p.seg: Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The Mysterious is
the progenitor of spontaneity,
and the great ancestor of all diversity.
Profound and obscure in its depth,
it is thus called subtle.
Vast and distant in its reach,
it is thus called wondrous.
Its height crowns the nine heavens,
its breadth envelops the eight directions.
Brighter than sun and moon,
swifter than lightning's flash.
Sometimes flickering like vanishing light,
sometimes floating like streaming stars,
sometimes shimmering in clear abysses,
sometimes misting like drifting clouds.
Through manifestations it becomes existence,
through hidden stillness it becomes non-existence.
It sinks into the great darkness below,
soars upward to the celestial pole above.
Metal and stone cannot match its firmness,
clear dew cannot equal its softness.
Square yet without angles,
round yet without compass.
Its coming none can see,
its going none can pursue.
Heaven is exalted through it,
earth is humbled through it,
clouds move through it,
rain falls through it.
It conceives the primordial unity,
molds the two polarities,
breathes forth the great beginning,
forges all creatures,
revolves the twenty-eight constellations,
creates from primordial chaos,
guides the spiritual mechanism,
breathes the four seasons,
encompasses silent emptiness,
unfolds brilliant beauty,
suppresses turbidity and elevates clarity,
measures out the Yellow River and Wei River,
increasing it doesn't overflow,
dipping from it doesn't deplete,
receiving doesn't bring glory,
losing doesn't bring decline.
Thus where the Mysterious dwells,
joy is endless.
Where the Mysterious departs,
forms decay and spirit vanishes.
The five tones and eight sounds,
the clear shāng and flowing zhǐ,
impair hearing.
magnificent and brilliant splendor,
injure vision.
Banquet ease and comfort,
clear wine and fragrant liquor,
disrupt nature.
Alluring looks and seductive postures,
lead-white cosmetics and pure complexion,
assault life.
Only the Mysterious Way
can endure eternally.
Those ignorant of the Mysterious Way,
though their glance be the divine instrument of life and death,
their lips the key to rise and fall,
their ornate towers overlook clouds and rain,
their patterned rooms display layered splendor,
silk curtains like gathering mist,
gauze canopies like parting clouds,
western beauties arrayed in leisure chambers,
golden cups gleaming in swift exchange,
clear strings strumming in unison,
Zhèng dances swirling in graceful motion,
mournful flutes soaring through clouds,
feathered canopies floating on ripples,
plucking fragrant flowers in orchid groves,
playing with red blossoms in pearl-filled pools,
climbing heights to gaze afar, forgetting all cares,
facing depths to look down, dismissing morning hunger,
entering banquets in brilliant thousand-gated halls,
riding out in splendid vermilion-carriage processions—
yet at joy's peak sorrow gathers,
fullness inevitably brings loss.
Thus music ends with sighs,
feasts conclude with heartache.
This is the inevitable course of reality,
like shadow following form, echo answering sound.
These borrowings are not true,
thus when things pass, something feels missing.
Now the Mysterious Way:
attained within,
maintained without,
used spiritually,
forgotten materially—
this is the essential teaching of contemplating the Mysterious Way.
Those who attain it are noble,
needing no yellow battle-axe's authority.
Those who embody it are rich,
requiring no rare treasures.
High beyond climbing,
deep beyond measuring.
Riding flowing light,
driving flying shadows,
traversing the six voids,
penetrating vast depths.
Emerging from the supremeless,
entering the bottomless.
Passing through the gate of boundlessness,
wandering the wilds of obscurity.
Drifting in hazy恍惚,
meandering in seeming模糊.
Swallowing nine splendors among clouds,
savoring six breaths in crimson mists.
Lingering in dim vastness,
soaring in subtle faintness,
treading coiled rainbows,
stepping on spinning stars—
this is what attainers experience.
Next are those truly knowing contentment:
the content can retreat unused,
nurturing light in mountain forests.
Coiling phoenix and dragon wings among tiny creatures,
cultivating vast energy in humble huts.
Ragged belts and rope ties,
not exchanged for dragon-emblazoned splendor.
Walking staff in hand,
not swapped for four-horse processions.
Hiding night-gems in mountain crevices,
avoiding other hills' polishing.
Sinking scales in dark abysses,
evading drilling and burning disasters.
Moving and resting knowing limits,
going nowhere without sufficiency.
Abandoning glorious morning blossoms,
avoiding dangerous overturned-car paths.
Chanting between dark cliffs,
while all things turn to dust.
Smiling under lush branches,
while vermilion gates become rope-hinged doors.
Holding plows in fields,
command tallies suddenly like whips.
Sipping bitter tea and spring water,
grand sacrifices same as coarse herbs.
Peacefully joyful in actionless realms,
gladly equalizing nobility and baseness in contentionless lands.
Embracing purity, preserving simplicity,
without desire, without worry,
perfecting genuineness, emptying forms,
dwelling peacefully, savoring blandness.
Vast and expansive,
equaling primordial unity in spontaneity.
Boundless and endless,
matching creation in harmony.
Like dark, like bright,
like turbid, like clear,
seeming slow yet swift,
seeming deficient yet full.
How could they abandon the shaman's seat,
leave the great craftsman's position,
cross ritual vessels to replace ignorant cooks,
discard ink-lines to aid hand-injuring laborers?
Not letting stinky-rat trivialities
become commoners' joys and sorrows.
Aloof, unwelcoming vulgar praise,
calm, unfearing unanimous slander.
Not letting external things muddy their utmost essence,
not letting profit and harm stain their purity.
Thus extreme wealth and honor
cannot tempt them—
what else could possibly please them?
Sharp blades and boiling cauldrons
cannot coerce them—
how could slander distress them?
Constantly unburdened by myriad troubles,
never mingled with external matters.
As for those wielding Suí pearls to shoot sparrows,
licking Qín hemorrhoids to join carriages,
climbing rotten ropes to rob nests,
swimming at Lǚliáng seeking fish,
morning as sovereign-calling guests,
evening as fox-and-bird leftovers—
beams bending, tripods overturning,
drowning unrevived—
this is what worldly people gallop to pursue,
but what the enlightened view with heartache and sorrow.
Thus the perfect person silences Sháo and Xià melodies and hides ornate pillars.
Flapping six wings over five-city ruins,
needing no reed-carrying defense.
Veiling scales and horns in unused lands,
relying no curved-cave preparations.
Below, no arrogant owl's cries,
above, no polar extremity's regrets,
none recognizing them—
how remote and far-reaching!"
Someone asked:
"Is it truly possible
to achieve immortality as an immortal?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Even with the sharpest vision,
not all things with form can be fully seen.
Even with the keenest hearing,
not all sounds can be completely heard.
Even with feet like Dàzhāng and Shùhài,
the places one commonly treads
are fewer than those untrodden.
Even with wisdom like Yǔ, Yì, and Qíxié,
what one has recognized is less than what remains unknown.
Among the myriad things in abundance,
what could possibly be absent?
Moreover, the ranks of immortals
fill the bamboo and silk texts.
How could the way to immortality
not exist?"
At this, the questioner laughed heartily and said:
"What has a beginning must have an end;
what exists must perish.
Thus, sages like the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, Confucius, and Dàn,
the wisdom of Qì Jí, Zhāng Liáng, and Chén Píng,
the eloquence of Zǐgòng, Yīng, Suí Hé, and Lì Shàng,
the courage of Mèng Bēn, Xià Yù, and the Five Dīngs,
all met death—
this is the constant principle of humanity,
the inevitable major outcome.
We only hear of plants withering before frost,
greenery fading in summer,
ears containing grains but not blooming,
withering before bearing fruit,
but never of enjoying a lifespan of ten thousand years,
or an endless period of longevity.
Therefore, the ancients did not seek immortality in their studies,
nor spoke of the supernatural in their words,
rejecting those heterodoxies,
adhering to this natural course,
classifying tortoises and cranes separately,
viewing life and death as morning and dusk.
To torment oneself and live austerely
engaging in futile endeavors,
is like carving ice or etching rot—
ultimately without certain success.
Why not instead unfold lofty strategies to save the world,
attracting prosperity in one's time,
letting purple and blue ribbons hang again,
with black oxen standing majestic,
exchanging ornate carriages for steady steps,
replacing cauldron fare with plowshares—
is that not splendid?
Often reflecting on the poet's criticism in 'Fǔ Tián',
deeply considering Confucius' assertion that all must die,
why grasp the formless wind,
catch elusive shadows,
seek the unobtainable,
walk an unreachable path,
abandon glory to face hardship,
forsake the easy for the extremely difficult,
like a madman chasing a wandering maiden,
bound to regret double loss,
or like Dān and Zhāng trusting biases,
hastening internal and external calamities.
Bān and Dí cannot sharpen tiles into fine needles,
Ōuyě cannot cast lead or tin into Gànjiàng swords.
Thus, what cannot be done,
even spirits cannot accomplish;
what cannot be achieved,
even heaven and earth cannot realize.
How could there be a miraculous formula in this world
to make the old young again,
or bring the dead back to life?
And you wish to prolong the life of a cicada,
granting it a lifespan of epochs,
or nurture the glory of a morning mushroom,
to accumulate months of existence—
is that not absurd?
I urge you to reflect deeply,
and not stray far into confusion."
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Where hearing is lost,
even thunder cannot make it heard;
where sight is abandoned,
even the sun, moon, and stars cannot make it seen.
Is it that the rumbling sound is too faint,
or the celestial sights too subtle?
Yet the deaf declare there is no sound,
the blind claim there is nothing.
How then could they appreciate
the harmony of pipes and strings,
the splendor of mountain dragons' brilliance,
or the elegant rhythms and dazzling scales?
Thus, if deafness and blindness lie in the physical senses,
one won't believe in Fēnglóng's thunder or the cosmic phenomena.
How much more for things subtler than these?
If darkness and stagnation cloud the mind,
one won't believe in the existence of Zhōu and Confucius in the past.
How then to convince them of the path of immortals?
Indeed, existence and demise, beginning and end,
form the general pattern.
Yet their variations and disparities,
some so, some not,
with transformations of myriad kinds,
wonders without fixed rules,
things identical but affairs different,
the root uniform, the branches divergent,
cannot be uniform.
Many claim that what begins must end,
but to lump them together uniformly
is not logical understanding.
Say summer must bring growth,
yet shepherd's purse and wheat wither then.
Say winter must bring decay,
yet bamboo and cypress flourish.
Say beginning implies an end,
yet heaven and earth are boundless.
Say life entails death,
yet tortoises and cranes endure long.
Intense yang should bring heat,
yet summer days may have coolness.
Extreme yin should bring cold,
yet harsh winters may have brief warmth.
All rivers flow east,
yet there are vast northward currents.
The earth's way is utmost stillness,
yet it may quake and collapse.
Water's nature is purely cold,
yet there are hot springs in warm valleys;
fire's essence should blaze,
yet there are cold flames at Xiāoqiū;
heavy objects should sink,
yet the South Sea has mountains of floating stone;
light things should float,
yet at Zāngkē there is a stream where feathers sink.
For all diverse categories,
one cannot judge by a single standard—
this has long been so.
Among living beings, the most intelligent
is none other than humans.
As creatures of noble nature,
they should be uniform.
Yet in wisdom and folly, integrity and wickedness,
beauty and ugliness, height and brevity,
purity and turbidity, chastity and licentiousness,
urgency and leisure, speed and slowness,
preferences in pursuits,
desires of ears and eyes,
their differences
are as vast as heaven and earth,
as opposed as ice and coals.
Why single out the difference of immortals,
surprised they do not die like ordinary people?
If we say all receive a fixed endowment of breath,
then the pheasant transforming into a clam,
the sparrow into a cockle,
soil insects growing wings,
river frogs taking flight,
water fleas becoming damselflies,
duckweed turning into maggots,
field mice becoming quails,
rotting grass into fireflies,
alligators into tigers,
snakes into dragons—
are these not so?
If we say humans receive a correct nature,
different from ordinary beings,
and Heaven bestows fate
without distinction,
then how explain Niú Āi becoming a tiger,
the Chǔ old woman a turtle,
Zhīlí turning into a willow,
the Qín woman into stone,
dying and reviving,
men and women swapping forms,
Lǎo Péng's longevity,
the youth's premature death?
What is the reason for this?
If there are differences,
then how can their variations be limited?"
As for immortals,
they nourish their bodies with medicinal substances,
prolong their lives through esoteric arts,
ensuring no internal ailments arise,
and no external afflictions enter.
Though they gaze long upon the world without dying,
their original forms remain unchanged.
If one possesses the true method,
there is nothing difficult about it.
Yet those with shallow understanding,
bound by conventions and clinging to norms,
all say they have never seen immortals in the world,
and thus claim such things cannot exist under heaven.
But how can what one's eyes have personally witnessed
be sufficient to speak of?
Between heaven and earth,
there is no greater expanse than this,
and within it, extraordinary wonders
are hardly limited.
We grow old beneath the sky
yet remain ignorant of what lies above;
we tread upon the earth our entire lives
yet know nothing of what lies below.
Even our own physical bodies, which we possess,
we cannot comprehend the workings of our minds and wills.
Lifespans lie within our grasp,
yet we cannot know how long or short they may extend.
How much more so for the profound principles of divine immortals,
the mysterious depths of the Dào and virtue?
To rely on our limited senses of sight and sound
to judge the existence of subtle mysteries—
is this not truly lamentable?
Suppose there is a sage of great talent,
who retreats from the world and remains unused,
concealing his brilliance and hiding his virtues,
abandoning falsehood and desires,
holding onto the purest simplicity in utmost sincerity,
leaving trivial matters beyond the vulgar trends,
yet few in the world can discern his worth,
and perhaps none can aspire to his conduct beyond fame,
or grasp his spirit within a humble form.
How much more so for immortals, with their different pursuits and paths,
who regard wealth and honor as misfortune,
consider glory and splendor as filth,
view precious treasures as dust and soil,
and see reputation as the morning dew,
treading on fiery blasts without being scorched,
stepping on dark waves with light footsteps,
flapping their wings to rise above the dust,
riding the wind as their chariot and clouds as their carriage,
soaring up to the Purple Heaven,
and dwelling below on Kūnlún.
How could the walking dead
ever witness them?
Even if they roam at play,
or pass through the human world,
hiding their truth and concealing their wonders,
outwardly appearing ordinary and common,
standing shoulder to shoulder and step by step,
who would be able to detect them?
If they were all like Jiāojiān with his pair of square pupils,
or Qiángshū with his double ears
protruding from the top of his head,
or Mǎ Huáng riding a dragon in travel,
or Zǐ Jìn personally driving a white crane—
or if they had scaly bodies and serpentine forms,
or golden carriages and feathered garments—
only then might they be recognized.
But since they are not like this,
how can those without penetrating vision perceive their forms,
or those without acute hearing hear their voices?
Since people do not believe
and often criticize and slander,
the true immortals, vexed by this,
withdraw even further into hiding.
Moreover, what ordinary people love,
the superior individuals detest.
What the vulgar value,
the utmost sages despise.
Even eminent scholars and great talents,
who nurture their vast spirit,
do not enjoy meeting shallow people
or those entangled in worldly dust.
How much more so for those immortals—
why would they anxiously seek to let the likes of straw dogs
know of their existence or what they seek,
and then be surprised that they are unknown?
If one's eyes can see only a hundred paces
and not with perfect clarity,
yet they take what they see as existent
and what they don't see as nonexistent,
then what is absent in the world
must surely be plentiful.
This is like measuring the sea with a finger,
declaring the water ended when the finger reaches its limit.
For a mayfly to assess a giant turtle,
or a morning mushroom to gauge a great cedar—
how could they ever achieve it?
Emperor Wén of Wèi, with extensive learning and broad knowledge,
claimed to have experienced all things,
saying there were no knives that could cut jade
or cloth that could be cleansed by fire.
But when he wrote the Diǎnlùn,
he firmly stated this view.
Not long after,
both items arrived.
The emperor sighed in amazement
and hastily retracted his argument.
Nothing is absolutely certain;
this illustrates the point.
Prince Sī of Chén, in his Shìyílùn, wrote:
"At first, I thought Daoist arts
were merely deceitful empty words meant to fool the people.
But after witnessing Emperor Wǔ test Zuǒ Cī and others,
ordering them to fast for nearly a month,
yet their complexions did not fade,
and their strength remained as before,
often claiming they could go fifty years without eating—
if this is true,
what doubt can remain?"
He also said:
"When Gān Shǐ made a live fish hold medicine in its mouth
and boiled it in bubbling fat,
the one without medicine
cooked and became edible,
while the one holding the medicine
swam playfully all day,
as if in water."
Also, using medicated powder on mulberry leaves to feed silkworms,
the silkworms lived until October without aging.
And feeding young chicks and newborn puppies with life-extending medicine,
they stopped growing altogether.
When a white dog was fed a darkening medicine,
in a hundred days, all its fur turned black.
Thus, I realized that the affairs of the world
cannot be fully known,
and to judge by conjecture
is unreliable.
I only regret that I cannot renounce sensual pleasures
to wholeheartedly study the way of longevity."
Those two Cáos, in learning, left no book unread;
in talent, they were the heroes of their era.
Yet initially, they denied such things,
only in later years to exhaustively explore principles and nature,
sighing in such a manner.
For those inferior to such men
to disbelieve in immortals
is hardly surprising.
Liú Xiàng, with his profound scholarship, delved into the subtle and mysterious,
traversing depths and distances,
and in reasoning, clarified truth and falsehood,
investigating existence and nonexistence.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn he compiled,
recording over seventy immortals—
if there were no truth to it,
why would he fabricate it?
Events of remote antiquity
cannot be witnessed firsthand;
all rely on records and hearsay from the past.
The Lièxiān Zhuàn clearly affirms their existence.
Yet since the book did not come from Zhōu Gōng's school,
and the matters were not handled by Zhòngní's hand,
people ultimately do not believe it.
If so, then all that ancient histories record
would be deemed nonexistent;
why single out just this one matter?
Vulgar people, greedy for glory and profit,
eagerly pursue fame and gain,
projecting their own minds
onto the ancients afar,
thus disbelieving that in the past, some fled the imperial abdication,
scorned the noble duties of ministers and chancellors—
like the likes of Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu,
or Lǎo Lái and Zhuāng Zhōu and their followers—
deeming it impossible.
How much more for immortals,
even harder to comprehend than this,
how can we expect everyone today to believe in them?
Many say Liú Xiàng was no sage,
so his compiled records
cannot be solely relied upon—
this is especially cause for sighing.
The chronicles of Lǔ did not match heaven and earth in virtue,
yet Zhòngní used them to compose the classics.
Sīmǎ Qiān did not shine like the sun and moon,
yet Yáng Xióng praised him for his factual records.
Liú Xiàng, a renowned Confucian and worthy of the Hàn dynasty—
how can his accounts
be simply discarded?
The reason people disbelieve that immortality can be learned,
and deny that lifespans can be extended,
is precisely because Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdí sought it without success,
and because Shào Jūn and Luán Dà's efforts showed no proof.
But one cannot, due to the poverty of Qián Lóu and Yuán Xiàn,
say that anciently there were no riches like Táo Zhū and Yī Dùn.
Nor can one, because of the ugliness of Wú Yán and Sù Liú,
claim that in the past there were no beauties like Nán Wēi and Xī Shī.
In endeavors, some fail to achieve their goals;
in farming, some crops do not yield;
in trade, some ventures bring no profit;
in warfare, some campaigns gain no merit.
How much more so in seeking immortality,
a most difficult task—
why must all who attempt it succeed?
Those two rulers and two ministers
may have sought without finding,
or started diligently but ended slackly,
or not encountered an enlightened teacher.
How can this suffice to conclude that there are no immortals in the world?
To seek eternal life,
to cultivate the ultimate Way,
the key lies in determination,
not in wealth and status.
If one is not the right person,
then high position and abundant riches
only become heavy burdens.
Why is this?
The methods of learning immortality
require tranquility, contentment, and simplicity,
cleansing oneself of desires,
looking inward and listening to one's inner self,
residing like a corpse without worldly thoughts.
Yet emperors bear the heavy responsibility of the world,
managing overwhelming governmental affairs,
their minds wearied by countless tasks,
their spirits racing across the universe.
If a single matter goes awry,
the kingly way is compromised;
if the common people err,
they say it is their own fault.
Strong wine disrupts their harmonious energy,
beautiful appearances damage their roots.
The ways in which their essence is cut, their thoughts impaired, and their purity diminished
cannot be fully detailed.
Mosquito bites keep one from sitting in peace,
swarms of lice attack so one cannot rest calmly.
The affairs of the world
are far more than just these.
How can one then obscure their senses,
practice internal contemplation and breath counting,
observe long fasts and maintain purity,
personally tend to the furnace,
rise early and retire late,
to refine the eight minerals?
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enjoyed a long reign,
the most prolonged in his dynasty,
having gained some small benefits from nurturing his nature.
But with a peck's worth of aid,
he could not meet the expense of a ton;
with the flow of field ditches,
he could not supply the drain of the vast ocean.
Immortal methods desire stillness and non-action,
forgetting one's physical form,
yet rulers strike thousand-dan bells,
beat thunderous drums,
with crashing and clamorous noises,
startling the soul and unsettling the heart.
Hundreds of skills and myriad changes,
exhaust the spirit and block the ears;
light and swift movements,
fishing in the depths and shooting at heights.
Immortal methods require love even for the smallest creatures,
harming no living being,
yet rulers have fiery wrath,
and executions of mass slaughter.
With a wave of the yellow battle-axe,
and the temporary grant of the executioner's blade,
corpses lie for a thousand miles,
blood flows in torrents,
and the penalty of beheading
never ceases in the marketplaces.
Immortal methods demand abstaining from foul and腥 scents,
fasting to cleanse the intestines,
yet rulers cook fat and slaughter plump animals,
butchering living beings,
with eight delicacies and hundred harmonies,
spread out before them,
simmering with spices,
savoring fine flavors to satiety.
Immortal methods call for universal love across the eight wildernesses,
seeing others as oneself,
yet rulers annex the weak and attack the ignorant,
seize the chaotic and overthrow the fallen,
expand territories and open up borders,
obliterating others' altars of grain,
driving living people
into lands of death.
Lonely souls in remote regions,
exposed bones rotting in the wilds.
At the Five Ridges, armies with blood-stained blades,
at the northern gate, heads of Dàyuān hung,
pits of the living buried,
tens of thousands in motion,
monuments to the dead piled high,
reaching up to the clouds,
exposed bones like overgrown grass,
filling mountains and valleys.
Qín Shǐhuáng caused nine out of ten households
to think of rebellion.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn left the world in turmoil,
with the population reduced by half.
If blessings have their benefits,
curses also have their harms.
Tying grass in gratitude knows virtue,
while empty sacrifices surely breed resentment.
Numerous troubles attack their vitals,
humans and ghosts alike harbor poison and hatred.
Those two rulers merely had the name of seeking immortality,
without the substance of cultivating the Way.
The shallow knowledge they had,
they could not fully practice;
the essential and profound secrets,
they never got to hear.
Moreover, they did not have Taoist masters
to compound the elixir of immortality for them.
Thus, failing to achieve eternal life
is no surprise.
I am but a common man,
further burdened by poverty,
with a home as destitute as Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's bare walls,
a belly suffering the hunger of Yìsāng's starvation,
enduring the cold of Róng Yí shut out at the door in winter,
the glare of Rú Zhòng's confined dwelling in summer.
Wishing to travel far but lacking boat or carriage,
wanting to undertake tasks but without servants to labor,
indoors, no enjoyment of fine silks,
outdoors, no joy of leisurely sightseeing,
sweet delicacies never touch my mouth,
colorful sights never meet my eyes,
fragrant scents never pass my nose,
the eight tones never reach my ears.
A hundred worries assail my heart,
numerous difficulties gather at my doorstep.
Living in the world like this,
there is nothing to cherish.
Some may obtain the essential secrets of the true path,
or encounter an extraordinary master,
yet still fret over their aging wives and young children,
cling fondly to their fox-and-hare-infested hills,
procrastinate until their eventual demise,
unaware of time's passage as they grow old,
knowing immortality is attainable yet failing to cultivate it,
troubled by the foul rat of vulgar customs but unable to abandon them.
Why is this?
The attachments of habitual affections are ultimately hard to dispel,
and the resolve to transcend worldly ties is not easily realized.
Moreover, those two emperors,
rulers of the four seas,
their indulged pleasures
were not limited to one pursuit,
their intimate favorites
were exceedingly numerous.
Even if forced to observe fasting for ten days or a month,
or dwell in solitude for a few days,
they would still be unable to endure it,
let alone abandoning inner chambers of lovely consorts within,
relinquishing external glory and majestic dignity,
refraining sweet delicacies with their mouths,
cutting off desires in their hearts,
turning their backs on splendor to journey alone,
seeking divine immortals in remote desolation—
how could they bear it?
Therefore, surveying past records,
those who attained the immortal path
were mostly men of humble station,
not people of power and status.
Furthermore, what Luán Tài knew
was truly shallow and meager;
craving honor and wealth,
brazenly seeking bribes,
flaunting falsehoods in reckless opportunism,
forgetting calamity through inaction—
such petty villainy and deceit
hardly proves the absence of immortals in the world.
Formerly, Gōu Jiàn paid respects to the gall bladder,
and his soldiers vied to tread through fire.
King Chǔ Líng adored slender waists,
and many in the state starved to death.
Duke Qí Huán craved exotic flavors,
and Yì Yá steamed his own son.
The Sòng ruler rewarded emaciated filial piety,
and those who wasted away filled households.
Whatever the ruler desires,
there is nothing that won't be delivered.
Emperor Hàn Wǔ recruited fāngshì,
treating them with excessive favor,
causing these individuals
to dare engage in empty fabrications.
If Luán Tài truly possessed the Way,
how could he have been executed?
Those who possess the Way
regard official ranks as boiling cauldrons,
see seals and ribbons as mourning garb,
view gold and jade as dirt and dung,
and behold magnificent halls as prisons.
How could they wring their hands with empty talk,
coveting glory and splendor,
dwell in vermilion-pillared chambers,
accept immeasurable rewards,
wear the seal of the Five Profits general,
marry the nobility of a princess,
wallow in power and profit,
never knowing satisfaction—
clearly, they had not attained the Way,
as can be decisively known.
According to the family records of Lǐ Shàojūn compiled by Dǒng Zhòngshū,
Shàojūn possessed the formula for immortality,
but his family was poor and unable to purchase the required medicines,
so he went to the Hàn court
to borrow the path to seek wealth,
and when his cultivation succeeded, he departed.
Also, according to the Hàn palace diaries,
just before Shàojūn was to leave,
Emperor Wǔ dreamed of ascending Mount Sōnggāo with him,
halfway up the path,
a messenger riding a dragon and holding a tally
descended from the clouds,
saying the Great Unity invited Shàojūn.
The emperor awoke
and told his attendants,
"From my dream,
Shàojūn is about to leave me."
Several days later,
Shàojūn was reported to have died of illness.
Much later,
the emperor had his coffin opened,
but no corpse was found—
only his clothes and hat remained.
According to the Xiānjīng (Classic of Immortals),
superior adepts ascend physically into emptiness,
called celestial immortals.
Middle adepts wander among famous mountains,
called terrestrial immortals.
Inferior adepts first die and then shed their husk,
called liberation-from-the-corpse immortals.
Now, Shàojūn must have been one who achieved liberation from the corpse.
In recent times, Hú Gōng took Fèi Chángfáng away.
And the dàoshì Lǐ Yìqī took his two disciples away,
all feigning death,
passing away,
and their families buried them.
After several years,
Chángfáng returned.
Also, an acquaintance saw Lǐ Yìqī with his two disciples in Pí County.
Their families each opened the coffins to look,
and the three coffins contained only a bamboo staff each,
with cinnabar writing on them—
these were all cases of liberation from the corpse.
In the past, Wáng Mǎng cited classics to disguise his wickedness,
but one cannot say that all Confucian scholars
are usurpers and thieves.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú used zither music to elope with Zhūo Wénjūn,
but one cannot claim that refined music primarily leads to debauchery.
Those choked by grains cannot blame Shénnóng for sowing crops,
those burned by fire cannot blame Suìrén for drilling flames,
those drowned cannot resent Emperor Xuān Yuán for inventing boats,
nor can drunkards condemn Dù Yí for creating wine.
How can we deny the existence of immortality
just because of Luán Tài's deceit?
This is like denying the existence of Yǐ Yǐn, Zhōu Gōng,
or Huò Guāng upon seeing Zhào Gāo and Dǒng Zhuó,
or denying Bó Qí and Xiào Jǐ
after encountering Shāng Chén and Mòdú.
Moreover, texts on transcendents contain methods
for summoning spirits and controlling ghosts,
and techniques to make people see apparitions.
Common folks hear of these
and dismiss them as fabrications,
some claiming ghosts don't exist,
others admitting their existence but denying controllability,
while others assert ghost-seers
are male xí or female wū shamans
by birthright,
not through learning.
Yet Hànshū and Grand Historian's records document
Shào Wēng of Qí,
appointed by Emperor Wǔ as General Wénchéng,
who manifested the Emperor's deceased consort Lǐ Fūrén
as if alive,
and revealed the Kitchen God—
explicit historical accounts.
Since esoteric arts can manifest ghosts
and enable non-seers to perceive them,
what else might they not achieve?
Ghosts frequently manifest through strange phenomena,
and classics abound with evidence
of their existence.
If commoners doubt ordinary spirits,
how much more would they distrust transcendents
dwelling in distant realms,
separated by purity from turbidity,
who ascend beyond
never to return—
invisible except to the enlightened?
Confucians and Mohists knew such tales
were unfit for moral instruction,
hence remained silent about them.
Is it any wonder the masses disbelieve?
Only discerning minds
who examine myriad methods
and obtain proof
can confirm their reality—
this cannot be forced.
Just as not seeing spirits
or transcendents
doesn't prove their non-existence.
All people, wise or foolish,
know they possess hun and pò souls;
when these partially depart, illness follows,
complete departure brings death.
Hence rituals exist to recall scattered souls,
and ceremonies to summon departed ones—
these closest of entities
accompany us from birth
until death,
yet none perceive them directly.
How can we deny their existence
merely through lack of perception?
Consider the ghost of Fǔshì demanding retribution,
King Chéng Tāng's wrathful spirit,
Shēn Shēng speaking through a fox,
Dù Bó avenging on King Xuān of Zhōu,
Péng Shēng manifesting as a black swine,
Rúyì appearing as a gray hound,
Guàn Fū haunting Tián Fěn,
Zǐyǐ assaulting Yān Jiǎn,
Rùshōu descending at Shēn,
Luán Hóu dwelling among commoners,
Sù Jiāng interpreting prophecies,
Xiào Sūn composing texts,
Shén Jūn speaking in Shànglín Park,
Luó Yáng serving in Wú court—
such spirit matters
recorded in bamboo and silk texts
are abundantly clear
and innumerable.
Yet skeptics still deny them;
how much more would they doubt rarer accounts
of immortality?
Demanding universal belief
is like asking mosquitoes to carry mountains
or frogs in wells to discuss oceans.
Commoners who've never seen dragons, qílín, or fenghuangs
declare them nonexistent,
dismissing ancient auspicious signs
as mere encouragement for rulers—
how then could they believe in transcendents?
Some dismiss Liú Xiàng's failed alchemy
as evidence that his pursuit of mysteries
and compilation of Lièxiān Zhuàn
are fraudulent.
Alas! This is like discarding
foot-long night-luminous pearls
for minute flaws,
or rejecting priceless Chúnjūn swords
for ant-nose imperfections—
lacking the discernment of Jīng Hé
or Fēng Hú's appraisal.
No wonder Lord Yǎn grew despondent
and Xuē Zhú sighed forever.
Alchemical methods reside in transcendence texts;
Huáinán King excerpted them
for his Hóngbǎo Zhěnzhōng Shū,
yet though recorded,
essential steps remain oral,
requiring personal instruction
for successful practice.
Moreover, ingredient names
are often altered,
preventing direct application.
Liú Xiàng's father Dé obtained the text
from Huáinán King's prison,
without proper transmission.
Xiàng himself, unversed in esoterics,
mistakenly assumed written words sufficed—
hence his alchemical failure.
As for his Lièxiān Zhuàn,
abridged from Ruǎn Cāng's text
with witnessed accounts,
it contains no falsehoods.
Even madmen's rhymes
are heeded by sages;
humble words
should not be dismissed.
When gathering radishes and mustard,
don't discard the roots—
shall we reject all classics
for occasional errors,
or deny the sun and moon's brilliance
because of occasional eclipses?
Foreign crystal bowls
are fused from five types of ash,
a technique now practiced in Jiāo and Guǎng regions.
Yet commoners refuse belief,
insisting crystal forms naturally
like jade.
Since natural gold exists,
why should they believe in artificial production?
Fools even deny that yellow lead and cosmetic powder
derive from transformed lead,
or that mules and jùxū
come from donkey-horse breeding,
claiming species are fixed—
how then grasp subtler truths?
Rarity breeds wonder—
this universal truth
stands confirmed.
Though heaven's light shines bright,
those under overturned pots
cannot perceive supreme truths.
Someone challenged by saying:
"Among humans, there are those like Lǎo and Péng,
just as among trees there are pines and cypresses,
endowed by nature,
how could this be learned?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Now, in molding and transforming creation,
nothing is more spiritual than humans.
Thus, those who grasp its shallow aspects
can then employ all things;
those who attain its depths
can then achieve long life and enduring vision.
Knowing that superior medicines prolong years,
they therefore take them to seek immortality.
Knowing that tortoises and cranes enjoy great longevity,
they thus imitate their daoyǐn to increase their years.
Moreover, the branches and leaves of pines and cypresses
differ from those of other trees.
The forms and appearances of tortoises and cranes
are distinct from those of other creatures.
As for Péng and Lǎo, they were still human,
not a different species with uniquely long lives;
their longevity resulted from attaining the Dào,
not from natural endowment.
Other trees cannot emulate pines and cypresses,
various creatures cannot learn from tortoises and cranes,
hence they die early.
But humans, possessing intelligence,
can cultivate the Dào of Péng and Lǎo,
and thus may share in their achievements.
If you claim there are no immortals in the world,
yet the records of past sages
mention nearly a thousand,
all with names and surnames,
and details of their deeds from beginning to end—
these are not empty words.
If you say they all uniquely possessed extraordinary qi,
yet their traditions all involved masters, practices, and ingestions—
they were not born knowing.
If you argue that the arts of the Dào cannot be learned,
then consider changing forms and appearances,
swallowing knives and spitting fire,
sitting here and vanishing there,
raising clouds and summoning fog,
calling forth insects and snakes,
gathering fish and turtles,
turning thirty-six minerals instantly into water,
dissolving jade into paste,
melting metal into liquid,
entering depths unwetted,
treading on blades unharmed—
such illusory transformations,
over nine hundred in number,
when practiced accordingly,
all prove effective without exception.
Why then refuse to believe that immortality can be attained?
The path to immortality is slow to achieve,
with many taboos.
Without a transcendent will
and strong ability,
one cannot persevere in it.
If some, half-hearted and doubtful,
abandon it midway,
they then say that the immortal path to long life
truly cannot be attained.
The immortal scriptures say:
'Ingest cinnabar and guard the One,
and you will endure as long as heaven;
revert essence and practice fetal breathing,
and extend life without limit.'
These are essential words of the ultimate Dào.
Even gentlemen among the common people
inwardly do not betray their hearts,
outwardly are not ashamed before their shadows,
above do not deceive heaven,
below do not break their word—
how much more so the ancient zhēnrén?
Would they fabricate empty texts
about things utterly unattainable
to mislead future generations?
What would they gain from it?
If one lacks the destiny for it,
they will never believe in the end,
so how can we force them to believe?"
Someone might challenge:
"The longevity of tortoises and cranes
is merely empty talk in the world.
Who has accompanied these two creatures from beginning to end to verify this?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"If one grasps the essentials,
then even beyond the eight extremes,
it's as clear as looking at one's palm;
distant ages hundreds of generations away
seem like the present time.
There's no need to have them in one's courtyard
or wait until they're within sight
to know about them.
The Yùcè Jì records
that thousand-year tortoises
display all five colors,
with two protrusions on their foreheads resembling horns.
They understand human speech,
float on lotus leaves,
or hide beneath clusters of yarrow plants,
with coiled clouds often above them.
Thousand-year cranes
sing according to the seasons,
able to perch on trees -
those not yet a thousand years old
never alight on trees -
their pure white feathers and crimson brains fully formed.
Seeing them thus,
one can recognize them.
However, aged creatures tend to be wise,
mostly dwelling deep in seclusion,
so humans rarely see them.
According to Yùcè Jì and Chāngyǔ Jīng,
it's not just these two creatures that are long-lived.
It says thousand-year pine trees
spread their branches around,
their tops ceasing to grow upward,
appearing from afar
like reclining canopies.
Within them reside beings -
some like green oxen,
some like green goats,
some like green dogs,
some like green humans -
all living ten thousand years.
Also stated:
snakes possess endless longevity;
macaques live eight hundred years then transform into apes;
apes live five hundred years then become jué.
Jué live a thousand years.
Toads live three thousand years;
qílín live two thousand years.
Téng Huáng horses
and Jí Guāng beasts
both live three thousand years.
Thousand-year birds
and ten-thousand-year fowl
all have human faces with bird bodies,
their lifespans matching their names.
Tigers, deer, and hares
all live a thousand years;
upon reaching five hundred years,
their fur turns white.
Bears living five hundred years
gain transformation abilities.
Foxes, jackals, and wolves
all live eight hundred years;
at five hundred years,
they skillfully assume human form.
Rats live three hundred years;
at one hundred years they turn white
and adeptly use humans for divination,
called Zhòng,
knowing annual fortunes and events a thousand lǐ away.
Such examples
are too numerous to record fully.
But the knowledgeable can name creatures upon encounter,
and the well-informed remain unperplexed by principles.
Why must one constantly interact with tortoises and cranes
to know this?
If one cannot recognize creatures,
then even garden plants,
field animals, and pond birds
remain largely unknown,
let alone remarkably exceptional ones?
The Shǐjì's 'Biographies of Tortoises and Divination' states:
'A man from between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
used a tortoise as bed support in childhood;
after growing old and dying,
his family moved the bed,
finding the tortoise still alive.'
This was at least fifty or sixty years -
without drinking or eating,
surviving so long without dying,
showing how vastly different it is from ordinary creatures.
Why doubt it could live a thousand years?
Immortal scriptures imitate tortoise breathing -
isn't there reason for this?
Thus, Chén Zhònggōng of Yǐngchuān,
a profound scholar,
recorded in Yìwén Jì:
'A fellow villager, Zhāng Guǎngdìng,
fleeing during turmoil,
had a four-year-old daughter
who couldn't walk far
nor be carried.
Deciding abandonment meant starvation,
but unwilling to leave her bones exposed,
he found an ancient large tomb at the village entrance
with a pre-existing hole on top.
Using a container and rope,
he lowered the girl into the tomb,
leaving several months' dry provisions and water before departing.
After peace was restored -
three years later -
Guǎngdìng returned home,
intending to collect the girl's bones
for proper burial.
Approaching the tomb,
he found the girl still sitting inside.
Seeing her parents,
she recognized them with great joy.
Her parents initially feared she was a ghost;
the father descended to approach her,
realizing she was alive.
Asked how she obtained food,
the girl said when provisions ran out, starving,
she saw a creature in the tomb corner
stretching its neck swallowing air.
Imitating it,
her hunger vanished,
practicing daily
until now.
Clothes and blankets left by her parents
remained in the tomb;
without moving about,
her garments didn't wear out,
so she didn't suffer cold.
Guǎngdìng searched for the creature described -
it was a large tortoise.
When the girl emerged and ate grain,
she initially had stomach pains and vomiting,
gradually adapting over time.
This sufficiently proves tortoises possess deathless methods,
and practitioners emulating them
can achieve equal longevity.'
Neither Sīmǎ Qiān nor Zhònggōng
were reckless storytellers.
Though countless insects and birds exist worldwide,
the ancients specifically cited these two creatures
to demonstrate their unique extraordinariness.
Understanding one aspect enables comprehension of the whole."
Someone might challenge by saying:
"Turtles can hibernate in earth,
cranes can fly in the sky.
If we ask humans to hibernate briefly,
or fly momentarily,
they still cannot do it.
How then can longevity be learned from them?"
Bàopǔzǐ replies:
"Many insects can hibernate,
numerous birds can fly,
yet we specifically cite turtles and cranes for their long-living nature
because their immortality
does not derive from hibernation or flight.
Thus, true masters only teach learning their daoyin to prolong life,
emulating their breath-eating to abstain from grains,
not learning their earth-hibernation or sky-flying.
Those who attain the Dào
can soar to the clouds above
or dive into rivers and seas below.
Hence, Xiāo Shǐ rode phoenixes through the void,
Qín Gāo mounted red carp in deep abysses -
these are verifications.
Why limit to momentary hibernation
or brief flight?
Dragons, snakes, jiāo, and chī,
jū, wèi, tuó, and lí
all can endure winter without eating;
when not eating,
they become plumper than when eating.
None understand their method.
Moreover, in singular excellences,
animals often surpass humans,
not just turtles and cranes.
Thus, Tàihào learned from spiders to weave nets,
Jīntiān followed jiù hù to regulate seasons,
Emperor Xuān awaited phoenix cries to tune pitch-pipes,
Táng Yáo observed míngjiá to know moons,
Guīzhōng knew the past,
qiánquè knew the future,
Yú Bó recognized flood-drought signs,
fúyóu knew hidden springs,
white wolves knew the Shāng's rise,
yuèzhuó foresaw the Zhōu's prosperity;
that turtles and cranes uniquely understand guiding nourishment
is unsurprising.
Furthermore, the immortal classics' longevity methods
number hundreds,
differing only in speed and complexity,
not all must emulate turtles and cranes.
Superior minds contemplate profoundly,
naturally comprehending mysteries,
hard to deduce transcendent profundities
from foolish conventions."
Some say,
"We moderns don't understand longevity principles -
how did ancients alone know?"
"This is ignorant talk,
not the view of the enlightened.
Scanning heaven's mysterious ways,
tracking celestial bodies' motions,
analyzing past cosmic interactions,
discerning future rise and fall,
observing cloud signs for omens,
interpreting hexagrams for fortunes,
moving three stones to determine campaign outcomes,
calculating nine talismans for fate divisions -
through single computations
exploring ghostly manifestations,
weaving six emotions
to handle ambiguous outcomes:
their roots are traceable,
forms and principles researchable,
yet mediocre minds
cannot penetrate profound studies,
let alone simple folk
straining over dregs,
unable to fathom subtleties.
Crude chisel-work
held untold secrets by Lún Biǎn;
simple cicada-catching
required divine skill from the hunchback -
it depends on the person,
stemming from utmost refinement.
How much more so with the transcendent Dào,
so profound and distant?
Seeking its roots,
truly不容易.
Even Sōng, Qiáo and their like
achieved effects
without necessarily understanding causes;
how much less ordinary people?
Since the practices can be learned,
ancients recorded and transmitted them
for discerning minds.
If you comprehend intuitively,
believe and cultivate;
if harboring doubts,
that's your own fate -
don't question why ancients alone knew this
or why you alone don't."
"I now know immortality is attainable,
I can abstain from grains,
I ensure liúzhū can fly,
huángbái can be sought -
if demanded to explain underlying principles,
I honestly don't know either.
If people deem existent only what thought can grasp,
nonexistent what it cannot,
then few things would exist under heaven!
Thus Lǎozǐ said:
using wildcat heads to treat rodent ulcers,
woodpeckers for dental caries -
these follow categorical correlations.
But crabs transforming lacquer,
hemp ruining wine -
these defy logical deduction.
Myriad phenomena arise diversely;
how can thought exhaust them?
Suppose with critical illness
needing good medicine,
you refuse treatment
until understanding Shénnóng and Qí Bó's original reasons
for using certain herbs - that's foolish indeed!"
Some say:
"Life and death are fated,
lifespan predetermined,
no medicines
can alter it.
Severed fingers reattached
won't heal;
spilled blood swallowed
brings no benefit.
How much less consuming foreign substances like pine/cypress
to extend short lifespans?
Highly improbable!"
Bàopǔzǐ says:
"If your argument requires
same-species substances
to be beneficial,
then severed fingers
and spilled blood
originate from one's body,
not different kinds -
why can't severed parts reconnect,
spilled blood be ingested?
I've repeatedly seen snake-salve ointment rejoin severed fingers,
mulberry-beans replace chicken/duck feet -
benefits from foreign substances
are undeniable.
If you need no external things,
should pounded flesh and treated bones
suffice for wound medicine,
boiled skin and scorched hair
cure baldness?
Soil/water differ from plants,
yet plants depend on them.
Grains aren't human,
yet humans need them to live.
Fat isn't fire,
water isn't fish,
yet exhausted fat extinguishes fire,
drained water kills fish.
Felling trees withers parasites,
cutting grass shrivels dodder,
absent river-crabs rot clams,
severed mulberries destroy silkworms.
Extend these analogies
to understand:
Gold/jade in orifices
preserve corpses from decay;
brine penetrating flesh
keeps jerky from rotting.
How much more so with life-enhancing substances
incorporated into oneself -
why doubt they confer longevity?"
Someone objected, saying:
"Books on immortality arts
appear plausible but are actually unfounded,
likely fabricated by meddlesome individuals,
not necessarily originating from Huáng-Lǎo's teachings,
nor witnessed by Sōng-Qiáo themselves."
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"If it were as you elegantly argue,
they should prove ineffective,
yet when testing minor techniques,
none fail to demonstrate efficacy.
I have repeatedly observed people using moon mirrors to collect water under evening moons,
solar reflectors to ignite fire from morning sunlight,
vanishing into formless concealment,
transforming appearances into different entities,
casting knotted scarves to make hares run,
pinning cinnabar ribbons to summon serpentine movements,
fruits ripening instantaneously,
dragons and fish swimming in bowls and plates -
all perform as described.
According to Hànshū, when Luán Dà first met Emperor Wǔ,
he tested him by making chess pieces
collide autonomously.
Later, Hòu Hànshū records Wèi Shǎng capable of sitting presence and vanishing absence,
while Zhāng Kǎi could summon clouds and raise fog,
all documented by reliable historians,
credible and evidenced.
These arts
are categorized under immortality techniques,
demonstrating they aren't fabricated.
Since minor techniques prove effective,
why would the path to longevity
be any different?"
Another questioned:
"If immortality can truly be attained through study,
soaring to celestial heights,
abandoning worldly customs,
then sacrificial rites
would remain unperformed.
Wouldn't ancestral spirits,
if conscious, starve?"
Bàopǔzǐ responded:
"I have heard that preserving one's body unharmed
constitutes ultimate filial piety.
How much more so attaining immortality,
living eternally with undimmed vision,
enduring as long as heaven and earth,
surpassing mere bodily preservation -
is this not far superior?
Indeed, ascending void realms treading light,
riding cloud-chariots under rainbow canopies,
sipping dawn mist's ethereal vapors,
inhaling the primordial essence of cosmic energies,
drinking jade nectar and golden syrup,
eating emerald fungi and vermilion blossoms,
dwelling in jade halls and gemmed chambers,
roaming freely through the Great Purity -
should ancestral spirits be conscious,
they would share my glory,
perhaps assisting the Five Emperors,
or overseeing countless divinities.
Rank would come unsought,
sustenance would be floral jades to savor,
influence commanding Luófēng's domains,
authority overwhelming Liáng Chéng's might.
Truly following this path,
its wonders beyond comprehension,
none would suffer starvation.
Among attained masters,
none surpass Bó Yáng.
Bó Yáng had a son named Zōng,
who served Wèi as general,
earning the fief of Duàngān through merit.
Thus present immortality seekers
may naturally have descendants
to maintain sacrifices -
how would worship
thereby cease?"
Another asked:
"Those who attain the Dào,
equipped with breathing techniques
and versed in medicinal essentials,
hear千里 through covered ears,
see the future with closed eyes,
some exchanging splendid steeds for dragon-steeds,
others abandoning the central realm for Péng-Yíng abodes,
while some linger among mortal customs,
wandering the human world
without severing ties for metaphysical pursuits -
their aspirations align,
yet their movements differ.
Why is this?"
Bàopǔzǐ answered:
"According to my late teacher,
immortals either ascend to heaven
or remain earthly,
essential is achieving longevity,
departing or staying according to preference.
Regarding golden elixir consumption,
those wishing earthly permanence
take half-doses reserving the remainder.
Should celestial ascent later beckon,
they consume the full portion.
With immortality assured,
sudden demise concerns vanish.
Sojourning terrestrially
or dwelling in famed mountains,
what worries remain?
Péng Zǔ stated
heaven hosts numerous senior officials and great deities,
where newly ascended rank low,
attending countless superiors -
merely increased labor.
Thus relentless ascent proves unwarranted,
hence his eight-century earthly stay.
Furthermore,
ancient immortals
sometimes grew feathered wings,
transforming and flying,
losing human essence,
assuming altered forms
like sparrows becoming clams,
pheasants transforming into sea-monsters -
this diverges from human Dào.
The human Dào entails savoring delicacies,
wearing light warmth,
harmonizing yīn-yáng,
holding official ranks,
maintaining keen senses,
sturdy bone joints,
radiant complexion,
aging without decay,
prolonged vibrant life,
free movement between realms,
unharmed by climate extremes,
unassailed by spirits and essences,
unaffected by weapons or toxins,
unburdened by emotions or reputation -
this constitutes true nobility.
Abandoning wives and children,
dwelling solitary in wilderness,
cutting off human connections,
isolated among trees and stones -
deserves no praise.
Previously, Ānqī Xiānshēng, Lóngméi, Nìng Gōng, Xiū Yáng Gōng, and Yīn Chángshēng
all consumed half-doses of golden elixir.
Remaining earthly
nearly a millennium
before departing.
Fundamentally speaking,
longevity seekers
cherish present desires,
not urgently craving celestial ascent,
nor considering flight superior to earthly existence.
If household immortality proves possible,
why rush heavenward?
Should ascension preclude earthly stay,
that presents separate considerations.
Péng Zǔ's words
accommodate human sentiments."
Someone asked:
"Should those pursuing the Way first establish merit and virtue,
is this correct?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Indeed so.
According to the middle chapter of the Jade Pendant Scripture,
establishing merit is paramount,
while eliminating faults is secondary.
For those pursuing the Way, rescuing people from danger to spare them calamity,
protecting people from illness,
and preventing untimely deaths
constitute the highest merit.
Those seeking immortality
must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, obedience, benevolence, and trustworthiness as their foundation.
If one fails to cultivate virtuous conduct
and merely focuses on techniques,
they will not attain longevity.
For major evil deeds,
the Director of Fate deducts a jì (twelve years),
while minor faults cost a suàn (one hundred days),
according to the severity of the offense,
thus the deduction varies in amount.
Every person's allotted lifespan
has its inherent measure;
if this measure is originally large,
then jì and suàn are hard to exhaust and death is delayed;
if what one is endowed with is originally small,
and offenses are numerous,
then jì and suàn are quickly exhausted leading to early death.
It also says,
one who desires to become an earth immortal
should perform three hundred good deeds;
one who desires celestial immortality,
perform twelve hundred good deeds.
If one has performed one thousand one hundred ninety-nine good deeds
and suddenly commits one evil act,
all previous good deeds are lost,
and one must start counting good deeds anew.
Thus, good is not measured by size,
nor evil by pettiness.
Even if one refrains from evil deeds,
but speaks of one's actions,
or demands recompense for almsgiving,
one loses the goodness of that particular deed,
though not all goodness is lost.
It further states,
if accumulated good deeds are insufficient,
even consuming elixirs of immortality
will be of no benefit.
If one does not take elixirs
but performs good deeds,
though immortality may not be immediately attained,
one can still avoid the calamity of sudden death.
I suspect that figures like Péng Zǔ
had insufficient merit,
hence could not ascend to heaven."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
I have studied books on nurturing life,
collected formulas for longevity,
and perused volumes
numbering in the thousands,
all emphasizing huándān and golden elixir as essential.
Thus, these two matters
represent the pinnacle of the Way to Immortality.
If consuming these does not confer immortality,
then there has never been immortality since ancient times.
In the past, when the central states fell into chaos,
all scattered in flight.
I traveled through several regions including Xú, Yù, Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Guǎng,
encountering hundreds of wandering Daoist priests.
Some were renowned,
seemingly beyond reach.
Yet they were largely similar,
their knowledge and insights,
whether profound or shallow,
insufficient to impress.
Though each possessed dozens of scrolls,
they couldn't fully comprehend them,
merely copying and hoarding them.
Some knew methods of breath circulation, grain abstention, and herbal remedies,
and their formula books
were roughly identical;
everyone had the Dàojī Jīng,
considering it supremely secret,
claiming it was written by Jūn Xǐ.
I informed them
it was actually composed by Wáng Tú, a military supervisor during the Wèi dynasty,
not an ancient.
Wáng Tú knew nothing of great medicines,
intending only to use breath circulation for ascetic practices seeking immortality,
composing this Dàojīng,
claiming it encompassed the entire Way,
thus greatly misleading people.
When I asked these priests about divine elixirs and golden elixirs,
and methods from the Three Sovereigns' Inner Script to summon celestial and earthly deities,
none knew anything;
most boasted, self-praised, and deceived,
claiming great longevity
or having roamed with immortals,
but few were worthy of deep discussion.
Some had heard of golden elixirs
but believed none existed today,
saying only ancient transcendent beings
could comprehend them.
Some obtained peripheral teachings,
lacking authentic scriptures.
Others had fragmented elixir recipes,
thinking these encompassed all alchemical methods.
Previously, Zuǒ Yuánfàng deeply contemplated in Tiānzhù Mountain,
where a spirit person bestowed upon him the Golden Elixir Immortal Scripture.
During the late Hàn turmoil,
he had no time to prepare it,
fleeing east of the river,
intending to seek famous mountains to cultivate this Way.
My granduncle Gě Xiān
received it from Zuǒ Yuánfàng.
He received the Great Clarity Elixir Scripture in three volumes, the Nine Cauldrons Elixir Scripture in one volume, and the Golden Elixir Scripture in one volume.
My teacher, Master Zhèng,
was a disciple of my granduncle Gě Xiān,
and received it from him,
but being poor, couldn't afford the medicines.
I served him personally,
sweeping and cleaning over time,
and finally received it through a covenant altar in Mǎjì Mountain,
along with oral secrets not written down.
Previously, no such texts existed in Jiāngdōng;
they originated from Zuǒ Yuánfàng,
who passed them to my granduncle,
who passed them to Master Zhèng,
who passed them to me,
hence other priests know nothing of them.
Yet I've possessed them for over twenty years,
lacking resources,
unable to prepare them,
only sighing deeply.
Some hoard gold full of chests,
accumulate money like mountains,
yet know nothing of this deathless method.
Even if they heard of it,
scarcely one in ten thousand would believe;
what can be done?
Drinking from the Jade Terrace makes one aware of the blandness of coarse brews;
beholding Kūnlún makes one realize the lowness of small mounds.
Once one learns the way of golden elixirs,
one no longer wishes to glance at minor formula books.
However, great medicines are hard to obtain quickly,
so one must temporarily use minor ones for support.
Yet consuming vast amounts of other medicines
may bring slight benefit,
but ultimately cannot confer longevity.
Thus, the essential saying of Lǎozǐ states:
If you do not obtain huándān and golden elixir,
you toil in vain.
The five grains can sustain life;
humans live with them,
die without them,
how much more so with top-grade divine medicines,
whose benefit to humans isn't it ten thousand times that of the five grains?
Golden elixirs as substances,
the longer they are heated,
the more marvelous their transformations.
Gold entering fire
never vanishes even after countless refinements;
buried,
it remains incorruptible forever.
Consuming these two substances
refines the human body,
thus enabling agelessness and deathlessness.
This relies on external substances to strengthen oneself,
like fat nourishing fire preventing extinction,
or copper rust applied to feet
preventing decay in water,
which borrows copper's strength to protect flesh.
Golden elixirs entering the body
permeate and nourish the vital systems,
unlike mere external application of copper rust.
Most in the world distrust the ultimate Way,
such skeptics are everywhere.
Yet if by chance an earnest seeker appears,
but fails to encounter these methods,
meets no enlightened teacher,
they cannot hear of this wondrous matter under heaven.
I now briefly outline the essentials of golden elixirs
for later like-minded enthusiasts.
Diligently seek them,
but do not cling to superficial formulas,
thinking them sufficient for transcendence.
Those who ultimately do not encounter them
should relinquish hopes for the unattainable.
Reflecting on these teachings,
one will surely realize it's like emerging from a stagnant pond to float on the vast ocean,
turning from firefly glow to face the sun and moon,
hearing thunder and recognizing the inadequacy of cloth drums,
seeing a giant whale and understanding the minuteness of tiny creatures.
If one chatters aimlessly,
with no profound understanding,
hoping to ascend with inferior medicines,
is it any different from whipping a lame donkey to chase the swift wind,
or rowing a small boat to cross a great river?"
Moreover, there are many minor elixir recipes,
but their preparation varies in depth,
so their potency differs.
Although some are superior and others inferior,
they cannot compare
to how a single-brewed wine
cannot match the richness of nine-times fermented liquor.
Yet even the lowest grade minor elixirs
still far surpass the highest grade herbs and plants.
All herbs and plants turn to ashes when burned,
while cinnabar produces mercury when heated,
and through accumulated transformations returns to cinnabar again.
How distant they are from ordinary herbs and plants!
Thus they can enable humans to achieve longevity—
only immortals have comprehended this principle.
How immeasurably distant
are they from ordinary people?
Ordinary people understand little
and marvel at much.
Some don't know mercury comes from cinnabar,
and when told, refuse to believe,
saying cinnabar is originally red—
how could it produce this white substance?
Others say cinnabar is just a stone,
yet when other stones are burned they all become ash—
why alone does cinnabar behave differently?
Such simple matters
remain incomprehensible to them—
when they hear of the Way of Immortality,
is it not fitting
that they laugh at its grandeur?
The ancient Perfected Ones, pitying those worthy of instruction in future generations,
created methods
meticulously designed to help them escape the calamity of death—
these can be called ultimate teachings.
Yet ordinary people stubbornly refuse to believe,
calling them empty words.
If they were empty words,
how could nine cycles of transformation,
achieved through counted days,
all proceed according to recipe?
The means by which the Perfected know these things
truly cannot be sought through conventional thinking.
In my youth I loved esoteric arts,
traveling on foot to inquire,
undeterred by danger or distance.
Whenever I heard unusual knowledge,
I rejoiced.
Though ridiculed and laughed at,
I never grieved.
Who knows if future generations won't surpass the present?
Therefore I write this to show those with understanding.
How could I merely admire the strange
and embellish empty talk,
wishing my book to circulate in the world,
gaining belief among common trends?
Strong sunlight cannot revive withered wood,
supreme wisdom cannot change the base fool.
Books are transmitted to the enlightened,
matters valued by the knowledgeable.
A farmer obtaining a vermilion bow would use it to scare birds,
southern tribespeople receiving royal robes would carry firewood in them—
how can those without understanding
be forced?
Ordinary people eat their fill all day,
yet cannot diligently pursue Confucian or Mohist studies,
nor attend to moral cultivation.
They merely wander aimlessly at leisure,
passing their days.
Their pursuits
involve nothing but fame or profit.
Some race hounds and falcons across plains,
others linger with overflowing wine cups,
some drown in music with beautiful women,
others indulge in fine silks,
some exhaust their muscles drawing bows,
others waste time on gambling.
Hearing supreme teachings, they act drunk;
seeing discourses on the Way, they nap by day.
They neglect self-cultivation,
moving toward death's domain,
unwilling to seek life-nourishing methods—
instead cutting themselves down,
tormenting themselves,
wasting away,
draining their vitality.
Those who know the Way treasure their knowledge secretly,
seeking nothing from others—
why should they force speech on them?
Common saying has it
that if immortality were possible,
the wealthy nobles of ancient times
should have obtained it themselves.
Since none did,
the Way doesn't exist.
But they don't realize ancient nobles
were just like modern ones—
all disbelieved and didn't seek it,
prioritizing immediate desires.
How could they obtain it?
Even if undecided,
if life might be extended
and immortality gained,
why not try?
A small success in testing
yielding just two-three hundred years
would still surpass dying young like ordinary people.
Worldly affairs are countless,
but Daoist arts are hardest to comprehend.
How can mediocre minds
declare no Way of immortality exists?
If mere common disbelief
means nonexistence,
then how too numerous
would be the world's wise ones?
Those who understand the Way and still cultivate it—
must they be utter fools,
inferior to ordinary people?
Some fear seeking immortality—
if unsuccessful,
they'd dread others' laughter,
considering them deluded.
But if their judgment errs
even slightly,
and immortality truly exists,
wouldn't successful ones laugh at them?
Even sun and moon can't illuminate everywhere—
how can human minds alone be trusted?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
According to the Yellow Emperor's Scripture of the Nine Cauldrons Divine Elixir,
the Yellow Emperor ingested it
and ascended immortal.
It also says:
Though breathing exercises
and herbal medicines
may extend life,
they cannot avoid death.
Divine elixirs grant endless longevity,
lasting as heaven and earth,
riding clouds driving dragons,
ascending and descending the Great Purity.
The Yellow Emperor transmitted it to Xuánzǐ,
admonishing:
This Way is supremely important—
must be taught only to the worthy.
If not the right person,
though they pile jade like mountains,
never tell them this Way.
Recipients must cast golden figures and fish into east-flowing water as covenant,
smearing blood as oath.
Without immortal bones,
one cannot perceive this Way.
Prepare elixirs in famous mountains,
uninhabited places,
companions not exceeding three,
first purify for hundred days,
bathe with five fragrances,
achieve utmost cleanliness,
avoid filth,
and contact with ordinary people.
Don't let unbelievers know,
lest they slander the divine medicine—
then the medicine won't succeed.
Success enables whole families to ascend immortal,
not just individuals.
People reject divine elixirs,
trusting herbs instead.
Herbal medicines
rot when buried,
dissolve when boiled,
char when burned—
cannot sustain themselves,
how give life to humans?
The Nine Elixirs
are essentials for longevity,
not for ordinary eyes and ears.
Millions swarm like insects,
knowing only greed for wealth—
aren't they walking corpses?
Preparation requires sacrifices,
with one scroll illustrating sacrificial methods.
The first elixir named Elixir Blossom.
First make Mysterious Yellow,
using realgar solution, alum solution, rock salt, brine salt, arsenopyrite, oyster shell, red halloysite, talc, and lead powder—each dozens of pounds—
to form Six-One Mud,
fire thirty-six days to complete.
Ingest seven days to become immortal.
Also pellet this elixir with Mysterious Paste,
place on fierce fire—
instantly becomes gold.
Also mix 240 zhu with 100 pounds mercury, fire it—
also becomes gold.
Gold formation means medicine succeeded.
If no gold forms,
reseal medicine and fire it again,
days as before—
none will fail.
The second elixir is named Shéndān,
also called Shénfú.
Taking it for a hundred days makes one an immortal.
One can traverse water and fire,
by applying this elixir to the soles of the feet,
and walk upon water.
Ingesting three dāoguī of it,
the Three Corpses and Nine Worms immediately decay,
and all illnesses are cured.
The third elixir is named Shéndān.
Taking one dāoguī,
for a hundred days makes one an immortal.
If given to the six domestic animals to swallow,
they too will never die.
It can also ward off the five weapons.
After taking it for a hundred days,
immortal beings and jade maidens,
mountain and river spirits,
all come to serve,
appearing in human form.
The fourth elixir is named Huándān.
Taking one dāoguī,
for a hundred days makes one an immortal.
Vermilion birds and phoenixes
soar and cover above,
with jade maidens arriving by the side.
Mixing one dāoguī with one jīn of mercury and heating it,
instantly produces gold.
Using this elixir to coat coins or objects,
they return the same day.
Writing with this elixir on a mortal's eyes,
all ghosts flee and avoid.
The fifth elixir is named Ěrdān.
Taking it for thirty days,
makes one an immortal.
Ghosts and spirits come to serve,
jade maidens appear before.
The sixth elixir is named Liàndān.
Taking it for ten days,
makes one an immortal.
Also, mixing it with mercury and heating,
also turns into gold.
The seventh elixir is named Róudān.
Taking one dāoguī,
for a hundred days makes one an immortal.
Mixing it with quēpén juice and taking it,
even a ninety-year-old man
can bear children.
Combining it with jīngōng and heating,
immediately produces gold.
The eighth elixir is named Fúdān.
Taking it makes one an immortal the same day.
Holding this elixir the size of a date pit,
all ghosts avoid.
Writing with the elixir on doors and windows,
myriad evils and numerous spirits dare not approach,
and it also wards off thieves, tigers, and wolves.
The ninth elixir is named Hándān.
Taking one dāoguī,
for a hundred days makes one an immortal.
Immortal boys and girls come to serve,
flying lightly and rising,
without needing wings.
Among these nine elixirs,
obtaining just one makes one an immortal;
it is not necessary to make all,
making them depends on individual preference.
Generally, taking the nine elixirs,
if one wishes to ascend to heaven, then go;
if one wishes to remain in the human world, it is also optional,
all able to pass without hindrance,
free from attainable harms.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
There is also the Tàiqīng Shéndān,
its method comes from Yuánjūn.
Yuánjūn,
is the teacher of Lǎozǐ.
The Tàiqīng Observing Heaven Scripture has nine chapters,
saying its upper three cannot be taught,
its middle three are not worthy of transmission in the world,
often sunk beneath the three springs,
the lower three chapters,
are precisely the upper, middle, and lower elixir scriptures,
totaling three volumes.
Yuánjūn,
is a great divine immortal,
able to harmonize yīn and yáng,
command ghosts, spirits, wind, and rain,
charioteer nine dragons and twelve white tigers,
all immortals under heaven are subordinate,
yet even he says it results from learning the Way and taking elixirs,
not naturally.
How much more so for ordinary people?
The scripture says:
The superior person attains the Way,
ascends to become a celestial official;
the middling person attains the Way,
dwells gathered at Kūnlún;
the inferior person attains the Way,
lives long in the world.
Foolish people do not believe,
calling it empty words,
from morning till night,
only do things seeking death,
completely not seeking life,
so how can heaven forcibly give them life?
Ordinary people only know fine food and good clothes,
music, beauty, wealth, and honor,
indulging hearts and exhausting desires,
those who suddenly end and perish,
carefully do not tell them of the divine elixir,
lest they laugh at the Way and slander the truth.
Transmitting the elixir scripture to the unworthy,
one's body will surely be unlucky.
If there are devout believers,
one may share the completed medicine with them,
but do not lightly transmit the formula.
Those who know this Way,
what need have they for princes and nobles?
For once the divine elixir is completed,
not only is there longevity,
but one can also make gold.
Once the gold is made,
take one hundred jīn and first conduct a great sacrifice.
The sacrifice has its own separate method in one volume,
not the same as the nine cauldrons sacrifice.
The sacrifice should separately weigh gold and label each.
Offer twenty jīn to Heaven,
five jīn to the sun and moon,
eight jīn to the Northern Dipper,
eight jīn to Tàiyǐ,
five jīn to the well,
five jīn to the stove,
twelve jīn to the River Earl,
five jīn to the earth god,
five jīn each to the doors, windows, village ghosts, spirits, and pure lords,
totaling eighty-eight jīn.
The remaining twelve jīn,
place in a fine leather bag,
on an auspicious day during the market's bustling hour,
silently leave it in a crowded place,
go straight away without looking back.
Only after using over a hundred jīn
can one freely use it.
If not first using gold to sacrifice to the spirits,
one will surely suffer calamity.
It also says,
the Way of longevity,
does not lie in sacrificing to ghosts and spirits,
nor in guiding and stretching exercises,
the essence of ascending to immortality,
lies in the divine elixir.
Knowing it is not easy,
doing it is truly difficult.
If you can make it,
you can endure long.
In recent times, at the end of the Hàn, Yīn Jūn of Xīnyě,
compounded this Tàiqīng elixir and attained immortality.
This man was originally a Confucian scholar,
talented and thoughtful,
skilled in writing poetry, elixir scriptures, eulogies, and prefaces,
describing his initial learning of the Way and following his teacher from start to finish,
listing over forty immortals he knew personally,
very clearly.
Making this Tàiqīng elixir,
is slightly harder than the nine cauldrons,
yet it is the superior method for ascending to heaven in broad daylight.
To compound it, one must first make huāchí, chìyán, gěn xuě, xuánbái, fēifú, and sānwǔ shénshuǐ,
then can one begin the firing.
The single-refined elixir,
taken for three years, leads to immortality.
The twice-refined elixir,
taken for two years, leads to immortality.
The thrice-refined elixir,
taken for one year, leads to immortality.
The four-times-refined elixir,
taken for half a year, leads to immortality.
The five-times-refined elixir,
taken for a hundred days, leads to immortality.
The six-times-refined elixir,
taken for forty days, leads to immortality.
The seven-times-refined elixir,
taken for thirty days, leads to immortality.
The eight-times-refined elixir,
taken for ten days, leads to immortality.
The nine-times-refined elixir,
taken for three days, leads to immortality.
If one takes the nine-times-refined elixir,
places it inside a divine tripod,
and after the summer solstice,
heats the tripod until it is hot,
placing a pound of Zhū'ér beneath the lid.
Wait in concealment,
awaiting the sunlight to shine upon it.
Suddenly, it will rise together with a hissing sound,
brilliant and radiant,
with divine light in five colors,
transforming immediately into Huándān.
Take and consume a small spoonful of it,
and you will ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Moreover, the nine-times-refined elixir
is sealed in an earthenware pot,
with chaff fire,
first gentle then fierce,
from one refinement to nine refinements,
the duration, slow or fast, varies in the number of days,
from this, one knows it.
With fewer refinements,
the medicinal potency is insufficient,
thus taking it requires more days,
and attaining immortality is slow.
With more refinements,
the medicinal potency is strong,
thus taking it requires fewer days,
and attaining immortality is swift.
There is also the Jiǔguāngdān,
which differs in method from the nine-refined elixir,
but is largely similar.
The method of making it
involves combining various medicines with fire,
to refine the five minerals.
The five minerals are:
cinnabar, realgar, white alum, azurite, and magnetite.
Each mineral undergoes five refinements, each producing five colors,
thus five minerals yield twenty-five colors,
each color weighing one liang,
and stored in separate vessels.
To revive the dead,
if less than three days have passed,
take a small spoonful of the green elixir and mix it with water,
bathe the dead person with it,
and also use a small spoonful to open their mouth and administer it,
and the dead will immediately come back to life.
To summon a traveling feast,
take the black elixir and mix it with water,
apply it to the left hand,
and whatever one requests verbally will arrive on its own,
capable of summoning all things under heaven.
To become invisible, foresee future events,
and halt aging to remain youthful,
take a small spoonful of the yellow elixir,
and one will immediately achieve longevity without aging.
Moreover, sitting still, one can see a thousand miles away,
knowing both auspicious and inauspicious events,
as if they were before one's eyes.
The fate of a person's life,
its prosperity and decline, longevity and premature death,
wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness,
are all known,
the methods for which are all in the middle scroll of the Tàiqīng Jīng.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Next, there is the Wǔlíng Dān Jīng in one scroll,
which contains five methods.
Using cinnabar, realgar, orpiment, sulfur, azurite, alum, magnetite, halite, and limonite,
also using liùyī ní,
and offering sacrifices in a divine chamber to combine them,
