it is completed in thirty-six days.
Also using the five emperors' talismans,
inscribed in five colors,
it too can make one immortal,
but it is not as effective as the Tàiqīng and Jiǔdǐng elixirs.
There is also the Mínshān elixir method,
which the Dàoshi Zhāng Gài tà obtained through deep meditation in a stone chamber on Mín Shān,
thus acquiring this formula.
The method involves smelting yellow copper,
to make a square mirror,
to collect water from the moon,
cover it with mercury,
and attract the essence of the sun's fire into it,
long-term consumption leads to immortality.
Also, take this elixir and place it in a realgar copper mirror,
cover it with mercury and expose it to the sun,
after twenty days, open and process it,
take with well water at dawn the size of a small bean,
for a hundred days,
the blind will be able to see,
all illnesses will heal on their own,
white hair will turn black again,
and lost teeth will regrow.
There is also the Wùchéngzǐ elixir method,
using Bāshā mercury placed in an eight-inch copper plate, with an earthen stove holding charcoal,
leaning on a three-cornered trench to support the plate,
pouring sulfur water over it,
always keeping it like mud,
consuming it for a hundred days leads to immortality.
There is also the Xiànménzǐ elixir method,
mixing one pound of elixir with wine,
using three shēng of wine to blend,
expose it to the sun for forty days,
taking it for one day,
will immediately expel the three worms and all diseases;
taking it for three years,
the path to immortality is achieved,
and surely two jade maidens will come to serve,
able to be commanded to summon a traveling feast,
this elixir can suppress all ghosts,
and the calamities from the dead in all directions that harm households,
and those who disturb others with construction,
hang it facing them,
and there will be no worries.
There is also the Lìchéng elixir,
which also has nine forms,
similar to the Jiǔdǐng but not as effective.
Its essential method further states,
take orpiment and realgar, smelt them to extract copper within,
cast it into a vessel,
cover it with three-year-old pure vinegar,
for a hundred days,
this vessel will grow red crystals,
several fēn long,
or sometimes five-colored Langgān,
take and process it for consumption,
it also grants longevity.
It can also be mixed with tùsī,
tùsī is the root when first sprouted,
its shape resembles a rabbit,
dig it up and extract its blood,
mix it with this elixir,
taking it leads to immediate transformation,
able to do as one pleases.
Also mixed with zhūcǎo,
taking it once,
enables one to ride the void and travel, it is said,
zhūcǎo looks like a small jujube,
planted, it grows three to four chǐ tall,
its branches and leaves are all red,
the stem like coral,
it likes to grow under the rocks of famous mountains,
when cut, its sap flows like blood,
if jade or the eight minerals, gold, and silver are placed into it,
immediately they can be kneaded like mud,
over time, they turn into liquid,
if gold is placed into it,
it is called gold syrup,
if jade is placed into it,
it is called jade nectar,
consuming either leads to longevity.
There is also the method of obtaining the fúdān, which says,
among all the waters under heaven,
those named dān,
such as Nányáng's Dānshuǐ and the like,
all have dānyú in them,
before the summer solstice, on the tenth night, watch for them,
dānyú will surely float by the water's edge,
with red light shining upward,
blazing like fire,
net them to catch,
though you may catch many,
do not take them all,
cut them to draw blood,
apply it to the soles of the feet,
then one can walk on water,
and dwell long in the depths.
There is also the Chìsōngzǐ elixir method,
take thousand-year-old léi juice and矾桃汁 to soak the elixir,
place it in a non-absorbent vessel,
seal its mouth with refined honey,
bury it three chǐ underground,
for a hundred days,
then squeeze the red fruit of the zhè wood,
take its juice, mix, and consume it,
it will make one's face, eyes, temples, and hair all red,
and grant longevity.
In the past, among the immortals of Zhōnghuáng, there was one called Chìxūzǐ,
could it be that he consumed this?
Another is Master Shí's elixir method:
take fledgling birds that have not yet grown feathers,
mix them with true cinnabar and beef and swallow them.
When they grow up,
their feathers will all turn red.
Then kill them,
dry them in the shade for a hundred days,
pound them together with their feathers and take a dose the size of a knife-tip,
and after a hundred days, one gains a lifespan of five hundred years.
Another is Kāng Fēngzǐ's elixir method:
use sheep, crow eggs, and sparrow blood,
combine with Shàoshì aconite juice,
mix with cinnabar and place inside a swan egg sealed with lacquer,
put it in mica water,
and after a hundred days it turns into red water.
Take one gě,
and immediately increase lifespan by a hundred years;
take one shēng and live a thousand years.
Another is Cuī Wénzǐ's elixir method:
put cinnabar into a duck's belly and steam it,
then consume it;
it makes people prolong their years,
and long-term consumption leads to immortality.
Another is Liú Yuán's elixir method:
put cinnabar into dark water liquid,
after a hundred days it turns purple,
and when held, it doesn't stain the hand.
Then mix it with mica water,
put it in a tube sealed with lacquer,
throw it into a well,
and after a hundred days it turns into red water.
Take one gě,
and gain a hundred years of life;
long-term consumption leads to longevity.
Another is Yuè Zǐcháng's elixir method:
combine azurite, lead oxide, mercury, and cinnabar,
place in a copper tube,
seal it with dried tile and talc,
steam it in white sand,
for eighty days.
Take a dose the size of a small bean,
and in three years, become an immortal.
Another is Lǐ Wén's elixir method:
wrap cinnabar in white silk,
boil it in bamboo juice,
calling it "red spring,"
then float it on boiling water to steam,
mix it with dark water,
take one gě,
and in one year, become an immortal.
Another is Yǐn Zǐ's elixir method:
mix mica water with cinnabar and seal it tightly,
place it in a golden flower pond,
take it out after one year,
take a knife-tip dose,
finish one jīn,
and gain five hundred years of life.
Another is the Tàiyǐ Summoning Souls Elixir method:
the five minerals used,
and sealing it with six-one mud,
are similar to the nine elixirs.
It excels at reviving those who have died suddenly within three days:
break a tooth and insert one pill,
along with a sulfur pill,
both sent down with water,
making them revive as soon as it enters the throat.
All say they saw a messenger holding a tally summoning them.
Another is Cǎinǚ's elixir method:
mix rabbit blood with cinnabar and honey, then steam it,
for a hundred days.
Take one pill the size of a sterculia seed,
three times a day,
until a hundred days,
and two divine maidens will come to serve,
and can be commanded.
Another is Jìqiū Zǐ's elixir method:
mix clear wine, sesame oil, hundred-flower sweet wine, and dragon fat,
seal with six-one mud,
heat with chaff fire,
mature in ten days.
Take one pill the size of a small bean,
finish the dose,
and gain a lifespan of five hundred years.
Another is Mò Zǐ's elixir method:
use mercury and five-mineral liquid in a copper vessel,
heat it over fire,
stir with an iron spoon,
for ten days,
it returns to being cinnabar.
Take one knife-tip dose,
all illnesses leave the body,
long-term consumption leads to immortality.
Another is Zhāng Zǐhé's elixir method:
use lead, mercury, and azurite water combined and sealed,
steam it in red millet,
mature in eighty days.
Mix with date paste to form pills,
take the size of a large bean,
for a hundred days,
lifespan five hundred years.
Another is Qǐlǐ's elixir method:
first levitate and collect jade dust from five minerals,
combine with cinnabar and mercury,
put in a large copper vessel and boil,
for a hundred days,
it turns five-colored.
Taking it leads to immortality.
With one hundred jīn of lead,
and a hundred knife-tips of medicine,
combine and fire to become white silver.
Mix with realgar water and fire it,
in a hundred days it becomes gold.
If the gold is too hard,
boil it in lard;
if too soft,
boil it with white plum.
Another is the Jade Pillar elixir method:
mix flower pond liquid with cinnabar,
cover and layer with azurite and sulfur powder,
put in a tube in sand,
steam for fifty days.
Take it for a hundred days,
and jade maidens, the six jiǎ and six dīng spirit maidens will come to serve,
can be commanded,
and know all affairs under heaven.
Another is the Zhǒuhòu elixir method:
mix golden flower liquid with cinnabar and seal in a dried tile,
steam for eighty days,
take the size of a small bean,
place on a plate,
harmonize it facing the sun,
its light connects upward with the sun.
Take the size of a small bean,
and achieve longevity.
Throw it into Dānyáng copper,
fire it to become gold.
Another is Lǐ Gōng's elixir method:
use true cinnabar and five-mineral water, one shēng each,
mix into a paste,
fire in a cauldron,
take out in thirty-six days.
Mix with liquid stone sulfur,
take for ten years,
and last as long as heaven and earth.
Another is Liú Shēng's elixir method:
use white chrysanthemum juice, paper mulberry juice, and ailanthus juice mixed with cinnabar and steamed,
for thirty days,
grind and take it.
In one year,
gain five hundred years of life.
An old man taking it becomes so youthful he's unrecognizable;
a youth taking it also doesn't age.
Another is Wáng Jūn's elixir method:
put arsenic and mercury into a chicken egg,
seal with lacquer,
have a hen incubate three of them.
Take on an auspicious day,
it halts aging;
children must not take it,
or they won't grow anymore.
Give it to newly hatched chicks or puppies,
and they also won't grow larger;
birds and beasts all show this effect.
Another is Chén Shēng's elixir method:
use white honey mixed with cinnabar,
put in a copper vessel and seal,
sink in a well,
for one cycle.
Take it for a full year,
and feel no hunger;
finish one jīn,
lifespan a hundred years.
Another is Hán Zhōng's elixir method:
cook lacquer and honey mixed with cinnabar,
taking it can prolong life and maintain vision,
standing in the sun without a shadow.
Beyond these,
there are still dozens of methods,
too numerous to detail.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The Gold Elixir is what the Great One ingested to become immortal,
no less potent than the Nine Cyclical Elixirs.
To prepare it, use one jin of gold according to ancient standards,
along with Xuánmíng Lónggāo, the Stone of Tàiyǐ's First Decade, ice stone, Purple Wandering Maiden, Dark Water Liquid, gold-dissolving stone, and cinnabar.
Seal it until it turns into liquid.
The scripture states:
Once the Gold Elixir enters the mouth,
one's entire body turns golden.
Lǎozǐ received it from Yuánjūn,
who said:
"This Way is of utmost importance,
appearing only once in a hundred generations.
Store it in a stone chamber.
When compounding it,
observe purification and abstinence for a hundred days,
avoiding contact with ordinary people.
Beside a famous mountain,
by flowing eastern waters,
build a separate retreat.
After a hundred days, it is completed;
ingesting one liang makes one immortal.
If not yet wishing to leave the world,
and instead becoming an earthly or aquatic immortal,
simply observe purification for a hundred days.
For those seeking ascension to heaven,
first abstain from grains for a year,
then ingest it.
Taking half a liang
grants longevity without death;
myriad harms and hundred poisons
cannot injure you.
You may keep wife and children,
hold official rank,
follow any desire,
with no restrictions.
If later wishing to ascend to heaven,
then observe purification
and take another liang,
and you will soar as an immortal.
Using the Gold Elixir in the method of Wēixǐ and Jùshèng,
take the Gold Elixir and mercury, combine and boil them
for thirty days.
Remove,
place in an earthenware jar,
seal with Six-One mud,
and set over fierce fire to cook
for sixty watches.
All transforms into elixir;
taking a small bean-sized amount makes one immortal.
With one knife-point of this elixir powdered
and one jin of mercury,
it instantly becomes silver.
Also, take one jin of this elixir, place over fire and fan it;
it turns into flowing red gold,
called Danjin.
Coating blades and swords with it
wards off weapons for ten thousand miles.
Using this Danjin for plates and bowls,
eating and drinking from them
grants people longevity.
Exposing it to sun and moon to obtain liquid,
like the Fangzhu obtaining water,
drinking it prevents death.
Mixing the Gold Elixir with yellow earth,
placing it in a Six-One mud jar,
and cooking over fierce fire
turns it all into gold,
usable for intermediary purposes.
Cooking it again over fire
transforms it all into elixir;
taking a small bean-sized portion allows one to enter famous mountains and great rivers as an earthly immortal.
With one knife-point of this elixir powdered, mercury instantly becomes silver.
Mixing one liang of silver with one jin of lead
turns all into silver.
The Gold Elixir Scripture says:
Cast eight liang of gold figurines into east-flowing water,
swear an oath by drinking blood,
then the oral formula is revealed.
If not following this method
but stealing the recipe to make it,
it will never succeed.
For those of sincere faith,
the medicine may be given,
but the texts must not be lightly transmitted,
lest both suffer calamity.
The celestial gods observe humans closely—
people just do not realize it."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The Nine Cyclical Elixirs truly represent the supreme method of immortal medicine,
yet compounding them
requires numerous varied ingredients.
If the four directions are clear and accessible,
they can be obtained in markets.
But if the nine regions are divided and separated,
the materials become unavailable.
Moreover, one must tend the fire for tens of days and nights,
monitoring the flame's intensity
without letting it deviate from the proper level—
extremely toilsome and difficult.
Thus, it falls short of the ease of compounding the Gold Elixir.
For the Gold Elixir, only gold is hard to obtain.
One jin of gold in ancient measure equals two jin today,
roughly worth just over three hundred thousand coins.
The other ingredients are relatively easier to gather.
Also, no fire-tending is needed;
simply place it in a Hua Pond,
and when the days are complete, it is done.
Altogether, about four hundred thousand coins can procure one dose,
sufficient to make eight people immortal.
However, if too little is compounded,
its energy is insufficient for mutual transformation—
like brewing a few liters of rice wine,
it will certainly not succeed."
Bàopúzǐ said:
Next there is the method of ingesting gold,
though not as effective as golden fluid,
it is far superior to other medicines.
Some prepare it by refining it with pig's pancreas fat and wine,
some treat it with ailanthus bark,
some dissolve it with thistle wine and magnetite,
some can draw it out to form a headscarf,
or immediately make it into liquid to ingest.
Some have taboos,
making it inferior to golden fluid.
Some combine realgar and orpiment to ingest it,
which can be stretched like leather,
but these are all methods for terrestrial immortals.
Silver and large pearls from clams
can all be transformed into liquid for consumption.
However, they require long-term use without interruption,
thus all are inferior to golden fluid.
Bàopúzǐ said:
To prepare this golden fluid and nine elixirs,
not only does it require money,
but one should also enter famous mountains,
cut off worldly affairs,
so few can accomplish it,
and even among millions of people,
only occasionally will one obtain the scripture.
Therefore, among those who write Daoist texts,
few discuss golden elixirs.
The foremost prohibition:
do not allow vulgar people who don't believe in the Dao
to slander, ridicule, or disparage it -
it will certainly not succeed.
Master Zhèng explained the reason:
when preparing such great medicines, sacrifices must be made,
whereupon the Great Unity Primordial Lord, Lǎojūn, and the Dark Maiden will come to inspect.
If the medicine maker doesn't seclude themselves in remote places,
allowing common fools to pass by and hear or see,
the various deities will blame the maker for not following scriptural precepts,
leading to evil people's slanderous words,
and will no longer aid the person,
allowing evil energies to advance,
and the medicine will not succeed.
One must enter famous mountains,
purify oneself for a hundred days,
abstain from the five pungent vegetables and raw fish,
avoid meeting common people,
only then can great medicine be made.
The purification ends only after the medicine is completed,
not just at the beginning of preparation.
Master Zhèng said,
Master Zuǒ told him
that various small mountains
cannot be used for making golden fluid and divine elixirs.
Small mountains generally lack proper deities as rulers,
mostly inhabited by spirits of wood and stone,
ancient creatures of thousand years,
blood-eating ghosts -
these are all evil energies,
not considering helping humans,
only capable of causing misfortune,
often testing Daoists,
who must use arts to protect themselves
and their disciples,
yet they might still ruin one's medicine.
Nowadays, medical practitioners,
when preparing good medicines or ointments,
don't want chickens, dogs, children, or women to see them.
If violated by these things,
they become ineffective when used.
Also, dyers hate being seen by evil eyes,
as colors lose their beauty.
How much more so for divine immortal medicines?
Therefore, ancient Daoists
making divine medicines
necessarily entered famous mountains,
not just ordinary mountains,
precisely for this reason.
According to immortal scriptures,
mountains suitable for concentrated preparation of immortal medicines include:

Huà Shān, Tài Shān, Huò Shān, Héng Shān, Sōng Shān, Shǎoshì Shān, Cháng Shān, Tàibái Shān, Zhōngnán Shān, Nǚjī Shān, Dìfèi Shān, Wángwū Shān, Bàodú Shān, Ānqiū Shān, Qián Shān, Qīngchéng Shān, Éméi Shān, Ruí Shān, Yúntái Shān, Luófú Shān, Yángjià Shān, Huángjīn Shān, Biēzǔ Shān, Dàxiǎo Tiāntái Shān, Sìwàng Shān, Gàizhú Shān, Kuòcāng Shān -
all have proper deities in these mountains,
some with terrestrial immortals among them.
They all grow glossy ganoderma,
can avoid great armies and calamities,
not just for making medicine therein.
If a Daoist ascends them,
the mountain deities will certainly aid their blessings,
and medicine will surely succeed.
If unable to reach these mountains,
large islands in the sea
can also be used for medicine preparation.
Like Wēng Zhōu, Dǎn Zhōu, and Zhù Yǔ in Kuàijī's east,
and Xúzhōu's Shēnjǔ Zhōu, Tàiguāng Zhōu, Yù Zhōu -
all are secondary choices.
Now that central plains' famous mountains are inaccessible,
reachable famous mountains in Jiāngdōng include:
Huò Shān,
in Jìn'ān;
Cháng Shān and Tàibái,
in Dōngyáng;
Sìwàng Shān, Dàxiǎo Tiāntái Shān, Gàizhú Shān, Kuòcāng Shān,
all in Kuàijī.
Bàopúzǐ said:
I, though unworthy, am a descendant of great officials,
though my talent insufficient for governing state affairs,
yet among my peers and friends,
those pursuing advancement,
few know more than me -
many soar through the Milky Way,
shining light to the morning sky.
The reason I cut off celebrations and condolences in my hometown,
abandoning contemporary glory and wealth,
is determined to travel far to famous mountains,
complete my written works,
then prepare divine medicines,
planning for longevity.
Common people all wonder why I leave my homeland,
turn from clear paths,
to personally farm in wooded marshes,
hands and feet calloused,
saying I have madness.
But the Dao and worldly affairs don't flourish together -
if not abandoning human duties,
how could I cultivate such aspirations?
Seeing clearly,
holding firmly -
why fear criticism or praise,
or be swayed by encouragement or discouragement?
I merely write my thoughts
to show future like-minded admirers.
Later those of unwavering resolve
will sacrifice
no differently than I.
Minor Divine Elixir recipe:
use three pounds of true cinnabar,
six pounds of white honey, mix well,
sun-dry and decoct daily
until pillable,
take ten sesame-sized pills each morning -
within a year,
white hair turns black,
lost teeth regrow,
body becomes moist and radiant,
long-term use
turns old men into youth,
achieving immortality.
Minor Elixir method:
one pound of cinnabar,
pounded and sifted,
add three liters of pure vinegar,
two liters of lacquer,
combine all three substances,
mix thoroughly,
heat over low fire until pillable,
take three sesame-sized pills,
twice daily -
in thirty days,
all abdominal illnesses cured,
three corpse worms removed;
after hundred days,
muscles and bones strengthen;
after thousand days,
Director of Fate erases death record,
lasting as long as heaven and earth,
shining like sun and moon,
changing form and appearance,
transforming unpredictably,
casting no shadow at noon,
even emitting separate light.
Minor Gold Ingestion method:
refine gold in clear wine,
about two hundred cycles,
removing when boiling -
should squeeze like mud between fingers;
if not boiling,
or not squeezing out between fingers,
continue cutting it,
immersing in clear wine repeatedly.
When ready,
take one pellet-sized pill,
or one pill
divided into smaller pills -
after thirty days,
unaffected by heat or cold,
divine beings and jade maidens attend you;
silver can also be ingested,
same method as gold.
Taking these two substances,
if dwelling in famous mountains' stone chambers,
one year leads to light ascent.
Even in human world, becomes terrestrial immortal -
do not recklessly transmit.
The Method of Ingesting Gold by Liǎng Yí Zǐ:
Take three jīn of lard from a pig raised on leather,
one shēng of pure bitter wine,
and five liǎng of gold.
Place them in a vessel,
heat it on an earthen stove,
put the gold into the fat,
repeating the immersion and removal a hundred times,
and do the same with the bitter wine.
Ingesting one jīn
grants a lifespan as vast as heaven and earth;
ingesting half a jīn
grants two thousand years of life;
five liǎng
grants twelve hundred years.
Regardless of the amount,
it can be ingested.
It should be prepared on auspicious days,
and taking it yields divine efficacy.
Do not transmit it to the unworthy;
if revealed to the unworthy,
the medicine will lose its potency and efficacy.
For those wishing to ingest corpse-shedding medicine,
they should take cinnabar.
Bào Pǔ Zǐ said:
Subtle and profound, it is hard to comprehend,
and many are doubtful.
How could my intelligence surpass others?
It is merely that I happen to have some partial understanding,
just as the crane knows midnight,
and the swallow knows the Wù-Sì days,
but that does not mean they understand other matters.
There is also evidence to verify
that attaining longevity is possible,
and that immortals are not born but made.
The wonders of the Dào
cannot be fully written down,
and what is near at hand
is not worth discussing.
In the past, Gēng Sāng toiled until his hands and feet were calloused,
and Wén Zǐ’s face became emaciated;
after long and arduous effort,
they received the great secrets—
surely there is a reason for this.
All living beings with round heads and breath,
who among them does not delight in life and fear death?
Yet glory, splendor, power, and profit tempt their minds;
fair faces and jade-like skin dazzle their eyes;
clear shāng and flowing zhǐ melodies disturb their ears;
love, hate, benefit, and harm agitate their spirits;
fame, achievement, and reputation bind their bodies.
These things come unsummoned,
and are achieved without learning.
Unless one is destined to become an immortal,
exhaustively comprehends principles, and gains unique insight,
recognizing change and adaptability beyond ordinary affairs,
and wields clear discernment in the realm of profound silence,
awakening to the intimacy or distance of body and fame,
and lamenting the lightning speed of life’s fleeting gap,
how can one abandon worldly pursuits to cultivate the remote,
suppress lingering desires,
cut off immediate cravings,
and practice the distant, hard-to-attain merits?
For existence arises from non-existence,
and form depends on spirit to stand.
Existence is
the palace of non-existence.
Form is
the abode of spirit.
Thus, liken it to a dike:
if the dike breaks, the water does not remain.
Compare it to a candle:
if the candle burns out, the fire does not stay.
When the body is weary, the spirit scatters;
when the breath is exhausted, life ends.
If the roots are depleted, even lush branches
will lose their green and leave the tree.
When the breath is tired and desires prevail,
the essence and spirit depart from the body.
Those who pass away do not return,
and once decayed, there is no life to restore—
this is what truly saddens those who have comprehended the Dào!
Why do they
disdain jade and value the shade?
Is there not a reason for it?
Therefore, those who nurture their nature in the mountains and forests,
and those who reject customs to follow their will,
compare lofty status to warts,
and regard all things as cicada wings—
are they merely boasting
and forcefully belittling worldly affairs?
It is because their vision is clear,
that they discard them as if forgetting.
Thus, they dwell in remote seclusion,
hiding their scales and concealing their brilliance,
restraining the eyes from desires,
dismissing sights that dim vision,
blocking the ears from distracting sounds,
avoiding noises that confuse hearing,
cleansing the profound mirror,
guarding the feminine and embracing the One,
concentrating the breath to achieve softness,
anchoring in tranquility and simplicity,
dispelling the evil emotions of joy and sorrow,
setting aside the glory and shame of gain and loss,
cutting off the poisonous sweetness of excessive life,
silencing excessive speech at its pivot,
listening inward to make hearing透彻,
gazing inward to see the formless,
nourishing the spiritual root in the dark crucible,
removing temptations in interactions,
eliminating shallow tasks,
restraining with contentment,
acting through non-action,
to fully preserve the heavenly principle.
Then, inhale the precious blossoms,
bathe the spirit in the Great Purity,
externally remove the five luminaries,
internally guard the nine essences,
secure the jade key at the Gate of Life,
bind the North Pole in the Yellow Court,
draw the three lights into the Hall of Light,
soar with the Primordial Beginning to refine the form,
gather spiritual liquid at the Golden Bridge,
long drive the white and retain the green,
condense clear spring in the dāntián,
draw deep pearls in the Five Cities,
the jade tripod simmers below,
the resplendent bird sings above,
exquisite flowers sprout,
the heavenly deer spews jade,
embody double cycles in the Crimson Palace,
hide the nine lights in the cavernous darkness,
clouds lush and blue connect to the sky,
long valleys deep and intersecting,
tread upon Qián and Duì,
summon the Six Dīng,
sit or lie in the purple chamber,
chew and inhale golden essence,
the radiant autumn fungus,
with vermilion blooms and emerald stems,
the gleaming precious ointment,
overflowing and sprinkling the night,
it cures hunger and quenches thirst,
and a hundred ailments do not sprout,
wandering freely on Wù-Sì days,
harmonious and balanced in drinking,
restraining the hun and controlling the pò,
bones firm and body light,
thus able to ride the wind and clouds to ascend void,
and join with the chaotic chariot to live eternally.
Yet, dust accumulating a foot high on a beam
cannot be achieved in a moment;
a mountain stream’s piercing clarity
cannot be attained in haste.
The problem lies in those who hear not believing,
those who believe not acting,
and those who act not persevering.
Those who succeed are very few and hidden,
while those who fail are numerous and visible.
People cannot perceive the hidden successes,
and only see the visible failures,
so they claim that there truly is no path to immortality in the world.
Bàopúzǐ said:
When the embankment is strong, water incurs no wasteful leakage;
when the fat is ample, fire has no fear of extinguishing.
The Lóngquán sword remains sharp by avoiding cutting;
axes and blades quickly dull through daily use.
Snow hidden away survives the summer by evading warmth;
ice stored deep endures the heat.
A single silk cloth veiling a mirror prevents scorching;
common plants partially covered pass through winter.
Soil is easily dissolved,
yet fired into tiles,
it lasts as long as heaven and earth.
Oak and tanoak decay rapidly,
but charred into charcoal,
they remain intact for eons.
A suckling pig raised leisurely dies late;
a fine horse climbing steep peaks perishes early.
Cold-adapted insects live doubled lifespans;
southern forests thrive in warmth.
Touched by killing frost, they wither;
bathed in warm sunlight, they flourish.
Though of the same category,
things thrive or decay differently—
how could there be fixed rules for autumn harvest
or winter storage?
Now human life,
its span of death and birth,
is less fragile than plants in cold weather,
yet the principles of prolonging life
and methods of restoration
are not merely the shallow benefit of warmth.
Why should the effect of longevity
be unattainable?
But worldly people cling to narrow habits,
deeming the path to immortality illusory,
calling the teachings of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ deceitful—
is this not regrettable?
If fools refuse to believe in herbal decoctions and acupuncture,
how much more would they doubt deeper truths?
They all say:
"If physicians like Yūfū, Biǎnquè, Hé, Huǎn, and Cānggōng
could surely cure illnesses,
why did they not avoid death?"
They also say:
"Wealthy families
surely lack no medical arts,
yet they die early—
this shows fate is natural."
To expect such people
to believe in transcendence
is like making oxen climb trees
or horses chase birds."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Minor elixirs like the Summoning Soul Pills
or modest medicines like Five Blossoms and Eight Minerals
can instantly melt solid ice
or enable floating on water,
sever ghostly influences,
ward off tigers and leopards,
dissolve accumulations in organs,
expel maladies from the vitals,
revive the suddenly dead from corpses,
recall startled souls from departure.
These are but ordinary medicines—
yet they can restore the dead to life.
How then could superior medicines
fail to make the living immortal?
Yuè Rén saved the Crown Prince of Guó from demise;
a northern physician revived Sū Wǔ after breath ceased;
Chúnyú Yī opened skulls to treat brains;
Huà Tuó cut abdomens to cleanse stomachs;
Wén Zhì delayed treatment to heal dire straits;
Zhòng Jǐng pierced chests to insert red cakes.
These mere techniques of physicians
achieve such feats—
how much more can the path of transcendence
accomplish anything?
Human death results from:
damage by desires,
aging,
harm by countless illnesses,
poisoning by toxins,
injury by evil energies,
assault by wind and cold.
Now through daoyin and breath control,
returning essence to nourish the brain,
moderate eating and drinking,
regulated activity and rest,
taking medicines,
visualizing spirits and guarding unity,
upholding precepts,
wearing talismans and seals,
and avoiding all life-injuring habits—
one may circumvent
these six harms.
Modern physicians have Kidney Qi Pills,
Internal Tonics for Five Networks Powder,
Bone-Filling Gǒuqǐ Decoction,
Huángqí Center-Fortifying Soup—
those who take them
become robust.
Lacquer Leaf and Green Flour,
common humble herbs,
were taken by Fán Ē,
who lived two hundred years,
remaining clear-eyed and sharp-eared,
still able to practice acupuncture.
This is recent fact,
recorded by reliable historians.
It is also said
one Wǔ Pǔ
learned the Five Animals Play from Huà Tuó,
using it instead of daoyin,
and lived over a hundred years.
Such superficial medicines and techniques
achieve this much—
how much more could their refined use accomplish?
If told that Lǐzhōng Sìshùn
can cure cholera,
Kuǎndōng and Zǐwǎn treat coughs,
Huánlú and Guànzhòng kill parasites,
Dāngguī and Sháoyào relieve colic,
Qínjiāo and Dúhuó expel winds,
Chāngpú and Gānjiāng alleviate damp paralysis,
Tùsī and Cōngróng replenish deficiency,
Gānsuì and Tínglì expel phlegm masses,
Guālóu and Huánglián heal diabetes,
Jìnǐ and Gāncǎo neutralize poisons,
Lúrú Yìrè mends wounds,
Máhuáng and Dàqīng treat cold damage—
worldly people still disbelieve,
preferring to kill for blessings
or consult yarrow stalks for curses,
rejecting good physicians' treatments
for shamans' confusion.
How then could they believe
in golden elixirs transcending mortality
or magic mushrooms prolonging life?
Formerly, Liúhóu Zhāng Liáng,
who devised unparalleled strategies,
whose wisdom was profound,
still believed immortality attainable.
His intelligence
surpassed ordinary people's,
yet he declared,
'I shall abandon human affairs
to wander with Chìsōng!'
He cultivated daoyin,
fasted from grains for a year,
planning ascension—
but Empress Lǚ coerced him,
seeking plans to secure the crown prince.
Compelled,
he devised the strategy inviting the Four Elders,
which succeeded as predicted.
Grateful, Empress Lǚ
forced him to eat,
thwarting his path.
According to Kǒng Ānguó's secret records,
Liáng obtained the immortality method from Huángshígōng,
not just military strategy.
It also says
Liáng studied under the Four Elders—
Lùlǐ Xiānshēng, Qǐlǐ Jì, and others—
all transcendents,
from whom he received divine formulas.
Though forced to eat by Empress Lǚ,
he later resumed cultivation,
secretly transcending the world—
unknown to people,
hence presumed dead.
Per Kǒng Ānguó's account,
Liáng achieved transcendence.
Also, Hàn chancellor Zhāng Cāng
chanced upon a minor technique:
sucking women's milk,
living 180 years.
This was a shallow method—
yet Cāng, practicing it,
tripled medium longevity.
How much more could complete methods
and secret marvels
fail to grant longevity?
This is recorded in the Book of Hàn,
not empty words.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Although taking medicine is the foundation of longevity,
if one can also practice breath control,
the benefits will be extremely rapid.
If one cannot obtain medicine,
but practices breath control to its fullest principle,
one can still live for several hundred years.
However, one should also know the arts of the bedchamber,
because if
one does not understand the techniques of yīn and yáng,
frequent labor and exhaustion
will make it difficult for breath control to be effective.
Humans reside within qì,
and qì resides within humans.
From heaven and earth to all things,
none can live without relying on qì.
Those skilled in breath control
use it internally to nourish the body,
and externally to ward off evils.
Yet ordinary people use it daily without knowing it.
In Wú and Yuè, there are methods of incantation and prohibition,
which have clear efficacy,
largely due to qì.
Those who know it can enter areas of great plague,
share a bed with the sick, and remain uninfected.
When traveling with dozens of companions,
all can be made fearless,
demonstrating that qì can ward off heavenly disasters.
Sometimes evil spirits or mountain sprites
invade households,
throwing tiles and stones at people,
or setting homes on fire.
Some appear visibly, coming and going,
while others are only heard in voice and speech.
But those skilled in prohibition can restrain them with qì,
causing them to cease immediately.
This shows qì can control ghosts and spirits.
Entering mountains and forests with venomous streams and vipers,
where ordinary people passing through briefly
are invariably harmed,
those skilled in prohibition can use qì to ward off dangers,
creating a safe area of several tens of lǐ,
ensuring companions remain unharmed.
They can also restrain tigers, leopards, snakes, and bees,
making them lie down unable to rise.
Using qì to prohibit metal wounds,
the bleeding stops instantly.
It can even reconnect bones and tendons.
Using qì to prohibit sharp blades,
one can tread on them unharmed,
or be stabbed without penetration.
If someone is bitten by a venomous snake,
using qì prohibition can cure them immediately.
In recent times, Zuǒ Cí and Zhào Míng, among others,
used qì to prohibit water,
causing it to flow backward one or two zhàng.
They also lit fires on thatched roofs,
cooked and ate food,
yet the thatch did not burn.
They drove large nails into pillars,
penetrating seven or eight inches,
then blew with qì,
and the nails shot out.
Using qì to prohibit boiling water,
they threw in about a hundred coins,
had someone reach in to stir and retrieve them,
and the hand was not scalded.
They prohibited water left in the courtyard overnight,
and despite severe cold, it did not freeze.
They could also prohibit all cooking within a lǐ from being completed.
And they prohibited dogs from barking.
Once, Wú sent General Hè to suppress mountain bandits,
among whom were skilled prohibitors.
Whenever battles ensued,
the government troops' swords could not be drawn,
and arrows from bows and crossbows turned back,
leading to repeated defeats.
General Hè, wise and resourceful,
said,
"I've heard that metal with edges can be prohibited,
and insects with venom can be prohibited.
But things without edges
or non-venomous insects
cannot be prohibited.
Since they can prohibit our weapons,
they surely cannot prohibit edgeless objects."
So he had many sturdy wooden clubs made,
selected five thousand strong elite soldiers as vanguards,
and they all attacked the bandits with clubs.
The bandits, relying on their prohibitors,
were completely unprepared,
and the government troops struck them with white clubs,
crushing the bandits.
The prohibitions indeed ceased to work,
and those killed
numbered in the tens of thousands.
Qì emanates from the body,
and its effects can reach such extents;
why doubt it can eliminate hunger, cure illnesses,
prolong life, and nurture nature?
Zhòngcháng Gōnglǐ,
a man of great talent and insight,
wrote in Chāngyán,
also discussing how "practicing qì can prevent hunger and illness."
He said, "Initially, I did not believe it,
but upon practicing it,
found it to be entirely true.
Methods of nurturing life,
as simple as this,
yet I have not mastered them—
is it not because my mind is preoccupied with worldly affairs,
and my thoughts sharpened by human matters?
Others who cannot do it
surely share this same ailment with me.
In the past, there was a wise teacher
who knew the way to immortality.
The ruler of Yān sent someone to learn from him,
but before succeeding, the teacher died.
The ruler was angry at his envoy,
intending to execute him.
An advisor said,
'What we fear most is death,
and what we value most is life.
Since he lost his own life,
how could he make our lord immortal?'
The ruler then did not execute him.
This advice was indeed sound.
Had he possessed an immortal method,
like the breath control I've heard of,
then the one who spoke of the teacher's death
might not have been unaware of the way,
but simply unable to abandon worldly affairs to practice it.
Thus, even knowing it was of no benefit—
it's not that there is no method for immortality.'"
He also said:
"In Mì County, Hénán,
there was a Bǔ Chéng,
who studied the Dào for a long time,
then bid his family farewell and left.
At first, his steps rose slightly higher,
until he entered the clouds and was seen no more.
This is what is called lifting the form in light flight,
ascending to heaven in broad daylight—
the highest form of immortality."
Chén Yuánfāng and Hán Yuáncháng,
both eminent scholars of Yǐngchuān,
close to Mì County,
the reason these two gentlemen believed in the existence of immortals in the world
was that their fathers and grandfathers had witnessed Bǔ Chéng achieving immortality and ascending to heaven.
This is yet another proof of immortality.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I have heard that those who share the same path and accord
understand without words, and trust is evident;
those whose paths differ and pursuits vary,
even with sincere advice, will be doubted.
For common, close-at-hand principles,
trivial matters of human choice,
where sinking and floating differ more than metal and feathers,
and black and white are distinct as ink and powder,
yet those holding doubts
often still cannot discern them.
How much more, then, when speaking of what lies beyond worldly ways,
showing them the most subtle truths—
they laugh loudly,
a response that has long existed,
not just today!
Where clarity reaches,
even in the dark obscurity of deepest night,
or objects as fine as a hair's tip,
it does not find them hard to see.
But where it does not reach,
even the blazing brilliance of sun and moon in the sky,
or the towering heights of Sōng and Dài mountains piercing the clouds,
cannot be perceived.
The Mysterious Sages Huángdì and Lǎozǐ,
with profound insight and unique vision,
revealed secret texts in famous mountains,
received immortal scriptures from divine beings,
shook off dust to cast aside burdens,
soared high into the vast beyond.
Metal and stone cannot match their firmness,
tortoises and cranes cannot equal their longevity.
Mindful of those with aspirations for the future,
pitying believers who lack guidance,
they handed down methods,
brilliantly clear and evident.
Small practice brings small gains,
great effort yields great results.
Yet those with shallow views,
clinging to their narrow ways,
are content with bitter weeds unaware of sweet honey,
drunk on thin wine unappreciative of rich brew.
They know to cherish life but not the way to nurture it,
fear death but disbelieve in methods to avoid it,
recognize that overeating stores up illness,
yet cannot restrain rich flavors in their mouths.
They know that excessive passions and desires lead to decay,
but cannot cut off their cherished desires.
Though I speak of the attainability of immortality,
how can I make them believe?"
Someone objected, saying:
"You possess no physique interwoven with the patterns of the Way,
no extraordinary features or penetrating bones,
your years do not match the long-lived Ānqī or Péng Zǔ,
your eyes have never beheld transcendent beings,
your ears have not exclusively heard extraordinary teachings—
how can you know that eternal life is attainable,
or that nurturing one's nature has verifiable proof?
If you claim to comprehend mysteries through mental attainment,
or operate transcendent insight through unique vision,
this I dare not accept.
When one lacks clothing to cover their skin,
or resources to plan for the evening,
yet speaks highly of Táo Zhū's methods,
equating themselves with Yī Dùn's strategies,
they invite ridicule from critics—
this is inevitable.
To cling to chronic illness while discussing Jīng Hé and Qūe's skills,
or repeatedly flee battles while claiming mastery of Sūn and Wú's calculations—
people disbelieve
because there is no evidence of efficacy."
I replied:
"The tiny fish swimming in a puddle
believes the world holds no vast oceans.
The worm twisting within a fruit pit
thinks the eight directions end at its edges.
Though told of boundless expanses,
or spoken to of the cosmos' immensity,
they dismiss it as empty talk
and refuse to believe.
Had my eyes square pupils,
or ears sprouting from my crown,
I would already ride flying dragons and mount auspicious clouds,
ascend flowing lightning and reach the inverted light—
how then could you question me?
If you saw me thus,
you'd call me a celestial deity, earthly spirit, or strange creature,
never attributing it to study's achievement.
I merely guide fellow seekers with prior understanding,
not forcing you and your kind
to believe.
If every household had transcendents,
visible everywhere and shoulder to shoulder,
even your obscured vision
would harbor no doubt.
But when those masters achieve the Way,
they tread azure skies and roam purple poles,
beyond ordinary perception—
none see or hear them,
so you deem them nonexistent.
People trust their assumptions,
rely on shortsighted views,
deem their judgments
flawless,
accustomed to the ordinary,
suspicious of the rare.
Though ear-pulled and palm-pointed,
they never awaken—
this persists from antiquity,
not merely today."
Someone said:
"Repeatedly hearing your wise words
leaves me no doubt about transcendence's existence,
but I still doubt my own capability.
Might I ask if there are essential methods
practicable alone?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"All Dao learning should progress from shallow to deep,
easy to difficult.
Sincere resolve and firm determination
overcome all obstacles;
doubt yields no merit—
this holds universally.
Roots not piercing earth
cannot yield cloud-touching branches;
sources not profoundly deep
cannot produce flowing streams reaching miles—
this never occurs.
Thus, without accumulated goodness and hidden virtue,
one cannot move divine spirits;
without genuine sincerity,
one cannot bond with teachers and friends;
without merit and labor,
one cannot discuss great trials.
Seeking essential methods without enlightened teachers
is impossible.
The Nine Elixirs and Golden Liquor
are paramount for transcendence,
but they require great effort and expense,
not swiftly accomplished.
Preserving essence and cherishing qì
are most urgent,
supplemented by minor medicines to prolong life
and learning basic techniques to ward off evils—
thus one gradually approaches refinement."
Someone asked:
"Techniques are numerous
and hard to master completely.
Besides the golden elixirs,
what others are worth cultivating?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Without obtaining the supreme essentials,
one must broadly know the minor ones,
for diverse methods collectively achieve longevity.
Broadly speaking,
like rulers governing states:
civil, military, rites, laws—
all are indispensable.
Narrowly speaking,
like artisans making carts:
shafts, crossbars, axles, pins—
none can be lacking.
Techniques involve
internally cultivating form and spirit
to prolong life and heal illnesses,
externally repelling evils
to keep harm at bay.
Compared to lutes:
a single string cannot produce all notes;
compared to armor:
one plate cannot block sharp blades.
Why?
All notes combined are indispensable,
as are plates where blades strike.
All nurturing life
should widely learn and grasp essentials,
broadly observe and skillfully choose.
Cultivating one thing exclusively
offers unreliable support.
Worse are enthusiastic dilettantes
over-relying on their specialties:
those knowing Xuánsù techniques
claim only bedroom arts
enable transcendence;
those understanding exhalation-inhalation
say only breath control prolongs life;
those knowing bending-stretching methods
declare only gymnastics prevents aging;
those knowing herbal formulas
insist only medicines ensure endless life.
Dao learning fails
through such one-sidedness.
Shortsighted individuals,
occasionally knowing one thing,
claim sufficiency,
while unrecognized genuines,
though obtaining good methods,
endlessly seek more,
wasting effort and time
with applications
lacking fixed intent—
both err.
Some, inherently dull-witted,
with shallow knowledge,
forcefully enter famous mountains,
braving venomous stings,
repeatedly injured,
ashamed to return.
Some get eaten by tigers or wolves,
slain by specters,
starve without grain-abstention methods,
freeze without self-warming techniques,
dying in ravines—
is this not foolish?
Diligent study surpasses not teacher selection.
If teachers' knowledge is narrow
and teaching incomplete,
they claim
Dao cultivation requires little.
'Requires little'
means possessing golden elixir essentials
obviates other methods.
But these are extremely rare;
why await uncertain great matters
while neglecting beneficial minor techniques?
Like managing a household:
claiming no need for other goods
presumes gold, silver, pearls, jade
held in hands or bosom,
sufficient for generations.
Without these,
how can one not broadly sow grains
and store abundant fruits and vegetables?
Thus, grain abstention, weapon avoidance,
ghost subjugation,
poison resistance,
illness healing,
mountain entry safeguarding from beasts,
water crossing protecting from dragons,
plague traversal without fear,
crisis evasion through invisibility—
these are minor matters
yet must be known.
How much more
should one learn beyond these?"
Someone asked:
"May I ask what taboos one must observe when cultivating the way of longevity?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"The most urgent taboos
lie in avoiding harm and injury.
According to the Inner Admonitions of the Yi, the Classic of Chìsōngzǐ, and the River Chart Record of Destiny Talisman,
heaven and earth have deities overseeing faults,
who, based on the severity of one's transgressions,
deduct from one's allotted lifespan.
When lifespan is reduced, one becomes poor, suffers decline and illness,
frequently encounters worries and troubles,
and when the lifespan is exhausted, one dies.
There are several hundred matters that warrant deduction of lifespan,
too numerous to discuss in detail.
It is also said that there are three corpse worms in the body,
and these three corpse worms,
though formless, are actually a type of soul, spirit, or ghost.
They desire to make humans die early,
so these corpse worms can become ghosts,
freely indulging and wandering,
enjoying human offerings and libations.
Therefore, every Gēngshēn day,
they ascend to heaven to report to the Director of Fate,
detailing human transgressions.
Also, on the night of the new moon,
the hearth god ascends to report human offenses.
Major offenses lead to the deduction of a jì.
A jì
is three hundred days.
Minor offenses lead to the deduction of a suàn.
A suàn
is three days.
I too cannot verify the truth of these matters.
However, the way of heaven is vast and distant,
and the ways of ghosts and spirits are hard to comprehend.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ and Qín Mùgōng both personally received golden edicts from the Supreme Deity,
clear evidence of their territories.
Mountains, rivers, plants, and trees,
wells, hearths, ponds, and marshes,
all possess essence and energy;
within the human body,
there are also hun and pò souls;
how much more so for heaven and earth, the greatest of all things,
should logically have spirits and intelligence.
Having spirits and intelligence, they should reward good and punish evil,
but their system is vast and the net is wide,
not necessarily responding immediately like a triggered mechanism.
Yet, reviewing various Taoist admonitions,
all state that those seeking longevity
must accumulate good deeds and perform meritorious acts,
be compassionate towards all things,
extend forgiveness from oneself to others,
extend benevolence even to insects,
rejoice in others' good fortune,
sympathize with others' suffering,
relieve others' emergencies,
rescue others from poverty,
not harm life with one's hands,
not incite disaster with one's mouth,
see others' gains as one's own gains,
see others' losses as one's own losses,
not exalt oneself,
not praise oneself,
not envy those better than oneself,
not flatter, be hypocritical, or secretly malicious,
only thus can one be considered virtuous,
receiving blessings from heaven,
ensuring success in all endeavors,
and making the pursuit of immortality achievable.
If one hates goodness and enjoys killing,
says yes but means no,
speaks differently behind others' backs,
opposes and perverts integrity,
cruelly mistreats subordinates,
deceives superiors,
betrays one's duties,
feels no gratitude for kindness received,
manipulates laws and accepts bribes,
indulges the crooked and wrongs the upright,
abandons public duty for private gain,
punishes the innocent,
ruins others' families,
seizes others' treasures,
harms others' bodies,
usurps others' positions,
suppresses the worthy,
slays those who surrender,
slanders immortal sages,
injures Taoist priests,
shoots flying birds with arrows,
cut open wombs and break eggs,
hunt with fire in spring and summer,
curse the spirits,
teach others to do evil,
conceal others' goodness,
endanger others for self-preservation,
claim others' achievements as one's own,
ruin others' good endeavors,
seize what others love,
separate flesh and blood,
humiliate others to win,
take full coins owed,
repay with shortchanged coins,
release floods or set fires,
use sorcery to harm people,
coerce the weak and frail,
exchange good for bad,
forcibly take or demand,
plunder to become rich,
act unjustly and unfairly,
be licentious and depraved,
bully orphans and oppress widows,
take lost items or accepted gifts,
cheat, deceive, and swindle,
enjoy gossiping about private matters,
hold onto others' shortcomings,
drag heaven and earth into affairs,
seek justice through curses,
borrow without returning,
exchange or loan without repayment,
have insatiable desires,
detest and reject loyalty and honesty,
disobey superiors' orders,
disrespect one's teachers,
mock others for doing good,
destroy others' crops,
damage others' utensils,
deprive others of their use,
serve others unclean food or drink,
use light weights and small measures,
narrow cloth and short lengths,
mix false with genuine,
seek profit through fraud,
lure others to take things,
step over wells or across hearths,
sing on the last day of the month or cry on the first.
Each such act
constitutes one offense,
and according to the severity of the matter,
the Director of Fate deducts suàn or jì from one's lifespan,
and when the suàn is exhausted, one dies.
Even having evil intentions without evil actions leads to deduction of suàn,
while committing evil deeds that harm others leads to deduction of jì.
If one dies before the suàn or jì is exhausted,
the misfortune will extend to their descendants.
Those who forcibly seize others' property
may have it accounted against their wives, children, and household,
leading to deaths
though not necessarily immediate.
If their evil deeds are insufficient to kill their family,
they will eventually encounter floods, fires, robbery, or theft,
or lose possessions,
or face government troubles or illnesses,
incurring medical expenses,
or costs for cooking sacrifices and offerings,
ensuring they pay fully for what they took.
Thus, the Taoist saying: those who wrongfully kill
will be killed in turn by weaponry.
Taking ill-gotten wealth,
regardless of resentment caused,
is like satisfying hunger with poisoned meat,
or quenching thirst with poisoned wine:
though briefly full, death follows.
For those who have committed evil deeds
but later repent,
if they have wrongfully killed,
they should seek to save those doomed to die to atone.
If they have taken others' property unjustly,
they should give to the poor to atone.
If they have falsely accused others,
they should recommend worthy individuals to atone.
All such acts must be doubled in goodness
to receive auspicious outcomes,
turning calamity into blessing.
If one can avoid all transgressions,
longevity is assured,
and the path to Taoist practice is swift.
Heaven is high yet hears the lowly,
and nothing escapes its notice.
Persist in doing good without slackening,
and you will surely receive auspicious reward.
Yáng Gōng accumulated virtue and gave alms,
continuing until his hair turned white,
and then received gold sent from heaven.
Cài Shùn was extremely filial,
and moved the spirits to respond.
Guō Jù killed his son for his parent,
and received the heavy reward of an iron pledge.
Yet good deeds are hard to do,
while evil deeds are easy to commit,
and foolish people point to Xiàng Tuó and Bó Niú
to claim heaven and earth cannot distinguish good from bad,
not knowing that those with outward fame
may lack inner virtue,
and open praise cannot absolve hidden sins.
If one doubts the great energy of yīn and yáng
based on the life and death of shepherd's purse or wheat,
one cannot grasp the profound.
This is why the highest scholars strive diligently merely to avoid offense,
This is why ordinary people fail to attain their desires. "
Someone asked:
"Before achieving moral integrity,
and without retreating to renowned mountains,
while the world differs from antiquity,
with thieves and robbers rampant,
how can one ward off daily calamities,
and guard against unforeseen disasters?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Regularly on Zhí days,
take earth from the Liùguǐ direction,
mix it with leaves of various fragrant herbs,
and plaster it on a square foot of your door—
then thieves will not come.
Alternatively, take earth from the south gate of the market,
earth from the Suìpò direction,
and earth from the Yuèjiàn direction,
combine and shape them into a human figure,
place it in the Vermilion Bird's position—
this also suppresses thieves.
In emergencies, enter a 'living ground' and stay—
then there will be no harm.
The world has living grounds,
a province has living grounds,
a commandery has living grounds,
a county has living grounds,
a township has living grounds,
a village has living grounds,
a residence has living grounds,
a room has living grounds."
Someone asked:
"A single room having a living ground—
isn't that too confined?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"The classics say,
in the utmost urgency,
hide beneath the chariot rail.
Thus,
within a single chariot,
there is also a living ground—
how much more so in a room?"
Someone asked:
"I've heard that to seek the way of longevity,
one should know of two mountains.
Unclear about these mountains,
where might they be located?
I hope for your enlightening words,
to dispel my confusion."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"They exist,
but not Huà or Huò,
nor Sōng or Dài.
The Mountain of Great Mystery,
hard to know but easy to seek,
neither heavenly nor earthly,
neither sinking nor floating,
perilous and remote,
towering and rugged,
harmonious energy coalescing,
divine intent roaming freely,
jade wells deep and profound,
irrigating ceaselessly,
a hundred twenty offices,
departments interconnected,
Lí and Kǎn positions aligned,
myriad dark mushrooms growing,
vermilion trees uniquely born,
their treasures all extraordinary,
gold and jade piled high,
sweet springs emerging from corners,
youth-renewing adepts,
draw from its clear streams—
if you can cultivate this,
you may rival Qiáo and Sōng—
this is the first mountain.
The Mountain of Long Valley,
vast and majestic,
mysterious qi drifting,
jade dew drizzling,
golden ponds and purple chambers,
nestled in its curves,
fools recklessly venture there,
only to return dead,
but those with the Way,
ascend without decline,
gather and consume huángjīng,
to achieve celestial flight—
this is the second mountain.
Both were secrets of ancient sages,
ponder them deeply."
Someone asked:
"I wish to hear about the methods for true humans to guard the body and refine the form."
Bàopúzǐ said:
Profound is your question.
Beneath the azure beginning, the moon and sun,
two halves rising together merge into one.
Emerging from that jade pond, entering the golden chamber,
large as a pellet, yellow as an orange,
within it a fine flavor sweet as honey,
if you obtain it, guard it well, do not lose it.
Once gone, it cannot be chased, the body will perish,
the pure white qi arrives subtle and dense,
ascending through the dark pass in three twists,
the central elixir radiant, peerless,
established at the gate of life, the form does not perish,
so profound and wondrous, hard to fully describe.
This is the oral teaching of the former masters—
those who know it fear not myriad ghosts nor five weapons."
Someone asked:
"I've heard that those who master the arts of the bedchamber
can attain immortality through this alone,
and also reverse disasters, absolve sins,
turn misfortune into blessing,
gain promotion in office,
double profits in trade—
is this true?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"These are all exaggerated, deluded words from shamanistic texts,
embellished by enthusiasts,
leading to inaccuracy.
Some are falsehoods fabricated by deceit,
to mislead the world,
concealing the true methods,
to attract followers,
gathering disciples
for worldly gain.
The arts of yin and yang,
at best, can cure minor ailments,
or prevent wasteful depletion.
Their principle has limits—
how can they bring immortality, avert calamity, or invite blessing?
Humans should not abstain from yin-yang union,
lest they incur illness.
But if indulging desires without restraint,
failing to regulate and express,
then life is shortened.
Those skilled in the art
can reverse the 'running horse' to nourish the brain,
return the yin elixir to redden the intestines,
gather jade dew from the golden pond,
draw the three fives to the splendid bridge,
keeping one beautiful in old age,
fulfilling one's natural lifespan.
Commoners hear that Huángdì ascended with 1,200 women,
and claim he achieved longevity solely through this,
not knowing he refined the nine elixirs
below Jīngshān,
above Dǐnghú,
and only then rode a dragon to heaven.
Huángdì may have had 1,200 women,
but that wasn't the sole means.
Even with a thousand medicines
and the nurture of three sacrifices,
without knowing the bedchamber arts,
there's little benefit.
Thus, the ancients, fearing reckless indulgence,
praised it in rhetoric—
but it shouldn't be fully believed.
Xuánsù compares it to water and fire:
water and fire can kill,
yet also give life—
it depends on whether one can use them.
Generally, knowing the essential method,
more women are better;
but without knowing the way,
even one or two can hasten death.
Péngzǔ's method is the most essential.
Other texts are laborious and hard to practice,
with benefits not matching their claims.
Few can accomplish them.
The oral teachings span thousands of words.
Those ignorant of them,
even taking hundreds of medicines,
cannot attain longevity."
Someone asked:
"The August Heaven is supremely divine,
and should bestow fate equally.
Why then do ordinary men like Qiáo and Sōng receive the lifespan of immortality,
while great sages like Zhōu and Kǒng lack the blessing of long life?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"The length of one's life
is truly determined by what one encounters.
Receiving vital energy and forming the embryo,
each is associated with specific constellations.
The Way of Heaven is non-action,
letting things follow their natural course,
showing neither intimacy nor alienation,
neither that nor this.
If one's fate is linked to the star of life,
then such a person will inevitably be fond of the Way of Immortality.
Those fond of the Way of Immortality,
will surely attain it through seeking.
If one's fate is linked to the star of death,
then such a person will not believe in the Way of Immortality.
Not believing in the Way of Immortality,
they will not cultivate its practices.
What one delights in and what one rejects,
are determined by what one has received,
to change, give, or take away,
is not within Heaven's power.
It is like metals and stones melting in the furnace,
or earthenware being shaped in the kiln;
although they are formed by these processes,
the sharpness or dullness of the copper and iron,
the straightness or crookedness of the pots and jars,
are matters of chance encounter,
and not again the affair of the furnace or kiln."
The person objected:
"The fine craftsman's creations,
all come from his hand.
The divine intelligence of Heaven,
what can it not do?
Yet you say that each person's life is determined by what they encounter,
and not crafted by that vast blue sky.
I am deeply perplexed by this,
and dare not accept it."
Bàopǔzǐ answered:
"When chaos divided and separated,
clarity and turbidity were displayed;
some rose and moved,
some descended and were still.
Even Heaven and Earth do not know the reason for this.
All things receive energy,
and also occur naturally.
They, along with Heaven and Earth,
are each a separate entity,
only their formation has sequence,
and their bodies have size.
Because of the greatness of Heaven and Earth,
we perceive the smallness of all things.
Because of the smallness of all things,
we perceive the greatness of Heaven and Earth.
Moreover, although the belly and back enclose the five organs,
the five organs are not made by the belly and back.
Although the skin and flesh wrap the blood and energy,
the blood and energy are not created by the skin and flesh.
Although Heaven and Earth contain all things,
all things are not made by Heaven and Earth.
It is like plants and trees relying on mountains and forests to sprout and flourish,
yet the mountains and forests have no deliberate action in it.
Fish and turtles depend on waters and marshes to reproduce and nurture,
yet the waters and marshes have no deliberate action in it.
Common people see the greatness of Heaven and Earth,
and the smallness of all things,
and therefore say that Heaven and Earth are the parents of all things,
and all things are the children and grandchildren of Heaven and Earth.
Now, lice are born from me,
but are they made by me?
Thus, without me, lice would not be born,
yet I am not the parent of the lice,
nor are the lice my children and grandchildren.
The midges bred in vinegar,
the mushrooms produced on wood and stone,
the larvae multiplying in filth and stagnation,
the green vines flourishing on pine branches—
these are not crafted by those four things.
All things fill the space between Heaven and Earth;
how is this any different?
Heaven has its sun, moon, cold, and heat;
humans have their sight, hearing, and breath.
Using the distant to infer the near,
using this to deduce that,
if humans cannot understand why their own bodies age, feel pain, or itch,
then that Heaven also cannot understand why its body expands, contracts, or has calamities and auspices;
if humans cannot make their ears and eyes always sharp and clear,
or their vitality and defense unceasing and unobstructed,
then Heaven also cannot make the sun and moon free from eclipses,
or the four seasons from losing their order.
From this we argue,
the matter of great longevity,
truly does not lie with Heaven and Earth.
Becoming an immortal or not,
is decisively a matter of what one encounters, not [Heaven's doing].
The one who sires me is my father,
the one who bears me is my mother.
Yet even they cannot ensure that my physical form is necessarily well-proportioned,
my appearance necessarily enchanting and beautiful,
my nature and disposition necessarily peaceful and harmonious,
my wisdom necessarily profound and far-reaching,
much less increase my strength,
or extend my years and life.
Instead, some are short and ugly, frail and weak,
some are swarthy and foul,
some deaf, blind, stubborn, or foolish,
some crippled, hunchbacked, or lame.
What one obtains is not what one desires,
what one desires is not what one obtains.
How much more so with the vast and expansive Heaven and Earth?
Parents are still closer [than Heaven and Earth].
I myself possess a body,
yet cannot make it forever strong and never aging,
always healthy and never ill,
my joy and anger never misplaced,
my plans and thoughts free from regret.
Thus, those who impart the energy and shape the form are the parents,
but the one who receives and possesses it is my own self.
Beyond this, none is more intimate than this relation,
none has more control than this.
Since these two cannot add to or subtract from me,
how could Heaven and Earth possibly know or intervene?
If indeed all people and things were made by Heaven and Earth,
then they should all be good without evil,
all successful without failure.
All living beings would belong to fulfilled kinds,
and there would be no spring withering sorrow for the catalpa and poplar!
You cite that Heaven could not give Zhōu and Kǒng the blessing of transcending the world;
this further shows that what one receives is natural,
not apportioned by Heaven and Earth.
Sagehood as a virtue,
is the ultimate of virtue.
If Heaven could endow them with the ultimate virtue,
yet caused their knowledge to be incomplete,
their achievements unestablished,
their positions not kingly or hegemon-like,
their lifespans not reaching a hundred years—
this is evidence that Heaven does not act deliberately.
The death of a sage
is not caused by Heaven's killing,
just as the birth of a sage
is not caused by Heaven's endorsement.
The worthy do not necessarily live long,
the foolish do not necessarily die young.
Goodness does not necessarily bring immediate fortune,
evil does not necessarily bring immediate disaster.
Life has no fixed year,
death has no constant lot.
A person of great virtue and wisdom
may blossom but bear no fruit.
A commoner like Dù Gōng
lived nearly two hundred years.
Bóniú was afflicted with disease,
Zǐxià lost his eyesight.
The utterly wicked Dào Zhí lived to old age with white hair,
the extremely evil Zhuāng Qiāo aged with yellowed locks.
Heaven's non-action
is clearly evident in this."
Someone said:
"Confucius stated that since ancient times all must die,
while Lǎozǐ claimed immortality can be attained through cultivation.
The sage's words,
are credible and evidence-based,
whereas Daoist teachings,
are extravagant and impractical."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Confucius,
is the sage of Confucianism;
Lǎozǐ,
is the sage who attained the Dào.
Confucianism is accessible and easily understood,
hence it has numerous followers.
The essence of Dào is profound and difficult to comprehend,
thus few achieve mastery of it.
The Dào
is the source of all diversity.
Confucianism
is the stream flowing from pure simplicity.
Before the Three Sovereigns,
the world was governed by the Dào.
Since the era of emperors and kings,
Confucianism has prevailed.
Discussants all recognize the淳朴 of ancient times,
while disparaging the frivolity of recent customs,
so why exclusively esteem Confucius and belittle Lǎozǐ?
This is like admiring flowers and foliage at the treetop
while ignoring the roots from which they grow.
How does this differ from valuing bright pearls while despising the deep pool,
cherishing the Héshì Bì while detesting Jīngshān,
not realizing that the deep pool
is where bright pearls originate,
and Jīngshān
is where the Héshì Bì was born?
Moreover, nurturing life
is but a byproduct of the Dào;
rituals and music
are the periphery of Confucianism.
The reason for valuing Confucianism
lies in its ability to transform customs and morals,
not merely in bowing and ceremonial movements.
The reason for honoring the Dào
is its transformative power without words,
not solely the matter of life cultivation.
If Confucianism and Daoism indeed have precedence,
then one cannot exclusively trust Confucius,
nor solely apply Lǎozǐ.
Since Confucius respectfully inquired of Bóyáng,
and expressed desire to compare himself to Lǎo Péng.
He also admitted to knowing fish and birds but not recognizing dragons,
metaphorically comparing Lǎozǐ to a dragon—
this clearly expresses his heartfelt admiration,
not empty words.
This is no different from
what Yán Huí described:
'Looked for it in front,
suddenly it appears behind;
the deeper you drill, the harder it becomes;
the higher you gaze, the more lofty it appears.'"
Someone asked:
"Since Confucius personally met Lǎozǐ, why didn't he follow him to learn the Dào?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"From this perspective,
it becomes clearer that endowed nature determines one's destiny,
and inherent inclinations are difficult to change.
Confucius recognized Lǎozǐ's profound mystery and rare excellence,
yet couldn't embrace the clarity and emptiness,
the fundamental principles and great essence,
that transcend form,
and enter the realm of ultimate Dào.
What he sought and received
was limited to worldly affairs only—
how could he pursue methods of immortality?
Considering his earnest intentions,
wholly dedicated to education and transformation,
he didn't concern himself with esoteric arts.
Though sagely in worldly matters,
Confucius couldn't achieve profound tranquility and mystical silence,
nor maintain self-preservation through non-action.
Thus Lǎozǐ admonished him:
'A skilled merchant hides his treasures as if possessing nothing;
a gentleman of great virtue appears simple as if foolish.
Rid yourself of arrogance and excessive desires,
pretentious manners and ambitious aspirations—
these are of no benefit to your person.'
This sufficiently shows Confucius wasn't free from worldly sentiments,
and wasn't suited for immortality cultivation.
Restlessly active,
striving to rectify the times,
gazing upward lamenting the phoenix's cry,
looking downward sighing over the bitter gourd,
anxious his worth might go unrecognized,
passionately wishing to serve even as a guard—
how would he willingly abandon his world-saving endeavors
to practice the impractical art of life cultivation?"
Another asked:
"Between Confucian and Daoist pursuits,
which is more difficult?"
Bàopúzǐ answered:
"Confucianism
is difficulty within ease.
Daoism
is ease within difficulty.
Abandoning social connections,
leaving behind wife and children,
renouncing fame and reputation,
sacrificing benefits and salaries,
depriving the eyes of dazzling sights,
restraining the ears from melodious sounds,
maintaining tranquil contentment and quiet withdrawal,
self-preservation through solitary goodness,
unmoved by slander when it comes,
unelated by praise when received,
unattracted when seeing nobility,
unashamed when dwelling in poverty—
this is the difficulty of Daoism.
No expectations of celebratory or condolence visits when going out,
no burden of caring for others when staying in,
no mental exertion on the Seven Classics,
no contemplation on calendrical calculations,
no suffering from astronomical computations,
no servitude to literary arts,
with numerous troubles reduced,
harmonious energy naturally increases,
acting through non-action, worrying not,
neither fearful nor apprehensive—
this is the ease of Daoism,
what's called ease within difficulty.
What Confucians cultivate
follows established precedents,
with principles for engagement and withdrawal,
speech and silence according to circumstances,
teachers readily found neighborhood by neighborhood,
books explained through commentaries resolving doubts—
this is the ease of Confucianism.
Delving into profundities and reaching distant truths,
mastering intricate classical texts,
comprehending the vastness of Hé-Tú and Luò-Shū writings,
mastering the myriad sayings of hundreds of schools,
accumulating virtue in humble alleys,
exhausting loyalty in serving rulers,
mentally engaging with celestial phenomena above,
contemplating wind and clouds below,
one matter unknown
renders actions unreasonable,
a single phrase improper
causes praise and blame indistinguishable,
every step becoming society's standard,
every word transmitted throughout the land—
this is the difficulty of Confucianism,
what's called difficulty within ease.
Judging both thoroughly,
Confucian practice involves more difficulties,
Daoist practice is simpler and easier.
I find the difficulties troublesome,
thus will abandon them for the easier path.
Those in the world who criticize me
are everywhere, shoulder to shoulder.
Those who can share profound understanding
I have yet to encounter.
But if like-minded people
must exist in the future,
then I wouldn't call this hope entirely rare."
Someone said:
"I have observed renowned individuals of high standing,
erudite scholars of vast learning,
who indeed exhaustively investigated principles and human nature,
and thoroughly examined the existence [of various phenomena]. There were many such individuals,
yet none ever claimed that lifespan could be extended,
or that immortality could be attained.
Your wisdom cannot compare with the sun and moon,
your thoughts cannot surpass those of ten thousand men,
yet you claim to possess the way of longevity -
this I dare not believe."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"I am but an ordinary man of modest talent,
with shallow insight and limited knowledge -
how dare I presume to consider myself exceptional with unique understanding,
or superior to all others in the world?
However, I have sought the hidden through the manifest,
and obtained the difficult through the easy.
By examining small verifications,
one can know the great effects;
by observing what has already occurred,
one can understand what has not yet been tested.
Moreover, those in the world who don't believe immortals exist between heaven and earth,
are unwilling to investigate.
They generally possess conventional talents,
skills suitable for official positions,
and have read classical texts and instructional books.
Using these to assess human affairs that are simple and easy,
and to distinguish what confuses ordinary people,
they assume that whatever doubts the masses have,
they alone can resolve;
that omens not yet apparent,
they can foresee.
Thus they believe they completely understand
the nature of all things,
and that nothing in the obscure and mysterious realms
eludes their comprehension.
If they claim there are no immortals,
then immortals certainly don't exist -
so firmly have they always held this view.
I often see vulgar Confucians, mediocre and commonplace,
who stubbornly cling to their ways and disbelieve profound matters -
their problem lies in possessing some intelligence,
yet being biased, rigid, and constrained,
burdened by their petty cleverness.
They refuse to be like those who are completely ignorant
and cannot even distinguish beans from wheat.
To view things through a narrow perspective like looking through a tube,
and then obstinately block what their intelligence cannot reach -
how is this different from using a short rope
to draw water from a well a hundred ren deep,
not realizing the rope is too short,
and then claiming the well has no water?
Common people hear the sound of fierce wind and fierce fire,
and say it's winter thunder from heaven;
they see clouds drifting west,
and say the moon is speeding east.
Even when others tell them [the truth],
they never awaken to belief -
this is because they excessively trust themselves.
Those who listen to sounds
all trust their own ears;
those who observe forms
all trust their own eyes.
Yet sometimes what people hear and see
appears true but is actually false.
If so, then our ears and eyes
are indeed not completely trustworthy.
How much more so with what the mind contemplates -
formless and soundless,
much harder to discern than sight and hearing.
Yet to insist on the most remote matters in the world
based solely on one's own mental conceptions,
declaring that divine immortals are mere fiction -
isn't this being blinded?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Beauty and ugliness are determined,
yet love and hate differ according to feelings,
so two eyes may not see alike.
Elegant and vulgar music have their inherent qualities,
yet likes and dislikes vary,
so two ears may not hear alike.
Truth and falsehood have their substance,
yet approaches and rejections contradict,
so two minds may not deliberate alike.
Some take ugliness for beauty,
some take turbidity for clarity,
some take loss for gain.
These three contradictions
are clearly recognizable -
so easily apparent,
yet ultimately these opposing views cannot be unified.
How much more so with the matter of divine immortals,
the most subtle of matters -
to expect everyone to believe in it
follows no reasonable principle.
If everyone could be made to understand,
what value would there be in the enlightened?
To wait for vulgar people to cease their deluded talk
would be like waiting for the Yellow River to run clear -
this would not take long!
The reason I cannot remain silent
is my hope that those who can go either way
might be guided and influenced.
As for those who cannot be moved,
the ancients already found no way to deal with them."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"That the ultimate truth is not easily understood,
and divine immortals are not readily believed -
this has been so for a long time,
how could it be only today?
The highest beings know this naturally,
the next level understand after being told,
but as for those who laugh loudly upon hearing it -
such people are everywhere.
In discussing this matter,
will I face the regret of many failures,
the fault of improper speech?
When things find no support,
then harm inevitably comes.
For abundant yang cannot make withered wood flourish,
divine intelligence cannot change stubborn natures set in their ways.
Zǐgòng could not please the rustic who captured horses,
