Gǔgōng could not dissuade the Róng and Dí tribes from wanting land.
Sometimes true principles cannot penetrate,
good words cannot prevail.
Ceremonial caps cannot be sold in Mán and Yuè lands,
red ceremonial shoes are not used by barefoot barbarians -
how can one force this?
To see jade and call it stone
doesn't mean the jade is not genuine -
it awaits a Hé Shì to recognize it.
To see a dragon and name it snake
doesn't mean the dragon lacks divinity -
it requires a Cài Mò to distinguish it.
The reason the Dào is valued
is that nothing can be added to enhance it,
and nothing can be taken away to diminish it.
The reason virtue is valued
is that hearing slander doesn't cause grief,
and seeing praise doesn't bring delight.
If they sincerely believe the world certainly has no immortals,
while I alone argue that they truly exist,
the longer we debate,
the more firmly they cling to their view.
This merely increases such disputes
without resolving their incomprehension -
should I indeed follow the principle of the interlocking rings?"
Someone asked:
"The ways of human affairs are manifold,
while attaining immortality is extremely difficult.
Unless one abandons some pursuits,
one cannot succeed in both.
The endeavors of literature and arts,
the duties involving sorrow and joy,
and the principles between ruler and subject—
how can they be neglected?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The essential path is not burdensome,
and what it requires is little.
Just worry about not establishing your will
and not having firm belief.
Why concern yourself with neglecting human affairs?
Those with great talent cultivate both sides,
so what difficulty is there?
Internally treasuring the way of nurturing life,
externally harmonizing with the world's glow,
cultivating oneself leads to long-lasting refinement,
governing the state leads to great peace.
Using the Six Classics to instruct common scholars,
imparting esoteric methods to kindred spirits,
wishing to remain briefly means halting to assist the times,
desiring to ascend means soaring to the heavens lightly—
these are the superior persons.
Those who assess their own capabilities
and cannot achieve both,
then abandon worldly affairs
to specialize in cultivating the Way and Virtue
are next in rank.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor bore the responsibility for all under heaven,
yet this did not prevent his ascent at Dǐnghú;
Péngzǔ served as a grand official for eight hundred years,
then went west to Liúshā;
Bóyáng served as the柱史,
Níng Fēng as the陶正,
Fāng Huí as the闾士,
Lǚ Wàng as the Grand Tutor;
Qiú Shēng served under the Yīn,
Mǎ Dān held office in Jìn,
Fàn Gōng dominated Yuè yet sailed the seas,
Qíngāo held office under Sòng Kāng;
Cháng Shēng lowered his aspirations to take up the whip,
Zhuāng Gōng concealed his ability in a minor post.
The ancients often attained the Way while supporting the world,
cultivating it while serving incognito in court,
because they had energy to spare.
Why must one cultivate in mountain forests,
completely abandoning the affairs of living people,
before achieving success?
There are also those whose hearts love quiet and silence,
whose natures detest noise and clamor,
who find joy in unrestrained freedom,
and see glory and office as sorrows.
Wearing rope belts and ragged clothes,
eating wild plants and handling plows,
they delight in their three joys,
maintaining constancy while awaiting their end,
not seeking a ignoble life,
not fearing a swift death,
declining offers of a thousand in gold,
disdaining the honors of ministers and chancellors.
Even without cultivation,
they often behave like this—
how much more so if they knew the way of immortals?
They would certainly refuse to enslave their bodies to the world.
Each follows his own will;
this cannot be discussed in sweeping terms."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"The world says a single good word
is worth more than a thousand in gold,
but this usually refers to the successes and failures of state affairs
or the good and bad in personal conduct.
As for informing people of the secrets of longevity
and imparting to them the methods of immortality,
this is not merely like those ordinary good words.
How could it be worth only a thousand in gold?
Suppose someone is ill and near death,
and another can rescue and cure him—
all would call this great kindness and significant aid.
Now if we follow the immortal classics,
refine the nine elixirs,
and prepare gold and jade,
then all under heaven can be made deathless.
The benefit is not just the merit of saving one person.
The virtue of Huáng-Lǎo
is truly immeasurable,
yet no one recognizes it,
calling it deceptive and false—
this is lamentable."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"To seek immortality,
one must grasp its essential principles.
The essentials lie in treasuring essence, circulating qì,
and taking the great elixir—these alone suffice,
with no need for excess.
Yet these three practices
have varying depths,
and without an enlightened teacher
or enduring hardship,
one cannot hastily comprehend them fully.
Though we speak of circulating qì,
there are multiple methods for doing so.
Though we mention bedroom arts,
the techniques therein
encompass nearly over a hundred practices.
Though we discuss taking medicine,
the formulas for medication
number roughly a thousand.
When first teaching others,
we start with the basics;
only through unwavering determination
and demonstrable diligence
are the essentials later revealed.
Thus, circulating qì can cure all ailments,
ward off epidemics,
subdue snakes and tigers,
staunch bleeding wounds,
enable dwelling underwater,
walking on water,
averting hunger and thirst,
and prolonging life.
Its core principle
is fetal breathing.
Those who master fetal breathing
can breathe without nose or mouth,
as if in the womb—
then the Way is achieved.
Beginners drawing qì through the nose
should hold it
while silently counting to one hundred twenty,
then exhale gently through the mouth.
Both inhalation and exhalation
should be inaudible to one's own ears,
ensuring more enters than exits.
Test by placing a goose feather at the nose and mouth—
exhalation should not stir it.
Gradually increase the count with practice;
prolonged effort reaches a thousand,
at which point the aged rejuvenate
day by day.
Circulate qì during living-qì hours,
never during dead-qì hours.
Hence immortals ingest the six qìs—
this is the meaning.
A day and night have twelve periods:
midnight to noon are living qì,
noon to midnight are dead qì.
During dead qì,
circulating qì is futile.
Masters of qì can
blow on water
to make it flow backwards several paces;
blow on fire
to extinguish it;
blow on tigers and wolves
to immobilize them;
blow on serpents
to make them coil motionless.
If someone is wounded by blades,
blowing stops their bleeding;
if poisoned by venomous creatures,
even unseen,
blow on one's hand from afar—
left for males,
right for females—
and the afflicted, even a hundred miles away,
are instantly healed.
For sudden severe illnesses,
swallow three nines of qì
for immediate recovery.
But human nature is restless,
few can cultivate this path tranquilly.
Another key: avoid overeating
and raw, rich foods,
which strengthen qì
and hinder retention.
Also restrain anger—
fury disrupts qì flow,
causing stagnation
or coughing fits,
hence few succeed.
My grand-uncle Xiāngōng
would dive to deep riverbeds
while drunk or in summer heat,
staying a full day—
all through fetal breath retention.
Bedroom arts span ten schools:
some repair injuries,
some treat diseases,
some harness yin to augment yang,
some extend lifespan—
but the core is returning essence to nourish the brain.
This oral tradition among adepts
was never written;
without it,
even famed medicines
cannot grant longevity.
Yet one must not abstain entirely from intimacy—
without union,
stagnation arises,
hence recluses and lonely souls
fall ill and die early.
Indulgence without restraint,
however, shortens life.
Only balanced moderation
prevents harm.
Without oral instructions,
none avoid self-inflicted injury.
Masters like Xuánsù, Zǐdū, Róngchénggōng, and Péngzǔ
recorded only fragments,
never committing secrets to writing.
Seekers of immortality
must diligently pursue them.
I convey these teachings from my master Zhèng Jūn
for future believers—
not mere speculation.
Yet I myself have not mastered all secrets.
Some practitioners
focus solely on bedroom arts
seeking immortality
while neglecting the golden elixir—
this is utter folly."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The Daoist texts originating from Huángdì and Lǎozǐ
are actually quite few.
Most are by later enthusiasts
who expanded upon their limited knowledge,
resulting in accumulated texts mountainous in volume.
The ancients were simple and unadorned,
and many lacked talent.
Their discussions of natural principles
were neither comprehensive nor thorough,
their supporting evidence
was not clearly presented,
all lacking essentials and being hard to understand.
Even when understood, their meaning wasn't profound,
insufficient to elucidate subtle teachings,
enlighten the perplexed,
encourage the motivated,
instruct beginners,
or show them the path to mystery
and the origins of fortune and misfortune.
Merely reciting them ten thousand times
yields nothing of substance.
Although one may wish to study broadly,
one should carefully select the good texts
before focusing on them.
As for non-essential Daoist texts,
they're not worth delving into.
Some late learners fail to distinguish the depth of authors,
and regarding anything labeled as Daoist teaching,
they fill boxes and baskets with copies,
exhausting their minds pondering them.
This is like searching a swallow's nest for phoenix eggs
or hunting eels at the bottom of a well.
No matter how diligent,
they seek what isn't there.
Nothing can be practically applied,
only wasting time needlessly,
exhausting themselves in vain labor,
gaining not an ounce of benefit.
They neglect contemporary affairs while advancing,
and lack longevity effects while retreating.
Then people all point and say:
'He cultivated the Dao so diligently,
yet couldn't transcend this world—
this proves there's truly no immortal method!'
They don't realize his quest for immortality
was like gazing at fish in the river
without any net—
not that the river lacked fish.
Furthermore, although the Five Thousand Character text came from Lǎozǐ,
it only discusses generalities briefly.
It never fully presents matters from start to finish,
offering nothing concrete to follow.
Merely memorizing this classic
without grasping essential teachings
is utterly futile—
how much more so with inferior works?
As for Wénzǐ, Zhuāngzǐ, Guān Lìng Yǐnxǐ and their followers,
their writings,
though tracing back to Huángdì and Lǎozǐ
and modeling metaphysical emptiness,
only elaborate broad principles
without ever expressing ultimate truths.
Some even equate life and death,
claiming no difference between living as conscript labor
and dying as rest.
Their distance from divine immortality
spans billions of miles—
how could they be worth indulging in?
Their parables and analogies
may have some value
for occasional use,
filling temporary needs,
yet later generations' slick-tongued flatterers
and immoral scoundrels
use Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ as hiding places—
isn't this regrettable?"
Someone asked:
"When sage rulers govern the world,
they treasure only the worthy.
If those studying immortality
refuse official positions,
and everyone cultivates the Dao,
who will assist in governance?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Those who turn from sage rulers to dwell in mountains—
this is why Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu are esteemed;
those who seclude themselves encountering virtuous rule—
this is why Zhuāng Bó is valued;
When Xuānyuán governed the world,
it could be called perfectly ordered,
yet Guǎngchéngzǐ didn't participate;
When Tángyáo possessed the empire,
it could be called great peace,
yet Wòquán didn't assist—
yet virtuous transformation wasn't diminished,
nor were talented officials lacking;
When Tiānyǐ revolutionized rule,
Wùguāng tied stones and drowned himself;
When Jīwǔ overthrew Shāng,
Bóyí and Shūqí starved on Western Mountain;
When Qíhuán prospered,
Xiàojì slept peacefully in his humble lane;
When Wèiwén excelled,
Duànmù Gànmù let hair flow free at Western River;
The Four Elders phoenix-like hid at Shāngluò,
yet didn't hinder Hàn's abundance of scholars;
Zhōu Dǎng stood unicorn-like in forest marshes,
yet didn't impair Guāngwǔ's suspended punishments.
When honor cannot move their hearts,
extreme wealth cannot shift their preferences,
they rinse their hats in blue waves,
neither submitting nor being disgraced,
making fragrant woods their towers,
steep peaks their mansions,
emerald orchids their fine beds,
green leaves their curtains,
wearing coarse cloth instead of royal robes,
eating wild herbs as fine cuisine,
never eating unless they farm themselves,
never clothing unless their wives weave—
through a thousand years,
such men occasionally appear.
How much more those who
entrust six relatives to their clans,
abandon households without regret,
reject glory like discarding footprints,
extinguish desires in their hearts,
climb lofty peaks alone,
companion echoes in famous mountains,
gaze inward at formless realms,
listen backward in deepest silence—
within the eight directions,
how many such exist?
Yet you fear rulers might lack ministers—
Someone said:
"Those who study immortality,
purify only themselves while neglecting the chaos in fundamental human relationships,
turn their backs on worldly rulers and harbor the arrogance of not serving as subjects.
I fear they will achieve no success in attaining longevity,
and instead will face the net of crimes closing in on them."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Now, Shíhù, Shànjuǎn, and Zǐzhōu from the northern regions,
were all men of great talent,
yet they submerged themselves in reclusion and unrestrained freedom,
nourishing their vast, righteous spirit.
The rise and fall of dynasties did not suffer because of them,
nor was the great transformation of the world impaired by their absence.
Moreover, those who study immortality,
may not necessarily possess the talent to govern a state,
nor be of use in court administration.
Gaining them would add no more benefit than a speck of dust or a drop of dew,
and losing them would not be felt even a hair's breadth of damage, would it?
Nowadays, the nine regions share the same abode,
and even those from remote wilderness come to serve,
with talents like Yuán and Kǎi piling up,
yet there is no use for them.
Scholars face delays in awaiting their turns for positions,
while no official post remains vacant even temporarily;
those long diligent sigh over slow promotions,
and the highly meritorious suffer the grievance of advancement by seniority.
Amid such flourishing abundance,
nothing surpasses this beauty,
and a lone individual,
is hardly what is lacking.
In the past, Prince Jìn abandoned his duty of attending to meals,
and relinquished the weight of being crown prince,
yet King Ling did not hold him accountable for unfilialness;
Yǐnshēng left behind his official responsibilities,
and turned away from the task of defense,
yet the Zhōu dynasty did not charge him with disloyalty.
Why so?
Because they truly understood that it was not out of contempt for the world or belittling their lords,
but simply because their preferences differed.
The will of a common man,
can sometimes be unshakable.
An enlightened ruler,
bears disgrace and excels in forgiveness,
knowing that people's hearts cannot be uniform,
and that choices of engagement or reclusion are matters of individual nature.
Not forcing, not forbidding,
he honors and amplifies their greatness.
Above, there is no biased heart of suspicion or resentment,
below, there is the utmost joy of fulfillment.
Thus, their brilliance and reputation are both proclaimed boundlessly,
and even the greedy, hearing of this, feel ashamed.
I have heard that when the auspicious wind rises, fur coats and stoves are set aside;
when the world's way is smooth, extraordinary men withdraw.
Now that the turmoil and chaos have been pacified,
plough oxen are rested and war horses released,
beacon fires cast no shadows,
weapons are stored away,
the mighty bows are sheathed,
and fine hounds are about to be cooked.
Zǐfáng stepped out of dark curtains to return to the alleyways,
while Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè laid aside their armor to take up fishing rods.
How much more so for those who study immortality,
not one in ten thousand,
why would the state grudge them for what reason?
Moreover, their endeavor lies in few thoughts and scant desires,
their pursuit in preserving the body and achieving longevity.
It involves no disgrace of contention,
bears no burden of harming customs.
What crime is there in that?
Besides, Mount Huà and Huò are immensely great,
the vast sea is boundless;
their heights do not await the arrival of flying dust to increase,
their depths do not rely on flowing puddles to fill.
A handful of soil cannot reduce their loftiness,
a dipper of water cannot diminish their breadth.
In an entire era, there are no more than a few immortals;
how could they possibly detract from the multitude of worldly affairs?"
Some may say:
"If the path to immortality could truly be sought and attained,
why is it not recorded in the Five Classics,
why did the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius not speak of it,
why did the sages not transcend this world,
why do the wisest not live forever?
If the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius were unaware of it,
then they cannot be considered sages.
If they knew but did not study it,
then there is no path to immortality."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The constellations that govern human destiny,
each have their correspondences,
as has been detailed in another chapter.
You might be said to wear a basin on your head while looking up,
unable to see the brilliance of the seven luminaries;
momentarily stretching your neck toward the great river,
unaware of the marvels in its deepest abysses.
What the Five Classics do not record is boundless,
what the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius did not speak of is not few.
Let me briefly mention to you but a ten-thousandth of it.
Though you may laugh heartily without cease,
constrained sentiments are hard to suddenly open,
yet let me allow you to hear its general outline.
Heaven and earth are the greatest of things.
Nine sages together completed the Classic of Changes,
sufficient to encompass yīn and yáng,
yet it cannot cover everything.
Now ask those proficient in the Changes:
the degrees of the celestial circumference,
the breadth and narrowness of the four seas,
the distances between cosmic realms,
how many lǐ in total?
What lies at the uppermost extreme,
what supports from below,
and when they revolve,
who pushes and pulls them?
The swiftness and slowness of the sun and moon,
the nine paths they traverse,
the length of darkness and light,
the seven stars alternating in position,
the expansion and contraction of the five planets,
coronas, parhelia, and eclipses,
the twenty-eight constellations encroaching and offending,
the emergence of comets and nova,
the anomalies of arrow-like vapors,
the omens of light and age,
the pole star remaining motionless,
the planet Jupiter moving uniquely eastward,
Xīhé externally radiant yet hot,
Wàngshū internally reflective yet cold,
the Milky Way seen above having moistening downward nature,
tides ebbing and flowing with variations in magnitude,
the five notes and six associations,
divining emotions of joy and anger,
cloud movements and vapor risings,
containing portents of fortune and misfortune,
Chán, Qiāng, Yóu, and Shǐ stars,
Xúnshǐ crimson threads,
Sìzhèn and Wǔcán stars,
Tiāngǒu and Guīxié phenomena,
some indicating success,
some confirming defeat—
those versed in the Changes,
cannot discuss these.
Then ask masters of the Spring and Autumn Annals, the four collections, Book of Songs, Book of Documents, and three Ritual texts,
all again will have no reply.
They all say these are entirely unrecorded in the canonical classics,
only Wū Xián, Gān Gōng, Shí Shēn, Hǎi Zhōng, Què Méng, and the Seven Luminaries records contain them all.
I would ask them:
Are these six schools' writings
considered teachings of the classics?
They will say no.
I would further ask:
Are figures like Gān and Shí
considered sages?
They will also say no.
Then since humans are born beneath heaven,
tread earth until old age,
yet seeking in the Five Classics finds nothing,
searching in the writings of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius yields nothing,
should we now consider it all illusory?
Heaven and earth are supremely vast,
what meets the eye
still cannot be fully understood,
how much more what is mysterious within mystery,
the ultimate of subtleties?"
Again asking ordinary people:
"The land where people ride clouds and are born from cocoons,
the people whose livers and hearts do not decay,
dwelling in nests and caves,
with single eyes or three heads,
horses with leisure and dogs with hooves,
long arms and interlocking thighs,
Huángchí with no males,
pierced chests and side mouths,
Lín Jūn lifting stones while floating earthen boats,
Shā Yī touching wood to birth dragon groups,
Nǚwā emerging from earth,
Dù Yǔ falling from heaven,
tiles flying and dogs speaking,
mountains moving and altars shifting,
entire armies
transformed in a single morning,
gentlemen becoming cranes,
commoners turning to sand,
Nǚ Chǒu leaning on withered trees,
Èrfù embracing fetters,
parasitic insects,
shedding shells to walk fleshy,
two-headed snakes,
strung to make bows,
unburnable wood,
heatless fire,
Chāngshǔ birds,
eyeless beasts,
headless bodies,
bodiless heads,
Jīngwèi filling the sea,
Jiāoràng trees alternating growth,
fire-washed cloth,
jade-cutting knives,
flames spitting brilliance,
grinding mud to filter water,
withering shrubs transforming shapes,
Shānkuí with forward heels,
Shí Xiū with nine heads,
Bìfāng with human faces,
Shǎoqiān subduing Bó Shuài,
Shèngqīng commanding Sù Shuāng,
Western Qiāng rising through tiger omens,
Xiānbēi strengthening by riding turtles,
Línyì ruling through divine registers,
Yōngshǔ emperoring through floating corpses,
salt goddess Yīnglái while insects flew,
vertical-eyed generations changing at Jīng peaks,
Wǔ Dīng leading snakes to topple cliffs,
Ròushèn fluttering wings over three seas.
Golden tablets and jade scripts,
discovered beside Yǔ's well.
Zhèngjī and balance mechanisms,
extracted from patterned stone.
All these wondrous affairs,
number in the thousands,
unrecorded in the Five Classics,
unmentioned by the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius—
can we still say these things do not exist?
As for southerners who can enter pillars and exit through ears,
Yù Kòu stopping arm water while drawing bows,
Bó Hūn treading thousand-ren heights on tiptoe,
Lǚliáng singing while leaning over abysses,
Duke of Sòng carving ivory leaves indistinguishable from real,
Gōngshū making wooden magpies soar,
Lí Zhū seeing fine hairs at a hundred paces,
Mèng Bèn exhibiting strength with ten-thousand jūn weights,
Yuè people reviving the dead with acupuncture,
Shù Hài surpassing accumulated thousands in footsteps,
Yǐng man wielding axe on nose plaster,
Zhòng Dū baring body in freezing weather—
these are all things the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius could not do,
can we still claim them nonexistent?
If sages truly have limitations,
then no wonder they didn't attain immortality;
not attaining immortality doesn't hinder being sages,
as sages occasionally have gaps in knowledge—
how can this suffice as your main argument?
Sages may equally accept departure or stay,
follow spontaneity,
having bodies but not selfish,
having life but not scheming,
existence and demise entrusted to heaven,
longevity and brevity left to fate,
thus not studying immortality—
why find this strange?"
Dì Wǔ Gōng eradicated demonic cults,
and enjoyed both longevity and nobility;
Sòng Lújiāng abolished mountain sacrifices,
and received eternal blessings;
Wén Wēng destroyed the temple of water spirits,
and achieved personal fortune and public peace;
Wèi Wǔ prohibited excessive worship customs,
and great prosperity came to him.
We must not forget past events,
for they serve as mirrors for the future.
Only bright virtue is fragrant,
the carefree live long,
the frugal do not die young,
the sorrowful age prematurely—
this is the natural principle.
What can external things accomplish!
If one's nourishment loses harmony,
and depletion remains unresolved,
hundreds of diseases will gather through the cracks,
while vital energy exhausts itself unnoticed.
Even the grand sacrifice of three animals,
how could it save such situation?
Common practices are mostly deceptive and false,
mutually deceiving and confusing,
growing worse over time.
They neither cultivate healing methods,
nor return from great delusion,
not seeking medicinal remedies,
but only focusing on erroneous prayers and sacrifices.
Endless supplications,
tireless divinations,
petty sorcerers
falsely predicting disasters,
when illness becomes critical,
they claim ignorance,
yet immediately perform rituals upon hearing,
causing immeasurable waste.
Wealthy families exhaust their treasures,
the poor borrow at double interest,
fields and homes are sold off completely,
chests and cabinets emptied without remainder.
If occasionally someone recovers,
they attribute it to divine blessing;
if someone dies,
they say ghosts didn't pardon them.
Even if mistakenly surviving,
with property depleted,
they eventually die from hunger and cold,
some turn to robbery and plunder,
others become thieves and scoundrels,
meeting death by weapons' points,
bringing upon themselves shameful punishments—
all these stem from such practices.
When belongings are exhausted on sacrificial expenses,
grains and silks lost to greedy sorcerers,
at time of death,
there's no money for coffins,
nor shrouds for wrapping,
leaving corpses to rot and be worm-eaten—
truly lamentable!
How deep is the common people's delusion,
reaching such extent!
Excessive worship and demonic practices
are forbidden by ritual laws.
Yet ordinary people
remain unenlightened.
Only rulers should strengthen laws:
offenders regardless of severity
should receive capital punishment,
reward those who report persistent sorcerers,
punish without pardon,
display them in public streets.
Within short time,
this will surely cease,
thus preventing people from freezing and starving sources,
stifling banditry's sprouts—
this is no minor kindness.
Previously, there were Zhāng Jiǎo, Liǔ Gēn, Wáng Xīn, Lǐ Shēn and others,
some claiming thousand-year age,
pretending minor arts,
sitting then vanishing,
changing forms and appearances,
deceiving common people,
gathering foolish crowds,
not aiming to prolong life,
nor to eliminate disasters and cure diseases,
but rather recruiting wicked factions,
inciting rebellions.
Not only did they face deserved punishment,
some even harmed good people,
deceiving ordinary folk,
seeking wealth and profit.
Money and silk piled like mountains,
riches surpassing nobles,
indulging in luxury,
wearing fine clothes, eating jade-like food,
concubines filling houses,
musicians forming rows,
assassins and death warriors
serving their purposes,
power overwhelming lords,
influence pressuring officials,
fugitives and escapees
finding shelter there.
All because officials failed to investigate,
leading to these troubles.
Considering the origins,
one can only sigh.
We are common people,
though understanding this principle,
not in position,
can do nothing!
Local officials,
suspecting divine power,
fear prohibiting it
might bring curses.
Even if somewhat willing,
their understanding incomplete,
and not essential duty,
nor urgent administrative matter,
plus their foolish wives and stubborn sons firmly believe,
petty subordinates
all say impossible,
many obstructing,
without sincere intention,
fearful advisors speaking unanimously,
thus causing doubt,
finally daring nothing—
making one wring wrists in frustration!
I personally witnessed several acquaintances
completely ignoring deities,
never praying lifelong,
enjoying extended years,
achieving high positions,
with flourishing descendants,
both wealthy and noble.
I myself also avoid such practices,
only sacrificing to ancestors seasonally.
Having traveled thousands of miles by land and water,
passing roadside temples
numbering about hundred,
yet coming and going directly,
never visiting any,
with no carriage accidents,
no stormy waves when crossing waters.
Often encountering epidemics,
relying on medicine's power,
frequently facing arrows and stones,
fortunately unharmed—
further proving ghosts and spirits' impotence.
Moreover, various demonic cults over hundred kinds,
all kill and blood-sacrifice,
only Lǐjiā Dào's inaction being slightly better.
Though not slaughtering,
often providing blessed food,
without limits,
market-bought supplies,
emphasizing abundance,
delicate fresh items
must be purchased,
sometimes feeding dozens in kitchen,
also costly,
not entirely pure and frugal either,
all should be prohibited.
Someone asked when the Lǐ family's teachings began.
I replied:
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Wú,
in Shǔ there was one Lǐ Ā,
who lived in a cave and ate no food,
and was seen through generations,
called the Lord of Eight Hundred Years.
People would often ask him about matters,
but Ā would say nothing;
they only observed his countenance.
If his expression was joyful,
then affairs were all auspicious;
if his face appeared sorrowful,
then affairs were all inauspicious;
if Ā wore a smile,
then there was great celebration;
if he sighed slightly,
then there was deep worry.
Such omens
never once failed.
Later, he suddenly left one day,
and none knew where he went.
Afterwards, there was a man named Lǐ Kuān
who came to Wú speaking the Shǔ dialect,
and could chant over water to cure illnesses quite effectively.
Thus, far and wide, people unanimously
claimed Kuān was Lǐ Ā,
and therefore called him Lǐ Bābǎi (Eight Hundred),
though in truth he was not.
From high officials down,
all flocked to his gate,
but later he became arrogant and aloof,
no longer easily accessible.
Guests would merely bow at his outer gate and leave;
such was his peculiarity.
Then, officials and commoners evading corvée duty
became Kuān's disciples, nearly a thousand constantly,
yet those who entered his inner circle and advanced in studies
only learned water chanting, three talismans, and guiding breath like sun and moon cycles,
utterly lacking essential self-cultivation methods, divine elixirs, longevity, or immortality techniques.
Swallowing breath and abstaining from grains
could last up to a hundred days or so,
but not longer,
showing the superficiality of his arts.
I know many who saw Kuān personally,
all saying he aged frail and haggard,
coughing and sneezing when moving,
eyes dim, ears deaf,
teeth fallen, hair white,
gradually becoming senile,
sometimes forgetting his own descendants,
no different from ordinary folks.
Yet people still claimed Kuān feigned ordinariness to deceive others;
how could that be so?
Wú once suffered a great plague,
killing over half the population.
Kuān's Daoist chamber,
called a retreat,
saw him contract the fever too.
Pretending to enter for fasting,
he died inside.
But his followers still called it transformation and release from the corpse as an immortal,
not true death.
Now, the method of immortals,
what sets them apart from世俗之人,
is precisely valuing agelessness and deathlessness.
Now, Kuān aged indeed,
died indeed;
this shows he hadn't attained the Dào,
clearly evident,
so what doubt remains?
If one claims he should be released from the corpse per immortal law,
why not stay in the world a century or two,
halt aging,
then depart?
It's not that the path to immortality doesn't exist under heaven,
but Kuān wasn't the right person for it.
The reason I elaborate in detail
is that Kuān's disciples teach each other,
spreading across the region south of the Yangtze,
numbering about a thousand.
Unaware of the inadequacy of Kuān's methods,
they uphold them undeserving of adherence,
hoping to transcend the world.
Thus, I wish to awaken them to this delusion.
The world has things that seem right but are wrong,
truly limitless.
I'll briefly recount old stories
to enlighten those who don't understand.
Once in Rǔnán, a man set a snare in a field and caught a river deer,
but the owner didn't notice.
A passerby saw it,
took the deer stealthily and left,
yet felt uneasy about taking it without cause.
Having some salted fish,
he placed one in the snare and departed.
The owner later came,
found the salted fish in the snare,
found it strange and thought it divine,
daring not to take it home.
Then the village heard of it,
built a house and established a shrine together,
calling it Lord Bào.
Later, more people worshipped there,
with vermilion pillars and painted beams,
bells and drums incessant.
If someone's illness happened to heal,
they'd say the god was effective,
and passersby
all offered sacrifices.
After seven or eight years,
the salted fish owner passed by the shrine later,
asked the reason,
and people explained it fully.
The owner then said,
"This is just my salted fish;
what divinity does it have?"
Thereupon, it ceased.
Also, one Zhāng Zhù from Nándùn,
plowing a dry field,
found a pear sapling
in the way of farming.
Zhù, pitying it,
wanted to take it home,
dug it up,
but couldn't leave immediately,
so wrapped its roots in damp soil
and placed it in a hollow mulberry tree,
then forgot to retrieve it.
Zhù later took a distant post and was away.
Afterwards, people from his village
saw a pear tree suddenly grow in the mulberry,
deemed it divine.
Someone with sore eyes
rested in the shade beneath it,
prayed to it,
saying, "If Lord Lǐ can heal my eyes,
I'll thank it with a piglet."
His eyes happened to heal,
so he slaughtered the piglet and offered it.
The story spread exaggerated,
saying this tree could make the blind see.
Far and wide, people unanimously
came to seek blessings,
often with horses and carriages crowding,
wine and meat abundant,
for several years thus.
When Zhāng Zhù returned from his post,
he saw it
and said,
"This is just the pear sapling I placed before;
how can it be divine?"
He cut it down, and it stopped.
Also, in Rǔnán, the Péng family tomb was near a main road,
with a stone figure at the entrance.
An old farm woman went to the market, bought some flatbreads, and returned.
The weather was hot,
so she rested under a tree at the tomb entrance,
temporarily placing the breads on the stone figure's head,
then suddenly left,
forgetting to take them.
A passerby saw bread on the stone figure's head,
found it strange, and asked about it.
Someone said,
"This stone figure is divine,
can cure illnesses;
those healed bring bread to thank it."
Thus, the word spread,
saying those with headaches should rub the stone figure's head,
those with stomachaches rub its belly,
and they'd also rub themselves accordingly,
and all were cured.
Then people came from afar to seek healing from the stone figure,
initially with chickens and pigs,
later with cattle and sheep,
erecting tents for it,
with constant music,
for several years thus.
Suddenly, the woman who'd forgotten the bread heard of it,
explained to people,
and only then did visits cease.
West of Luòyáng there was an ancient large tomb,
which had collapsed and accumulated much water.
The tomb contained much limestone,
and the limewater was effective in treating sores.
In the summer,
when travelers suffering from sores felt feverish and restless,
they saw the clear, good water in this tomb,
and so washed themselves in it.
Their sores happened to heal.
Upon hearing this, all those afflicted with illness
went to wash themselves there.
Gradually, some even drank it to treat internal ailments.
People living near the tomb
then built a temple at the tomb site and sold this water.
Those who came to buy it often made offerings in the temple,
so that wine and meat were constantly present.
As more and more people came to buy,
the water ran out.
So the water sellers often secretly added other water at night to supplement it.
Those who lived too far to go in person
would take advantage of travelers or send messengers with containers to buy it.
Thus, the water sellers became very wealthy.
Some said there was no deity,
and the authorities issued a ban,
so the tomb was filled in,
and the practice ceased.
Also, when Mǎ Shì was serving as the Tàishǒu of Xīnggǔ,
an old acquaintance came to him seeking aid.
Mǎ had this person stay outside,
falsely claiming he was a divine immortal or a Dàoshi,
who could cure any illness instantly with his touch.
He also had eloquent speakers travel around,
creating false praise for him,
saying he could make the blind see again
and the lame walk immediately.
Thus, people gathered from all directions like clouds,
flocking to him as to a market.
And money and silk piled up like mountains.
He also ordered all those seeking treatment,
even if not cured,
to tell others they were cured,
for then they surely would be;
but if they said they were not cured,
then they would never be cured.
Such was the way of the method,
and one must believe it.
So when later arrivals asked those who came before,
the earlier ones always said they were cured,
and none dared say they were not.
Within ten days,
he amassed great wealth.
Most people are clever in small matters but foolish in large ones.
When they hear of methods for prolonging life and immortality,
they dismiss them as empty fabrications,
yet gladly believe in demons, evil spirits, and ghosts,
engaging in drumming, dancing, and sacrificial prayers.
What are called deities
are often deceptions like that of Mǎ Shì.
I briefly record these few incidents
as a warning to those still unawakened."
Someone asked:
"There are those in the world who know nothing of the Dào, arts, methods, or techniques,
yet live peacefully and enjoy long lives.
Why is that?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"In such cases,
some may have hidden virtue and good deeds,
which bring them blessings and protection;
some are endowed with inherently long lifespans,
hence they age slowly and die late;
others are simply fortunate to avoid disasters and injuries by chance.
It is like after a hunt has passed through,
some birds and beasts are left behind;
after a great fire has swept by,
occasionally some unburned grass and trees remain.
For protecting the body and warding off harm,
one should cultivate defenses that guard the form,
and carry talismans and swords inscribed with celestial patterns.
Sacrificial prayers are of no benefit.
One should rely on one's own inviolability,
not on the hope that ghosts and spirits will not invade.
However, contemplating the mysterious and holding fast to the One,
embracing the light and circulating it around the body,
can ward off evil and malign influences,
and help one pass through inauspicious events,
but it cannot prolong lifespan
or eliminate physical illnesses.
Those who follow nature without practicing methods
may not necessarily fail to live out their natural years,
but they have no means to resist the rampant harm of violent ghosts
or the spread of great epidemics.
Storing armor and helmets,
keeping raincoats and bamboo hats
is for the sake of war and rain.
If fortunately there is no attack or battle,
and the weather is not continuously cloudy,
then having them or not is just the same.
But when arrows and stones descend like fog,
and flying blades cross like smoke,
then the plight of the naked is known.
When heavy rain pours like a river,
and white snow fills the sky,
then the hardship of standing exposed is felt.
One should not, due to the triviality of wild herbs and wheat,
doubt the great energy of Yīn and Yáng,
misleading later learners and idle scholars
into thinking that methods and arts are of no benefit."
Someone asked about the precedence between Confucianism and Daoism.
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The Dào
is the root of Confucianism;
Confucianism
is the branch of the Dào.
Previously, the techniques of yīn and yáng
were abundant with taboos,
making people constrained and fearful;
while Confucians were broad but lacking essentials,
laborious with little achievement;
Mòists were frugal but difficult to follow,
impossible to practice universally;
Legalists were severe and lacking kindness,
damaging benevolence and righteousness.
Only the teachings of the Dàoist school
enable people to concentrate their essence and spirit,
acting in accordance with the formless,
embracing the strengths of Confucianism and Mohism,
summarizing the essentials of the School of Names and Legalism,
moving with the times,
adapting to changes in circumstances,
concise and easy to understand,
achieving much with little effort,
devoted to preserving the simplicity of the great ancestor,
guarding the source of true genuineness.
Yet Bān Gù, because Sīmǎ Qiān prioritized Huáng-Lǎo over the Six Classics,
called Qiān erroneous.
Now Qiān's extensive knowledge,
comprehensively synthesized the obscure and hidden,
sifted through the merits and faults of affairs,
verified the integrity and corruption of ancient people.
His critiques
were truly based on spontaneity,
his judgments of praise and blame
all followed the ultimate principle.
He did not falsely praise,
nor conceal flaws,
nor conform mindlessly to vulgar opinions.
Liú Xiàng, a towering intellectual of his time,
called it a true record;
thus Bān Gù's criticism
cannot be relied upon.
Gù was indeed a pure Confucian,
who did not comprehend the meaning of the Dào,
indulging in what he was accustomed to,
making it hard to reach a balanced judgment.
Now, what is called the Dào,
is it merely about nurturing life?
The Yì Jīng says:
'The way of heaven
is called yīn and yáng;
the way of earth
is called soft and hard;
the way of humanity
is called benevolence and righteousness.'
It also says:
'The Yì contains four aspects of the sage's way,
and if it is not the right person,
the way does not operate in vain.'
Moreover, in a well-governed and prosperous age,
it is called having the Dào,
while in a perilous state with a chaotic ruler,
it is called without the Dào.
Also, those who sit and discuss the Dào
are called the Three Dukes,
and when the state possesses the Dào,
it is shameful to be poor and lowly.
All references to the Dào
span from the two cosmic forces above
down to the myriad things below,
none are not governed by it.
But Huáng-Lǎo grasps its root,
while Confucianism and Mohism manage its branches.
Those recognized as possessing the Dào today
are broadly knowledgeable about past and present,
able to observe heaven and examine earth,
traverse changes and delve into subtleties,
understand the cycles of rise and fall,
comprehend the essence of order and chaos,
with minds free of doubt,
and no question they cannot answer—
why must they practice longevity techniques,
or admire the practices of Sōng and Qiáo?
Yet scholars with tunnel vision,
make blind assertions and瞎说,
hearing of those dwelling in mountain forests,
devoted to the work of Bó Yáng,
they slander and laugh, saying,
'That is a minor path,
not worth considering.'
Alas!
Those holding glowworms within confined walls
cannot see the brilliance of heavenly light;
those befriending minnows and shrimp in puddle waters
do not recognize the vastness of the four seas;
they value the depth of great rivers,
but do not know they originate from Kūnlún;
they treasure the harvest of millet and grain,
but are unaware they sprout from fertile soil.
Now if they only know to esteem Confucianism,
but not that its success comes from the Dào.
The Dào
is what molds the Hundred Schools,
casts the two cosmic forces,
germinates all classes of beings,
and ferments moral relationships.
The world has many shallow people
and few profound ones,
the few cannot overcome the many,
which has long been the case.
Thus, though Sīmǎ Qiān was superior, he received no praise,
while Bān Gù, though inferior, received no criticism.
Yet things are valued when scarce,
and cheap when abundant;
in human affairs,
is it not the same?
Hence, wild greens cover the plains,
while rare orchids seldom appear;
thorny bushes blanket the fields,
yet towering trees occasionally rise;
sand and gravel are countless,
but pearls and jades are very rare;
falcons flock in flight,
while phoenixes rarely emerge;
vipers and lizards fill the marshes,
yet dragons are seldom seen;
Bān Gù having many followers
is only natural.
The Dào
internally cultivates the self,
externally governs the state,
enabling the seven governors to follow their courses,
the two energies to harmonize,
the four seasons not to lose their rhythm of heat and cold,
wind and rain not to bring destructive disasters,
the jade candle manifesting signs of peace,
clear sweet wine displaying tokens of virtuous governance,
whirlwinds and rainbows ceasing their ominous displays,
storm clouds and rain-birds folding their wings,
sunlight shining brightly,
bountiful grains fully ripening,
epidemics not spreading,
calamities and chaos not arising,
watchtowers not being built,
weapons not being used,
decisions made without discussion yet appropriate,
trust without covenants,
unity without bonds yet firm,
success without planning,
motivation without rewards,
order without punishments,
attainment without seeking,
cessation without prohibitions,
ruling above without being burdensome,
leading without causing anxiety,
influence spreading before commands are issued,
customs transforming before orders are given—
this is the governance of the Dào in the world.
Thus when the Dào flourishes,
the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors rule effortlessly with abundance.
When the Dào declines,
later ages strive anxiously yet achieve inadequacy.
Only with abundance
can non-action lead to beautiful transformation.
Only with inadequacy
do harsh penalties and rampant wickedness arise.
The masses grumble below,
the celestial spirits rage above.
Either great floods run wild,
or extreme drought scorches the land,
mountains and valleys change form,
winter thunder and summer snow occur,
bloodshed floats shields,
corpses pile into mounds,
mass burials of surrendering troops number tens of thousands,
bones exchanged and children traded as food,
city walls higher but rams more ingenious,
moats deeper but ladders more clever,
laws clearer but robbers more numerous,
treaties frequent but rebellions more severe,
like frightened waves disturbing fish and turtles in the depths,
dense nets agitating birds in the marshes,
numerous wolves distressing beasts in the forests,
fierce fires boiling small fish in the cauldron.
There are cases of rulers and ministers swapping positions,
fathers and sons turning blades on each other,
only then do loyalty and righteousness gain fame in a crumbling state,
filial piety earns praise in a ruined family.
Epidemics arise and shamans become valued,
morality collapses and Confucianism and Mohism gain importance.
From this perspective,
the precedence between Confucianism and Daoism
can be determined."
Someone asked:
"In ancient times, Chìsōngzǐ, Wángqiáo, Qíngāo, Lǎoshì, Péngzǔ, Wùchéng, and Yùhuá were all true men,
yet they all served in the world,
not fleeing far into seclusion.
But since middle antiquity,
those who practice the Way,
without exception drift away to remote hiding places, cutting off all traces.
Why is this?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"In remote antiquity, purity and simplicity prevailed;
cunning and artifice had not yet sprouted.
diligently studied it,
Those who believed in the Way
merely remained silent.
while those who did not believe
did not pass their lips;
Slanderous words
did not reside in their breasts.
malicious intentions to harm others
Therefore, the true men moved leisurely among the people,
not hastily ascending to distant realms.
In the decadent customs of later ages,
deceit and artifice deepened,
the transformative power of profound tranquility was abandoned,
and factions of wicked customs multiplied.
Since they did not believe in the Way,
they delighted in ridicule and slander,
calling the genuine and correct demonic falsehoods,
regarding divine immortals as absurd delusions,
some saying they delude the masses,
others claiming they disrupt the community.
Hence, superior individuals feel ashamed to dwell among them.
The enlightened men of old
prevented troubles at their inception,
withdrew at the first sign of trouble,
not waiting until dawn if night fell,
acting upon perceiving the subtle signs,
not lingering until the day's end.
Thus, when Zhào harmed Míngdú,
Zhòngní immediately turned his carriage around;
when the sweet wine was no longer set out,
Mùshēng departed like a shooting star;
when the enemy was numerous and they were few,
Huà Yuán left them.
How much more so for the wise and discerning,
whose pursuits and aspirations fundamentally differ?
What attachment could make them stay in such a place?
When the deep pool dries up and the pond is drained,
the flood dragons do not swim there;
when the nest is overturned and the eggs gathered,
the phoenix does not roost;
when slanderous words are spoken in the house,
the soaring gulls do not descend;
when common flowers are cut in spring,
the auspicious zhī and míng plants do not bloom;
since the vulgar world detests correctness,
contempt and侮辱 are sure to come.
How could those who possess the Way
not soar aloft, shaking their wings beyond the winds and clouds,
and swiftly hide their tracks in the realm of profound silence?
It is not that the mountains and forests possess the Way,
but those who practice the Way must enter the mountains and forests,
truly wishing to distance themselves from that foul stench
and approach this purity and tranquility.
Those who enter the nine chambers for refined contemplation,
preserving the true unity to summon spirits,
neither enjoy noise and clamor nor associate with filth and defilement.
And those who compound the great medicine of the golden elixir,
refining the flying essence of the eight minerals,
are especially wary of foolish people with sharp tongues
and the knowledge of ordinary folk.
The bright spirits will not descend because of them,
and the immortal medicine will not be completed.
This is no minor prohibition.
Remaining among people,
there may be those with shallow views who slander them to the authorities,
bringing upon them accusations and penalties;
or there may be visits from relatives and old friends,
dragging them into celebrations and condolences.
It is better to withdraw into seclusion, cutting off all such ties,
to avoid these stinking rats.
Their solitary journey far away,
finding contentment in the mountain peaks,
is there not reason for it?
Some say:
Superior individuals attain the Way amid the three armies;
middle individuals attain the Way in the bustling cities;
inferior individuals attain the Way in the mountains and forests.
This refers to when the immortal medicine is already completed,
and they do not yet wish to ascend to heaven.
Though they are amid the three armies,
swords and blades cannot harm them;
though they are in the bustling cities,
human calamities cannot touch them.
But inferior individuals have not reached this stage,
so they remain in the mountains and forests.
This does not mean that those of the highest grade,
when first learning the Way, should remain in the three armies or bustling cities to attain it.
If that were so, then Huáng and Lǎo could have remained until now without leaving."
Someone asked:
"That the Dao is the root source,
and Confucianism the later branches,
I have already heard explained.
But what exactly are
the minor differences between them today?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The teachings of bowing and rising,
the intricate rituals of three thousand rules,
the methods of attack and defense, advance and retreat,
the principles of valuing righteousness over life,
the matters of joy and sorrow, rites and music,
the strategies for governing the world and aiding customs—
these are the concerns of the Confucians.
Rejecting external things and discarding wisdom,
cleansing oneself of cunning and change,
forgetting wealth and disdaining nobility,
blocking encouragement and discouragement,
not worrying over poverty,
not glorying in success,
not grieving over slander,
not delighting in praise—
these are the pursuits of the Daoists.
Confucians offer sacrifices to pray for blessings,
while Daoists tread the correct path to ward off evil.
What Confucians cherish is power and profit;
what Daoists treasure is desirelessness.
Confucians are anxious for fame and gain;
while Daoists embrace unity to perfect themselves alone.
What Confucians discuss
are the ledgers of mutual contention.
What Daoists practice
are the teachings that dispel emotions.
As for the Daoists,
in their actions,
they excel at self-cultivation to accomplish tasks;
in their dwelling,
they excel at taking what others do not contend for;
in their governance,
they excel at cutting off calamities before they arise;
in their giving,
they excel at aiding things without claiming virtue;
in their movement,
they excel at observing the people to focus their minds;
in their stillness,
they excel at residing cautiously without distress.
This is why they are the sovereign leaders of the hundred schools,
the ancestral source of benevolence and righteousness.
The principle of their minor differences
is roughly as described;
from beginning to end, in rise and fall,
this has not changed."
Someone said:
"The Ruists,
exemplified by the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
base their teachings on the Six Classics,
which serve as the foundation for governing the world and preserving righteousness,
and as the standards for personal conduct and behavior.
Their influence is far-reaching and their work esteemed,
their affairs are grand and their language elegant,
constituting immutable institutions for states and families.
Yet those who follow the Dào,
disregard ritual teachings,
ignore the great moral principles,
companion with foxes and badgers in the marshes,
associate with apes and monkeys in the forests and hills,
rejecting society in a solitary manner,
neighboring with trees and stones.
This is like the confusion of one who runs east
while forgetting the sweetness of the sunflower."
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Elaborate rhetoric and dazzling displays,
are not valued by the straightforward;
dispelling ignorance and rescuing the confused,
is what I have long been content with.
I truly do not wish to argue with you about the validity of principles,
nor debate gains and losses with clever words.
Yet seeing a child fall into a well,
would move any benevolent person;
witnessing a blind man bump into a pillar,
would stir anyone who advocates universal love.
Thus I shall outline the main points,
roughly presenting one aspect.
Those who embody the Dào to shape all things,
and treasure virtue to prolong life,
are the followers of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ.
Huángdì could bring peace and prosperity to the world,
and also ascended as an immortal,
so he cannot be considered inferior to Yáo and Shùn.
Lǎozǐ both integrated ritual teachings,
and achieved longevity,
so he cannot be considered lesser than the Duke of Zhōu or Confucius.
Thus Confucius sighed with a desire to compare himself to Lǎozǐ,
and I have never heard him speak any critical words.
Yet ordinary people in these decadent times,
unable to find the right path,
cultivate Ruist and Mohist teachings while slandering Daoism.
How is this different from descendants cursing their own ancestors?
This shows ignorance of one's origins,
and is truly excessive.
The arm of a dwarf
cannot topple Mount Sōng or Huà;
the leg of the Jiāoyáo people
cannot fathom the vast ocean.
Often I see mediocre Ruists who cling to outdated ways,
busy with their familiar practices,
lacking broad understanding of principles,
admonishing the stubborn and commanding the unruly,
elaborately decorating their harsh words,
slandering and accusing Daoism,
discussing the dregs of its teachings,
like watching a steed pass by a crack
—when they touch upon the profound depths of its spirit,
they drown and lose themselves.
Like quails flapping their short wings
to ride the waves of the ocean god,
or flies with their feeble bodies
attempting to climb the steep cliffs where apes dwell,
such tasks are beyond their capacity,
only hastening their exhaustion.
Yet they chatter while confined to their narrow views,
their hearing unable to grasp the vast,
their sight unable to penetrate the distant,
and wish to rise on tiptoe to embrace the three lights,
or puff their bellies to rival the thunder god.
Is this not blindness?
For only by ascending the lofty celestial pole
can one realize the extreme lowness of a well or valley;
only by witnessing the bright sun shining in the sky
can one recognize the shabbiness of common brass.
I was not born with knowledge,
nor did I believe in youth;
at first I was also confused,
just like you.
But having witnessed the profound cultivation of these mysteries,
I regret not escaping my confusion earlier.
The matters of the Five Classics,
with their clear and exposed commentaries,
can still be incomprehensible
to beginning learners.
How much more so the golden tablets and jade scrolls,
the scriptures of immortality,
with their essential teachings
often left unwritten?
Only upon mounting the altar and smearing blood on lips
are oral instructions transmitted.
If one is not the right person,
even if offered territories and linked cities,
or halls filled with gold and jade,
these teachings are not recklessly revealed.
The pointers are profound and the return distant;
even with the texts in hand but without a master's instruction,
one would look up without seeing the head,
look down without knowing the heel.
How could you possibly comprehend this in detail?
Those who attain immortality
may ascend to the Great Clarity,
or soar through the purple heavens,
visit Mysterious Continent,
or dwell on Mount Kūntóng,
listen to the music of the Heavenly Court,
enjoy feasts of magical mushrooms,
travel abroad with Sōng Qiáo and Wáng Zǐqiáo beyond the inverted shadows,
and feast with Chángyáng in jade chambers upon returning.
Why would they need to companion with foxes and badgers or associate with apes?
This shows you speak without understanding.
The Dào
allows one to wander with rainbows,
soar through crimson skies,
traverse the six directions with vast cliffs,
going wherever the mind wishes.
Solitary rejection of society
is not considered sorrowful.
Gathered fattened sacrificial animals,
though adorned with embroidered trappings,
when considering their joy,
how can they compare to the extraordinary unicorn leaving the herd to roam alone,
or the auspicious light breaking from its mate to enjoy abundant blessings?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
The Shénnóng's Four Classics state,
"Superior medicines enable one's body to be at ease and life prolonged,
ascending to become celestial spirits,
roaming freely above and below,
commanding myriad numinous beings,
growing feathers on the body,
with feast preparations instantly arriving."
It also says,
"The five zhī fungi, as well as consuming cinnabar, yùzhá, zēngqīng, realgar, orpiment, mica, and tàiyǐ yǔyúliáng,
each can be taken individually,
all enabling one to fly and attain longevity."
It further states,
"Medium medicines nurture one's nature,
inferior medicines eliminate illnesses,
enabling poisonous insects not to attack,
ferocious beasts not to assault,
malignant energies not to circulate,
and various evil spirits all to be warded off."
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì also says,
"Pepper and ginger ward off dampness,
calamus enhances hearing,
jùshèng prolongs life,
wēixǐ repels weapons."
These are all the utmost words of the highest sages,
truthful records of esoteric techniques,
clearly written and luminous,
yet people in the world ultimately do not believe them—
this is truly lamentable.
Among immortal medicines, the highest is cinnabar,
next is gold,
next is silver,
next are the various zhī fungi,
next are the five jades,
next is mica,
next are bright pearls,
next is realgar,
next is tàiyǐ yǔyúliáng,
next is shízhōnghuángzǐ,
next is stone cassia,
next is quartz,
next is stone brain,
next is stone sulfur,
next is stone terrace,
next is zēngqīng,
next are pine and cypress resin, poria, dìhuáng, maimendong, wood jùshèng, chónglóu, huánglián, stone felt, paper mulberry fruit, and xiàngchái,
also known as tuōlú.
Some call it immortal's staff,
some call it Xīwángmǔ's staff,
some name it tiānjīng,
some name it age-repeller,
some name it earth bone,
some name it gǒuqǐ.
Tiānméndōng,
sometimes called dìméndōng,
or yánméndōng,
or diānjí,
or yínyángshí,
or guǎnsōng.
That which grows on high ground,
with short roots and sweet taste,
and fragrant qi, is superior.
That which grows in lowlands near water,
with leaves thin like pondweed and slightly yellow,
long roots and mostly bitter taste,
and foul-smelling qi, is inferior,
yet still consumable.
However, it tends to make one's qi descend,
and its benefits are particularly slow.
After consuming it for a hundred days,
all will be more effective than shū and huángjīng,
and one can steam it when entering the mountains.
If boiling and eating it,
taking enough can enable grain abstinence.
If one has the resources, it can be taken as an elixir,
or made into powder,
and also by squeezing its juice to make wine,
though taking the powder is especially good.
People of Chǔ call tiānméndōng bǎibù,
but there is actually a bǎibù herb,
whose roots all number about a hundred,
similar and uniform,
though their sprouts are slightly different.
True bǎibù sprouts resemble báxiè,
only suitable for treating coughs and killing lice,
not fit for consumption—
one must not mistake them.
Like huángjīng, also called báijí,
but actually not the báijí used for making paste.
According to the Běncǎo, many medicinal herbs share names with other plants,
only the precise and learned can distinguish them—
this cannot be overlooked.
Huángjīng is also called rabbit bamboo,
called rescuer from poverty,
called hanging pearls.
Consuming its flowers is better than its fruit,
consuming its fruit is better than its root,
but the flowers are hard to obtain in quantity.
Obtaining ten hú of fresh flowers,
when dried yields only five or six dǒu,
and the daily consumption is merely three gě,
impossible to prepare without great effort.
Only after consuming huángjīng for ten years
can one greatly reap its benefits.
Both are inferior to shū for grain abstinence;
shū as an elixir makes one robust and healthy,
able to carry heavy loads and traverse dangers,
but not as sweet and tasty as huángjīng, which is easier to eat.
In famine years, it can substitute grain for the old and young;
people unable to distinguish it
call it dried rice.
As for the five zhī fungi,
there are stone zhī,
wood zhī,
grass zhī,
flesh zhī,
and mushroom zhī,
each with about a hundred varieties.
The stone mushroom,
the stone elephant mushroom grows on famous mountains by the sea,
and on the shores of islands where rocks accumulate.
Its form resembles flesh with a head, tail, and four limbs,
quite similar to living creatures.
It attaches to large rocks,
preferring high peaks and perilous places,
sometimes hanging upside down or attached upward.
The red ones are like coral,
the white like cut fat,
the black like glossy lacquer,
the green like kingfisher feathers,
the yellow like purple gold,
and all are brilliantly translucent like solid ice.
On dark nights, from three hundred paces away,
one can see their glow.
The larger ones weigh over ten jīn,
the smaller three to four jīn.
Unless one has long maintained utmost purity,
and carries the Lǎo zǐ Rù Shān Líng Bǎo Wǔ Fú,
one cannot see these beings.
Whenever encountering any mushroom,
first place the Kāi Shān Què Hài Fú on it,
then it can no longer hide or transform away.
Slowly choose an auspicious day,
set up a ritual offering with wine and dried meat,
pray and then gather it,
all while walking the Yǔ steps from under the sun, holding one's breath.
If one obtains the stone elephant mushroom,
pound it thirty-six thousand times,
take a fāng cùn bǐ dose,
three times a day.
After consuming one jīn,
one gains a thousand years;
ten jīn,
then ten thousand years.
It can also be shared for others to consume.
The jade fat mushroom,
grows on jade-bearing mountains,
often in precarious, hanging locations.
Jade ointment flows out,
and after ten thousand years or more,
it congeals to form a mushroom,
resembling the shapes of birds and beasts,
with no constant color,
mostly like dark mountain or pale water jade.
It is also bright and clear like crystal.
Obtain and powder it,
mix it with heartless grass juice,
and in a moment, it turns into liquid.
Drink one shēng,
and gain a thousand years.
The seven-bright and nine-light mushrooms,
are both stone,
growing on high mountain cliffs near water,
shaped like plates or bowls,
not exceeding a foot in diameter.
They have stems and bases connecting them,
rising three to four inches,
those with seven holes
are called seven-bright,
those with nine holes are called nine-light.
Their lights are like stars,
within over a hundred paces,
their glow is visible at night.
Their lights are distinct,
can scatter but not merge.
Often obtained by waiting during the autumn equinox,
pound and take a fāng cùn bǐ dose,
upon entering the mouth, the body suddenly feels warm,
the taste sweet and delicious.
After consuming one jīn, one gains a thousand years,
making one's body glow,
lighting the dark surroundings like the moon,
enabling night vision.
The stone honey mushroom,
grows in the stone doors of Shǎoshì Shān,
inside the doors are deep valleys,
impassable.
Throw a stone into the valley,
and after half a day, its sound is still heard.
Over ten zhàng outside the door is a stone pillar,
on the pillar lies a reclining cover stone,
about a zhàng in height and diameter.
One can see the honey mushroom falling from the stone door into the reclining cover,
after a long while,
a drop falls,
like residual leakage from a roof after rain,
only occasionally.
Yet the honey mushroom falls incessantly,
but the reclining cover never overflows.
On the door, characters are carved in tadpole script,
saying that consuming one dǒu of stone honey mushroom grants ten thousand years of life.
Various Dàoshi have pondered the place,
but none can reach it.
The only way is to attach a bowl to a sturdy bamboo or wood pole to catch it,
yet no one has managed to do so.
According to the inscription on this stone door,
someone in ancient times must have obtained it.
The stone cassia mushroom,
grows in stone caves of famous mountains,
resembling a cassia tree but being stone.
About a chǐ tall,
and a chǐ in diameter,
bright and pungent in taste,
with branches.
Pound and consume one jīn to gain a thousand years.
Shí zhōng huáng zǐ,
can be found in many places,
especially in Qìn Shuǐ Shān.
Inside large rocks,
the rock is often moist and not dry.
Break the rock through dozens of layers,
to obtain it.
Inside the large rock,
it appears red-yellow and fluid,
like an egg within its shell.
It should be drunk immediately,
or it will harden into stone,
and no longer suitable for consumption.
The method is to drink it before it hardens;
once solidified, it should be powdered and taken.
Breaking one rock,
may yield up to one shēng,
or as little as a few gě.
It can be taken in one dose.
Although not obtainable in large quantities,
if taken successively,
totaling the amounts consumed,
reaching three shēng,
grants a thousand years of life.
One may wish to consume more,
but it is hard to obtain.
The stone brain mushroom,
grows in talc,
also similar to shí zhōng huáng zǐ in form,
but not always present.
Break about a thousand large talc stones,
to possibly get one piece.
When first broken open,
inside the stone,
it shines with five colors and moves on its own.
Consuming one shēng grants a thousand years.
The stone sulfur mushroom,
found in all five sacred mountains,
but abundant in Jī Shān.
Local legends say Xǔ Yóu consumed it here for longevity,
hence he no longer cared for wealth and honor,
and declined Emperor Yáo's abdication.
Stone sulfur elixir,
is the red essence of stone,
a type of stone sulfur.
Both seep out between cliffs and banks,
the moist ones can be formed into pills for consumption,
the hardened ones can be powdered and taken.
There are one hundred twenty such varieties,
all are stone mushrooms,
recorded in the Tài Yǐ Yù Cè and Chāng Yǔ Nèi Jì,
too numerous to list in full.
As for the Wood Mushroom,
when pine and cypress resin sinks into the ground for a thousand years,
it transforms into Pórilíng,
and after ten thousand years,
a small plant grows on top of it,
resembling a lotus flower in shape,
named Mùwēixǐzhī.
It glows when viewed at night,
feels very smooth when held,
does not burn when set on fire,
and repels weapons when carried.
If you attach it to one chicken and mix it with twelve other chickens in a cage,
step back twelve paces,
and shoot twelve arrows,
the other chickens will all be injured,
but the one carrying the Wēixǐzhī will remain unharmed.
It should be picked from the direction of the life gate,
dried in the shade during the Liùjiǎ days,
for a hundred days,
then ground and taken in doses of one square cùn bǐ,
three times a day.
After consuming one whole piece,
one will live three thousand years.
The thousand-year-old Guāmù tree
has roots beneath it shaped like a seated person,
seven cùn long,
and when carved, it bleeds.
Applying its blood to the soles of the feet
allows one to walk on water without sinking;
applying it to a person's nose before entering water
causes the water to part,
enabling one to stay at the bottom of deep pools;
applying it to the body makes one invisible,
and to become visible again, wipe it off.
It can also cure illnesses:
for internal abdominal ailments,
scrape and take one dāoguī dose;
for external swellings and pains,
scrape one dāoguī dose according to the affected area,
and rub it on the swollen or painful spot;
all will heal immediately upon contact.
For example, if the left foot is afflicted,
then scrape and apply it to the left foot.
Also, scrape it and mix with Jùshèng to make a candle;
at night, shine it all over the ground,
and where there are gold, jade, or treasure hoards,
the light will turn blue and droop downward;
dig with a spade to obtain them.
Grind it into powder,
and after consuming ten jīn, one will live a thousand years.
Also, pine branches that are three thousand years old
contain accumulated resin in their bark,
shaped like a dragon,
named Fēijiézhī.
Large ones weigh ten jīn;
grind and take it,
and after consuming ten jīn,
one gains five hundred years.
There is also Fántáozhī,
whose plant is like a rising dragon,
with flowers and leaves like red silk,
and fruits like a kingfisher bird,
standing no more than five chǐ tall.
It grows in the shade of famous mountains,
on soil near east-flowing springs.
Wait for it during the Lìxià solar term,
obtain it, grind, and take it;
consuming one whole plant grants five thousand years.
Shēnchéngzhī
is red and glowing,
and when its branches and leaves are tapped,
they sound like metal or stone.
If broken and reattached,
it immediately restores itself.
Mùqúzhī
parasitizes large trees,
resembling a lotus flower,
with nine stems in a cluster,
and a taste that is sweet and pungent.
Jiànmùzhīshí grows in Dūguǎng,
its bark like that of a python,
and its fruit like a luán bird.
Taking any of these three mushrooms
allows one to ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Huánglúzǐ, Xúnmùhuá, Xuányèhuá—
these three mushrooms grow in Tàishān, Yàoxiāng, and Fènggāo.
Those who obtain and take them
will all live a thousand years.
Huángtánhuánzhī
is a thousand-year-old yellow plant,
with roots beneath like a three-hú vessel,
located one or two zhàng from the main stem,
connected by fine roots resembling threads.
Obtain it, grind, and take it;
consuming one whole piece makes one an earth immortal, never dying.
There are another hundred and twenty kinds of these,
each with its own illustration.
Among herb mushrooms, there is Dúyáozhī,
which sways without wind,
its stem as thick as a finger,
red as cinnabar,
with plain leaves resembling amaranth.
Its root has a large core like a dou measure,
surrounded by twelve smaller ones like eggs,
arranged around the main root in four directions,
like the twelve celestial stems.
They are about a zhàng apart,
all with fine roots,
like white hairs connecting them.
It grows on high mountains and deep valleys,
with no grass around it.
Obtain the large core, grind, and take it;
after consuming it all, one gains a thousand years.
Taking one of the smaller pieces grants a hundred years,
and it can be shared with others.
Carrying the large root makes one invisible;
to become visible, turn left and remove it.
Niújiǎozhī
grows on Hǔshòu Shān and Wúbǎn,
shaped like scallions,
uniquely growing like an ox horn,
three or four chǐ long,
and green in color.
Grind and take one square cùn bǐ dose,
three times a day.
After a hundred days,
one gains a thousand years.
Lóngxiānzhī
looks like ascending dragons supporting each other,
with leaves as scales,
and roots like coiled dragons.
Taking one piece grants a thousand years.
Mámǔzhī
resembles hemp with a red stem
and purple flowers.
Zǐzhūzhī
has yellow flowers,
red leaves,
and fruits like plums but purple,
with twenty-four branches connected,
hanging like strung pearls.
Báifúzhī
is four or five chǐ tall,
resembling plum trees,
often blooming during heavy snow,
and bearing fruit in late winter.
Zhūcǎozhī
has nine bends,
each bend with three leaves,
and each leaf with three fruits.
Wǔdézhī
looks like a multi-storied pavilion,
with a square stem,
and leaves displaying five colors each, distinct and unmixed,
the top like an inverted canopy,
often with sweet dew inside,
and purple energy rising several chǐ.
Lóngxiánzhī
often grows in opposing pairs in mid-spring,
with three nodes and twelve branches,
and roots below like a seated person.
All these herb mushrooms,
another hundred and twenty kinds,
should be dried in the shade and taken,
enabling one to live as long as heaven and earth,
or to attain a thousand or two thousand years.
The Fleshly Excrescence refers to the ten-thousand-year-old toad,
with horns on its head,
and beneath its chin, there are eight characters in vermilion script written twice over.
It should be captured at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
dried in the shade for a hundred days.
Using its left foot to draw on the ground
will create flowing water.
Carrying its left hand on one's person
wards off the five weapons;
if an enemy shoots at you,
the arrows from bows and crossbows will turn back toward them.
The thousand-year-old bat,
white as snow,
hangs upside down when gathered,
due to the heaviness of its brain.
Obtain these two creatures, dry them in the shade, powder them, and ingest them;
it will enable a person to live for forty thousand years.
The thousand-year-old spiritual turtle
is adorned with five colors;
the male has two bones on its forehead that protrude like horns.
Bathe it in sheep's blood,
then carve out its shell,
roast it over fire, pound it, and take a square-inch spoonful,
three times a day,
until one whole turtle is consumed,
to live a thousand years.
When walking in the mountains,
if you see small people riding carriages or horses,
seven or eight inches tall,
they are Fleshly Excrescences;
capture and ingest them to become immortal.
The wind-born beast resembles a marten,
blue in color,
as large as a wildcat,
born in the great forests of the Southern Sea.
Set nets to catch it,
pile several cartloads of firewood to burn it;
when the wood is consumed, the beast remains in the ashes unburned,
its fur unscorched,
impervious to chopping or stabbing,
feeling like a leather bag when struck.
Strike its head dozens of times with an iron hammer to kill it;
once dead, it opens its mouth toward the wind,
and in a moment revives and runs away.
Plug its nose with stone calamus to kill it.
Take its brain, mix it with chrysanthemums, and ingest it;
after consuming ten jin,
one gains five hundred years of life.
Also, the thousand-year-old swallow
has its nest entrance facing north,
mostly white in color with a stubby tail.
Capture it, dry it in the shade,
powder it, and ingest one to live five hundred years.
In total, there are another hundred and twenty kinds,
all of which are Fleshly Excrescences.
Fungus Excrescences
may grow deep in the mountains,
under large trees,
or beside springs.
Their shapes may resemble palaces,
carriages and horses,
dragons and tigers,
human forms,
or flying birds,
with varying colors.
There are also a hundred and twenty kinds,
each with its own illustration.
One should always take the Yu step to gather them,
carve them with a bone knife,
dry them in the shade, powder them, and take a square-inch spoonful,
enabling one to ascend to immortality;
the medium grade grants several thousand years,
the lower grade a thousand years.
To seek the Excrescence herbs,
enter a famous mountain,
necessarily in the third or ninth month,
the months when the mountains open to yield divine medicines.
Do not go on inauspicious mountain days;
it must be during Tianfu time,
especially favorable when the Three Marvels converge.
Exit through the Three Marvels auspicious gate to the mountain,
on a Six Yin day,
during Mingtang time,
carry the Lingbao talisman,
lead a white dog,
hold a white chicken,
with a peck of white salt
and the mountain-opening talisman and proclamation,
place them on a large rock,
grasp a handful of Wútáng grass to enter the mountain;
the mountain spirits will be pleased,
and you will surely obtain the Excrescence.
Also, when gathering and ingesting Excrescences,
choose days of Wang, Xiang, Zhuan, and He harmony,
with heavenly stems and earthly branches mutually generating each other as best.
These various Excrescences are found in many famous mountains,
but ordinary Taoists,
with unfocused minds,
filthy conduct and shallow virtue,
and unaware of mountain-entry techniques,
even with the illustrations,
do not recognize their forms,
and thus ultimately cannot obtain them.
Mountains, regardless of size,
all have ghosts and spirits;
if these spirits do not give the Excrescence to a person,
even if one treads on it,
it remains invisible.
Also, mica has five types,
which most people cannot distinguish.
The method is to hold it up to the sun,
observe its color,
and examine it in detail
to know.
Simply viewing it in a shaded place,
one cannot see its mixed colors.
With all five colors present and predominantly blue, it is called Yúnyīng,
best ingested in spring.
With all five colors present and predominantly red, it is called Yúnzhū,
best ingested in summer.
With all five colors present and predominantly white, it is called Yúnyè,
best ingested in autumn.
With all five colors present and predominantly black, it is called Yúnmǔ,
best ingested in winter.
With only blue and yellow colors, it is called Yúnshā,
best ingested in late summer.
Glistening pure white is called Línshí,
which can be ingested throughout the four seasons.
Methods for ingesting the five micas include:
using cassia, onion, and crystal to dissolve it into water;
or exposing it to dew in an iron vessel,
simmering it with dark water into liquid;
or combining it with saltpeter in a tube, burying it to form water;
or mixing it with honey to make a paste;
or steeping it in autumn dew for a hundred days,
then pounding it in a leather bag into powder;
or combining it with Wúdiān grass and Ailanthus blood to form a pill.
Ingesting it for one year
cures all diseases;
taking it long-term for three years,
an old man reverts to a youth;
five years without interruption
enables one to command ghosts and spirits,
enter fire unburned,
enter water unwetted,
tread on thorns without skin injury,
and meet immortals.
Moreover, other substances rot when buried
and char when put to fire,
but the five micas, when placed in fierce flames,
do not burn over time,
and when buried, never decay,
