thus enabling longevity.
It is also said
that after ingesting for ten years,
cloud qi often covers the person above;
ingesting the mother to attract the child
follows the principle of nature.
Also, when viewing it toward the sun,
if a dim, pure black color appears,
it is unfit for ingestion,
as it causes urinary diseases and sores.
Even when taken with water,
it should first be steeped for a hundred days
in water from a thatched roof's eaves
or flowing eastward river water or dew,
then rinsed to remove earth and stones,
before it can be used.
Wèi Shūqīng of Zhōngshān ingested it;
over time, he could ride clouds and travel.
He sealed the formula in a jade box,
and after he ascended to immortality,
his son named Shì,
along with the Hàn envoy Liáng Bó,
obtained it, followed the formula to prepare and ingest it,
and both ascended to immortality.
Furthermore, realgar must be from the Wǔdū Mountains,
pure and unadulterated,
with a red color like a rooster's comb,
shining brightly and brilliantly—
only then can it be used.
If it is merely pure yellow resembling realgar's color,
without a red glow,
it is not suitable for making elixirs of immortality,
but can be used in medicines to treat illnesses.
The methods of taking it as a remedy
include steaming or boiling it,
or taking it with wine,
or first dissolving it with saltpeter into water and then solidifying it,
or wrapping it in pig's intestine and steaming it under red clay,
or mixing it with pine resin,
or refining it with three substances,
until it stretches like cloth,
white as ice.
Taking any of these can make one live long,
cure all diseases,
expel the three corpse worms,
erase scars,
turn white hair black,
and regrow lost teeth.
After a thousand days, jade maidens will come to serve,
allowing one to command them,
and even summon a mobile kitchen.
Moreover, jade maidens often have yellow jade as a mark,
as large as a millet grain,
on their noses—
these are true jade maidens.
Those without this mark
are demons testing humans.
Jade is also an elixir of immortality,
but it is hard to obtain.
The Jade Classic says:
"Those who ingest gold will live as long as gold;
those who ingest jade will live as long as jade."
It also says:
"Those who ingest Xuánzhēn,
their lifespan knows no bounds."
Xuánzhēn
is another name for jade.
It enables the body to fly and rise lightly,
not just as an earthbound immortal.
However, the path is slow to achieve;
one must ingest one to two hundred pounds
before effects are known.
Jade can be dissolved into water with black rice wine or Sanguisorba wine,
or liquefied into paste with scallion juice,
or made into pills for ingestion,
or burned into powder.
Taking it for over a year,
one can enter water without getting wet,
enter fire without being burned,
blades will not injure,
and all poisons will not harm.
Do not use finished jade objects,
as they harm people without benefit;
one must obtain raw jade
to be usable,
with white jade from the Kingdom of Yútián being especially good.
Next, jade from the territory of Xúshàn Pavilion in Nányáng and from the waters of Lúróng in Rìnán is also excellent.
Chìsōngzǐ used the blood of a mysterious creature to soak jade into water and ingested it,
hence he could ride smoke up and down.
Ingesting jade powder or taking it with water
both grant immortality.
The reason it is considered inferior to gold
is that it often causes fever,
similar to the effects of cold-food powder.
If taking jade powder,
one should every ten days take one knife measure each of realgar and cinnabar,
then wash with cold water to disperse the effects,
and walk against the wind—
then fever will not occur.
Dǒng Jūnyì once gave jade liquor to a blind man to drink,
and his eyes were healed in ten days.
There was a man named Wú Yánzhì,
who wished to ingest jade,
but obtained an incomplete Jade Classic formula,
completely unaware of its procedures and taboos.
He gathered many jade guī, zhāng, rings, and discs,
as well as numerous items used for swords,
intending to prepare and ingest them.
Later, I explained to him these were unusable,
and he sighed, saying:
"One must be meticulous in such matters;
not only is there no benefit,
it nearly caused disaster."
Also, silver is only inferior to gold and jade,
but can lead to earthbound immortality.
The method of ingestion
involves dissolving it in wheat water,
or taking it with vermilion herb wine,
or refining it with dragon fat.
However, taking just three doses,
each as large as a pellet,
is beyond the means of poor Taoists.
Moreover, pearls over an inch in diameter can be ingested;
taking them grants longevity.
Soaking them in fermented milk turns them into liquid like mercury;
they can also be dissolved with pumice water and wasp nests,
wrapped with red snake gall and combined,
stretched to three or four feet long,
and taken as pills.
If taken while abstaining from grains,
one becomes immortal and lives forever.
Pure lacquer that does not stick
can make one communicate with spirits and live long when ingested.
The method of taking it
involves putting ten large "gutless princes,"
or said to be large crabs,
into it,
or using mica water,
or jade water to combine and ingest it.
All nine worms will be expelled,
bad blood will exit through the nose,
and within a year, the six jia spirits will bring a mobile kitchen.
Cinnamon can be combined with scallion juice and steamed into water,
or taken with bamboo sap,
or mixed with the brain of a "knower of the future,"
or said to be a turtle,
and ingested.
After seven years,
one can walk on water,
living forever without death.
Jùshèng, also called sesame,
prevents aging when ingested,
resists wind and dampness,
and rejuvenates the aged.
Peach resin soaked in mulberry ash water
cures all diseases when taken;
long-term use makes the body light and radiant,
glowing like the moon in dark nights.
Taking it in large amounts allows one to abstain from grains.
The red fruit of the citron tree,
taken for a year,
reverses aging in the old,
enabling clear vision and seeing ghosts.
Once, the Taoist Liáng Xū, aged seventy, took it
and became younger;
by 140 years old,
he could write at night,
outrun galloping horses,
and later entered Qīnglóng Mountain.
Sophora seeds placed in a new jar sealed with mud
for over twenty days
until their skins rot,
then washed and taken like soybeans daily,
primarily nourish the brain.
Long-term use
keeps hair from turning white and grants longevity.
Formulas from Xuánzhōng vines,
such as Chǔ fēilián, Alisma, Rehmannia, Coptis, and the like,
over three hundred kinds in total,
all can prolong life
and be taken singly.
Língfēi powder, Wèijué pills, Zhìmìng pills, and sheep blood pills
all preserve youth and ward off aging.
In the mountains of Lì County, Nányáng, there is the Sweet Valley Water,
which is sweet because
on both sides of the valley grow sweet chrysanthemums,
and their blossoms fall into the water.
Over many generations,
the water's flavor has thus changed.
The residents living by this valley
all do not dig wells,
but consume the Sweet Valley Water entirely.
Those who drink it all live to old age,
with the oldest reaching 140-150 years,
and the youngest not less than 80-90,
with no premature deaths,
all due to the power of these chrysanthemums.
Therefore, former Ministers Wáng Chàng, Liú Kuān, and Yuán Wěi,
who all served as governors of Nányáng,
upon taking office,
often ordered Lì County to send forty hú of Sweet Valley Water monthly for their consumption.
These gentlemen mostly suffered from rheumatism and dizziness,
and all recovered,
but they couldn't gain as much benefit
as the valley's residents,
who had been drinking this water since childhood.
Also, chrysanthemums resemble yì flowers,
distinguished only by sweetness and bitterness:
chrysanthemums are sweet, yì is bitter,
as the saying goes, "bitter as yì."
Nowadays, true chrysanthemums exist in various places,
but are scarce.
They mostly grow by water,
with Gōushì Mountain and Lì County having the most.
The immortal recipes call them "sun essence" and "renewal,"
"full cycle"—all names for one chrysanthemum,
though its root, stem, flower, and fruit have different names.
The theories are very elegant,
but recent users have seen almost no effect,
precisely because they don't obtain the true chrysanthemum.
The Sweet Valley Water, having absorbed the chrysanthemum's essence,
is hardly worth mentioning,
yet its residents
all attain longevity.
How much more could proper medicine
not bring benefits?
My late grandfather, a court official, once served as magistrate of Línyuán.
He said there was a Liào family in this county
that enjoyed long lives generation after generation,
some over a hundred years,
others eighty or ninety.
Later, they moved away,
and their descendants began dying young.
Others living in their old house
resumed the pattern,
with subsequent generations living long.
From this, it was realized the house was responsible,
though the reason was unknown.
Suspecting the well water was unusually red,
they dug around the well
and found dozens of hú of cinnabar buried by ancients
a few feet from the well.
The cinnabar essence had seeped into the well via spring water,
hence drinking it conferred longevity.
How much more could ingesting refined cinnabar achieve?
I also heard of a Zhào Qú from Shàngdǎng
who suffered from leprosy for years,
untreated by many,
and was near death.
Some said he wouldn't survive,
so he was abandoned.
Later, his family, to avoid misfortune,
prepared provisions
and left him in a mountain cave.
In the cave, Qú
lamented his misfortune,
grieving day and night,
weeping for a month.
A passing immortal saw him
and took pity,
inquiring in detail.
Qú, recognizing an extraordinary being,
kowtowed and begged for mercy.
The immortal then gave him a bag of medicine
and taught him how to take it.
After about a hundred days,
his sores healed completely,
his complexion became radiant,
and his skin turned jade-smooth.
The immortal visited again,
and Qú thanked him for the gift of renewed life,
begging for the formula.
The immortal told him,
"This is just pine resin.
This mountain has plenty of it.
Refine and take it,
and you can live eternally."
Qú returned home,
his family first thinking him a ghost,
were greatly shocked.
Qú then took pine resin long-term,
his body becoming lighter,
strength increasing hundredfold,
climbing heights and crossing dangers
all day without tiring.
At 170 years old,
his teeth didn't fall out,
nor hair whiten.
One night, resting,
he suddenly saw a light in the room, mirror-bright,
and asked others,
but none saw it.
Over time, it grew,
illuminating the room like daylight.
Another night, he saw two fairy maidens on his face,
two to three inches tall,
fully formed,
just small,
playing between his mouth and nose.
This continued for about a year,
the maidens gradually growing
until they emerged beside him.
He often heard lute and zither music,
smiling joyfully alone.
After about 300 years among humans,
his appearance like a child's,
he entered Bàodú Mountain,
surely becoming an earth immortal.
Hearing of Qú's pine resin use,
people competed to take it.
Those with many laborers
used carts and donkeys
to fill their houses with it.
Those taking it longer
stopped within a month
without noticing great benefits,
showing how hard it is to find the determined.
Also, during Emperor Chéng of Hàn's reign,
hunters in Zhōngnán Mountain
saw a person without clothes,
body covered in black hair.
The hunters,
wanting to catch them,
found the person leaping over pits and valleys,
as if flying,
impossible to catch.
So they secretly watched the location
and captured them in a coordinated effort,
finding it was a woman.
Questioned,
she said, "I was a palace maid of Qín.
Hearing rebels from Guāndōng arrived,
the Qín king surrendered,
palaces burned,
I fled in panic into the mountains.
Starving with no food,
near death,
an old man taught me to eat pine needles and pine nuts.
At first, they were bitter,
but later I adapted,
ceasing to feel hunger or thirst,
cold in winter,
or heat in summer."
This woman must have been a palace maid of Qín's last king, Zǐyīng,
surviving to Emperor Chéng's time,
about 200 years later.
They took her back,
fed her grains,
but she initially found them smelly and vomited,
taking days to adjust.
After about two years,
her body hair fell out,
and she aged and died.
Had she not been found,
she would have become an immortal.
A Wén family from Nányáng
recounted their ancestor
who, during the late Hàn turmoil,
fled into the mountains,
starving and near death.
Someone taught him to eat zhú,
ending his hunger.
Decades later, he returned home,
looking younger,
stronger than before.
He said in the mountains,
his body felt light, ready to leap,
climbing heights and traversing dangers
for days without fatigue,
walking in ice and snow
without feeling cold.
He often saw on a high cliff
several people sitting opposite playing board games,
or reading,
who looked down at him.
He overheard them ask,
"Should this one be called up?"
One replied, "Not yet."
Zhú is also called shān lín,
or shān jīng.
Thus, the Divine Medicine Classic says:
"To seek eternal life,
always take shān jīng."
In ancient times, the Eight Immortals
each ingested one substance
to attain terrestrial immortality,
living for several hundred years each,
before combining them into the Divine Elixir and Liquid Gold,
thus ascending to the Great Purity.
If a person combines all eight substances,
refines and consumes them,
but fails to gain their power,
it is because the medicinal properties counteract and inhibit each other.
Hán Zhōng consumed calamus for thirteen years,
growing hair all over his body,
able to read ten thousand words a day,
memorizing them all,
and remaining unshivered in winter while bare-chested.
Moreover, calamus must grow on rocks,
with nine or more nodes per inch,
and the purple-flowered variety is especially excellent.
Zhào Tāzǐ consumed cinnamon for twenty years,
growing hair on his feet,
walking five hundred li a day,
and lifting a thousand jin with strength.
Yíménzǐ consumed schisandra for sixteen years,
acquiring a complexion like a jade maiden,
remaining dry when entering water,
and unscathed when entering fire.
Chǔ Wénzǐ consumed rehmannia for eight years,
gaining night vision with a glow,
and strength to arm a crossbow by hand.
Lín Zǐmíng consumed atractylodes for eleven years,
growing ears five inches long,
becoming as light as flying,
able to leap over ravines of about two zhang.
Dù Zǐwēi consumed asparagus root,
serving eighty concubines,
fathering one hundred thirty children,
and walking three hundred li a day.
Rén Zǐjì consumed poria cocos for eighteen years,
with immortal jade maidens following him,
able to appear and disappear at will,
no longer eating grains,
scars from moxibustion all vanishing,
face and body glowing like jade.
Língyáng Zǐzhòng consumed polygala for twenty years,
fathering thirty-seven children,
remembering everything read at a glance,
sitting here and vanishing there.
The Immortal Classics say:
Although one may ingest the leaves of plants,
and live for several hundred years,
if neglecting the Divine Elixir,
one will never become an immortal.
From this, it can be reasoned
that herbs merely prolong life,
and are not the medicine of immortality, as is clear.
Before one can make the elixir,
one may consume them
to sustain oneself temporarily.
Someone asked:
"When taking medicinal substances,
is there a proper sequence or timing?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"According to the Regimen of Ingestion by Zhōng Huángzǐ,
medicine for curing illness
should be taken before meals;
medicine for nurturing nature
should be taken after meals.
I consulted Master Zhèng about
why this is so.
Master Zhèng said,
this is easy to understand:
when using medicine to attack disease,
it should be taken when one has not eaten,
while the stomach is empty,
allowing the medicine's power to circulate easily;
if taken after meals,
the medicine would only attack the food and exhaust its strength;
if one wishes to nurture nature,
but takes the medicine before meals,
its power has not yet circulated,
and is driven downward by the food, unable to be retained,
thus rendering it ineffective."
Another question was asked:
"When people take medicine to nurture their nature,
it is said there are specific compatibilities,
is this true?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"According to the Jade Strategy Record and the Enlightening Classic,
both use the five notes and six affiliations
to determine the year and destiny of a person.
Zǐ and Wǔ belong to Gēng,
Mǎo and Yǒu belong to Jǐ,
Yín and Shēn belong to Wù,
Chǒu and Wèi belong to Xīn,
Chén and Xū belong to Bǐng,
Sì and Hài belong to Dīng.
Those obtained in one word
are Gōng and Earth.
Those obtained in three words
are Zhǐ and Fire.
Those obtained in five words
are Yǔ and Water.
Those obtained in seven words
are Shāng and Metal.
Those obtained in nine words
are Jué and Wood.
If one's destiny belongs to Earth,
one should not take blue/green medicine;
if belonging to Metal,
one should not take red medicine;
if belonging to Wood,
one should not take white medicine;
if belonging to Water,
one should not take yellow medicine;
if belonging to Fire,
one should not take black medicine.
This is based on the principle of the Five Elements,
where Wood overcomes Earth,
Earth overcomes Water,
Water overcomes Fire,
Fire overcomes Metal,
and Metal overcomes Wood.
As for the great medicine of golden elixir,
there is no discussion of compatibility or incompatibility.
One word: Gōng.
Gēngzǐ Gēngwǔ,
Xīnwèi Xīnchǒu,
Bǐngchén Bǐngxū,
Dīnghài Dīngsì,
Wùyín Wùshēn,
Jǐmǎo Jǐyǒu.
Three words: Zhǐ.
Jiǎchén Jiǎxū,
Yǐhài Yǐsì,
Bǐngyín Bǐngshēn,
Dīngyǒu Dīngmǎo,
Wùwǔ Wùzǐ,
Jǐwèi Jǐchǒu.
Five words: Yǔ.
Jiǎyín Jiǎshēn,
Yǐmǎo Yǐyǒu,
Bǐngzǐ Bǐngwǔ,
Dīngwèi Dīngchǒu,
Rénchén Rénxū,
Guǐsì Guǐhài.
Seven words: Shāng.
Jiǎzǐ Jiǎwǔ,
Yǐchǒu Yǐwèi,
Gēngchén Gēngxū,
Xīnsì Xīnhài,
Rénshēn Rényín,
Guǐmǎo Guǐyǒu.
Nine words: Jué.
Wùchén Wùxū,
Jǐsì Jǐhài,
Gēngyín Gēngshēn,
Xīnmǎo Xīnyǒu,
Rénwǔ Rénzǐ,
Guǐchǒu Guǐwèi.
The Pace of Yǔ method:
First lift the left foot,
right foot passes over left,
left foot joins right.
Next lift the right foot,
left foot passes over right,
right foot joins left.
Then lift the right foot again,
right foot passes over left,
left foot joins right.
In this way, three steps
should cover exactly two zhang and one chi,
leaving nine footprints behind.
A minor divine formula:
use three jin of true cinnabar,
one jin of white honey,
mix and sun-dry, then boil,
until it can be formed into pills.
Take ten pills the size of hemp seeds each morning,
within less than a year,
white hair will turn black again,
lost teeth will regrow,
the body will become moist and radiant,
with long-term use,
an old man can revert to youth,
and constant use leads to immortality without death.
The Minor Elixir of Gold recipe:
Melt the gold and immerse it in clear wine,
two hundred times out,
two hundred times in,
then it will boil.
When squeezed, it passes between the fingers,
making it like mud.
If it does not boil or when squeezed does not pass between the fingers,
then melt it again in the wine repeatedly.
Take one pill the size of a pellet when finished;
one may also divide one pill into smaller pills with liquid.
After taking it for thirty days,
regardless of cold or warmth,
divine beings and jade maidens will descend.
Silver can also be ingested as an elixir,
using the same method as gold.
Taking these two substances,
one may dwell in stone chambers on famous mountains,
and in one year, achieve ethereal ascent.
If taken in the human world,
one becomes an earthly immortal;
do not recklessly transmit this.
Liǎngyí Zǐ's method for ingesting melted gold:
three catties of pig's omentum fat,
one dou of strong vinegar,
take five taels of gold,
place in a vessel and decoct it,
remove from the furnace,
put the gold into the fat,
a hundred times in and a hundred times out,
the same with the vinegar.
Ingesting one catty of gold,
lifespan rivals heaven and earth;
eating half a catty of gold,
lifespan two thousand years;
five taels,
twelve hundred years.
Regardless of the amount,
it can be ingested.
It should be made on auspicious days,
then it is divinely effective;
do not transmit it to others,
if transmitted,
the medicine will not succeed nor be divine.
If one wishes to take medicine to expel the corpse-entities,
one should ingest cinnabar.
The method for ingesting cinnabar:
one catty of cinnabar,
pounded and sifted,
add three sheng of strong vinegar,
two sheng of pure lacquer.
Combine all three substances,
mix them thoroughly,
decoct over a low flame,
until it can be formed into pills.
Take three pills the size of hemp seeds,
twice daily.
After forty days,
all ailments in the abdomen are cured,
and the three corpse-entities depart;
taking it for a hundred days,
muscles and bones become strong;
taking it for a thousand days,
the Director of Fate erases the death register,
one is preserved with heaven and earth,
faces the sun and moon,
alters form and changes appearance,
transforms unfathomably,
casts no shadow at noon,
and moreover emits a distinct light.
Someone asked:
"If immortality must be attainable,
the sages would have cultivated it already,
yet the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius did not pursue it,
which shows that this Way does not exist, as can be known."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Sages are not necessarily immortals,
and immortals are not necessarily sages.
Sages receive their mandate,
but do not encounter the path to longevity;
they only wish to eliminate the cruel and remove the treacherous,
pacify dangers and quell violence,
establish rites and create music,
set forth laws and bequeath teachings,
rectify improper customs,
change wayward practices,
support rulers in peril,
aid states showing signs of collapse,
edit the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
compile the Hé and Luò writings,
author classics and decrees,
harmonize the Yǎ and Sòng hymns,
instruct the young and ignorant,
respond to summons from various states,
their chimneys never gathering smoke,
their mats never warming.
Their affairs are overwhelming and boundless,
lasting the whole year without end;
how could they then shut out sound and obscure sight,
turn vision inward and hearing backward,
practice breathing and guiding exercises,
maintain long fasts and perpetual purity,
enter chambers to refine their forms,
climb mountains to gather herbs,
count breaths and contemplate spirits,
abstain from grains and purify themselves?
As for those who seek immortality,
they only need unwavering determination and utmost faith,
diligence without slackness,
ability to be serene and tranquil,
then it can be attained;
it does not require great talent.
Having the lofty integrity to enter worldly life
becomes a heavy burden for practitioners of the Way.
If one can combine the great medicine,
and grasp the essentials of guarding the One and nurturing the spirit,
then longevity and enduring vision are achieved;
how could they compare to the limitless tasks that sages cultivate?
Moreover, what the world calls sages
are all sages who govern the world,
not sages who have attained the Way.
Sages who have attained the Way
are Huángdì and Lǎozi.
Sages who govern the world
are the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius.
Huángdì first governed the world and then ascended as an immortal;
this was a rare case of one capable of both.
Ancient emperors and kings
carved inscriptions on Mount Tài,
seventy-two of which can still be read,
while those worn away
are too numerous to count;
yet only Huángdì is recorded as an immortal,
which clearly shows the truth.
People in the world consider those exceptionally skilled
in what others cannot match
as sages.
Thus, those peerless in playing board games
are called chess sages;
hence, Yán Zǐqīng and Mǎ Suímíng today bear the name of chess sages.
Those supremely skilled in history and writing for their time
are called calligraphy sages;
hence, Huáng Xiàng and Hú Zhāo today bear the name of calligraphy sages.
Those exceptionally skilled in painting beyond others
are called painting sages;
hence, Wèi Xié and Zhāng Mò today bear the name of painting sages.
Those especially clever in carving and cutting
are called wood sages;
hence, Zhāng Héng and Mǎ Jūn today bear the name of wood sages.
Thus, Mèngzǐ called Bóyí
the sage of purity;
Liǔxià Huì,
the sage of harmony;
Yī Yǐn,
the sage of responsibility.
If I may elaborate and discuss it,
then sagehood is not confined to one matter.
Bān Shū, Chuí, and Dì
were sages of mechanics;
Fù, Biǎn, Hé, and Huǎn
were sages of healing;
Zǐ Wéi and Gān Jūn
were sages of divination;
Shǐ Sū and Xīn Liào
were sages of augury;
Xià Yù and Dù Huí
were sages of physical strength;
Jīng Kē and Niè Zhèng
were sages of courage;
Fēi Lián and Kuāfù
were sages of swiftness;
Zǐyě and Yánzhōu
were sages of musical knowledge;
Sūn, Wú, Hán, and Bái
were sages of military strategy.
Sagehood
is the ultimate title in human affairs,
not limited to literature and learning alone.
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
'Robbers have five ways of the sage.
Guessing correctly what people hide
is clarity;
entering first without hesitation
is courage;
exiting last without fear
is righteousness;
knowing what is appropriate to attempt
is wisdom;
dividing spoils equally
is benevolence.
Without this Way, no one has ever become a great robber in the world.'"
Someone said:
"The Way of the sage
cannot be scattered branch and leaf,
but must be gathered and combined wholly,
only then can one be a sage."
I responded to him, saying:
"Among the disciples of Confucius,
seventy-two achieved mastery,
yet each grasped only one aspect of the sage's teachings,
showing that sagehood can be divided.
It is also said:
Yan Yuān possessed all qualities in miniature form,
demonstrating that sagehood varies in depth.
Furthermore, the Book of Changes states:
There are four ways of the sage:
those who value words esteem its phrases,
those who value action esteem its changes,
those who make implements esteem its images,
those who practice divination esteem its prognostications.
This clearly proves that the Way of the Sage can be divided.
Why then should those skilled in the Way and its virtue who attain immortality,
not be considered sages who have obtained the Way?
If there were no sages who obtained the Way,
then could the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius be considered sages who brought order to the world?
Since they are not identical,
why demand that they be combined?
According to the Classic of Immortality, those who attain immortality
all received their destiny by encountering the energy of immortals,
a natural endowment.
Thus, while still in the womb,
they already contained the nature of believing in the Way,
and when they gained consciousness,
their hearts loved these matters,
inevitably encountering enlightened teachers and obtaining their methods.
Otherwise,
they would neither believe nor seek,
and even if they sought, they would not obtain.
The Jade Pendant Scripture on the Origins of Destiny states:
Human fortune and misfortune
are determined at conception and the reception of energy,
all receiving the essence of the constellations above.
Those encountering sage constellations become sages,
those encountering worthy constellations become worthies,
those encountering literary constellations become literary,
those encountering martial constellations become martial,
those encountering noble constellations become noble,
those encountering wealthy constellations become wealthy,
those encountering lowly constellations become lowly,
those encountering poor constellations become poor,
those encountering long-lived constellations become long-lived,
those encountering immortal constellations become immortals.
There are also constellations of immortal sages,
constellations of sages who bring order to the world,
constellations combining both types of sages,
constellations of nobility without wealth,
constellations of wealth without nobility,
constellations combining wealth and nobility,
constellations of early wealth followed by poverty,
constellations of early nobility followed by lowliness,
constellations combining poverty and lowliness,
constellations of incomplete wealth and nobility,
constellations of loyalty and filial piety,
constellations of viciousness and evil.
These cannot all be recorded,
but their general outline is as such.
Human life fundamentally has predetermined destiny,
as the theory of Chēzi Zhāng states.
If one does not receive the destiny of immortality,
then one certainly lacks the heart that loves immortality,
for there has never been one who loved it not yet sought its practice,
nor one who obtained it without seeking.
From ancient times to the present,
there have been those of high talent and clear understanding
who did not believe in immortals,
and ordinary people who studied and attained immortality.
While A might have broad discernment yet be blind to immortality,
B might lack broad understanding yet particularly grasp its principles.
Is this not all driven by heavenly mandate?"
The Daoist tradition treasures and keeps secret the arts of immortality,
and among disciples,
it particularly emphasizes careful selection.
Only after prolonged refinement to the utmost essence
are they then instructed in the essential formulas.
How much more so for ordinary people,
who fortunately do not believe or seek it themselves—
why should one force such knowledge upon them?
Since one cannot transform them to make them believe,
it would only invite ridicule and hasten slander.
Therefore, those who have attained the Dao
take different paths from ordinary people in their actions,
and dwell in separate places.
They do not wish to speak with them,
nor mingle their persons with them.
Even separated by a thousand miles,
they still fear it is not enough to distance themselves from the troubles and labors that assail;
even erasing their tracks,
they worry it is insufficient to avoid the disgrace of defamation and insult.
High status cannot tempt them,
wealth cannot sway them;
why would they willingly boast to vulgar scholars,
saying, "I possess the methods of immortality"?
This is precisely why Zhōu Gōng and Confucius had no means to know the way of immortality.
Moreover, Zhōu Gōng and Confucius,
though indeed men of high talent and profound learning,
still had many minor skills
in which they were not versed.
Having them juggle balls or play with swords,
leap over blades or dart through narrow gaps,
walk on poles or climb flagpoles,
pick from trays or scale tables,
hang from cliffs of ten thousand ren in steepness,
swim in the unfathomable depths of the Lǚliáng waters,
lift a thousand jun with their hands,
tread on raging whirlwinds with their feet,
wrestle tigers or cage leopards,
catch flying arrows in mid-air—
these are things ordinary people can do,
yet Zhōu Gōng and Confucius could not;
how much more so for things beyond these?
The thoughts in others' minds,
the direction a louse's head points,
the shades of red and purple beyond a wall,
the blades of grass under a forest,
the books within a chest,
the treasures buried underground,
the birds and beasts in dense woods and deep marshes,
the fish and turtles in deep abysses and vast pools—
if one were to ask Zhōu Gōng and Confucius to discern their colors in detail,
distinguish their names,
list their quantities,
and verify their existence,
they might not be able to know them all,
let alone things far beyond these.
Sages, if they do not eat, grow hungry;
if they do not drink, grow thirsty;
scorched, they feel heat;
frozen, they feel cold;
beaten, they feel pain;
cut, they suffer wounds;
with age, they grow old;
injured, they fall ill;
when their breath ceases, they die.
In these respects, they share much in common with ordinary people,
while what sets them apart is minimal.
What makes them surpass others
lies solely in their extensive talents and far-reaching thoughts,
eloquent speech and lofty writing,
complete virtue and pure conduct,
and matters of forceful instruction and broad knowledge;
how could they possibly excel in everything?
Since they have already composed classics and codes,
bringing peace to the rulers and order to the people,
to further expect them to fully understand the way of immortality,
and achieve eternal life without death,
to demand this of sages—
is that not asking too much?
I have heard that profound words offend common ears,
and truthful speech inevitably goes against the crowd.
When Confucian scholars finish reading this book of mine,
they will surely say I am slandering the sages.
How could that be my intention?
I only wish to exhaust the principles of things;
when principles are exhausted and matters fully examined,
it may seem like defaming Zhōu Gōng and Confucius.
Ordinary people think sages descended from heaven,
divine and spiritual beings,
omniscient,
and omnipotent.
They so deeply revere their names
that they dare not judge them by actual events,
believing that what sages do not do,
no one else can accomplish;
what sages do not know,
no one else can know—
is that not laughable?
Now, let us verify this with recent events;
I hope it may bring enlightenment.
The birds of Wánshān,
with their cries of selling life and mourning death—
Confucius did not know of them;
can one then say Yán Huí alone could partially understand them?
Hearing the wailing of a woman on Tàishān,
he asked about it
and only then learned a tiger had killed three of her family members;
he also did not understand why the woman had not moved away,
and only realized after her reply.
Seeing a bird-catcher netting only fledglings,
he could not discern the reason,
and only understood after asking.
When he wished to bury his mother,
he did not know where his father's grave was,
and had to be told by others.
After the tomb was decided and collapsed,
he again did not know of it;
only when his disciples informed him
did he shed tears.
Suspecting Yán Yuān of stealing food,
he falsely claimed he wished to sacrifice to ancestors
to test the deceit of brushing off dust.
When the stables burned,
he did not know if anyone or any horses were injured.
When Yán Yuān fell behind,
he assumed he had died.
Traveling through over seventy states,
he could not foresee that people would inevitably not employ him,
yet he rushed about anxiously,
without even warming his mat.
He did not know the people of Kuāng would surround him,
and still took that route.
Asking Lǎozi about ancient rites,
there were aspects of the rites he did not comprehend.
Inquiring of Tánzǐ about bird officials,
there were offices he did not recognize.
On the road, not knowing the ferry,
he sent someone to ask,
yet did not realize the person asked
would mock him and not tell the way—
if he had known, he might not have asked.
Alighting from his carriage to chase the singer of the phoenix,
he did not know the other would not stay.
Meeting Nánzǐ, he did not realize it would be of no benefit.
All such instances,
too numerous to list fully,
show that his not knowing the methods of immortality
is hardly surprising.
Moreover, vulgar Confucians say:
"What sages cannot do,
no one else can do."
Yet the Dàng people live in water,
Liáng Mǔ transformed through fire,
Bó Zǐ endured extreme heat,
Zhòng Dū withstood bitter cold,
Zuǒ Cī escaped death through military execution,
Gān Shǐ fasted for years without eating,
Fàn Yì was cut but not penetrated,
Biē Líng revived after floating as a corpse,
Shǎo Qiān captured hundreds of ghosts,
Cháng Fáng contracted the earth's veins,
Zhòng Fǔ borrowed the form of a morning duck,
Zhāng Kǎi blew to raise clouds and mist—
it is unheard of that Zhōu Gōng or Confucius could do such things."
Some ordinary people say:
"Zhōu Gōng and Confucius could do these things,
but they chose not to."
I replied to him:
"If one must not seek evidence from clear texts,
but point to things with empty words,
then I could equally claim that Zhōu Gōng and Confucius could flap their wings and soar,
hover across the eight extremities,
summon clouds and bring rain,
move mountains and lift wells,
but simply chose not to.
Once we stop using recorded texts and witnessed events as evidence,
what limits remain?
If it must be as you say,
I could also claim that Zhōu Gōng and Confucius had already ascended as immortals,
but since this method cannot be used to instruct the world,
fearing that everyone would know immortality is attainable,
all would abandon their family duties,
discard official careers to climb dangers and plunge into depths,
cultivating this path,
resulting in households without descendants,
states without ministers and officials,
both loyalty and filial piety lost,
the great moral order certainly disrupted,
therefore Zhōu Gōng and Confucius secretly practiced it themselves,
keeping it hidden from others,
outwardly feigning final death,
while inwardly possessing the reality of ascension.
If so,
how would you refute me?
Nor can this necessarily be deemed impossible.
The Língbǎo Scripture contains three chapters: Proper Mechanism, Balanced Flight, and Turtle Bestowal,
all concerning arts of immortality.
When the King of Wú quarried stones to build his palace,
amidst the gathered stones,
he discovered texts with purple patterns on golden slips,
but being unable to read them,
he sent a messenger to consult Confucius,
deceiving him by saying:
'While the King of Wú was at leisure,
a red sparrow carried this text and placed it in the palace,
but we cannot understand its meaning,
so we consult you from afar.'
Confucius examined it
and said:
'This is the method of Língbǎo,
the technique for long life,
which Yǔ employed,
hidden in the watery regions,
extending his years to match heaven and earth,
paying homage in the Purple Court.
When Yǔ was about to transform into an immortal,
he sealed it in a stone casket within a famous mountain,
and now the red sparrow carries it—
this must be a heavenly bestowal.'
From this, we can deduce that Xià Yǔ did not die,
and Confucius knew it;
how can we be sure Confucius did not secretly cultivate this path?
Even if sages did not practice these things,
we cannot say they lack efficacy.
Human likes and dislikes
vary greatly among individuals;
to judge by appearances alone,
how can that be reliable?
If something truly matches one's inclinations,
even trivial matters will be pursued;
if it does not resonate with one's spirit,
even significant ones will not be learned.
Preferring bitterness over sweetness
is already common;
craving profit while abandoning righteousness
is also countless.
'The great treasure of the sage is position,
and what gathers people is wealth.'
It is also said:
'Wealth and honor
are what people desire,'
yet in the past, some declined the throne of emperor,
refused the wealth of the entire realm,
scorned high-ranking offices,
turned down offers of jade and silk,
pursued the lofty purity of mountains and forests,
and were content with the humble work of fishing—
such individuals are too numerous to count.
It is also said:
'The relations between men and women, and eating and drinking,
are where great human desires lie.'
Thus, lust cannot be admonished away,
and delicious food can make one forget sorrow.
Yet there were those who fasted and renounced delicacies,
kept no wives or concubines,
transcended alone,
roamed with boundless satisfaction,
found joy in their own reflection,
and rinsed in streams, forgetting flavors—
again, too many to record.
Human nature loves beautiful faces and forms,
slender bodies and soft flesh,
yet Huángdì sought the homely Mómǔ,
and Lord Chén cherished the unattractive Dūnqià.
Human noses delight in fragrance,
hence sulfur, turmeric, iris, orchid, storax, dark gall, plain glue, thoroughwort, and bedstraw,
priced like precious jade,
yet women by the sea
chase men with strong odors,
following them incessantly.
King Wén of Zhōu relished unappetizing pickles,
not exchanging them for the taste of grand sacrifices.
Emperor Míng of Wèi enjoyed the sound of hammer and chisel,
not trading it for the harmony of string and wind instruments.
Each person has their own will;
how can we demand uniformity?
If Zhōu Gōng and Confucius themselves
did not believe in the path to immortality,
just as the sun and moon have places they do not illuminate,
sages have things they do not know,
how can we say that because sages did not practice it,
there are no immortals in the world?
That is like blaming the three lights for not shining under an overturned pot."
Someone asked:
"Did the immortals of antiquity
all attain it through learning,
or were they endowed with unique energy?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"What kind of question is that?
They all carried satchels and followed teachers,
accumulating effort and diligence,
braving frost and danger,
combing wind and bathing rain,
personally sweeping and cleaning,
enduring hardship and toil,
first proving themselves through faithful conduct,
finally tested with peril and hardship,
their nature steadfast, their actions pure,
their hearts free of resentment or doubt,
only then did they enter the hall and reach the inner chamber.
Some grew weary and stopped midway,
some felt resentful and retreated,
some were tempted by glory and profit,
and returned to worldly pursuits,
some were led astray by heresies,
losing their serene aspirations,
some started in the morning and expected success by evening,
some sat cultivating but stood up expecting results.
As for those who see wealth and beauty without inner conflict,
hear worldly talk without discouragement,
among ten thousand people,
one such is already many.
Thus, those who attempt it are as numerous as ox hair,
but those who succeed are as rare as unicorn horns.
Those who draw strong bows
exert force to release the arrow;
those who cross great rivers
ensure safety after reaching the other side;
if a well does not reach the spring,
it is as if not dug;
if one step is not taken,
it is as if not gone.
The journey's accumulation
is not reached in a moment's shadow;
the height of the sky
is not piled up in one basket.
Yet those climbing steep heights fear being near the top with insufficient strength,
and those cultivating the Way suffer from almost succeeding but their will failing.
Thousands of granaries and myriad boxes
are not gained from one ploughing;
the tree that reaches the sky
does not grow in ten days;
the unfathomable abyss
begins from a puddle;
the wealth of Táo Zhū
must accumulate over hundreds and thousands.
If others retreat while I advance,
this is how Yīnzǐ attained the ultimate Way.
Revering the end as the beginning,
this is how Xiànmén achieved the cloud-dragon.
If my will is sincere and firm,
what are they to me?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Common people not only fail to nurture life,
but instead engage in what harms it.
Finite resources
cannot sustain endless consumption;
the flow of rivers
cannot fill a bottomless vessel.
When anyone's income is small but expenses large,
it remains insufficient,
let alone when there's not a zīzhū's worth coming in,
yet thousands going out?
Regardless of age,
everyone has ailments,
only differing in severity.
And the vital energy each receives varies in amount,
those with more deplete slowly,
those with less exhaust quickly.
Those who understand the Dào supplement and remedy it,
first restoring what was,
then seek measured benefits.
If taking herbs could make one soar in flesh and bones by day's end,
or guiding qi change one over a month to grow feathers varied,
then none in the world would doubt the Dào.
The worry is that the gain of a shēng or sháo isn't firm,
while the cost of zhōng and shí follows incessantly,
the foundation not solid,
yet frost and ice attack together.
Not realizing the fault lies with themselves,
they instead claim the Dào is useless,
thus abandoning pills and powders, quitting breathing exercises.
Hence it's said: not that long life is hard,
but hearing of the Dào is;
not that hearing is hard,
but practicing it is;
not that practicing is hard,
but persisting to the end is.
A skilled craftsman can give the compass and square,
but cannot make one adept;
a wise teacher can impart manuals,
but cannot make one act.
Cultivating the Dào is like sowing grain,
achieving it like harvesting the store.
Though the field be fertile,
the water rich,
if one misses the season,
and plowing isn't thorough,
with crops covering the ridges,
unharvested and uncut,
even many acres
yield nothing.
Ordinary folks not only fail to recognize benefit as benefit,
but also don't know harm as harm.
Harm is easy to know and quick,
benefit hard to perceive and slow.
If people don't grasp the easy,
how can they recognize the hard?
Harm is like fat consumed by a lamp,
unseen,
yet suddenly gone.
Benefit is like sowing seedlings,
unnoticed,
yet suddenly lush.
Therefore, in cultivating body and nature,
be meticulous in small things,
not dismissing minor gains as trivial and neglecting them,
nor ignoring small harms as harmless and taking no precaution.
For greatness comes from accumulating smalls,
billions from units.
If one can cherish the subtle,
achieve the manifest,
then one is nearly understanding the Dào."
Someone asked:
"In ancient times, were there those who became immortal without any practice?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"None.
Some followed enlightened teachers,
accumulating effort and diligence,
and were bestowed with ready-made elixirs.
Others received secret formulas,
made them themselves,
detached from worldly affairs,
unburdened by common speech,
so recorders only preserved their names,
unable to detail how they attained immortality,
hence the gaps.
Of old, Huángdì could speak at birth,
command all spirits,
deemed a heaven-given natural body,
yet still couldn't attain the Dào by mere sitting.
So he ascended Wángwū to receive the cinnabar classic,
went to Dǐnghú to obtain flowing pearls,
climbed Kōngtóng to consult Guǎngchéng,
visited Jùcí to serve Dàwěi,
journeyed to Dōngdài to honor Zhōnghuáng,
entered Jīngǔ to seek advice from Juānzǐ,
in Dào cultivation learned from Xuánnǚ and Sùnǚ,
in astrology consulted Shānjī and Lìmù,
in divination inquired of Fēnghòu,
in diagnosis received from Léi Qí,
in warfare adopted the five tones' strategies,
in understanding spirits recorded the words of Báizé,
in geography wrote down Qīngwū's theories,
in healing injuries compiled the art of metal smelting.
Thus he mastered all secrets,
exhausted the Dào and truth,
and ascended by dragon to great heights,
becoming boundless with heaven and earth.
Yet according to immortal scriptures,
both Huángdì and Lǎozǐ served Tàiyǐ Yuánjūn to receive essential teachings;
how much more those inferior to these two lords—
could there be any who became immortals unaided?
I've not heard of it."
Someone said:
"If Huángdì was truly an immortal,
what of his tomb at Qiáoshān?"
Bàopǔzǐ answered:
"According to Jīngshān Jīng and Lóngshǒu Jì,
after Huángdì consumed the divine elixir,
dragons came to welcome him,
his ministers, longing and nostalgic,
with nowhere to direct their thoughts,
took his table and staff,
building a temple to offer sacrifices;
or took his clothes and cap,
burying them to guard.
Lièxiān Zhuàn says:
Huángdì chose his own day of departure,
left for seventy days,
returned after seventy days,
was buried at Qiáoshān,
the mountain suddenly collapsed,
the tomb empty with no corpse,
only his sword and shoes remaining.
Though these accounts differ,
the essence is his immortality.
Tales of Huángdì's ascension abound in Dàoist texts and various schools,
but Confucians, unwilling to promote wonders,
open alternative paths,
focus on rites and teachings,
deem immortal affairs
unfit to guide customs,
thus claim his death
to curb public fancy.
Zhū Yì, Luán Bā, and Yú Gōng,
who benefited the people,
had temples built for them while alive.
Also, ancient virtuous men,
after passing,
had their achievements engraved on lasting vessels by subjects.
And today, when officials transfer,
if loved by people,
virtue-praising stelae are often erected—
this is akin to Huángdì's temple and tomb,
how can it prove his certain death?"
Someone asked:
"Peng Zu lived eight hundred years,
An Qi lived three thousand years—
these lifespans far exceed the ordinary.
If there truly were a way to avoid death,
why didn't they simply become immortals?
Is it not because our endowed fate and received qi
inherently have their own lengths,
and they merely happened to obtain more,
but the principle cannot be extended,
thus they could not escape withering and demise?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"According to the Classic of Peng Zu,
he assisted Emperor Kù and Yáo,
passed through the Xià dynasty to the Yīn as a senior official.
The king of Yīn sent palace maidens to learn the arts of the bedchamber from him,
which proved effective.
Wanting to kill Peng Zu,
to cut off his methods,
Peng Zu became aware and fled.
At the time of his departure, he was over seven to eight hundred years old,
but he did not die.
The Records of Huáng Shígōng state:
More than seventy years after Peng Zu left,
his disciples saw him west of the Liúshā Desert—
clearly, he did not die.
Moreover, Peng Zu's disciples,
Qīngyī Wūgōng, Hēixuégōng, Xiùméigōng, Báitùgōngzǐ, Lílóugōng, Tàizújūn, Gāoqiūzǐ, Bùkěn lái—seven or eight individuals,
all lived for several hundred years,
and during the Yīn dynasty, each ascended to immortality.
How much more so would Peng Zu be willing to die?
Also, the Biographies of Immortals recorded by Liú Xiàng states that Peng Zu was an immortal.
As for Master Ān Qī,
he sold medicine by the seashore,
and people in Lángyá passed down accounts of seeing him through generations,
reckoning he was already a thousand years old.
Qín Shǐhuáng invited him for conversation,
lasting three days and three nights.
His words were lofty,
his meaning profound,
broad and well-supported.
Shǐhuáng found him extraordinary,
and bestowed upon him gold and jade,
worth tens of millions.
Ān Qī accepted them and placed them at Fùxiāng Pavilion,
and left a letter saying,
'After several thousand more years,
seek me on Pénglái Mountain.'
Thus,
it is evident that when he met Shǐhuáng, he was already a thousand years old—
he did not die.
Moreover, Shǐhuáng was harsh, violent, arrogant, and stubborn,
precisely the kind in the world who should not believe in immortals.
Nor was he one to accept unfounded answers.
Yet when he questioned Ān Qī about matters of longevity,
Ān Qī's responses were fitting and proper,
making Shǐhuáng awaken and understand,
believing that there must be a path to immortality in the world.
Not only did he bestow generous gifts,
but he was also willing to learn the art of immortality,
only lacking an enlightened teacher,
and being deceived by the likes of Lú Áo and Xú Fú,
he thus could not attain it.
Had Master Ān Qī's words lacked evidence,
within those three days and three nights,
he would have been thoroughly refuted,
and Shǐhuáng would surely have boiled, cooked, or slaughtered him,
not escaping the calamity of the cauldron and chopping block—
how could he have received such generous favors then?"
Someone asked:
"In the world, there are those who ingest medicines,
practice breath control and guiding exercises,
yet still cannot avoid death—
why is that?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Without obtaining the golden elixir,
but merely consuming herbal medicines and practicing minor arts,
one can prolong years and delay death,
but cannot attain immortality.
Some only know to take herbal remedies,
but are unaware of the essential techniques for restoring youth,
thus ultimately lacking the principle for long life.
Others do not understand carrying divine talismans,
practicing prohibitions and precepts,
contemplating the body's spirits,
and preserving the True One—
these can only prevent internal illnesses from arising
and ward off wind and dampness.
If suddenly evil ghosts and powerful malign forces,
mountain spirits and water poisons harm them,
they will die immediately.
Some lack the methods for entering mountains,
causing mountain gods to bring disaster upon them,
then demonic ghosts test them,
fierce beasts injure them,
stream poisons strike them,
venomous snakes bite them—
leading to numerous fatal incidents,
not just one kind.
Some begin cultivating the Dao late in life,
having already deeply damaged themselves beforehand,
making it difficult to repair and restore.
The benefits of repair and restoration
have not yet taken root,
when illness strikes again—
how can such debilitating conditions
possibly lead to longevity?
Some grow old practicing Daoism and attain immortality,
while others practice young but fail—
why is this?
Those who are old received abundant vital energy originally,
and having abundant vital energy means minimal damage,
minimal damage means easy nourishment,
hence they attain immortality.
Those who are young received little vital energy originally,
and having little vital energy means deep damage,
deep damage means difficult rescue,
hence they fail to become immortals.
Consider hibiscus and willow trees:
cut and planted, they regenerate;
upside down, they grow;
horizontal, they also grow.
Nothing surpasses these trees
in ease of growth.
Yet if planted too shallow,
and not given time,
constantly carved or stripped,
shaken or uprooted,
even if buried in fertile soil
and soaked with spring rains,
they still cannot escape withering—
because their roots are unstable,
unable to sprout buds,
their vital energy cannot consolidate through sap and fluid.
The human body as an entity
is easily harmed and hard to nourish—
compared to these trees,
it falls far short.
Yet what attacks and destroys it
exceeds carving and stripping,
surpassing shaking and uprooting.
Those who aid it are few,
those who ruin it are many—
death becomes inevitable.
Exhaling the old and inhaling the new
uses qi to grow qi,
but when qi is greatly depleted, growth is difficult.
Taking medicines
uses blood to enrich blood,
but when blood is nearly exhausted, enrichment is hard.
Running until panting and choking,
coughing or feeling full,
straining the body with effort,
constantly short of breath—
these are signs of qi damage.
Lusterless complexion,
dried skin like cured meat,
parched lips and pale veins,
withered muscle texture—
these are evidence of blood depletion.
With both signs declining externally,
the spiritual root withers internally.
In such state,
without superior medicine,
there is no rescue.
All who practice Daoism yet fail,
or seek life but meet death—
it's not that they lack qi and blood.
Rather, what makes qi and blood in their bodies
has lost its source,
leaving only branches and streams.
Like embers entering water:
the fire dies but smoke doesn't cease instantly;
or a severed tree:
branches and leaves may still live.
Both have smoke
and have leaves,
but what makes them smoke and leaves
has already perished.
People consider the day they feel ill
as the start of disease,
just as taking the day breath stops
as the sign of bodily death.
They only blame wind-cold and summer-dampness,
not knowing wind-cold and summer-dampness
cannot harm strong, sturdy people—
they merely afflict those with weak bodies and scant qi
who cannot endure them,
thus becoming infected.
How to compare?
Suppose several people,
similar in age and vitality,
equal in diet and nourishment,
together enter desert lands,
braving severely cold nights,
black ice forming below,
cold wind snapping branches in nightly terror,
coughs and spittle freezing on lips—
then among them only some will catch cold,
not all necessarily falling ill.
It's not that cold qi favors some,
but that some bodies cannot endure it.
Thus eating the same food,
some alone fall ill—
not because the food is uniquely toxic.
Using equal vessels to drink equally,
some stay sober, some get drunk—
not because wine's potency varies.
Similarly exposed to scorching heat,
some alone die of heatstroke—
not because heaven's heat plays favorites.
Taking the same medicine,
some become dizzy and distressed—
not because its toxicity loves or hates.
Therefore when gusting winds hit a forest,
withered branches break first;
when great waves strike cliffs,
cracked seams crumble first;
when fierce fires sweep plains,
dry grasses burn first;
when dragon bowls fall to ground,
the brittle ones shatter alone.
From this we see:
those lacking the Dao
already have inherently ill bodies,
activated by wind, cold, summer-heat, and dampness.
If one can ensure vital qi doesn't decline,
form and spirit guarding each other,
nothing can harm them.
All Dao practitioners
should worry about starting late,
not about starting early.
Those relying on youthful vigor
and peak physical strength
to overexert themselves
will accumulate numerous ailments,
their lives fragile as morning dew—
without great medicine,
only taking herbs,
they may surpass ordinary people
but cannot extend their ultimate limit.
Thus the Immortal Classics say:
'The foundation of nurturing life is avoiding harm.'
These are essential words.
Shénnóng said:
'With hundreds of illnesses unhealed,
how can one attain long life?'
How true these words are!"
Someone asked:
"What is referred to as harming oneself,
is it not merely about the indulgence in desires?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Why limit it to just that?
However, the essence of longevity
lies in the methods of rejuvenation.
Superior individuals who understand this
can extend their years and eliminate illnesses;
those of lesser attainment avoid self-inflicted harm.
If one is still young and robust and knows rejuvenation,
consuming yīn elixirs to nourish the brain,
gathering jade fluids from deep valleys,
even without medicinal herbs,
one can still live three hundred years,
though not achieving immortality.
Those who lack the proper techniques
are compared by the ancients to holding hot soup in an ice cup,
or preserving fire in a feather pouch.
Moreover, contemplating beyond one's intellectual capacity
and straining the mind
causes harm;
attempting to lift what exceeds one's strength
and forcing exertion
causes harm;
excessive grief and melancholy
cause harm;
extreme joy and elation
cause harm;
frantic pursuit of desires
causes harm;
prolonged talking and laughing
cause harm;
irregular sleep patterns
cause harm;
drawing bows and bending crossbows
cause harm;
heavy intoxication and vomiting
cause harm;
sleeping immediately after satiation
cause harm;
jumping, running until breathless
cause harm;
exuberant shouting and weeping
cause harm;
absence of yīn-yáng interaction
causes harm;
accumulated harm leads to premature demise,
and premature death contradicts the Dào.
Therefore, the methods of nurturing life include:
not spitting too far,
walking without rushing,
ears not straining to hear,
eyes not gazing too long,
sitting not to the point of prolonged stiffness,
lying down before exhaustion,
clothing before feeling cold,
undressing before feeling hot,
not eating only when ravenous,
and not overeating when dining,
not drinking only when parched,
and not overdrinking when hydrating.
Generally, overeating leads to accumulations and blockages,
overdrinking results in phlegm and stagnation.
Avoid excessive toil or idleness,
do not rise too late,
prevent profuse sweating,
shun excessive sleep,
eschew reckless carriage and horse riding,
refrain from straining the eyes with distant views,
limit consumption of raw and cold foods,
avoid drinking alcohol in the wind,
minimize frequent bathing,
curb ambitious and far-reaching aspirations,
discard plans for novel contrivances.
In winter, avoid extreme warmth,
in summer, shun utter coolness,
do not sleep uncovered under the stars,
do not expose shoulders while sleeping,
severe cold and heat,
fierce winds and heavy fog,
all should be avoided.
When the five flavors enter the mouth,
avoid any predominance,
thus too much sourness harms the spleen,
too much bitterness harms the lungs,
too much pungency harms the liver,
too much saltiness harms the heart,
too much sweetness harms the kidneys,
this is the natural principle of the five phases.
Generally, when we speak of harm,
it may not be immediately felt,
but over time it erodes longevity.
Therefore, those skilled in nurturing life
follow seasonal rhythms in rising and resting,
maintain harmonious routines in activity and repose;
regulate and benefit muscles and bones
with methods of stretching and bending;
ward off diseases and ward off pathogens
with techniques of inhalation and exhalation;
circulate yíng and wèi energies
through methods of tonification and purgation;
moderate labor and leisure
with principles of giving and withholding.
Restrain anger to preserve yīn energy,
suppress joy to nurture yáng energy.
Then first consume herbs to remedy deficiencies,
later ingest golden elixirs to secure endless vitality,
the principles of longevity
are fully contained herein.
As for those who insist on following their whims,
claiming broad understanding and acceptance of fate,
unbound by unconventional teachings,
indulging passions and exerting force,
not seeking prolonged life,
upon hearing these words,
they pass like wind through the ears,
lightning across the eyes,
leaving no impression.
Even if their bodies wither in indulgence,
their breath ceases amidst silken luxury,
and they are content with it,
how could one discuss life-nurturing matters with them?
Not only would they not accept it,
they would deem it demonic falsehood.
To expect their belief
is like offering a bright mirror to the blind,
or playing music for the deaf."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Heaven and Earth's greatest virtue is called life,
and life favors living beings.
Therefore, what the Daoist tradition keeps most secret and values most highly
is nothing more than the methods for attaining longevity.
Thus, they are transmitted only after blood oaths,
and if transmitted to the wrong person,
the warning lies in heavenly punishment.
Earlier masters did not dare to impart them lightly to others;
they required that seekers be extremely diligent,
and even then, they would choose only the most refined to teach.
How much more so for those who neither love nor seek it,
or who seek it without sincerity—
how could one flaunt and peddle it to inform them?
Those whose destiny does not align with immortality,
even if they daily see immortals gathered in the world,
will still insist that they are a different kind of people,
that there are such beings separately under heaven,
some calling them ghosts and demons in disguise,
or saying they偶然 encountered them in nature—
how would they ever admit that these are attained through cultivation?
If their hearts disbelieve,
even if Chìsōngzǐ and Wángqiáo spoke directly into their ears,
they would still consider it demonic falsehood.
Yet there are occasionally those who recognize and believe,
but they suffer from not being able to diligently seek out enlightened teachers.
Those who understand the essential and attain the true Dao
are indeed very rare,
not to be encountered hastily.
However, those who know it
are merely few,
but they have never been completely absent from the world.
It is because seekers are neither widespread nor sincere
that those destined for immortality
are bound to encounter them eventually.
Yet there are those who seek but do not find,
but there are none who obtain it without seeking.
In the world, there are countless deceitful individuals plotting for wealth,
who falsely assume the title of Daoist priests.
They cannot be counted.
However, these people are not entirely ignorant;
they all have a superficial understanding,
some recklessly seek fame,
adding to it the concealment of evil and pretense of falsehood.
And those fond of such matters,
unable to distinguish true from false,
merely flock to inquire,
bringing deception upon themselves,
and are restrained by them,
not allowed to venture out,
to broadly seek extraordinary scholars and unique individuals,
and are told,
'The Dao ends here.'
This misleads many who have the aspiration,
lamentable and infuriating indeed!

Some hear of those who know how to disperse the five clouds, fly the eight minerals, transform the nine elixirs, smelt yellow and white, create jade from water, turn cinnabar and jade, condense frost and snow in divine furnaces, or gather divine mushrooms on Sōng Mountain,
then many slander them, saying,
'These methods are known only to Chìsōngzǐ and Wángqiáo;
for people in this world to claim knowledge of them
is all falsehood.'
Then those with shallow views,
unaware that these words are deceitful fabrications,
immediately abandon their intentions to seek afar.
Alas,
this is something to sigh over!
Time flies like a gust,
briefly young, suddenly old,
so swift
it can be compared to nothing;
a hundred years of life
is but over thirty thousand days.
In youth, one knows little;
in decline, joy and pleasure fade together;
childhood ignorance and senile confusion
take away decades,
and dangers, narrow worries, and illnesses
follow one after another;
the years of one's life
are roughly halved.
Considering those destined for a full century,
with happy laughter and peace,
it is no more than fifty or sixty years,
gone in a moment;
with sorrow and senility,
it's but six or seven thousand days,
gone in a blink.
How much more so for those who live a full hundred years—
not one in ten thousand!
Reflect on this,
and there is no reason to laugh at summer insects or morning fungi.
This is the ultimate sorrow of those who do not know the Dao.
There is a common saying:
'A person in the world
loses a day each day,
like leading an ox or sheep to the slaughterhouse;
with each step forward,
death draws nearer.'
This analogy may be crude,
but it holds true.
The reason enlightened ones do not worry about death
is not that they do not wish to avoid it,
but that they simply do not know how to escape it;
and empty anxiety
benefits nothing.
Thus, it is said they are content with heaven and know their fate,
hence they do not worry—
not that they do not desire long life.
Duke Zhōu pleaded to replace King Wǔ,
and Confucius dragged his staff in sorrow—
this shows that even sages do not welcome swift death.
Common people see Zhuāng Zhōu's metaphor of the great dream,
and thus compete to promote theories equating life and death.
These are deceptive paths forcing understanding,
outwardly making contrarian statements,
all of which Confucius would have condemned as breaking laws deserving punishment.
Now observe those who speak thus:
when afflicted with illness, they quickly resort to acupuncture;
when facing danger, they greatly fear death.
Yet a widespread flaw of decadent customs
is not honoring true faith,
turning away from classics to study philosophical texts,
and if one does not engage in clever arguments against reason,
they are called rustic,
not in line with Lǎo-Zhuāng teachings.
Thus, those without backbone who follow the crowd
drift into untenable theories,
unable to turn back.
Lǎozi made longevity and enduring vision his task,
while Zhuāng Zhōu valued wagging his tail in the mud,
not being a turtle caught in a net,
or an ox adorned with embroidery,
starving and begging for grain from the River Earl—
from this, we know he did not equate life and death.
Later learners fail to examine truth and falsehood,
latching onto a single phrase—
is that not mistaken?
Moreover, to descend deep under the nine springs,
into the endless long night,
first becoming food for ants,
finally merging with dust and soil—
it makes one's heart burn with dread,
involuntarily sighing.
If one's heart holds the will to seek life,
why not set aside unimportant matters
to cultivate the mysterious and subtle art?
If they do not believe, let it be.
For those who do believe,
the trouble is that worldly attachments are not fully eradicated,
preventing full dedication to nurturing life,
attempting it only in spare moments amid worldly affairs.
Hence, some who undertake it
often start too late and mostly fail.
What ordinary people eagerly pursue
is power, profit, and desires.
If one's body is not preserved,
even with high office and heavy authority,
mountains of gold and jade,
and countless beauties,
they are not truly ours.
Therefore, superior individuals first attend to the matter of longevity;
with longevity assured, one can act freely.
If not yet ascended to mystery and left the world,
one can temporarily be an earth immortal among humans.
Like Péng Zǔ and Lǎozi,
they lived among people for centuries,
not losing the joys of human relations,
then gradually ascended in peace—
a magnificent affair indeed.
However, it absolutely requires a good teacher;
if the teacher is inadequate,
there is no way to succeed.
In the past, the Hàn Empress received the Shàngshū from Xiàhóu Shèng,
rewarding Shèng with a hundred jīn of gold,
and countless other items.
When Shèng died,
she granted his family two million coins,
and wore plain mourning for him for a hundred days.
When Emperor Chéng was heir apparent,
he studied the Analects with Zhāng Yǔ.
Upon ascending the throne,
he enfeoffed Yǔ as Marquis within the Pass,
with a fief of a thousand households,
appointed him Grand Master of Brilliantly Meritous,
and bestowed a hundred jīn of gold.
Later, he promoted him to Chancellor,
advancing his rank to Marquis of Ānchāng.
When Yǔ grew old and requested retirement,
he was given a comfortable carriage with four horses,
a hundred jīn of gold,
and tens of thousands of coins.
When Yǔ fell ill,
the Emperor personally visited him,
bowing at his bedside.
When Emperor Zhāng was heir apparent,
he studied the Classic of Filial Piety with Huán Róng.
After the Emperor's accession,
he appointed Róng as Minister of the Imperial Clan.
The Emperor visited Róng's residence,
had Róng sit facing east,
and provided a table and staff.
Gathering hundreds of officials and students from the Imperial Academy,
the Emperor personally held the texts and lectured.
He bestowed upon Róng the title of Marquis within the Pass,
granting him a fief of five thousand households.
When Róng fell ill,
the Son of Heaven visited his home,
alighting from his carriage upon entering the lane,
hastening forward with scrolls in his arms,
observing the etiquette of a disciple.
Upon Róng's passing,
the Emperor donned plain mourning garments for him.
All these gentlemen,
though not capable of storming cities or battling in the wilds,
repelling enemies or expanding borders,
hoisting banners and proving their loyalty,
praying for distant frontiers,
transforming primordial achievements,
or displaying prowess in remote lands,
were revered so greatly
merely for mastering a single classic,
expounding its chapters and sentences.
Such lofty esteem
was accorded only to those who could discourse on the words of the deceased.
Even the exalted status of an emperor
bowed humbly to honor them.
In the world, there are those who wish to practice the path of immortality,
yet refuse to humble themselves before worthy teachers;
instead, they press urgently,
demanding the essential secrets—
how could they possibly obtain them?
What benefit does a learner's reverence and diligence bring to the teacher's own knowledge?
Yet without it,
the learner's heart is not fully committed;
without full commitment,
the teacher's guidance will not be thorough;
without thorough guidance,
how can all the secret formulas be acquired?
Forced by circumstance, the teacher may reveal only superficial aspects—
how could that suffice to achieve the work of immortality?
There are also those with fair appearances and eager enthusiasm,
whose faith lacks deep roots in heart and spirit;
driven by personal desires,
they feign humility outwardly,
but within days,
negligence emerges.
If they encounter a wise teacher,
who observes the changes in newcomers' attitudes,
testing them over time,
thus withholding instruction
to gauge their resolve,
then such individuals,
with their falseness exposed in action,
will ultimately not be teachable,
and even if taught, the teacher cannot speak fully or reveal the truth;
without complete understanding, the practice yields no benefit.
Take Chén Ānshì, for example,
only thirteen years old,
originally a servant in Guàn Shūběn's household,
who first attained the way of immortality.
Shūběn, at seventy with white hair,
bowed to Ānshì morning and evening, saying,
"The Way is revered, virtue is precious;
whoever attains the Way first is the teacher.
I dare not neglect the rites of a disciple."
Thus, Ānshì imparted to him the essential methods,
and Shūběn too ascended to immortality.
Humans first receive their essence and spirit from Heaven and Earth,
later inheriting qi and blood from their parents;
yet without an enlightened teacher
to instruct them in the path of transcending the world,
there is no way to avoid death.
Like striking a stone that leaves sparks,
their allotted years wither and fade.
From this perspective,
the grace of an enlightened teacher
truly surpasses that of Heaven and Earth,
and is far weightier than that of parents.
Should we not revere them?
Should we not seek them out?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The ancients were simple and upright,
valuing action over words,
thus those who governed did not prize literary eloquence,
and those who cultivated the Way did not exalt rhetoric.
As customs declined and grew shallow,
external adornment became increasingly elaborate,
with texts piling up like mountains in Confucian schools,
while esoteric writings also proliferated among the masters of arts.
Beginners
could not immediately be taught the essential principles.
Moreover, it is human nature to delight in abundance of both fundamentals and details.
Therefore, later knowers of the Way,
such as Gān Jí, Róng Sōng, Guì Bó, and various schools,
each wrote thousands of chapters,
yet most contained instructional admonitions,
unwilling to clearly reveal the ultimate direction and meaning.
The truest formulas
were sometimes only orally transmitted,
or written on no more than a foot of silk,
kept within one's collar belt,
and unless one followed a teacher for a long time,
accumulating effort and undergoing trials,
could not be obtained.
Miscellaneous disciples
were each taught according to their diligence,
the duration of their hardships,
their level of intelligence,
and the capacity of their will and strength to discern,
receiving different teachings;
over hundreds and thousands of years,
occasionally someone might exhaust the secrets hidden
in their bags, pillows,
or under their sleeves—the essential tenets.
Some were only given formulas to prepare medicines;
once the medicine was made, they received a share,
enough to make them immortal,
yet the master never passed on the written method throughout the year.
Thus, among Daoist priests in the world,
those who knew the art of golden elixir
were fewer than one in ten thousand.
Those with narrow views
believed that the methods of immortality must be fully contained in voluminous books
or in rituals of sacrifice and prostration.
But longevity is controlled by the great medicine alone,
not obtained through sacrifices and offerings.
In the past, during the Qin and Han dynasties,
grand prayers were promoted,
worshipping the Great Unity, the Five Deities,
the Chén Bǎo, the Eight Deities, and the like,
using cattle, sheep, grains, and silks,
spending billions in coins,
yet achieving no benefit at all.
How much more so for commoners,
lacking in virtue,
neglecting self-cultivation,
who wish to use triple sacrifices and wine offerings,
praying to ghosts and deities,
to seek extended life—
how deluded they are!
Some enthusiasts,
sincerely wishing to practice the Way,
fail to diligently seek enlightened teachers
or compound extraordinary medicines,
but instead day and night recite and lecture on unimportant books,
numbering thousands of volumes,
reaching old age without benefit,
then claim there truly are no methods of immortality in the world.
Others knock their heads at their doors,
facing empty seats,
cooking sacrificial animals,
burning incense to beg for blessings,
yet the sick do not recover,
deaths follow one another,
fortunes are depleted and wealth exhausted,
with nothing miraculous,
still they do not repent or realize,
blaming themselves for insufficient devotion.
If with such diligence
they sought a teacher who knows the methods,
and with such expenses
supplied the cost for buying medicines,
they would surely attain immortality, longevity, and transcendence.
How is this different from tilling a rocky field until old age,
hoping for a harvest of a thousand granaries?
Though effort is exhausted,
it misses the mark.
It is like heading to Chǔ but taking the road to Yān—
though the horse is fine, it does not arrive;
not that the travel is slow,
but the path is wrong.
Some, trusting by nature and prone to believe others,
lack the intelligence to verify truth and falsehood,
or gauge depth and shallowness;
their broad learning is inherently narrow,
unable to appreciate things.
Later generations, stubborn and shallow,
hastily finding someone,
a self-praising individual,
who claims to possess secret texts,
then serve and follow them.
But mediocre people and charlatans,
often outwardly assume the name of having the Way,
their fame exceeding reality,
due to exaggeration and deceit,
inwardly harboring greed and impurity,
seeking only profit,
when asked to do something,
they forcibly mutter,
bowing and modulating their voices,
as if the knowledge they guard is profound and unobtainable.
When requests are made,
depending on what is sought,
they bow and smile,
perhaps promising later,
thus making the unaware
unable to desist,
thinking their service is insufficient,
and their gifts too meager.
Then, with sincere belief,
they become even more reverent,
bribing with rare treasures,
performing slave-like duties for them,
not shirking heavy burdens or distant travels,
not avoiding dangers or perils,
hoping to accumulate toil to prove themselves,
enduring hardship and pleading pitifully,
in hopes of hearing extraordinary teachings.
Yet they vainly pass the years,
emptily abandoning the support of their parents,
forsaking wives and children without pity,
braving frost and treading on ice,
following year after year,
wasting resources and effort,
ultimately achieving nothing.
Those teachers initially deceived them,
but later may feel ashamed,
confused within,
truly empty and lacking,
with no methods to teach,
how could they possibly help others achieve?
I have personally seen many such people,
perhaps over ten individuals.
Some call themselves by lofty names,
long dwelling in the world,
with some claiming they are three or four hundred years old,
merely changing names,
falsely calling themselves sages,
living among humans,
with many serving them,
but I prefer not to write their names.
They wander commonly in society,
where ordinary folks cannot distinguish beauty from ugliness,
jointly praising them,
increasing their absurd falsehoods,
for those cunning and deceitful people,
vainly generating flowery reputations,
their influence gradually spreads,
and none can discern the truth.
Thus, sometimes even noble individuals, failing to carefully observe,
and relying only on their ears,
are misled in their learning—
often because of such people,
it invariably makes one sigh.
Whenever I see these types,
deceiving the world,
scheming for power and profit,
sooner or later they suffer calamity and punishment;
though the net of heaven is wide,
it ultimately leaves nothing out.
But it is regrettable for those with sincere aspirations who are misled.
Most people chase empty reputations,
rarely able to verify the truth.
Hearing that so-and-so has many disciples,
up to a hundred or so,
they assume there must be something extraordinary,
and rush to compete,
gathering to follow and serve,
wasting time to honor those foolish and crude individuals.
They do not seek the essence,
while those teachers gain strength from their disciples.
Some thereby become wealthy;
though followers pursue them for long,
there is no way to achieve humanity,
and foolish people do not realize such individuals are not worth serving.
