Why do they never awaken?
How lamentable!
Searching for a sky-touching tree
on a mound only a few feet high;
straining a cow's hoof print
for a fish that swallows boats—
though the time spent is long,
how can it be found?
Alas!
Future learners,
while making seeking a teacher their priority,
must also urgently take care to choose carefully.
Crude and narrow-minded individuals,
with shallow conduct and scant virtue,
little merit and sparse karmic connections,
It is insufficient for fulfilling the way of a complete person,
nor does it serve as a task to repay others' great kindness.
Deeply contemplate its essence,
do not let it be in vain."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Those so-called masters of the Way,
skilled in deception and fraud,
deceive their students;
moreover, they conceal their shortcomings and ignorance,
ashamed of not knowing,
pretending as if broad learning is enough,
ultimately unwilling to seek guidance from those superior to themselves,
foolishly clinging to their limitations,
standing like facing a wall;
not only remaining silent and inactive,
but also harboring jealousy towards those who truly possess the Way and slandering them,
fearing that their reputation might surpass their own.
Do such individuals truly have any intention towards the methods of longevity?
They merely wish to attract disciples,
scheme for their wealth and resources,
to indulge their own desires and passions.
Yet they do not realize that heaven, though high, hears what is below,
and they will inevitably suffer the consequences.
The poor should not falsely claim to be rich,
the lowly should not vainly claim to be noble,
how much more so when it comes to matters of virtue and the Way, which they lack in reality,
yet they vainly support followers and disciples?
Even ordinary people
should not harbor jealousy towards the good,
let alone masters of the Way,
who should especially live with loyalty, trust, and contentment,
how can they allow such narrow-mindedness to dwell in their hearts?
Though humans cannot see or hear the divine,
the divine finds it easy to see and hear them.
This is no different from being outside a silk curtain,
unable to observe inside the hall,
yet acting arrogantly,
thinking others cannot see them.
This is like stealing a bell,
which clangs loudly,
and, disliking others hearing it,
covering one's own ears.
And those who are spiritually blind and deaf,
only wish to monopolize glorious reputations,
gather followers exclusively,
seek external fame,
internally plan for wealth and power,
their envy of those better than themselves
is even more intense than ordinary people's struggles for power.
Thus, they use their tongues as blades,
turn slander and praise into factions,
friendly in speech but distant in heart,
united in appearance but divided in action,
outwardly speaking of shared ideals,
inwardly carrying the venom of wasps and scorpions,
this is detested by both heaven and humanity,
a summons to disaster.
When studying the Five Classics,
one should still not feel ashamed to ask those below,
to advance virtue and cultivate knowledge,
daily achieving brightness.
As for the crude skills of archery and charioteering,
the elementary arts of writing and arithmetic,
the exposed tasks of farming and sericulture,
the minor techniques of carpentry,
one still needs a teacher's instruction to fully understand their principles,
how much more so for the methods of nurturing longevity,
wishing to prolong life and transcend the world,
this is no different from rescuing the dying.
How can one cling to the fear of the name of asking for instruction,
and forever remain in the plight of ignorance,
unchanged until old age,
unrepentant at death,
such are the profoundly benighted among heaven's people.
It makes others feel ashamed and alarmed for them,
yet those who do this do not even reflect on their own actions.
As Confucian scholars, one should still remain steadfast and preserve simplicity,
outwardly appearing plain and unadorned,
knowing yet acting as if not,
possessing yet acting as if without,
not allowing mediocre people to fully praise them,
if praised, not responding unless asked,
and if answering,必定谦让而后言.
How much more should those who are masters of the Way
forcibly claim to know what they do not,
to have what they lack,
vainly boasting and showing off,
to scheme for illicit gains?
Those who are lost and do not know to turn back,
persist even more in their errors,
if there is a way to practice this,
I believe they would not be ashamed to reform.
I do not say this lightly,
indeed, I speak for a reason,
as they say, one cannot remain silent when troubled by something.
I merely pity the foolish,
unable to bear seeing an infant fall into a well.
If someone reads this and awakens,
it is like one herb of the immortal medicine,
what more can I do!
If one refuses the bitter medicine,
the danger is imminent,
this can be known without waiting for a pulse diagnosis."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"If there is a capital crime,
and someone can save the person,
they will not begrudge the toil or shame nor fear humble pleas,
and will surely achieve the merit of preserving life.
Now, among the mixed and vulgar masters of the Way,
those who do not obtain the great method of the golden elixir,
it is certain they cannot achieve longevity.
Even if they can heal illnesses with life-restoring effects,
abstain from grains and remain without hunger for years,
command ghosts and spirits,
sit and vanish or stand and disappear,
see a thousand miles away,
know the rise and fall of others,
dispel hidden evils from obscurity,
foresee fortune and misfortune before they emerge,
it still does not benefit their lifespan,
yet they feel ashamed to seek and ask,
embarrassed to serve those more advanced,
this is cherishing a moment's humiliation,
while accepting endless pain,
they fail to see the analogy.
The ancients had a saying,
life, for me,
is of great benefit.
Considering its nobility,
even the title of emperor
cannot compare to this method.
Considering its weight,
even possessing the wealth of the world
is not enough to exchange for this art.
Hence, there is the metaphor of a dead king willing to be a living rat.
Governing a state and achieving peace,
cultivating the self and achieving life,
do not come automatically,
all require effort to attain.
Cherishing the empty name of avoiding shortcoming,
ashamed of the temporary toil of learning from a teacher,
even if they claim not to be foolish,
I do not believe it.
Now, if someone could avoid certain death and face a lesser punishment,
they would gladly rejoice at escaping heavy for light,
freeing themselves from scorching burns to preserve their life,
enduring the pain,
as if reborn.
People simply do not know the day they will die,
so they do not worry temporarily.
If they truly knew,
and even punishments like amputation or nose-cutting
could extend their life,
they would certainly do it.
How much more so merely personally sweeping and cleaning,
holding towels and exerting effort for those superior to oneself,
to be taught the way of immortality,
how could that be considered hardship?
Yet the obstinate fear it.
Suppose there is someone
ashamed to run quickly and waits to be burned by wildfire,
embarrassed to flee the wind and ends up drowning in deep abysses,
the world would surely call them ignorant,
and all would laugh at their failure to avoid danger,
yet none find it strange that they do not fear real disaster,
why is that?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"In the past, many have written about the Way,
all striving for broad, floating, and clever words,
to exalt mysterious and empty meanings,
none have thoroughly discussed the steps to longevity,
or admonished the ailments of practicing the Way,
as diligently as I have.
Truly wishing to make the lost know to turn back,
lose at sunrise in the east,
gain at sunset in the west,
pulling the rope after falling into the well,
is better than sinking completely.
But for those who cherish the beauty of illness and reject the harsh medicine,
there is nothing to be done.
Who among humans is without fault?
To err and be able to correct it,
is like the eclipse of the sun and moon,
following the example of Yán Huí.
Also wishing to make future lovers of the life-nurturing Way
careful in whom they trust,
thus I exhaust my sincere advice and good strategies,
without adorning with excessive elegance,
words spoken are pointed and direct,
writing down is painfully frank,
regretting only that in pursuing longevity, I must suppress falsehoods,
what more is there to seek?"
Bàopǔzǐ stated:
"I deeply reflect upon those who study the Daoist arts and nurture life,
yet follow teachers who are not the right persons,
ultimately achieving nothing,
causing later generations with aspirations,
upon seeing their failure to attain longevity,
to consequently claim that under heaven there truly are no methods to become immortals.
Generally, those who seek to transcend life on their own,
yet are inevitably unable to discipline their bodies and restrain themselves to cultivate the mysterious and subtle,
will merely advance without gaining the means to secure official emoluments,
and retreat without achieving the merit of delaying old age,
internally harming their own beings,
and externally discouraging future aspirants.
That immortality can be attained through study,
is as evident as millet and grains being obtainable through sowing and planting,
very clear indeed.
However, there has never been a case of harvesting fine crops without tilling the land,
nor gaining eternal life and transcending the world without diligence."
Someone asked:
"May I ask if those who abstain from grains can achieve longevity?
How many methods are there in total,
and which one is the best?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Those who abstain from grains can only save the expense of food provisions,
but it alone cannot make people live long.
I've inquired of those who have long practiced grain abstention,
and they say they have slightly fewer illnesses and pains,
better than when they ate grains.
Those who take atractylodes or consume huángjīng,
or take the Yǔyúliáng pills,
twice a day,
for three days,
find themselves more energetic,
able to carry loads and travel far,
feeling light and not exhausted.
Those who take various mineral medicines,
some lasting five to ten years without hunger, or those who swallow breath, use talismans, or drink sacred water,
only avoid hunger,
but their physical strength cannot handle labor.
Although Daoist texts say that to attain longevity,
the intestines must be clear;
to achieve immortality,
the intestines should have no waste.
They also say,
those who eat plants are good runners but foolish,
meat-eaters are strong and fierce,
grain-eaters are wise but not long-lived,
and breath-eaters become divine and immortal.
This is just the biased view of one school of breath cultivation,
not to be followed exclusively.
If one wishes to take the great golden elixir,
it's best to fast for about a hundred days first.
If unable to do so,
taking it directly is fine,
though achieving immortality will be slightly delayed,
with no major hindrance.
In times of famine,
if hiding in mountains and forests,
knowing this method
can prevent starvation.
Otherwise,
there's no urgent need to abstain,
as rushing into it brings little great benefit.
Moreover, when people suddenly stop eating meat,
upon smelling rich and fresh scents,
they cannot help but feel desire in their hearts.
If not yet ready to renounce the world and leave family,
to dwell in caves and cliffs,
it's unwise to forcibly give up all flavors
and cause oneself suffering;
better not to abstain from grains but to regulate hunger and fullness.
There are nearly a hundred methods,
such as taking dozens of pills of mineral medicine to center oneself,
enabling one to avoid hunger for forty to fifty days.
Refining pine, cypress, or atractylodes
can also help maintain centeredness,
but it's not as effective as the great medicine,
lasting no more than ten years.
Some methods avoid hunger for a hundred or two hundred days,
while others require daily intake
to stave off hunger.
Some involve eating a full meal of delicious food first,
then taking medicine to preserve the ingested food,
preventing digestion,
allowing abstinence for three years.
To resume eating grains,
one should take sunflower seeds and lard to purge it,
whereupon the undigested food is expelled,
unchanged as before.
In Luòyáng, there was a Daoist named Dǒng Wēiniǎn,
who often stayed at the White Society,
completely abstaining from food.
Chén Zǐxù served and attended him,
learning the Dao over time
and eventually obtaining his method:
grind about ten herbs like gāncǎo, fángfēng, and xiànshí into powder,
first take a spoonful,
then swallow twelve pebble-like stones the size of sparrow eggs,
sufficient to avoid hunger for a hundred days.
Then take the powder again,
maintaining energy and complexion as before.
To resume eating grains,
drink a sunflower seed decoction to expel the stones,
after which one can eat.
Another method uses Chìlóng xuè and Qīnglóng gāo,
made with water of dānshā and zēngqīng,
placing stones into it,
and in a short while,
the stones soften and can be eaten.
If not taken promptly,
they dissolve completely.
Eating these stones to satisfaction
makes one strong.
There's also Yǐnshí sǎn,
where a spoonful is added to a peck of white stones,
boiled with water,
quickly cooking them like taro,
edible as a grain substitute.
Zhāng Tàiyuán, his whole family, and dozens of disciples
lived in seclusion in the Línlǘ Mountains,
using this method to eat stones for over ten years,
all remaining plump and healthy.
But it requires white stones,
unlike Chìlóng xuè and Qīnglóng gāo,
which can use any found stones,
though boiling is necessary,
involving the hassle of firewood.
Some use talismans,
some use water,
some both talismans and water.
Others use dried dates,
nine a day,
with one or two shēng of wine.
Some consume the energy of the twelve two-hour periods,
starting from midnight,
from nine-nine to eight-eight, seven-seven, six-six, five-five, and stopping.
Some face east in spring to ingest the green energy of Jupiter,
directing it to the liver;
in summer, ingest the red energy of Mars,
to the heart;
in the last month of each season, ingest the yellow energy of Saturn,
to the spleen;
in autumn, ingest the white energy of Venus,
to the lungs;
in winter, ingest the black energy of Mercury,
to the kidneys.
Also, the Zhōngyuè Daoist Xī Yuánjié ingested the essence of the six wù cycles,
with great effect.
For instance, in the jiǎzǐ decade,
there's the essence of wùchén,
so throughout the ten days,
constantly face the chén direction and swallow energy,
and when the next jiǎ cycle comes, face its wù direction.
The Gān Shǐ method
summons the six jiǎ and six dīng jade maidens,
each with their names,
using incanted water to drink,
which can also prevent hunger in oxen and horses.
Some meditate on the name of the spirit in the spleen,
named Huángchángzǐ,
while closing the mouth and swallowing internal energy,
all with genuine effects.
I've seen many who abstained from grains for two or three years,
all light-bodied with good complexion,
resistant to wind, cold, heat, and dampness,
mostly without being overweight.
Though I haven't seen those who didn't eat for decades,
ordinary people die within about ten days without grains,
yet these practitioners have lasted years and remain normal,
so why doubt it can't last long?
If all grain-abstainers were emaciated,
one might constantly worry
it couldn't be sustained.
But asking those who practice it,
all initially had less energy,
then gradually became stronger,
improving month by month,
year by year.
Thus,
it can be prolonged without concern.
Those who achieve longevity and the Dao
all do so through taking medicines and swallowing energy,
and those who succeed are not mistaken.
Those who take medicines and abstain from grains
almost all experience initial weakness.
But those using only talisman water or single breath intake
all become thin and weak within forty days,
after which they become strong.
Master Zhèng said:
I never drank much alcohol,
but once in the Copper Mountains,
abstaining from grains for about two years,
I could drink several dǒu without getting drunk.
From this, it can be inferred
that not eating makes one more resistant to toxins,
which is a sign of being less prone to illness.
I asked how he got wine in the mountains?
Master Zhèng said,
first brew good yúnyè wine without filtering,
then mix with powders of cinnamon, aconite, licorice, and five or six other herbs to form pills,
dry them in the sun,
and put one pill the size of an egg
into a dǒu of water,
instantly turning it into fine wine.
There's also the Yellow Emperor's Yúnyè Quán method,
using fermented rice and seven or eight herbs combined,
take one shēng,
and add one shēng of water to it,
like adding water to thousand-year vinegar.
It never runs out,
always tasting good and unchanged,
very beneficial to drink.
Also, using talisman water to abstain from grains,
though it first causes emaciation,
it's good to know as an option,
in case of sudden famine
when there's no time to prepare medicines,
then talisman water is the best choice."
There was a certain Féng who,
merely ingested breath alone,
having abstained from grains for three years already.
Observing him climbing mountains on foot,
he carried about a hectoliter's weight,
remaining untired throughout the day.
Moreover, he occasionally drew his bow,
yet barely spoke,
and when he did speak, he refused to be loud.
When asked, he said,
abstaining from grains depletes essence and wastes energy,
which is the greatest taboo.
I have also repeatedly seen superficial Taoists
who, wishing to boast of their strangeness,
seek fame for not eating,
but in truth do not know the method,
only pretending not to eat soups and rice.
As for drinking wine,
they consume over a dou by midday,
with dried meats, dried fish, tai fu, dates, chestnuts, chicken eggs, and such,
constantly in their mouths.
Some eat large amounts of meat, swallowing the juices
and spitting out the dregs,
with tens of jin passing through their mouths all day,
this is simply making fine food instead.
Generally, wine drinkers who only drink wine and eat dried meats without consuming grains
can all endure for half a year to a year without distress,
but this is not called grain abstention.
In Wú, there was a Taoist named Shí Chūn,
who whenever he practiced breath circulation to treat illnesses for others,
would not eat,
waiting until the patient recovered,
whether it took a hundred days,
or a month before he ate.
Emperor Jǐng of Wú heard of this and said,
"This cannot last long,
he will surely starve to death."
So he summoned and locked him up,
assigning people to guard him.
Chūn only asked for two or three sheng of water,
and after over a year like this,
Chūn's complexion became even brighter and more cheerful,
his energy and strength as before.
Emperor Jǐng asked him,
"How much longer can you endure?"
Chūn said, "Unlimited,
possibly several decades,
only fearing old age and death,
not worried about hunger."
Then he released and dismissed him.
According to Chūn's words,
it shows that grain abstention cannot prolong life.
Nowadays, there are also those who have obtained Chūn's method."
Someone asked about the method to avoid cold.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Some, on the day of Lìdōng (Start of Winter),
take talismans of the sixth Bǐng and sixth Dīng,
or close the mouth and circulate the energy of five fires twelve hundred times,
then they won't feel cold throughout the twelfth month.
Some drink Tàiyáng wine,
or take Zǐshíyīng Zhūqī powder,
or take one male pill,
followed by two female pills,
which can also make one endure a day and night without cold.
Female pills use realgar, zengqing, alum stone, and magnetite.
Male pills use orpiment, cinnabar, and chalcanthite.
However, these do not benefit life extension."
Someone asked about the method to avoid heat.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Some, on the day of Lìxià (Start of Summer),
take talismans of the sixth Rén and sixth Guǐ,
or circulate the energy of the sixth Guǐ,
or take Xuánbīng pills,
or take Fēishuāng powder.
But these require the bark of the Xiāoqiū tree,
and the blood of a black snake traveling north at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
so few can compound them.
Only Yòu Bózǐ and Wáng Zhòngdū,
these two men dressed in heavy fur,
exposed under the summer sun,
surrounded by ten stoves' fire,
did not claim heat,
nor did their bodies sweat,
likely using this method."
Someone asked about the method to ward off the five weapons.
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"I heard that the Great Emperor of Wú once received essential methods from Master Jiè,
saying that merely knowing how to write the characters for the Big Dipper and the sun and moon,
makes one unafraid of blades.
The emperor tested this on several tens of attendants,
who often charged ahead in battle,
and were never injured for life.
Master Zhèng said,
merely reciting the names of the five weapons is also effective.
The sword is named Dàfáng,
governed by the star Xū;
the bow is named Qūzhāng,
governed by the star Dǐ;
the arrow is named Pánghuáng,
governed by the star Yínghuò;
the blade is named Shīshāng,
governed by the star Jiǎo;
the crossbow is named Yuǎnwàng,
governed by the star Zhāng;
the halberd is named Dàjiàng,
governed by the star Shēn.
Before battle,
often silently invoke them.
Some make Chìlíng talismans on the fifth day of the fifth month,
placing them in front of the heart.
Some at noon on a Bǐngwǔ day,
make Yàn Jūn's dragon-tiger three-pouch talisman.
Year talismans are changed yearly,
month talismans monthly,
day talismans daily.
Some wear the Xīwángmǔ military faith talisman,
or the Yínghuò Vermilion Bird talisman,
or the Nánjí Shūojīn talisman,
or carry the Quèrèn talisman,
Zhùróng talisman.
Some apply Yùzhá powder,
or bathe in forbidden scallion soup,
or take Mùjīng to make the six yin general talisman,
pointing it at the enemy.
Some at the moment of a lunar eclipse,
use the blood of a three-year-old toad with eight characters under its throat,
to write on their blades or swords.
Some carry Wǔwēi talismans or Yínghuǒ pills.
Some, when crossing blades,
step on the Dipper and tread on the celestial net,
calling out to the elders of the four directions,
also with clear effect.
People in this era,
also have methods to ward off the five weapons,
and there are often such cases."
Someone asked about the method of concealment.
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"There are five divine methods,
sitting disappearing and standing vanishing among them.
But they do not benefit lifespan matters,
and if done without reason among humans,
it leads to strange reputations,
not worth recklessly practicing.
They can prepare for military chaos and crises,
used only when unavoidable,
to escape danger.
Master Zhèng said,
taking the Dàyǐn talisman for ten days,
to conceal, turn left;
to appear, turn right.
Some apply Yùtái pills on the body;
or use Shézú powder,
or carry Límǔ grass,
or break Qīnglóng grass,
to hide under the six Dīng;
or enter a bamboo field,
and hold the soil of the celestial pivot;
or go to the Hé Lóng stone chamber,
and hide in the shade of the cloud canopy;
or submerge in the Qīnglíng abyss,
to pass the path of the dark gate;
or ride the Tiānyī horse to roam the purple chamber;
or ascend to the bright hall of Tiānyī;
or enter the jade maiden's golden cabinet;
or turn the back to the assistant and face the official,
standing under the triple canopy;
or cast off headscarf and shoes, use gallbladder decoction and child's clothing talisman,
Zǐ Jū Méng rén,
Qīngyè Guìgěng,
six jiǎ parents,
Pìcè glue,
Bó Mǎ mud pill,
Mùguǐ's child,
Jīnshāng mugwort,
some can become a child,
or an old man,
or a bird,
or a beast,
or grass,
or a tree,
or one of the six domestic animals,
or rely on wood to become wood,
or rely on stone to become stone,
rely on water to become water,
rely on fire to become fire,
this is what is called changing form and altering appearance,
but not complete concealment."
Someone asked:
"Emperor Wǔ of Wèi once captured Zuǒ Yuánfàng and put him in shackles,
yet he managed to free himself naturally.
What method did he use?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"I cannot know exactly what methods Master Zuǒ employed.
However, having examined various formula texts,
there are those who take coix seeds three times monthly,
combined with three to five yīn elixirs,
or use paired yang embryos,
or the jumping insect that travels eastward on the seventh day of the seventh month,
or the single garment of the dragon child on stone on the fifth day of the fifth month,
or the thunder wedge on the summer solstice,
or the twenty-one character celestial script,
or self-removing father's blood,
or the jade child's surplus grain,
or combine the mountain lord's eye,
the river earl's surplus grain,
and floating cloud dregs to apply them -
all can achieve self-release.
However, Master Zuǒ's transformations were boundless,
and may not have come from these methods.
Using the six jiǎ transformations oneself,
one's true form cannot be captured."
Someone asked:
"Can those who practice the Way avoid illness?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Those who exhaust the principles of nurturing life,
having taken spiritual medicines,
and persistently practice breath circulation,
performing daoyin exercises morning and night,
to stimulate and move the nutritive and defensive energies,
preventing any blockage,
supplemented with bedroom arts,
regulating diet,
avoiding exposure to wind and dampness,
and not worrying about what cannot be achieved -
thus can avoid illness.
But the problem for those living among people
is that their determination cannot be focused,
their practice lacks constancy,
and they suffer from laziness and lack of diligence,
so they inevitably develop ailments.
If one merely has faith in the Way
but lacks self-benefitting practices,
with one's lifespan in isolation and emptiness,
and the body facing the danger of damage,
then the three corpse spirits will take advantage of declining months and dangerous days,
when entering the realm of fatal illness,
summoning evil energies,
recklessly inviting ghosts and spirits,
to come cause disaster and harm.
When the six calamities converge
and the three punishments align,
the disaster will surely be great.
For those still relatively healthy,
various diseases will arise,
while those with pre-existing conditions
will have them activated.
Therefore, ancient practitioners of the Way
all simultaneously cultivated medical arts
to rescue themselves from immediate misfortune.
Common Daoist priests
do not understand this principle,
relying only on what they've heard,
which largely doesn't concern healing methods.
Unable to withdraw from society and live in seclusion,
focusing on internal practices
to repel illness and pain,
when sickness reaches them,
they have no means to treat it,
making them inferior even to ordinary people specializing in decoctions.
This is what is called advancing without attaining Hándān's gait,
while retreating losing Shòulíng's meaning.
I have seen the Golden Casket Green Bag collection of Cuī Zhōngshū's Yellow Silk Formulas and about five hundred volumes of various formulas compiled by Dài Bà and Huá Tā.
Gān, Hú, Lǚ, Fù, Zhōu, Shǐ, Gān, Táng, Tōng, Ruǎn, Nánhé and others
each compiled collections for sudden death emergencies,
some containing one hundred ten,
some ninety-four,
some eighty-five,
some forty-six formulas.
People consider them exhaustive
and unsurpassable.
But examining them thoroughly,
I find them quite incomplete,
with many urgent diseases not fully covered,
moreover confused and mixed up,
lacking systematic organization,
making consultation
not immediately accessible.
For treating sudden emergencies,
they all use expensive medicines,
often dozens of types,
which unless one is wealthy and lives in the capital,
cannot normally stockpile,
nor quickly obtain.
They also frequently have people use acupuncture for treatment,
with moxibustion methods unclear about locations and measurements,
merely naming the body's cavity points and nutrient transport points.
Unless one is an experienced physician familiar with Mingtang flow injection and side diagrams,
how can one understand them?
What I have compiled in one hundred volumes,
titled Jade Case Formulas,
categorizes diseases by name,
organized by type continuously,
without confusion or mixing,
with its emergency treatment section in three volumes,
all straightforward and simple,
concise yet easily verified,
where between hedges and paths,
looking around reveals medicines everywhere,
for all urgent diseases,
none left unprepared for,
with this formula collection at home,
doctors become unnecessary.
Most doctors inherit family traditions,
having reputation without substance,
merely cultivating empty fame
to seek wealth and profit.
Poor scholars and retired gentlemen
cannot afford their services,
and those who can often end up misled,
so understanding the essentials oneself
is better than inviting ignorant physicians.
Doctors cannot be quickly found when needed,
and when found, they may not readily serve,
allowing minor ailments in the flesh
to become deep-seated calamities in the vitals,
reaching the point of being incurable.
Moreover, for sudden urgent illnesses,
traveling far to seek advice
mostly results in unnecessary deaths."
Someone asked:
"Regarding future fortune and misfortune,
safety and danger, staying or leaving,
knowing these can preserve one's person -
is there a Way for this?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Gazing upward at celestial patterns,
looking down to examine terrestrial features,
divining winds and energies,
arranging counting rods for calculation,
deducing with three chess pieces,
pacing the nine palaces,
examining the eight trigrams,
investigating where flying and hidden energies gather,
diagnosing anomalies among things,
foretelling good and ill fortune through turtle shells and yarrow stalks—
these are all inferior arts and common skills,
tiring and unreliable.
But to see all under heaven without leaving the curtained chamber,
that is to enter the realm of the divine.
Some use the Three Sovereigns' celestial writings
to summon the Directors of Fate and Calamity, the lords of the Five Peaks,
the spirits of the field paths, outpost chiefs, and the Six Dīng,
making them visible to people,
and by questioning them on various matters,
then good and bad fortune become clear,
as if held in the palm of the hand;
nothing far or near, hidden or deep,
cannot be known in advance.
Some summon the Six Yīn Jade Maidens—
the method takes sixty days to complete,
and once complete, they can be commanded long-term.
Some make offerings to invoke the Eight Scribes,
the Eight Scribes being
the essences of the eight trigrams,
which also suffice to foresee the unformed.
Some take géhuā and autumn miscanthus, hemp pollen, a dāoguī measure or a fāngcùnbǐ spoonful,
and suddenly feel as if about to sleep,
then hear someone speak to them of matters they cannot decide,
and good or ill fortune is immediately determined.
Some use a bright mirror nine inches or larger to reflect themselves,
concentrating their thoughts,
and after seven days and seven nights, they see divine beings,
whether male or female,
old or young;
once shown,
they know in their hearts affairs from a thousand miles away
and events yet to come.
Some use one bright mirror,
some use two,
called sun and moon mirrors.
Some use four,
called four-direction mirrors.
The four directions mean
when reflecting,
one is placed each in front, behind, left, and right.
Using four mirrors reveals many coming spirits.
Some have vertical eyes,
some ride dragons or drive tigers,
their caps and robes in colors
unlike those in the world,
all depicted in classical texts.
To cultivate this path,
first memorize in the dark the names, titles, and positions of the spirits to be summoned,
and recognize their attire and caps.
Otherwise,
when they suddenly arrive, you might forget which spirit it is,
or become startled and fearful,
which can harm people.
Practicing this,
it's best to be in tranquil, secluded forests or foothills,
where external forms don't meet the eye,
and outside sounds don't enter the ears;
then the path is sure to succeed.
The Three Youths, Nine Maidens, Festival Longevity Lord,
the nine-headed serpent-bodied hundred and twenty officials—
even if they come, do not stare intently.
If some question you,
or scold you angrily,
do not answer either.
Some may have dazzling attendants,
strongmen in armor,
riding dragons or driving tigers,
with noisy pipes and drums—
do not look up or speak to them.
Just concentrate on the true form of Lǎojūn;
when Lǎojūn's true form appears,
rise and bow twice.
Lǎojūn's true form:
visualize it—
surname Lǐ, name Dān,
courtesy name Bóyáng,
body nine feet tall,
yellow complexion,
beak-like mouth,
prominent nose,
elegant eyebrows five inches long,
ears seven inches long,
forehead with three lines running top to bottom,
feet bearing the eight trigrams,
using a divine turtle as a bed,
in a golden tower and jade hall,
silver steps,
clad in five-colored clouds,
wearing a layered crown,
holding a sharp, pointed sword,
followed by a hundred twenty yellow children,
with twelve blue dragons on the left,
twenty-six white tigers on the right,
twenty-four vermilion birds in front,
seventy-two black tortoises behind,
led by twelve qióngqí beasts,
followed by thirty-six bìxié creatures,
with lightning and thunder above,
shining and brilliant.
This account comes from immortal scriptures.
Seeing Lǎojūn extends one's lifespan,
makes the heart like the sun and moon,
and omniscient."
Some ask about the method for strengthening teeth.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Nourish them with the flowery pool [saliva],
soak them with sweet liquor,
and tap the teeth three hundred times at dawn—
they will never loosen.
Next, hold rehmannia decoction in the mouth,
or xuándǎn soup,
and pills of snake fat, alum stone, or jiǔjí powder.
Then loose teeth will firm up,
and any worm infestation will heal.
Also, taking língfēi powder
can make lost teeth regrow."
Some ask about the method for sharp hearing.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Practice dragon guidance and tiger pulling,
bear stretching and turtle swallowing,
swallow flying, snake coiling, and bird extending,
heaven bending and earth tilting,
keeping the red and yellow light
from leaving the cavern chamber [dantian],
ape perching and rabbit startling—
do this twelve hundred times,
and hearing will not deteriorate.
For those already deaf,
fumigate with black turtle,
or wrap jí thorn heads, sheep dung, cassia twigs, and sparrow-cassia to plug the ears;
or use wolf's bane and cooked kudzu,
or monkshood and onion juice,
combined and inserted into the ears,
or pour steamed carp brain into them—
all can cure."
Some ask about the method for brightening vision.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Draw the rising light of the triple burner,
summon the great fire from the southern li,
wash with bright stones,
warm with sunlight,
and burn a bǐngdīng clear-sight talisman,
mixing it with wine to wash the eyes—
the ancients could write at night this way.
Or boil turnip seeds in vinegar until cooked,
sun-dry them,
powder and take a fāngcùnbǐ spoonful,
three times daily,
until one dǒu is finished—
then one can see at night.
Or use dog gall to decoct a powder of green sheep, turtledove, abalone shell, and motherwort flowers,
or use clove, Chinese goldthread, and breast milk decoction to apply.
All various eye ailments will heal,
and vision will become exceptionally clear and bright."
Someone asked about the method of climbing steep heights, traversing dangerous terrain, and traveling far without exhaustion.
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Only by consuming the great elixir
can one make the body light and strength vigorous,
laboring without fatigue.
If one is newly entering the mountains and forests,
and the body is not yet fully robust,
it is appropriate to wash the feet with Yúnzhū powder, Bǎihuā sweet wine, and Xuánzǐ decoction,
and use Hǔdǎn pills, Zhūmíng wine, Tiānxióng crane fat pills, Fēilián decoction of Qiūmáng, Chēqián, and Zéxiè powder.
After using them for ten days,
not only will one not get exhausted when traveling far,
but it will also make one walk faster,
up to three times the normal speed.
If one can ride the qiāo,
they can roam throughout the world,
unrestricted by mountains and rivers.
There are three methods of riding the qiāo:
the first is called the dragon qiāo,
the second is the tiger qiāo,
the third is the Lúlǔ qiāo.
Either ingest talismans and concentrate intensely,
if wanting to travel a thousand lǐ,
then concentrate for one shí.
If concentrating for twelve shí day and night,
then one can travel twelve thousand lǐ in one day and one night,
but cannot exceed this.
Beyond this, one must concentrate again,
following the previous method.
Or use jujube heartwood to make a flying chariot,
fasten with ox leather straps and connect rings and swords to pull its mechanism,
or visualize five snakes, six dragons, and three oxen intersecting with the celestial force and ride them,
ascending forty lǐ high,
named Tàiqīng.
Within Tàiqīng,
the qi is very strong,
capable of overwhelming a person.
The master said that when a kite flies higher,
it simply stretches its two wings straight,
no longer needing to flap them to advance on its own,
because it gradually rides the strong qi.
When a dragon first rises through the clouds,
it ascends to forty lǐ,
then moves on its own.
These words come from immortals,
and are passed down among the common people,
but are truly beyond ordinary people's understanding.
Moreover, riding the qiāo requires long fasting,
abstaining from pungent vegetables,
and avoiding blood-based foods.
After one year,
one can then ride these three qiāo.
Even if again ingesting talismans,
concentrating on the five dragon qiāo allows the farthest travel,
the others not exceeding a thousand lǐ.
The ascent, descent, stay, and departure
all have their own methods,
and must not be done arbitrarily.
If one does not observe these taboos,
they should not recklessly ride the qiāo,
lest they face the disaster of falling."
Someone said:
"In the chapters of Lǎozǐ and the Guīwén scripture,
it is said that after medicinal warfare,
in the years of metal and wood,
there will surely be a great epidemic,
with only one in ten thousand surviving.
May I ask the method to avoid it?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"The secret method for immortals to enter pestilence involves
visualizing one's body as five jades.
The five jades
follow the colors of the four seasons:
green in spring,
red in summer,
yellow in the last month of each season,
white in autumn,
black in winter.
Also visualize wearing a golden headscarf,
and the heart as a blazing fire,
as large as a dou measure,
then there is nothing to fear.
Another method:
visualize the hair spreading to cover the body,
each strand
has a large star attached to it.
Also visualize forming the seven stars of the Big Dipper,
with the bowl covering the head,
and the handle pointing forward.
Also visualize the qi of the five zàng organs,
emanating from both eyes,
surrounding the body like clouds and mist:
green qi from the liver,
white qi from the lungs,
yellow qi from the spleen,
black qi from the kidneys,
red qi from the heart.
When the five colors are intricately mixed,
one can even share a bed with the infected.
Either perform Yǔ steps and call upon the Jade Maiden of the direct day,
or hold the breath and visualize strongmen
wielding thousand-catty golden hammers,
one hundred twenty men for self-protection.

Or use Shèguǐ pills, Chìchē shǐzhě pills, Guànjūn pills, Xúchángqīng powder, Yùhán essence powder, Qīngnián dàoshi fumigation pills, Cuīwén yellow powder, Cǎoyù wine, Huángtíng pills, Huángfú, Lǎozǐ collar talisman, Chìxūzǐ peach blossom talisman;
all have good efficacy."
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The scriptures of the divine immortals contain twenty-five volumes on the methods of yellow and white,
with over a thousand entries.
Yellow refers to
gold.
White refers to
silver.
The ancients kept their methods secret and revered,
not wishing to speak of them directly,
hence they concealed them in such terms.
Some titled their chapters Gēng Xīn,
as Gēng Xīn also signifies metal.
However, most are profound and subtle, hard to comprehend,
with only a few that can be clearly understood.
Many people doubt these matters as false and fanciful,
just like those who do not believe in immortals.
I once studied the scriptures of the nine elixirs and the liquid of gold and silver under Lord Zhèng,
and thus sought further to learn the five volumes of the central classic on yellow and white.
Lord Zhèng said,
he had once attempted these methods with Lord Zuǒ in the Tóng Mountains of Lújiāng,
and they succeeded.
Yet the diligence and hardship of purification and taboos
are no different from those for golden elixirs and divine immortal medicines.
Commoners often ridicule my fondness for delving into unorthodox paths,
saying I strive to force understanding upon what is incomprehensible in the world.
But why would I do so?
If I wished to use such matters
to showcase literary skills for posterity,
then the over two hundred volumes of my external essays and miscellaneous writings
would suffice to convey my ideas to future generations,
with no need for this.
Moreover, this inner volume
consists of straightforward words,
without embellishment.
I also know that discussing these topics
will lead many to call them impractical and irrelevant,
unlike discussing everyday, immediate principles
that can resonate with the masses.
Yet the reason I cannot refrain from these matters,
knowing they do not appeal to worldly ears,
and still write about them,
is truly because I have witnessed their efficacy,
and the masters who transmitted them were not deceitful.
But I am poor and lack resources,
and have encountered many hardships in fate,
with unavoidable predicaments,
compounded by blocked roads,
making it impossible to obtain the necessary ingredients,
so I never had the chance to attempt their creation.
If I now tell people
that I know how to make gold and silver,
yet suffer from hunger and cold myself,
how is it different from being unable to walk
while selling medicine for lameness,
expecting others to believe?
It truly cannot be achieved.
However, principles do not always align with wishes,
and one cannot judge everything uniformly.
The reason I diligently record this in writing
is to let future scholars who seek the unusual and appreciate truth
see my book and understand the intent behind discussing the Way.
As for the arts of transformation,
what cannot they accomplish?
The human body is inherently visible,
yet there are methods to conceal it.
Spirits and ghosts are inherently hidden,
yet there are ways to reveal them.
There are many who can perform such feats.
Water and fire exist in heaven,
yet they can be harnessed with sundials and mirrors.
Lead is naturally white,
yet it can be reddened to form cinnabar.
Cinnabar is naturally red,
yet it can be whitened back into lead.
Clouds, rain, frost, and snow
are all energies of heaven and earth,
yet they can be created with medicines,
indistinguishable from the real.
As for flying and crawling creatures,
wriggling beings,
endowed with forms by creation,
they have fixed natures.
Yet when they suddenly change their old bodies,
transforming into different entities,
the variations are endless,
beyond full description.
Humans, as beings,
are valued for their intelligence and spirituality,
yet men and women can alter their forms,
become cranes or stones,
tigers or apes,
sand or turtles,
and such cases are not few.
As for mountains turning into abysses,
deep valleys becoming hills,
these are also great transformations of nature.
Transformation
is a natural process of heaven and earth;
why doubt that gold and silver cannot be made from other substances?
Compare it to fire obtained from a burning mirror,
or water from a moon mirror:
are they any different
from ordinary fire and water?
When a snake becomes a dragon,
or straw turns into fat,
it is no different from what occurs naturally.
Yet the origins and causes
are all natural interactions;
only those who exhaust principles and understand nature
can grasp their essence,
and only those who trace beginnings to ends
can comprehend their true state.
Those with narrow views and limited knowledge,
confined to their nests and caves,
guess at profound mysteries beyond measure,
dismiss divine transformations as absurd,
and because the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius did not speak of it,
or ancient texts do not record it,
they deem it all untrue—
is that not ignorant?
Moreover, commoners, because Liú Xiàng failed to make gold,
claim there is no such Way in the world,
like seeing farmers suffer flood or drought with no harvest
and saying the five grains cannot be sown and grown.
Wú Dàwén, the internal historian of Chéngdū,
learned and knowledgeable,
also said he once served the Daoist Lǐ Gēn,
and saw him melt lead and tin,
tossing a small bean-sized amount of medicine into the cauldron,
stirring it with an iron spoon,
and upon cooling, it turned into silver.
Dàwén obtained the secret formula,
but when he wished to attempt it himself,
after a hundred days of purification,
he was detained by official duties,
and never succeeded,
often sighing that human life is full of shortcomings.
Also, Huán Jūnshān spoke of Chéng Wěi, a court gentleman of the Hàn,
who was fond of the arts of yellow and white.
He married a woman from a family that knew such methods.
Wěi once accompanied the emperor but had no timely clothing,
and was greatly worried.
His wife said,
"Allow me to procure two bolts of silk."
The silk arrived before them without cause.
Wěi, following the Hóng Bǎo text from his pillow,
attempted to make gold but failed.
His wife went to see him,
as he was fanning charcoal to heat a tube,
which contained mercury.
She said,
"I wish to test something with you."
She took medicine from her pouch,
added a small amount to it,
and after a mealtime, opened it—
it had turned into silver.
Wěi, astonished, said,
"The Way is near you,
yet you did not tell me earlier—
why?"
She replied,
"To obtain it, one must have the destined fate."
So Wěi coaxed her day and night,
even selling fields and homes to provide fine food and clothing,
but she still refused to tell him.
Wěi then conspired with companions to beat and subdue her.
She always knew of it,
and told Wěi,
"The Way must be transmitted to the right person;
meeting such a one on the road, I would teach it instantly.
But if it is not the right person,
one who agrees in word but not in heart,
even if torn limb from limb,
the Way will not be revealed."
Wěi pressed her relentlessly,
until she went mad,
ran naked,
smeared herself with mud,
and eventually died.
More recently, the former governor of Lújiāng, Huà Lìngsī,
a man of great talent and broad learning,
well-versed in many subjects,
often disbelieved in unorthodox matters.
Later, a Daoist explained the methods of yellow and white,
and he had him attempt it:
melting lead in an iron vessel,
adding a powdered medicine,
it turned into silver.
Then, melting this silver
and adding another medicine,
it became gold.
He also learned from this Daoist the method of clear vision,
and before a hundred days of practice,
while lying at night, he could see the celestial patterns and his surroundings clearly,
unaware of any houses or fences.
Moreover, his concubine named Yáohuá, who had died,
appeared in form,
and spoke with him as in life.
Again, when sacrificing at the temple,
he heard the temple deity respond to his bow,
and the bed seemed to move with a sound.
Lìng Sī then sighed, saying,
"In the world, indeed, there is nothing that does not exist;
although the Five Classics do not record it,
one cannot arbitrarily judge based on personal opinion.
However, those unacquainted with esoteric arts,
suddenly hearing this,
how could they not be startled and find it strange?"
Moreover, the art of alchemy (huángbái shù) is also like compounding divine elixirs:
both require fasting and purification for over a hundred days,
and one must also understand prescription texts thoroughly,
with intentions aligned—only then can it be practiced.
It is not something that turbid and defiled individuals,
or the unintelligent,
or those rarely involved in occult arts can accomplish.
Among them, some require oral instructions,
all of which should be transmitted by a teacher.
Also, one should enter deep into the mountains,
in pure and clean places,
not wanting ordinary, foolish people to know of it.
Yet Liú Xiàng attempted it within the palace,
having palace attendants supply the needs for the task—
they certainly were not fasting and purified,
nor could they sever human affairs,
preventing people from coming and going.
How could success be achieved under such conditions?"
Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn states:
"Shǐ Zǐxīn was appointed as a secretary to the chancellor,
had a building constructed,
and mobilized clerks, soldiers, and government slaves to supply it,
yet failed to produce gold.
The chancellor himself felt his strength insufficient,
so he reported to Empress Dowager Fù.
The empress dowager was no longer interested in gold for profit,
but hearing that successful gold could be used to make longevity medicine,
she became eager for it,
then appointed him as a court gentleman,
housed him in the Northern Palace,
and had envoys attend to him.
How could such a divine method be performed in the palace,
with ordinary people混杂ly participating in its making?"
In the common practice of dyeing silk fabrics,
one still does not want mixed company to see it,
for seeing it will ruin it;
how much more so for the transformations in alchemy?
In all matters, regardless of size,
one must grasp the essentials.
If the method is not obtained,
even recklessly making wine, sauce, vinegar, or stews will fail,
let alone great undertakings?"
I once consulted Master Zhèng, saying:
"Lǎojūn said,
'Do not value goods that are hard to obtain.'
And in the most well-governed ages,
all cast gold into the mountains,
discarded jade into the valleys.
I wonder why the ancients considered gold and silver precious yet left behind methods for them?"
Master Zhèng replied to me:
"What Lǎojūn meant
refers to those who dig through sand and split rocks,
overturn mountains and drain deep pools,
travel thousands of miles without regard for distance,
heedless of being crushed or drowned,
in seeking rare curios,
thereby hindering the people's seasons,
not knowing when to stop,
to adorn what is useless.
As for those who wish to practice the Way,
aspiring to seek longevity,
yet also engage in trade,
not upholding honesty and humility,
braving depths and crossing dangers,
plunging into risks chasing profit,
not sparing their bodies and lives,
and not cultivating few desires.
But when genuine persons make gold,
they intend to ingest it themselves to attain divinity,
not to gain wealth.
Therefore, the scriptures say:
'Gold can be made,
and the world can be transcended.'
Silver can also be ingested,
but it is not as effective as gold."
I objected:
"Why not ingest the gold and silver of the world instead of transforming and making it?
Making it means it is not genuine,
and not genuine implies fraud and falsity."
Master Zhèng answered me:
"The gold and silver in the world are all good,
but Daoist priests are mostly poor.
Hence the proverb says:
'There are no fat immortals or rich Daoists.'
Disciples and masters, whether ten or five in number,
how can they obtain gold and silver to supply themselves?
Nor can they travel far to gather them,
so it is appropriate to make them.
Moreover, the gold transformed and made
is the essence of various medicines,
superior to that which is natural.
The Xiān Jīng says:
'Cinnabar essence produces gold.'
This is the theory of using cinnabar to make gold.
Therefore, where cinnabar is found in the mountains,
below it there is often gold.
And when gold is successfully made, it becomes a true substance,
identical inside and out,
un-diminished even after a hundred smeltings.
Thus, the formula states:
'It can be used to make nails.'
Demonstrating its hardness and strength.
This accords with the natural Dào.
So, being able to do this—
how can it be called fraud?
Fraud refers to using céngqīng to coat iron,
making the iron red like copper;
or using egg white to transform silver,
making the silver yellow like gold—
both are external changes without internal transformation.
As for mushrooms and fungi,
they grow naturally,
yet the Xiān Jīng has methods to plant mushrooms using five minerals and five woods;
when the mushrooms grow,
they are picked and ingested,
no different from natural mushrooms,
both enabling people to attain longevity—
this is similar to making gold.
Pheasants transforming into clams,
sparrows transforming into cockles,
are just the same as natural ones.
Therefore, the Xiān Jīng says:
'Flowing pearl, nine cycles turned,
father does not tell son;
transformed into gold and silver,
naturally they act upon each other.'
It also says:
'Those who take cinnabar turned into gold
and ascend as immortals
are superior practitioners;
those who consume mushrooms and practice dǎoyǐn,
swallowing breath to live long,
are middle practitioners;
those who feed on plants and trees,
reverting after a thousand years,
are inferior practitioners.'
It further states:
'Gold and silver can be made by oneself,
such is their natural property;
longevity can be learned and attained.'
The Yù Dié Jì states:
'All under heaven, vast and varied,
can achieve longevity;
the trouble lies in hesitation,
hence they do not succeed.'
Condensing mercury into gold
can produce nails.
The Tóng Zhù Jīng says:
'Cinnabar can be made into gold,
river chariot can be made into silver;
success is immediate upon standing,
and what is made is genuine.
If you attain this Dào,
you can immortalize your body.'
Huángshānzǐ says:
'Heaven and earth possess gold,
I can make it;
two yellow and one red,
instantly achieved without doubt.'
The Guī Jiǎ Wén states:
'My life lies with me, not with heaven;
returned elixir forms gold for myriad years.'
How could the ancients deceive me?
But the problem is that those who know this Dào are often poor,
and the medicines may be extremely cheap yet grow in distant lands,
not obtainable in times of chaos.
For instance, róngyán and lǔxián are cheap substances;
in peaceful times, they are practically worthless,
but now, regardless of price, they cannot be bought.
Qiānglǐ shídǎn,
sought by the millions for one jīn,
is also unobtainable.
Merely knowing the formula
is the same as not knowing it at all—
one can only sigh deeply over this.
Those who possess the method
may suffer hunger and cold, unable to compound it,
while the wealthy and noble, in turn, do not know the method.
Even if they come to know it,
none believe in it.
Suppose they somewhat believe,
they already have abundant gold and silver themselves—
would they be willing to spend their visible wealth to purchase the medicines,
fearing the regret of abandoning the tethered to chase the flying?
Thus, none are willing to act.
Moreover, calculating the cost of buying medicines
against the value of the resulting substance,
there is especially great profit,
yet it additionally requires fasting, abstinence, and toil—
therefore, none can bring themselves to do it.
Moreover, without the oral instructions from a clear-sighted master,
one truly should not attempt it lightly."
Now, the medicines of physicians
are extremely superficial and obvious,
yet their commonly effective formulas
are still kept secret.
Thus, formulas mention using Rear Palace Wandering Maiden,
secluded side glue,
Fēngjūn's mud pill,
wooden ghost child,
golden shāng zhī,
flying jūn root,
crouching dragon liver,
white horse sweat,
floating cloud dregs,
dragon child's cinnabar garment,
nocturnal light bone,
hundred-flower sweet wine,
winter Zōu fasting, and the like,
all of which are common things,
yet without oral instructions,
they remain unknowable,
how much more so the arts of yellow and white?
Those who can perform them today
do not keep them secret merely because they are expensive,
but because once this Way is accomplished,
one can achieve longevity.
The Way of longevity
is the ultimate Way,
hence the ancients valued it.
All the drug names found in formula books
may sometimes share names with common drugs but are actually different,
like Héshàng Chànǚ,
which is not a woman;
Língyáng Zǐmíng,
not a man;
Yǔyúliáng,
not grain;
Yáojiāng,
not water.
When commoners see formulas using lóngdǎn, hǔzhǎng, jītóu, yāzhí, mǎtí, quǎn xuè, shǔwěi, niúxī,
they all assume they are creatures of blood and qi;
seeing quēpén, fùpén, fǔlì, dàjǐ, guǐjiàn, tiāngōu used,
they think they are iron or earthenware vessels;
seeing Húwáng Shǐzhě, Yǐgū Xīnfù, Yězhàngrén, Shǒutián Gōng, Dàiwényù, Xúchángqīng used,
they take them as people's names.
Even common, simple herbs
may sometimes be unknown,
how much less can anyone fully understand
mysterious and secret formulas?
It's no wonder
that Liú Xiàng failed in making gold.
Once one grasps the essentials,
there's no need for sage-like great talent to accomplish it;
any ordinary person can do it.
Was Liú Xiàng a foolish man?
He simply failed because he lacked the oral instructions.
Now, I will record concise and effective methods
to bequeath to like-minded people of the future.
First, take realgar from Wǔdū,
cinnabar-colored like a rooster's comb,
bright and free of夹杂石,
in any amount,
but not less than five catties.
Pound it into powder,
mix it with ox gall,
and cook it until dry.
Take a red earthen pot holding one dǒu,
first layer with powdered róngyán and shídǎn
to a thickness of three fēn,
then add the realgar powder,
to a thickness of five fēn,
and cover again with róngyán.
Repeat this process
layer by layer until finished.
Then add crushed charcoal pieces the size of date pits,
to a thickness of two cùn.
Mix earthworm soil and róngyán into mud,
coat the outside of the pot,
cover it with another pot,
seal both with mud three cùn thick,
ensuring no leakage.
Let it dry in shade for one month,
then heat with horse dung fire,
for three days and three nights.
After cooling,
open it,
and tap out the copper,
which flows like smelted copper or iron.
Cast this copper into a tube,
and use the tube to hold cinnabar water.
Again, heat with horse dung fire,
for thirty days, then open the furnace,
tap to obtain the metal,
and again make it into a tube,
to hold cinnabar water once more.
Heat with horse dung fire for another thirty days,
open, take out, and pound it for processing.
Take two parts of raw cinnabar
and one part of mercury;
mercury
is water silver,
and it will instantly solidify into gold.
Bright and beautifully colored,
it can be used for nails.
Method for making cinnabar water:
Process one catty of cinnabar,
place it in a fresh bamboo tube,
add two liǎng each of shídǎn and xiāoshí,
layering above and below,
seal the tube opening,
and secure it with a lacquered bone ball.
Once dry,
immerse it in strong bitter wine,
bury it in the ground
three chǐ deep,
and in thirty days, it turns into water,
red in color and bitter in taste.
Method for making gold as received by Jīn Lóu Xiānshēng from Qīng Línzǐ:
First, forge tin
into a square six cùn wide,
one cùn two fēn thick,
mix red salt with ash juice
into a mud-like consistency,
apply it to the tin
evenly to one fēn thickness,
and stack it in a red earthen pot.
Typically, for ten catties of tin,
use four catties of red salt,
seal the edges firmly,
and heat with horse dung fire
for thirty days.
Open and inspect;
the tin will appear ashy throughout,
with bean-like clusters inside,
which is the gold.
Combine and process in an earthen jar,
heat with charcoal and blow,
and after ten refinements, it is complete.
Typically, ten catties of tin
yield twenty liǎng of gold.
Only earthen pots from Chángshā, Guìyáng, Yùzhāng, and Nánhǎi are usable.
The local people there
make earthen pots for cooking,
and they are plentiful.
Method for making red salt:
Use one catty of cold salt,
one catty of cold water stone,
one catty of cold feather níng,
and one catty of white alum,
combine in an iron vessel,
and heat with charcoal fire
until all dissolve and turn red,
then remove for use.
Method for transforming gold as received by Jiǎolǐ Xiānshēng from Jìqiūzǐ:
First, take two parts of alum water stone,
place in an iron vessel,
add charcoal fire to boil,
then add mercury as desired,
stir to mix well,
after six or seven boils,
pour on the ground to form silver.
Then take one part each of cinnabar water and zēngqīng water,
two parts of realgar water,
heat in a lì vessel over low fire to boil,
stir frequently
to mix well,
then add charcoal fire to boil again,
place this silver inside,
amount as desired,
allow six or seven boils,
pour on the ground to solidify,
and it becomes high-quality purple polished gold.
Method for making realgar water:
Process one catty of realgar,
place in a fresh bamboo tube, add two liǎng of xiāoshí each time,
layer above and below,
seal with a lacquered bone ball,
immerse in strong vinegar,
bury three chǐ deep,
and in twenty days, it turns into water.
The method for making zēngqīng water
and alum stone water is the same,
only using different tubes.
A minor method for making gold
A large iron cylinder was completed,
with an inner diameter of one foot two inches,
and a height of one foot two inches.
A small iron cylinder was completed,
with an inner diameter of six inches,
polished to a shine.
One jīn of red halloysite,
one jīn of saltpeter,
one jīn of mica,
one jīn of hematite,
half a jīn of sulfur,
four liǎng of azurite,
one jīn of gypsum,
all were pounded together, finely sieved,
mixed with vinegar,
and applied inside the small cylinder,
to a thickness of two fēn.
One jīn of mercury,
half a jīn of cinnabar,
half a jīn of liángfēi.
To make liángfēi, ten jīn of lead were placed in an iron pot,
set on a furnace and heated uncovered,
until the lead melted,
then three liǎng of mercury were added,
and the early rising substance was skimmed off with an iron spoon,
named liángfēi.
Stirred until well mixed,
with the disappearance of mercury as the sign,
placed in the small cylinder,
covered with mica on top,
and sealed with an iron lid.
The large cylinder was placed on the furnace,
melted lead poured into the large cylinder,
submerging the small cylinder,
leaving half an inch above,
using the melting of lead as the sign,
heated with a fierce fire,
for three days and three nights until completion,
named purple powder.
Ten jīn of lead were melted in an iron vessel,
for about twenty days,
then transferred to a copper vessel,
waiting for the lead to melt,
adding seven square cùn bǐ of purple powder,
stirred,
and it turned into gold.
To make silver,
mercury was placed in an iron vessel,
adding over three cùn of purple powder,
heated until well combined,
poured into water,
and it turned into silver.
Wǔ Chéngzǐ's method:
Made an iron cylinder nine cùn long,
five cùn in diameter,
pounded three jīn of realgar,
mixed equally with earthworm soil,
combined to make a paste,
applied inside to form a three-cùn diameter,
with a four-cùn opening,
added two gě of cinnabar water,
placed over horse dung fire,
dried thoroughly,
inserted into a copper cylinder,
sealed tightly with a copper lid,
built up with yellow sand,
covered with layered earthworm soil paste,
ensuring no leakage from the top,
placed in a furnace with charcoal,
having three cùn of charcoal,
until the cylinder mouth glowed red,
cooled and opened,
the realgar all adhered to the copper cylinder,
repeated as before.
Three jīn of refined realgar,
all descended into the cylinder,
extracted and mixed equally with yellow sand,
combined to make a furnace,
the furnace size could vary.
When ready to use,
the furnace was placed in charcoal fire,
until the furnace glowed red,
mercury was added,
when the silver moved, lead was added,
yellow rising from the sides meeting in the center,
poured onto the ground,
becoming gold.
After making about fifteen hundred jīn,
the furnace's power was exhausted.
This gold was soaked in wine made from牡荊 (Vitex negundo) and red millet,
for a hundred days,
becoming soft and malleable.
Taken in pellets the size of small beans,
one pellet per dose,
three times a day,
after consuming one jīn,
the three worms and dormant corpses
along with all diseases would vanish,
the blind would see,
the deaf would hear,
the aged would rejuvenate to their thirties,
unharmed by fire,
immune to all evils, poisons, cold winds, summer dampness;
after three jīn,
one could walk on water,
mountain and river deities
would come to serve and protect,
lifespan matching heaven and earth.
Boiling one pellet with zhūxuè red grass,
and wiping the eye corners,
enabled seeing ghosts and underground objects,
and writing at night;
applying goat blood to a pellet,
throwing it into water,
fish and dragons would immediately emerge,
and could be caught;
applying green goat blood and red rooster blood to a pellet,
hanging it on the city gate,
prevented plague within one lǐ;
applied to the foreheads of cattle, sheep, and livestock,
they would not fall ill,
and tigers or leopards would not attack;
applying tiger bile and snake fat to a pellet,
throwing it from the direction of the monthly celestial stem towards the enemy army,
the army would chaos without cause,
harming each other and fleeing;
applying ox blood to a pellet and throwing it into a well,
the well would boil,
thrown into flowing water,
the water would reverse flow for a hundred steps;
applying white dog blood to a pellet,
throwing it into a shrine or house,
the ghosts and deities would appear,
and could be commanded;
applying rabbit blood to a pellet,
placing it in a six-yīn location,
jade maidens of the traveling kitchen would arrive instantly,
serving sixty to seventy people;
applying carp gall to a pellet,
holding it while entering water,
the water would part for ten feet,
allowing breathing underwater and movement,
walking in rain without wetting clothes;
boiling a pellet with purple amaranth,
swallowing the juice,
prevented hunger for a hundred days;
boiling a pellet with magnetite,
placing it in the hair bun,
when facing enemies,
blades and arrows would not hit,
if shot at,
the arrows would turn back on the shooter;
mixing a pellet with soil from the Liùdīng and Liùrén directions,
hiding it on one's person made one invisible,
holding a pellet in the mouth,
facing north and blowing towards fire,
the fire would extinguish;
on gēngxīn days during shēnyǒu hours,
throwing a pellet towards a tree in the west,
the tree would wither that same day;
with another pellet,
performing Yǔ steps and throwing it at tigers, wolves, or venomous snakes,
they would die immediately;
grinding a pellet to write on stone would penetrate it,
writing on metal would enter it,
writing on wood would sink in,
all writings penetrating the texture,
unable to be removed by carving;
for those who died suddenly within a day,
taking a pellet with water from the monthly celestial stem direction,
making them swallow it,
and spraying water on the dead person's face,
would revive them;
applying fox blood and crane blood to a pellet,
placing it in the hand,
pointing at things,
they would change as spoken,
like mountains moving or trees relocating,
all visible to people,
though in reality, they did not move.
In all gold and silver making,
altars were set up for Tàiyǐ, Xuánnǚ, and Lǎozǐ with offerings,
following the method for making the nine elixirs,
constantly burning five incenses,
ensuring the fragrance never ceased.
Once the gold was made,
three jīn were first thrown into deep water,
one jīn into the market,
only then could it be used freely as desired.
Someone asked about the methods for entering mountains.
Bàopúzǐ said:
"All those who practice the Way and prepare medicines,
or avoid turmoil to live in seclusion,
invariably enter the mountains.
However, those unaware of mountain-entry techniques
often encounter disasters.
Hence the proverb:
Beneath Tàihuà Mountain,
scattered white bones lie in disarray.
This speaks of knowing only one aspect
without comprehensive preparation;
though possessing the will to seek life,
one instead meets violent death.
Mountains regardless of size
all contain divine spirits -
large mountains host great spirits,
small mountains host minor spirits.
Entering mountains without proper methods
inevitably brings calamities:
some suffer illnesses and injuries,
or terror and unrest;
some witness strange lights and shadows,
or hear peculiar sounds;
some see giant trees break without wind,
rocks fall without cause,
striking and killing people;
some become confused and run wildly,
falling into pits and valleys;
some encounter tigers, wolves, and venomous creatures attacking them.
One must not enter mountains lightly.
The appropriate months are March and September -
these are the months of mountain opening -
and one must further select auspicious days and favorable hours within these months.
If matters require prolonged stay beyond these months,
one may still choose favorable days and hours.
All who enter mountains
should first purify themselves for seven days,
avoiding defilement,
carry mountain-ascent talismans when departing,
and perform the Three-Five Body Protection method.
Furthermore, the Five Peaks have years of calamity -
just as the Nine Regions
experience cycles of decline and prosperity -
when they receive flying talismans and lethal energies,
then the local rulers should not act.
According to the Duke of Zhōu's City Records,
the celestial divisions correspond to regions
where disasters may reach -
these can be avoided but not averted through rituals.
The same applies to dwellings,
and likewise for mountains and peaks.
Great taboos include: never entering the Eastern Peak
during first or second months of jiǎ-yǐ-yín-mǎo years;
never entering the Southern Peak
during fourth or fifth months of bǐng-dīng-sì-wǔ years;
never entering the Western Peak
during seventh or eighth months of gēng-xīn-shēn-yǒu years;
never entering the Central Peak
during the transitional months of wù-sì years;
never entering the Northern Peak
during tenth or eleventh months of rén-guǐ-hài-zǐ years.
Not only for Tàihuà, Huòshān, Héngshān, Tàishān, and Sōnggāo Mountain
are these years prohibited -
the corresponding directions of all peaks
share the same restrictions.
Furthermore, aged creatures among all things
can assume human form through their essence,
dazzling human vision and constantly testing people,
though unable to alter their true forms in mirrors.
Therefore ancient mountain-entering Daoists
all hung mirrors over nine inches in diameter
behind their backs,
whereupon old demons dared not approach.
When testing creatures approached,
they would gaze into their mirrors:
if immortal beings or benevolent mountain spirits,
their mirror reflections remained human;
if bird, beast, or evil demon,
their true forms appeared in the mirror.
Moreover, when old demons approach,
they necessarily retreat walking backward.
One may turn the mirror toward them
and observe from behind -
if old demons,
they will lack heels,
while those with heels
are mountain spirits.
Formerly Zhāng Gàità and Ǒu Gāochéng
both meditated intently in Shǔ's Yúntái Mountain stone chamber
when suddenly a yellow-robed, hemp-hatted figure
approached saying:
'Hard at work, Daoists?
How you suffer in seclusion!'
The two gazed into their mirror
to see a deer reflected.
They challenged it:
'You mountain-old deer,
how dare you counterfeit human form?'
Before words faded,
the visitor became deer and fled.
Below Línlǜ Mountain stood a lodge
housing ghosts -
lodgers there
would die or fall ill.
Nightly dozens would appear
in yellow, white, or black garments,
male and female.
Later Zhì Bóyí lodged there,
sitting by lamplight chanting scriptures
when midnight brought a dozen visitors
sitting opposite Bóyí
playing dice games together.
Bóyí secretly mirrored them
to reveal a pack of dogs.
Grasping his candle, Bóyí rose
and pretended to accidentally singe their clothes with embers,
producing the smell of scorched fur.
Bóyí drew his small knife
and stabbed one captive -
first human cries,
then death revealed a dog.
The remaining dogs fled,
ending the hauntings -
all through the mirror's power.
Superior adepts entering mountains
carry the Three Sovereigns' Esoteric Script and Five Peaks' True Form Charts,
summoning local mountain spirits
and consulting demon registers,
calling regional earth gods and mountain guardians for inquiry -
whereupon tree/stone monsters
and mountain/stream essences
dare not test them.
Next best: erect seventy-two spirit-suppressing talismans
to control hundreds of evils' manifestations,
together with Vermilion Office Seal and Primordial Encasement's twelve seals,
sealing the four directions of one's dwelling -
again preventing evil approaches.
Next best: hold the Eight Powers scepter
wearing Lǎozǐ's jade tablets,
enabling mountain spirit command -
how would they dare cause harm?
I heard these words from Master Zhèng,
though cannot fully comprehend such matters.
My teacher often instructed disciples:
'Those seeking the Way
like those anxious about family poverty
or distressed by low position -
how could they fail to obtain it?
Only worry about insufficient dedication,
pursuing nearness while forgetting distance,
hearing teachings with delight,
earnestly leaning forward -
yet soon
suddenly forgetting as if discarding,
failing to secure hairbreadth gains
while accumulating mountain-sized losses.
How then reach subtle mysteries of profound teachings,
achieving the boundless and sublime?'"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Major mountain-entry taboos:
first month wǔ days,
second month hài days,
third month shēn days,
fourth month xū days,
fifth month wèi days,
sixth month mǎo days,
seventh month jiǎzǐ days,
eighth month shēnzǐ days,
ninth month yín days,
tenth month chén-wèi days,
eleventh month jǐchǒu days,
twelfth month yín days.
Auspicious mountain-entry days:
jiǎzǐ, jiǎyín, yǐhài, yǐsì, yǐmǎo, bǐngxū, bǐngwǔ, bǐngchén -
the above days are highly auspicious."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"According to Secret Nine Heaven Records and Supreme Unity Dunjiā texts,
large-month mountain taboos:
3rd, 11th, 15th, 18th, 24th, 26th, 30th days;
small-month taboos:
1st, 5th, 13th, 16th, 26th, 28th days.
Entering mountains these days
ensures testing by mountain spirits.
Furthermore, requests will go unfulfilled,
and endeavors will fail.
Not only Daoists -
any commoner entering mountains these days
faces misfortune
and encounters with tigers, wolves, and venomous creatures."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The true nature of heaven and earth,
the auspicious and inauspicious aspects of yīn and yáng,
are vast and difficult to comprehend in detail.
I do not necessarily claim they exist,
nor do I dare guarantee their non-existence.
However, Huángdì and Tàigōng both believed and relied on them,
and recent eminent figures like Yán Jūnpíng and Sīmǎ Qiān all used them as basis,
while classical texts contain references to days of governing calendars, clarifying seasons, and hard-soft attributes.
An ancient saying states,
'The auspicious day is only Wù.'
This has its origins.
When kings establish the office of Grand Historian,
for conferring titles and appointments,
conducting affairs at ancestral temples,
or performing suburban sacrifices to heaven and earth,
they all select auspicious times;
yet recent talents and mediocre persons,
considering themselves beyond conventions,
in their actions and deeds,
feel ashamed to choose favorable days -
is this not foolish and ignorant?
Whenever I observe people entering mountains today,
if they don't obtain the proper timing and day combinations,
there will be evidence below,
so one cannot enter lightly.
According to the Yùqián Jīng:
'Those wishing to enter famous mountains
must know the secret arts of Dùnjiǎ,
though the text doesn't explain the matter in detail.'
And the Língbǎo Jīng states:
'Entering mountains should be on Bǎo days and Yì days,
if on Zhuān days it is very auspicious,
while on Zhì days or Fá days means certain death,'
again not explaining everything in detail.
I had aspirations to enter mountains from youth,
therefore I studied Dùnjiǎ texts,
which amounted to over sixty volumes.
Since one cannot master them quickly,
I compiled their essentials,
creating a portable reference,
though it's not suitable for writing down.
Now I discuss the general outline,
thinking enthusiasts wishing to enter mountains
should seek out those with knowledge,
who ultimately won't be lacking in the world.
The Dùnjiǎ Zhōngjīng says:
'To seek the Way,
use Tiānnèi days and Tiānnèi hours
to subdue ghosts and spirits,
and apply talismans.
Using Tiānqín days and Tiānqín hours to enter famous mountains
will cause hundreds of evils, tigers, wolves, poisonous insects, and thieves
to dare not approach people.
Exit through Tiāncáng,
enter through Dìhù.
Generally, Liùguǐ constitutes Tiāncáng,
while Liùjǐ constitutes Dìhù.'
It also says:
'To avoid chaotic times,
disappear into famous mountains,
ensuring no worries or troubles,
use the Shàngyuán Dīngmǎo day,
named the time of Yīndé,
also called Tiānxīn,
where one can hide and disappear,
so-called "white sun land-submergence",
where sun and moon give no light,
and neither humans nor ghosts can see you.'
Also:
'Those seeking immortal path entering famous mountains,
on Liùguǐ days at Liùguǐ hours,
also called Tiāngōng days,
will certainly attain transcendence.'
Also:
'When going into mountain forests,
take grass from Qīnglóng with left hand,
break half and place under Féngxīng,
pass through Míngtáng into Tàiyīn,
walk with Yǔ steps,
chant three times:
"Nuògāo Great Yīn,
General Dúwén,
your descendant Wáng Jiǎ
do not reveal to outsiders;
make those who see Jiǎ
consider him bundled firewood;
those who don't see Jiǎ
consider him non-human."
Then break the held grass and place on ground,
take soil with left hand to apply between nose and lip,
hold grass with right hand for concealment,
left hand placed forward,
walk with Yǔ steps,
arrive under Liùguǐ,
hold breath and stop,
humans and ghosts cannot see you.
Generally Liùjiǎ is Qīnglóng,
Liùyǐ is Féngxīng,
Liùbǐng is Míngtáng,
Liùdīng is Yīnzhōng.
☵☲ Compared forms Jìjì guà,
first and second positions cannot bear nine-step count,
yet following accordingly, each step is seven chi.
Also stated:
one chi equals two zhang one chi,
looking back at nine steps.
Also Yǔ step method:
Stand upright,
right foot forward,
left foot behind,
then advance right foot again,
bring left foot beside right foot -
this is one step.
Then advance right foot again,
then advance left foot,
bring right foot beside left foot -
this is two steps.
Then advance right foot again,
bring left foot beside right foot -
this is three steps.
In this manner,
the method of Yǔ steps is complete.
All who practice hundreds of arts under heaven
should know Yǔ steps,
not just for this matter."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The Língbǎo Jīng states:
So-called Bǎo days
refer to days when earthly branches produce heavenly stems,
like using Jiǎwǔ or Yǐsì days.
Jiǎ
is wood.
Wǔ
is fire.
Yǐ is also wood,
Sì is also fire,
because fire is produced by wood.
Also called Yì days
are days when heavenly stems produce earthly branches,
like Rénshēn or Guǐyǒu days.
Rén
is water.
Shēn
is metal.
Guǐ
is water.
Yǒu
is metal,
because water is produced by metal.
So-called Zhì days
are days when heavenly stems overcome earthly branches.
Like Wùzǐ or Jǐhài days.
Wù
is earth.
Zǐ
is water.
Jǐ is also earth,
Hài is also water,
according to five phases principle,
earth overcomes water.
So-called Fá days
are days when earthly branches overcome heavenly stems,
like Jiǎshēn or Yǐyǒu days.
Jiǎ
is wood.
Shēn
is metal.
Yǐ is also wood,
Yǒu is also metal,
because metal overcomes wood.
Others all follow this pattern,
extending and elaborating,
