all can be understood."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Enter famous mountains
on Jiǎzǐ opening-removing days,
with five-color silks each five cùn,
hang on large rocks,
and what you seek will certainly be obtained.
Also stated:
Entering mountains should know Liùjiǎ secret incantation.
Chant:
'Lín bīng dòu zhě,
jiē zhèn liè qián xíng.'
Nine characters total,
constantly chant them secretly,
and nothing cannot be warded off.
The essential way is not complicated -
this refers to this."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The form of the mountain spirit in the mountains,
is like a small child with a single foot,
it walks backward,
and enjoys coming to harm people.
When a person enters the mountains,
if they hear a loud human voice speaking at night,
its name is Qí,
knowing this and calling it by name,
then it dares not harm people.
Another name is Rènèi,
which can also be used to call it.
There is another mountain spirit,
like a drum and red in color,
also with one foot,
its name is Huī.
Another may appear like a person,
nine feet tall,
wearing fur and a bamboo hat,
named Jīn Lěi.
Or like a dragon with five colors and a red horn,
named Fēi Fēi,
upon seeing any of these, call them by their names,
and they will not dare to cause harm."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"In the mountains, there are large trees,
some that can speak,
it is not the tree that can speak,
its spirit is named Yún Yáng,
calling it by name brings good fortune.
Seeing firelight in the mountains at night,
is all caused by long-dried wood,
do not find it strange.
Seeing a Hú rén in the mountains at night,
is the essence of copper and iron.
Seeing a Qín person,
is the essence of a hundred-year-old tree.
Do not be alarmed by them,
they cannot cause harm.
Seeing an official among the mountains and waters,
its name is Sì Jiào,
calling it by name brings good fortune.
Seeing a large snake wearing a hat and headscarf in the mountains,
its name is Shēng Qīng,
calling it by name brings good fortune.
Seeing an official in the mountains,
if only hearing its voice but not seeing its form,
calling out to people incessantly,
throw a white stone at it and it will stop;
another method is to use a reed as a spear to stab it, which brings good fortune.
Seeing a ghost in the mountains coming to call someone,
seeking food without ceasing,
throw white cogon grass at it and it will die.
For mountain ghosts that often confuse people and make them lose their way,
throw a reed staff at them and they will die.
On Yín days in the mountains,
those who call themselves Yú lì,
are tigers.
Those who call themselves Dānglù Jūn,
are wolves.
Those who call themselves Lìng Zhǎng,
are old raccoon dogs.
On Mǎo days, those who call themselves Zhàngrén,
are rabbits.
Those who call themselves Dōng Wáng Fù,
are elks.
Those who call themselves Xī Wáng Mǔ,
are deer.
On Chén days, those who call themselves Yǔ Shī,
are dragons.
Those who call themselves Hé Bó,
are fish.
Those who call themselves Wú Cháng Gōng Zǐ,
are crabs.
On Sì days, those who call themselves Guǎrén,
are snakes from the shrine.
Those who call themselves Shí Jūn,
are turtles.
On Wǔ days, those who call themselves Sān Gōng,
are horses.
Those who call themselves Xiān Rén,
are old trees.
On Wèi days, those who call themselves Zhǔ Rén,
are sheep.
Those who call themselves Lì,
are river deer.
On Shēn days, those who call themselves Rén Jūn,
are monkeys.
Those who call themselves Jiǔ Qīng,
are apes.
On Yǒu days, those who call themselves Jiāng Jūn,
are old chickens.
Those who call themselves Bǔ Zéi,
are pheasants.
On Xū days, those who call themselves by human names,
are dogs.
Those who call themselves Chéng Yáng Gōng,
are foxes.
On Hài days, those who call themselves Shén Jūn,
are pigs.
Those who call themselves Fù Rén,
are gold and jade.
On Zǐ days, those who call themselves Shè Jūn,
are rats.
Those who call themselves Shén Rén,
are bats.
On Chǒu days, those who call themselves Shū Shēng,
are cows.
Simply knowing the names of these creatures,
then they cannot cause harm."
Someone asked about methods to avoid venomous snakes while living in mountain wilderness.
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"In ancient times, Yuánqiū had many large snakes,
but also produced fine medicinal herbs.
When the Yellow Emperor was about to ascend there,
Guǎngchéngzǐ taught him to carry realgar,
and all the snakes departed.
Nowadays, if one carries five taels or more of Wǔdū realgar,
with color like a rooster's comb,
and enters mountain forests and vegetation,
they need not fear snakes.
If a snake bites a person,
applying a small amount of realgar powder into the wound
will also provide immediate healing.
Although there are many snake species,
only the pit viper and green-gold snake cause the most critical bites.
Without treatment,
they can kill within a day.
If someone unaware of treatment methods
is bitten by these two snakes,
immediately cut the wounded flesh with a knife and throw it to the ground.
The flesh will sizzle like fire roasting,
quickly burning completely,
but the person will survive.
During July and August when these snakes' venom is most potent,
if they cannot bite humans,
their unexpressed venom
makes them bite large bamboos and small trees,
which immediately wither and dry up.
Nowadays, when Daoists enter mountains,
they only know general principles
but not the methods to avoid snakes,
which is no trivial matter.
Before entering mountains,
one should prepare at home
by first learning prohibition techniques,
visualizing the sun, moon, Vermilion Bird, Black Tortoise, Azure Dragon, and White Tiger
to protect one's body.
Then when walking through mountain vegetation,
take three breaths from the left and hold them,
blowing into the mountain grasses,
envisioning this breath becoming red like clouds and mist,
spreading across dozens of miles.
If accompanied by others,
regardless of number, have them form ranks
and blow breath toward them.
Even if stepping on snakes,
snakes won't dare move,
and one will scarcely encounter them.
If seeing a snake,
face the sun and take three breaths from the left,
press tongue against palate,
pinch the Dūguān point with hand,
close the Tiānmén,
block the Dìhù,
then press the snake's head with an object while coiling it by hand,
draw a prison on the ground to contain it,
and one can even play with it.
Though it may coil around one's neck,
it won't dare bite.
If unaware of prohibition methods,
exhale breath to blow on it,
and it still cannot escape the prison.
If others are bitten by snakes,
take three breaths from the left and blow on them,
and they'll heal without further pain.
Even from over ten miles away,
one can remotely direct breath,
calling the person's name,
for males visualizing my left hand,
for females my right hand,
and they will also heal.
According to Jiè Xiānshēng's method,
when staying in mountains,
visualize five colored snakes, one of each,
then hold breath and pierce them with bent green bamboo and small wood,
stepping left with Yǔ steps,
visualizing thousands of centipedes
clothing one's body,
then depart—
ultimately not encountering snakes.
Some carry dried ginger and monkshood behind their elbows,
or fumigate with burned cow/deer horn,
or carry Wáng Fāngpíng's realgar pills,
or place pig earwax and musk pills under toenails,
all being effective.
Moreover, musk deer and wild boars both eat snakes,
Also, the Rì bird and Yīng turtle
both eat snakes.
Thus southerners entering mountains
carry Yīng turtle tails
and Rì bird beaks to ward off snakes.
For snake bites,
scrape these two substances to apply on wounds,
also providing immediate healing.
Rì
is another name for the Zhèn bird.
Also, southerners entering mountains
carry live centipedes in bamboo tubes.
When centipedes detect snake territories,
they move within the tubes.
Thus carefully inspecting grasses,
one will surely find snakes.
Large snakes over ten feet long
with bodies thick as arm spans
—when centipedes see them,
they can use breath to immobilize them,
and the snakes immediately die.
When snakes see centipedes on banks,
large snakes flee to deep valley waters,
while centipedes float immobilizing on water.
People see bluish objects
large like threads
descending straight to snake locations.
Soon snakes surface dead.
Thus southerners use ground centipede powder for snakebite treatment,
all achieving immediate healing."
Someone asked:
"In the valleys and mountains of Jiāngnán,
there are many poisonous evils,
is there a way to ward them off?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"In the central plains and high plateaus,
the soil and climate are clear and harmonious,
in the famous mountains of superior regions,
such creatures are completely absent.
Now in the wilds of Wú and Chǔ,
where summer heat and dampness steam oppressively,
even on proper peaks like Héng and Huò,
there are still many poisonous creatures.
There is also the duǎnhú,
also called yù,
also called shègōng,
also called shèyǐng,
which is actually an aquatic insect,
shaped like a singing cicada,
resembling a three-part cup,
with wings that enable flight,
eyeless but with sharp hearing,
in its mouth there is a crosswise object like a horn-bow,
when it hears human sounds,
following the object in its mouth like a horn-bow,
using breath as arrows,
it then uses water to shoot people,
those hit on their body immediately develop sores,
those whose shadow is hit also fall ill,
though not immediately developing sores,
those who don't know how to treat it will die.
The illness resembles major cold damage disorders,
within ten days all die.
There is also the shāshī,
found both in water and on land,
after new rain and before dawn or dusk,
those traveling will inevitably have them attach,
only during intense sun when grass is dry,
are they somewhat scarce.
They are as large as the tip of a hair,
initially attaching to a person,
they immediately enter beneath the skin,
where they are feels like prickly needle sensations,
slight contact causes great pain,
they can be picked out with a needle,
bright red like cinnabar,
moving about when placed on a fingernail.
If not picked out,
the insects burrow to the bone,
then travel throughout the body,
their effect similar to the shègōng,
both can kill people.
When people walk in areas with these insects,
each time returning to where they stay,
should always use fire to roast all over the body,
then these insects will fall to the ground.
If carrying the Eight Substances Musk Pill, or Dùshì Pill, or Hùmìng Pill, or Yùhú Pill, or Xījiǎo Pill, or Qīxīng Pill, or jìnǐ,
all can ward off shāshī and duǎnhú.
If suddenly unable to obtain these medicines,
just carrying good raw musk is also fine.
Mix realgar and garlic in equal parts and pound together,
carrying one pill the size of a chicken egg is also good.
If already affected by them,
applying this medicine to the sores can also cure.
Chew red amaranth juice,
drinking it or applying it can also cure.
Wǔjiā root and xuángōu grass with fūténg,
these three items can each be used singly,
can be pounded and taken as juice, one or two shēng.
Also, shègōng insects hibernate in mountain valleys in winter,
during heavy snow, search for them,
where these insects are,
the snow does not accumulate,
vapor rises as if steaming,
should dig there,
not more than one chǐ into the ground then obtained,
dry in shade, powder, and carry,
in summer automatically wards off shègōng.
If a Daoist knows one prohibition formula,
and comprehends hundreds of prohibitions,
constantly maintains prohibitions and guards the True One,
then hundreds of poisons dare not approach,
no need to rely on various medicines."
Someone asked:
"When Daoists dwell in mountains,
perching among rocks and caves,
not necessarily having the warmth of thick bedding,
how can they make themselves unafraid of wind and dampness,
may I ask the method?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Jīnbǐng Powder, Sānyáng Liquid, Chāngxīn Pill, Hūncǎo Nàidōng Brew, Dúyáo Paste, Yīnyú Xuánhuá Powder, Qiūdìhuáng Blood Pill,
all need not be taken more than fifty days,
can make one unafraid of wind and dampness for ten years.
If taking golden elixir great medicine,
although not yet ascending voidly and lightly rising,
the body does not receive ailments,
even sleeping in wind and dampness,
cannot be harmed.
Taking these seven medicines,
all are for those beginning to learn the Way.
Master Yáo only took Sānyáng Liquid,
then lay naked on ice,
completely without cold shivering.
These were tested by Master Jiè and Liáng Yǒudào lying on stones,
and in autumn and winter facing wind and cold,
already tried and proven effective,
a secret method."
Someone asked about methods to ward off snakes and dragons when crossing rivers and seas.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"When Daoists must travel across great rivers,
should first at the water's edge,
break one chicken egg,
mix a little powder with fragrant dust,
stir together in vessel with water,
wash themselves with it,
then unafraid of wind waves, flood dragons, and dragons.
Also wear the Dōnghǎi Xiǎotóng Talisman, and Water-Control Talisman, and Pénglái Slip,
all repel hundreds of harms in water.
Also the Liùjiǎ Sānjīn Talisman, and Wǔmù Prohibition.
Another method,
facing the river first pray:
Rolling tumbleweed, rolling tumbleweed,
Hébó leads ahead warding off flood dragons,
ten thousand disasters vanish, heaven clear and bright.
Also, the Jīnjiǎn Record says,
on the fifth month's bǐngwǔ day at midday,
pound five minerals,
cast the copper.
The five minerals are:
realgar, cinnabar, orpiment, alum stone, and zēngqīng.
All powdered,
bathed in golden flower pool,
placed in Liùyī Shén furnace with bellows below,
fired with cassia wood,
when copper forms, refined with hard charcoal,
have young boys and girls tend the fire,
take male copper to make male sword,
take female copper to make female sword,
each five and a half cùn long,
taking earth's number,
to suppress water essence.
Wear them when traveling by water,
then flood dragons, giant fish, and water spirits dare not approach.
To know copper's male and female,
have young boys and girls both pour water on the copper,
pouring when the copper is red-hot in fire,
then the copper naturally divides into two sections,
the protruding one is male copper,
the indented one is female copper,
each engraved with names for identification.
When entering water,
wear male on left,
female on right.
If only riding boats without personally wading,
on yang days wear male,
on yin days wear female.
Also, celestial script large characters,
there is the Běidì writing,
copy on silk and wear,
also wards off wind waves, flood dragons, and water insects."
Someone asked:
"Methods to ward off hundred demons in mountains, rivers, and temples."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Daoists often wear Tiānshuǐ Talisman, and Shànghuáng Zhúshǐ Talisman, Lǎozǐ Left Contract, and guard True One contemplating three division generals,
demons dare not approach.
Next, study the Hundred Demons Register,
know the names of all under heaven's demons,
and Báizé Diagram, Jiǔdǐng Record,
then all demons automatically retreat.
Next, take Chúnzǐ Chìshí Pill, and Zēngqīng Yèguāng Powder, and Cōngshí Wūyǎn Pill, and swallow Báishíyīng Zhīmǔ Powder,
all make people see demons,
then demons fear them."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"There is the Lǎojūn Huángtíng Zhōngtāi Forty-Nine True Secret Talisman,
enter mountains and forests,
on jiǎyín day write in cinnabar on white silk,
at night place on table,
offer it to the Northern Dipper,
with a little wine and dried meat each,
state one's own name,
bow twice then receive it,
place inside the collar,
wards off mountain and river hundred demons, myriad essences, tigers, wolves, insect poisons.
Not only Daoists,
those avoiding calamity entering mountains in chaotic times,
should also know this method."
Mountain Entry Talisman
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"The five talismans above
are all Lǎojūn's mountain-entry talismans.
Write them with cinnabar on peachwood boards,
inscribe the characters largely,
making them fill the boards completely,
then place them on doors and gates,
and on all four directions and corners,
as well as along paths and key locations,
within fifty paces
of one's dwelling place,
to ward off mountain spirits and demonic apparitions.
They can also be applied
to beams and pillars inside the house.
Whether residing in mountain forests or temporarily entering mountains,
all can use them,
so that no creatures dare cause harm.
Three talismans should be connected on one board.
I suppose you are not of the Gě clan."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"This talisman is also Lǎojūn's mountain-entry talisman,
applicable to beams and pillars inside the house.
All who dwell in mountain forests or temporarily enter mountains
should use it."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"This is the mountain-entry talisman to ward off tigers and wolves, transmitted by the immortal Chén Ānshì.
Write two talismans with cinnabar on silk,
making them distinct from each other.
Always carry them at your dwelling place,
four pieces each.
When moving, pluck and take them along—
greatly mysterious!
The mountain-opening talisman uses thousand-year ivy to name the mountain's gate,
opening treasure texts, ancient scripts, gold, and jade,
all revealed yet kept secret.
The method to the right is like this,
largely similar with minor variations."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"This talisman was worn by Lǎojūn,
a divine seal against ghosts, snakes, vipers, tigers, and wolves.
Carve it on date-heart wood two inches square,
bow twice and wear it—
it has remarkable divine efficacy.
It is the talisman of the immortal Chén Ānshì."
Mountain-entry talismans to carry
These three talismans,
when also placed around ox and horse stables and pig pens,
ward off tigers and wolves."
Someone asked:
"I've heard of Tán Chāng in the past,
who could walk on water
or dwell underwater for long periods—
by what method?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Mix scallion juice with cinnamon,
take seven pills the size of wútóng seeds,
three times daily.
After three years,
one can walk on water.
Zhèng Jūn said that merely practicing breath-holding up to a thousand cycles,
over time enables dwelling underwater for about a day.
Obtain a true tōngtiān rhinoceros horn over three inches long,
carve it into a fish shape,
hold it in the mouth to enter water—
the water will part for the person,
creating a three-foot square
where one can breathe underwater.
Also, the tōngtiān rhinoceros horn has a red vein like a thread,
running from base to tip.
Place rice in the horn among chickens—
when they peck at it,
before reaching within inches,
they startle and retreat.
Thus southerners sometimes call it 'frighten-chicken rhinoceros.'
Place this horn on grain piles—
no birds dare gather.
On heavily foggy, dewy nights,
set it in the central courtyard—
it remains completely dry.
This rhinoceros dwells in deep mountains;
on dark nights,
its horn glows brightly like a torch.
Using the horn as a fork-guide,
stir poisoned liquid with it—
white foam surges up,
completely neutralizing the poison.
Stirring non-poisonous substances
produces no foam.
Thus it is known.
When traveling in foreign lands with venomous regions,
before eating or drinking elsewhere,
always stir with the horn first.
If someone is struck by a poisoned arrow near death,
pierce the wound with this rhinoceros fork—
the sore will foam and heal.
The tōngtiān rhinoceros neutralizes poison because
this beast exclusively eats poisonous plants
and thorny bushes,
never casually consuming soft, smooth vegetation.
It sheds its horn annually in mountain rocks;
if humans take it,
they must carve a replica matching its color and shape
to substitute—
the rhinoceros won't notice
and will shed again there the next year.
Other rhinoceros horns also ward off evil and detoxify,
but not as marvelously as the tōngtiān.
Some take the Six Wù Talisman for a thousand days,
or combine red-spotted spiders and seven-layer water striders
with Féng Yí's water-immortal pills—
this too enables dwelling underwater.
Merely applying it to the soles
allows walking on water.
Even scalp grease can make metal float on water—
how much more effective these methods!"
Someone asked:
"Many Daoists practice in mountain forests,
where tigers and wolves abound—
how to ward them off?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"Ancient mountain travelers
all carried the Huángshén Yuèzhāng seal,
four inches wide
with 120 characters.
Placing its clay impressions in all four directions
within a hundred paces of one's dwelling
keeps tigers and wolves from approaching.
Seeing fresh tiger tracks,
imprint the seal along them—
the tiger leaves;
imprint against them—
the tiger returns.
Carrying this seal in mountain forests
also eliminates fear of tigers and wolves.
Not only does it ward them off—
against malevolent mountain, river, or temple gods causing fortune or misfortune,
using the seal's clay impressions
to block their paths
nullifies their power.
Once a giant turtle in Shítóu's waters,
dwelling in a deep pool
called 'Turtle Pool,'
haunted people
and spread sickness.
A Wú dàoshi named Dài Bǐng
once saw it,
made hundreds of Yuèzhāng clay seals,
boated across the pool throwing them in.
After a while,
a giant turtle over ten feet long
surfaced, not daring to move—
he struck it dead,
and the sick all recovered.
Many small turtles emerged
and died lined up on the shore.
If suddenly meeting a tiger in mountains,
perform the Three-Five Ban—
the tiger will retreat.
The Three-Five Ban method
requires oral transmission—
writing cannot convey it fully.
One method:
visualize yourself as a Vermilion Bird,
thirty feet long,
standing on the tiger's head—
then hold your breath,
and the tiger leaves.
If staying overnight in mountains,
secretly take a hairpin,
hold breath and point it at the White Tiger constellation—
then fear nothing.
Another method:
hold a knife in the left hand while holding breath,
draw a square on the ground,
chant:
'Shade of Héng Mountain,
sun of Tài Mountain,
no thieves arise,
no tigers roam,
city walls unbroken,
sealed by golden pass.'
Then swing the knife toward the White Tiger constellation at midday—
and fear nothing.
Some use the Great Ban,
swallowing 360 breaths,
left taking right to shout at tigers—
tigers dare not rise.
Using this method in mountains,
one fears no tigers.
Some use the Seven Stars Tiger Step,
or Jade Spirit Talisman, Eight Powers Five Victories Talisman, Lǐ Ěr's Great Peace Talisman, Central Yellow Canopy Seal Script, and sulfur powder,
burning ox or sheep horns,
or erecting the Western Peak Lord's Mountain Ban Talisman—
all have proven effective.
These four talismans are omitted."
This talisman is Lǎojūn's mountain-entry talisman,
described below as written.
It can also be applied to indoor beams and pillars.
All who dwell in mountain forests or enter temporarily
can use it.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I have heard from my teacher:
If a person can know the One,
all things are accomplished.
One who knows the One
knows everything.
One who does not know the One
cannot know anything.
The Dao arises from the One,
its nobility has no equal,
each residing in its place,
symbolizing heaven, earth, and humanity,
hence it is called the Three Ones.
Heaven attains the One and becomes clear,
earth attains the One and becomes tranquil,
humanity attains the One and lives,
spirits attain the One and become divine.
Metal sinks and feathers float,
mountains stand firm and rivers flow,
look for it but it cannot be seen,
listen for it but it cannot be heard,
preserve it and it remains,
neglect it and it perishes,
face it and there is good fortune,
turn away from it and there is calamity,
protect it and blessings are boundless,
lose it and life withers and energy exhausts.
Lǎojūn said:
Indistinct and elusive,
within it there are images;
elusive and indistinct,
within it there are substances.
This refers to the One.
Therefore, the Immortal Scriptures say:
If you wish for long life,
guarding the One must be clear;
think of the One until hungry,
the One provides food;
think of the One until thirsty,
the One provides drink.
The One has a surname, given name, and clothing color,
for males it is nine fen tall,
for females it is six fen tall,
sometimes located below the navel at two point four cun in the lower dāntián,
sometimes in the heart region at the crimson palace golden tower, the middle dāntián,
or between a person's eyebrows,
retreating one cun is the bright hall,
two cun is the chamber of insight,
three cun is the upper dāntián.
This is what Daoists value,
passed down through generations by blood oath, orally transmitting its name.
The One can complete yin and generate yang,
regulate the progression of cold and heat.
Spring attains the One to sprout,
summer attains the One to grow,
autumn attains the One to harvest,
winter attains the One to store.
Its greatness cannot be measured by the six directions,
its smallness cannot be compared to a hair's tip.
In the past, Huángdì went east to Qīngqiū,
passed Fēng Mountain,
met Master Zǐfǔ,
received the Inner Texts of the Three Sovereigns,
to command and summon myriad spirits;
went south to Yuánlǒng, beneath Jiàn Tree,
observed where hundred spirits ascend,
picked Ruògàn's blossoms,
drank from Dānluán's waters;
went west to see Zhōnghuángzǐ,
received the formula of nine additions,
passed Kōngtóng,
followed Guǎngchéngzǐ to receive the Scripture of Spontaneity;
went north to Hóng Dī,
ascended Jùcí,
met Great Wěi Jūn and Huánggài童子,
received the Divine Fungus Chart,
returned and climbed Wāngwū,
obtained the Golden Formula of Divine Elixir.
Arriving at Éméi Mountain,
met Celestial True Huángrén in the Jade Hall,
inquired about the Way of True One.
Huángrén said:
Since you already rule the four seas,
yet seek long life again,
is that not greedy?
The details cannot be fully explained,
I will roughly mention one aspect.
As for the immortal recipe for long life,
only the golden elixir suffices;
for guarding the form and warding off evil,
only the True One is unique,
hence the ancients especially valued it.
The Immortal Scriptures say:
The Ninefold Cycled Elixir,
the Scripture of Golden Liquor,
the Formula of Guarding the One,
all are within the Five Cities of Kūnlún,
stored in jade caskets,
inscribed on golden tablets,
sealed with purple clay,
stamped with the central seal.
I heard from my former teacher:
The One is in the great abyss of the North Pole,
with the bright hall in front,
the crimson palace behind;
towering like a canopy,
golden towers arching high;
the Dipper on the left, the Ladle on the right,
waves surging, soaring skyward;
dark fungi cover the cliffs,
vermilion grass lush and delicate;
white jade peaks towering,
sun and moon shedding light;
passing through fire and water,
traversing the mysterious and touching the yellow;
city walls and gates interwoven,
curtains and canopies of precious stones;
dragons and tigers standing guard,
spirits and immortals by the side;
without giving or taking,
the One rests in its place;
neither slow nor hasty,
the One settles in its abode;
able to be leisurely and prepared,
the One does not depart;
guard the One and preserve the true,
then you can communicate with spirits;
reduce desires and moderate food,
the One then remains with breath;
with a blade at the neck,
think of the One and survive;
knowing the One is not difficult,
difficulty lies in persistence;
guard it without loss,
and you can be boundless;
on land, ward off fierce beasts,
in water, repel flood dragons;
fear not specters and goblins,
nor venomous insects;
ghosts dare not approach,
blades dare not strike.
This is the general outline of the True One."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"I have heard from my teacher that
among the various classics of the Daoist arts,
the methods of contemplation, concentration, and visualization
that can repel evil and protect the body
number in the thousands.
Such as containing shadows and hiding forms,
guarding the form without life,
the nine transformations, twelve metamorphoses, twenty-four births, etc.,
visualizing the various spirits within one's body,
and the methods of inner vision to see them—
these are too numerous to count,
and each has its effectiveness.
However, some involve visualizing thousands of objects for self-defense,
which are mostly cumbersome and difficult,
enough to greatly weary one's mind.
If one knows the Way of Guarding the One,
then all such methods can be discarded,
hence it is said that knowing the One brings all matters to completion.
Receiving the oral formula of the True One
has clear written instructions;
one must smear the blood of a white sacrificial animal,
receive it on a day of Wáng and Xiàng,
use white silk and white silver as pledges,
engrave a metal contract and divide it—
to lightly disclose or recklessly transmit it
will cause its spiritual power to be ineffective.
If a person can guard the One,
the One will also guard the person.
Thus, sharp blades cannot wield their sharpness,
and all harms cannot manifest their malevolence;
one can succeed even in failure,
and find safety alone in danger.
If in haunted temples,
beneath mountain forests,
places of great pestilence,
among graves and tombs,
dens of tigers and wolves,
or abodes of venomous snakes,
one guards the One without negligence,
all evils will flee far away.
If one suddenly forgets to guard the One,
they may be harmed by hundreds of ghosts.
For those who are plagued by nightmares while sleeping,
immediately go to the central courtyard and gaze at the Fǔ star,
clench firmly and guard the One,
and the ghosts will depart.
If it is cloudy or rainy,
simply remain indoors,
facing north and visualizing the Fǔ star.
If surrounded by soldiers or bandits,
with no escape route,
urgently enter the Yin of Liùjiǎ,
crouch down and guard the One,
and the five weapons cannot harm you.
Those who can guard the One
may travel ten thousand miles,
join the army,
cross great rivers—
without needing to divine days or choose hours,
commence work or move residences,
enter new houses—
all without consulting geomancy or astrological calendars,
and without avoiding the deities of Tàisuì, Tàiyīn, Jiāngjūn, Yuèjiàn, or evil influences,
or taboos of fate and year,
yet never encounter calamity or misfortune.
This is a method tested and proven by past sages."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"The Way of the Mysterious One
is also an essential method.
There is nothing it does not ward off,
sharing the same efficacy as the True One.
The first chapter of my Inner Chapters is titled 'Chàng Xuán'
Guarding the Mysterious One is even easier than guarding the True One.
The True One has a surname, given name, height, clothing color, and appearance;
the Mysterious One is simply perceived as such.
Initially seek it at midday,
as the saying goes: 'Know the white, guard the black,'
so that even desiring death is unattainable.
However, one must first undergo a hundred days of pure fasting
before it can be sought and obtained,
and it usually takes only three or four days to acquire it.
Once obtained and guarded,
it will not depart again.
While guarding the Mysterious One,
also visualize your body
dividing into three persons.
Once the three are visible,
further increase them—
up to several tens of persons,
all identical to oneself.
Concealing or revealing them
each has its oral formulas—
this is the so-called Way of Dividing Forms.
This is how Zuǒ Jūn, Jì Zǐxùn, and Gě Xiāngōng could be in dozens of places in a single day,
such as having a guest in the hall
with one host conversing,
another host at the gate welcoming guests,
and yet another by the water fishing—
leaving guests unable to distinguish the true host.
My teacher said that guarding the One while cultivating the bright mirror
allows one to divide into dozens of persons once the mirror method is mastered,
with clothing and facial features
all identical."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"My teacher said that to seek longevity,
one must diligently ingest the great medicines;
to attain spiritual communion,
one must achieve the metal-water division of forms.
Once forms are divided, one can see the three hún and seven pò within their body,
and commune with celestial spirits and earthly deities;
all become accessible,
and the gods of mountains and rivers
can be commanded."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Life is precious,
death is fearsome.
Yet those who cultivate longevity, nurture nature, and avoid death
invariably begin with diligence,
ultimately achieving enduring vision.
After mastering the Dao,
effort becomes minimal.
Before mastery is attained,
no effort is spared.
Gathering herbal medicines,
laboring in mountains and marshes,
decocting, preparing, and concocting—
all require physical strength.
Scaling heights and traversing dangers,
toiling day and night without rest—
without utmost determination,
one cannot persevere long.
And when seeking to complete the golden elixir and ascend to heaven,
the great medicines required
all cost money,
impossible to procure hastily.
One must engage in farming, herding, trade, or peddling to raise funds,
accumulating years of diligent effort
before the elixir can be compounded.
When the time for compounding arrives,
one must again fast and purify,
severing all human affairs.
Facing numerous challenges,
one must additionally practice spirit contemplation and guarding the One,
repelling evils and protecting the body,
constantly like a ruler governing a state
or a general awaiting the enemy—
only then can the achievement of longevity be attained.
Those with keen intelligence and great wisdom,
endowed with the capacity to manage worldly and save customs,
who cultivate this path—
are certain to succeed.
Superficial and mediocre individuals,
even with aspiration and fondness,
cannot persevere to the end.
Thus, a person's body
resembles a state.
The positions of chest and abdomen
are like palaces and chambers.
The arrangement of the four limbs
is like suburbs and borders.
The divisions of bones and joints
are like the hundred officials.
The spirit is like the ruler,
blood like the ministers,
and qì like the people.
Therefore, knowing how to govern the body
enables one to govern the state.
Cherishing the people ensures the state's stability;
nurturing the qì ensures the body's wholeness.
When the people scatter, the state perishes;
when the qì is exhausted, the body dies.
The dead cannot be revived,
the perished cannot be restored.
Thus, the ultimate person eliminates troubles before they arise,
treats illnesses before they manifest,
attending to them before any issue occurs,
not pursuing them after they have passed.
The people are hard to nurture yet easily endangered;
qì is hard to purify yet easily turbid.
Therefore, applying authority and virtue preserves the altars of land and grain;
cutting off desires and cravings stabilizes blood and qì.
Then the True One will reside within,
the three and seven will be guarded,
all harms will be repelled,
and lifespan will be extended."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"My master said that by taking the great elixir of gold and cinnabar,
although one has not yet left the mortal world,
no hundred evils can approach.
If one only consumes herbs and minor preparations of the eight minerals,
it may suffice to cure illnesses and prolong life,
but it is not enough to ward off external calamities.
One might be assailed by ghosts,
or lightly bullied by mountain spirits,
or invaded by spectral demons—
only by guarding the True One
can one fear none of these beings.
Next best is carrying divine talismans.
If one is completely ignorant of these two methods while seeking longevity,
it is perilous indeed.
If you close three of the four gates,
thieves may still enter—
how much more if all are open?"
Someone said:
"I am but an ignorant man,
confined to Confucian teachings,
knowing only the classics of Five Canons, Three Histories, and Hundred Schools,
along with frivolous poetry,
and pointless short essays.
I have devoted my thoughts to preserving these,
for many years now.
Born into an era of many troubles,
with chaos unceasing,
weapons of war raised high,
literary arts are not valued—
I've merely wasted effort,
straining my mind to the utmost,
probing subtleties and seeking hidden meanings,
yet ultimately failing to secure an official post,
or escape farming fields;
moreover, it has harmed deep contemplation,
and done nothing for lifespan.
With gray hair signaling dusk,
my pure aspirations wane,
I wish to turn from delusion,
to seek the path of life,
but in haste, without guidance,
I have no direction,
as if crossing a great river
without knowing how to reach the other shore.
Since you, sir, have thoroughly studied ancient texts,
and also mastered esoteric secrets,
may I ask how many volumes of Daoist writings exist,
and could you tell me their titles?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I too share your ailment.
In the past, I was fortunate to meet my brilliant master, Master Zhèng,
but regret that as a disciple, I was not wise enough
to penetrate the hardest and highest truths.
At that time, though I performed menial tasks as a disciple,
being of shallow talent and insight,
and still young and vigorous,
my mind was not focused,
worldly attachments not fully shed,
I could not gain much,
which I deeply regret.
Master Zhèng was then over eighty,
previously his hair had been graying,
but within a few years it turned black again,
his complexion radiant and cheerful,
he could draw a strong bow shooting a hundred paces,
walk several hundred lǐ a day,
and drink two dǒu of wine without getting drunk.
Whenever he climbed mountains,
his body was light and agile,
scaling heights and crossing dangers,
young men chasing after him
often couldn't keep up.
His diet was no different from ordinary people's,
and he was never seen abstaining from grains.
I asked his earlier disciple Huáng Zhāng,
who said that when Master Zhèng returned from Yùzhāng,
at Juégōu Pǔ,
he encountered strong winds repeatedly.
Hearing there were many bandits ahead,
companions urged him to stay
and wait for others,
as everyone had little food,
but Master Zhèng gave his rice to comfort them,
and though he ate nothing himself,
for fifty days he felt no hunger.
No one saw him perform any special act,
so it's unknown how he did it.
He could write finely by lamplight,
surpassing younger men.
He understood music theory,
played the qín excellently,
while sitting leisurely,
with several attendants present,
he would answer questions orally,
his speech uninterrupted,
yet his ears could simultaneously listen
to those playing strings beside him,
correcting their rhythms
without the slightest error.
I became Master Zhèng's disciple late,
and requested to see medical texts;
he told me:
'The essential Way fits on a foot of silk,
enough to transcend the world—
no need for many.
But after broad study,
it far surpasses not seeing them.
It helps understand human intent,
and provides simple techniques
to protect beginners from various afflictions before they achieve mastery.'
So he first showed me nearly a hundred volumes of less important Daoist instructional and disciplinary texts,
gradually revealing them.
I had already seen many,
and consulted him on doubtful points in those I'd previewed.
Master Zhèng said:
'You have a talent for discernment,
and can be taught.
But what you know,
though extensive, is not refined,
and your mind is on external studies,
unable to focus solely,
so you're not yet fit for deep and far-reaching exploration.
I will now show you better texts.'
He also promised to gradually give me short texts written on silk,
and over the years,
collecting what I saw,
it should have amounted to about two hundred volumes,
but in the end, I couldn't obtain them.
Other disciples all performed servant duties,
gathering firewood and farming,
only I, being frail,
couldn't handle other labor,
yet having no way to contribute,
I often personally swept,
wiped beds and tables,
ground ink and held candles,
and helped Master Zhèng copy old texts.
He treated me like his earlier disciples,
telling me,
'Every volume of miscellaneous Daoist texts contains valuable insights,
but you should compare their refinement and coarseness,
and choose what to practice,
not memorize everything,
wasting time and straining your mind.
Once the golden elixir is achieved,
all these become unnecessary.
Sometimes teaching may be required,
so you should grasp the fundamentals,
starting from the shallow and simple,
to encourage learners,
without expecting precise steps or origins.'
Master Zhèng also refused to let anyone copy his books first;
one had to understand their meaning thoroughly,
and though they could be borrowed long-term,
no one dared secretly copy a single character.
Master Zhèng was originally a great Confucian scholar,
who later embraced the Dào,
yet continued teaching the Book of Rites and Book of Documents.
His demeanor was noble and bright,
his character upright and disciplined,
all who met him felt reverence.
Whenever asking questions,
we always waited for his gentle expression,
not daring to be presumptuous.
When books were in my possession,
even for a month,
enough to copy much,
I dared not steal a transcription,
precisely because Master Zhèng was sharp,
and if by chance he found out,
losing his favor would mean small gain at great cost.
Yet at the start of seeking instruction,
I didn't dare ask for more,
only making occasional requests after consideration.
Thus, I only knew how to drink from the river,
but couldn't fill my belly.
However, among over fifty disciples,
only I received the Scripture of the Golden Elixir and the Inner Script of the Three Sovereigns, along with the Pillowbook Record of the Five Phases;
others didn't even get to see the titles of these books.
Though I didn't obtain all other texts,
I noted their names,
and now I'll tell you,
so later generations who love books
can search widely for them.

they are one volume each.
Next are various talismans,

including the Self-Originating Talisman, Golden Light Talisman, three scrolls of the Great Mystery Talisman, Heaven-Penetrating Talisman, Five Essences Talisman, Stone Chamber Talisman, Jade Strategy Talisman, Pillow Talisman, Youth Talisman, Nine Spirits Talisman, Six Lords Talisman, Xuāndū Talisman, Huángdì Talisman, Shàoqiān's Thirty-Six General Talismans, Life-Extending Divine Talisman, Tiānshuǐ Divine Talisman, Forty-Nine Truth Talismans, Tiānshuǐ Talisman, Azure Dragon Talisman, White Tiger Talisman, Vermilion Bird Talisman, Black Tortoise Talisman, Red Embryo Talisman, Seven Mechanisms Talisman, Nine Heavens Troop-Deploying Talisman, Nine Heavens Talisman, Lǎojīng Talisman, Seven Talismans, Great Warding-Off-Calamity Talisman, Xuánzǐ Talisman, Wǔxiàojīng's Yānjūn Dragon-Tiger Three Pouches Weapon-Warding Talisman, Bāoyuán Talisman, Shěnxī Talisman, Yǔqiāo Talisman, Disaster-Dispelling Talisman, Eight Trigrams Talisman, Jiàngān Talisman, Thunderbolt Talisman, Wànbì Talisman, Eight Majesties Five Victories Talisman, Wēixǐ Talisman, Jùshèng Talisman, Cǎinǚ Talisman, Xuánjīng Talisman, Jade Calendar Talisman, Běitái Talisman, Yīnyáng Great Suppression Talisman, Pillow Talisman, ten scrolls of Cure All Illnesses Talismans, ten scrolls of Spirit-Subduing Talismans, twenty scrolls of Húgōng Talismans, nine scrolls of Jiǔtái Talismans, ten scrolls of Liùjiǎ Spiritual Communication Talismans, five hundred scrolls of Liùyīn Mobile Kitchen, Dragon Embryo, Stone Chamber, Three Metals, Five Woods, Life-Protection Talismans, Jūnhuǒ Summoning and Control Talisman, ten scrolls of Jade Axe Talismans,
all of which are major talismans.
The remaining minor ones
cannot be fully recorded."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Master Zhèng stated that talismans originated from Lǎojūn,
all being celestial script.
Lǎojūn could communicate with spirits,
and the talismans were all bestowed by them.
The reason modern users experience few effects
is due to their long history
and frequent errors in transcription.
Moreover, lacking sincere faith,
their application becomes ineffective.
Comparing them to writing characters,
an erroneous talisman
not only brings no benefit
but may cause harm.
Even with known characters,
people still make copying errors.
Hence the proverb:
'After three copies,
"fish" becomes "lǔ",
"xū" becomes "hǔ".'
This illustrates the point.
The characters for 'seven' and 'scholar'
differ only in stroke curvature and length.
Yet current talismans bear unreadable script,
where errors go undetected,
so none realize their inconstancy.
Some practitioners achieve singular efficacy with talismans,
just as certain individuals naturally emit fragrance when using musk,
an innate quality untransmittable.
Nevertheless,
one must obtain error-free talismans
and use them with upright mind.
Though effects may be slower than with innate bearers,
benefits will still manifest.
For Daoists seeking immortality,
the primary focus should be on medicines,
while talismans and swords merely ward ghosts and evil.
Claims that major talismans can confer transcendence
should not be solely relied upon.
In former Wú times, Jiè Xiàng
could read talismanic script
and detect errors.
When tested with assorted healing and spirit-subduing talismans
stripped of labels,
he identified each by name.
Those containing errors
he corrected for others.
Since then,
none have possessed such knowledge."
Someone asked:
"Among transcendent medicines,
none surpass golden elixirs –
this we have learned.
Dare we ask which talismanic texts
are considered most divine?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"From Master Zhèng I learned
the most revered Daoist texts
are the Three Sovereigns' Esoteric Script and Five Peaks True Form Charts.
Ancient transcendents and perfected beings
guarded this Way sacredly,
never transmitting it
to those lacking transcendent destiny.
Recipients waited forty years between transmissions,
swearing blood oaths
with personal pledges as covenant.
Various famous mountains and five peaks
all housed these texts,
hidden in secluded stone chambers,
where destined seekers
entering mountains with utmost sincerity
would witness mountain deities
revealing them personally.
Like Bó Zhònglǐ,
who obtained them in mountains,
erected altars with silk offerings,
and copied a version before departing.
Possessing these texts,
keep them in pure places.
Before any undertaking,
first announce to them
as serving ruler and parent.
The scripture states:
'Housing the Three Sovereigns' Script
wards off evil spirits,
epidemic energies,
and sudden calamities.
If gravely ill near death,
those with sincere faith
holding this text
shall surely survive.
Childbirth women breathless in labor holding it
will deliver immediately.'
Daoists seeking longevity
carrying it into mountains
repel tigers, wolves, mountain spirits,
five poisons, and hundreds of evils –
none dare approach.
Crossing rivers and seas,
they repel flood dragons
and calm winds and waves.
Mastering its methods
enables transformation and construction.
Without consulting geomancy or selecting days,
households avoid misfortune.
For building new homes or tombs,
copy the Earth Sovereign Script dozens of times,
spread over land,
and next day observe
where yellow marks appear –
construct there
for family prosperity.
During others' burials,
with your name on paper,
secretly insert into their tomb
undiscovered,
to prevent sudden disasters and theft.
Conspirators against you
will suffer self-inflicted harm.
After purifying fasting for hundred days,
this text summons celestial deities, Directors of Fate, and Year Guardian,
daily touring five peaks and four rivers,
shrine deities –
all appearing humanoid,
consultable on fortune, safety,
and causes of illnesses' supernatural afflictions.
Another eighteen-character version worn in clothing
ensures safe long voyages
free from storm worries.
Households keeping Five Peaks True Form Charts
ward off weapons and rebellion;
would-be harm-doers
suffer reversed consequences.
Occasional Daoist recipients
failing benevolence and compassion,
impure or unrighteous,
risk family-destroying calamities –
never treat lightly."
Among the arts of transformation,
the greatest is only the Mòzǐ Wǔxíng Jì,
originally in five volumes.
In the past, before Liú Jūn'ān ascended to immortality,
he excerpted its essentials,
making one volume.
Its methods use medicines and talismans,
enabling one to fly up and down,
disappear without a trace,
smile and become a woman,
frown and become an old man,
crouch and become a child,
grasp a staff and it becomes a forest,
plant something and it grows edible melons and fruits,
draw on the ground and it becomes a river,
gather soil and it forms a mountain,
summon a feast while seated,
raise clouds and ignite fires,
there is nothing it cannot do.
Next is the Yùnǚ Yǐnwēi in one volume,
which also transforms forms into birds, beasts,
and metals, wood, stones, and jades,
summons clouds and brings rain over a hundred lǐ,
similarly creates snow,
crosses great waters without boats or bridges,
divides the body into a thousand people,
rides the wind to fly high,
enters and exits without gaps,
can exhale breath in seven colors,
sit and see the eight extremes,
and things underground,
emit light ten thousand zhàng long,
brighten dark rooms,
also a great art.
However, it requires pacing dozens of stars,
intricate and hard to recognize,
few can master it.
The Huáinán Hóngbǎo Wàn Bì
does not compare to this book.
There is also the White Tiger Seven Transformations method,
taking the skin of a white tiger killed on the third day of the third month,
raw badger blood, tiger blood,
purple ribbons,
sandal straps,
duckweed,
planting them together on the third day of the third month.
The first growth resembles sesame,
bearing fruit,
then planting these seeds,
each generation differing.
After seven plantings,
use the fruits in combination,
can also change form and appearance,
fly or dive at will,
similar to Mòzǐ and Yùnǚ Yǐnwēi,
beyond this, not worth discussing."
The purpose of broad reading
is to let those who love the Way know the names of extraordinary books.
Zhèng Jūn was not only versed in the Five Classics and knew the path to immortality,
but also mastered the Nine Palaces and Three Wonders, calculated astronomy, and the prophecies of the Hé and Luò rivers,
all with profound research.
In the first year of Tài'ān,
knowing the chaos of the declining age,
and that Jiāngnán would boil like a cauldron,
he shouldered his books and held recipes of immortal medicines,
leading his close disciples,
eastward to Huò Shān,
and none know where he is.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
"To seek bright pearls,
if not from the depths of Hépǔ,
one cannot obtain the night-shining gem of the black dragon.
To gather beautiful jade,
if not from the cliffs of Jīng Shān,
one cannot get the foot-long jade worth multiple cities.
To learn from a teacher and inquire about the Way,
if not with the right person,
leaving means delaying hopes of gain,
staying means ultimately achieving nothing,
wasting effort and hindering progress,
later, even with deep regret,
it is too late.
Even shallow, common matters in the world,
cannot be known by sitting idly,
let alone the affairs of immortals?
Even sages and the wise,
cannot comprehend them on their own,
not attainable through sequential thought,
nor by analogical seeking.
Truly, one's teacher
must be profound and broad,
like dipping water while crossing the vast sea,
or cutting wood in a long forest,
where the worry is only insufficient strength,
not scarcity of resources!
What tigers and leopards leave behind,
is what wildcats and mice fight over.
What Táo Zhū discards,
is what Yuán and Yán lack.
Those who follow a teacher,
if they do not find one with deep insight and vast knowledge,
but meet an isolated and ignorant person,
whose knowledge is inherently narrow,
with short sources and hurried flow,
when giving to others,
they are stingy and unwilling,
when sharing to teach,
it is shallow and unremarkable,
what they treasure is already imprecise,
if they further select the crude to teach others,
how can there be any achievement?
It is like borrowing grain from the door of Yí Qí,
or complaining of cold at the house of Qián Lóu,
what you get is only acorns and coarse cloth,
certainly no grand feast or silks and furs.
Some cling to mediocre teachers,
never awakening.
Some fortunately meet knowledgeable ones,
but do not diligently seek,
this loss is from unawareness,
and cannot be reclaimed.
To know a person's depth,
is indeed not easy.
The ancients found it difficult,
for good reason.
White stones resemble jade,
treacherous flatterers resemble the worthy.
The worthy hide themselves more,
having but as if not,
the treacherous boast more,
empty yet seeming solid,
without utmost clarity,
how to distinguish them?
Those who keep seeking mediocre teachers without leaving,
not knowing their ignorance yet persisting,
truly believe it sufficient.
Those who see a wise person but do not serve them,
not knowing their depth and thus not inquiring,
truly think them no different.
Those who know the essential Way,
desire nothing from things,
do not seek worldly fame,
why would they flaunt themselves among the vulgar?
But shallow individuals,
mostly boastful and self-proclaiming,
using stern looks and rare sounds to disguise falsehoods,
enough to dazzle late learners,
and dare to make grand claims.
Saying,
they have climbed famous mountains,
seen immortals.
Hearing hastily,
without clear verification,
few detect their falseness.
I have often seen miscellaneous, scattered Daoists,
visiting nobles' doors,
specifically having followers create empty reputations,
claiming they are already four or five hundred years old.
When people ask their age,
they pretend not to hear,
smiling and nodding,
saying eighty or ninety.
Shortly after, they claim,
'I practiced grain-abstinence on Huàyīn Shān for fifty years,
then on Sōng Shān's Shǎoshì for forty years,
again on Tài Shān for sixty years,
and with someone on Jī Shān for fifty years,'
telling all they've been through to companions,
just so,
wanting others to calculate the total,
making them hundreds of years old.
Then, among those fond of such ways,
none fail to gather like smoke and mist,
crowding their gates.
Some practitioners occasionally possess innate physical abilities,
perceive ghosts and spirits,
and are somewhat capable of internal divination,
knowing people's future and past events,
yet they truly cannot affect fortunes for better or worse.
They are like yarrow stalks and tortoise shells.
When ordinary people witness minor validations,
they immediately hail them as divine beings,
claiming they must be omniscient.
Otherwise,
some excel in talisman water and incantation techniques,
effectively treating evil influences,
but may not understand the path to immortality.
Some cultivate miscellaneous arts,
enabling them to see ghosts and monsters,
yet it does not benefit their lifespan.
When questioned about the golden elixir method,
they generally know nothing.
Upon careful examination,
most deceive the world,
seeking wealth and profit,
stopping at nothing.
These individuals share the same end as burglars
though their paths differ.
Relying on empty words
is inferior to demonstrating evidence through actions.
For the late-awakening later learners,
I shall explain analogous cases,
using counterfeit examples as proof.
In the past, there was Gǔ Qiáng,
who consumed herbal formulas
and practiced Róng Chéng's dark feminine arts,
remaining intelligent and not severely frail
at around eighty years old.
Contemporaries thus called him an immortal,
or the millennia-old elder.
Yángzhōu's Inspector Jī heard and invited him to Yídū for testing.
Upon arrival,
he mumbled and hesitated,
seeming to know much
yet withholding full disclosure.
Consequently, enthusiasts
gathered like echoes to sound,
clinging like shadows to form,
converging like clouds and mist,
competing in admiration,
with gifts flowing continuously,
often leaving him surplus money.
Even Luán and Lǐ's reverence in the Hàn dynasty
could not surpass this.
He regularly consumed tiānméndōng without cessation,
revealing his lack of golden elixir mastery.
Though Gǔ Qiáng had briefly studied texts,
he recognized ancient affairs.
He claimed to be four thousand years old,
daring falsehoods
without shame.
He stated he had seen Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng,
describing them vividly and accurately.
The world says Yáo had eight-colored eyebrows,
but it was untrue;
rather, his brow-ends were upright,
resembling the character "eight."
Yáo was tall with a beautiful beard,
drinking over two hú of wine daily,
yet people exaggerated it to a thousand zhōng—
impossible,
as I repeatedly saw him heavily drunk.
Though a sage,
he aged and governed
less effectively than in youth.
Upon banishing the Four Fiends
and promoting Yuán and Kǎi,
he relied on Shùn.
Shùn was an orphan from a humble family,
but with exceptional talent,
he farmed incognito at Lìshān,
fished at Léizé,
and pottered by the sea,
unappreciated by contemporaries.
I observed him morally transforming people wherever he was;
his eyes had double pupils,
indicating noble destiny,
so I often encouraged and comforted him:
"Cherish lofty ideals,
fear not lacking wealth;
the Fire Virtue ends,
the Yellow Essence rises,
the mandate descends—
who but you shall inherit it?"
Yet his father was stubborn,
his brother vicious,
constantly plotting to kill Shùn.
I often admonished them:
"This child will glorify your lineage,
benefiting all under heaven—
not just your family—
do not mistreat him."
Soon he received the throne,
recalling my prophetic words.
He also said:
"When Confucius's mother was sixteen or seventeen,
I divined she would bear a noble son.
Upon Shēng Zhòngní's birth,
he was truly extraordinary,
standing nine feet six inches tall,
his forehead like Yáo's,
his neck like Gāo Yáo's,
his shoulders like Zǐ Chǎn's,
though from the waist down, three inches shorter than Yǔ.
Despite
poverty and obscurity,
he loved ritual vessels even as a child.
I knew he would achieve greatness.
As he grew,
his profound discourse amazed,
attracting numerous disciples
numbering thousands.
I delighted in his words,
often visiting him,
regretting only my lack of study,
unable to discuss in detail.
He urged me to read the Yì Jīng,
calling it a superb text,
which he privately cherished,
wearing out the leather bindings thrice,
breaking three iron pointers,
gaining great enlightenment.
In the fourteenth year of Lǔ Āi Gōng,
a unicorn was captured westwards
and died.
Confucius asked me about it,
and I told him
it was an ill omen.
He wept sorrowfully.
Later, he had a nightmare
and wished to see me.
It was mid-fourth month, intensely hot,
so I could not go;
soon I heard he fell ill and died in seven days,
his expression still vaguely memorable."
He also said:
"Qín Shǐ Huáng brought me to Péngchéng,
to retrieve a Zhōu dynasty cauldron.
I told the emperor
it was a divine artifact:
it emerges with virtue,
vanishes with tyranny.
Cultivate yourself,
and it will come naturally,
not by force."
The emperor initially doubted me,
but pulling it indeed failed.
He then apologized:
'You are truly a far-sighted wise man.'"
He also clearly described Hàn Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ;
such accounts
are too numerous to record fully.
Contemporaries recognized them
as amusement.
Yet ordinary listeners
believed his words.
Moreover, Gǔ Qiáng grew senile,
forgetful of events.
Inspector Jī once gave him a jade cup,
but he later claimed,
"Ānqī Xiānshēng gifted this to me."
He later fell ill and died at Shòuchūn in Huáng Zhěng's home.
Zhěng suspected he had transformed and left.
About a year later,
they opened his coffin to check,
and the corpse remained intact.
These are cases of fame without substance,
causing the world to disbelieve in immortals,
all due to such frauds confusing truth with falsehood.
The governor of Chéngdū, Wú Wén,
spoke of one Cài Dàn from Wǔyuán,
who loved the Dao but lacked a proper master and essential practices.
He abandoned his family's livelihood,
merely chanting day and night texts like the Huángtíng, Tàiqīng Zhōngjīng, and Guāntiān Jiéxiáng,
various books of little urgency,
never ceasing his recitations,
believing the Dao was fully contained within them.
Yet he never understood how to apply them,
only admiring their flowery rhetoric and deceiving himself.
He also taught that reading them a thousand times
would naturally yield their meaning,
persisting in this for a long time.
His family grew distressed by it,
as it consumed their clothing and food
without producing any marvels.
He himself felt ashamed and resentful,
unable to justify it,
so he left his home,
claiming he had achieved immortality.
He then fled to remote mountains in another land,
but did not know how to gather herbs and plants for fasting,
only selling firewood to exchange for food and clothing.
After three years of this,
suffering hunger, cold, and hardship,
some people recognized him,
but he deceitfully pretended not to know them.
Eventually, unable to endure, he returned home,
dark, thin, and gaunt,
barely human in appearance.
His family asked him,
"Where have you come from?
Did you not attain immortality after all?"
He then deceived them, saying,
"I did not ascend to heaven,
but became an earthly immortal instead.
Moreover, my initial rank is low,
and I must serve the earlier accomplished immortals,
gradually advancing over time.
Previously, I was herding several dragons for Lǎojūn,
among which a five-colored dragon was the finest,
the one Lǎojūn often rode.
He ordered me to guard and watch it,
but I was negligent,
playing games with the junior immortals instead,
and suddenly lost that dragon,
which then vanished without a trace.
For this crime, I was reprimanded
and sent to the foot of Kūnlún Mountain,
to weed three or four qǐng of land.
The grasses were all fine and dense,
with much overgrowth and weeds,
making the toil indescribably arduous.
By the rules, it would take ten years to be pardoned.
Fortunately, immortals like Wò Quánzǐ and Wáng Qiáo came on an inspection,
and I pleaded with them,
so they all exerted effort on my behalf,
temporarily releasing me to return.
I must now cultivate myself further to seek departure again."
Thus, he eventually died of old age.
Initially, upon Cài Dàn's return, he claimed
to have come from Kūnlún,
and his relatives and old acquaintances eagerly asked him,
"What is Kūnlún like?"
He replied:
"Heaven's height in miles is not questioned,
but when you look up at it,
it seems no more than a dozen zhang from the sky.
There is a Tree of Grain on top,
forty-nine zhàng tall,
with ears as large as a cart.
There are trees of pearls, jade, shātáng, lánggān, and bìguī,
jade plums, jade melons, and jade peaches,
whose fruits resemble worldly peaches and plums in shape,
but are luminous, translucent, and hard.
They must be washed with water from the Jade Well,
then they soften and can be eaten.
Whenever the wind rises,
the branches, flowers, and leaves
of the pearl and jade trees
strike each other,
naturally producing the five tones,
clear and mournful, stirring the heart.
As I was exiled and disheartened,
hearing this, I could not help but feel sorrowful and sad.
I also saw that on Kūnlún Mountain,
each side has four hundred and forty gates,
each gate four lǐ wide.
Inside are five cities and twelve towers,
below the towers are Green Dragons and White Tigers,
and serpents over a hundred lǐ long,
whose mouths and teeth are like three-hundred-hù ships.
There are giant bees ten zhàng long,
whose venom can kill elephants.
There are also divine beasts,
named Shīzi Bìxié, Sānlù Jiāoyáng,
Copper-Headed, Iron-Browed, Long-Tusked, Chisel-Toothed, and the like,
thirty-six kinds in all.
If one knows all their names,
then no evil ghosts or beasts in the world
dare to harm people.
The deities include Wútóu Zǐ, Dàojǐng Jūn, Xīlù Gōng, Zhōnghuáng Xiānshēng, and Liùmén Dàfū.
Zhāng Yáng, styled Zǐyuān,
fully guards the Jade Palace.
Without carrying Lǎojūn's Bamboo Messenger Tallies and matching contracts,
one cannot enter.
Five rivers all emerge from the mountain's corners,
surrounded by the Ruò River,
where not even a goose feather floats,
and no flying bird can cross.
Only immortals can traverse it.
Above are divine birds and divine horses,
such as Yōuchāng, Jiāomíng, Ténghuáng, Jíguāng,
all able to speak human language and never die.
Truly, it is a magnificent and swift immortal abode,
but alas, I could not roam there freely.
At that time, hearing Cài Dàn's words so clearly,
many believed him.
Also, in Púbān, Hédōng, there was one Xiàng Mǎodū,
who entered the mountains with his son to learn immortality.
After ten years, he returned home,
and his family asked him the reason.
Mǎodū said:
"After three years of intense meditation in the mountains,
an immortal came to welcome me,
and we rode a dragon together to ascend to heaven.
After a long while,
I looked down at the earth,
dark and obscure,
not yet reaching the top above,
but already extremely far from the ground.
The dragon traveled very swiftly,
with its head raised and tail lowered,
making one on its back
feel perilously frightened.
Upon reaching heaven,
we first passed the Purple Mansion,
with golden beds and jade tables,
dazzling and brilliant,
truly a noble place.
The immortal gave me a cup of flowing rosy clouds,
and drinking it ended all hunger and thirst.
Suddenly, I missed home,
and when I went before the Heavenly Emperor,
I breached etiquette in my audience,
was reprimanded and sent back,
told to cultivate and accumulate more merits,
only then could I return again.
In the past, Liú Ān, the Prince of Huáinán, ascended to heaven and saw the Supreme God,
but sat cross-legged and boasted arrogantly,
calling himself 'the solitary one,'
and was thus exiled to guard the heavenly kitchen for three years.
Who am I to compare?
Hence, in Hédōng, Mǎodū was called the Reprimanded Immortal.
There are many such people in the world,
of various kinds,
and one must be very cautious.
Such wild tales exist,
and some still fail to see their falsehood,
let alone more subtle deceptions
that embellish similarities to real events.
Without utmost clarity,
how can one discern them in haste?
There are even those who impersonate famous Daoist masters of the past,
like Bái Hé,
said to be eighty-seven hundred years old,
occasionally appearing among mortals,
then suddenly leaving,
with none knowing his whereabouts.
In Luòyáng, there was a Daoist
well-versed in many matters
and skilled in esoteric arts,
who consulted Hé on various doubts and difficulties.
Hé would immediately explain and resolve them all
without any obstruction,
thus considered profoundly knowledgeable.
People did not know his exact age,
but believed he was nearly a thousand years old, if not more.
Later, he suddenly left,
and none knew where he went.
Then, someone north of the Yellow River claimed to be Bái Hé,
and people from near and far vied to serve him,
generously bestowing gifts upon him.
But Bái Hé's disciples and family,
hearing he had reappeared,
were overjoyed
and went to see him,
only to confirm it was not him.
The imposter then fled and disappeared.
The Five Classics and Four Divisions
are but straw dogs already displayed,
the dregs of bygone days.
What is called a "footprint"
is produced by the foot but is not the foot itself.
The "writings" were created by sages but are not the sages themselves,
yet Confucian scholars travel thousands of miles carrying satchels to seek their teachers;
how much more should one diligently seek and exhaustively inquire
about the Way of Long Life,
which is valued by Perfected Persons?
However, one must carefully distinguish their authenticity from falsehood!
I fear that the likes of Gǔ Qiáng, Cài Dàn, Xiàng Màn-dū, and Bái Hé will never cease to exist in the world.
Those with a taste for such matters, upon examining this book of mine,
may slightly refine their judgment of what is good and bad.
Moreover, the Immortal Scriptures say:
"The pupils of immortals' eyes are all square."
I met a man in Luòyáng named Bái Zhònglǐ,
who told me his pupils were indeed square—
truly, he was an extraordinary man!"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
There was a Master Huáibīng,
who despised the unrest of roaming about,
and lamented the toil of spitting out and grasping.
He ceded fertile lands to others,
and instead tilled the salty wastes himself.
He concealed his six wonders by tying his bag,
holding precious gems without revealing them.
His clear voice went unheard,
his brilliant writings unseen by the world.
He turned his back on the splendor of vermilion gates,
preserving his tranquility in a humble thatched hut.
He severed tracks at the gates of the wealthy,
nourishing his vast spirit among recluses.
He considered glory and prominence unfortunate,
viewing jade and silk as mere grass and dirt.
He upheld divine norms beyond the clouds,
alone rejecting the present to follow antiquity.
Sheltered by towering majestic peaks,
resting on fragrant mats of emerald orchids.
Gargling with the clear liquid of flowing mists,
consuming the essence of the eight minerals.
His thoughts soared as if dwelling at the edge of a rainbow,
his mind drifted as if neighboring inverted shadows.
The myriad things could not disturb his harmony,
the four seas were insufficient to muddy his spirit.
Then, a young nobleman pursuing power heard of him,
and sighed with emotion, saying:
"A fine steed with a strong neck in an empty valley
is a disgrace to Sūn Yáng;
an era of peace leaving behind a talent unmatched in the world
is the fault of those who recognize the true.
How can we allow the outstanding to fulfill their solitary virtue,
leaving the sacred court lacking the service of Yuán and Kǎi?"
So he visited and persuaded him, saying:
"Merely hearing of flapping wings and straightening the body,
unable to soar fiercely through the nine heavens,
or ascend to the profound zenith—
those who can order human relations
are not necessarily heroic.
Now, you, sir, wield a blade that cuts decisively,
conceal resplendent literary talents,
ponder over texts in untrodden marshes,
and gather elegance among beasts and birds.
You display dragon patterns in the dark night,
sink precious stones into deep abysses,
lie dormant in midsummer's heat,
and hide blossoms in the heart of spring.
Even if you lower the curtain and ponder deeply,
exhaust your brush and unleash eloquence,
mysteriously aiding the Supreme Ultimate,
expounding the fundamental origins,
making wooden figures smile joyfully as if with clever grins when speaking of happiness,
and causing puppet faces to weep profusely when telling of sorrow;
diminishing the light until a goose feather sinks in weak water,
or resisting weight until jade and stone float on flying waves;
separating the intimate until liver and gall become distant lands,
or uniting the disparate until myriad differences harmonize as one;
harsh in argument like autumn frosts and spring sternness,
gentle in speech like icy branches blooming with flowers;
toppling heights until majestic peaks crumble,
elevating lows until deep pools tower;
finding fault with purity by relying on dark night's glow,
saving turbidity by instantly clarifying the Yellow River—
yet you cannot shower great blessings upon all beings,
nor establish grand merits for the imperial house.
Your name will vanish with the morning dew,
your body perish with the mayfly.
Overlooking the lofty treasures of the sages,
forgetting the sigh over the river's flow in old age—
I secretly believe, sir, this is not acceptable.
"It is said the greatest are heaven and earth,
next, the ruler and his subjects.
The ancient sages, concerned for their time,
longed to practice their Way;
three months without a ruler,
and they grew anxious.
Ashamed that the present sage ruler does not match Yáo and Shùn,
pitying these common folk who cannot be enfeoffed house by house,
some thus leaped like dragons bearing tripods,
others sang like phoenixes tapping their horns,
not waiting for wheeled rushes to move,
nor depending on King Wén to rise.
Submerging at first, soaring later,
they waxed and waned with the times,
advancing with the benefit of purposeful action,
retiring without the burden of a drenched tail,
preserving themselves through wisdom,
transforming society through propagation.
Causing those bathed in orchid breezes to bend their branches,
and cleansed in clear waves to shed their filth—
like submerged shadows responding to a bright mirror,
or squares and circles conforming to compass and square.
Thus, their merits reached high and low,
their kindness moistened the eight directions.
The reason for the grandeur of the Táng era,
the reverence of Chóng Huá,
the tripartite division by Lord Wén of the West,
the revolution of Jī Fā,
the rectification by Huán and Wén,
the response to heaven by Hàn Gāo—
none failed to gather wise men as their six wings,
entrusting heroes as their boats and oars.
If each clung to the loftiness of ear-washing,
and all held to the lot of paired plowing,
then the transformative power of examining antiquity would not be established,
the brilliance of wisdom would not shine,
the songs of enlightened and able rulers would not be sung,
and the all-encompassing net of heaven would not be spread.
"Thus, those who conceal their talents are prized for adapting to change,
the heroic and exceptional valued for expressing wonders and quelling chaos.
If the shining sun hides its light behind clouds,
the beauty of the sky's brightness remains unseen;
if a roaring tiger sheathes its teeth and claws,
the swiftness of its pounce remains unshown;
if the Tài'ē sword hides its edge unused,
the power of its instant cut remains unrevealed;
if fine steeds limp without galloping,
the speed that chases the wind remains unmanifested;
if all are silent, then Zǐgòng is no different from the mute;
if all are blind, then Lí Zhū is no better than the sightless.
You, sir, purify yourself but neglect the disorder of great relationships,
find contentment but forget the duty of securing the ruler,
living with the burden of missed opportunities,
dying without the resonance of metal or stone.
Even ordinary men would feel indignation—
how can one of great refinement be so heedless?
"When the cord is stretched, the wood straightens;
when uprightness advances, wickedness withers.
With Yú's promotion, the four villains were executed;
with Xuānní in office, Shǎomǎo was beheaded.
Just as thunderclaps drown out drumbeats,
and the morning sun dims firefly candles.
If one does not save the sick from calling back their souls,
there's no use displaying the exceptional skills of the Yuè people;
if one does not encourage in times of turmoil,
there's no way to know the extraordinary foresight.
Folding arms high to watch others drown
is not the benevolence of refusing to tread;
embracing the Way but confusing the state
is not the task of a true creator.
If we wait for the central hall to grow grass that foretells the sun,
the morning sun to abound with the phoenix's song,
the suburbs to host the unicorn beast,
the wilds to gather forests of interlocking branches,
long banners rolled and unraised,
weapons stored and nowhere to be found,
and Shǎobó about to retire after success—
then who can be plucked from obscurity?
I deeply hope, sir, you will not long remain lost in return!"
Thereupon, Master Huáibīng stood in serene solitude gazing into the distance,
his spirit wandering the celestial thoroughfares,
his emotions and consciousness stretching far and wide,
as if nothing else existed around him.
He bowed his head and replied:
"Alas!
Are such words truly spoken?
For the perfect person acts through non-action,
dwelling in spirit within the vast emptiness,
not enslaving his will to salaries and profits,
thus harm and disgrace cannot befall him;
he does not tread perilous paths,
hence stumbling and falling cannot trouble him.
Though coarse vegetables may not suffice,
his mind finds contentment in simplicity;
though living among common folk in humble attire,
his heart rejoices as if possessing lands.
Residing in the abode of Yìliáo,
closing the gate of Qiánmù,
befriending companions like Zhuāng Lái,
dwelling in a narrow lane's humble home,
steadfast as a mountain unshakable,
how could he harbor thoughts of advancement or retreat?
For excessive desires disturb harmony,
thus he abandons worldly affairs without a second glance;
as those in high positions bear deep worries,
he turns away from power and profit without lingering doubt.
His nobility does not come from rank,
nor his wealth from possessions.
Soaring with the great péng bird,
he does not entangle his wings with rotten rats;
taking Fán Xǔ's hardship as solemn warning,
he finds joy unchanged in simple fare like dān piáo.
"Moreover, the universe is vast and remote,
yet human life is fleeting,
as brief as a white steed's shadow across a gap,
resting in the boundless interim,
swift as a shooting star's momentary glimpse,
fleeting like an arrow's lightning pass.
Let us then wander at ease and find self-contentment,
why should we torment our bodies with external matters!
The luán bird does not entangle in nets,
the lín beast does not fall into traps,
observe these birds and beasts,
they still know to avoid harm,
how much more should those in the dusty world,
ever be unwary?
As for Yāolí destroying his family to prove merit,
Jì Xìn burning to death to deceive Chǔ,
Chén Jiǎ cutting his throat to vindicate his brother,
Zhòng Yóu sacrificing his life to be minced,
Yíngmen falling on his sword to show loyalty,
Niè Zhèng moved by kindness to slaughter and mince,
Jīng Kē having his knees severed to repay Yān,
Fángōng bearing sorrow to offer his head,
all are the delusions of the foolish,
hardly what the wise would choose!
"For those with ample emoluments bear heavy responsibilities,
those with high ranks endure mental toil.
Thus the Qìyuán recluse fished with his line,
disregarding the honor of ministers and chancellors;
Bó Chéng wielded the plow,
scorning the status of feudal lords.
Yáng Yuè found peace in a butcher's stall,
Yáng Zhū grudged a single hair.
Those who seek by fluke,
blinded by desires,
like birds alighting without choosing trees,
serve without considering the times,
covet advancement without heeding the disaster of overreaching,
accept posts without calculating the ruin of incompetence;
discussing glory and honor, they cite Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng to save themselves from drowning,
speaking of calamitous regret, they avoid mentioning overturned tripods and forget;
they await the river dragon's sleep to pluck the bright pearl,
dwell in the favor of high position hoping to avoid trouble;
addicted to momentary safety,
blind to inevitable danger;
lacking the morning mushroom's brief glory,
yet expecting the great chūn tree's longevity;
it is like treading on thin ice awaiting summer's day,
climbing a rotten branch expecting strong winds;
like deep-water fish attracted by fragrant bait,
marsh pheasants swallowing poisoned grains;
chewing spoiled meat to satisfy hunger,
drinking poisoned wine to quench thirst.
"In the past, Jīzǐ wept upon seeing ivory chopsticks,
Confucius sighed forever hearing of burial figurines,
for they discerned the significant from the subtle,
perceived the end from the beginning.
Yet the ignorant tread on triggers unaware,
how profound is foresight's difficulty,
and how deep the obsession with profit and desire!
Zhōu Chéng, though virtuous, believed slanderous tales,
the Duke of Zhōu, though sage, fled to Southern Chǔ,
entrusting his grief to the owl's song,
barely spared by the golden casket.
Moreover, enlightened rulers
are not found in every age;
slander that finds favor
never lacks at any time.
Virtue does not arise from violent winds that flatten crops,
deeds are not praised for bearing jade tokens as great talent,
lamentation is futile,
and so it should be.
"With prolonged soaking,
even strong glue and lacquer dissolve;
under constant influence,
even bone and flesh part ways;
accumulated dust and feathers
can sink a boat or break an axle;
words repeated thrice
can create a market tiger.
Thus Jiāng Chōng, distant and lowly,
was no kin to the crown prince,
yet a stepmother by pretence,
was no closer than Bó Qí to his father;
but the false accusation of a wooden figure
destroyed the affection between father and son;
the deceit of a bee in the sleeve
