shattered the love of natural kinship.
How much more elsewhere
can one be certain of anything.
Alas!
This is why Wǔ Yún, loyal yet adrift, met a corpse's fate;
sorrowful!
This is why Bái Qǐ, upholding duty, cut his own throat.
It is enough to make the clear mirror shudder,
and the skilled craftsman dizzy with confusion.
"Further, some wish to push their limited talents to rectify conformity,
relying on singular correctness to critique widespread errors.
Yet they fail to see that though metal overcomes wood,
an awl cannot fell the Dèng Forest;
though water conquers fire,
a cupful cannot extinguish a burning mountain.
An inch of glue cannot clear the Yellow River's muddiness,
a foot of water cannot cool the Xiāoqiū's heat.
Therefore, those who preserve both body and reputation are rare,
while those who laugh first and wail later are many.
Fearing calamitous regret yet not extinguishing the desire for glory,
dreading slander and disgrace yet not abandoning contentious impulses,
is like hating dampness yet swimming in deep abyss,
despising shadows yet avoiding shade,
drilling a boat to stop a leak,
burning fiercely to halt boiling.
"This seven-foot body,
endowed by one's birth,
should not be received whole and returned damaged;
the heart within the square inch,
controlled by oneself,
should not be set adrift in dissipation.
Farming with one's hands to eat,
digging wells to drink,
coarse cloth to cover oneself,
thatched hut for shelter,
playing and chanting for joy,
breathing to prolong life,
roaming freely among bamboo and texts,
entrusting emotions to the profound brush,
maintaining constancy while awaiting life's end,
this is indeed sufficient.
Moreover, where the Dào resides, there is honor,
where Dé prevails, there is nobility.
Using a Suí pearl to shoot sparrows
is not the act of the wise.
Why must one await power to shine,
or depend on salary to be sated!"
"Moreover, those who find peace in poverty regard the lack of wealth as richness,
and those content with humility take not holding office as glory.
Thus, Yòu'ān drifted across the sea to purify his spirit,
while Húzǐ willingly retreated to farming.
Féng and Bǐ bore the guilt of virtuous conduct,
Xìn and Bù faced punishment despite great achievements.
A single branch suffices to furl a phoenix's feathers—
why trouble with lush forests?
A small pond is enough for dragon scales to float—
why seek the vast sea?
Wild greens are finer than the eight delicacies,
cold spring water sweeter than fine wine;
straw sandals are fairer than red ceremonial shoes,
coarse robes lovelier than embroidered gowns;
holding a staff brings more peace than wielding axes,
the rustling of branches pleases more than strings and flutes;
thatched roofs outshine vermilion pillars,
unhewn beams are dearer than carved rafters;
climbing high peaks serves as terraces and towers,
rugged cliffs with dripping springs make splendid abodes;
accumulating writings builds granaries of thought,
treasuring profound discourse as gold and jade;
discarding the petty attachments of commoners,
renouncing the desires of the servile;
roaming the nine marshlands with joy,
casting aside wisdom to transcend the mundane.
Like the inchworm curling,
concealing brilliance, preserving simplicity;
displaying clumsiness and reticence,
knowing when to stop, ever content.
Then, savoring the fragrance of orchids,
soaring like wind and floating clouds;
basking in the light of the nine suns,
riding wings to lofty wanderings;
perching high on the wútóng tree,
alighting below on Xuánzhōu.
How does this compare to biting the bit, stalled at the trough,
or being adorned like a sacrificial ox!"
The Career-Seeking Noble retorted:
"Those who enter but do not exit
are called obsessed with favor, forgetting retreat;
those who advance but do not return
are deemed unfit and without righteousness.
Hence, the enlightened see their bodies not as their own,
but accept what comes their way.
In hiding or prominence, silence or speech,
nothing is fixed.
When it's time to stop, they stop;
when it's time to act, they act.
When silks gather and
court torches are lit,
the way of the gentleman flourishes,
and heaven favors their appearance.
But if fate brings slander's triumph in hard times,
they stay within doors,
tied like a sack, unused.
Dragons rise or phoenixes rest,
as the season demands.
The ancients avoided danger without entering,
or fled at a glance, not lingering—
fearing the fire on Wūshān
might burn both orchid and weed alike.
Now, the sage emperor steers destiny,
the world peaceful, the Way prosperous;
benevolence reaches all living beings,
gracious winds blow far and wide;
awe subdues distant realms,
favor moistens the nine borders;
emulating earth's virtue to bear all,
mirroring the sky's vault in lofty canopy;
divine transformation brings clouds and rain,
mysterious grace flows abundant and deep;
the four gates humbly welcome broadly,
the ruler seeks talents to aid governance.
This is a rare chance in a thousand years,
a unique moment since creation split.
Yet you, sir, admire the lopsidedness of reclusion,
unaware of the harm in rejecting splendor;
focusing on Shàn Bào's inner cultivation,
blind to the external risks of confronting tigers.
It's like hearing someone drowned while wading,
then claiming all boaters fail;
or judging all heirs monstrous
based on Shāng Chén's vicious rebellion."
The Ice-Heartened Scholar replied:
"The sage's transformation is indeed grand,
as you eloquently argue.
Matters of engagement or withdrawal
are personal to each.
Thus, even with Yáo and Shùn ruling,
Jīyǐng had its nest-dwelling hermits;
under the Xià sovereign's reign,
remote marshes held plow-wielding worthies.
Was it due to fear of peril?
Rather, each followed what suited them.
Therefore, holding one's aspirations high,
not serving kings or lords,
preserves the symbols in the hexagrams,
a commoner's steadfast grip;
Yánzhōu maintained integrity,
and the sage approved of it."
"The reason I wander free in hills and gardens,
hiding traces in marshy wilds,
is truly that my talent lacks governance skill,
my ability falls short in ruling people.
With multitudes of scholars rising like clouds,
elite talents gathering like scales,
civil and military filling the court,
all affairs already well-managed,
I'd not wish to add my faint glow beside sun and moon,
tap pottery shards next to a great bell,
offer a light fan in deep winter's chill,
flaunt furs and stoves in summer's heat—
sure to be discarded as useless,
hastening untimely ridicule.
If I can clasp classics and compose works,
preserving truth and earning fame,
contributing to latter-day culture;
but if forced beyond my capacity,
I'd stumble into blame,
regretting like the little fox.
So, I dwell on my strengths
to safeguard my weaknesses.
Though I've no merit at court
or glory in battle;
yet guiding the younger generation,
broadening the Way, nurturing rectitude,
different paths lead to one goal—
I'm no burden to the people.
A humble man guarding his integrity,
how can I match Xǔ Yóu?
In this sage age, forgiven and tolerated,
roaming free as in Táng's time,
isn't that acceptable!"
The Career-Seeking Noble, stirred and self-doubting,
solemnly changed expression,
saying:
"Your words, sir, support teaching,
texts expose deceit and error;
promoting calm to curb restless strife,
reviving Confucian ways to save fading wisdom.
Without those who step out,
who would order human relations?
Without those who withdraw,
who would instruct the young?
Under heaven, across the land,
all are subjects and people.
Why must those with official caps be right,
and those content in poverty be wrong?
Those lost in Yúnmèng's clouds
need a guide to find the way;
those adrift on the vast sea
must look to the pole star to return.
Now, hearing your wise instruction,
I realize my blindness.
I'll shoulder my robes and cap,
spur my nag to chase your steed,
embrace your kindness to advance,
unashamed to learn from you."
Bào Pǔzǐ remarked:
I once roamed Yúntái Mountain,
and visited a recluse,
meeting an official there.
The official said:
"With brilliance above,
ruling all eight directions,
Huá and Yí alike submit,
distant lands serve the court;
yet you, sir, follow Bó Chéng's remote path,
mingling with birds and beasts.
But times change, customs differ,
worldly duties aren't fixed—
thus, eating from trees, dwelling in hills,
casting off external burdens—
what was ancient purity and loftiness
is today's evasion.
A gentleman foresees danger before it forms,
cuts off calamity ere it arrives.
Aren't you avoiding Zhāng Yì's inner fever
only to meet Shàn Bào's external harm?
Fearing fullness, you resist thought,
forgetting the near worry of chaotic crowds,
dodging the shallow risk of ox tracks,
only to fall into unfathomable depths,
shunning muddy puddles that wet the feet,
yet plunging into forge fires unawares?"
The recluse answered:
"Those fixated on young mice
can't grasp the zōuyú's intent;
those busy with courtyard grains
how can they know the yuānluán's distant aim?
Like jiāomíng insects laughing at the roc,
morning mushrooms marveling at the great chūn,
puddle frogs doubting the sea turtle,
well snakes scoffing at the yìnglóng.
You, swayed by encouragement and deterrence,
how can you perceive the sublime tune of profound expanse?
I'm blessed to live in an age like Yáo and Shùn's—
why worry about not fulfilling such a man's aspirations!"
The recluse replied:
"You may be said to cling to anthills,
amuse yourself with fox-haunted mounds,
never having ascended Lángfēng to touch the rainbow clouds;
play in muddy streams,
wade through stagnant ponds,
never having floated on the Southern Ocean or crossed the Milky Way.
Generally speaking, those with noble aspirations
need not care about official positions,
nor must they achieve military merits.
The highest state is to forget oneself,
the next is to be free from fame,
able to soar above the crowd with wings outstretched,
and gallop beyond conventional tracks,
accomplishing what ordinary people cannot,
sacrificing what those of limited talent cannot sacrifice,
unmeasured by worldly standards in scarcity or abundance,
serene and pure, unstained by fame and position,
their pristine virtue sufficient to cleanse the filth of a hundred generations,
their lofty conduct enough to stir the turbid waters of the future.
Why must one wear vermilion and purple robes,
don official caps and ride in carriages,
adorn oneself with sacrificial oxen's embroidered trappings,
swallow the fragrant bait like Zhān Hé,
morning becoming the blazing heat that scorches the sky,
by evening turning into the cold ashes of seasonal extinction!
"The quail doesn't exchange its brushwood for the heights of clouds,
the royal sturgeon doesn't trade its deep cavern for the vastness of the sea,
tigers and leopards feel sorrow when entering grand mansions,
swans and phoenixes contain grief when climbing high peaks.
All creatures have their own minds,
content with what suits them best.
None are not at ease when following their nature,
and distressed when displaced from their proper place.
Those who engage with worldly affairs
are everywhere in great numbers,
a single day without a ruler,
and they become restless and anxious.
They are like the accumulated jade of Lántián,
the abundant timber of Dènglín forest,
for skilled craftsmen and great artisans
to use as they please.
Why must one force fish to perch or sink birds underwater!
Splendid withdrawal and lofty wandering
were approved by ancient sages;
some may emerge, others remain hidden,
each following their own preferences.
"What scholars value
is establishing virtue and establishing words.
As for filial piety, friendship, benevolence and righteousness,
pure and lofty conduct in one's vocation,
this may be called establishing virtue.
Exhaustively studying the ancient classics,
producing brilliant writings,
this may be called establishing words.
Though Shàn Zhèng had no achievements in governing people,
he cannot be considered inferior to vulgar officials;
though Confucius had no military merits,
he cannot be deemed lesser than Hán Xìn or Bái Qǐ.
To preserve both body and reputation
is considered the highest achievement.
Living in seclusion to pursue one's aspirations
was praised by earlier people.
Though Yí Qí were but humble men,
unwilling to compromise,
the ancients sighed in admiration,
saying they would not lower themselves or suffer disgrace.
Speaking of not lowering themselves
clarifies the nobility of reclusion;
speaking of not suffering disgrace
recognizes the defilement of being constrained.
The purity of sages
was praised by Mèng Kē,
who also said heavenly nobility is more valuable than official seals.
Cultivating aspirations while abandoning glory
was esteemed by Xún Qīng,
for when one is complete in Dao and righteousness,
one may look down upon kings and dukes.
Yet what worldly people fear is only power,
what they value is only profit.
Those of great virtue who remain obscure
are called mediocre men;
those of small capacity in great positions
are called eminent scholars.
Some risk dangers and perils,
casting away life and forgetting survival,
abandoning their bodies beneath thousand-ren cliffs,
seeking fleeting glory and splendor,
compared to those who lightly regard the world but cherish a single hair,
how distant they are indeed!"
The official said:
"Those who withdraw into obscurity,
content with mountains and marshes,
bearing no worldly honors,
unrestrained and self-indulgent,
of no use to their time,
sniffing at salaries and benefits,
truly are things of no benefit to the world,
what about this?"
The recluse replied:
"The qilin doesn't bark at guards,
the phoenix doesn't herald the dawn,
the téng huáng doesn't pull plows,
the prayer official doesn't manage the kitchen.
Moreover, casting great light without exclusion,
spreading warm, nurturing breezes
is the sun's role;
shining brilliantly in dark nights,
smelting metal and stone for practical use
is fire's function.
The world cannot go long without the sun,
cannot endure a single day without fire,
yet their magnitudes
cannot be equated.
Beyond the rivers and seas,
encompassing the two realms of heaven and earth,
rising to become clouds and rain,
descending to form hundreds of streams;
yet for daily use,
they cannot match a well several ren deep,
for irrigating fields and gardens,
they are not as effective as ditches and channels.
Comparing their sizes,
which is more vast?
Jié and Zhòu
were emperors;
Confucius
was a minor official.
Now if someone is compared to Jié and Zhòu,
none fail to become angry;
if compared to Confucius,
none fail to be pleased.
Thus nobility and baseness indeed do not lie in position.
Therefore Mèngzǐ said,
Yǔ, Jì, and Yán Yuān,
if they exchanged places, would all act the same.
Zǎi Yǔ also said
Confucius was far more worthy than Yáo and Shùn.
When commoners are equally praised with kings,
when Confucian scholars esteem the heights of Táng and Yú times,
it is due to virtue alone,
why must it be official position!
"Moreover, those who commune with the numinous and ascend through creation,
holding heaven and earth in their embrace,
vast and unimpeded, worldly affairs don't lodge in their minds,
boundless and undisturbed, honor and disgrace don't muddy their purity,
what the vulgar desire
cannot stain their spirit,
what confuses ordinary people
cannot shift their resolve.
Glory and splendor
are like wens and tumors;
the myriad things
are like cicada wings.
If this is so,
how could they willingly contort their limbs,
bend their posture up and down,
force themselves to accept what they dislike,
seek what they have discarded,
put on happy faces to gain advancement,
bend their bodies to avoid demotion,
fear that common people might disapprove,
worry about their own decline,
bend a dragon's abyss to serve as an awl,
suppress a divine drum to sound like a common battle drum,
push a yellow battle-axe to fit a sickle's grasp,
or fold a magnificent banner to enter a wolfberry thicket?
Gǔgōng leaned on his staff and abandoned his throne,
Yuè Yǐ entered a cave to escape his,
Jì Zhá withdrew to farming to relinquish his,
Lǎo Lái tended gardens to distance himself from it,
following their preferences,
none could change them.
Thus, pure and unadulterated,
this is true wealth;
the body not subjected to servitude,
this is true nobility.
As for those who receive official tallies and territories,
these are what's called salaries and benefits,
not true wealth and nobility.
Moreover, those with high offices bear heavy responsibilities,
those with great achievements incur others' envy,
only in poverty and lowliness
does no one contend with me,
allowing me to long treasure
this carefree state."
To seek knowledge without studying,
is like wishing for fish yet having no net—
though the heart is diligent, nothing is gained;
to broaden and deepen in the pursuit of truth,
is like relying on the wind when needing to travel—
the body is not wearied, yet one reaches far.
With cosmetics applied, Xīshī becomes even more beautiful,
while the unsightly blemish is concealed;
with profound mastery of classics, the talented gain deep insight,
and the dull-witted awaken to understanding.
Fine timber may reach the clouds,
yet cannot be called a tower or pavilion
without the craftsmanship of Bān and Yǔ;
one may be naturally bright and clear,
yet cannot be deemed a noble person
without understanding the principles of human relations.
To cover a thousand miles in a single morning,
one must rely on steeds swift as shadows;
to cross vast waves and journey afar,
one must depend on boats and oars;
to see the world beyond without leaving the hall,
one must proceed through books;
to fathom profound mysteries without straining the spirit,
one must obtain enlightened teachers.
Thus, vermilion and green dye alter plain silk,
and instruction transforms the ignorant.
When dark clouds part and the great light shines,
the forms of all things are no longer hidden;
when scrolls are unrolled to examine past and present,
the nature of heaven and earth is fully revealed.
How much more so for spirits and gods?
And how much more for human affairs?
Clay can be fired to rival the hardness of gold and jade,
warped wood can be worked to conform to the ink-line;
wild beasts can be trained for battle formations,
livestock can be taught to advance and retreat;
submerged fish can be stirred by sound,
and mechanical devices can be moved by sincere intent—
how much more possible for beings endowed with the five virtues and supreme intelligence!
The horse that responds to the rein
is the result of training;
the bird of prey that strikes fiercely
is tamed through practice.
They and ordinary horses or wild eagles
are originally of the same kind,
yet these are valued for their refinement,
while those are despised for their rawness.
If flowing water never ceases,
it will surely merge with the vast sea;
if one piles baskets of earth without rest,
it will equal the height of the highest peak.
In great surging rivers,
dragons and serpents swim in schools;
with daily effort and monthly progress,
virtue is established and the Way perfected.
Only then can one be rectified.
To dream of Qiū and Dàn,
how can it merely free one from the bonds of ignorance!
Once Zhòng Yóu wore a cock-feather cap and boar-tusk girdle,
with cicada-shaped ear ornaments,
brandished a sword and danced,
boasting of the sturdy bamboo of the southern hills,
wishing to follow his stubborn nature;
yet Confucius, skilled in guidance,
imbued him with moral teaching,
turning him into a disciple who entered the hall,
and ascended among the four categories of wise men.
Zǐzhāng was a rustic man,
and originally fierce and cunning,
but steeped in the teachings of the Way,
he became a transformed renowned scholar,
able to stand as an equal to kings and dukes—
how could this be merely escaping vulgarity!
Thus, the wise grieve at life's fleeting swiftness,
and lament vanishing without renown;
they are moved by the profound teaching of hearing the Way at dawn,
and awaken to the universality of penetrating subtlety;
they heed the clear warning of impending decline,
and realize that lack of reflection leads to recklessness;
they do not idle away days in satiety,
nor waste a single moment of time;
they draw inspiration from the flowing river to strengthen resolve,
and mourn the lightning speed of the fleeting gap;
they cut off trivial distractions,
and reduce worldly non-essentials;
they cleanse the heart of anxiety over poverty,
and discard the filth of excessive desires;
they cease the amusements of hunting and gambling,
and correct the laziness of napping and dozing;
knowing that idle thought is useless,
they stride forth on the path of sages.
Learn to accumulate knowledge,
question to discern clearly,
advance virtue and cultivate practice,
review the old to understand the new.
Now, the Duke of Zhōu, a supreme sage,
read a hundred chapters daily.
Confucius, endowed by heaven,
wore out the leather thongs of his books three times.
Mò Dí, a great worthy,
filled carts with writings.
Zhòngshū, a man for the age,
never glanced at his garden gate.
Ní Kuān carried classics while weeding with a hoe,
Lù Shēng cut reeds to copy books,
Huáng Bà studied while imprisoned in shackles,
Nìng Yuè labored day and night to double his efforts—
thus they could explore the depths of the Way,
and probe its subtle words,
viewing ten thousand ages as if one day,
knowing the eight wildernesses as their own courtyard;
examining the waxing and waning of the seven luminaries,
tracing the transformations of the three and five;
discerning the rise and fall yet to come,
verifying good and ill in the past;
grasping the mysteries of heaven and earth in their palms,
recognizing the unformed as if already complete.
Therefore, they achieved great virtue and grand deeds,
topping their generation,
with pure radiance and fine reputation,
spreading boundlessly.
Moreover, hearing of the Shāngyáng bird, one warns of great floods;
inquiring about the bird-tipped arrow, one governs the eastern regions;
consulting about the duckweed fruit, one speaks of its color and taste;
asking of the earth-dog, one recognizes the grave-sheep;
perusing the "Língbǎo" scripture, one learns of hidden mountains;
through the divided sacrificial meat, one discusses the full cart;
observing the scattered Bi constellation, one distinguishes the signs of yin and yang;
from the winter locust, one detects errors in the intercalary month—
what divinity is there in this?
It is all learning.
Even children's rhymes aid the ears and eyes of sages,
how much more the vast breadth of the Fén and Suǒ classics!
Talents and natures have their superior and inferior,
and the capacity for thought varies in depth.
Some know early and mature soon,
while others need repeated guidance before understanding.
Those who grasp quickly and practice timely
are like the feet of thoroughbreds;
those who comprehend slowly and awaken late
are like the wings of quails and sparrows.
Though the former may fly to extreme heights,
if they stop and do not advance,
they will not surpass a few steps;
though the latter may progress inch by inch,
if they press on without ceasing,
they can cross mountains and marshes.
Is not the difference between brilliance and obscurity in learning just like this?
For in youth, the will is focused and hard to forget,
while in age, the spirit scatters and is easily lost.
Thus, pursuing learning must be done early;
once it becomes refined and concentrated,
practice and nature unite,
no different from the natural self.
If one possesses exceptional talent
but misses the prime years due to circumstances,
though lost in the morning sun,
it may be regained in the evening dusk.
Then we know that late sowing in fertile soil
is better than leaving the field barren all year.
The metaphor of the sun and candle—
these words are indeed apt.
The ways of the world are fraught with difficulties,
and Confucian teachings have fallen into decline;
the paths of Wén and Wǔ
are on the verge of withering away.
Some drown in sounds and sights,
others rush down roads of rivalry and pursuit.
Those who, though poor and isolated, master the six arts—
with the caliber of Zǐyóu and Zǐxià—
are suppressed deep as the nine springs;
while those who ride the wind and cling to phoenix wings—
with the quality of nags and mediocrities—
still hover proudly above the rosy clouds.
Those who abandon the root for the branches
are called diligent cultivators of near-success;
those who embrace the classics and seek within
are labeled as impractical and pedantic.
Thus, all don dusty rain-gear,
bear frost and tread ice,
clutching gold and grasping silver,
lifting clear wine and leading fat livestock,
to take the shortcut of crooked paths,
planning to plant in the morning and reap by evening.
As for those who lower their curtains and rest on high pillows,
letting their spirits wander through the Nine Canons,
refining the profound meanings and exploring the hidden truths,
savoring the Way while dwelling in tranquility,
firmly establishing unshakable integrity,
displaying their purity after the winter's harshness,
not measuring the world to follow its tracks,
nor drifting like duckweed with the crowd—
such individuals are indeed rare.
Those who are anxious and eager for advancement,
frustrated and stifled by stagnation,
how could they abandon the broad path of easy and swift success
to guard the blocked road that is difficult and sure to lead to a dead end?
This is why the riverbank is left unmanned,
and why the "Zǐ Jīn" ode was composed.
It is what causes those who grieve for the customs to ache with heartfelt sighs,
and those who worry about the Way to bear sorrow and sink into deep thought.
The alternation of cold and heat,
the end of adversity leading to prosperity,
the cyclical rise of civil and military virtues—
these are the constant patterns of nature.
We hope that all bandits will be cleansed away,
and a revival is at hand;
the seven luminaries follow their courses,
the old state is renewed,
wielding the celestial broom to sweep widely,
stoking the great furnace of the nine yang,
operating the great pivot at the imperial center,
opening the profound model to guide all things.
To mold and shape the multitude of beings,
crafting the outstanding talents,
washing away the accumulated dust,
eradicating evil and restoring righteousness.
Sheathing the spears and shields,
storing away the bows and arrows,
reviving the schools of the Pìyōng,
gathering the state's scholars,
cultivating literary virtue,
emitting golden sounds,
resonating with jade-like tones.
Bringing down wind and clouds from their hidden beginnings,
presenting bundles of silk at the hills and gardens,
enabling the phoenix that has folded its wings
to soar in the clear void;
the steed with a sturdy neck
to gallop a thousand miles.
Let those who harbor brilliance yet are suppressed,
who have exhaustively studied and broadly learned—
the likes of Shēn Gōng and Fú Shēng—
receive the dark and crimson silks,
ascend the cattail-lined carriages,
vent their pent-up feelings,
express their steadfast principles,
reveal their persons,
practice their Way,
so that the sage age may follow the lofty tracks of Táng and Yú,
gallop on the broad path of peace,
with the mysterious flow moistening the nine realms,
and benevolent winds reaching everywhere without exception.
The five punishments are set aside, and songs of praise arise;
harmonious energy pervades, and auspicious grain grows—
is this not splendid!
In the past, the Second Emperor of Qín
did not value Confucian teachings,
abandoned the Way of the former sages,
and practiced laws of punishment and imprisonment.
The people saw no virtue,
hearing only of slaughter.
Thus, they were confused and knew not the path of return from delusion,
ruined yet unaware of how to save themselves,
ultimately falling from the heights of the clouds,
and crushed to powder in the unfathomable depths.
From the highest to the lowest,
how can we not take warning!
Bàopúzǐ says:
Those who focus their vision on the autumn hair
fail to see the brilliance of celestial patterns.
Those who indulge their minds in trivial matters
remain unaware of the vastness of the Confucian Way.
Those who relish in rotten fish forget the fragrance of angelica;
those lost in great errors cannot find their way back.
Wood that is marked by the ink line does not yield crooked cuts;
those imbued with the teachings of the Way do not become wicked.
The art of self-cultivation
has no better method than learning.
The breadth of learning lies in tirelessness,
and tirelessness lies in firm resolve.
If resolve is not firm,
then the poor and lowly will anxiously strive for livelihood,
while the rich and noble will sink into indulgence and pleasure.
Thus, those with profound and broad learning
are rare across the ages;
while those who face the wall in ignorance
stand shoulder to shoulder and follow in each other's footsteps.
If humble scholars till the fields by day to feed themselves,
and by night, by the light of firewood, pursue their studies,
and if those in office use their leisure from feasts
to occasionally observe and encourage virtue,
then the world would have no "flesh-gazers,"
and there would be no lack of disciples like Zǐyóu and Zǐxià.
There are also those afflicted by hunger and cold,
unable to obtain even coarse vegetables,
their skin suffering from wind and frost,
their mouths lacking even chaff and bran,
with no means to seek a teacher outside,
and urgent needs at home morning and night,
where setting aside the plow halts farming,
and holding a book neglects support for their family—
though they may lack in studies,
they are to be pitied.
This is what is called the steed capable of a thousand miles
trapped beneath a salt cart;
the ore fit for a red blade
never passing through Ōuyě's forge.
As for the sons of nobility and princes,
leisurely and indulging in luxury and pleasure,
dallying amidst silks and satins,
ignorant of the hardships of farming,
their eyes weary of dark and yellow hues,
their ears fatigued by music of Zhèng and Wèi,
their noses sated with orchids and musk,
their tastes dulled by rich foods,
in winter, clad in the luxurious warmth of sable and fox,
in summer, draped in the flutter of sheer gauze,
riding out in Qìng Fēng's light carriages,
feasting indoors in splendid, radiant chambers,
adorning pillars and beams with vermilion and emerald,
accumulating endless treasures in chests and boxes,
displaying enchanting beauties to amuse their hearts,
drowning in strong wine until deeply intoxicated,
leading in drinking gatherings when active,
commanding in games of chance when seated.
They neither understand literary compositions,
nor regard scholars as more than weeds,
their speech and writing lack classical foundation,
and they err in drawing analogies.
In deep discussions, they are defeated as soon as the debate begins;
faced with doubts, they wither before their time.
Even if they could argue like Shū Mài,
how would they differ from the blind and deaf!
Bàopúzǐ says:
I have heard that the heir of the emperor
must enter the Great Academy,
to receive teachings and inquire about the Way.
Those who are ranked among the state's scholars
learn the duties of a minister,
so that they may later become rulers;
learn the duties of a son,
so that they may later become fathers.
Thus, one studies before taking office,
not learning governance through administration,
for wielding a knife and injuring by cutting—
this is what Zhèng Qiáo lamented.
To follow passions and indulge desires
is to be called inhuman.
Yet the noble and leisurely youths,
born within deep palaces,
raised in the hands of women,
have never known the toil of worries and fears,
never taken them to heart.
Some, still in swaddling clothes,
are bestowed with high-ranking offices;
barely old enough to wear the cap and gown,
they occupy clear and prominent positions.
Wielding the power of life and death,
holding the authority over promotions and demotions,
determining honor and disgrace through grants and takings,
sensing advantages and harms on their lips,
their likes and dislikes never ceasing,
praise and blame roaring in their ears.
Suspicions and resemblances,
seemingly right yet wrong,
arise from opportunities without cause,
using trusted positions to craft clever words,
the changes of interactions and plots,
with countless twists and turns,
beyond the detailed calculations of clever strategies,
unfathomable by the finest ink.
Without the learning of methods and arts,
how can they discern the true from the false in right and wrong?
How can they grasp the events of past and present?
The principle of self-awareness,
free from deception and falsehood—
without it, how can they avoid the disaster of a toppled nest and overturned cart!
The ancient sages, while in high positions,
never forgot the perils,
loving their sons and wishing to teach them the right principles.
Through carving and polishing, grinding and discussing,
they kept them from falling into depravity and falsehood.
They selected wise teachers to shape them,
chose good friends to gradually influence them,
urged them to read extensively,
showed them examples of success and failure,
enabling them to understand the future by examining the past,
and comprehend the present by observing others.
They guided them onto the straight path,
restrained them within the bounds of discipline,
with caution as if treading on the edge of a ten-thousand-ren abyss,
and trepidation like riding a galloping horse over thin ice.
Thus, they could avoid many regrets and errors,
preserving their purity and good fortune.
In the past, the Dòu family benefited from the legacy of teachings,
while Huò Yǔ suffered disaster due to willful behavior.
Zhōngshān and Dōngpíng found peace through their love for antiquity,
but Yānlà faced danger due to ignorance.
Not forgetting past events
serves as a valuable mirror for the present.
Tāng and Wǔ were influenced by Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
and their rise was vigorous;
while Xīn and Guǐ were tainted by flatterers,
and their downfall was sudden.
Friends and teachers
should be selected with particular care.
One must choose scholars of humble background and virtuous conduct,
who stand firm through hardship,
and are respected for their integrity.
Those well-versed in classics like Dǒng Zhòngshū and Huán Róng,
or steadfast and upright like Gōng Suì and Wáng Jí,
can expound daily on the ultimate principles of loyalty and filial piety,
solemnly demonstrating the paths to survival and ruin,
thus cleansing impurities,
warding off evil and correcting deviations.
They ensure restraint of desires and adherence to laws,
guiding one into virtuous training.
By the end of the Hàn dynasty
and the late years of Wú,
this was no longer the case.
Officials were chosen based on their robes and carriages,
appointed through the empty praise of cliques,
bearing the titles of teachers and friends,
but lacking any substantive guidance.
Not only were they useless,
they actually caused harm.
Thus, what they lectured on
was not about morality;
what they recommended
was not for loyalty or benefit.
Instead, they focused on new tunes and beautiful women,
light bodies and skilled hands,
judging the clarity and muddiness of songs,
discussing the length and shortness of pipes and strings,
comparing the speed and slowness of dogs and horses,
debating the best places for outings,
evaluating the quality of various paths,
assessing the fineness of carvings,
competing in the skill of board games like tánqí and chūpú,
calculating wins and losses in fishing and hunting contests,
critiquing the beauty of singing girls and concubines,
pointing out the vulgarity of clothing,
arguing over the quality of horses and carriages,
and discussing the craftsmanship of bows and swords.
They sought out the strange and unusual,
without limit,
their excesses
growing daily and monthly.
When discussing palaces,
they envisioned distant jade towers and gem chambers,
emulated nearby Ēpáng and línguāng palaces,
considered thousand-door万户 residences cramped,
deemed Kūnmíng and Tàiyè pools shallow and crude,
laughed at thatched roofs as unworthy,
and saw earthen steps as rustic.
The people's strength was exhausted in labor,
savings wasted on non-essentials,
building earth mounds to rival Sōng and Huò mountains,
digging canals to imitate the Nine Rivers;
ascending magnificent towers reaching the clouds,
opening ornate windows at the sky's edge.
Lewd music blared to confuse the ears,
silk sleeves waved to dazzle the eyes,
with melodies from Púshàng and Běilǐ
rising one after another;
shouting and yelling,
they turned day into night.
Lingering among wine cups,
immersed beside strings and rhythms.
Some erected lush green canopies,
others hunted fierce birds in the suburbs,
galloping swift feet on steep heights,
exposing subordinates to the blazing sun,
setting out with torches,
returning under the stars,
neglecting official duties,
abandoning rewards and punishments.
Some floated ornate boats on vast waters,
spread dense nets across green rivers,
dangled fragrant bait in rippling pools,
released boating songs over clear depths,
shot high arrows to bring down light swans,
cast deep lines to hook hidden fish;
others set traps in forested foothills,
formed great circles around mountains and marshes,
arrayed red banners over lush grass,
galloped swift horses across plains,
unleashed hounds to bite cunning beasts,
sent falcons to strike flying birds,
powerful crossbows killing wild rhinos,
long spears slaying bears and tigers.
Thus,
they remained unweary for years,
continuing without end.
Moreover, they added seasonal banquets,
farewells and celebrations,
inviting close friends for frequent gatherings,
welcoming honored guests bearing gifts.
Worldly affairs
were endlessly bustling.
Hence, elegance and correctness drifted away,
while frivolity and indulgence deepened.
They distanced themselves from Confucian learning,
far and remote.
Few could perceive the principles of rise and fall,
extricate themselves from drowning,
abandon the perilous path of ruined virtue,
and tread the great way of lasting peace.
Indeed, such individuals were very rare.
Alas!
This is why those who preserve the state and secure their families are extremely few,
while those who collapse and weep in despair are countless.
Now, with a sage and enlightened ruler above,
studying antiquity to aid the world,
strengthening dikes to prevent breaches,
clarifying praise and blame to encourage and deter;
it is hoped that the imperial clan and nobility,
along with the wealthy and young,
will surely compete in promoting Confucian arts,
moderate their literary pursuits,
set aside the non-urgent ideas of Lǎo-Zhuāng,
(the character "idea" is redundant)
and focus on the true path of the Six Classics.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
When the clear and mysterious parted and rose upward,
the turbid and yellow separated and sank down.
The distinctions between noble and humble, authority and subject,
thus became evident.
The ancient sages drew from the two cosmic forces,
and established the way of ruler and minister;
setting up officials and dividing duties,
the harmonious and prosperous transformation flourished.
Those who rule others
must first cultivate themselves to lead the world,
eliminate partiality to balance the kingly way,
discard personal feelings to manifest supreme impartiality,
and embrace the universe to encompass all diversity.
Once truth and falsehood are discerned beyond objects,
add self-reflection;
once listening and receiving are keen in interactions,
add self-awareness.
Like diverting water to promote goodness,
or cutting strings to discard evil,
display virtue and block wrongdoing,
employ the intimate and value the worthy,
so that the compass exhausts its roundness,
the square fulfills its angles,
the straightedge extends its line,
and the axe delivers its cut.
No tool is tasked beyond its measure,
no talent is employed beyond its capacity.
Examining names and demanding substance,
repeatedly reflecting and diligently showing compassion,
establishing instructive norms to demonstrate the ultimate standards for the people,
carefully appraising praise and blame to highlight encouragement and deterrence,
clarifying checks and balances to prevent overstepping and excess,
scrutinizing right and wrong to avoid obscurity and regret.
In granting rewards,
there is no luck that defies reason;
in imposing penalties,
there is the concealment of many clans.
Shaping them with the six arts,
guiding them with loyalty and trustworthiness,
governing them with kindness and harmony,
unifying them with rites and punishments.
Promoting the humble to alleviate suppression,
stirring the clear stream to clarify good and evil.
Ensuring that things follow no deceitful path,
and affairs exceed no improper bounds.
Those who serve in court and govern the people
must not encroach on others' duties or overstep their authority;
those who lead armies into battle
dare not fear danger or cling to life.
Pleasing the near to win over the distant,
cultivating culture to attract allies.
Enriching the wealth and grain of the hundred surnames,
broadening the path for moral advancement,
eliminating the multitude of cunning and deceitful tasks,
then enforcing punishments and upholding laws,
judging cases with compassion and respect;
when benevolent transformation prevails,
flaws and faults are concealed,
and the five teachings are administered with leniency.
Externally, gathering many scholars in civil and military affairs,
internally, establishing harmonious kinship to solidify the realm,
ensuring that close and distant relatives support each other,
like the tail protecting the body.
Though branches flourish, there is no worry of harming the root;
though streams surge, there is no tendency to turn against the source.
Firm as rocks and mountains standing tall,
blocking any covetous ambitions.
Seeing the downfall of the Sānmiáo,
one knows that rivers and sources cannot be relied upon;
witnessing the loss of Yìyōu,
one realizes that steep barriers are insufficient to depend on.
Though the Jiāng and Hàn rivers still flow,
the powerful Chǔ suffered capture and humiliation;
though the Jiàngé pass remains intact,
Zǐyáng's clan was exterminated.
The four peaks and three paths,
indeed do not belong to one family;
golden walls and boiling moats,
are not as good as human harmony.
Defense lies beyond the seas,
not in mountains and rivers.
Thus, wise rulers embrace fear of inadequacy,
and are more than eager to correct their errors.
Even with successful plans and achieved goals,
they still ponder dangers and do not rest;
even after winning battles and expanding territories,
they guard against arrogance and remain vigilant day and night.
Emulating the vast heavens to cover all afar,
following the thick earth to bear all widely.
Employing double brilliance to reveal subtleties,
contemplating the distant and considering the unmanifested.
Drawing on spring's warmth to nurture growth,
modeling autumn's frost to discipline beings.
Consulting widely to compare similarities and differences,
balancing impartially to weigh all opinions.
Humbling oneself to fully understand the sentiments below,
crediting achievements to encourage future efforts.
Governing with strategy,
then from start to finish, efforts can be exhausted;
regulating with measures,
then disparities can be aligned.
Lofty as the Lángfēng peak piercing the clouds,
so those below cannot lightly assess its weight;
profound as an abyss of ten thousand ren,
so close attendants cannot measure its depth.
Thus, the ruler's flow and source are inexhaustible,
and the talents of all officials are fully displayed;
my boundaries have no limits,
while their measure can be confined.
Issuing commands and decrees,
they roar like startling thunder,
unswayed by deceitful arguments to alter their correctness.
Designing laws and creating systems,
they shine like the seven luminaries adorning the sky,
unbent by personal likes or dislikes to distort their truth.
With grand strategies covering afar,
they amass like dense clouds gathering high.
Abiding in steadfastness to accomplish tasks,
they stand firm as Mount Sōng and Dài rooted in the earth.
Foreseeing hidden changes before they sprout,
discerning slander and praise from glib tongues.
Not allowing sincerity to dissipate in carved deceit,
not letting unity be diluted by duality.
Though capable of decisive judgment,
one must broadly accept even grass and firewood gatherers' advice;
though striving for inclusiveness,
one must clear the ears of insidious flattery.
When people suffer hunger and cold,
grieve for them and blame oneself;
if the hundred surnames commit crimes,
consider it one's own fault.
When auspicious signs arrive,
reflect on receiving divine protection;
if encountering heaven's wrath,
think of the Sānglín confession of fault.
Not hesitating to change strings when the tune should be altered,
not ashamed to turn back from the path of morning errors.
With a tiger's gaze to alert secrecy,
like a qilin standing to connect with the distant.
If no old man is seen beating the soil in joy,
feel ashamed to hear harmonious music played;
if people suffer grain shortages,
feel ashamed to face a feast spread.
Residing in soaring towers scraping the sky,
then fear the laborers' toil and exhaustion;
savoring delicate delicacies under the moon,
then worry about missing the timely farming season;
listening to feasts of pipes and strings,
then grieve over excess in leisure and pleasure;
viewing dazzling displays of ornate beauty,
then fret over the severity of taxes and levies.
Following Fàngxūn's coarse furs,
matching Wèiwén's plain silks;
emulating the low palaces of the Xià dynasty,
recognizing the unbuilt dew terrace;
learning from the Zhānghuá palace's summoned disasters,
realizing the Ēpáng palace's swift ruin.
Reading covenants and oaths, then reflect on broken promises of the past.
Indulging in pleasures, then sense the bewitchment of Bāo and Dá.
Launching campaigns, then assess strength and timing,
not allowing a hundred li to bear the grief of weeping;
executing punishments, then set aside emotions and follow reason,
not letting wronged souls like Chīyí cling to injustice.
Heeding the lesson of Cāotóng's Dùbó,
and the man-standing hog's cry.
Deposing the嫡 heir warns of Jìn Xiàn's great folly.
Establishing a庶 son recalls Liú Biǎo's ended lineage.
In hunting, rejoice not in catching beasts but in gaining scholars,
recognize the joy of casting nets wide to attract the distant,
favoritism fears the cunning slander of sleeve wasps,
and Fēiyàn's monopolized favor.
Sole reliance realizes the tyranny of deer called horses,
and Gōng Xiǎn's hatred of integrity.
Accepting advice recalls Hàn Zǔ's spitting out food,
and Xiào Jǐng's execution of Cuò.
Offering sweet delicacies,
then shun Yí Dí.
Indulgent flattery and appeasement,
then reject Luán Jī.
Eliminate the flattery of steamed child,
embrace the kindness of releasing a fawn.
Learn from the white dragon to cease recklessness,
observe the thin fish to curb insatiability.
Guard against the human swine mutation within the six palaces,
halt the quest for sweat-blood horses beyond remote lands.
Remove vicious dogs to prevent drunken excess,
buy horse bones to attract wind-chasing steeds.
Salute the angry frog to encourage bravery,
avoid the mantis to inspire martial spirit.
Heed Gōnglú's honest words,
tolerate Bǎojiǎ's upright integrity.
Pluck useless hairs from the back and belly,
grasp the utility of six wings soaring skyward.
Boil the reed-like tongue to quiet the Sīyuán's admonitions,
break the twisted raft to guide Liáng Bó's virtue.
Banish Dān Jī to end infatuation's迷,
dismiss Zǐxiá to block the peach's惑.
Hide fish in the deep abyss,
wield the handle of sharp tools.
Do not fear the hassle of moving firewood,
to save the cost of being scorched.
Drum the cultivation of integrity and shame,
clarify the standards of examination and testing.
In anger, do not transgress the law to inflict cruelty;
in joy, do not exceed the constitution to bestow excessive rewards.
Sever affection for those beloved,
and pardon not the offenders;
discern goodness in those despised,
and neglect not the meritorious.
Lower yourself to accept loyalty,
and heed unpleasant advice without avoidance.
Broadly seek counsel even from slander,
and though suppressed, do not reject it.
Overlook minor flaws to employ great talents,
forget recent faults to remember distant achievements,
enabling figures like Cáo Guì and Mèng Míng to demonstrate their renewed efficacy,
while Wèi Shǎng and Zhāng Chǎng establish feats of washing away shame.
The treacherous minister who once harmed the state,
now displays grand merit in restoration;
the freed captive like Zuǒ Jū,
utters lofty strategies to cease warfare.
Then owls transform into phoenixes,
and wicked falsehood turns to loyal integrity.
Sharp blades flourish in barren salt flats,
and luminous pearls arise from muddy marshes.
With keen talents gathered,
all achievements harmonize,
humbly deferring westward,
to invite the talents of mentors and friends;
honoring the elderly,
to emphasize filial and fraternal conduct.
Thus, those hidden in depths look up and come forth,
and dwellers in mountains descend and assemble.
Brilliance flourishes within to assist,
while fierce generals guard the frontiers without.
Governance excels above,
and all things incline below;
kindness emanates nearby,
and blessings extend afar.
The wise exert strength in their duties,
and the common people yield borders in marshlands.
Then, abolish intricate laws,
and stir the clear breeze of great harmony.
With ceremonial chariots and jade silks,
draw out the eminent from rural retreats;
all talents gathered,
to deliberate on the gains and losses of the Way.
Reduce the multitude of shepherds,
return to the purest of unfermented wines,
promote the gates of benevolence and deference,
block the ford of flashy rivalry,
commend the conduct of righteous integrity,
and expand the standard of virtuous simplicity.
Make adherents of virtue feel like budding plants rejoicing in sweet rain,
and those returning resemble flowing streams joining the great river.
The common people find peace,
as green leaves adorn long branches;
even barbarians look up in awe,
like stars tethered to the North Pole.
Thus, the seven governance spheres do not disrupt the cosmic order,
and cold and warmth follow their seasons without error.
The four auspicious beasts appear,
while magical fungi glow resplendently.
Sweet dew drizzles down by night,
and abundant grain sways gracefully, filling bins.
The red drought demon is chased by divine pools,
and dark plagues are restrained in the vast north.
All rivers show no signs of turmoil,
the Southern Winnowing Star quiets storms that flatten crops,
things do not wither out of season,
and no sighs of grievance are heard among people.
Prisons stand empty,
and the five punishments are suspended.
Where the royal calendar does not reach,
and court officials do not set foot,
those in fur coats and hides,
dwelling in mountains or hiding by seas,
all joyfully reform their ways,
moved to communicate through interpreters,
divine birds tribute in vermilion courts,
jade rings are offered from the western extremes.
The round-headed people swiftly turn good,
as vapors follow a strong wind;
remote lands heed commands,
like echoes responding to a clear sound.
Truly, this is the pinnacle of rise and prosperity,
the path of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Thus, the ancestral temple can be secured for eternity,
and the royal lineage flourish for a hundred generations.
For deep roots ensure lush foliage,
and contented subjects bring peace to the ruler.
If horses are untamed,
even Zào Fǔ cannot achieve a thousand-mile journey;
if the people are unallegiant,
even Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn cannot attain the beauty of universal harmony.
Horses pushed to extremes produce erratic behaviors,
leading only to worry and collapse;
when the people are impoverished, many revolt,
and disaster inevitably erupts.
How can one not be vigilant, awaiting the dawn!
How can one not tremble, considering the dangers!
If a ruler does not ponder order and chaos with clarity,
nor deeply reflect on signs of downfall,
even with vision sharp enough to see autumn hairs at a hundred yards,
ears keen to distinguish the nuances of all music,
literary skill that drops gems from the brush tip,
martial prowess that crushes enemies in the palm,
a mind storing recitations of ten thousand texts,
a mouth broadcasting eloquence like surging waves,
it still avails nothing against collapse,
nor rescues from disintegration.
Why?
Because they do not focus on the great essentials,
but attend to trivialities,
stagnating in minor tasks,
and overlooking the fundamental principles.
If truly able to handle affairs with caution,
as if facing deep abysses or treading on thin ice,
in safety, not forgetting the warning of riding a runaway horse,
in existence, not neglecting the fear of potential ruin,
grasping the key points to manage details,
holding the Way's principles to guide all talents,
with Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ exerting full strength to avert conflict,
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shěn devoting ability to govern the state,
uniting the ruler's heart to achieve resolute determination,
and strategists collaborating to offer long-term plans;
then the ruler, though leisurely in jade chambers,
carefree atop cloud-high towers,
with sweet wine spoiling in feathered cups,
and musicians weary from dance and music,
can still govern with folded sleeves by relying on the worthy,
and rest on high pillows while demanding accomplishments.
Why must one dwell in the narrow confines of thatched huts,
eat the bland broth of simple fare,
personally labor like a gatekeeper,
endure the toil of self-sacrifice,
to then extend kindness to the common people,
and spread the Way beyond the seas!
The deluded and confused ruler,
however, does not act thus.
In governance,
some are benevolent but indecisive,
allowing right and wrong to blur,
where the upright go unrewarded,
and the wicked unpunished.
Others are harshly cruel,
or purely威严 without grace,
imposing excessive penalties,
showing no forgiveness or consideration.
With roots exposed and foundations crumbling,
perilous as a nest on a curtain,
yet they compare themselves to the sun and sky,
and assume the firmness of Mount Tài,
claiming that embodying brilliant virtue is not hard to achieve,
and that cautious vigilance is not worth considering.
Thus, the innocent and guiltless,
suffer arbitrary punishments for show,
the people see no virtue,
hearing only of executions.
Appointing officials, they deem those who comply as worthy,
promoting talents, they favor those close and familiar.
High ministers are ranked,
but entrusted to the empress's clan;
decisive power in consultations,
is given to flattering sycophants.
Those promoted are distant relatives beyond the nine degrees,
without assessing their capability;
those trusted are petty talents skilled in fawning,
while the upright are despised;
those demoted follow popular opinion,
without investigating the truth;
those favored are chosen for fine reputations,
without examining their actual achievements.
Officials in charge of key governance and people,
generals commanding armies and campaigns,
some corrupt and ruin their posts,
others selfishly disrupt the court,
some weak and bungle affairs,
others timid and lose military advantages.
Ultimately unaware,
and unwilling to dismiss them,
the ruler instead draws them closer,
hoping for late improvements.
Small vessels bearing great loads,
lead inevitably to disaster.
Talented individuals of broad vision without support,
may wear coarse clothes and live in hidden retirement,
or sink into poverty and obscurity,
holding to the Way but keeping silent,
with no means for the people to benefit from their strength,
hence the frequency of decline's calamities,
which thus abound.
Yet he neither hears nor peruses
the warnings in the classics and canonical texts,
indulging in frivolous amusements and revelries,
wholly devoted to these pursuits.
He elevates tower views but lowers moral virtue,
expands parks and gardens but narrows recruitment and acceptance,
deepens ponds and marshes but shallowens kindness and trust,
delights in dogs and horses but detests blunt admonishments,
values pearls and jades but disdains wisdom and strategy,
enriches silken garments but restricts benevolence and grace,
delays relief aid but hastens tax collections,
diligently hunts but neglects farming,
emphasizes land annexation but轻视s people's lives,
promotes entertainers but demotes scholars and elegance,
favors court favorites but slights warriors,
immerses in music and beauty, forgetting all state affairs,
prioritizes feasting and travel over hearing petitions and judgments,
imposes numerous harsh labors but spares rewards and recognition,
crafts expensive, unnecessary objects of fancy,
and pens up animals that consume grain without benefit.
Thus, for peril and downfall, one cannot blame heaven;
for weakness and decline, one cannot fault others.
Good and ill fortune stem from oneself—
were King Tāng and King Wǔ exceptions?
In the past, King Wén of Zhōu buried exposed bones,
and all under heaven praised his benevolence.
King Zhòu of Shāng carved out Bǐ Gàn's heart,
and the world condemned his tyranny.
When hopes rest on one in the public eye,
praise and blame spread swiftly.
The key to gain and loss
lies not in quantity.
For when praise accumulates, even distant tribes submit willingly,
and it cannot be obtained falsely;
when censure piles up, even Huáxià turns离心,
and it cannot be remedied with words.
Therefore, small acts of good, though not greatly beneficial,
must not be left undone;
minor evils, though causing no immediate harm,
must not be left unaddressed.
If one gives rein to desires and passions,
without sharing joy with all under heaven,
then worries arise with none to relieve them.
Undermining the foundation while hating the height,
unaware that collapse below leads to ruin above,
thus downfall comes with none to support it.
Then the reins slip from my hands,
divine favor is lent but not returned,
efforts toil while wealth depletes,
the people cannot bear their fate,
grievances brew below,
heaven's wrath stirs above,
Tián Chéng steals all of Qí from within the tent,
Jī Chāng gains trust from the western neighbor,
followers like Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng,
raise swords with great cries,
others like Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ,
brandish spears like a storm,
cloud ladders scale hundred-zhì walls,
bright blades clash beneath the palace gates,
flying blades thrust inward,
imperial guards crumble outward,
only then does one sorrowfully yearn for great sages of distant ages,
wield a broom to welcome reclusive wise men,
admire Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng in mountain retreats,
seek out Sūn Wǔ in the wilds,
yet find no place to receive wise counsel,
ponder good strategies but have none to ask,
like trying to fetch water from the sea
after a great mansion has burned down,
or building boats in distant lands
when floods overwhelm the house.
Lofty reputations
cannot be built on arrogance and stinginess;
and the fēngsacrifice at Tài Shān
is not easily achieved through self-indulgence.
The wisest rulers drive their chariots with double whips,
still fearing they cannot keep pace with the past;
yet mediocre lords stroll slowly, holding the reins,
thinking themselves superior.
Some dwell in safety yet ponder danger,
others live in peril yet seek ease.
Some achieve merit and stable rule,
neither negligent nor wasteful,
while others hang by a thread or balance on stacked eggs,
yet remain unawakened.
Without the downfall of King Zhòu and Jié,
how could we value the lofty salvation of wise rulers?
Reflect on this, ever mindful,
almost there, almost there!
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
In the times of Yáo and Shùn,
they studied antiquity with reverence and wisdom,
yet still awaited the assistance of all lords,
to achieve grand success.
Thus they could glorify the emperor's deeds,
and all accomplishments solidified,
the four gates stood solemn,
all offices functioned in order,
barbarians caused no turmoil in Huáxià,
and the palace roof nested singing phoenixes.
Comparing it to the head
and the limbs,
though there is a distinction between noble and humble,
they truly rely on each other as one body.
The ruler must assign duties based on ability,
to prevent the disaster of overturning a carriage;
the minister must accept posts according to talent,
thus avoiding the calamity of exile.
Those who, like shadows and echoes,
bow and obey every command,
are but corpses in office, clinging to life.
Those who defy orders and risk the ruler's displeasure,
steadfastly selfless,
are the pillars that secure the state.
Those who anticipate and迎合 the ruler's wishes
are flatterers and sycophants;
those who correct errors and rectify faults
are the loyal backbones of the state.
They must be ready to face the axe and block to offer upright advice,
lean against the cauldron to speak fully.
If loyal yet distrusted,
or remonstrating without effect,
they may await dismissal;
if certain death brings no remedy,
only adding to the ruler's faults,
they may leave.
In action,
they rely on nothing but the teachings and classics;
in stillness,
they follow only the laws and regulations.
No room for favoritism or requests,
upholding law without regard for private ties.
Enforcing penalties without bias against the disliked,
granting rewards without favoring the obsequious.
Not usurping authority to seize power,
nor discussing purity while tolerating filth.
Advancing, they think of speaking out to correct errors;
retreating, they consider recommending worthies without obstruction.
Rising early and retiring late,
concerned that affairs may not be well;
frugal in person and restrained in ambition,
as if whipping a horse over thin ice.
Accepting advice and recommending scholars,
without boasting of it;
unjust profits,
without harboring them in heart.
In court, they maintain integrity as sharp as a whetstone and straight as an arrow;
in personal conduct, they emulate the purity of the lamb.
Facing danger and crisis,
they forget family and disregard life.
Holding the balance of judgment,
they remain impartial, without bias.
They emulate the guidance of Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn,
admire the ingenious plans of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng,
follow Zhōu Bó's wholehearted loyalty,
match the straightforwardness of Bāo Yán and Bāo Xuān,
tread the virtuous path of Yǎn Yīng and Hóng Yàn,
hold fast to the steadfastness of Méng Tián and Wáng Jiǎn till the end,
content with the fate of being boiled or burned,
wary of the disaster that befell Hán Xìn and Yīng Bù for losing loyalty.
Departing, they do not shirk toil;
returning, they do not count merits;
attributing achievements to others, taking blame upon themselves,
yielding precedence to subordinates,
wholly sincere and reverently cautious,
as if heaven's majesty were ever before them;
day and night devout and alert,
as if a boiling cauldron stood beside them.
Bearing the weight of trust,
they take Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng as models;
exerting strength across the land,
they follow the examples of Jí Fù and Shào Gōng;
serving the departed and caring for the living,
they exhaust loyalty without turning back;
combating those who violate law,
they strike like hawks against sparrows;
defending the borders,
they admire the lofty deeds of Wèi Jiàng and Lǐ Mù;
governing the masses and comforting the people,
they aspire to the virtuous transformation of Wén Wēng and Xìn Chén.
For the utmost loyal have nothing with which to betray the state,
how much less those who harbor wisdom to deceive their superiors?
Those bound by duty fear not the extinction of their lineage,
how much less would they shirk demotion or disgrace?
Thus they can preserve hard-won honors to glorify their ancestors,
entrusting their goodness to the songs of the people.
The sacrificial vessels of Kūnwú,
the skilled inscribe with merits.
Gāo Yáo and Hòu Jì,
what men were they
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When a minister's achievements are not grand,
he feels ashamed of drawing an empty salary;
when his accomplishments are not abundant,
he is embarrassed by undeservedly high rank and appointments.
Walking in trustworthiness and thinking of obedience,
heaven and man will support him;
fearing fullness and dwelling in humility,
he will ultimately have blessings.
Every step he takes treads the measures of the Way,
every gesture he makes follows the plumb line;
though praise and honor may be delayed,
regret and disgrace will certainly be far away.
As for those who harm the superior to cling to the inferior,
abandon public duty to pursue private gain,
flatter and crookedly follow,
adding water to water,
even if the ruler's actions are erroneous,
they ingratiate and praise them as good.
Repeatedly presenting curios and treasures,
they lead their lord into evil.
With clever words they ruin governance,
with pleasing expressions they seek favor,
above blinding the ruler's clarity,
below blocking the path for advancing worthies;
externally forming friendships beyond the borders,
internally cultivating cliques that betray the public.
Though their talent may suffice to cover up wrongs,
and their words to gloss over faults,
usurping authority like Zhào Gāo,
dominating the court like Dǒng Zhuō,
none have failed to end with their bodies greasing the sharp blades,
and their families perishing in boiling water and fire.
Yet the foolish and blind abandon the upright for the crooked,
forsake the genuine for the false,
personally witnessing collapse and ruin,
yet not changing their course;
the gathering of calamity and disaster
does not descend from heaven.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Ministers are likened to limbs,
thus hands and feet.
Treading on ice or handling heat,
they cannot refuse.
Therefore, the ancients compared them to the earth:
dig it, and water springs forth;
plant in it, and a hundred grains flourish;
the living stand upon it,
the dead enter into it.
They accomplish much without expecting reward,
toil exhaustively without daring to complain.
Understanding this method clearly
is essential for preserving oneself.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When a minister's duties are clearly divided, there is order;
when authority is too broad, there is much stagnation.
Without the strength of Mèng Bēn or Wū Huò,
one cannot lift the weight of multiple men;
without being outstanding among ten thousand,
one cannot oversee the affairs of different offices.
This is why Hán Hóu established penalties for overstepping,
and Zǐ Yuán feared the disaster of incompetence.
If one's talent and strength are peerless,
both civil and military abilities are genuine,
internally possessing the lofty strategies of a confidant,
externally having the far-reaching plans to repulse the enemy,
though affairs are numerous, they are managed even better,
handling two paths and succeeding in both,
without them, the constant principles are destroyed,
yet entrusting them to another, there is no suitable person—
then combining duties is permissible;
if one is not such a vessel,
one should measure and withdraw,
for a carriage shaft bearing too heavy a load
rarely avoids breaking.
Ordinary people covet glory,
not considering future troubles,
once they themselves have fallen and drowned,
the disaster reaches the ruler and parents—
is this not lamentable!
All decline tasks beyond the axe's capability,
yet none yield offices they cannot bear.
Alas!
This is why Chén and Lǐ warned against insufficient strength,
and why Zǐfáng wisely retreated to avoid fullness.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who soar and perch without choosing the tree
will surely be birds caught in the net.
Those who enter service without assessing the times
will surely be men in peril and disgrace.
When the time is gained,
one soars like the responding dragon viewing the radiant clouds;
when the time is lost,
one is desolate like a giant fish stranded on a high plain.
Therefore, the wise conceal their ability to await the moment,
hide themselves to act when needed.
If a high cliff is about to collapse,
it cannot be held by thin threads;
if the Dragon Gate boils and surges,
it cannot be blocked by handfuls of soil.
Then they do not act recklessly for petty gains,
nor venture into danger hoping for luck.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The Duke of Zhōu's regency in the king's place,
Yī Yǐn's deposing of Tài Jiǎ,
Huò Guāng's dethroning of Chāngyì,
Sūn Chēn's removal of the Shàodì—
these are called abandoning the norm to use expediency,
to secure the altars of grain and soil.
Yet the Duke of Zhōu was slandered and troubled,
with rumors filling the roads;
Yī Yǐn ultimately met execution,
with heavy fog for three days;
Huò Guāng nearly brought disaster upon himself in his lifetime,
and his family was soon destroyed;
before the mulberry shade had moved, Sūn Chēn
found his head and feet separated.
Their laughter had not yet faded,
and wailing had already reached them.
If one does not support in danger,
what use is such a minister?
Even with seven remonstrating ministers,
a ruler without the Way cannot be saved.
This led to the likes of Wáng Mǎng
giving rise to their treacherous schemes,
citing past events externally to cover wrongs,
harboring the heart of wolves and jackals internally—
all stemming from Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
laying the foundation for this disorder.
Future gentlemen
should deeply consider this.
The matter of deposing rulers,
though minor in compliance, is major in transgression,
and cannot be prolonged.
The deceit of summoning the king
was already condemned and restrained.
How much more so removing a ruler—
how can such evil be permissible!
These all calculated their actions and succeeded,
only to suffer calamity later.
As for those who begin with secret plans and expediency,
and are betrayed by greedy men,
exterminating their entire clan and lineage;
while other families are enfeoffed—
such cases are not few.
If there are treacherous sycophants abetting arrogance and chaos,
like Jié's Gānxīn and Tuīduō,
Zhòu's Féi Lián and È Lái,
and Lì's partisans,
replacing them with loyal and good men—
is that not easier?
Remove the multitude of evils at the ruler's side,
banish the wicked clans to the four borders,
hold troops and maintain strength,
uphold the straight path and abide by the law,
strictly wield the axe of authority,
sternly hold the plumb line,
clearly reward and invariably punish,
tolerating no offense without pardon,
appoint the worthy and employ the capable,
granting trust only to the loyal,
acting without arbitrary control,
requesting permission before proceeding;
if the ruler has errors or faults,
advise him correctly based on principle.
Trembling with caution,
never forgetting respect,
ensuring the state's eternal peace above,
and oneself remaining free of trouble below.
When achievements are made, not dwelling on them,
begging to retire and withdraw,
selecting highly capable loyalists,
advancing them to replace oneself—
is that not more than ample?
Why must one seize the sovereign's seal and ribbons,
endangering the ruler one serves!
The ruler
is heaven,
is father.
If the ruler can be deposed,
then heaven can be changed,
and father can be replaced.
Those whose merit overshadows the age go unrewarded,
whose might shakes the ruler endanger themselves.
Even those solely victorious in battle and conquest,
with unmatched merit and labor,
still face the bow discarded once birds are gone,
the hound boiled once hares are caught.
How much more so those who depose their ruler,
yet hope for the later lord's favor—
how is this different from a child carrying his parent to abandon in the valleys,
taking another to raise instead,
and saying, "I can be as filial as Bóyú or Zēng Shēn,
but my parent is unfit to serve,
so I cast them away."
Even if he offers three sacrificial animals daily,
attends morning and evening,
could he be pitied and believed?
Those like Huǒ Guāng,
though they were promoted in rank and advanced in nobility at the time,
receiving immeasurable rewards and gifts,
were all honored through schemes;
was this truly the sincerity of such men?
To take in a discarded wife and then speak ill of her former husband's faults,
or to buy a servant and then slander the cruelty of the former master—
even ordinary, mediocre people
would find it unjust.
Why?
It deeply wounds their kind,
which is a natural sentiment.
Thus, Yuè Yáng was estranged for his tolerance of cruelty,
while Qín Xī was cherished for his excessive kindness.
Yet people of the world truly believe Tāng and Wǔ were right,
and Yī and Huǒ were virtuous,
which is to encourage each other in rebellion.
Moreover, the deposed rulers
were not necessarily entirely wrong.
Some assisted young sovereigns,
wielding authority and power,
but their crimes grew great and evils accumulated,
causing concern for future harm;
while they still held power,
they were replaced,
prolonging the disasters of the near term.
The merit of devising strategies
was calculated for self-interest,
not necessarily for the state.
Once authority was seized heavily,
life and death were decided by a single word.
The deposed sovereigns,
having lost the divine vessel,
bore the blame for all downstream crimes,
with none not attributed to them.
Though aware of this,
who dared to speak out?
Without a Dōngmóu or Zhūxū to execute their plans,
without a Nánshǐ or Dǒnghú to attest to their crimes,
in the days to come,
who would redress it?
Only the insightful can retrospectively realize that the evils of Jié and Zhòu were not as heinous as portrayed,
and the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ not as glorious.
What is recorded in historical texts
invariably exalts the ruler and subordinates the minister,
strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches.
The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals
is that Heaven cannot be opposed.
The great sages, in composing the classics,
taught serving the father and the ruler.
The people's life lies in three relationships,
upheld with equal devotion.
Yet to endorse depositions and successions,
opening the door to unprincipled acts,
leads to subordinates overriding and superiors declining,
making it hard to uphold teachings.
Conventional scholars, immersed in a fish market,
trapped in sophistry,
argue that discussing Tāng and Wǔ is like eating horse liver,
and those who critique such matters
are unaware of expediency in change,
valuing the promotion of good without defying order,
not realizing it contradicts reason and rebels against righteousness.
Previous writers,
failing to analyze with grand principles,
placed those with such sentiments on the edge of a sharp blade,
or atop a crumbling mountain,
which is no way to prolong life
or avoid danger.
Though edicts and honors briefly flourished,
and generous rewards suddenly gathered,
it was no different from a sacrificial ox adorned with embroidery,
or deep-water fish enticed by weeds and wheat,
like the thirsty quenching their thirst with cloudy-day wine,
or the hungry sating themselves on spoiled meat.
Yet writers collectively praised it,
making it a celebrated tale,
deeming unpardonable crimes as wise adaptation,
causing distress and lasting sighs.
Some admonish me that such words offend the sages,
and I will surely be criticized.
I reply:
"Shùn and Yǔ underwent trials both internal and external,
before receiving the mandate from Wén Zǔ.
Even if there were faults,
how could they harm the sages?
In the past, Yán Yánnián accused Huǒ Guāng of unprincipled conduct in court,
and at that time, all present were solemn,
with no one to refute him.
Moreover, I offer a warning to the world,
without direct accusations,
why worry about common talk?"
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
To exhaust one's duty without concealment
is possible.
But to have one's words heeded and oneself safe
requires timing.
When the time is adverse,
treacherous and malicious individuals envy those they cannot match,
flattering superiors and suppressing subordinates,
detesting the upright and honest,
fearing public criticism and exposure of their evils,
thus striving to eliminate those better to avoid punishment.
Enlightened rulers do not appear in every era,
and mediocre rulers are confused about right and wrong,
unable to accept loyal advice,
sometimes even divulging crucial words.
Then, those like Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn,
craft clever words to fabricate resemblances,
using public pretense to sell private wickedness.
They make those who offer ways to longevity
instead face capital charges;
those who present plans for stability
quickly suffer life-threatening disasters.
Hence it is said:
The difficulty lies not in speaking,
but in the timing of the discourse.
Even with a worthy advising a sage,
acceptance is not guaranteed,
so Yī Yǐn sought Tāng's attention
up to seventy times.
With wisdom told to a fool,
it will not be heeded,
thus Wén advised Zhòu,
but it was never accepted.
If words are not trusted,
that is tolerable.
But cases like Lǐ Sī executing Hán Fēi,
Páng Juān mutilating Sūn Bìn,
Shàngguān slandering Qū Yuán,
Yuán Àng framing Cháo Cuò,
are too numerous to record.
Being a minister is not easy,
and there is more than one path to hardship!
Those who press forward without turning back
achieve merit only after death;
while those who hide their talents awaiting the right time
rarely get a single opportunity in a hundred.
Ministers with high merit appear once in an era;
those who fall into icy traps
fill the history books.
Alas,
how exceedingly rare
it is to encounter the right time!
From this perspective,
I know that those like Lǚ Shàng by the Wèi River,
or Fù Yuè among the cliffs,
bearing the tools to assist kings,
holding transcendent talents,
grasping fishing rods or hoes,
grow old and die among the common folk,
without meeting a King Wén or Emperor Gāozōng—
this is inevitable.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
The swift steed's gallop
depends on Zào Fǔ's driving;
Yǔ and Jì's ordering of all affairs
met with the rulers of Táng and Yú.
Thus, they could travel a thousand li without toil,
and praises arose through courteous yielding.
But if Zāng Pǐ rode Sùshuāng,
or Yīn Xīn faced the three benevolent men,
wishing to gallop freely,
the reins would be tight and the yoke oppressive;
wishing to offer full loyalty,
disaster would strike like a released trigger.
Hence, the carriage overturns on dangerous paths,
and the state falls, never to recover.
Thus, a fine steed is ruined by a clumsy driver,
and a wise scholar stumbles in a dark age.
Zhòngní could not stop the ruler of Lǔ from departing,
Yàn Yīng could not prevent Cuī Zhù's rebellion.
Their talents were sufficient,
but their rulers were not.
The ruler is like a vessel,
the minister like an object;
if the vessel is small and the object large,
they cannot accommodate each other.
A child abandons gold to chase butterflies,
a Yuè person discards delicacies for frogs and tadpoles—
they not only fail to appreciate the good,
but also cannot recognize the bad.
If not used,
even treasures hold no value;
if not supported,
harm will surely come.
In the past, Lord Líng of Wèi heard sage words and was repeatedly startled,
while Lord Xiào of Qín listened to lofty talks and fell asleep,
yet they wished to weave a tapestry of peace and prosperity,
and reap the rewards of capable governance—
it was like walking backward to catch up with a galloper,
or heading to Chǔ by way of Yān.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The Southern Ocean draws tributary streams to form its unfathomable depths;
the Mystic Garden piles up rocks to reach heaven-scraping heights.
When tall towers pierce the clouds,
they rely on the accumulation of many rafters;
when wheels are curved and carriage-poles straight,
there is no material that goes to waste.
Thus, when assistants like Yuán and Kǎi rise to office,
transformative governance reaching Heaven is achieved;
