when talent for averting conflict is comprehensive,
then conspiracies to seize the throne subside.
This is why Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world yet did not interfere with it,
and why Duke Líng of Wèi, though arrogant and willful, faced no danger.
When many strengths combine,
even ten thousand jun can be lifted;
when the wisdom of the multitude is employed,
all tasks can be accomplished.
Thus, a creature with many legs may die but not disintegrate,
and a state with many scholars may face turmoil but not perish.
Yet swords and halberds are not adept at sewing,
awls and drills cannot be used for striking and cutting,
oxen and horses cannot bark and guard,
chickens and dogs cannot pull carriages.
Employ their strengths,
and no task will be futile;
avoid their weaknesses,
and no talent in the world will be discarded.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
One who abandons a light boat to cross a boundless ocean
will not necessarily reach the other side;
one who lacks good ministers yet desires great peace
has never been heard to succeed.
When wild swans and phoenixes soar through the void,
it is by the power of their six wing feathers;
when deep-dwelling dragons fly to the sky,
it is with the aid of clouds and mist.
Thus, attracting the worthy and employing them
is the ruler's essential task;
achieving merit and accomplishing deeds
is what the talented and outstanding aspire to.
To delight in orderly governance yet neglect the wise
is no different from wanting to travel a long road but discarding the fine steed!
To pluck the stagnant from the hills and gardens,
to promote the obscure who have been overlooked,
to assign positions that exhaust their talents,
and to grant emoluments matching their achievements—
this is how a ruler treats the worthy.
To labor diligently day and night in public service,
to exhaust heart and strength in all affairs,
to advance the good and dismiss the wicked,
and to act knowing nothing should be left undone—
this is how a minister repays one who recognizes his worth.
There may be recluses in the world,
but there is no sovereign who stands alone.
A scholar may delight in withdrawal and have no worries,
but a ruler cannot achieve order without ministers.
Thus, Fù Yuè and Lǚ Shàng did not anxiously seek fame and advancement,
for when virtue is complete, one slights kings and dukes.
Yet Yīn Gāo and Zhōu Wén dreamed of obtaining the worthy,
for great achievements require excellent assistants.
The trouble lies in being born deep within the palace,
reared in the hands of women,
unaware of the hardships of farming,
ignorant of the principles of worry and fear,
inheriting the family and continuing the line,
yet blind to rise and fall.
Their urgent concerns lie in extravagance,
their paramount tasks in amusement and feasting,
engrossed in hunting,
immersed in heavy drinking and pleasure,
startling their ears at wanton music,
shifting their gaze at beautiful colors.
Employing their keen hearing and sharp sight
only for these two things,
they discern and evaluate people
without applying their spirits,
knowing only that playthings can delight the heart,
unaware that extraordinary men can secure the state.
Rhinoceros horns, ivory, pearls, and jade
arrive effortlessly from ten thousand miles away;
yet instruments that stabilize collapse,
though capable of action, sink unknown within the four borders.
When the illness of the two minions has taken hold, then they seek a good physician;
when the calamity of the bending roof beam has gathered, then they think of counselors—
how is this different from digging a well only when a fire breaks out,
or planning the fields only when hunger is felt!
Even common servants cannot be made to exhaust their strength without安抚,
so how can one obtain sudden service without prior cultivation?
Some say:
"A tail larger than the body
cannot be wagged;
a minister wiser than the ruler
cannot be employed.
Thus, one who forces down what the mouth cannot hold will choke;
one who relies on a talent not his match will be slighted."
Bàopǔzǐ says:
"How deceptive
are these words!
In the past, the young lord of Jīng assumed the ministerial duties,
truly relying on twenty-five elders
to achieve benevolent peace.
Zǐ Jiàn left home to govern a great state,
truly because he had many superiors to himself,
and attracted their broad benefits.
Duke Huán of Qí killed his elder brother and took the throne,
behaving like birds and beasts,
wearing his hair loose and indulging in wine,
with three hundred women's quarters,
yet he entrusted governance to Zhòng Fù,
and thus became hegemon;
after Yí Wú passed away,
calamity and chaos repeatedly arose.
When Lǔ employed Jìzǐ for over twenty years,
there were no flawed policies internally,
no invasions or losses externally;
after his passing,
decline and suffering echoed and gathered.
Is it not that when talent is not equal to the task,
the achievement is as it was;
when one takes charge of affairs oneself,
the disaster is as it is!"
"Hàn Gāo's strategies in the dark tent,
securing victory a thousand miles away,
were not as good as those of Liáng and Píng;
in training troops, the more the better,
invincible wherever they went,
he was not as good as Xìn and Bù;
yet by employing them together,
he accomplished the imperial enterprise.
Thus, rapid steps and accumulated strides
are not like riding a swift-footed steed;
chasing what flies and runs
is not like borrowing the skills of hawks and hounds.
A powerful crossbow is hard to draw,
yet it can shatter solid targets and reach far;
a great boat is hard to steer,
yet it can carry heavy loads and cross deep waters;
a fierce general is hard to control,
yet he can avert conflict and expand borders;
a lofty worthy is hard to approach,
yet he can properly order the constant relationships.
"In the past, Lǔ Āi was a mediocre ruler,
yet Zhòngní, the supreme sage,
dared not fail in his devotion;
Qí Jǐng was of low ability,
yet Yàn Yīng, a great worthy,
dared not withhold his sincerity.
How can a minister compete with his ruler in measuring the extent of wisdom and strength,
or calculate the superiority of capacity,
requiring a Yáo or Shùn to serve him!
What ruler is not one's lord?
What people are not to be directed?
To feel ashamed if his ruler does not equal Táng or Yú—
this is also the intention of the enlightened."
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Yóu Yú was among the Róng,
and Duke Mù of Qín worried greatly.
Chǔ executed Dé Chén,
and Duke Wén of Jìn rejoiced.
Yuè Yì departed, and Yān fell to ruin;
Zhǒng and Lí entered, and Yuè became hegemon.
States shattered and families lost—
all due to losing men of talent.
Is it merely that having them is weighty,
and lacking them is light?
Liǔ Xià Huì's tomb
could still blunt the edge of a mighty foe,
how much more if he were seated in the court!
Duàn Gān Mù's reclusion
could still repel an invading attack,
how much more if he were placed in high office!
Zhì Dū's image
made fierce enemies tremble with fear.
Kǒngmíng's corpse
still caused a great state to sheathe its blades.
Using such men to resist insult,
the land will surely not be invaded;
leading armies with such men,
the ruler will surely not be humiliated.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler presents bundles of silk in poor alleys,
raises sunken feathers in withered forests,
dispatches raised carriages to river bridges,
opens the four gates tirelessly,
not grudging gold and jade,
not considering a thousand miles far,
not fearing to humble himself,
not ashamed of lowly words,
but takes obtaining the worthy as his foremost duty,
and gaining scholars as his precious treasure.
Those who recommend them receive the highest rewards,
those who obscure them are stealing their positions.
Thus, the Duke of Dàn presented gifts at humble cottages,
and Qín Shào bowed to Zhāng Shēng in reverence.
When Zōu Zǐ crossed the border,
the Lord of Yān wielded a broom to welcome him;
before Zhuāng Zhōu had eaten,
King Huì of Zhào stood in awe.
Lord Píng of Jìn received Hài Táng,
and dared not sit properly even with numb feet;
the ruler of Qí visited Jì Qiū,
and did not refuse the labor despite frequent visits.
King Chǔ accepted flogging from Bǎo Shēn,
● Jiǎn removed his armor at the public lodge,
Though they lowered their high status and suppressed pride,
humbling themselves before inferiors,
they ultimately broadened their vision to enhance clarity,
and borrowed others' ears to expand their hearing.
Like dragons soaring and tigers crouching,
it was fitting indeed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
All value benevolence,
yet none can achieve governance through pure benevolence;
all despise punishment,
yet none can maintain order among people by abolishing penalties.
Some say:
"When an enlightened ruler governs the world,
the wind bends the grass.
When the Way prevails and transformation is pure,
what use is there for punishment?"
I thus argue:
"Virtuous teaching
is like ceremonial robes for sacrifices;
penal punishment
is like armor against sharp blades.
If virtuous teaching governs the cunning and violent,
it is like using ceremonial robes to block sharp spears;
if punishments are applied in peaceful times,
it is like wearing armor in temple halls.
Thus benevolence is the tool for nurturing things,
while punishment is the instrument for rectifying wrongs.
When I wish to benefit them,
but they intend harm,
adding benevolence brings no repentance,
without punishment, it does not cease.
Punishment assists benevolence—
this can thus be known.
For example, preserving the primal breath through controlled breathing,
inhaling and exhaling,
visualizing internally with absorbed scenes,
imitating bear hangs and bird stretches
are longevity techniques.
Yet they are arduous and slow,
with few practitioners succeeding;
those who can master them
are one in ten thousand.
When illness is severe and pain intense,
the body exhausted and life endangered,
one must resort to acupuncture and stone needles,
treating with potent methods.
If abandoning the methods of Hé and Què,
to admire the ways of Sōng and Qiáo,
then the dead would be numerous.
Governing with benevolence
is not without merit.
However, the common people are crafty and deceitful,
chasing profit while forgetting righteousness.
If not restrained by authority,
and corrected by punishment,
aspiring remotely to the customs of Fúxī and Shénnóng,
then chaos cannot be controlled,
and the disaster will be profound and great.
Using killing to stop killing—
how could one delight in it!
"The creation of the Eight Trigrams
exhausts principles and fulfills nature,
clarifying penalties and employing prisons,
as seen in the hexagram Shìhé;
the use of bonds and ropes
is preserved in the hexagram Xíkǎn.
Thus, the use of punishment has a long history.
Reaching the time of Xuānyuán,
whose sage virtue was especially lofty,
yet he personally led campaigns,
fighting hundreds of battles,
corpses piled at Zhuōlù,
blood flowed at Bǎnquán,
still he could not prevent rebellions in his time,
nor store away shields and spears.
How could he make all百姓 virtuous,
with people committing no crimes, thus needing no governance?
Such a thing has never existed.
In the flourishing eras of Táng and Yú,
they modeled heaven in applying punishments,
banishing and exiling offenders,
and the world submitted.
Emperor Wén of Hàn practiced profound silence,
rivaling the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng,
yet he adjudicated four hundred cases,
with many dying from flogging.
Master craftsman Shí never abandons the ink line,
thus there are no crooked woods;
an enlightened ruler never abolishes punishments,
thus there is no decadent governance.
"For the way of heaven and earth
cannot be purely benevolent,
thus spring reveals nurturing harmony,
while autumn wields the stern force of execution;
when warm winds blow, withered plants sprout,
when white dew condenses, lush flowers wither.
Thus all things flourish,
and the year's work is accomplished.
If warm without cold,
then creeping insects do not hibernate,
and roots and plants thrive in winter.
If lenient without strictness,
then villains and rebels arise together,
and sharp tools remain unused.
Thus, clear rewards preserve correctness,
necessary punishments prevent evil.
Among tools for encouragement and deterrence,
none is more essential.
Observing the people to establish teachings,
balancing leniency and severity,
so the timid cannot be bullied,
and the stern do not harm kindness.
The five punishments encompass
up to three thousand crimes,
showing the line must not be bent;
when the Minister of Justice carries out executions,
the ruler refrains from feasting,
showing laws cannot be abolished.
If the line is bent,
then treachery sprouts;
if laws are abolished,
then disaster and chaos proliferate.
"Fallen states lack not decrees,
but suffer from decrees too numerous to enforce;
defeated armies lack not prohibitions,
but suffer from prohibitions established but unheeded.
Thus evils spread rampantly,
and inferiors defy their superiors.
Rewards should fit the merit, not necessarily be heavy;
punishments should match the crime, not necessarily be cruel.
If whipping is abandoned at home,
then servants become lazy;
if campaigns cease in the state,
then subordinates show irreverence.
Love relies on respect to endure,
thus rituals are established to honor it;
virtue requires authority to last,
thus punishments are created to solemnize it.
Bān and Chuí never discard compass and square,
thus circles and squares conform to objects;
enlightened rulers never abandon laws and measures,
thus cunning deceit cannot unleash its tricks.
Táng and Yú were benevolent as heaven,
yet did not pardon the four culprits;
Lord Jī was friendly to brothers,
yet did not spare his two uncles.
Confucius' execution of Shǎozhèng Mǎo,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's killing of his nephew,
shedding tears while upholding the law—
all were acts of necessity.
Thus punishing one to deter ten thousand,
sacrificing few to benefit many,
compared to combing hair,
the beneficiaries are numerous;
compared to cutting a abscess,
the preserved is great.
Thus acupuncture's sharp pain is endured
to cure illness;
punishments' harshness is not abandoned
to remedy flaws.
The six armies stand like forests,
not all are brave.
Charging into blades and fire
is feared by human nature.
Yet encouraging with gentle words
rarely inspires sacrifice;
intimidating with execution
makes all strive to attack.
Thus relying on cheerful motivation
is less swift than stern commands;
using诱导 and persuasion
is less uniform than penalties and killings.
Thus Ān Yú enforced strict laws influenced by deep valleys,
and Wèi Zǐ harshly punished ash-tossing due to aversion.
Using what they fear
to prohibit what they trifle with,
strict yet unviolated,
is the art of preserving the people.
Those who understand healing techniques
prevent diseases before they arise;
those who grasp the essence of order and chaos
avert future disasters.
If using light penalties to forbid heavy crimes,
or thin laws to protect great interests,
the more regulations are displayed,
the more offenders multiply,
like digging a pit to block a road—
not the intention of benevolent people.
"Those skilled in governance
must first rectify themselves to lead others,
manage the intimate to regulate the distant,
never twisting laws to suit personal intentions,
ensuring punishment without pardon for crimes.
Like Shí Què sacrificing affection to eliminate kin,
or Duke Wén of Jìn suppressing emotions to execute Dī Jié.
Thus benevolence is
the cosmetics of governance;
punishment is
the reins and whip for ruling the age;
cosmetics are not most vital to the body,
yet reins and whip cannot be lacking for a moment.
Should solemn reverence slacken slightly,
negligence and laziness arrive;
if authority and dignity relax briefly,
all evils stir in hearts.
When anger is due but withheld,
treacherous ministers become tigers;
when execution is warranted but not carried out,
great bandits emerge.
Rivers erode banks over time,
mountains rise from minute beginnings.
A thousand-zhàng tree
starts from a tiny sprout;
fire from drilling wood
can be quenched by a ladle of water;
unhatched swan eggs
can be crushed in a palm.
But when riding storm winds to scorch vast plains,
or spreading six wings to soar above dawn clouds,
even the wise and brave cannot control it.
Thus enlightened rulers tackle difficulties while easy,
eliminate evils while minute,
not indulging goodness to foster chaos,
nor hesitating with axe in hand.
Therefore punishment as a tool
is the state's sacred instrument,
held personally by the ruler,
never lent to others,

If their words were put into practice,
then shackles should be burned,
prisons demolished,
officials dismissed,
penal codes abolished,
weapons melted down,
city walls leveled,
treasuries dispersed,
tallies destroyed,
border passes removed,
and measures smashed.
Glue up Lí Zhū's eyes,
plug Zǐyě's ears.
Drift freely without constraints,
return to natural herding;
neither teach nor manage,
forgetting each other in rivers and lakes.
The court silent as if无人,
the people never interacting till death.
This can be discussed theoretically,
but is difficult to implement practically.
"Conventional scholars merely hear that Zhōu rose through benevolence,
while Qín fell due to severity,
yet fail to realize that Zhōu's success didn't stem purely from benevolence,
nor was Qín's loss due solely to severity.
Formerly Zhōu employed corporal punishment,
amputating feet and cutting off noses.
At the Mèngjīn pledge,
latecomers were beheaded,
rewards and punishments strictly enforced,
with oaths of executing families.
Examining their actions,
they were not entirely benevolent.
By their declining age,
laws were disregarded and texts manipulated,
rulers became harsh and cruel,
edicts couldn't extend beyond the court,
rituals, music, and military campaigns,
no longer originated from the sovereign.
Subordinates competed fiercely,
transforming into long serpents.
They attacked roots and blocked sources,
destroyed caps and tore ceremonial crowns.
Some were drowned in the Hàn River,
others exiled like swine.
The failure of losing control,
arose from lack of severity.
When Qín first rose,
it appointed capable officials.
Figures like Wèi Yāng and Yóu Yú,
established laws internally;
while Bái Qǐ and Wáng Jiǎn's types,
conquered externally.
Annexing the weak and attacking the confused,
gaining prestige and establishing hegemony,
devouring neighboring states,
chewing up various powers,
expanding territories and repelling barbarians,
transforming like dragons with dragon-like vision,
actually relied on clear rewards and certain punishments,
to lay the imperial foundation.
Descending to its end era,
arrogant in success,
extremely luxurious and excessive.
Adding威虐 to this,
building万里 walls,
over a thousand detached palaces,
bells, drums, and female musicians,
readily available without moving.
The Líshān project,
majority taxes,
conscripting the poor,
cruel burying of scholars,
northern campaigns against Xiǎnyǔn,
southern expeditions to Bǎi Yuè,
deploying millions of troops,
lasting decades.
The world suffered separation sorrows,
households harbored resentment sighs.
White bones piled like mountains,
empty sacrifices spread across fields.
Xú Fú's departure加重ed the people's hatred,
Zhào Gāo's entry gathered wolf-like factions.
The world wanted rebellion,
nine out of ten homes emptied.
Their reason for collapse,
was it really due to severe punishments?
This shows Qín gained through severity,
not lost through it.
"Moreover punishment is like a blade,
the skilled use it to achieve success,
the clumsy to self-harm,
governing with principles aided by punishment,
can prevent deceit and falsehood,
reforming凶邪 intentions.
If the net breaks and order tangles,
offending heaven,
applying punishment unreasonably,
danger必定 speeds.
Just as water and fire can sustain life,
they can also kill people,
depending on whether one can use them properly.
"If tumors aren't removed,
yet refusing to practice Yuèrén's techniques,
longevity like Lǎo Péng's is hard to achieve.
When treacherous factions abound,
without strict impeachment systems,
no long-term blessing can be seen.
Simply select those like Zhǎng,
entrusting them with legal governance;
choose those of Zhào Chén's kind,
assigning them to investigate offenses.
Enlightened rulers pay attention above,
loyal officials exert sincerity below,
attacking evil like sparrowhawks seizing birds,
seeing disorder sprouts like weeding fields.
Rewards not mistakenly given,
punishments not missing crimes,
then太平's path isn't hard to follow.
If orders aren't violated,
perhaps punishments could be abolished for governance,
but I dare not agree."
Someone said:
"Then can punishments truly assist education and promote goodness,
serving as models without error?
What about ancient corporal punishments,
should they be restored?"
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"Why not!
Formerly Zhōu used corporal punishment,
lasting seven hundred years.
Hàn abolished it,
their reign shorter.
Replacing it with flogging,
mostly caused deaths.
Outwardly having light punishment names,
inwardly containing killing reality.
Regarding crimes,
when not capital offenses,
only exile and caning remain below,
if meeting amnesties,
bodies remain unharmed;
shaving regrowing hair,
beating healing wounds,
hardly punishes near-death crimes.
Now removing corporal punishment,
leaves no intermediate penalties between death and others,
so near-death crimes只能 end with exile/caning,
making severity inappropriate.
Moreover criminals are rare but occasional,
killing seems too severe,
while whipping seems too light,
such offenders are numerous.
Now without corporal punishment,
these near-death crimes,
often go unpunished properly.
"Now unless plotting rebellion or great treason,
harming sovereign or kin,
or military offenses during war,
and murderers,
replacing death with corporal punishment,
would sufficiently warn凶人.
The punished can still perform labor,
capable of productivity,
not cutting off life's continuity,
yet终身 disabled,
people witnessing it,
all shudder,
also deterring potential offenders,
demonstrating for the future,
surpassing execution.
Execution,
isn't insignificant.
But after three days' exposure,
buried and discarded,
many remain unaware,
most don't witness it.
Whereas corporal punishment provides ample warning.
Formerly Wèi debated this repeatedly,
all great Confucians and learned scholars,
thoroughly understanding profound principles,
all advocated restoring corporal punishment,
while opponents refuted,
all unreasonably.
Wèi Wǔdì also agreed.
Only because frontiers weren't pacified,
distant peoples couldn't comprehend ultimate principles,
suddenly hearing central states amputated limbs,
cut ears and noses,
would immediately deem it cruel,
thus temporarily suspended,
awaiting universal unification.
Learned Yáng Zǐyún also supported restoration.
But its abolition is long-standing,
those discussing principles,
don't consider it urgent."
Bàopǔzǐ said:
The reason Mount Huá and Mount Huò can tower to the sky's height
is due to their massive foundations below;
the reason Emperor Yáo and Emperor Shùn could achieve lofty merits
was truly reliant on having excellent assistants.
Even if one possesses the hand of a Sūn Yáng,
but lacks the feet of a qíjì steed,
then one cannot reach a thousand miles.
Even if one has the talent to examine antiquity,
but lacks supportive aides to exert strength,
then there is no way to consolidate various achievements.
Though a ruler's wisdom may parallel the sun and moon,
and his spirit discerns the unseen,
yet myriad affairs cannot be managed alone,
minute details cannot be personally overseen—
he must rely on eyes for distant observation,
borrow ears for broad listening,
truly needing official departments
to support and assist him.
Thus, sage rulers all sincerely seek worthies from the heart,
considering recommending talent their primary task,
bestowing silks upon recluses in hills and gardens,
dispatching ornate carriages to cliffs and marshes,
laboring in seeking people,
but resting easily when employing the capable.
From high ministers down
to lowly clerks,
all who discuss the Way and govern the state
hold their positions competently.
The ruler is reverent and non-interfering,
yet governance is peaceful and punishments set aside;
transformation permeates without exception,
and all states are tranquil.
Establishing offices and dividing duties
is like constructing a house:
if one component is unfit,
it becomes the cause of collapse.
Yet those recommended for office
were tested by four criteria;
high ministers and the nine ranks
emerged from this system,
necessarily selecting outstanding and brilliant talents.
But by the end of the Hàn dynasty,
during the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng,
power left the imperial house,
government fell into the hands of treacherous ministers,
the net of law leaked and defenses crumbled,
customs decayed and teaching collapsed.
They suppressed virtuous integrity and promoted flattery,
dismissed those who walked the righteous path and advanced the wealthy.
Striving through force became common practice,
obtaining by any means without shame:
some presented family treasures to sell themselves,
others offered letters from influential persons;
some had noble and prominent fathers or brothers,
receiving appointments by family reputation;
others bowed low and bent their knees,
gaining acceptance through practiced obsequiousness.
If the scale is unbalanced,
then light and heavy are mistaken;
if the measuring vessel is inaccurate,
then less and more become confused;
if the marking line is not applied,
if standards are tilted,
then impurities indeed abound.
Using such men to govern people
leads to cruelty and wolf-like greed—
they exact taxes and amass wealth
to recoup their costs of buying office;
placing them in the court
creates chaos worse than tangled threads.
Employing the inept and mediocre
to form cliques and support,
yet expecting customs to reform like grass bending to the wind,
and all affairs to prosper—
how is this different from hanging shards and demanding luminous pearls,
or plucking an untuned string and seeking clear music?
How can one not clarify the murky and elevate the submerged,
sift through the good and bad,
strictly enforce examination methods,
and sternly guard against the greedy?
This is the step toward decline and ruin—
how can one not fear it?
In ancient times, when feudal lords presented scholars,
if suitable, it was called meritorious,
and the meritorious had their ranks raised and titles advanced;
if the presented scholars were unsuitable, it was called faulty,
and the faulty were demoted in rank and lost territory.
Even then, they could not stop poets from quietly satirizing incompetence,
nor prevent worthy recluses from remaining in forests and hills.
Moreover, if recommendations carry no penalty for lacking talent,
and acceptances bear no risk of unfitness,
once measurement loses its standard,
how can excess or deficiency ever be corrected?
The outstanding solitary talent
hides his ability awaiting the right price;
the petty and frivolous
use connections to seek quick advancement.
Precisely because he awaits his value,
the former sinks into poverty and distress;
precisely because he seeks speed,
the latter jumps and leaps by cunning.
When owls flock and fly,
then phoenixes hide in seclusion;
when wolves block the road,
then qílín flee afar.
Promote the good and teach,
and the unvirtuous will stay away;
if the deceitful and false are honored,
then heroes and elites vanish secretly.
Noble characters feel ashamed to stand with the base,
the pure-minded are disgusted to join the gluttonous lot.
If recommendations and appointments are both erroneous,
then all the worthy withdraw into silence;
when all the worthy are silent,
then the wicked and evil draw each other in;
when the wicked and evil draw each other in,
then the path of petty men grows;
when the path of petty men grows,
then monsters stand shoulder to shoulder.
This is why hymns of praise do not arise,
and cries of complaint resound loudly.
Those of high ability and great talent,
relying on their capability to surpass others,
bend or stretch, silent or speaking,
leaving it to heaven and fate,
their poverty or success, gain or loss,
entrusted to nature—
how can they not fall behind those with factions,
and reside beneath those with power?
The extraordinary man,
not acting against propriety,
firm as a mountain, deep as a still pool,
is known by few;
those who chase and scramble,
blindly slander and destroy him,
so the ruler who longs for worthies
never learns where extraordinary talents lie,
and the man who embraces the Way,
willing to contribute his strength, finds no one to follow.
Even if he possesses the capability of a Jì or a Xiè,
and bears measure surpassing the age,
he sinks and stagnates until death,
unable to gain appointment.
Meanwhile, those with factions and power
gather in crowds like fish scales,
while men are scarce and offices empty—
how can one not pick and use them?
Yet those who arrive are also unworthy.
In the time of Emperors Líng and Xiàn,
eunuchs held power,
a host of villains wielded authority,
endangering loyal and good officials.
The central government failed in selection above,
and the provinces and commanderies trivialized recommendations below.
When selection fails above,
then governors and prefects are not the right men;
when recommendations are trivialized below,
then the xiùcai and xiàolián do not get the worthy.
Thus people of the time said:
"Recommended as xiùcai,
but he knows no books;
selected as xiàolián,
yet his father lives apart.
The poor and pure are muddy as sludge,
top-ranked fine generals timid as chickens."
They also said:
"The ancients, wishing to advance, diligently recited classics;
today's men, aiming for office, avoid managing livelihoods."
Such was the depth of their resentment.
At that time, official titles were hung up for sale,
as if displayed in market stalls;
those competing for advancement bought them,
just like market traders.
The wealthy advanced directly without distinction,
while the empty-handed watched the road and withdrew.
Those with abundant goods obtained high offices,
while those with little wealth received lowly positions.
Thus, the Eastern Garden accumulated money from selling offices,
and Cuī Liè was mocked for the stench of copper.
The subordinates emulate their superiors,
the ministers intensify their rulers' actions.
Therefore, flatterers and favorites
alone gained intimate audiences.
Local evaluators,
the Zhōngzhèng and the Ministry of Personnel,
all became chief brokers,
each setting their price.
How could impoverished scholars
have any hope of principle?
This was indeed the case.
Moreover, evil and upright are distinct,
like ice and charcoal;
those who hate integrity
despise those outside their faction.
Those who distort standards
fear others criticizing them;
those who achieve success through improper means
worry that discourse may not praise them.
Thus they jointly fabricate false accusations,
slandering virtuous character,
flaws and burdens proliferate wildly,
with none daring to rescue or uplift.
Hence, Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sǔn received slander like Shāng Chén,
while Confucius and Mòzǐ were stained with the filth of Dào Zhí.
Those upholding integrity and residing in purity
were trampled into the mire,
while the cunning and artfully deceitful
soared high among rainbows.
And ordinary men with shallow understanding,
unable to distinguish evil from upright,
called those adhering to principle stagnant,
and deemed those treading crooked paths adaptable.
How could those customs flowing with the wind
and drifting with the waves
return to personal virtue
or labor in thought over learning?
Thus, all abandoned the toil of discipline
and rushed toward the swiftness of bribery.
This truly was the reason the Hàn dynasty collapsed,
a lesson future generations should deeply heed.
Someone said:
"Your discourse on the imperial examinations of the late Hàn
truly diagnoses its ills.
Now, to guard against past errors,
avoid the path of the overturned cart,
change the strings of bygone eras,
prevent laxity in laws from recurring,
make the rustic songs of Púshàng
return to the proper tones of peace and joy,
so that ailments in the muscles
do not become chronic obstructions—
is there a method for this?
Scholars may have majestic demeanor and impressive appearance,
elegant reputation to spare,
yet harbor emptiness and void within,
lacking solid foundation.
Selecting by appearance
may not necessarily yield the worthy;
gradual preliminary testing
cannot be done hastily.
What should be done then?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"To know others is wisdom,
difficult even for the highest sages.
Now, to expect governors and prefects all to discern fine talent before employment,
and safeguard character and conduct throughout—
this is truly not easy.
But if they collectively set aside private feelings,
exhaust their intelligence,
remain unmoved by profit and desire,
unbent by connections and entreaties,
then for those they wish to recommend,
they must clarify thoughts to examine them,
broadly consult to detail them,
cultivate their reputation and investigate their actions,
compare consistencies to guard against false appearances.
Ensure their kin praise their filiality and friendship,
their community acknowledges their trustworthiness and righteousness.
For those who have held minor office,
look for evidence of loyalty and integrity,
and capability in handling affairs—
then a small piece of brocade can reveal skill,
piercing a rat can display courage.
"Moreover,
both Xiùcái and Xiàolián should, as before, be tested on classics and answer policy questions,
to prevent deceitful responses to accusations,
and it must be ensured that those who fail are not appointed,
with officials penalized by confinement.
For those whose recommendations miss the mark,
the Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu should be dismissed,
or at least demoted.
If more pass than fail,
subsequent promotions must not exceed former levels.
If accepting bribes to recommend the unfit,
upon discovery and verification, they should be stripped of titles,
confined for life,
not pardoned by amnesty decrees,
the recommender sharing the guilt with the recommended.
Trying this method now
for a year or two,
many Xiùcái and Xiàolián will inevitably fail,
sufficient to reveal how long imperial recommendations have been imprecise.
Beyond this,
many will surely cultivate virtue and diligent study.
"Furthermore,
for all officials in post,
those committing public offenses
should be dealt with according to law;
those guilty of corruption and bribery,
if not deserving death,
after serving sentences or upon amnesty,
should all be confined for life,
or at least twenty years for lighter cases.
Thus,
unclean officials
will surely transform into Bó Yí and Shū Qí.
If officials take bribes in office,
amassing mountains of gold,
and upon discovery can easily secure relief,
returning to post within days after dismissal—
even Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú would turn into Dào Zhí.
In that case,
even if all recommended scholars are qualified,
it cannot compensate for the poor quality of officials."
Someone said:
"Eloquence need not match action;
even if one passes classic tests and policy responses,
must they possess administrative talent?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The ancients used archery to select men,
how much more so classical learning?
If we discard this,
I see no better method than this.
Lush grass does not flourish in barren soil,
great fish do not live in small waters,
wise sayings do not come from mediocre mouths,
lofty writings do not fall from stubborn brushes.
Thus, unrolling the 'Hóng Fàn' reveals Jīzǐ's capacity for statecraft,
perusing the nine strategies shows Fàn Jū's vision for governing,
studying Guǎn Zhòng's texts
clarifies his ability to quell chaos,
reading Shēn Bùhài's writings
shows his mastery of kingly rule.
Now, if Xiàolián must be tested on classics without error,
and Xiùcái must answer policy questions without missing the point,
they cannot remain obscure or ignorant.
Fine generals of high rank are chosen for courage,
yet still tested with policy questions—
how much more so literary scholars?
Even if we cannot guarantee all are worthy and capable,
it must be better than no testing at all.
Now, let all under heaven due for recommendation
dare not neglect diligent study.
This alone,
its lasting benefit to customs and education,
is not small.
If the realm fears the cost of reckless recommendations,
if all cease seeking by luck,
turn from competing for trivialities,
return to the root of learning,
Confucian principles will greatly flourish,
private bribes will gradually cease,
rare talents can be employed,
and offices will not remain vacant."
Someone said:
"You wish to tighten examination laws,
but the penalty of confinement,
is harsh and severe,
frightening many.
Tight reins and frequent whipping
are not Bó Lè's way;
strict defenses and harsh laws
are shameful in virtuous governance."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Medicines that fill the bones and supplement the flesh
are excellent for nourishing the body and prolonging life,
but cannot rescue one from the urgency of sunstroke or drowning.
Administrations that emphasize tolerance and包容污垢
may suffice to govern the simple and honest,
but cannot save from the changes of decline and decay.
When tigers and wolves press upon you,
if you do not brandish spears and wield swords,
but instead play the qín and chant poetry,
I have never seen one's person preserved thereby.
When a blazing fire reaches the house,
if you do not run to fetch water,
but instead bow and yield, circling about,
I have never seen the fire extinguish itself.
Now to discuss this with those who wish to sell their strategies,
is to discuss catching thieves with Zhí."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"Now the whole land is unified under one rule,
the nine regions share the same customs;
the king's institutions and government decrees
truly ought to be uniform.
Even small measures and vessels
cannot be allowed to differ frequently,
how much more the standards for men of talent,
can they be uneven and without restraint?
Though the region south of the Yangtze is distant,
closely bordering the sea corner,
yet it has been imbued with the transforming Way,
following ritual and teaching,
for already over a thousand years.
Though temporarily separated in the past,
it was not a full century,
and the affairs of Confucian learning
were not entirely neglected either.
Only because its territory is narrower than the Central Plains,
thus the number of men of talent
cannot equal theirs in quantity.
But as for those high in virtuous conduct and talent,
such as Zǐyóu and Zhòngrèn and their kind,
they have not been inferior to those of the upper states.
In the past when the scholars of Wú were newly subjugated,
their tribute scholars were suppressed by not being examined.
Now peace has lasted nearly forty years,
yet still they are not examined,
thereby causing the Confucian pursuits of the southeast to decline compared to the past.
This treats them the same as the left-lapped barbarian tribes,
it is not the way to distinguish them.
Moreover, the noble man still loves others with ritual,
how much more should he, as their kind and easy-going parent!
Laws can invite trouble,
decrees can damage transformation,
this is what is meant.
Now if tribute scholars are never again examined,
then they will all surely cultivate appearances and compete,
vying for empty fame;
who would again open books to receive learning?
This is what is called: to indulge them is precisely to ruin them.
"There are those whose nature inherently loves antiquity,
whose hearts delight in arts and literature.
They study not for salary,
savoring the Way, forgetting poverty,
like Fǎ Gāoqīng and Zhōu Shēngliè.
Those whose learning is refined yet do not serve, pursuing glory and profit,
are one in ten thousand.
As for the likes of Nìng Yuè, Ní Kuān, Huáng Bà,
the reason they strongly forced themselves to diligently pursue the classics,
was not by natural inclination,
but all due to suffering and hardship,
wishing to extricate themselves through classical studies.
Had it not been the era of Emperor Hàn Wǔ,
then the likes of Zhū Màichén and Yán Zhù
would not necessarily have studied books.
Now if the path to wealth and honor
fortunately has easier ways than studying,
and they fundamentally lack a natural love for it,
would they be willing to labor in vain,
holding brooms as students,
traveling far to seek teachers and inquire about the Way?
In an age of rising military affairs,
martial prowess is valued, civil arts dormant;
common people view Confucian scholars as slaves,
seeing classical texts as dirt and dust—
why is this?
Because reputation and benefit lie elsewhere.
Not using them is like selling ceremonial caps among the Yuè barbarians,
or parading bearded snakes in Huáxià.
Now if near and far were treated uniformly,
with clear examinations and tests,
then many would surely carry satchels a thousand lǐ
to seek teachers and friends,
converting the expenses of ritual gifts
to buy records and texts—
this would not wait till day's end."
Bàopúzǐ said:
Men of talent and learning fit for the xiùcái and xiàolián selections
are already hard to come by.
Even if such men, as in the Huán and Líng emperors' time,
were recommended as officials without first using wealth and goods
to secure favor with the ministry chiefs,
then even if they mastered all classics with commentaries,
and answered every question posed,
they would still be falsely accused,
prevented from passing.
I often regret that the authorities then
did not seriously guard against this.
I propose that for the new year's tribute examinations,
this year we should have Confucian officials and talented scholars
prepare various policy questions in advance,
sufficient for comprehensive use.
Collect them, forbid keeping drafts, store them in the palace,
seal them shut;
at the examination time,
promptly assign them.
Thus personal influences and connections are cut off.
Those due to answer policy questions
should all be gathered in one place,
with high-selected officials from the ministries personally supervising.
Also strictly prohibit communication and movement,
dismissing them only after completion.
Violators will be punished without pardon.
Thus,
the wings of favoritism are blocked.
An enlightened ruler relies on his own inability to be deceived,
not on others not deceiving him.
Why then feel ashamed to strictly enforce this system?
If the method of examining classics is established,
then the empire need not establish school officials,
and people will diligently pursue learning joyfully themselves.
According to the Four Categories, there is also clear understanding of laws and decrees;
now among those in office,
regardless of rank,
all are ignorant of laws and decrees.
Some have subtle words hard to comprehend,
and petty officials are often stubborn;
to have them decide legal cases,
entrusting them with life and death matters,
lightly treating the people's lives,
is to hand them to the ignorant.
When senior officials do not know the law,
deceived by subordinates unknowingly,
and also deciding their oral and written statements,
confused and unable to understand the law applied,
whether they eat or not, ask or not,
not assigning it to the responsible officer—
some judge cases by whim,
stumbling, not careful about laws and decrees—
we could also have honest and good officials
all take those who understand the statutes and test them like examining classics,
employing the higher ones according to their ability and rank.
Thus,
the empire will surely have fewer officials manipulating the law,
and fewer unjust legal cases."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"In the friendships of companions,
they should not be superficial and promiscuous.
Facial without heart—
Yáng Xióng criticized this.
Therefore, even if one is prominent in rank and famous,
matching in family status and age,
but if our paths differ in principle,
and pursuits and aspirations conflict,
I have never bonded with them.
Some are proud of their early advancement,
walking high, looking far;
some neglect old friends in decline,
or scorn and discard later acquaintances as vulgar;
some judge people by office, not discussing virtue;
if one does not encounter a true friend,
withering in rural obscurity,
even if deeply talented and wise,
with pure conduct and high integrity,
it is impossible;
if one's advancement happens to coincide,
with prominent rank and official access,
even if ignorant and mediocre,
they will surely associate.
Such people,
though they can make soil insects fly like clouds,
or quails soar to the sky,
holding knife and ruler in hand,
speaking fortune or disaster with their mouth,
gaining which makes ice bloom,
losing which withers in spring,
I find their chattering spine-chilling,
ashamed to share the same age with them."
Poverty and success,
cannot be sought.
Yet frivolous individuals,
those without distinction,
lack the integrity to swiftly criticize faults,
instead traveling by starlight at night,
guarding the gateways,
flattering with ingratiating smiles,
using humble words and pleasing expressions,
carrying wine and gifts,
constantly seeking to curry favor;
after long toil and accumulation,
they are still met with rejection and refusal,
so they resort to relying on elders to mediate connections.
When accepted,
their joy exceeds that of prisoners released from confinement;
when rejected,
their distress is sharper than the grief of illness or bereavement.
Success and obstruction are fated,
the Way values integrity,
prosperity and adversity are left to nature,
why trouble over the paths and crossings?
Alas, petty people,
are they not despicable!
Human sentiments differ,
how far apart they are!
I often sigh with emotion,
feeling ashamed on their behalf.
In the past, Zhuāng Zhōu saw Huìzǐ's multitude of carriages,
and discarded his surplus fish.
I lament that worldly scholars are not diligent in striving for the highest ideals.
Observing their endless bustle,
those galloping through the dust,
do not diligently build virtue and achievements,
nor focus on fundamentals and self-cultivation,
but instead seek high connections,
forming cliques,
claiming no principle is more crucial,
nor any contemporary matter more urgent.
They regard those who stand firm and independent
as awkward, stingy, and unrefined;
while those with servile expressions and fawning glances
are deemed knowledgeable about the times.
When this becomes custom and habit,
all chase after trivialities,
drifting and evading, rushing forward,
truly lamentable.
Some, with little virtue but high position,
arrogant and overambitious,
are startled by wealth and profit,
yet doze off at the sight of exceptional scholars.
Those in ragged clothes, leaning on staffs,
wearing coarse garments and carrying satchels,
even if their writings are brilliant and competitive,
their learning surpasses Róng's profundity,
are treated like dust and chaff,
without any welcome or guidance.
As for those like Chéng Zhèng, Wángsūn, Luó Póu and their ilk,
riding fat horses, clad in light silks,
bearing gold and jade,
even if their brushes cannot gather on paper,
unable to distinguish beans from wheat,
they are welcomed with haste,
spitting out food, gripping hair in eagerness.
I only regret not being in a position,
having an axe but no handle,
unable to cleanse the nation's filth to the four borders,
casting it to the northern wastes.
Though they may be illustrious,
their power to decide with authority can move mountains and drain seas,
their shouts can make clay statues ascend clouds,
approaching their gates,
I have no time for it.
Yet many lower their wills and put on pleasant faces,
crawling on knees to advance,
seeking friendship with such people,
hoping for their benefits.
How sad!
That people's intentions are so unequal,
how vast the gap in their worthiness!
The reason I, born in a sage's era, remain in hardship and lowliness,
originally looking back and seeing nothing,
now find others ahead, beyond reach,
is there no cause for it!
Yet if one's nature cannot endure it,
each follows their preferences,
living or dying by this,
I cannot change it.
Some may challenge:
"Times change, eras transform,
ancient and modern duties differ,
conduct is established by oneself,
fame is achieved through others.
Gold and jade cross unfathomable depths
by relying on light boats;
the divine bird gathers in the dark heavens
by the force of the whirlwind;
fragrant orchids emit strong scents
by the work of the clear breeze;
humble scholars rise from rural gardens
by the aid of understanding friends.
Now, sir, in your associations, you insist on clarifying conduct and career,
in your close ties, sifting hearts and natures,
standing alone and isolated,
losing and abandoning renowned circles,
making enemies for a lifetime,
incurring resentment from common customs,
does this align with harmonizing light to encompass all,
the noble principle of shared methods?
If friendships required matching wisdom,
then humble huts would not lower for the noble Duke of Zhōu;
if wanderings required equal talent,
then Confucius would have no disciples entering his chamber."
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"I have heard that those who befriend carefully do not lose people,
while those who associate broadly often regret later.
Thus, past sages first chose, then befriended,
not first befriended, then chose.
Your argument
is a strategy for advancement;
my adherence
is the will of a retiring scholar.
You speak of jade floating and birds soaring,
all having their reasons,
truly another school of thought.
I believe it's better to be an unpolished gem,
a roc that does not fly,
an orchid that does not waft,
a scholar without a faction—
does it
(what?)
diminish the substance of night-shining jade,
the vastness of the hanging sky,
the fragrant flora,
or the immortal orchid?
Moreover, when reputation exceeds reality,
position surpasses talent,
those holding it rarely escape disaster and disgrace;
how can associating with them bring honor and fortune!
"From this perspective,
befriending them and succeeding,
even if achieving status, is not honorable;
sheltering under them and erring
is like shading under a rotten tree about to collapse.
They cannot even prevent their own downfall,
how could they save me from shattering my head!
I have heard that a great man, self-possessed and detached from external things,
regards ordinary people
as forced encounters when unavoidable;
even if they number in thousands,
they are like fleas and lice accumulating on clothes,
or warts clustering on the body.
Losing them, even by tens of thousands,
is like flying dust leaving Mount Sōng and Tài,
or dead branches falling from the Dèng forest.
How can having them be beneficial,
or lacking them felt as a loss?
"Moreover, friends
must be chosen for integrity, honesty, and broad knowledge,
rectifying omissions and rejecting errors,
in life, no words of plea,
in death, no excuses,
consistent from start to end,
unchanging through heat and cold.
Yet such people are truly hard to find,
some silent, some speaking, on different paths,
some with differing loves and hates in heart,
some close in prosperity, distant in decline,
some forgetting trust at sight of profit.
In today's world,
they are like birds and fish forming companions,
ice and charcoal sharing a vessel—
hoping for lasting union,
how can it be achieved!
Even father and son, by nature,
should share likes and dislikes,
yet Yán Huí and Zǐsī,
differed in fair judgment;
Nánshān Bóqí,
debated right and wrong.
Faces apart, hearts divergent,
this has long been so.
To lump them all together,
is it not difficult!
"Worldly people,
in friendships, do not consider ideals,
chasing fame and following trends,
warm when coming, cold when leaving;
seeing faults, they do not correct them,
observing confusion, they do not rescue;
with benefits, they monopolize without sharing,
with harm, they evade and do not sympathize;
if an opportunity arises, they take first without yielding,
facing a chance, they sell others to secure themselves.
In all such cases,
it is better to have none than such friends."
"It is not that the world entirely lacks worthy individuals to befriend,
but those who bring benefit are few while those who create burdens are many.
The wisdom to discern others' character,
even the greatest sages find difficult.
To strive to encourage nearby talents,
yet be deficient in judging people,
and insist on broadening one's social connections,
while wanting them all to be individuals
who can endure hardships without changing their devotion,
share dangers and bear burdens together—
I have not seen such people to be plentiful.
Though one might search for fine jade on molehills,
or seek phoenixes in wrens' nests,
it would not be as difficult.
How dare I claim that south of Lántián,
or within the Cinnabar Cave,
such things do not exist!
I merely state their rarity."
"People's principles differ,
just as gold sinks and feathers float.
The divergence in aspirations and preferences,
is like fire rising and water descending.
If they cannot be aligned,
even the ingenuity of Creation,
the craftsmanship of the Great Mass,
cannot make them the same—
how can they be forced?
My innate nature is slow and dull,
added to a Heaven-bestowed earnestness and laziness;
all playful pastimes,
such as弹棋 and board games,
I detest witnessing;
and activities like running swiftly,
hunting, and arrogant sightseeing,
I do none of them;
I particularly dislike jesting and frivolity.
All these things
are what the current age favors,
and none fail to indulge in them,
yet I lack them all,
hence my close friendships are especially distant.
Moreover, being straightforward,
I am inclined to speak loyal and sincere words,
which, like medicine and stones,
few gladly accept.
Also, I wish to urge others with learning,
admonish them against rushing and competing,
stop their gambling,
restrain their indulgence in drink—
these are things ordinary people do not enjoy.
"To break one's squareness and blend like tiles,
going against one's feelings to conform to customs,
requires effort that people cherish,
which I greatly cannot bear.
And to expect daily improvement in friendships,
how can it be achieved?
Knowing this yet not debating or changing it,
can it not be said to be ignorant of the times,
clumsy in handling great matters?
Starting friendships but not finishing them,
uniting only to part again,
then both parties suffer a reputation for lack of magnanimity,
and lose the beauty of a complete end.
With depth, affection arises;
with shallowness, grievances form—
this is the natural principle.
Should one not choose carefully?
To clap backs at banquets,
hold hands briefly,
wanting many in number and all to be perfect—
this is what I fear."
Someone said:
"Then can one do without friendships altogether?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"How can that be!
Why must those who fear water abandon boats and oars?
Why must those wary of injury discard axes and adzes?
The way of friendship
has been esteemed since ancient times.
If heaven and earth do not interact, there is no peace;
if superiors and inferiors do not communicate, wills diverge.
Without peace, the two energies are blocked;
with divergent wills, the state loses its foundation.
Yet starting is very easy,
ending is ultimately difficult.
The worry lies in bonding with the wrong person,
failing over small disputes while forgetting greater matters.
The Yì jīng praises numerous orchids,
the Shī jīng sings of a hundred friends;
though one has brothers,
they are not like friends.
Reflecting on the three beneficial friendships,
the great sage commended them;
they increase closeness among disciples,
and prevent harsh words from arising;
they are the force by which Guǎn Zhòng avoided execution and achieved hegemonic success,
and Zǐ Yuán left his low post to ride in a red carriage.
Such is the power of friendship.
"A single string cannot produce the harmonious sounds of Sháo and Xià;
one color cannot create the brilliance of the dragon robe;
one flavor cannot match the sweetness of Yī's cauldron;
a lone tree cannot achieve the lushness of the Dèng Forest.
The Xuánpǔ Garden reaches the sky,
truly by the accumulation of many stones.
The Southern Sea is vast and boundless,
indeed requiring the convergence of numerous streams.
Raise a bright mirror, and tilted caps are seen;
let Xīhé shine, and crooked shadows are noticed;
apply the straightening tool, and warped thorns are corrected;
form good friendships, and the way of supporting benevolence is expanded.
The enlightened know this,
so in seeking companions, they choose those better than themselves;
in forming bonds, they select those with shared aspirations.
In seclusion, they discuss the Way and advance virtue;
in public, they unite hearts and soar together.
In obscurity, they engage in fishing and farming;
in prosperity, they collaborate on worldly affairs.
In safety, they refine righteousness;
in danger, they support each other.
Ashamed to let Tán and Kěn monopolize the depth of face-to-earth sincerity,
not allowing Wáng and Gòng to独占 the beauty of dusting off hats.
Thus,
the value of friendship is esteemed.
"Yet truly, it is not easy to know others;
power and profit give rise to partings;
accumulated slander ruins neck-cutting covenants;
gradual erosion dissolves the strength of glue and lacquer.
Hence, there are sighs over forgotten pure feelings,
or grudges over minor slights;
thus, the bond of Yuán Bó and Jù Qīng
is uniquely celebrated in the past;
the betrayal between Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú
is repeatedly seen today.
Reflecting on the past and anticipating the future,
it is truly lamentable.
The phoenix does not perch on the same branch as owls;
the qilin does not herd with wolves;
clear springs do not mix with muddy floods;
the benevolent and wise do not dwell with the cruel and dark.
Why?
Gradual influence shifts straight paths,
and close proximity to violence breeds harm."
Someone asked:
"May I ask, can the way to maintain perfect friendships be explained?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"A noble person, even when ending a friendship, uses no harsh words;
how much less would they speak differently to those they differ with?
They would die for a friend;
how could they compete for fame and status?
In good friendships, be intimate but not disrespectful,
harmonious but not identical.
When seeing faults in others,
admonish them with a serious expression;
when told of one's own errors,
quickly reform without resentment.
Do not refrain from speaking due to offending others;
do not reject advice due to grating on one's ears;
do not use clever arguments to cover wrongs;
do not employ flowery words to gloss over faults;
do not appear alike while spirits diverge;
do not feign agreement while hearts disagree;
do not agree face-to-face and resent behind backs;
do not envy others' superiority;
shield their shortcomings and highlight their strengths;
conceal their failures and proclaim their successes;
externally, avoid contentious calculations;
internally, discard the burden of heart rivalry.
Only then is the goodness of 'The Deer Cry' preserved,
and the criticism of 'Felling Trees' ceases.
If one lightly joins without valuing separation,
easily deepens ties but finds thinning difficult,
starting as close as body and shadow,
ending as distant as stars apart,
utmost joy turning to deep hatred,
assistance becoming enmity—
the regret of not being cautious
is unavoidable.
In the past, the Hàn dynasty declined,
the imperial reins slackened,
public duty was neglected,
and a custom of rivalry formed.
To oppose the times was considered noble;
to save the world was seen as self-disgrace.
Rituals between noble and base were ruined,
and great ethical order fell into chaos.
Those in power
did not strive to fulfill their duties;
they abandoned fundamentals for trivialities,
turning from substance to seek reputation.
Those who neglected royal affairs were praised;
those accumulating deceit were credited with great achievements.
All flew on wheels with doubled whips,
traveling by starlight without sleep,
braving cold and heat,
to rush to powerful doors,
buying empty fame from influential mouths,
purchasing undue positions from families selling offices.
Some fought over desires,
even slaughtering each other."
Thus, Gōngshū Wěicháng was distressed by such circumstances,
but lacked the power to rectify them,
and could not bear to witness it.
So he vented his frustration by writing a treatise,
closed his doors and severed social ties—
this was indeed driven by righteous indignation and purpose.
Yet it was like straightening a crooked pole by bending it too far the other way,
not an enduring principle for normal conduct.
One should merely avoid factions of incompatible kinds
and guard against the roots of flattery and corruption.
Why must one strip naked to defy others,
or cease eating grains to criticize fine cuisine?
When social interactions go awry,
repeated remonstrance fails to stop it,
leading eventually to great chaos.
Thus, what ritual and righteousness reject
may rightly be severed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The swift Yǎoniǎo can strain its sinews to outrun shadows,
but cannot tread on ice or traverse depths;
the fierce tiger can roar like thunder while hunting,
but cannot leap through clouds to soar in the void.
The great swan cannot flap its wings within a cage,
nor the nimble falcon strike like lightning beneath low eaves.
If this is true for creatures,
so it is for humans.
Thus, one who harmonizes yīn and yáng
may not master all conducts or refine documents;
one who expounds the Five Constants and Nine Virtues
need not excel in minor purities or trivial rules.
Huìzǐ,
a model for chief ministers,
could not steer a boat across turbulent waves;
Hàn Gāozǔ,
a paragon of divine prowess,
could not manage estates or uphold discipline;
Huáiyīn,
foremost among fine generals,
could not farm or trade to avoid hunger and cold;
Zhōu Bó,
a pillar of the state,
could not answer queries on finances or legal cases.
If we discard strengths for weaknesses,
then transcendent talents will go unused;
if we demand perfection in minor rites,
then world-saving achievements will be obscured.
Heaven cannot flatten its northwest,
Earth cannot raise its southeast,
sun and moon cannot shine into crooked caves,
nor gales stir waves in a well’s depths.
To pick teeth, pine and catalpa are less useful than a short bamboo sliver;
to clean ears, beams and pillars比不上 a wren’s feather;
to shoot birds, gold is less valuable than a clay pellet;
to sew, a long sword比不上 a few-inch needle.
Why tether an elephant to catch mice,
or leash a great Péng bird to herald dawn?
Thus, Jiāng Yá sold refreshments
(possibly “gruel”) unsold,
yet became mentor to Wén and Wǔ;
Jiǎng Shēng fumbled as a minor official,
yet later strode alone among the highest ranks.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Elegant writings and lush prose
are not for the blind to enjoy;
outstanding talents
are not for the shallow to recognize.
If vision cannot perceive things,
then imperial robes and coarse hemp seem equal;
if discernment cannot engage,
then the brilliant and the平庸 are deemed alike.
Eyes that do not see
miss beauty that stirs the soul;
where none befriend,
harm soon arrives.
Moreover, loves and hates, preferences and aversions,
differ across ages;
times change, customs shift,
the same object holds varying worth.
Like the Huáng jade of Xiàhòu,
once valued at linked cities,
if sold today,
would be cheaper than copper or iron.
Thus, past eras honored recluses seeking virtue,
while today mountain-dwelling scholars are deemed unworthy.
So a pillar of a sage age
becomes a criminal in benighted times;
the integrity of yesteryears
becomes weakness in decadent eras.
Great individuals,
those who walk the path,
their lofty faith is not just a wall many ren high,
their profound depth not merely like the Lǚliáng abyss,
thus the shortsighted cannot appreciate them,
and the shallow cannot fathom them.
Hence, they are scorned for differing from the norm,
and hated for not seeking favor;
if unvalued and unused,
what more need be said?
Some even cast dust on white jade,
raise blemishes on jade-like skin,
mock flaws in unison,
attack those who stand alone,
as Zēng Shēn bore robbery’s stigma,
Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu suffered slander of theft.
Unless one’s clarity rivals hanging stars,
with mystic vision to reveal subtleties,
how can one sift mud to extract submerged jade,
or clear streams to pick sinking pearls?
If jade tablets in markets go unsold,
how much more when hidden in unhewn stone?
If a rare scholar knocking on horns is rejected,
how much more when buried in obscure pastures?
Sūn Bìn longed to display his strategies,
but Sīmǎ cut his feet;
Hán Fēi wished to achieve governance,
but Lǐ Sī killed him;
Jiǎ Yì, passionate,
bearing statecraft methods,
was spurned by warriors;
Zǐ Zhèng, loyal and good,
equipped to save crises,
was ensnared by Gōng and Xiǎn.
This is why Hé Shì hugged his uncut jade and wept blood,
and Qín Xī vented fury by dashing his head.
Now jade and stone are easier to distinguish than worthiness and folly,
yet love for treasure runs deeper than for talents.
With easily distinguishable treasure,
matched by deep affection,
still one may suffer severed toes,
and slander across generations.
How much more for hard-to-know sages,
not urgently desired,
where slanderers paint snake feet on the formless,
and treacherous ministers fear loyalty harming them,
as the crooked dread the carpenter’s line,
and the naked at night hate bright candles.
Thus, high praise and fine conduct
are suppressed, unraised;
fabricated slanders
take shape before the fact.
Without a Chǔ man’s weeping recommendation,
one in ten thousand never meets chance,
which is only fitting.
Those who mistake jade for stone
will also take stone for jade;
those who deem the wise foolish
will also call fools wise.
Taking stone as jade
brings no great harm;
but taking fools as wise
is a symptom of ruin.
For a state showing such symptoms, though existing, will surely fall,
as a pulse indicating death means life is doomed.
Can we not be cautious?
Alas,
how sorrowful!
None reflect on this.
Of old, even Confucius, a supreme sage,
was hindered in the east by men of Qí,
blocked in the south by Zǐxī.
Wén Zhǒng, a great worthy,
was initially scorned in Chǔ customs,
later wandering idly by fishing lines.
To achieve merit in competitive times,
is it not difficult?
Gems like Jiélǜ and Xuánlí
only a Táo or Yī could purchase;
a weight of a thousand jūn
only a Bēn or Huò could lift.
The melody “White Snow”
only a Líng or Sù could play;
a talent surpassing peers
only an enlightened ruler can employ.
Yet the pearl that glows in night’s darkness
does not diminish its quality for lack of seekers,
to cheapen itself in market;
the great bell and Zhōu tripod
do not lighten their substance if buried,
to be lifted by dwarfs;
the Yuèyáng and Yúnhé zithers
do not cease their music if unplayed,
to compete with vulgar tunes;
a virtue crowning the crowd
does not, though submerged, take shortcuts,
or compromise with common trends.
Thus, the Hé jade becomes stagnant goods,
pliant timber is discarded as useless,
the ore for a red dagger
never enters Ōu Yě’s forge;
the group of Yuán and Kǎi
ultimately miss the call at the four gates.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
I have a friend named Jūlíng Xiānshēng,
who is serene, content, tranquil, and plain,
with form and spirit so harmonized that they forget each other,
outwardly not adorning himself with a countenance to startle the foolish,
inwardly not harboring a mind that seeks to contain everything.
He immerses his spirit in the ancient classics and edicts,
finding such joy that he forgets all sorrows.
By day, he competes for the last rays of Xīhé's sunlight,
by night, he basks in the lingering glow of Wàngshū's moon,
no path is too distant for him to explore,
no word too subtle for him to scrutinize.
Yet, his carriage tracks never mark the lands of the powerful and influential,
his letters never pass through the courts of the noble and mighty.
Thus, his fame does not extend beyond his humble door,
his person never leaves the fields and farmlands.
Thereupon, Yìliàng Dàfū waited and challenged him, saying:
"I have heard that when the hidden dragon arises, dark clouds gather to attend it,
and when the transformative rain of the Way moistens the earth, extraordinary talents flourish.
Thus, on the broad highways, there are songs of success,
and from the sacrificial tripods and stands, traces of soaring ambition emerge.
If offered for sale, one can reap immeasurable wealth,
if spurred on, one can surpass the highest advancements.
Shine your brilliant light in the Valley of the Rising Sun,
spread your great brightness across the nine heavens.
Achieve merits that overshadow the present age,
let your reputation resound without end.
For the path that is but a few feet away, if one does not tread it,
even feet that chase the wind cannot reach it;
beneath the pillars and beams, though most lowly, if one does not move,
even the wings of a swan or a phoenix cannot attain it.
How much more so if one rests their feet in the remote wilderness,
folds their wings on the dark branches of the parasol tree,
how can one emulate speed to chase the light,
or flap lightly to rise into the azure skies?
The years of life pass swiftly and do not last long,
existence in this world drifts rapidly and does not return,
the wise, treading on frost, know that solid ice is sure to come,
at the beginning, they realize that all living things must have an end.
The six dragons hasten their course in the great chaos,
the flowery peak suddenly announces the dusk,
this is why the ancients, reflecting on the flowing stream, turned to sigh,
gazing at the passing gap, were moved to sorrow.
You, sir, possess the extraordinary capacity of a generation-defining talent,
embodying brilliance and greatness that surpass the ordinary,
your sharp intellect surges like waves,
your six stratagems lie suppressed, stored in deep abysses;
yet you cannot ride the whirlwind to soar high,
or raise your pure radiance to the nine mysteries,
your vessel is not displayed among the sacrificial utensils,
your body is not spared the toil of carrying firewood,
as if playing harmonious music in a land of the deaf,
selling ceremonial caps in a region where people wear their hair loose.
In vain, you forget to awaken in the literary forest,
intently focusing on exhausting the divine,
cherishing fine jade within your bosom,
spilling pearls and gems from the tip of your brush,
personally suffering the frugality of constant emptiness,
your spirit wearied by the pursuit of firm heights,
it is like burying a foot-long jade disc under heavy soil,
sealing brocade in layered chests,
ultimately without the wealth of exchange,
who will appreciate the treasure hidden in obscurity?
"If a dragon-steed is tethered,
how can it be distinguished from a lame donkey;
if a red blade sheathes its edge,
how is it different from a leaden knife.
The sturgeon does not dwell in ox hoofprints,
the great peng bird does not linger in蒿 thickets.
I hope, sir, that you will leave the dragon-snake's den,
ascend the path of advantage and visibility,
forsake the solitary purity of your doorstep,
observe the two mice and awaken to distant truths,
cross the desolate valley to climb high,
don bright colors to change your plain attire,
compete with the startling gale at dawn,
not circling about and missing the mark,
gather fame and honor in lofty places,
resonate with the celebratory blessings of bells and tripods.
Bó Chéng was but a solitary figure,
is picking ferns truly worthy of much admiration?"
Jūlíng Xiānshēng replied:
"I have heard that the workings of the spirit are profound and distant,
chaotic, vast, and obscure,
fortune and misfortune intertwine in the space between reliance and潜伏,
rise and fall are entangled in the meeting of fullness and emptiness;
the swift runner cannot escape the shadow chasing his body,
the one who delights in success cannot avoid the collapse that follows logic;
those who rectify the flow at its end,
are not as good as those who stand firm in governance before signs appear;
those who tidy up what has already occurred,
cannot match those who return to the root beyond primal simplicity.
Therefore, those who understand the inchworm,
gladly bend to preserve extension;
those who recognize通畅 and blockage,
do not grieve or rejoice over adversity and prosperity.
Moreover, the great potter molds things,
the great image flows into forms,
the restless and the calm have different preferences,
soaring and sinking diverge in nature.
Gold and treasures value their heaviness,
feathers pride themselves on their lightness.
The narrow-minded are bound by filth and defilement; the profoundly subtle wander freely in the mysterious and pure.
The stagnant pond接纳 runoff and overflows,
the vast sea吞 hundred rivers yet never fills.
Minnows and shrimp leap joyfully in the mud,
the red dragon soars fiercely in the high heavens.
Those who chew on fragrant bait,
satisfy their desires and rush to their death;
those who savor emptiness and blandness,
embrace heavenly harmony and move toward life;
those who recognize the divine opportunity,
foresee the absence of signs and are not confused;
those who are blind to good and ill fortune,
touch a strong crossbow and are not alarmed.
Each adheres to what they prefer,
how could they be willing to change their pursuits?
"I have heard that the five jades cannot cut themselves out from Mount Sōng's peaks,
the flying snake cannot glide like lightning without mist,
the dragon's abyss cannot sever rhinoceros without being wielded,
the great bell cannot emit a洪 sound without being struck.
Golden mushrooms need the autumn wind to shimmer brilliantly,
the oriole awaits the warmth of spring to sing beautifully,
the fine steed does not recklessly gallop into danger,
the nobleman does not achieve goals deceitfully to ruin his name.
When fate is blocked, one sinks into disuse,
when the time is right, one soars high in the heavenly court.
A scholar considers self-promotion as not noble,
a woman considers self-matchmaking as not chaste.
Why must one abandon the lofty standard of washing the ears,
and imitate the dry glory of bearing the sacrificial stand?
In times of poverty,
then Yǒu Yú danced contentedly while potting and fishing,
Shàngfǔ was driven away by a foolish old woman,
Fàn Shēng came to be humiliated by a drowning basket,
Hóng Shì hid his奇 talents in plowing and herding;
and when they achieved success,
then Huáiyīn cast aside his fishing rod and became a lord,
Wén Zhǒng removed his straw sandals and wore the blue绶,
Fù Yuè left his mortar to discuss the Way,
Guǎnzǐ shed his fetters to become a high minister.
For the nobleman hides his talent to await the right moment,
accumulates virtue to have the means to act,
not appearing when the time is not right,
not serving a ruler who is not his own,
poverty and success depend on what one encounters,
advancement and withdrawal are not bound by attachment.
In stillness,
he becomes the model for recluses;
in action,
he stands as the paragon of the Yuán and Kǎi.
Some apply their thoughts to establishing words,
others inscribe their merits on the vessels of the state.
Different paths lead to the same end,
their ultimate aim is one.
"A scholar can perform deeds worthy of honor,
but cannot make society necessarily honor him;
he can possess talent fit for use,
but cannot make the world necessarily use him.
Wearing coarse cloth, eating plants, setting traps for rabbits,
then his heart is joyful and content,
as if he will live this way终身,
wearing official caps, riding in light carriages,
adorned in vermilion and double purple,
then it is as if he has always had them.
Always like a commoner in spirit,
this is the mindset of the ultimate man.
If the treasures on the mat are not accumulated,
if the integrity within the narrow walls is not pure,
it is my fault.
If those who understand are few,
fame and position do not come,
if jade is taken for stone,
if the phoenix is called a quail,
it is not my fault.
To be anxious about being recognized,
distressed by stagnation and obstruction,
is the sentiment of the common people;
to nurture one's spirit with vastness,
to be淡 and free from desires,
is the aspiration of the无忧.
When the time comes, the Way is practiced,
those with great capacity do not rejoice excessively;
between heaven and earth,
those who know fate do not worry.
As for pursuing goods worth ten thousand in gold,
only to seek a sale for a hundred or ten,
often losing the essence for the trivial,
I have no time for such things."
A disciple asked:
"I have heard that in the late Hàn dynasty,
during the reigns of Líng and Xiàn,
the evaluation of characters was perverse and excessive,
the heroic and exceptional were impoverished and stagnant,
the greedy and gluttonous gained their ambitions,
names did not match reality,
value was not based on the substance,
considering those who were connected as worthy,
and those who were cold and isolated as foolish.
What was the reason for this?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The rumbling of thunderous chariots
may go unheard by some;
the seven luminaries traversing the heavens
may go unseen by others.
How could this be solely due to physical deafness or blindness!
The obscurations of mind and spirit
are likewise so.
Thus, those who hear profound sayings yet fail to comprehend
are not without ears;
those who witness extraordinary brilliance yet remain unknowing
are not without eyes;
it stems from their hearing not reaching the subtle,
and their sight not grasping the exceptional.
Those with great wisdom and far-reaching vision
stand firm like mountains;
those with petty capacities and narrow aspirations
drift like floating duckweed.
Precisely because they are mountain-like,
nothing can shake them;
precisely because they are duckweed-like,
they flow without stagnation.
Comparing them to goods,
those sealed and stored awaiting sale -
only the most precious remain difficult to vend;
those advertised with drumbeats -
though common and flawed, are quickly exhausted.
Measuring them as timber,
those rooted in Sōng and Dài peaks
though towering a thousand ren high,
casting shade over ten thousand mu,
remain unrecognized;
while saplings planted along main roads
though crooked, twisted, and quick to decay,
still find employment.
Thus ancestral temples contain ritual vessels of withered poplar,
while remote valleys hold uncut catalpas and oaks.
Therefore those stealing false glory
soar like lizards into the clouds;
those losing true worth
sink like jade dragons into the abyss.
Hence quails ride winds to soar high,
while divine phoenixes fold wings in hidden retreat;
lead blades fill the treasured Tài'ē scabbards,
as dogs and sheep usurp the roles of tigers and wolves.
The artful deploy precious bribes as strong wings -
then no height remains beyond reach;
ride factional alliances as boats -
then no distance remains un-crossed.
Sustained by dawn-rising vigilance,
enhanced by anticipatory flattery,
their glib adulation resembles eloquence;
their hearsay peddling resembles scholarship;
their sinister hearts and gentle appearances resemble benevolence;
their foul deeds and clean words resemble integrity;
their eagerness to expose others' faults resembles loyalty;
their disregard for taboos resembles frankness -
thus they often prosper.
Moreover, those who respect me
wish to benefit me,
while those who ignore me
cannot earn my affection -
this is natural principle.
"The worthy are always few while fools are many;
the multitude band together concealing flaws,
the few stand isolated without support.
Sycophants mutually promote blocking righteous paths,
while sages in low positions go unrecognized.
The principle of uprooting weeds collapses,
as hordes of incompetents rise;
