the soaring dragon falls from heights,
weeping blood in endless streams.
Thus Zǐxī banished the supreme sage Confucius,
Zāng Cāng slandered the era-defining Mèng Kē.
These two sages could not escape such misfortune -
how much less worth mentioning those beneath them!
This calamity likely emerged with creation itself,
plaguing more than just one age.
Surveying ancient times,
we mostly find this same affliction.
When lame nags raise heads in royal chariots,
while thoroughbreds herd in remote woodlands;
when incompetents enjoy sinecures,
the state withers in distress;
subordinates usurp while superiors decline -
truly this is the cause.
Some lie worm-ridden unburied,
some flee to Shēn and Hài's domains,
some hang tendons from temple beams,
some meet doom at Wàngyí Palace -
all from promoting the false,
while neglecting loyal competence.
"Thus enlightened rulers labor to summon worthies,
eagerly selecting the exceptional;
clearing obstructions,
strictly preventing blockages.
Where talent proves truly trustworthy,
they ignore butcher or fisherman origins;
where counsel proves soundly applicable,
they extract it from garrison troops.
Some raised from beneath oxen's mouths
are elevated above officials;
some rescued from shackles
are entrusted with state重任.
Thus they achieve glorious merit,
expanding territories pacifying distant lands,
gaining authority establishing achievements,
establishing enduring legacies.
"The straightening cord
is hated by warped timber;
the pure and impartial
are enemies of the treacherous.
If rulers cannot employ profound mirrors to detect hidden truths,
they must rely on powerful recommendations.
Yet observing past power-monopolizers,
their recommendations consistently favored allies,
their appointments prioritized self-interest.
They destroy what they fear while advancing what they love;
what they fear embodies perfect impartiality,
what they love shares their selfishness.
Perfect impartiality employed breaks factions,
widespread selfishness established steals sovereign authority;
factions broken leads to flourishing peace,
sovereign authority stolen begins decline toward ruin.
Destroying what they fear, they worry accusations lack severity -
even amputating noses and feet
still fails to satisfy,
so elimination alone brings relief;
advancing what they love, they suffer praise's inadequacy -
even promoting beyond rank
still fails to gratify,
so endangering others secures themselves.
Thus the innocent die wronged,
the blameless get dismissed -
this has always existed.
"Therefore those embodying Dao uniting with truth,
towering in solitary excellence,
with transcendent talent and measure,
embracing frost treading ice,
thoughts spanning heaven and earth,
capacities matching Yuán and Kǎi,
grasp classics behind humble gates,
deep as still waters firm as mountains.
They prefer purity preserving obscurity,
shaming sycophancy for shallow accord.
Finding joy in hunger within narrow alleys,
they cultivate noble integrity;
concealing abilities preserving authenticity,
they await heaven-allotted years' completion.
Not emerging in unpropitious times,
not acting against ritual.
Wearing coarse cloth chewing vegetables,
yet without depression;
reaching gray hairs in obscurity,
yet without resentment.
How could they compress Tài Mountain's cliffs
to fit mortise-and-tenon confines;
furl sky-shading wings
for crowing-rooster duties?
How could they join official ranks,
suppressed beneath mediocre youths?
Abandon phoenix groves
for thorny thickets,
compete with owls for rotten rats,
bending principles for petty gains!
"Moreover, great worthies appear extremely awkward,
their flavor profoundly plain,
serene self-sufficient,
placidly unassuming.
Known by few yet unworried,
unused by times yet unperturbed.
Though some days lack wild-herb soups,
they won't exchange for immoral feasts;
though hemp robes lack winter durability,
they refuse joy in unprincipled furs.
They'd rather loose hair rest high,
guarding what they already possess,
never bending backs lowering brows,
seeking what they don't yet need."
When virtue is shallow and position lofty,
he does not associate;
when name contradicts reality,
he does not draw close;
the chase after glory and splendor,
he does not pursue;
the powerful, knight-errant, crafty, and authoritative,
he does not engage with;
commonplace theories and trivial debates,
he does not answer;
the paths where shoulders are shrugged in flattery,
he does not follow.
In appearance foolish but in ambition far-reaching,
with a soiled face but pure conduct.
Firm as Mount Sōng and Tài,
no balance can measure him;
vast as the blue sea,
no bushel can gauge him.
Steep is his height of multiple ren,
concealed is his richness of a hundred officials.
Observing those frivolous thieves,
they are like wild grass.
His conduct transcending the world,
soars high above the autumn clouds;
his spirit abandoning customs,
dwells distantly at the edge of the Nine Mysteries.
Though poor and lowly,
he cannot be coerced by might;
though in peril and hardship,
he cannot be moved by profit.
"The endeavors he upholds,
can be heard of but not fully known;
the principles he holds fast to,
can be seen but not discussed.
Thus, those who resent him,
unite in voice and glare askance;
those who love him,
are few and weak and of no help.
It is like trying to fill a breached river with a handful of soil,
or extinguish a prairie fire with a liter of water.
Thus, the war drum silences the thunder's roar,
while the small drums indulge in the sound of large bells.
Fragrant orchids are cut down,
while stinking abalone is worn and cherished.
Dark aromatic wine is cast aside without shame,
while thin ale is poured exclusively at the Round Mound.
Sweating-blood steeds are driven away with drooping ears,
while lame donkeys gallop in imperial carriages.
This is why the ancients embraced stones and sand,
went to the flowing waters for fish-burial,
unable to bear sharing the same era.
Enough!
Alas!
"Yet discarding the dark Lí jade in the mud,
is not because the night-shining pearl is unreal,
but because none recognize it;
casting the red lú bow without bending it,
is not because the Fánruò bow lacks strength,
but because none appreciate it.
Thus, the Qióngyáo jade awaits a Jīng Hé to reveal its worth of linked cities,
the Wūhào bow needs a Péng Méng to demonstrate its power of piercing armor,
the flying rabbit horse waits for a Zǐyù to soar and gallop,
and the outstanding person meets a知己 to exert his strength.
If fine jade does not emerge from deep cliffs,
a good bow does not pierce a hundred layers of armor,
steeds like Jì and Lù do not pull vermilion carriages,
and a man destined for the age does not tread on nobility and power,
then who would know his ability to radiate brilliant colors,
to halt cloud-borne birds at a thousand ren,
to unleash extraordinary tracks chasing the wind,
and to achieve myriad merits in all affairs?
His lack of encounter,
also prevents him from being mixed with tiles and stones,
equally cheapened as rotten wood,
aligned with inferior steeds,
and regarded equally as common mediocrity!
Alas!
With a bow of brambles and arrows of thorns, hoping for a master archer in Qúguǎng,
driving a tired nag, seeking to follow the tracks of King Mù of Zhōu,
discarding axes and adzes, yet wanting double the skill of Bān and Mò,
neglecting fine talent, yet expecting the constant principles to be ordered,
is it not difficult?
Though fame and reality may be overlooked in one lifetime,
virtuous reputation can be sought in the future.
Rejoicing in heaven and knowing fate,
what worries and what sorrows?
Being content with the times and accepting one's lot,
what resentment and what regrets!
Bàopǔzǐ says:
It is often said that those with unmatched courage and strength
are the tools of great generals;
those well-versed in order and chaos
are the talents for the Three Ducal Offices and Nine Ministers.
Yet Zhāng Fēi and Guān Yǔ, a match for ten thousand men,
both lost their heads and brought disgrace to their lords,
dying in inappropriate places;
Kǒng Róng and Biān Ràng, whose literature surpassed the common,
yet neither understood governance,
failing wherever they were.
Dèng Yǔ, Mǎ Yuán, and Tián Kuàng were mere field scholars,
yet excelled in employing troops;
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn did not study the classics,
yet surpassed as chief ministers.
Thus, knowing people is indeed not easy.
To test them before employing,
risks the disaster of a broken leg and overturned tripod;
to judge by words and appearance,
may encounter the seemingly right but actually wrong,
with true and false mixed and confused.
Yet people consider it very easy,
passing through ears and eyes,
thinking they can grasp it thoroughly.
I am deeply skeptical of this,
and dare not agree.
Distinguishing good from bad,
observing form to capture spirit,
depends on the person,
and cannot be forced.
Unless one is as discerning as the sun and moon,
hearing the soundless,
it is advisable to clarify carefully,
advancing gradually in employment,
not appointing suddenly.
Lightly granting sharp tools,
once taken back is very difficult,
and the damage done is already great.
Do not rely on one incident to blindly guarantee the rest;
those who agree with you,
may not necessarily be usable;
those different from you,
may not necessarily be negligible.
Some may challenge:
"In heaven, there are hanging signs,
on earth, there are forms,
so gazing at mountains and measuring rivers,
their height and depth can be deduced;
wind rising and clouds flying,
good and bad fortune can be predicted.
The wise, seeing trees not withered,
realize fine jade is in the mountain;
seeing banks not dry,
sense bright pearls are in the deep.
When a comet appears,
one knows the sturgeon is about to die;
when the sun and moon are eclipsed,
one recognizes the Qílín are fighting.
Huà and Huò mountains need no praise,
for their boundless weight is known;
rivers need no measuring,
for their immeasurable depth is set.
The wings of the swan,
the feet of the Lùqí steed,
though not yet flown or run,
their lightness and speed are certain.
The Háocáo sword,
the Xú shì dagger,
though not yet wielded in strike,
their instant cutting is undoubted.
The young Bó beast has a look that can swallow an ox,
the young eagle has a demeanor that overpowers raptors.
Where plants flourish, the soil must be fertile;
where fish are large, the waters must be vast.
A tiger's tail does not attach to a fox's body,
an elephant's tusk does not emerge from a rat's mouth.
Shū Yú's insatiable greed,
was seen in his newborn appearance;
Shí Wǒ's sign of annihilating his clan,
was evident at the opening of his amniotic sac.
Shēn Tóng detected the Wū Chén who stole a wife,
Zhāng Fù knew the Chén Píng who would become noble.
The reason Fàn Lǐ vanished traces at the Five Lakes,
was because Gōu Jiàn had bee-like eyes and a bird's beak.
The reason Zhào people gave up thoughts of contending,
was because Bái Qǐ had a sharp head and a direct gaze.
When King Wén met Lǚ Shàng,
before the mulberry shade had moved,
he knew he was worthy as a teacher.
When Xuándé saw Kǒngmíng,
before the sundial's shadow changed,
he had already entrusted him as his heart and mind.
Guō Tài, a man of moderate talent,
was still able to understand people.
Thus, upon entering Yǐngchuān, he befriended Lǐ Yuánlǐ;
arriving in Chénliú, he bonded with Fú Wěimíng;
entering Wàihuáng, he grew close to Hán Zǐzhù;
reaching Púhēng, he took Qiú Jìzhī as his teacher;
stopping at the schoolhouse, he accepted Wèi Dégōng;
observing a farmer, he promoted Máo Jìwěi;
he recognized Mèng Mǐn's uniqueness while he was carrying burdens,
and warned Yuán Ài that he would surely fail.
In the end, his words proved true,
without a single error.
He must have been able to discern the sharp from the dull through signs and appearances,
understand urgency and leisure through voice and breath,
judge brightness and darkness from actions,
distinguish clarity from turbidity in wealth and desire,
observe appropriateness in giving and taking,
assess truth and falsehood in words and deeds,
examine conduct within the private chambers,
and verify outcomes against promises.
The test of good and bad—
is it not indeed easy?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"I do not mean that people are entirely unknowable,
nor that understanding them lacks any principle.
It is just that this art resides in great clarity,
not something anyone can claim for themselves.
Yet scholars of the world each say they can do it,
hence such sayings exist,
to caution against reckless trust.
Those with majestic appearances are not necessarily virtuous,
and those with frail forms are not necessarily foolish.
Those who roar are not necessarily brave,
and those who are calm are not necessarily timid.
Some have the same outward signs but different intentions,
others differ in temperament yet pursue the same goals.
It is not like heaven and earth having constant patterns,
or mountains and rivers having fixed boundaries.
Things also may be distant yet easy to know,
or near yet hard to predict,
just as the eye can perceive the celestial path,
but cannot see around one's own neck;
the ear can hear thunderclaps,
but cannot discern the sound of tiny insects or lice.
Táng Jū, Lǚ Wàng, Fán Xǔ excelled at reading appearances,
but only knew longevity, early death, poverty, wealth, official rank, and status,
unable to discern the breadth or harshness of one's nature,
or the purity or baseness of one's aspirations and conduct.
Even emperors found it difficult,
let alone ordinary people!
And you, sir, cite examples of judging by form,
questioning discussions of spirit,
without cultivating the root,
nearly missing the point.
"Arrows missing the target
can still pierce fine hairs.
But consistently hitting the mark cannot be considered skillfulness.
Shūxiàng's mother,
the Shēn family's son—
they were not without occasional successes,
but could not do so consistently.
Táo Táng, in examining antiquity, erred in appointments;
Lord Jī, despite his reverence and wisdom, mistakenly entrusted.
Confucius could foresee rise and fall from distant signs,
yet recently missed Dàntái due to physical appearance.
Yánzhōu discerned clarity and turbidity across millennia,
but overlooked an extraordinary scholar right before him.
The difficulty of knowing people
is indeed this severe.
Were all those Guō Tài evaluated
superior to the highest sages?
But his successes
were evident and easy to recognize;
his failures
went unrecorded by others.
"Moreover, what is truly valuable
lies in spotting outstanding talent among the unknown,
foreseeing a swift steed on Wú's slopes,
plucking a pearl-bearing clam from the deepest abyss,
pointing out a luminous treasure within piled stones.
Like Cài Yōng recognizing an unmatched instrument from ashes,
or Zhāng Héng selecting bamboo with extraordinary resonance before its use.
In gatherings of the six armies,
or meetings in marketplaces,
to observe briefly at a glance,
without being misled,
probing hidden thoughts and schemes,
determining lifelong conduct and outcomes—
this is the unique, untransmittable marvel.
If, as in your discussion,
one must wait to examine complete or flawed conduct,
observe the goodness or ugliness of actions,
this is like weighing silk after it's been measured,
or cloth after it's been yarded,
then slowly discussing its weight in ounces,
or the length of the bolt—
anyone can do that,
why would it trouble the wise and discerning!"
Bàopǔzǐ says:
One who emulates the encompassing of heaven and earth,
spreads brightness to reveal subtlety;
whose writings shine like the sun and are complete in form,
and whose clear insight penetrates the divine—
is a sage.
One endowed with lofty purity,
who upholds high standards beyond the mundane,
humbles their intellect as if foolish,
and neither repeats errors nor flatters—
is a worthy.
One who dwells in quietude and non-action,
treads the straight path with fairness—
is a Daoist.
One who fulfills rites for the living and dead,
preserving body and hair to spread their name—
is a filial person.
One who extends compassion to all beings,
always empathizing with others—
is a benevolent person.
One who dedicates their life to the nation,
unchanging through peril—
is a loyal person.
One who discerns subtle principles hard to perceive,
foresees future changes—
is a perceptive person.
One who gauges order and chaos to adapt,
judging when to advance or retreat for self-preservation—
is a wise person.
One who accepts fortune and misfortune with equanimity,
following nature without obstruction—
is an enlightened person.
One who won't bend principle for gain,
nor stoop to compromise—
is an elegant person.
One whose actions match their bearing,
always clear and without regret—
is a dignified person.
One pure as ice and frost,
untainted by power or profit—
is an incorruptible person.
One steadfast through all seasons,
undaunted even in danger—
is a righteous person.
One who keeps their word through long trials,
unchanging despite decline—
is a trustworthy person.
One who composes sharp prose,
with brilliant and fair expressions—
is a literary person.
One who acts with fierce determination,
wielding arms to quell troubles—
is a martial person.
One who masters profound classics,
exhausting principles through ancient wisdom—
is a Confucian scholar.
One focused on essential meanings,
cherishing every moment for moral growth—
is a beneficial person.
One who knows hoarding invites loss,
facing wealth as if discarding it—
is an honest person.
One unchanged by gain or loss,
unswayed by desires—
is a steadfast person.
One who aids the distressed tirelessly,
bearing others' burdens as their own—
is a sincere person.
One who maintains purity to the end,
never evading duty—
is a principled person.
One with sharp wit and elegance,
whose concise speech resolves stagnation—
is an eloquent person.
One who credits others from humble posts,
growing more respectful in prosperity—
is a humble person.
One who strengthens clan harmony,
adhering to righteousness—
is an obedient person.
One decisive in critical moments,
impartial in judgment—
is a capable person.
One who distinguishes truth from falsehood,
resolving doubts with fairness—
is a rational person.
One who tracks celestial movements,
deducing cycles of rise and fall—
is a strategist.
One who charges blades fearlessly,
confronting beasts in wilds—
is a brave person.
One who commands respect through demeanor,
unyielding in upholding laws—
is a stern person.
One who invents tools for utility,
mastering arts and music—
is an artistic person.
One who defies tyranny unafraid,
undaunted by oppression—
is a shrewd person.
One diligent day and night,
toiling tirelessly on heights—
is an industrious person.
One calm amid slander,
fearless against threats—
is a resilient person.
One unmoved by fame,
steadfast in adversity—
is a composed person.
One who acts when sure,
unswayed by doubts—
is a decisive person.
One who follows rules in conduct,
avoiding opportunistic gains—
is a cautious person.
One reverent in observing rites,
faultless among kin—
is a good person.
One who walks the simple path desirelessly,
unchanging through time—
is a plain person.
Of all these traits,
if one possesses none,
and treads not the path of goodness—
they are a base person.
A disciple requested:
"We have heard the categories of virtuous conduct;
now regarding the deeds of the wicked,
which can serve as warnings to common customs,
I hope you would bestow instructions in writing."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Those who fail to support their parents,
damaging the Way and endangering themselves,
are perverse people.
Those who harbor evil falsity to steal glory,
seeking self-benefit while forgetting life,
are rebellious people.
Those who turn from the proper path of benevolence and righteousness,
temporarily endangering others for self-preservation,
are vicious people.
Those fond of contention without satiety,
specializing in vilifying the upright and harming the straightforward,
are evil people.
Those who exceed proper standards with hurtful harshness,
with hearts delighting in killing and comfortable with cruelty,
are brutal people.
Those who adorn heretical doctrines to gradually influence,
fabricating slanders against the loyal and steadfast,
are slanderous people.
Though clever in speech but contrary in action,
actually practicing filth while pretending purity,
are sycophantic people.
Not tracing origins of right and wrong,
arbitrarily loving victory and unleashing anger,
are violent people.
Arranging minor virtues to gain trust,
secretly harboring poison without affection,
are treacherous people.
Following the wind of indication for temporary acceptance,
measuring the ruler's mind to support wrongs,
are flattering people.
Speaking without considering consequences,
fond of light promises without substance,
are empty people.
Seeing profitable positions and forgetting righteousness,
abandoning integrity for temporary gains,
are greedy people.
Seeing dazzling beauty and becoming mentally agitated,
adorned in fine silks with wicked thoughts,
are lustful people.
Seeing accomplished matters with doubt and confusion,
acting with failed plans and much regret,
are obtuse people.
Turning from classics to self-appointment,
ashamed to ask those better than themselves,
are damaging people.
Knowing good deeds but not reaching them,
though doing much without accomplishment,
are inferior people.
Abandoning virtue without cultivation,
serving power to gain favor,
are corrupt people.
Treading dangerous paths for lucky speed,
pushing bribes to compete for passage,
are wicked people.
Already arrogant and rude,
fond of humiliating superiors,
are ferocious people.
When suppressed wrongly then self-accusing,
in matters without hardship yet trembling with fear,
are timid people.
Arguing trivial disputes before crowds,
speaking fully to the wrong person,
are shallow people.
Unaware of matters' feasibility,
though aspiring but never reaching,
are stubborn people.
Knowing wrongs but not correcting,
hearing good rules yet worsening,
are confused people.
Without compassionate kindness,
lightly cutting off relatives and old friends,
are cold people.
Resenting others' achievements,
rejoicing in others' disasters,
are envious people.
Monopolizing wealth while轻视ing righteousness,
seeing poverty without relief,
are stingy people.
Risking extreme danger for luck,
planting failure without regret,
are foolish people.
Sentiments petty and biased,
ambitions solely for profit,
are petty people.
Releasing hawks and hounds on plains,
addicted to gambling without end,
are obsessed people.
Forgetting hierarchical differences,
delighting in extravagant ornaments,
are wasteful people.
Indulging in music and beauty at feasts,
neglecting celebrations and condolences of human relations,
are dissolute people.
Neither minded toward cultivation,
nor diligent in household duties,
are lazy people.
Without dignified restraint,
often casual and unthinking,
are frivolous people.
Viewing morality like drunkenness,
hearing commerce like turbulent waves,
are foul people.
Relying on shallow errors,
unaware of choices' merits and faults,
are clumsy people.
Disliking the worthy without respect,
hearing profound words like deafness,
are arrogant people.
Seeing scarlet and purple undistinguished,
though ear-pulled unawakened,
are blinded people.
Hesitating against morality,
risking ritual punishment regardless,
are chaotic people.
Every action receiving ridicule,
every word spoken violating reason,
are inept people.
Serving chieftains like slaves,
encountering decline and betraying kindness,
are wicked people.
Abandoning poor and humble old friends,
disdaining scholars with haughty posture,
are proud people.
Discarding fading charms for expanded desires,
not for office or learning but distant travels,
are wanton people.
Without pure steadfast loyalty,
betraying nurturers for profit,
are treacherous people.
Facing agreement with surface compliance,
separating with behind-the-back destruction,
are hypocritical people.
Practicing bullying and self-assertion,
rejecting loyal advice unaccepted,
are obstinate people."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"Human talents are hard to know,
truth and falsity sometimes resemble.
Some scholars have handsome features,
elegant demeanor and appearance,
pleasing to behold,
comfortable to interact with,
dignified like dragon and tiger,
movements forming perfect规矩.
Yet minds obscured and spirits blocked,
talents unfit for anything,
all they possess mentally,
attaches only to skin-deep.
Mouths cannot utter remarkable words,
brushes cannot compose half a sentence;
in office cannot govern people,
outward cannot command troops;
managing affairs ruins them,
carrying missions brings disgrace.
Actions inappropriate,
positions untenable.
This is the first difficulty in distinction.
Some scholars appear plain and haggard,
looks short and ugly,
voices soft and weak,
movements awkward and stiff.
Yet containing excellence and treasured qualities,
classics mastered and conduct elevated,
abilities surpassing Yuán Kǎi,
writings flourishing like spring woods.
In office achieves all accomplishments,
in military completely victorious alone.
This is the second difficulty in distinction.
Some scholars have profound strategies,
tactics reaching divine level,
wisdom encompassing success and failure,
thoughts penetrating mysteries,
talents covering multiple skills,
natural capacity unlimited;
yet mouths don't convey hearts,
brushes don't exhaust meanings,
in casual encounters,
no different from ordinary.
This is the third difficulty in distinction.
Some scholars have sharp adaptability,
artful speech splendid and bright,
employing analogies,
gushing like springs and fierce like wind;
yet what mouths discuss,
bodies cannot perform;
skilled in understanding antiquity,
deficient in managing present,
governing brings chaos,
ruling people causes resentment.
This is the fourth difficulty in distinction."
There are scholars who outwardly appear reverent and respectful,
with devout expressions and cautious words,
yet inwardly distant and negligent,
their hearts scattered and unrestrained,
accepting responsibilities without concern,
holding positions without managing them.
This is the fifth type difficult to distinguish.
There are scholars who can hit targets with arrows,
enter empty-handed into battle,
ride backwards on standing horses,
mastering all five weapons;
yet they are physically weak and shallow in thought,
quick-handed but timid at heart,
appearing unmatched in practice,
but proving ineffective in actual combat.
They flee at the sight of dust,
lose their spirit upon hearing the enemy.
This is the sixth type difficult to distinguish.
There are scholars who appear straightforward and slow,
sparing in speech and plain in appearance,
negligent in minor matters,
not exhibiting petty courage,
restrained and cautious in speech,
enduring offenses without retaliation,
holding back like folded wings,
appearing weak and compliant.
Yet they possess strong courage and firm principles,
fearing no powerful opponent,
where righteousness demands,
they face death as returning home,
even if torn limb from limb,
they won't change their stance.
This is the seventh type difficult to distinguish.
There are scholars who are filial, friendly, gentle and virtuous,
modest and refined,
practicing faithfulness and obedience,
avoiding improper conduct,
content in poverty with pure aspirations,
their integrity pure as ice and frost;
yet they are slow and impractical,
failing to grasp essential matters,
missing opportunities when they arise,
achieving nothing in their endeavors,
remaining passive in their positions,
failing in assigned tasks.
This is the eighth type difficult to distinguish.
There are scholars whose conduct is lofty and aloof,
with stern and steep character,
proud and arrogant,
looking down on peers and scorning customs,
not strictly disciplined,
not guarding against small faults,
following their whims freely,
acting as if no one else is present,
condemned by factions,
criticized by commentators,
not befriended by fellow scholars,
overlooked in evaluations.
Yet in court they maintain upright dignity,
doing all they know should be done,
loyal in serving superiors,
clear-minded in governing subordinates.
This is the ninth type difficult to distinguish.
There are scholars who are broad-minded and universally helpful,
humble and accepting of others,
concealing flaws and hiding imperfections,
gentle, respectful, honest and clean,
hardworking, modest and retiring,
saving the endangered and keeping promises,
entrusted with lives without doubt,
charged with orphans reliably;
yet being purely good but ignorant of authority,
benevolent but indecisive,
unable to reward the good,
unwilling to punish the evil,
sufficient in loyalty and chastity,
but lacking in practical ability,
hesitant in decision-making,
abandoning laws to imitate wrongs,
mixing right and wrong,
ultimately ending in failure.
This is the tenth type difficult to distinguish.
Things may appear similar but actually differ,
seeming so yet not so.
To discern without error,
to perceive the spirit through the form,
even sages would find it difficult,
let alone ordinary people?
Therefore in employing talents and selecting scholars,
in recommending intimates and making friends,
one cannot but choose carefully,
cannot but examine thoroughly.
As for the confusion in character changes,
beginning right but ending wrong,
like Wáng Mǎng who initially surpassed Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
but later exceeded Zhào Gāo in tyranny,
this is beyond what average talent can foresee.
If scholars were as easy to distinguish
as the wren from the swan,
the fox and rabbit from the dragon and unicorn,
then the Four Fiends wouldn't have held office in Yáo's court,
Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū wouldn't have endangered the Zhōu dynasty,
Zhòngní wouldn't have misjudged Dàntái Mièmíng,
Yánlíng wouldn't have regretted the lost gold,
Yī Yǐn wouldn't have labored for seventy years,
Xiàng Yǔ wouldn't have regretted suspecting Fàn Zēng.
The problem lies in stones like wǔfū confusing with jade,
owls resembling phoenixes,
frozen ice appearing like crystal,
smoke mistaking for clouds,
hence those who make no mistakes are few.
Even emperors find it difficult,
how much more so ordinary people!
Only with great clarity,
profound insight into subtleties,
spiritual measurement of things,
thought illuminating darkness,
can one recognize uncut jade in mountains,
know pearls in rivers.
For scholars among the difficult to distinguish,
to have no regret in selection,
making good and bad clearly separated,
praise and blame all appropriate.
Then Wǔ Dīng and Jī Chāng wouldn't govern alone,
while Fù Yuè and Lǚ Shàng wouldn't be permanently rejected,
Gāo Jiàn and Zǎi Pǐ couldn't accomplish their evils,
Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn would have no place for their falsehoods.
This roughly covers the essentials of selecting scholars,
the general principles of choice.
For finer details in seeking,
it depends on the individual,
certainly not something writing can fully elaborate.
Your nephew Liú Jūn Shìyóu's argument states:
"Human relationships begin with husband and wife,
their union mirrors heaven and earth.
Therefore the great wedding ceremony
was valued by the ancients,
to join two families in harmony,
continuing the ancestral foundation.
The host bows to welcome at the gate,
receives instructions at the temple,
with black and red betrothal gifts,
personally handing the carriage reins,
if the groom has three years' mourning,
he informs the woman's family,
who accepts without daring to change.
After the great mourning ends,
they seek the groom's permission,
if the groom declines,
only then she may marry elsewhere.
This honors respect and deference.
How can there be litigation before marriage?
But recent generations treat it lightly,
damaging morals and corrupting customs,
actions lacking righteousness,
promising but not fulfilling,
fighting and bringing shame,
clogging government offices.
Now for those disputing marriages,
before cohabitation,
allow righteous dissolution,
returning double the wedding feast cost,
giving back betrothal gifts.
For those who have divorced twice,
return double the betrothal gifts.
For those divorcing three times,
return triple the betrothal gifts.
Thus,
the divorced won't litigate,
the greedy won't profit from repeated marriages,
this is essential for royal governance,
an eternal unchangeable law."
Bàopǔzǐ replies:
"Liú Jūn laments the decline of virtuous deference,
deplores how people's disputes damage customs,
though speeding to litigation,
households become insufficient,
the value of harmony,
will thus be lost.
Creating honest words to restore worldly losses,
establishing good plans to save drifting ways,
the noisy customs,
will thereby change,
the shameless trends,
will thereby shift.
Covering all true and false,
certainly hard to find fault.
Truly an eternal law for governing the state,
a substantial discussion of great benefit."
As one of limited understanding,
I fail to grasp the ultimate principle,
but having hastily received your inquiry,
I privately have doubts.
The formation of marital unions
should by principle involve no coercion;
one party selects and seeks,
the other consents only if pleased.
If a light promise leads to later regret,
the fault lies with the woman's family.
Breaking their word and abandoning trust,
they arbitrarily give and take as they please.
Yet strict precautions and severe regulations
have been unable to stop this.
Now if we loosely permit such license,
merely demanding double the betrothal gifts—this is what the poor fear,
while those rich in wealth
may then fulfill their wishes.
A later suitor
might possibly prosper,
assisting with the supplementary betrothal gifts,
which would certainly be done willingly.
But then the initial family must remain silent,
unable to voice a word.
Judging by human feeling,
how can they be without resentment and lament?
For those who will not submit,
facing death is like returning home;
calamities of bloodshed
are then likely to arise.
Now if we merely begrudge the minor disgrace of litigation
and instead construct unbearable great hatreds,
this is what is called sparing the trouble of minor nuisances
while forgetting the cruelty of devastation and ruin.
Even one who buys goods at the market,
if another raises the price and snatches them away,
would rarely endure it without indignation—
how much more so when it is a wife awaiting marriage who is seized!
If this method is implemented,
it will cause those entering marriage,
even after presenting respects and performing the wedding ceremony,
to still harbor fears of being robbed.
Why?
Master Liú's argument
uses the sharing of the nuptial cup as the cutoff point,
which is firm indeed.
Then, although the woman's family may have received betrothal gifts for years,
they would always wield the power of changing their mind,
relying on the possibility of repeated seizures,
and would surely be negligent in choosing a son-in-law.
If slightly dissatisfied with the groom,
they could then repent and change,
entangling themselves in enmity and inviting disaster—
nothing could be worse than this.
The ancients designed laws,
considering matters from beginning to end,
stopping problems at their start and preventing them in their bud,
with thoughts exceedingly refined;
yet not addressing the path of arbitrary seizure,
and deciding with the rule of reporting the marriage—
could there be a resolution?
Suppose a woman possesses beauty that topples cities, peerless and unmatched,
and encounters powerful, influential men
whose eyes delight in her alluring appearance,
their hearts forgetting ritual bounds.
With resources amassing a thousand in gold,
their feelings know no stinginess.
Returning tenfold the betrothal gifts
would still not daunt them,
let alone merely doubling them?
The Huá clan did not hesitate to kill Kǒng Fù and take his wife;
a man of Chǔ, fetching a bride for his son,
took her for himself because of her beauty.
Judging by this,
would they hesitate to exhaust their household assets to help the woman's family repay the previous suitor's due?
Petty men are frivolous and fickle;
a mere squint becomes a grudge.
They also delight in abandoning the declining and pursuing the flourishing,
shunning the cold and rushing to the hot.
If this method is enacted,
many will surely seize from the poor and lowly to give to the rich and noble.
I wonder, my lord,
what method you have to prevent such abuses!
Some say:
"Make the woman's family accept betrothal gifts regardless of amount,
and on the same day report the marriage.
Afterwards, have contemporaries sign their names on a separate document,
necessarily ten people or more,
ensuring coverage for distant travel and deaths.
Also order the woman's father, brothers, or uncles
to reply to the groom's family with a letter,
necessarily handwritten on one sheet.
If there is change of heart and the evidence is clear,
the woman's parents and brothers
shall all be punished with penalties.
In this way,
might we nearly eliminate lawsuits!"
Bàopúzǐ says:
What the eyes favor
should not be followed;
what the ears enjoy
should not be indulged;
what the nose delights in
should not be given free rein;
what the mouth craves
should not be pursued;
what the heart desires
should not be unrestrained.
Thus, what dazzles the eyes
must be captivating looks and fresh adornments;
what seduces the ears
must be charming tones and licentious sounds;
what beguiles the nose
must be fragrant plants and aromatic scents;
what tempts the mouth
must be rare delicacies and fine flavors;
what misleads the heart
must be power, profit, and fame.
If all five are deluded,
then to inherit disasters that harm the self—
is that not indeed certain?
Therefore, the wise strictly regulate their innate nature,
not recklessly exerting spirit to chase after things.
They restrain themselves with calm contentment,
and enhance themselves with long-term planning.
In suppressing passions,
they are more rigorous than dikes preparing for a breach;
in controlling nature,
they exceed rotten reins guiding a galloping horse.
Thus they can internally preserve long life
and externally avoid conflicts and encumbrances.
For hunger and cold are hard to bear,
yet the pure-minded do not accept unrighteous grain or silk;
poverty and lowliness are difficult to endure,
yet the noble do not dwell in the glory and rank of danger and chaos.
When calculations are sound, the ability to endure is complete;
when the Way prevails, things that harm nature are discarded.
Fine wine, with its immediate taste,
is a poisonous substance that breeds illness.
It offers not the slightest benefit,
but has massive harm like mountains.
Gentlemen through it ruin their virtue;
petty men through it hasten their crimes.
Those addicted and deluded by it
rarely escape calamity.
Scholars of the world
also know this is so,
yet they can neither abstain entirely
nor are they willing to moderate.
Indulging the immediate desires of heart and mouth,
they lightly summon the root of disaster—
like one feverish and thirsty indulging in cold drinks:
though it suits them momentarily, it endangers their body.
Both minor and major chaos and ruin
are invariably linked to wine.
Yet common people drink deeply and drown in it.
At the start of the feast,
they are reserved and orderly,
words sparse, demeanor proper,
chanting the "tranquil" of the "Dew Lies Heavy,"
singing the "joyful" of "In Hào,"
raising cups to "myriad years of life,"
nurturing the principle of "gentle mastery."
Before the sun has moved a shadow's length,
bodies grow light and ears hot.
Then glass and conch vessels are used together,
and the rules for full penalties and leftover drinks become urgent.
Drunk yet not stopping,
they pull out linchpins and throw them in wells.
Then mouths gush and noses overflow,
drenching heads and leading to disorder.
Repeatedly they dance, whirling and leaping,
leaving their seats and moving about;
some shout, some bawl,
like boiling water, like bubbling soup.
Some argue to win debates,
some giggle alone,
some talk without a partner,
some vomit over mats and tables,
some trip over fine performers' feet,
some lose caps and loosened sashes.
The chaste and good cast glances like Huá Dū,
the timid emulate Qìng Jì in leaping swiftness,
the slow and heavy tumble like weeds in turbulent waves,
the orderly and solemn leap like deer and fish.
Those usually tongue-tied about the weather
all clap and sing in tune;
the humble and non-competitive
all raise their hems for lofty interactions.
The demeanor of integrity and shame is destroyed,
and the malady of wild error erupts;
the nature of baseness is exposed,
and the attitude of arrogance and obstinacy emerges.
When essence is turbid and spirit disordered,
judgments become inverted.
Some dash about in chariots or on horseback,
rushing into ravines and valleys without fear,
considering the nine-bend slope as flat as an anthill;
others climb perilous heights and tread on crumbling edges,
unaware even if they fall,
viewing the depths of the Lǚliáng Gorge as mere ox hoofprints.
Some vent hatred on objects,
others rage drunkenly against wives and children;
they inflict cruel injustice on servants and slaves,
and wield sharp blades against the six domestic animals;
they set fierce fires in their homes,
and cast precious treasures into deep waters;
they redirect fierce anger onto passersby,
and inflict violent harm on scholarly friends.
There are those who insult and slaughter revered rulers,
indeed;
and those who offend violent men and thereby suffer distress,
indeed.
Though their speech may prize rhetoric,
it is vexatious and contrary to reason;
their bows and prostrations are many in vain,
laborious and mournful, not reverent.
Ministers and sons breach etiquette before their sovereigns and parents,
the young and lowly act insolently in the presence of elders.
They deem refined conversation as slander,
and take loyal advice as personal affront.
Then they draw white blades, forgetting the peril of consequences,
and brandish clubs and staves, heedless of what lies ahead or behind.
They forge blood-spilling enmities,
inviting the calamity of capital punishment.
When the young bully their elders,
the community imposes severe censure;
when one insults another's father or elder brother,
the sons and younger brothers will seek vengeance;
when one exposes what others conceal,
even strong men cannot endure it;
when one's schemes are deeply harsh,
even the sober cannot forgive it.
In an instant, they stir up numerous troubles,
and tie a hundred ailments deep in the vitals.
A galloping team cannot retrieve past regrets,
and though they wish to reform, they find no path of return.
This is what the wise deeply guard against,
yet the foolish cannot avoid.
The disasters and ruin they cause
are too numerous to record.
Yet in joyous gatherings,
none refrain from it,
with cups raised high and toasts filling the ears,
regardless of one's capacity.
They measure every drop left in the cup,
taking delay as a slight against themselves.
Pouring the entire vessel for the respected,
earnestness turns into disrespect.
Urged to hold back, they do not;
pressed to finish, they do not comply,
whence arise resentful looks and harsh words.
Now, when wind affects the organs and viscera,
it causes confusion and dizziness,
and in severe cases,
one harms and deludes oneself.
If struck by such an illness,
all worry and fear,
swallowing bitterness and enduring pain,
desiring a swift recovery.
As for the harm drunkenness does to one's nature,
how does it differ from this?
Yet one will seclude indoors to escape the wind,
but cannot cut off attachment to节制 alcohol.
If one feared alcohol as they fear the wind,
and hated drunkenness as they hate illness,
then the faults of indulgence would be blocked,
and the errors of lingering over drink would cease.
Now, wind as an ailment
still allows time for treatment,
but the transformation brought by alcohol
occurs in a mere breath.
When it leads to stupor and chaos,
one is between existence and oblivion,
seeing Tài Shān as a pellet,
viewing the vast ocean as a bowl,
looking up to shout at the falling sky,
bending down to cry at the collapsing earth,
lying down awaiting tigers and wolves,
throwing oneself into wells or fire,
without considering it evil.
When one uses their body thus,
how can they still cherish the rites of reverence,
or guard against the excesses of joy and anger?
In the past, when Yí Dí was shunned,
Great Yǔ prospered.
With hills of dregs and ponds of wine,
King Zhòu and Jiǎ of Xià perished.
Fēng Hóu incurred guilt,
for bearing a cup on his forehead.
Liú Biǎo decayed into ruin,
with his three elegant cups.
Liú Sōng rotted his intestines,
from drinking to escape the heat.
Guō Zhēn went mad,
from never a day without drunkenness.
The violent brevity of Lord Xìnlíng's life,
the disordered governance of Xiāngzǐ,
Zhào Wǔ's loss of popular support,
Zǐfǎn's execution,
Hàn Emperor Huì's shortened lifespan,
Guàn Fū's extermination of his clan,
Chén Zūn's murder,
Jì Bù's alienation and dismissal,
Cáo Zhí's removal and demotion,
Xú Miǎo's prohibition from speech,
all were due to this thing.
Many in the world love and enjoy it,
but few caution against or fear it,
they are many, we are few,
how can good advice be applied?
I only wish you would节制 it.
In the past, when famine struck and grain was expensive,
drunkards killed each other,
whereupon regional rulers imposed alcohol prohibitions,
reiterating strict orders,
with officials conducting searches,
arresting, flogging, and parading offenders to shame them,
and more than half died under whipping.
The stricter the prevention,
the more the offenders.
Some even brewed in underground cellars,
or carried wine in oiled bladders.
The people's fondness for this
can be called profound.
I, a humble commoner,
entrust these empty words in writing,
yet know not what to do.
Moreover, those governing the people may establish laws,
but cannot abstain from this thing themselves,
lenient with themselves but strict with others,
so even with orders, they are not followed,
not practicing what they preach,
the common people do not trust them.
Teaching in this way,
how can the teaching prevail?
Prohibiting in this way,
how can the prohibition hold?
Those who sell alcohol
would be destitute if they lost this trade,
so they offer bribes and gifts,
relying on powerful connections,
and the subordinate officials dare not intervene.
The powerless alone desist,
while the influential monopolize the market.
Setting up stoves for exclusive profit,
they then double the price,
yet people buy from them,
acting openly without fear,
for the law is light and the profit heavy,
how can they avoid it?
Someone may object:
"The downfall of Jié of Xià and Zhòu of Shāng,
the brutality of Lord Xìnlíng and Emperor Huì of Hàn,
were due to faults of music and women,
not just alcohol!
To judge it today based on ancient troubles,
and cut it off now,
is like saying that since Bāo Sì caused the fall of Zhōu,
rulers should abolish the six palaces,
or because the Ēpáng Palace endangered Qín,
kings should live in thatched huts.
I have heard that the heavens display the star of the wine banner,
and the earth spirit manifests the transformation of the hollow mulberry,
offering firewood at round mounds,
burying offerings in marshlands,
using ceremonial vessels for libations,
to invoke the descent of gods and spirits,
for wine is part of ritual.
A thousand zhōng and a hundred gū -
such was the drinking of Yáo and Shùn.
Only with wine was there no limit -
such was the capability of Zhòngní.
Jī Dàn never cleared away wine and dishes,
hence he could establish rituals and create music.
Hàn Gāo danced about greatly drunk,
hence he could slay the serpent and rally troops.
Yú Gōng drained a full hú,
and his judgment in legal cases became even clearer.
Guǎn Lù tilted his head back for three dǒu,
and his pure discourse became brilliantly elegant.
Yáng Yún never let wine leave his lips,
and thus the "Tài Xuán" was completed.
Zǐ Yǔ got drunk without awareness,
yet his hegemonic achievements were accomplished.
When a bottle of láo was poured out,
the masses of the three armies were pleased.
When the解毒之觴 was circulated,
even horse thieves were moved.
To dispel worries and complete rituals,
to record merits and celebrate returns,
to summon deities and unite people -
without this there is no means to do so.
Within, hastening the various elders;
without, leading honored guests -
like the Huái and Shéng rivers,
it is valued by the "Chūn Qiū".
Speaking from this perspective,
how can it be prohibited?"
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
The constellation of the wine banner -
indeed exists.
It is like the hanging images that manifest brightness,
none greater than the sun and moon;
the origins of water and fire,
are therein present.
Yet to regulate and control them,
is to nurture life and achieve merit;
to use them improperly,
is to be burned or drowned to death.
How can one rely on the hanging images in heaven,
and claim that water and fire do not kill people?
Among the means to sustain life,
none comes before food;
when food is excessive,
it truly causes abdominal masses.
How much more so for the poisonous substance that is wine!
Those like Xià Jié, Yīn Zhòu, Xìnlíng, and Hàn Huì who indulged in the decadent music that destroys states,
and drowned in the chaotic beauty that topples cities,
all had their natures intoxicated by wine,
their tendencies formed by drunkenness,
thereby leading to the excesses of extreme passions,
forgetting the methods of self-cultivation.
I discuss its root,
you recognize its branches,
claiming it is not the calamity of wine -
from where then does the calamity arise?
This is only knowing that heavy rain soaks clothes,
without knowing the clouds and vapor that produce it;
only worrying that flying dust irritates the eyes,
without perceiving the whirlwind that causes it.
A thousand zhōng and a hundred hú -
these are unreasonable words,
impossible matters,
which the wise do not believe.
The difference of the sages lies in their intelligence and talent,
but as for their physical forms, they cannot surpass others,
having the height of seven chǐ or three zhàng,
or being ten thousand times larger.
How could a single day's drinking
possibly reach such amounts?
Zhòngní feared the alteration of his nature,
and dared not approach disorder.
Zhōu Gōng bowed a hundred times daily,
with dried dishes and clear wine.
The highest sages were cautious and apprehensive,
still being like this -
how much more so for ordinary people,
can they be without regret?
Hàn Gāo responded to heaven,
received the mandate to revolutionize,
even if he hadn't been drunk,
he would still have slain the serpent.
Yú Gōng was intelligent and perceptive,
clear in hearing and judgment,
handling matters great and small according to circumstances,
without missing what is crooked or straight.
Therefore punishments were not indiscriminately applied,
and there were no resentful people in the world.
But his capacity for drinking
did not immediately mean neglecting affairs.
If speaking of great drunkenness,
all become without knowledge.
The talent for resolving doubts -
how does it rely on wine?
I have not heard that Gāo Yáo, Fǔ Hóu, Zǐ Chǎn, or Shì Zhī
had to be drunk to adjudicate cases.
Guǎn Lù was young,
rarely engaged in intense debates,
so he borrowed the power of wine to boost his courage.
If he exceeded his limit,
he would certainly become confused and erroneous.
As for his piercing the slightest details through hexagrams,
seeking the transformations of ghosts and spirits,
reading complexions to determine prosperity and decline,
listening to bird calls to know the future,
awaiting wind and clouds to ascertain good and bad fortune,
observing steles and cypresses to recognize disaster and blessing -
how could he again require wine
to then examine these?
Yáng Yún was a thorough scholar,
of high talent and far-reaching thoughts,
the richness of his brilliant vision,
was endowed by heaven -
how could he rely on external things
to aid his writing?
As for his frequent drinking,
it was due to occasional preference;
or perhaps he had an illness,
to facilitate the effect of medicine.
Zǐ Yǔ's indulgence of his will
was probably already predetermined.
Even if he hadn't been drunk,
he would still have ultimately achieved the same result.
The bottle of láo pleasing the masses -
this is a metaphorical parable.
If indeed rewards and punishments are fair and proper,
authority and kindness appropriately applied,
with long-term strategies deployed freely,
responding to opportunities without fixed methods,
then officers will think resolutely,
and people will gladly exert themselves.
If it is not so,
even if wine flows like an abyss,
what would it contribute to victory or defeat?
Mù Gōng gave drink to thieves -
a rash expedient,
abandoning law and fostering evil -
what is there to greatly praise!
How can it compare to being cautious?
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Worldly affairs continue to exist,
but ritual teachings gradually decay.
Respect and deference are not esteemed,
arrogance has become customary.
Among companions at drinking gatherings,
some squat, some sit sprawled.
In the hot summer months,
they bare their heads and expose their bodies.
Their main activities are solely gambling at pitch-pot and playing liubo and弹棋,
their discussions limited to the realm of music and beauty,
their steps never leaving the side of silken trousers and fine fabrics,
their wanderings never departing from the doors of powerful and wealthy drinking companions.
One does not hear the words of pure conversation discussing the Way,
but only vulgar language and mockery given priority.
They consider such behavior lofty and profound,
and those not like this foolish and uncouth.
Thus the mediocre people who chase after trends,
the commoners who follow customs,
those who admire them are like night insects flying toward bright candles,
those who learn from them are like light feathers responding to whirlwinds.
In jesting talk,
sometimes it reaches up to ancestors,
sometimes it extends down to women.
Those who initiate it strive to make it deeply cutting,
those who retaliate fear their response isn't heavy enough.
Those who start it don't consider the consequences of being answered,
those who join in are ashamed if their light words don't silence others.
The cutting of Zhōu's grain,
the reaping of Wēn's wheat,
truly arose from revenge and hatred,
which could not be stopped.
The sharp-tongued support the strong and side with the powerful,
the eloquent borrow sharp words to stab at shields.
They consider those who don't respond as clumsy and inferior,
those who stop first as defeated losers.
Like this,
the language of mutual hostility -
how can it remain silent!
When those with talent and thought do it,
they are still skilled at seizing opportunities,
following established forms,
citing antiquity to illustrate the present,
with subtle words and raised principles,
elegant yet amusing,
hitting the mark without causing injury,
not poking at what people avoid,
not offending what people cherish.
As for when the clumsy do it,
then they twist the straight and gather the crooked,
making people feel astonished,
the beautiful and the ugly -
regarding what should be absolutely avoided,
how could it be merely without benefit!
Then there are those who indulge in alcohol,
and those with aggressive tendencies,
who cannot endure restraint,
shake their sleeves and draw thorns,
coming to blows with hands and feet,
hurling ugly words at their elders,
turning joy into enmity,
severing friendships and ruining themselves,
creating rifts that lead to disaster.
Some throw cups and ladles in anger,
others expose each other's private secrets.
In the past, Chén Líng was struck by arrows,
the Guàn clan was annihilated,
not because of heavenly decree,
but through the consequences of their own words.
The pivot's movement
governs honor and disgrace;
the warning of the double-sealed lips
does not deceive us!
Even roaring thunder cannot recall misspoken words,
even Bān's wheel cannot polish away the stain of such speech.
Though one may not think thrice before uttering refined words,
one can still cease joking banter to prevent the sprouting of disaster.
Honor your speech,
respect your dignified manner,
so that words bear no oral faults,
and posture shows no arrogant bearing,
making you worthy of emulation and admiration,
commanding awe and affection.
This is indeed the excellent method to avoid disgrace,
the essential way to preserve friendships.
Moreover, those who disrespect others
do not love their own parents;
those who take fighting lightly
do not value the bodies inherited from them.
Both fall into unfiliality—
can we not be cautious?
Yet the deluded lack self-awareness;
the emotionally driven shun unwelcome advice.
They harbor flaws without the needle of honest critique to cure them,
lost in confusion without a compass to guide their reflection.
Sycophantic petty men
laugh and praise their goodness;
those who agree to their face
clap and applaud their achievements.
This further blinds the confused to their errors,
making them think they possess Dùn's wit and extraordinary eloquence,
unaware that this is the banner summoning trouble, the tally inviting harm, the relay station for slander, the cart that overturns them.
Is it merely diminishing their reputation in records,
tarnishing their virtuous name for posterity?
Even with lifelong caution,
one cannot undo a single morning's mistake;
even with the wealth of Táo Zhū,
one cannot redeem the error of a few words.
Thus, a hair's breadth of loss
leads to a thousand-mile deviation;
words that wound others
inflict pain like swords and spears.
Accumulating tiny things makes them prominent,
piling up shallows forms depths.
A swan's feather can sink a dragon boat,
many light loads can break a strong axle,
a spark can burn a hundred-xún hall,
a worm can topple a tree of joined girth.
Why did ancient sages act so cautiously and humbly,
while modern men are so recklessly arrogant?
Therefore, noble scholars of high standing
turn away at the sight of dust;
frivolous and shallow individuals
flock like shadows to the echo.
In planning affairs, they lack the aid of the wise;
in perilous times, they gain no benefit from mutual critique.
The good historian suspends his brush,
finding no worthy deeds to record;
speakers fall silent,
with no admirable tales to pass on.
Their good name unestablished,
their ill repute spreads far,
leaving behind lasting damage,
inviting ridicule from future generations,
with nothing to emulate at the start,
nothing to commemorate at the end.
This is indeed the shame of the aspiring.
How can one bear to act thus?
To err and not correct it
is truly to abandon the smooth road for thorny thickets,
to spurn fine fare for poison weeds.
Is this not what is called: deeming small virtues useless and not doing them,
small vices harmless and not ceasing them,
until evil accumulates beyond concealment,
and crimes grow too great to resolve?
I wish for people to reform their unbridled conduct,
rid themselves of arrogant and stingy faults,
discard the disease of boastfulness and one-upmanship,
cease mocking and improper speech,
so that Zhào Shèng's gate sees no departing guests,
and Huáng Zǔ's club finds no use.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
Some do not cultivate pure virtue to earn respect,
but rely on force to inspire fear.
When in a crowd,
they stand erect, refusing to sit,
vie for the central position,
change expressions and tone at will,
pushing others aside for their own comfort.
If thwarted,
they retreat resentfully.
When walking out,
in narrow paths,
they disdain to yield way,
whip their horses to charge ahead,
shoving others into danger.
Those who do not immediately step aside
are further harassed and jostled.
Alas,
how wrong!
They say the ancients were humble and unassuming,
yielding shade and giving way,
laboring modestly and honoring scholars,
uncompeting with others,
standing as if too weak for their clothes,
walking as if with no room for themselves—
how vastly different these are from them!
When virtue is abundant and conduct pure,
even with deep self-abasement,
people still honor them.
If one's actions are not noble,
even with violent behavior,
people will not respect them.
If outwardly they command others' bodies,
but inwardly lose their hearts,
it is what is called being detested,
not being respected.
In the past, before Zhuāngzǐ had eaten,
the King of Zhào stood by his side;
when Zōu Yǎn entered the border,
the Lord of Yān held a broom in welcome;
in Kāng Chéng's village,
even rebels bowed in reverence;
at Lín Zōng's courtyard,
all were humble and solemn.
Not because they were subdued by force.
Wealth obtained through theft
is not praiseworthy, even if immense;
intimidating others with vicious virtue
brings no honor, even if feared.
Yet the common folk do not despise such acts.
So hearing their words
is like the hooting of owls arriving;
seeing their faces
is like the apparition of ghosts.
Where they arrive,
it is as if monsters have gathered;
on the road,
it is worse than encountering a pack of tigers.
Fools who act thus
boast of being heroes;
petty men who emulate them
see it as a stepping stone to power.
Chaos knows no end,
truly because of this.
Yet those who dare do this
are not necessarily obstinately stupid.
Mostly, they are descendants of officials,
from families with powerful connections,
who initially strove to do good deeds
to steal a false reputation.
Once their name is roughly established,
their true nature is unleashed.
Some use wealth and beauty to befriend the powerful;
some seize the moment to snatch glorious positions;
some marry into noble families;
some manipulate praise and slander to grasp authority.
Vessels full, ambitions overflow,
attitudes shift, flaws emerge,
cliques form, connections widen,
paths clear, steps rise higher.
Pure discourse can no longer restrain them,
rules and measures can no longer correct them,
until they become flies on a steed's head,
rats in the temple walls.
To those above them,
they bow and scrape in servitude.
To those beneath them,
they act tyrannically to control them.
Thus, they do not listen to their betters,
or pretend not to hear;
their inferiors dare not speak,
or if they do, cannot stop them.
Pest insects harm the grain,
but frostfall wipes them out.
Villainous heroes disrupt the group,
but strict times bring their downfall.
Those who cultivate personal integrity
can only refuse to serve them,
not follow their example.
With an axe but no handle,
what can one do?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The Book of Songs praises the ospreys,
valuing their distinction.
In rites,
men and women without a matchmaker's arrangement
do not meet,
do not sit together,
do not exchange inquiries,
do not share clothing or belongings,
and are not allowed to hand things directly to each other.
When sisters return after marriage,
brothers do not share a mat to sit with them.
Outside matters are not brought inside,
and inside matters are not taken outside.
Women do not go beyond the gate to see off or welcome guests,
and when they go out, they must cover their faces.
On the road, men keep to the left,
women to the right.
These are the wise regulations established by the sages to emphasize distinction and prevent gradual decay.
Moreover, between husband and wife,
one might say intimacy exists,
yet men do not stay indoors during the day unless ill,
and when nearing death, they avoid dying in the hands of women,
let alone with others!
In the past, the woman of Lǔ did not seclude herself in deep quarters,
leading to the incident of Tā Hù's carriage;
Confucius's wife did not keep hidden within the household,
sparking the disaster of Huá Dū;
Shǐ Jī lacked precautions,
resulting in regret over the mixed lineage;
Wángsūn was not strict,
suffering the disgrace of having his door blocked.
Yet nowadays, common women
abandon their silkworm-raising and weaving duties,
neglect their tasks of dark headbands,
do not spin their hemp,
but instead dance frivolously in the market.
They forsake the affairs of household management,
and cultivate friendships with widespread socializing.
They take turns visiting relatives,
raising torches under the stars,
ceaseless in their travels,
often accompanied by many attendants,
with dazzling displays filling the roads,
maids, servants, clerks, and soldiers
mingling chaotically like a market,
engaging in lewd banter along the way,
detestable and abominable.
Some stay overnight at others' homes,
or return late at night,
play in Buddhist temples,
watch fishing and hunting,
climb heights and overlook waters,
leave their domains for celebrations and condolences,
open carriages and lift curtains,
wandering through cities.
They drink from cups by the roadside,
play stringed instruments and sing while walking,
encouraging each other to elevate such behavior,
making wrongs customary.
This gives rise to opportunities,
and there is nothing they won't do.
It is the source of teaching licentiousness,
an extreme lack of urgency.
Only by setting an example for one's wife
can the family and state be rectified.
I hope all gentlemen
can somewhat prohibit and stop this.
Women having no external affairs
is how to prevent gradual decay.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Frivolous and shallow individuals,
whose deeds place them in high positions,
form friendships based on wealth and support,
and having roughly attained fame and status,
then betray rites and violate teachings,
claiming to be unrestrained and natural.
Though their talents do not surpass others,
they force themselves to be unrestrained and broad-minded,
considering those arrogant and unbridled as magnanimous,
and those who cherish and uphold integrity as stingy and narrow.
Thus, during the year-end drumming, idle good-for-nothings,
after getting drunk and flushed,
form cliques and groups,
associating without discrimination,
while exceptional scholars and great Confucians
might not be received even if separated only by a fence.
They recklessly go wherever they please,
no matter how far, they will arrive,
hand in hand, sleeves linked,
roaming and gathering,
entering others' halls and rooms,
gazing at people's women,
pointing out flaws and assessing features,
commenting on beauty and ugliness.
Do they not understand what such actions amount to?
Some, without notifying the host,
rush forward together,
before proper attire is arranged,
without even peeping or listening,
break through doors and bolts,
climb over broken walls and slip through gaps,
as if raiders have arrived.
If concubines or maids hide but are caught unprepared,
they search even hidden corners,
pulling and dragging them out,
which is indeed a bizarre affair.
A gentleman in his own home
does not even overlook his family's unpreparedness,
so he raises his voice upon entering,
and looks down when ascending the hall.
Yet to intrude upon others' homes—
what principle justifies that?
However, those unrestrained fellows,
spineless and fond of following trends,
consider those who engage in this as intimate,
and those who reject it as disrespectful,
truly believing it's unavoidable in today's world.
Hence, with noisy clamor,
they enter rooms to see wives,
sitting knee-to-knee in cramped spaces,
exchanging cups at close range,
playing licentious and seductive melodies,
using words to stir feelings like those that moved Wén Jūn,
shouting and brawling,
jesting in ugly and lewd ways,
reaching the depths of vulgarity and filth.
Then they laugh and disrupt the great principles between men and women,
trampling on the "no decorum" warned in "Xiàng Shǔ."
The downfall of Jié and Zhòu,
the destruction of Zhōu and the fall of Chén,
all arose from lack of propriety,
let alone among commoners!
For if trust does not come from the heart,
repeated oaths are useless;
if the spirit is fully engaged,
physical forms can be forgotten.
The interactions of gentlemen
are based on shared morality and righteousness,
and closeness through mutual aspirations,
thus they are plain yet enduring.
The connections of petty people
are tied by power and profit,
and intimacy through frivolity and disrespect,
thus sweet but ultimately ruinous.
Why must one gather in inner chambers for banquets
to show sincerity,
or have wives and concubines drink together
to establish affection and intimacy?
The ancients, guarding against the crooked paths of licentiousness and ruin,
preventing the beginnings of decadence and evil,
were truly utmost in their efforts.
Those who cultivate this are gentlemen,
those who violate it are wrongdoers.
Yet if prohibitions are lax, then in high palaces there will be men climbing walls;
if the net has holes, then in mulberry groves there will be eloping women.
To indulge and let it run wild
is like igniting a fierce fire in Yúnmèng,
or releasing pent-up waters from a great height—
can it be extinguished with brooms and besoms,
or blocked with handfuls of soil?
However, customary practices become ingrained,
and all say:
"This is what is commonly done in the capital and superior states,
by princes, nobles, and the esteemed."
I often refute them, saying:
"The central states
are where rites originated.
How could rites be like this!
It is a phenomenon of decline and chaos,
not the old customs of a well-governed era."
Now, Lǎodān,
the epitome of purity and emptiness,
still dared not face what he desired,
to prevent his heart from being disturbed.
If even Liǔxià Huì, with his pure and lofty conduct,
were repeatedly exposed to lewd banquets,
it would inevitably stir emotions within him,
showing in his expression,
especially since those of truly indifferent emotions are fewer than one in ten thousand,
and those who can suppress their emotions are rare.
Such matters as these—
how can they be perpetuated?
Although impoverished scholars are aware that such customs should not be promoted,
they lack both reputation and influence,
how can they rectify them!
I often sigh over this,
thus frequently incurring the dislike of these cliques,
and being labeled as rustic and simple-minded,
incapable of adapting to the times.
I aspire to remain true to myself,
so how could I abandon my own principles
to follow what others deem acceptable!
Lamentable matters are not few,
mostly like this.
Alas,
there is nothing I can do about it!
Those who are tainted by corrupt customs
and sink into degradation along with them—
how would they be willing to accept straightforward, unwelcome advice
and reverse their far-flung eastward rush?
Bàopúzǐ says:
Among the common people, there is a practice of teasing the bride,
amidst large crowds,
in front of relatives,
using foul language to question her,
demanding disrespectful replies.
Such vulgar and defiling acts
are unbearable to discuss.
Some press her with beatings,
or tie her feet and hang her upside down.
Drunken guests, intoxicated and unruly,
know no limits,
to the extent that some cause injuries leading to bleeding,
or even broken limbs—
truly lamentable.
The ancients, moved by parting, would not extinguish candles;
grieving for replaced kin, they refrained from music and rites.
According to ritual,
the groom felt ashamed and did not receive congratulations.
Now, since we cannot fully follow the old codes,
at least for those whose virtue is respected in the village,
and whose words are trusted by scholars,
it is fitting to sternly correct and rebuke such practices.
Why go with the flow
and perpetuate these corrupt customs?
Yet, as these practices have long been carried out among the people,
none realize their wrongness.
They cannot be stopped by mere refined discourse,
nor without severe penalties.
Thus, they disparage the Duke of Zhōu and find fault with Confucius,
considering arrogance and unrestraint as transcending the world.
Some, due to unforeseen events,
sneakily seize honor and rank;
others, relying on powerful connections,
soar high and stand out.
Thereupon, they become proud and boastful,
their spirits towering above all things,
walking tall and gazing far,
smug and self-satisfied.
Looking back at those stuck and isolated,
even if truly talented and exceptional,
they dismiss them like grass.
Some recline on pillows to receive guests,
or claim illness to keep them away,
wishing for crowds of scholars to form forests at their gates,
and cavalry to clog the alleys,
calling it noble and esteemed,
deeming it necessary.
In terms of status and position,
the Duke of Zhōu was diligent in spitting out food and holding his hair to welcome talents;
comparing in fame and reputation,
Confucius was earnest and skilled in guidance.
Both valued diligence and humility,
not considering arrogance and neglect as virtues.
By the end of the Hàn dynasty,
it had changed.
Hair unkempt and disheveled,
clothes draped loosely without belts.
Some received guests in informal attire,
others sat sprawled naked or with legs apart.
Gatherings of friends,
outings for tasteless amusements,
lacked earnest efforts to cultivate virtue,
or diligent pursuit of learning,
correcting faults and remedying errors,
discussing principles and refining meanings.
When they met,
they no longer recounted separations,
or inquired about well-being.
Guests would enter calling for servants,
hosts would see guests and call for dogs.
If one did not do so,
they were not considered intimate
and were shunned as not part of the clique.
At gatherings,
they crouched like foxes and drank like cattle,
scrambling for food and fighting over portions.
Grabbing and gulping down large amounts,
without any sense of shame,
considering those who joined in as sophisticated,
and those who did not as inferior.
All day, no words touched on righteousness,
all night, no beneficial admonishments were heard.
Falsely invoking Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
they prized spontaneity and indulgence,
claiming great deeds ignore minor rites,
and superior men are unbound by rules,
deeming whistling proudly and acting recklessly
as embodying the Dào.
Alas,
what a pity,
is it not sorrowful!
Thus, they mocked clans to express camaraderie,
and engaged in extreme vulgarity to deepen bonds.
They considered leaning and stretching legs as enchanting and elegant,
while viewing those with upright and stern demeanor as country bumpkins;
treating those who pointed stubbornly as vigorous and fresh,
and those who spoke eloquently as stammering and abrupt.
All those frivolous individuals,
though adept at flattering and conforming to trends,
broadly connecting with fellow drifters,
mutually praising and promoting each other,
quickly achieving prominence,
are mostly slick on the surface,
but hollow and empty inside.
They resemble the Shǔ people’s metaphor of the gourd bottle—
not a single page of text in their minds,
their knowledge limited to matters of wine and roasted meat.
So-called arrogance toward bright virtue,
deafness following ignorance,
reckless pursuit of wealth,
greed for food and drink—
as recorded by Zuǒ Qiumíng,
they are the worthless sons.
If asked about the subtle teachings of the Fén and Suǒ documents,
the nature of spirits and ghosts,
the transformations of all things,
the wonders of distant lands,
the grand rites of court and ancestral temples,
the ceremonies of suburban sacrifices and imperial worship,
the origins of the three beginnings and four starts,
the principles of yīn-yáng, pitch-pipes, and calendars,
the models for military, state, and altars,
the similarities and differences in ancient and modern reforms,
they become bewildered and lost,
mumbling and looking around,
dazed and confused,
silent and blank.
Though inwardly aware of their ignorance as if facing a wall,
outwardly they cover up their shortcomings,
unwilling to admit faults,
forcing grand speeches,
saying:
These are trivial old tales,
fit only for impoverished scholars who pore over texts,
chanting towards dried-up bamboo strips,
crawling to guard yellowed scrolls—
not worth asking our kind.
Though they truly know the harm of lacking learning,
the value of great Confucians,
the errors in what they emulate,
the mistakes in what they belittle,
yet they remain迷失 and unrepentant,
because those who are unrestrained suffer no setback in advancement.
If noble persons reprove them with admonishing words,
and for those who fear no authority and persist in evil unrepentantly,
lower their social ranking,
then they should surely fear, melt like ice, and reform,
swiftly retracing their eastward rush.
Bàopúzǐ says:
When the turbid and clear separated and formed,
and all things transformed and came to life,
some feathered tribes could respond to calls,
and some furry kinds had knowledge of speech.
The jué monkey recognized the past,
the guīzhōng beast knew the future,
the dark swallows understood yin and yang,
and insects could sense distant springs and streams—
even yarrow stalks and tortoise shells could not surpass them,
nor could Gān and Shí outdo them.
It is only because humans lacked ritual
that they did not rank among noble natures.
In the earliest antiquity,
people had no social classes;
the Lord on High lamented the extreme crudeness of their chaotic state,
and pitied the despicability of their nest and cave dwellings.
Therefore, He constructed buildings to separate them from flocks of birds and beasts,
and established ritual codes to differentiate ranks of authority and dignity.
He taught them circling movements,
instructed them in bowing and yielding,
standing like a bent chime stone,
cupping hands as if embracing a drum,
the etiquette of walking quickly or slowly, ascending and descending,
the demeanor of gazing, receiving, and responding—
amounting to as many as three thousand rules.
These served as dikes to check excess,
and are urgent matters of human principle.
Hence, dignity stands first in the Qū Lǐ,
and appearance heads the five matters;
leaving the gate requires solemnity in meeting guests,
and solitude at home calls for caution in self-reflection.
Yán Huí straightened his attire after nightly bathing,
Zhòng Yóu tied his cap string when facing death;
if respectful demeanor is briefly abandoned,
laziness and negligence soon follow.
To pacify superiors and govern the people,
there is no other way but this.
For humans having ritual
is like fish having water.
If fish lose water,
though they may gasp briefly for life,
their withering and decay can surely be expected.
If humans abandon ritual,
though they may seem alive outwardly,
it is a step toward disaster and ruin.
Lǔ upheld the rituals of Zhōu,
and violent troops did not attack;
Wèi honored Duàn Gānmù,
and sharp-helmeted soldiers turned their banners back.
Great Chǔ had a million armored troops,
yet collapsed like dried leaves shaken loose;
strong Qín relied on Hángǔ Pass's perils,
but lacked the solidity of a plucked willow.
Was this not due to abandoning the three fundamentals and losing their roots?
Moreover, in times of comfort and ease, emotions are stirred,
and the long duration of chaos and turmoil
has caused customs and teachings to deteriorate,
restraining rituals to be abandoned,
and a culture of negligence to form.
People nowadays face the delusion of misguided governance,
commoners encounter the disorder of a broken moral net,
like fish escaping the water net,
or trapped beasts breaking free from land snares.
Since the era of turmoil and loss,
things have constantly changed:
caps, shoes, and clothing,
sleeves and cuffs barely regulated,
altering with the sun and moon,
no longer fixed in form.
Now long, now short,
one wide, one narrow,
suddenly high, suddenly low,
sometimes coarse, sometimes fine,
adornments without constancy,
taking sameness as pleasure.
Those fond of novelty
imitate them morning and night—
the so-called "the capital favors big eyebrows,
distant regions all follow with half-foreheads."
I am truly an ordinary man,
