clumsy at following trends;
unable to keep up with changing attire,
I do not change,
and where there is no harm,
I have never altered.
Though pointed at and laughed at,
I pay no heed.
Is it that I wish to defy the crowd?
Truly, I consider it non-essential.
The superior state excels in many ways over Jiāngbiǎo,
yet some practices are acceptable, others not.
A noble person practicing ritual
does not seek to change customs—
meaning when in a foreign land away from home,
one does not alter the ways of their native place.
How much more so in one's parents' homeland—
why must one abandon the old and strain to learn anew?
In Wú, skilled calligraphers
include Huáng Xiàng, Liú Zuǎn, Cén Bórán, Zhū Jìpíng,
all unparalleled masters of their generation;
just as in the central states, there are Zhōng Yuáncháng, Hú Kǒngmíng, Zhāng Zhī, Suǒ Jìng,
each exquisite in their own region,
all using ancient styles,
fully adequate for their purposes.
I say: discarding long-practiced methods
to toil painfully learning central states' script
is still unnecessary,
let alone changing one's speech sounds
to mimic northern tongue—
unable to master it well,
it seems shameful and laughable,
like failing to learn Hándān's walk
and earning the mockery of crawling instead.
This is but a minor issue;
there are even those in mourning
who imitate central states' weeping,
making it suddenly devoid of genuine grief.
In the past, Zhōng Yí and Zhuāng Xì
never forgot their native accents,
and the ancients praised them.
Confucius said:
"Those who have lost a parent
are like infants who have lost their mothers.
Their cries—how could they be ordinary sounds!"
Better to have excess grief and insufficient ritual
than to weep merely to vent sorrow—
what matters grace or clumsiness?
Yet some embellish their tones—
this is not called heartfelt pain.
I also hear that nobles in deep mourning,
or those ill,
take mineral powders and frequently eat to diffuse the drug's effect,
treating drinking as vital to life.
When ill and critically weak,
unable to bear wind and cold,
they surround themselves with curtains, cushions, and mattresses,
settling wherever comfortable.
Thus, petty men with wealth and power
no longer stay in mourning quarters,
often residing in separate rooms,
on high beds with thick bedding,
enjoying fine food and heavy drink,
sometimes with close guests,
filling cups and draining them,
until dead drunk,
saying:
"This is the way of the capital, Luòyáng."
Is it not a pity!
In my homeland,
virtuous gentlemen of former times,
facing grave difficulties,
or combined with old age and decline,
though ritually only required to wear mourning hemp,
and not to grieve to emaciation,
all exceeded in sorrow, consuming only gruel,
never tasting sweetness.
Even unworthy people then
strove to emulate and improve themselves;
yet people now choose such ways—
how vastly different they are!
Moreover, many do not understand,
claiming that most central states people in mourning are extravagant—
but this is entirely untrue.
I hear that Xuān, Jǐng, Wén, and Wǔ, the four emperors of Jìn,
while mourning parents, all emaciated beyond regulation,
and did not follow the Wáng family's twenty-five-month rite,
but observed the seven-month mourning.
At that time, all under heaven in deep grief
took the four emperors as their model.
Why do people nowadays not hear of this,
but falsely slander the noble—
is it not deluded?
Bàopúzǐ says:
Born into families of worldly nobility,
residing in influential positions,
most, without expecting arrogance, find it comes naturally.
Unless one possesses extraordinary caliber,
it is hard to avoid the fault of excess.
For laboring humbly and emptying oneself
attracts many followers;
arrogance and haughtiness
drive many away.
Many followers are a sign of security;
many departures are a symptom of danger.
The pivot of survival and demise
lies herein.
To treat it lightly
is indeed blindness!
There are also those who start from lowly origins,
rising from obscurity to prominence,
merely by hunching shoulders and hiding tracks,
crouching and standing sideways,
lowering brows and bending knees,
flattering the powerful and influential,
seizing opportunities by chance,
surpassing others out of turn,
feathers growing into wings,
shedding their cicada shells in the spring soil,
then becoming self-important,
eyes not following their feet,
filled with self-satisfaction,
viewing others as mere mustard seeds.
Some host lavish banquets with dense gatherings,
pipes and strings clamoring noisily,
later guests crowd the gate,
yet they no longer receive them.
Or among those of similar background,
they show particular favor to some,
which may not be entirely deserved either.
Simply put,
they only frequently engage with those
who continuously send gifts,
with wine vessels never empty.
As Mèng Kē said, "To love without respect
is to raise them like pigs."
Yet many practice this,
claiming it is the way of self-respect.
The way of self-respect
lies in humbling oneself to the lowly,
maintaining modesty to cultivate oneself,
not in what is described here.
Rather, it is a corrupt custom of decadence,
an incurable malady,
that so many partake in it
is truly lamentable.
As for great individuals and monumental talents,
with vast capacity and far-reaching grace,
they tread high paths alone,
serene and self-content,
their bodies adrift in the currents,
their spirits ascending beyond the nine heavens,
their inner virtue sufficient,
they discard external things,
with torn hats and broken shoes,
clad in rags and rope belts,
how would they deign to compete with vulgar people in obsequious flattery,
cultivate fawning expressions of sycophancy,
mimic the garrulous petty officers of Shànglín,
or create the cacophony of spring cicadas and summer flies!
Judging by appearance,
demanding beauty,
vulgar people only see the coarseness of their exterior,
unable to perceive the profundity of their spirit,
focusing on the surface,
ignoring the heart and mind,
though they harbor extraordinary talents,
surpassing the world and transcending peers,
their actions can enlighten the methods of the entire era,
their words suffice to resolve confusions of past and present,
containing brilliance while remaining reserved,
speaking only of what is lawful,
yet thatch and weeds cannot stir the resonance of ten thousand jun bells,
dwarfs cannot appreciate the grandeur of towering heights,
thus they are ridiculed,
deemed ordinary and foolish.
Those not from the Hàn riverbanks
cannot discern bright pearls in the mud-covered clams;
those who have not wept blood
cannot recognize night-lustrous gems within layered cliffs.
Tiny insects dwelling in the eyebrows of mosquitoes
laugh at the great roc that fills the sky;
inch-long minnows swimming in puddles of ox hoofprints
do not value the giant fish that traverse the seas.
Thus, their paths and achievements cannot intersect,
their intelligence cannot reach each other.
It is naturally incompatible,
and nothing to be greatly surprised about.
The reason I criticize this and cannot remain silent
is my hope that gentlemen in positions
will not judge people by appearance,
but encourage humility and self-restraint,
to eternally preserve the heavenly order.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
People hearing of Dài Shūluán and Ruǎn Sìzōng's disdain for customs and self-indulgence
consider it great magnanimity,
yet without assessing that their own abilities do not match those of such disdainful figures,
they admire and emulate them.
Some with disheveled hair or bareheaded,
some naked or squatting rudely,
some washing feet in crowded places,
some relieving themselves in front of others,
some leaving guests to eat alone,
some serving wine only to their close ones,
these are acts of barbarians,
not the refined practices of Zhūxià.
With the talent and learning of Dài and Ruǎn,
they still suffered from their own eccentricities,
their gains and losses hardly balancing out,
had the two gentlemen respectfully adhered to constraints,
acted earnestly in interactions,
and cautiously in their duties,
how much further could they have reached!
Moreover, those far inferior to them,
hastily following in their footsteps,
will quickly incur disaster and endanger themselves,
in the blink of an eye,
not only failing to be treated with virtuous respect!
In the past, Xī Shī, ill, lay by the roadside,
her beauty enchanting,
fragrant like orchids and musk,
passersby all admired her looks and pitied her illness,
pausing with concern.
Then a village girl, emulating her,
feigned illness by the road,
but being ugly in form,
and emitting a foul odor,
travelers all detested her appearance and loathed her smell,
turning away and covering their noses,
hurrying past quickly.
Now people without the natural grace of Dài and Ruǎn,
but imitating their arrogance,
are like that ugly girl unaware of her own measure.
Even emperors hold the rites of disciples to the Sān Lǎo and Wǔ Gēng,
to lead people in reverence.
A person without courtesy
is deeply flawed.
To disrespect others surely means not honoring one's own parents,
for if one wishes others to respect them,
they must first show self-respect.
Failing to cultivate good deeds,
one becomes a wicked person;
without great achievements,
one remains a petty person.
Zhòu, for his tyranny,
was called the "lonely one";
Zhòngní, though a minister's attendant,
was deemed the "uncrowned king."
Thus, a gentleman's worth lies not in wealth or status.
Now, committing acts that violate rites,
yet disliking to hear criticism of hastened death,
is like carrying a pig and resenting mention of its stench,
or throwing oneself in mud and forbidding talk of dirt.
In the past, Xīn Yǒu saw those sacrificing with disheveled hair,
and knew the Róng tribes would rise.
I observe the era of Huái and Mǐn,
when customs favored arrogance and irreverence,
treating themselves as barbarians,
later the Qiāng and Hú tribes ravaged Xià,
invading and plundering the capital,
and realizing this matter,
it was a foreshadowing omen.
Now the land tends toward peace,
with signs of revival,
why not jointly correct past errors,
and cultivate the beauty of harmony and dignity!
Only by entering a den of tigers and wolves
does one appreciate the bravery of Bēn Yù;
only in a society where rites are abandoned
does one recognize the unwavering integrity of the refined.
With the decline of moral transformation,
and the drift into waywardness,
scholars and Confucians
should collectively regret it,
and rightly feel heartfelt sorrow together,
correcting and rectifying it.
If strength is insufficient,
and nothing can be done,
then at least maintain the integrity of bamboo and pine,
unchanged even in the harsh cold.
How can one rush to compete with the vile and base,
seeking acceptance from such crowds!
The farther one strays from the Way,
the more it calls for sorrow and lament.
If there are those who loftily uphold integrity,
steadfast and unshifting,
not drifting like tumbleweed to follow the crowd,
nor altering their elegance to adopt vulgarity,
people cannot recognize their goodness through mere dislike,
and thus, for those who differ from themselves,
they collectively treat them as enemies and refuse to acknowledge them.
Alas,
can decay and corruption truly prevail so?
A noble person can act with unwavering brightness and principled rigidity,
forming no factions with the vulgar,
stirring clear waves to agitate the muddy flow,
grasping strong arrows to chastise the multitude of wrongdoers.
At most, they may not be tolerated,
and fail to attain wealth and honor.
If the heavenly nobility truly resides within oneself,
standing independently and unyielding through this,
what bitterness or regret is there to bear?
Yet to instead chop at one's roots and crumble like tiles,
eating dregs and clutching mud,
cutting feet to fit shoes,
destroying squares to fit circles—
is that not utterly extreme!
A person of principle cannot make others respect him, yet his resolve cannot be seized;
he cannot make others not hate him, yet his path cannot be bent;
he cannot prevent others from insulting him, yet honor still lies within him;
he cannot stop others from rejecting him, yet his integrity cannot be altered.
Thus, with destiny settled and plans decided,
persuasion or discouragement cannot interfere;
rejoicing in heaven and knowing fate,
worry and fear cannot enter;
in hardship and toil, he grows firmer,
in poverty and adversity, he holds no regret.
If one can truly apply their heart in this way,
how could they ever willingly bend like grass or float lightly,
seeking to fit a square peg in a round hole,
emulating the actions of those whom propriety has cast aside!
Bào Púzǐ said:
I have heard that in the late Hàn period, those without virtue
ranked and graded each other,
a crowd of arrogant and haughty individuals
who did not adhere to the restraints of the Way.
They became chief bullies and dominant figures,
with connections in all directions,
all betraying ritual teachings to indulge in depravity and aberration,
slandering the truly upright,
harming those outside their clique,
their mouths accustomed to foul speech,
their bodies performing corrupt deeds.
All they said and did
made it unbearable for people to even discuss.
What the ancients called "comprehensive understanding"
meant comprehending the Way and virtue,
attaining benevolence and righteousness.
How could it mean understanding defilement and attaining lewdness and evil!
It is like the robber Zhí,
who claimed to possess five paths of the sage.
Such customs damage and destroy human relations,
more severely than the arrival of bandits and thieves.
They cannot endure long,
but is the harm merely the ruin of a single set of clothing!
As for the descendants of noble families,
and officials in positions,
disregarding canonical punishments,
they all went bareheaded and exposed their bodies,
sitting sprawled when receiving guests.
This not only disgraced their official posts,
but also spread contamination to the common people.
Later generations and younger folks,
seeing that some of them had already attained pure status,
or frivolously stolen empty fame,
and then imitated their actions themselves,
led ordinary people to believe that in establishing oneself in the world,
nothing was more admirable than this.
Those who uphold ritual restraints find it bitter and difficult,
and most of them end up poor and lowly;
those who indulge in arrogance and license find it pleasant and easy,
and practitioners of this swiftly advance.
Thus, vulgar people all abandon the former for the latter.
In the world, some lack pure conduct from youth,
yet grow up to buy office and attain wealth and honor.
Perhaps their knowledge is sufficient to embellish themselves,
and their cliques enough to pull each other up.
Then, unscrupulous youths
point to them as proof,
saying:
"They indulge their passions and desires without hindering their splendor,
while those who restrain themselves and follow the Way cannot escape poverty and lowliness."
They do not realize that the honored and prominent may be fortunate,
while the suddenly fallen may be unlucky,
neither due to their conduct.
Yet those called "four-way, eight-direction connected"
love to aid and attach themselves to their own kind.
Shoes来不及 tied,
sashes来不及 fastened,
they join hands ascending halls,
link sleeves entering chambers,
going out they sit knee-to-knee,
invited to meetings they come directly,
favors received are plentiful,
requests entrusted are often heard,
desires are invariably met,
in discussions they are indulged,
in trouble they are rescued,
when recommended, a lame donkey gains the value of a fine steed,
when slandered, even Xiàojǐ receives the calumny of Shāngchén.
Thus, when petty men rush forth,
it is like releasing accumulated water from a towering dam,
or setting fire to dry grass in the Yúnmèng marshes.
To hope for solemn and harmonious dignity,
with later generations having models to follow,
is like trying to dry ice by roasting it,
or making ashes blaze by heaping them.
Bào Púzǐ said:
Officials of the Three Terraces and Nine Ranks
sit and discourse on the Way;
provincial governors and commandery administrators
grasp the guiding principles and lift the key points.
The higher the office,
the more ample its affairs,
yet the concentration of toil and complexity,
lies uniquely with the district magistrates.
From them emerge all labor services,
towards them converge all exactions and demands.
Even if governors and administrators are worthy, if magistrates are incompetent,
then state affairs will not be accomplished,
myriad duties will have gaps,
and the damage and ruin will hardly stop at just one region!
Magistrates especially ought to be selected for talent,
more urgently than officials in the central ministries.
If the wrong persons are appointed,
the reason is none other than
the failure to practice utmost impartiality,
while following selfish intentions goes unchecked.
Sometimes elder relatives are esteemed and powerful,
so their sons and brothers are chosen based on reputation;
sometimes high-ranking individuals make requests,
so mediocre types are appointed despite incompetence;
sometimes it is due to long-held inclinations,
or relatives who are no strangers.
Knowing they are unsuitable, yet such types are still employed.
Occasionally, there are satisfactory cases,
not entirely without hits.
But overall, the unrefined are in the majority.
Those who can prove themselves effective,
diligently cultivating purity and restraint,
serving diligently day and night,
to seek public acclaim,
fearing their achievements and reputation may be unimpressive,
ashamed if their patrons made a mistaken recommendation—
such men are few!
Mediocre and base individuals,
petty in capacity and narrow in ambition,
crave wealth and bribes,
aiming only for riches,
indulging passions and desires,
without stop or satisfaction.
The supervising officials,
knowing they have enough evidence,
rely on their superiors to impeach and investigate them.
Though they should eventually be dismissed,
fearing they might incur enmity,
and instead suffer slander themselves,
they dare not confront or offend them,
thus indulging their greed and cruelty.
Under such circumstances,
how can the common people not suffer hardship and poison, leading to separation and fragmentation!
When the fragmented are numerous,
they cannot but gather and become bandit hordes.
A hall a hundred fathoms high
can be burned by a spark of wind;
a dam a thousand zhang long
can be breached by an ant's nest.
How can one not take deep precautions!
How can one not make changes!
Yet those who wield the scales
sometimes abandon impartial judgment to follow personal whims;
those who hold the axe handle
often bend the plumb line to favor those who side with them.
Those selecting officials do not choose people for the sake of the office,
and those seeking positions do not consider themselves unqualified.
Thus, when they assume governance, administration becomes neglected;
when they shepherd the people, the people become dispersed.
Some are corrupt, arrogant, and extravagant, oppressing the common folk;
some are harsh, cruel, and severe, breeding much resentment and rebellion;
some are ignorant, obtuse, and confused, throwing all affairs into chaos;
some are negligent, sluggish, and lax, leading to decay and ruin;
some delight in launching unnecessary projects, exhausting the people's strength;
some harbor fugitives and carry out violent acts;
some are ignorant of laws and decrees, easily deceived and manipulated;
some indulge in music, wine, and sensual pleasures, sinking into dissipation;
some are engrossed in board games and gambling, neglecting governmental duties;
some are absorbed in hunting, excursions, and drinking, forgetting all matters of state;
some pay no heed to litigation, throwing penalties and prisons into disarray.
The common people cannot endure it,
and rise up to become bandits and rebels.
When faults and crimes come to light,
they are imprisoned among thorny bushes.
This tarnishes the ruler's wisdom,
adds to the complexity of penal codes,
and the suffering of the people
has already run deep!
Employing the wrong person
is like adorning a wooden horse with ornate trappings—
how could it gallop with the wind?
Or using a clay dragon to bring rain—
how could it shine its light across the heavenly thoroughfare?
If those who hold the nation's reins
and issue the royal commands
would carefully examine candidates as one would good medicine,
not allowing the lame to stand among thoroughbreds,
and if those who seek recklessly and obtain undeservedly,
blind to their own limitations,
would consider the risk of stumbling midway,
not yoking worn-out nags to a phoenix carriage,
then why worry that all achievements would not prosper,
or that the four evils would not retreat?
The Three Sovereigns would hardly suffice to be four,
and the Five Emperors would find it hard to be six!
Bàopúzǐ said:
When talent meets great enlightenment,
even before the mulberry's shadow moves,
a bond as strong as metal and orchid is already forged.
When great ability encounters deep insight,
there's no need for repeated trials—
mutual understanding is already clear.
Soaring like a swan geese riding a strong wind,
dancing like a legendary fish treading on startling clouds.
If obscurity could be overlooked,
then Jiāng Zǐyá would not have been employed by the Zhōu.
If distance and low status could be rejected,
then Máo Suí would not have been honored in Zhào.
If only long-standing virtue warranted political trust,
then Nìng Qì would not have risen in Qí.
If reliance were placed solely on established fame,
then Chén Píng and Hán Xìn would not have been recorded in Hàn.
The wise focus on the major and overlook the minor,
free from jealousy and greed,
thus they can establish authority and achieve merits,
bringing peace to heaven and earth.
How could they be willing to weigh each stick of firewood before burning,
or count every grain before cooking,
picking out flaws and discarding examples,
parting hair in search of flaws?
Some say:
"Ancient writers
had great talent and profound thoughts,
so their texts are obscure and hard to understand;
modern people have shallow ideas and limited strength,
so their writings are exposed and easy to see.
Comparing this easily understood
to that hard to comprehend
is like matching a ditch to a river,
or an anthill to Mount Tài.
Thus, if water does not spring from Kūnlún,
it cannot surge as a great stream flowing east;
if books do not come from the brilliant,
they cannot possess the grand tone that reaches far."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Those who discuss narrow views
cannot be asked about the boundlessness of the nine heavens;
those accustomed to constraints
cannot be urged to have outstanding unique insights.
The scholars of the past
were neither ghosts nor gods;
though their physical forms have melted away long ago,
their spirit and essence
are spread across the pages.
Their feelings appear in their words,
their main ideas can be grasped.
Moreover, the obscurity in many ancient texts
is not necessarily because the ancients intentionally made them hard to understand;
sometimes it's due to changes in language over time,
or differences in dialects,
passing through chaos and turmoil,
being buried and stored for long,
with bamboo strips rotting and breaking,
many parts lost,
some pieced together残缺ly,
some missing chapters and sentences,
hence they are hard to know,
seeming as if extremely profound.
Take the Shàngshū,
a collection of governmental affairs,
yet it is not as elegantly rich and splendid as the modern edicts, military documents, and memorials;
the Máo Shī,
with its flowery and colorful phrases,
cannot match the vast richness of 'Shànglín', 'Yǔliè', 'Èr Jīng', and 'Sān Dū'.
So, how can it be
that ancient philosophical works
surpass those of modern authors?
But those who cling to the past,
chattering about what they cherish,
have ears but no eyes—
how would they acknowledge this?
They regard the ancients' works as divine,
and modern writings as shallow,
valuing the distant and despising the near—
this has been so for a long time.
"Hence, a new sword gains value with fake engraving,
and a worthless prescription is treasured for its false label.
Thus, though ancient books are plain,
vulgar Confucians claim they fell from heaven;
though modern writings are like gold and jade,
common people equate them with tiles and pebbles.
Ancient books, though numerous,
are not all perfect;
they should serve as mountains and abysses for scholars,
enabling writers
to identify, cut, fish, and hunt within them.
Yet, they are like the trees of Dōng'ōu,
the forests of Chángzhōu:
though there are many catalpas and wingnuts,
one cannot call them the magnificent spectacle of a great hall,
the grand beauty of a splendid house;
or like the marshes of Yúnmèng,
the swamps of Mèngzhū:
though fish and meat are abundant,
one cannot call them the lavish feast of frying and roasting,
the fine flavors of Yú Dí.
Modern poetry and ancient poetry
both have meaning and principle,
but differ in beauty.
Comparing them to scholars,
both may have moral conduct,
but if one excels in arts and literature,
they cannot be considered the same;
comparing them to women,
both may possess national beauty,
but if one is uniquely skilled in a hundred arts,
they cannot be mixed as no different.
If both discuss palaces,
how does the ode of Xīsī for the royal寝宫
compare to Wáng Yán's rhapsody on the Lingguang Hall?
Similarly speaking of hunts,
how do the poems of Shū Tián about Lúlíng
compare to Xiàng Rú's description of Shànglín?
Both praising sacrifices,
how do the verses of Qīngmiào and Yúnhàn
compare to the brilliance of Guō's Southern Suburb sacrifice?
Equally recounting expeditions,
how do the works 'Chūjū' and 'Liùyuè'
compare to Chén Lín's vigor in 'Wǔjūn'?
Thus, citing these examples can awaken understanding.
Recently, Xiàhóu Zhàn and Pān Ānrén both composed poems to supplement the lost,
such as 'Báihuá', 'Yóugēng', 'Nángāi', 'Huáshǔ', and the like.
All erudite Confucians and highly talented connoisseurs of literature
agree that among the ancient three hundred poems,
none suffice to match the works of these two worthies.
"Moreover, in ancient times all things were pure and simple,
while today everything is adorned and decorated.
Times shift and the world changes -
this follows the natural principle.
As for woolen brocades being both beautiful and durable,
they cannot be said to be inferior to straw rain capes;
covered carriages being both elegant and sturdy,
they cannot be considered worse than solid-wheeled carts.
Writing is like speech -
if people converse
deliberately to show their knowledge
(sound?)
even when Hu and Yuè people meet,
they ultimately cannot understand each other.
Using this method for teaching and admonishment,
how could people comprehend it!
If speech should aim to be easily understood,
then why should writing prize being difficult to comprehend?
Just as boats and carriages replaced walking,
and writing superseded knot-tying,
later creations often surpass earlier practices.
The achievements that have followed one another by thousands,
cannot be enumerated in detail.
Everyone knows this
and finds modern times more convenient than the past -
why should only literature be inferior to antiquity?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
For securing the state and governing the people,
nothing is better than rites,
which thoroughly organize human relations
and are indeed comprehensive.
However, the ceremonies for capping, wedding, drinking, and archery
are excessively trivial!
Although human relations value having rituals,
they should only serve to distinguish hierarchy and express respect.
Why insist on the complexity of ascending/descending and bowing/saluting,
or the endless kneeling, rising, and prostrating!
In the past when the world was peaceful
and all regions were tranquil,
antiquarian officials
occasionally practiced these rites,
even to the point of lecturing and testing for months,
supervising with whips and canes,
practicing day and night,
neglecting sleep and food.
After studying for seasons,
being tested in one day,
holding scrolls while performing,
moving according to written texts,
with punishments of demotion and exile
looming over them,
mistakes still occurred,
and the essential meaning was missed.
To consider this as regular routine for common people
is extremely difficult to implement.
This is what Mòzǐ meant by 'generations cannot exhaust the learning,
nor can one lifetime complete the practice.'
The ancients consulted grass-cutters and wood-gatherers,
widely debated children's rhymes -
even madmen's words
were considered for selection.
As for Mòzǐ's theories,
they cannot be entirely rejected.
Though he expanded penal codes,
opened pathways,
dealt with human affairs,
and prepared the kingly way,
he couldn't elaborate everything in detail.
His criticism of lavish burials
and satires against ritual complexity
should not be discarded.
Since the Jiàn'ān era,
Wǔ and Wén of Wèi
established funeral customs
that emphasized simplicity and frugality -
this shows Mòzǐ's way
has practicable elements.
I believe that after chaos subsides
and court and country are tranquil,
the ruler's institutions
should create new precedents.
We should appoint learned scholars
capable of making judgments,
free from rigid conservatism,
to revise the Three Ritual Classics,
discarding the unnecessary,
organizing their origins and developments,
consolidating their content,
and grouping them by category.
The repetitive and elaborate explanations,
differently worded but similarly meant, should be preserved;
the impracticable should be removed.
Without causing harm,
we can ultimately simplify and implement them,
preventing obscurity
and further confusion.
The ritual objects for auspicious and inauspicious occasions,
vessels like zǔ, dòu, gū, and zhì,
regulations for clothing, headwear, vehicles, and ornaments,
the beauty of banners and distinguishing colors,
standards for palace buildings reflecting rank,
protocols for court feasts and host-guest etiquette,
variations in sacrificial and burial ceremonies,
methods for suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
rites for state altars and mountains-rivers -
all can be reduced,
ensuring simplicity and frugality.
Simplicity makes compliance easier,
frugality reduces expenditure;
easy compliance eliminates hassle,
reduced expenditure means lighter burdens;
no hassle means officials make fewer errors,
lighter burdens mean no harsh demands on suppliers.
The minutiae of bowing, resting, and saluting,
the forms of ascending, descending, and circling -
make them sufficient for conducting affairs
without trivial complexity.
Arrange items separately,
for easy reference and use.
Currently the Five Rituals are confused and mixed,
with miscellaneous decorations tangled together,
branching and scattering like leaves,
duplicating and overlapping,
interpenetrating one another.
Even classical scholars researching them
often encounter obstacles;
disputes and objections increasingly diverge endlessly,
with different principles and multiple interpretations,
growing year by year, month by month.
Unless supremely learned,
none avoid confusion and frustration.
Hesitating at crossroads,
toiling in thickets of doubts,
exhausting spirit and thought,
examining cases and precedents -
some spend whole years
without achieving clarity.
Such diligent study yields bitterness,
with no way to resolve doubts;
groaning while analyzing,
haggard while debating,
studying until gray-haired without establishing oneself,
wasting time and days,
neglecting other occupations,
exhausting later generations -
truly endless!
The resulting commentaries and annotations
exceed the original texts.
Now if we harmonize with varied customs,
classify and categorize,
delete the non-essential,
raise the main principles,
adjust the ordinances,
making them bright as sun and moon,
clear as the definite five colors,
we can spare scholars ten-thousandfold labor,
end the trouble of academic disputes,
so future understanding observers
will admire them more than we admire the Zhōu dynasty.
This resembles reforming stone-cooking and abandoning blood-sacrifices -
nothing to fear or avoid,
yet people regretfully cling to nostalgia,
like pushing carts slowly after leaving nest-dwellings.
However, conventional adherents
suddenly hearing this proposal
will inevitably be shocked by its novelty,
calling it the raving of a madman.
The Three Sovereigns didn't continue each other's music,
the Five Emperors didn't inherit each other's rites,
yet they all transformed customs,
secured states and governed people alike.
Some reforms, some continuations,
additions and deletions all aiming at improvement -
why must we ride boats up mountains,
whip horses across rivers,
wear armor in temple halls,
or don heavy furs in midsummer!
If ancient practices were truly unchangeable,
then coffins shouldn't replace firewood burials,
nor should clothing replace nakedness."
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The canonical classics are the deep sea of the Way and righteousness,
while the philosophical writings are the rivers and streams that augment its depth.
Looking up and comparing them,
they are like the auspicious star assisting the three luminaries;
looking down and analogizing them,
they are like the woods and thickets embellishing Mount Sōng.
Although their paths differ,
they converge in the advancement of virtue;
though they diverge in their steps,
they unite in promoting transformation.
Thus, the comprehensive person traces the origins to encompass the branches,
grasps the guiding principles to achieve unity.
The ancients lamented the rarity of talent,
hence they said that a hundred generations pass as if following footsteps,
not discarding the gem that shines at night because the uncarved jade is not from Kūnlún,
nor rejecting words that aid teaching because the book did not come from a sage.
Therefore, rustic poems from the lanes,
and stern oaths from the army,
even if their words are crude and metaphors simple,
and their texts do not fill ten lines,
are still compiled and recorded,
ranked next to the canonical decrees.
The words of the hundred schools,
share the same principle with what is good.
Like those carrying water,
though their vessels differ, they put out the fire alike;
just as acupuncturists,
though their techniques vary, they treat illnesses equally.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
numerous writings have multiplied,
though their meaning is deeper than the mysterious abyss,
and their rhetoric more abundant than waves,
applying them can bring auspicious signs from heaven,
elicit good omens from the earth,
summon the ringed pheasant from beyond the wilderness,
secure peace within Huáxià's walls,
quell the steps of calamity nearby,
and bestow long-lasting blessings afar.
Yet, as there are no sages in this age,
their eloquent words go unnoticed,
so they cannot gallop like fine steeds on a thousand-mile path,
nor be compiled with the ancient ways in the end of the Three Sovereigns' texts.
Those who are constrained,
shackled in shallow narrowness,
clinging to trivial glosses,
despise the unusual and disdain the different,
deeming them unimportant.
Some say petty arts are not worth observing,
others claim breadth confuses the mind,
not realizing that combining small weights can equal a mountain's mass,
gathering hundreds and tens can reach billions in number,
as multiple colors combine to make rich patterns beautiful,
and various sounds blend to harmonize like Sháo and Huò music.
Some value and love the shallow, trivial writings of poetry,
while neglecting the deeply beautiful and richly broad philosophical books,
considering sharp, profound words as foolish clumsiness,
and taking empty, flashy rhetoric as exquisite skill,
thus inverting truth and falsehood,
confusing jade with stone,
equating grand music with rustic songs,
and matching dragon insignia with common attire.
So many are like this,
truly lamentable and regrettable!
Some say:
"Though writings are abundant,
they only serve to display rhetoric and adorn language,
offering no remedy for gains and losses,
unlike the unspoken teaching of virtuous conduct.
Thus, Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn rank first, while Zǐyóu and Zǐxià come second.
In the framework of the four disciplines,
learning is fundamental and conduct secondary,
yet composing writings is indeed a minor matter,
and you, sir, do not praise its source,
but solely value its branches,
is that acceptable?"
Bàopǔzǐ replies:
"Virtuous conduct involves action,
its strengths and weaknesses are easily seen.
Literary works are subtle and refined,
their essence hard to discern.
What is easily seen is coarse,
what is hard to discern is refined.
Precisely because it is coarse,
it can be measured with fixed standards;
precisely because it is refined,
evaluation becomes difficult to unify.
Thus, I set aside the easily seen coarseness,
to discuss the hard-to-discern refinement,
is that not acceptable!"
Some say:
"Virtuous conduct is the root,
literary works are the branches.
Hence in the order of the four disciplines,
literature does not rank highest.
Then, what is put on paper
is the dregs of trivial matters;
what can be transmitted
is like straw dogs after the sacrifice.
The hierarchy of high and low,
is thus recognizable.
The essence of literature,
can it be heard?"
Bàopǔzǐ says:
"The trap can be discarded only after the fish is caught;
if the fish is not yet caught, the trap cannot be done without.
Writing can be abolished only after the Way is practiced;
if the Way is not yet practiced, writing cannot be done without.
As for the grandeur or brevity of literary traces and rhythmic schemes,
the density of phrasing and event comparison,
the length of origins and arrivals,
the depth of implication and guidance—
the disparity is so vast,
that even the gap between heaven and a hair's tip
cannot比喻 its distance;
their contrast is such,
that even the brilliance of the three lights
cannot compare to their magnitude and minuteness.
Dragon's pool lead and iron ingots
are insufficient to比喻 their sharpness and bluntness;
wild goose feathers and piled gold
cannot match their lightness and weight.
Clear and turbid, uneven,
each endowed with its own master,
bright and obscure not of the same class,
strong and weak each with different energy,
yet common scholars only see those who can wield the brush on paper,
and generalize them as one category.
This is why Bóyá forever missed Zhòngzǐ,
and the Yǐng man's axe remained unused.
For though carvers are numerous,
only Bān and Dí are renowned for peerless skill;
though lute players abound,
only Kuí and Xiāng knew the difficulty of true understanding.
A thousand steeds in the stable,
yet the qíjì stands out with unmatched value;
tens of thousands of beauties counted,
yet Wēishī possesses a transcendent appearance.
Truly, some far surpass the multitude.
"Moreover, literature and virtuous conduct,
are like ten feet to a zhang (ten feet),
to call it a minor matter,
has never been heard before.
What heaven displays through images,
why Táng and Yú are so named,
the great man's tiger-like brilliance,
the nobleman's leopard-like patterns,
Chāng and Dàn determining sagehood with a single character,
Confucius following the richness of Zhōu,
all are literature.
The Eight Trigrams born from what the eagle and hawk embody,
the Six Jiǎ derived from what the spiritual turtle carries,
where literature exists,
even if lowly, it is still noble,
the hide of dogs and sheep
cannot compare.
Besides, the root need not all be precious,
the branches need not all be worthless.
Like brocade relying on plain fabric,
pearls and jade dwelling in clams and stones,
clouds and rain born from a tiny patch of sky,
rivers and seas starting from a small beginning.
Thus, though literature may be the younger sibling of virtuous conduct,
it cannot be called a minor matter."
Some say:
"The deeds of the present age
mostly fall short of antiquity,
and literary compositions
are likewise so.
Is this due to the decline of vital energy,
a natural principle?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"Though the sayings of the hundred schools
vary in their starting points,
all emerge from the thoughts of profound scholars,
taking form through the hands of talented men.
Compared with the ancients,
they are not necessarily inferior.
Some possess profound and expansive subtlety,
matching the creators,
inwardly opening unfathomable deep sources,
outwardly spreading inexhaustible far-reaching currents.
Their ancestral foundation is lofty,
their elaboration exquisite.
Their transformations are not confined by the square and compass of rules,
their comprehensive understanding not obstructed by the narrowness of a single path.
Thus, those with biased tastes for sour and salty
cannot know their flavor;
those with limited capacity for thought
cannot grasp their spirit.
When the winged dragon rises leisurely,
gazing around as it reaches the clouds,
and the sweat-blood steed paces slowly,
breathing across a thousand miles,
how can the mole cricket wonder at their attaining heights without steps,
or the lame nag fret that they surpass it not gradually?
As for those who gallop within the confines of poetic discourse,
circulate among biographies and records,
yet view grand uniqueness with ordinary feelings,
measure the boundless with narrow capacity,
seek the most refined with the coarsest means,
fathom the profound with shallow understanding—
even if they begin in childhood,
and continue until hoary age,
they will still not attain it.
Those who appreciate swiftness necessarily praise it as good,
while those who do not understand
necessarily condemn it as bad—
this is the natural principle.
Thus they deem what they cannot comprehend as empty and false,
sincerely believing it to be so;
they未必 intentionally oppose sentiment to harm things.
Moreover, common practice generally honors the ancient past as divine and slights the contemporary:
Though there may be steeds that chase the wind,
they are said not to match those driven by Zàofù;
though there may be treasures worth multiple cities,
they are said not to match what the Chǔ man wept over;
though there may be swords that cut through metal,
they are said not to match those forged by Ōuyě;
though there may be medicines that revive the dead,
they are said not to match those compounded by Hé and Què;
though there may be people who surpass the crowd,
they are said not to match those recorded in bamboo and silk;
though there may be books that benefit the world,
they are said not to match the遗留 writings of former ages.
Thus, Zhòngní was not esteemed in his own time,
and the Great Mystery was ridiculed by his peers.
Common scholars often say
today's mountains are not as high as ancient ones,
today's seas not as vast as ancient ones,
today's sun not as hot as the ancient sun,
today's moon not as bright as the ancient moon—
how would they concede that today's talented men
are no less than the dry bones of antiquity!
Valuing what is heard,
disparaging what is seen—
this is not a malady confined to one age.
Those of old who broke their lutes and cut their strings
surely had reason to do so!
Bàopúzǐ said:
Surveying past records
up to recent times,
the decline of the Way and decay of customs
reached their extreme in the late Hàn.
Eunuchs and their ilk in high positions
wielded the sacred vessels,
grasped the state's authority,
abolished the upright and promoted the crooked,
harmed benevolence and injured righteousness,
squatting in opposition, bearing secret hatred,
following the deaf, obeying the dim,
forming groups of like evil,
drawing in factions of the wicked.
They amassed wealth in great stores,
knowing no limit,
yet would not disperse a trifle of meager goods
to aid the pure and impoverished in their distress.
Advancement in office was unattainable without ample wealth;
legal cases would not be decided fairly without substantial bribes.
High in rank and powerful in influence,
with strength enough to promote talent,
they would not utter a syllable of recommendation
for outstanding men who could benefit the times.
Those they employed
did not extend beyond relatives of their wives and concubines;
the favors they bestowed
did not reach beyond mediocre minions in their inner circle.
They heeded no warning from the reproach of Zāng Wén's usurpation of position,
pursued no remembrance of Xiè Hú's selfless righteousness,
distributed emoluments as if to Wáng Lín,
conducted affairs as if guided by Fāng Huí.
Thus, though worthies filled neighboring houses,
their gates received no compassion like that of Zhèng Yáng;
though noble figures gathered in crowds,
they met no recommendation like that of Bào Shēng.
They suppressed the independent,
advanced those who attached themselves to them—
this is why Fán Jī covered her mouth,
and Féng Táng sighed forever.
Those in power were mostly idle consumers and complacent faces,
obscuring virtue and blocking worth,
envying the meritorious and endangering them,
detesting the pure and white and repelling them,
shunning loyal admonishment and entrapping them,
disliking the uniquely upright and rejecting them,
while the soft and fawning received the protection of lavish adornment,
and the square and angular suffered the calamity of slander and abandonment.
They nurtured jackals and wolves while exterminating unicorns,
cultivated thorns while cutting down cassias.
Thus, the arrogant and unrestrained, drifting like duckweed,
were called grand and magnanimous;
the harsh, treacherous, and venomous
were called impartial and upright;
those with pleasing looks and quick wit but hollow within
were called brilliantly perceptive;
those with sharp tongues and clever words currying favor
were called exemplars of purity and beauty;
the rash, frivolous, and conceited
were called towering and magnificent;
the debauched and base without restraint
were called unrestrained and unfeigned;
those greedy and rapacious without satisfaction
were called broad-minded with far-reaching integrity;
the disheveled and slovenly who associated with the unworthy
were called universally amiable and broadly loving;
those who twisted classics, deceived sages, and glorified error
were called followers of Zhuāng and Lǎo;
mockers and scoffers who insulted and despised
were called free-spirited with elegant charm;
those who abandoned principles to conform, echoing in response
were called unsurpassed talents;
those relying on powerful patrons to push goods and tread crooked paths
were called knowing change and understanding trends;
the lazy who glanced at documents and signed blankly
were called having great enterprise and high ambition;
those exceeding their merit by relying on powerful relatives
were called peers of the four nobles;
those purchasing fame and rank by bribing powerful families
were called lightly valuing wealth and honoring righteousness;
those forming cliques with false praise, deeds contradicting words
were called meeting friends through culture;
practitioners of heterodox arts feigning supernaturalism
were called spiritually connected divine men;
fortune-tellers deceiving with omens of fortune and misfortune
were called wondrous knowers of the future;
those with mere brute courage in horsemanship and spearplay
were called supreme generals;
those echoing popular hearsay with conventional talk
As for those of sterling integrity and lofty conduct,
with clear spirits and broad tolerance,
who do not flatter with smiles to seek favor,
nor twist words to betray their conscience,
who tread frost and snow,
adhering to righteousness without improper alliances,
upholding the Way and promoting rectitude,
standing firm and unyielding in solitude,
their branches unshaken even by fierce winds,
their integrity unchanged despite personal hardship,
who in advancement offer forthright admonitions and just arguments,
attacking faults and correcting shortcomings,
and in retreat maintain sincerity and block selfish desires,
acting on all they know to be right—
such individuals are deemed foolish and obstinate.
Those who rise early and retire late,
serving diligently in public office,
worrying over gains and losses,
exerting all efforts in governance—
are considered petty and vulgar officials.
Thus, the wise adopt a reserved demeanor and retreat into seclusion,
the noble and talented feign ignorance while keeping silent,
the marginalized strive to choose better paths,
the constrained feign compliance while practicing reclusion at court,
the knowledgeable withhold their secret strategies,
the brave refrain from displaying their valor,
loyalty and outspokenness withdraw,
while the wicked and malevolent gain power,
evil flows unchecked and cannot be stemmed,
false paths open wide and cannot be blocked.
This leads to the collapse of authority above and disorder below,
with bandits and thieves proliferating,
eunuchs usurping the sovereign's might,
high officials dying at the hands of lowly men.
Loyal worthies and esteemed scholars
are labeled as factions,
imprisoned, captured, and executed,
while the world laments in anguish,
the innocent and guiltless
meet disaster behind closed doors.
Tiny smoke rises from within the walls,
yet the blaze spreads across the universe;
a small crack appears in a minute space,
yet waves flood to the four corners.
Fortified cities are sacked by common rebels,
impenetrable moats are crossed by a mere reed,
mighty troops dissolve like ice at the sight of dust,
conscripted soldiers turn their weapons and flee,
sharp blades reach the inner chambers,
barbarians plunder the forbidden precincts,
grains sprout in the ancestral temples,
weeds flourish on the jade steps,
cloud-kissing towers become dens for foxes and hares,
imperial gateways turn into paths for tigers and leopards,
eastern halls reduced to ashes in the dust,
the people scorched and plunged into abyssal fires,
harming families and ruining the state,
earning condemnation in historical records,
with no praise from honest historians,
no virtuous echoes in metal or stone.
Why is this so?
It is due to the nature of people.
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
In the late era of Wú,
different times shared the same maladies,
knowing past failures there,
yet unable to change course here.
Witnessing the chaos and decline not far behind,
they still follow the tracks of overturned carts,
seeing the struggle for petty gains like beasts,
while forgetting the shared calamity,
mocking the complacency of lice,
unaware that different events bring equal disaster.
Observing the sinking of competing boats,
they fail to see that different paths lead to the same drowning.
I was born in the Jìn era and did not witness it,
but my teacher, Master Zhèng,
who experienced it firsthand,
often instructed me thus:
In the late period of Wú,
the maladies were especially severe:
the worthy went unused,
dregs and filth disrupted order,
laws and discipline slackened and fell into disarray,
allowing even the most heinous to escape.
Those offering rich bribes were placed ahead in examinations,
official posts went to the powerfully connected,
without wealth or influence,
one had no hope for years.
The virtuous and noble,
though talented, were suppressed and sunk;
the cunning and powerful,
soared to high offices like clouds.
The ruler was benighted above,
ministers deceived below,
without cliques, one gained nothing,
without contention, one advanced not,
the custom of betraying public trust intensified,
the path of integrity was thus ruined.
Thus, sparrows rode gusts to soar skyward,
rotten boats sped on swift waves like lightning,
while phoenixes folded wings in thorny thickets,
and imperial prows stalled in stagnant waters, unraised.
Those holding reins of power,
officials governing the people,
were either relatives of the empress dowager,
or sycophantic flatterers.
In office, they lacked the loyalty to correct errors,
in retreat, they had no skill in adjudicating disputes,
in empty talk, their words were icy pure,
in conduct, they were muddier than mire.
They felt no shame for sinecures,
no fear of provoking war's disaster,
turning slander and praise into silken webs,
replacing farming with displays of power.
Their carriages and robes shone like mirrors,
their grand houses attracted flocks of birds.
Their rebukes faster than thunder,
their dispensation of fortune and doom swift as spirits,
their influence overshadowing lords,
their accumulations richer than the state treasury.
Outdoors, they paraded with guards like Zhái Huáng's,
indoors, they lounged in halls adorned with jade and carvings.
Their servants formed armies,
their homes turned into markets,
their cattle and sheep covered plains and marshes,
their fields and ponds spanned thousands of miles.
They feigned frugality like fish-skin robes,
usurping the repute of Zhào Xuān and Píng Zhòng.
Outwardly, they praised the integrity of Táo Kǎn and Wén Xìn,
yet inwardly harbored the corruption of Ān Chāng and Dǒng Dèng.
Though guests received no fine treats,
and the hungry got not a grain of aid,
their halls brimmed with gold and jade,
their chambers overflowed with concubines,
their merchant fleets numbered thousands,
their rotting grain filled myriad storehouses,
their gardens rivaled the Shànglín Park,
their mansions usurped the Tàijí Palace's grandeur,
their dogs and horses glutted with fine meats,
their treasures buried in vaults.
In receiving scholars,
they showed not the thinness of reed down;
in serving themselves,
they indulged in extreme luxury.
Some never opened law books,
yet stole positions of chief justice;
ignorant of where desks stood,
they occupied pivotal posts;
unaware of the Five Classics' names,
they enjoyed Confucian officials' salaries;
unfamiliar with seasonal documents,
they sat in editorial seats.
Their brushes never wrote boldly,
yet they received honors for critical discussions;
with lowered brows and drooping wings,
they filled roles for impeachment reports;
unable to discern fine from coarse in people,
they were tasked with evaluating character;
ignorant of military strategy in heaven, earth, and man,
they strutted under command canopies;
repeatedly disgraced as defeated generals,
they retained prestigious vanguard titles;
unable to tell wheat from barley,
they shamefully held advisory positions near the throne.
Like fish with dragon patterns,
seeming yet not being,
they rejoice in water,
but grieve at sight of otters.
Even under the threat of execution,
or tempted by city-toppling treasures,
they cannot wield rhinoceros-horn blades,
nor race nags to catch the wind.
Not that they fear severe punishment,
nor dislike generous rewards,
but their nature cannot be forced,
leaving no alternative.
To expect them to harmonize all affairs,
and greatly aid in major tasks,
is like placing a thousand tons on a tiny boat,
seeking a thousand measures in a pint jar,
tethering a straw dog and demanding hound-like results,
or raising barnyard fowl and expecting falcon's feats.
Their uselessness
is thus abundantly clear!
The ruler of Wú did not reflect on this,
nor did he increase his vigilance at night,
but entrusted important responsibilities
to flattering and mediocre individuals.
The crisis was more urgent than a drawn bow,
and the signs of downfall were as clear as the sun and moon.
Yet he believed himself as secure as a towering mountain,
thinking he could emulate the eras of Táng and Yú.
His eyes were weary from gazing at dazzling beauty,
yet he did not observe the gains and losses of governance;
his ears were filled with decadent music,
yet he did not discern the right and wrong of advice;
grain and silk were wasted on trivial competitions,
yet he did not use them to relieve the hunger and cold of his soldiers;
his heart delighted in flattery and charm,
yet he did not contemplate the profound principles of survival and demise.
Truly, he underestimated the roots of rise and fall,
and neglected the gravity of the ancestral temple.
Mr. Zhèng also recounted
that his teacher, Master Zuǒ, lived in seclusion at Tiānzhù,
emerging without seeking wealth or rank,
and not befriending feudal lords.
Yet his heart yearned for peace,
and he secretly grieved for his homeland.
Sighing deeply in his humble abode,
he told his disciples:
"The Hàn dynasty must shine again,
and the Yellow Essence will rise once more,
taking the pivot at Tàiwēi,
and turning the purple canopy to the constellation Chúnshǒu.
Uniting heaven's principles to govern all things,
its radiance will reside in Eastern Xià,
with benevolent winds reaching beyond the borders,
and profound grace permeating the world.
Envoys from distant lands will come in succession,
and tributes will fill the court.
Vast and majestic,
it will reach high and low,
maintaining peace and upholding culture,
continuing traditions with ease.
Yet the five strings lie silent,
and the south wind goes unsung;
above, the ruler does not enjoy the ease of governing effortlessly,
below, the people do not hear songs of prosperity.
The flying dragon soars but does not alight,
the abyssal serpent coils but does not leap;
the zōuyú is obscured in darkness,
and vermilion flowers sprout but do not bloom.
Yīn and Yáng clash in discord,
cold and heat lose their proper rhythm,
the seven celestial bodies signal disaster,
hills and valleys shift their places,
and thunderous rumbles
occur in the month of the dragon's dormancy,
while frost and killing cold descend in the season of Zhūmíng.
The jade candle does not illuminate,
sweet springs do not flow,
the suburbs are filled with fortifications,
and bountiful harvests do not thrive—why is this so?
Truly, it is because the four villains are not removed,
and the yuánkǎi are not promoted:
the employed are not virtuous,
and the virtuous are not employed.
"Yet those with lofty principles and broad vision,
clad in coarse garments but harboring jade-like virtue,
guarding tranquility and pure aspirations,
free from worldly desires,
hiding in deep obscurity,
finding contentment beyond the world,
acting only in accordance with propriety,
appearing only at the right time,
unperturbed in hardship,
unrepentant in poverty,
joyful in heaven's will and accepting fate,
blending glory and disgrace into one,
showing no delight in advancement,
no sorrow in retreat—
such men would rather die in obscurity behind tiled windows,
how could they ever flaunt themselves to advance,
displaying their priceless treasures
to compete with the sale of common stones?
The ways of Confucius and Mòzǐ
were once not practiced,
and Mèng Kē and Yáng Xióng
also lived in hardship and obscurity.
Having virtue but not the times—
this has always been so.
With no Lí Zhū in the world,
black and white become confused;
lacking a Guǎn Qīng in this age,
thoroughbreds and nags are mixed together.
Gravel accumulates in golden chests,
while jade and gems are discarded in ditches;
the master craftsman is distant and forgotten,
and fine wood goes unrecognized.
Alas,
how sorrowful!
I was born at an inopportune time,
neither too early nor too late,
and I shall witness the land of Wú transformed into Jìn,
and the southern people turned into northern slaves."
His words still echo in my ears,
yet the Sūn clan has already borne their coffins in surrender.
Bàopǔzǐ, hearing this, remarked:
"The words of these two gentlemen
can serve as a warning for the future.
Therefore, I record them in this work,
so that later generations may know that the loss of the state of Wú
was not decreed by heaven.
If we conceal the faults of the state,
without the slightest criticism,
then why value Dǒng Hú's honest brush,
and would Jiǎ Yì be mocked for his 'Guò Qín' essay?"
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"I have a friend, the Master of Seclusion,
who admires the uncontested land of Qǐnqiū,
and chose barren soil to build his home.
Devoted to literature and arts,
he neglected farming,
repeatedly missing harvests,
with hunger showing on his face.
Someone challenged him, saying:
'Heaven knows that ritual depends on full granaries,
and generosity stems from abundant wealth.
Nobility arises from surplus,
while frugality comes from want.
Thus, ten thousand coins are praised in poetry,
and food and goods head the eight government policies.
Farming oneself lays the foundation for matching heaven's virtue,
and plowing together brings unyielding joy.
A remarkable man, in his dwelling,
advances to soar with phoenixes,
and retreats to engage in livelihoods like Táo Zhū and Bái Guǐ.
In office, he must aid kings and hegemons;
at home, he must amass great wealth.
Therefore, the ancients divided fertile lands for profit,
diligently tilling with their own hands,
sowing beans in abundance,
cultivating fine vegetables luxuriantly,
harvesting grains to fill countless granaries,
amassing stores in the millions,
riding out in processions for hunts,
and returning to enjoy jade-like feasts in noble attire.
Yet where you, sir, reside,
in drought, the valleys blow dust,
in heavy rain, floods overwhelm the hills;
the land has no sprouting crops,
the water no budding plants.
Coarse grains are absent from your bins,
and firewood is lacking in your kitchen.
Content with your aim to wait for a rabbit,
calm without plans to advance or retreat—
I fear the fate of Shǒuyáng
will soon be seen today;
the hardship of Dānshān
may arrive at any moment.
Others shudder for you,
yet why are you so calm and unworried?
To see opportunity and not act
cannot be called wisdom;
to stay put without moving
is the way of the common crowd.
Can it be that those accustomed to rotted fish forget orchids,
and the greatly confused change their nature?
Why has it taken you so long to awaken, sir?
I am perplexed,
and do not understand your reasoning.
Ceremonial robes do not ward off arrows,
and ancient texts do not relieve hunger and cold.
Why not seek fertile fields in the suburbs,
engage in the noble work of farming yourself,
set aside the impracticalities of the six arts,
and gather abundant harvests to relieve want?'"
Master Qiánjū said:
"One cannot compel the deaf to discern refined and vulgar music,
nor demand the blind to distinguish vermilion from lacquer.
One cannot speak of the vast ocean to a frog at the bottom of a well,
nor discuss classical scholarship with the vulgar.
If you recognize the minor achievements of an old farmer,
yet fail to understand the profound ignorance of one who faces a wall (unenlightened),
how is this different from picking up grains of sand while discarding the Suí-Hé jades,
turning toward a flickering candle while turning away from the bright sun?
Preferences cannot be measured with a single standard,
choices cannot be exchanged between you and me.
Those who wish to ascend Lángfēng Peak or scale Sōng and Huà mountains
will not linger on small mounds;
those intent on roaming the Southern Ocean,
sailing the vast seas,
have no leisure to wander by puddles.
Thus, one who attunes their ears to the Jiǔsháo music
cannot find pleasure in the songs of Bā country;
one accustomed to feasting on grand sacrifices and lavish spreads
cannot find satisfaction in the taste of bitter herbs.
The kūn-péng soars high into the red sky,
while the wagtail flutters proudly in overgrown woods;
though their paths and heights differ,
both achieve the ultimate in flight.
The twilight of dawn and dusk is brief,
the morning mushroom knows not the full day.
The mayfly darts through its inch of sunlight,
the wild horse rests only after the sixth month,
the minnow splashes about exposing its scales,
while the divine dragon remains unused in unfathomable depths.
When actions and paths go astray,
how can one attain their aims?
Though I may lack even coarse meals to fill my belly,
I am content as if with feasts fit for a tripod.
Thus, Lièzǐ did not let his poverty
make him covet the salary of Zhèngyáng;
Zēng Shēn did not for his impoverishment
exchange for the wealth of Jìn and Chǔ.
"To gather subtle words before they fade
is the distant legacy of Zhōu and Confucius;
to labor diligently for profit
makes one a sinner in the eyes of Mencius.
Those who journey far cannot master all forked paths,
those who act cannot simultaneously till and study.
If the body is weary but the spirit content,
what harm is there in living frugally?
Moreover, dwelling in barren land brings toil,
and toil brings purity without seeking it.
Residing in fertile land brings ease,
and ease brings extravagance without learning it.
Purity
is where blessings gather;
extravagance
is where disasters converge.
When blessings gather,
even the humble can become prominent,
the declining can revive;
when disasters strike,
even the strong can weaken,
the existing can perish.
This occurs without appointment yet inevitably meets,
unsummoned yet comes of its own.
Thus, the noble person who wishes to straighten the branches
must first correct the roots;
who wishes to stop the flow
must dam the source.
So when the work of virtue is established,
the gate to extravagance closes.
Jiāng Wàng, with his utmost virtue, ceased farming without replanting,
Shùn, the great sage, fished without depleting the nets,
thereafter the jade huáng tablet marked the fortune of Yíngqiū,
his great achievements ranked among the twenty highest;
why must one ridicule him as lazy
and assess talent by judging appearance?
When two people divide wealth,
taking less is considered integrity;
I now relinquish the world's abundance,
dwell in this region's barrenness,
forsake Ānchāng's fertile lands,
choose the desirelessness of Běiguō,
truly, if one can minimize all things,
where is there not sufficiency?
The North Star, by remaining unchanged, is honored by all stars;
the Five Peaks, by not moving, are revered as foremost among mountains.
The cricket, though it moves often, is not valued;
birds and fish, when sated in deep waters, encounter peril.
I shall soon cultivate the overgrown fields of the nine classics,
sow the fine grains of the six virtues,
whose fields surpass the highest grade of soil,
whose harvest fills all between heaven and earth.
Why must tilling and weeding be the priority?
In the past, Bèiyī used discarding wealth to stop theft,
the Gēng clan used analogy to curb greed,
Liú Guǎng scattered gold to avert disaster for his descendants,
Shū Áo chose barren land to eliminate desires' worries,
Niú Quē incurred robbery by carrying treasures,
Táo Gǔ attracted calamity through hoarding.
Gains and losses are clear;
can we not learn from them?"
Then the questioner was silenced,
for a long time his mouth agape but unable to speak,
his head bowed, unable to lift it.
With a sigh of regret,
he began to understand that those who establish immortal words
do not let property disturb their harmony,
those who pursue achievements behind lowered curtains
do not let peeping at the garden strain their eyes.
To call the yuān-phoenix with the sweetness of a stinking chick,
to beckon the fierce tiger with a crab's strategy,
is that not shallow?
Shameful,
your lack of foresight!
Bàopǔzǐ said:
"In the past, when the Han flame dimmed,
dragons fought and tigers contended,
the nine regions split apart,
three powers stood like tripods.
There was a Master Lètiān,
who fled the turmoil, drifting like tumbleweed,
wandering to Mín and Yì,
initially befriended by Wénxiū,
but in the end unrecognized by Kǒngmíng.
Yet his speech was lofty, his conduct upright,
standing alone, unswayed by the crowd,
feared by contemporaries,
with none to befriend him.
Despite the power of those two lords,
they could not oppose the majority,
leaving this gentleman suppressed among thorns,
his age advancing to the mulberry and elm (old age),
yet his humble cloth unchanged.
Though the ruler of the time longed for worthies,
he remained unheard and unknown;
those in high positions
neither recommended nor presented him.
He hid in the narrow lanes of Wǔ,
dwelled in a thatched hut with a rope-fastened door,
in public, neglecting affairs of governing the world,
in private, forgetting carts for livelihood,
his meals of coarse grains often empty,
not knowing morning what the evening would bring.
Then a conventional young master came and questioned him, saying:
I have heard that those with the talent of Yī and Lǚ
do not long linger in poverty and lowliness;
those possessing the methods of Yīdùn
do not endure hunger and cold.
The perceptive value knowing change,
the wise prove themselves through sufficiency.
Thus, Fàn Lǐ, when he went out, destroyed Wú and made Yuè hegemon,
becoming an assistant for the ages;
when he entered, he traded and made a living,
amassing wealth of ten thousand gold.
Poverty is among the six extremes,
wealth among the five blessings,
the "Book of Songs" praises abundance,
The Yì jīng values gathering people;
dangle fragrant bait and eels and sturgeon will come;
offer generous rewards and the resolute will strive;
this is why Chángqīng doffed his calf-nose apron to grasp the vermilion banner;
why Qūnì descended from his mat door to enjoy a fiefdom;
why Bùwéi feasted on a city of a hundred thousand households;
why Marquis Zhāng was rescued from the hardship of prison.
Thus, Xiàxiāng's frugality brought him the hour of regret and blame,
while the漂嫗's abundance granted her a thousand-gold reward.
You, sir, lack Shàobó's remarkable strategy,
focusing solely on the Six Classics with sharp concentration,
overlooking the real disaster of lacking provisions,
admiring the empty fame of immortality,
ashamed to seek office by crooked means,
embarrassed to pursue glory through ostentation,
hoping for the hunt of King Wén of the West,
waiting for the Yellow River to run clear.
Content with Lièzǐ's starved complexion,
transcending the spirit while neglecting the body,
how is this different from drawing a fine steed
to replace the toil of walking;
pointing to the distant sea
to quench a parched thirst;
spreading a fishnet atop a towering peak;
casting a fishing line from the tip of a tall tree?
Though you may think yourself well-placed,
you cannot avoid being deemed impractical.
Nothing achieves merit after death,
nothing thrives against its time.
Now the land is divided like a melon,
heroes compete by force;
deceitful flatterers run rampant,
disrupting Xià and defying fate;
humble talents rush like stars across dual paths,
wolves and jackals clash with bared teeth.
Those in power roll up sleeves to dispute grievances,
scholars tread dusty, winding roads;
pure Confucians abandon imperial ways for Five Hegemons' tactics,
erudite students forsake the Four Disciplines for monthly critiques.
Those with full baskets
advance from the wilds;
those lacking resources
retreat from court;
holders of gold and silver
push through golden gates to ascend jade halls;
reciters of classics
forge lifelong enmities and are cast into mud;
those with rich gifts
see tiles and stones become jade tablets;
those with meager requests
find dragon steeds abandoned in woodlands;
those with many allies
soar with whirlwinds to the clouds;
those with few connections
swim with lame turtles in puddles.
A clod of earth cannot stop Pénglí's boiling waves,
how can a lone worthy reverse the deviant flow's error?
Now you, sir, have at home not a peck of grain in store,
abroad no bundles of gifts to offer.
Though you bear brilliance like dragons and phoenixes,
adorned with patterns like tigers and leopards,
spewing words like surging waves,
displaying them like brocade and embroidery,
you freeze and starve within your humble walls—
what plan or strategy is there to lament?
Why not float a light boat on swift currents,
hoist a flying sail to journey far?
Trade rare treasures from north to south,
gather gold and jade from Jiǔyí Mountain.
Follow Cuī Liè's distant footsteps,
secure a noble rank in these clear times?
Why toil only in writing and scholarship,
when will you ever shed your mortal coil?
Suffering alone for fame's sake
is what even Huáng-Lǎo would mock!"
Master Lètiān replied:
"Mastering the Six Arts,
comprehending the Eight Symbols—
this is true wealth.
Soaring with brush and elegant prose,
virtuous words endless—
this is true nobility.
Seek benevolence and it arrives,
what more is there to abandon?
Dwelling in deep abysses to nurture the spirit,
transcending all things to find contentment,
leaving dust and peril behind,
clarifying the soul in silent mystery.
Without peering out windows, one sees afar,
discerning subtle words without confusion.
Even if offered ministerial posts,
I'd remain steadfast, unchanged.
Why should I fret over poverty and vie for profit with merchants,
grieve hardship and compete for advancement with the mediocre?
If you believe trade can amass treasures,
farming can avert hunger,
do you not see that chasing deer ignores rabbits,
and long journeys arrive slowly?
Moreover, Shàngfǔ once wielded a butcher's knife,
yet his white head produced wonders;
a weight of myriad jūn,
unmoved by rushing winds;
before the Sháo music's nine movements end,
the divine bird delays its display.
Thus, those awaiting the whirlwind to ascend the heavens
do not despise bending among the weeds;
those galloping with orchid-tendoned steeds over sixty thousand
do not fight paths with lame donkeys.
Great filial piety fears risks that shame parents,
hence Zǐchūn trembled descending the hall;
supreme wisdom prizes not hard-won wealth,
so Táng and Yú discarded gold as metaphor.
The wise avert calamity before it comes,
the discerning consider harm when hearing gain,
yet you advise me to sail boats,
zealously seeking to enrich my household,
urging me to shoot sparrows with the Suí pearl,
wrest meat from a tiger's mouth,
lightly risking my body to the unfathomable,
braving steep dangers for distant gains,
forgetting the clear warning of skin and hair,
pursuing sunken treasures in hopeless depths.
Should wheels burn and cliffs collapse,
trees uprooted, stones flying,
Yáng Hóu towering like mountains,
great waves heaping high,
light boats drifting like dust,
strength contradicting heart,
following sighs and tears to no avail,
then you'd understand the perceptive see the subtle."
"Once, Huí and Xiàn were famed for pure hardship,
Chén Píng escaped peril having no gold;
Guǎnghàn lost his life craving profit,
Niú Quē turned to ashes carrying treasure.
Commoners die unjustly for clutching jade,
plump foxes invite disaster with fine fur.
Now you urge me toward theft-inducing trades,
press me with thief-attracting schemes,
proffer poisoned wine in toast,
mistaking it for life-lengthening advice.
A scholar takes the Three Sovereigns' works as gold and jade,
the Five Canons as lutes and zithers,
lectures and practice as bells and drums,
the Hundred Schools as panpipes and reeds,
letting flavor-seekers feast on words,
virtue-drunkards awaken to righteousness,
transcending vulgar customs in lofty steps,
surpassing myriad eras to spread renown,
galloping freely alone ahead—
why soil myself with lust for goods?
Hoard much and lose abundance,
favor modesty, shun excess;
hold night-shining pearls and be quickly cut open,
follow overturned carts and surely tumble;
overload and sink the boat,
crave victory and kill your life.
Such are the concerns of inferior men,
not the pursuits of highest virtue."
Then the questioner felt utterly lost,
begging to be enrolled as the least disciple,
to forever treasure the fine prescription for long life.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
Disciples debated whether benevolence or wisdom comes first,
each holding their own view,
and consulted me.
I told them:
"The Three Lights' glorious images represent Qián,
bearing all endlessly represents Kūn;
Qián possesses benevolence and also wisdom,
Kūn has benevolence but lacks wisdom.
The measure of high and low—
is it not clear?
Only the sage
aligns with Heaven's virtue.
Thus, Táng Yáo headed the canon with reverent wisdom,
Zhòngní began his work with illuminating righteousness.
'Brilliance above'
honors the sovereign;
'wise protection of self'
marks the odes' highest path.
Even crawling insects and flying bugs
can possess benevolence,
for their affection spreads in nurturing,
sorrow shows in their chirps.
Yet they enter traps without suspicion,
caught in nets unawares.
Having benevolence without wisdom,
they rush together into disaster and perish;
hidden scenes easily consume life,
building houses to avoid nests,
selecting grains to replace poison,
making clothes to alter nakedness,
crafting boats to cross impassable waters,
using oxen and horses to relieve carrying and walking,
establishing ranks to quell chaos,
inventing tools to prepare for uncertainties,
creating writing to govern officials,
instituting rites and laws to solemnize customs—
all are deeds of great wisdom,
not what the biased can discern."
"If the mind does not deviate from benevolence but the understanding does not extend to statecraft,
the disaster of peril and ruin
cannot be prevented,
and this can be known.
To anticipate prosperity and decline before signs appear,
to probe hidden affairs while they are still formless,
to point out latent transformations beyond conventional reasoning,
and to resist slander before it takes root—
these are the achievements of understanding.
To extend compassion even to insects,
to endure offense without retaliation,
to change sacrificial animals upon seeing their fear,
to avoid treading on growing grass—
these are the practices of benevolence.
Thus, understanding is a matter of talent,
while action is a matter of conduct.
The conduct of sacrificing oneself to achieve benevolence can be accomplished through effort,
but the understanding that discerns the profound and mysterious is difficult to borrow.
The distinction between the refined and the coarse
is clearly vast.
To embody compassionate benevolence
without the discernment of understanding
leads to confusion between false and true,
disorder between red and purple,
inability to distinguish calculations,
and failure to recognize the wicked and the upright.
Unaware of safety and danger,
one cannot even preserve oneself—
how could one have the leisure to establish and save others?
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu did not lack brotherly love,
yet he wept while eliminating his kin;
Shí Què did not lack natural kindness,
yet he severed personal ties to serve the public.
For they saw the essence of affairs with clarity,
not drowning in immediate emotions,
and thus became pure ministers.
Using righteousness to cut off affection,
setting aside benevolence to employ understanding,
using strategy to restrain benevolence—
benevolence may be temporarily abandoned, but understanding must never be lacking.
King Tāng and King Wǔ took power by force but governed with compliance,
truly acting without benevolence.
Yet they responded to Heaven and initiated revolution,
relying on their understanding.
Xú Yǎn cultivated benevolence to make neighboring states pay homage,
externally abandoning the defense of city walls and moats,
internally lacking preparations of weapons and armor,
leading to the destruction of his state and family—
this was the disaster of lacking understanding."
The disciple said:
"Confucius lamented that benevolence is a heavy burden and a long road,
and also said,
'If a man is not benevolent, what has he to do with ritual?'
As for sagehood and benevolence,
how dare I claim them!
Mencius said,
'Benevolence
is the dwelling;
righteousness
is the path.'
'If a man lacks a heart of compassion,
he is not benevolent.'
The Three Dynasties gained the world through benevolence
and lost it through lack of benevolence.
These are all maxims of the sages and worthies,
clear evidence in the records.
Yet you, Master, value understanding,
for which I have not seen classical support.
I, your humble student, am ignorant
and privately perplexed."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The ancients said,
'To love benevolence without loving learning
leads to the obscuration of folly.'
You are close to this.
In the past, when the six states devoured each other,
with wolves and tigers competing by force,
exalting cunning and despising morality,
崇尚杀戮而废弃谦让,
