Mencius sought to suppress greed and cruelty,
and elevate benevolence and righteousness—
how could he not diligently and earnestly
exclusively praise benevolence?
Yet not a single word
says that benevolence surpasses understanding.
It is like during an epidemic,
when physicians and shamans are valued,
and all voices in unison
only discuss medicines—
can one then say that the skill of acupuncture
surpasses the way of long life and immortality?
Moreover, I believe that matters of benevolence and understanding
are spread throughout the texts,
intending to directly reveal principles,
highlighting the essential spirit,
raising one corner as an example.
Yet you use them daily without knowing,
saying there is no basis for understanding!
The Qián hexagram speaks of the great understanding that ends and begins,
with the six positions timely formed.
This establishes Heaven with understanding,
encompassing all.
The Kūn hexagram says, 'How great! The myriad things are born through it,'
showing Earth's virtue of benevolence,
which merely receives and follows.
The order of priority
is not brilliantly clear!
The Book of Songs says,
'Brilliantly bright is the high Heaven,
shining down upon the earth below.'
'Brilliantly bright is the Son of Heaven,
his fair fame unceasing.'
The Book of Changes says,
'When the king is understanding, all receive his blessings.'
'To aid darkly the spiritual and intelligent,'
'spiritual and understanding.'
This shows that understanding merges with the divine,
truly not something pure benevolence
can hope to match.
Confucius said 'intelligent, discerning, divine, and martial,'
not 'benevolent in hearing';
also said 'in the past, the understanding kings governed the world,'
not 'benevolent kings.'
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'The bright virtue is abundant,'
not 'benevolent virtue.'
The Book of Documents says 'the sovereign is understanding,'
not 'benevolent.'
Lǎozǐ, praising the highest scholar,
said 'understanding and penetrating in all directions,'
and in discussing decline,
said 'when the Way was lost, then virtue appeared;
when virtue was lost, then benevolence appeared.'
The Book of Changes says 'the king faces south toward understanding,'
not 'toward benevolence.'
'I desire benevolence,
and benevolence is at hand.'
Also, 'practicing benevolence depends on oneself,'
meaning everyone can do it.
But as for intelligence and discernment,
how can they be forced?
Thus Mencius said,
whenever anyone sees a child about to fall into a well,
all will rush to save it.
From this perspective,
all have a benevolent heart,
only in degrees of thickness or thinness,
while the distinction of intelligence is occasional.
In the past, Cuī Zhù did not kill Yàn Yīng,
and Yàn Yīng said Zhù was greatly unbenevolent
but had minor benevolence.
Thus, even treacherous ministers and villainous sons
can still possess benevolence."
The disciple said again:
"The Book of Changes states that the way of humanity
is benevolence and righteousness,
so nothing is greater than benevolence for humans."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"The reason for saying so
is that benevolence lies in action,
which can be achieved through effort,
while understanding enters the divine,
requiring Heaven-given talent—
this is not meant for instruction in the old ways.
Bàopúzǐ said:
A weight of ten thousand jūn
must begin with zī and zhū;
towering to the clouds,
it must start with minute measures.
Thus, flowing streams gather to form the boundless expanse of the Southern Sea,
and ordinary accumulations lead to the Mystic Garden reaching heaven's heights.
Bàopúzǐ said:
Those who wield swift whips on galloping steeds
leave shadows behind without toil;
those who ride winds and waves
cross dangers without capsizing.
Thus, with Yuán and Kǎi dividing duties,
the merit of modeling Heaven was achieved;
with Yī and Lǚ taking on the world's burden,
the work of revolution was accomplished.
Bàopúzǐ said:
Jade boats and gem-like sails
have no use for crossing rivers;
golden bows and jade strings
lack the ability to shoot arrows.
Thus, those who are upright and pure but lack administrative skill
are not instruments for quelling chaos;
those who are refined and elegant but devoid of governance strategy
are not talents for assisting brilliance.
Bàopúzǐ said:
The Lángfēng and Mystic Garden
do not borrow height from anthills;
Xuánlí and Jiélǜ gems
do not rely on common jade for their beauty.
Thus, the heroic and outstanding, standing apart from the crowd,
startle with the fragrance of secluded orchids;
the lofty and independent,
make the sounds of all birds resonate.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Ice and charcoal do not flaunt their abilities in cold and heat,
fine jades do not prove their worth yet their substance is evident.
Thus the gentleman is reverent to himself,
unconcerned about having no supporters;
the perfect man remains still as a corpse,
his mind free from slander or praise.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A fierce gale can topple mountains,
yet cannot muster strength to pluck a hair;
fire can melt metal and stone,
yet cannot blaze fiercely to dry dampness.
Thus Huáiyīn excelled at warfare,
but was clumsy in strategies of governance;
Jiànghóu stabilized the state,
yet lacked ready responses in audience.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who chase fame do not consider sacrificing their lives difficult,
those who value their bodies do not burden their feelings with base desires.
Thus Jì Xìn willingly became ashes without regret,
while Yáng Zhū equated a single hair to a city of jade.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Small fish cannot comprehend the distant vision of the divine dragon,
ducks and egrets do not know the swan is no match for them.
Thus paired plowmen laugh at Chén Shèng for casting aside his plow,
the shallow-minded sneer at Kǒngmíng for sitting with clasped knees.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The sharpness of the Chúnjūn sword,
is tested on rhinoceros hide;
the goodness of Xuāncí,
is proven through clear examination.
Thus if lumped together, Yuánkǎi and a petty man show no difference;
if employed equally, the thoroughbred and the nag are indistinguishable.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Vessels not like ritual gui,
must advance sharply but retreat swiftly;
capacity matching Yī Lǚ,
though starting late arrives early.
Thus the wren tires its wings,
yet cannot fly beyond the reed tips;
the young phoenix rises slowly,
but with a glance soars to the blue sky.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When decline ends, it is followed by prosperity;
when darkness peaks, clear light shines at dawn.
Thus one who hung its head at Wú's slope,
gallops a thousand miles in freedom;
one coiled in the ninefold abyss,
treads on rainbows to leap high.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Nine segments and four joints,
are why algae display their spirit;
broken branches and crushed leaves,
are why fragrant herbs increase their scent.
Thus Yíwǔ in fetters,
achieved the feat of restoration;
Yìnghóu in hardship and disgrace,
earned merit by entering Qín.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Listen to competitors' details,
then benefits align and enmity forms;
good and bad differ in path,
then matters diverge and knots arise.
Thus Mómǔ and the goitered woman,
hated to see Xīshī's stunning beauty;
Shāng Chén and Xiǎo Bái,
once heard of Yánzhōu's retreat to farming.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When purity and flaw differ in trace,
the declining feel shame and regret;
when strong and weak are of different classes,
the lifters of tripods are envied.
Thus Huáiyīn's prominent promotion,
made common clerks resentful of his surpassing;
Wǔ'ān's high merit,
led Fàn Jū to fabricate tales to ruin his affairs.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
For a fatal illness,
do not withhold bitter medicine;
for rotten timber,
do not accept carved ornament.
Thus Bǐgān did not spare himself,
and had his heart cut out in utter loyalty;
Tián Fēng saw the subtle signs,
and was slaughtered for his straightforward words.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The lone tong tree from Yìyáng,
cannot produce mournful sounds without strings;
the lone bamboo from Dàxià,
cannot emit clear notes without blowing.
Thus with low rank, even Jì and Xiè could not achieve prosperous governance;
with weak authority, even Yī and Zhōu could not reach peace and prosperity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those climbing heights must beware of reaching too high;
those crossing depths find disaster in an overloaded boat.
Thus in Western Qín, Lǐ Sī longed for Shàngcài;
in Eastern Yuè, Wén Zhǒng regretted his fullness and arrogance.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Hard and soft have unchangeable substances,
steadfast and pliant have natural dispositions.
Thus even after a hundred smelts, southern metal does not lose its genuineness;
in peril and hardship, a resolute man does not lose his integrity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If not by the right way,
then wealth and honor are not worth holding;
if背离ing benevolence and discarding righteousness,
even a hundred years of life are not worth regretting.
Thus Biàn Suí carried stones to throw into the abyss,
Zhòng Yóu willingly went to the blade.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
High and low cannot be leveled by one standard,
food and salary cannot transform through encouragement or discouragement.
Thus Huì Shī worried about having too few followers,
while Zhuāng Zhōu feared too many ways to catch fish.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Advance and retreat differ as ice from charcoal,
agitation and calm vary as flight from sinking.
Thus Mò Dí found joy in calloused feet,
while the hermit Jí found delight in abandoning the world.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who please the heart inspire deep affection even with shallow acquaintance;
those who offend the spirit grow more distant despite long interaction.
Thus with shared views, one feels close even in a brief meeting;
with differing paths, one feels no love even with white hair.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The Yúhuáng with its pheasant heads,
is a fine vessel for crossing rivers,
but if rowed by northern barbarians,
it will sink and drift in the waves.
Púshāo and sweat-blood horses,
are swift steeds for rapid travel,
but if driven by one not Zàofǔ,
they will stumble and fall on dangerous paths.
Qīngpíng and Háocáo swords,
are the finest of sharp blades,
but if wielded by one not Yǔ or Yuè,
there is the risk of self-injury.
Strong soldiers and sharp troops,
are divine tools for quelling chaos,
but if used by one not wise,
they quickly bring the disaster of self-destruction.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Heaven's order has an unchanging constant尊,
without礼, one faces the heavy刺 of swift death.
Thus the beasts of Xuánzhōu,
though able to speak, cannot be among noble sacrifices;
the Qióngqióng carrying its mate,
though entrusting life, cannot practice benevolence and righteousness.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Slander cannot be silenced with clever words,
real hatred cannot be dispelled with empty matters.
To dispel it not by the right way,
to silence it not by reason,
is like embracing ice to驱 cold,
adding stoves to repel heat,
chasing light to escape shadow,
piercing a boat to stop leaks.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
An enlightened ruler appoints men,
not letting them exceed their capacity;
a loyal minister holds office,
not daring to go beyond his measure.
To recklessly grant what does not match his talent,
to vainly appoint what he cannot bear,
is like using a冰碗 to hold boiling soup,
wrapping烈火 in reed down,
hanging ten thousand jun on a rotten rope,
doubling the load on a small boat.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Leopard-fur robes,
are not for those carrying firewood;
nine movements and six variations,
are not for the deaf;
high songs and distant harmonies,
are not for the平庸 and foolish;
forgetting self to achieve results,
is not for those with shallow virtue.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When the people's wealth is exhausted yet demands continue,
when their strength is spent yet labor does not cease,
to expect no resentment or lament,
to plan for lasting peace,
is like severing roots to graft branches,
cutting the back to patch the belly,
carving eyes to widen sight,
gouging ears to enhance hearing.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Laws have no fixity,
yet one admires expediency following the times;
merit not doubling the past,
yet one favors constant change to suit the vulgar,
like cutting down a tall horse to fit a low cart,
shaving the ankle to match a crooked shoe,
shortening a long sword for a small scabbard,
trimming a foot-long jade to fit a narrow box.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The giant fish that calms the waves
does not emerge from the narrow confines of remote valleys;
the phoenix that perches on towering trees
does not flourish in the lowly soil of anthills.
The canonical maxims of the Nine Domains
do not issue from the mouths of the vulgar and base;
the lofty strategies inscribed on metal plates
do not arise from the thoughts of common folk.
Observing a branch of a hundred arm-spans,
one can know its trunk is not slender;
reading profound and expansive writings,
one can perceive the author's depth and erudition.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Lush mulberry groves
cannot alleviate the chill of cypress wood;
fertile lands surrounding the city walls
cannot resolve Qián Áo's covering his face with his sleeve.
Yet silken fabrics and fine linens,
are produced from these very sources;
thousands of granaries and myriad chests
thereby come into being.
Thus, those with far-reaching vision value the root,
while the short-sighted attend to the branches.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The coarse-minded are bound to form,
the refined in knowledge grasp the spirit.
Those who trace origins to see the end
have threads they can follow;
those who obtain it before any sign appears
need no external causes.
Hence, seeing heaven and earth by day
does not merit being called clear-sighted;
discerning the finest details at night
is what makes one peerless.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Blossoms glowing in spring
cannot remain fresh long when separated from the branch;
the fish that swallows boats
cannot survive leaving the water.
Thus, those with a fine reputation but undeserving reality
inevitably lack unyielding integrity;
those in high position with unmatched capability
cannot avoid defeat that invites invasion.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Enduring the pain of bitter medicines
is to cure life-threatening diseases;
bearing the heavy chill of armor
is to ward off the hail of arrows;
maintaining the austerity of pure conduct
is to achieve preeminent accomplishments;
heeding deeply unsettling advice
is to avoid the confusion of losing one's way.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If a phoenix competes for grains in the courtyard,
it is demeaned by chickens and ducks;
if a dragon's scales are mixed among fodder animals,
it is seen as one of the sacrificial beasts.
Thus, the Shang elders dwelled on heights to broadcast their transcendent integrity,
and Biàn Suí plunged into the depths to preserve his reputation of discarding worldly things.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A well dug but not cleaned will accumulate mud;
fine grain not weeded will be overrun by tares.
Learning without reflection leads to numerous obstructions;
studying without precision results in prolonged confusion and wasted effort.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Hoarding ten thousand gold in chests,
though frugal and unused,
is no different from being poor.
Harboring elegant talent in one's breast,
without expressing it in writing,
is no different from being vulgar and base.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Nánwēi and Qīngqín,
supremely beautiful,
yet must await rich adornment to enhance their loveliness;
Yán Huí, Zǐgòng, Zǐyóu, and Zǐxià,
though brilliantly talented,
truly needed the ancient texts to broaden their wisdom.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Vermilion curtains and layered nets,
silk canopies casting deep shade,
then ugly features are hidden;
vermilion lacquer applied with care,
dazzling with intricate patterns,
then dry wood is concealed.
Thus, mastery of the Six Arts transforms the base into gentlemen;
accumulation of widespread praise elevates the isolated to noble company.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Where dense forests flourish,
feathered tribes gather like clouds;
where dark abysses stretch vast,
scaly schools vie to approach.
Where virtue is abundant and achievements broad,
many will give their allegiance;
overlooking flaws and employing talent,
attracts those far and gathers those near.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The steed that seeks flight with shadow-outpacing feet
cannot gallop freely at Lǚliáng;
the creature that swims through waves and depths
cannot climb steep heights or scale dangers.
Thus, Lì Zhū could discern autumn down at a hundred paces,
but could not distinguish the refinement or vulgarity of the eight tones;
Zǐyě could harmonize transcendent, sublime music,
but could not point out white and black at close range.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When the four avenues of hearing are widely open,
even Xīhé submits his light;
when a ten-thousand-ren depth empties itself,
even puddle waters converge.
Thus, when the path of broad inquiry is expanded,
unusual knowledge gathers completely;
when the courtyard torch shines brilliantly,
exceptional scholars come knocking;
when the slander-posting tree is erected,
errors are inevitably known;
when the drum for daring remonstrance is hung,
straightforward advice is inevitably offered.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
All who can speak praise Yáo,
yet Yáo's governance was not always perfect;
the whole world condemns Jié,
yet Jié's actions were not entirely wrong.
Thus, one withered branch
does not harm the lushness of a vast forest;
wormwood sprouting in winter
does not dispel the harshness of autumn's end.
Xīshī has her flaws but they cannot diminish her beauty,
for her beauty is abundant;
Mómǔ has her merits but they cannot save her ugliness,
for her ugliness is profound.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Personal well-being and reputation
are hard to achieve together;
merit and spirit
are seldom both fully attained.
Those who fragment their virtue
suffer but find security;
those who adapt to the world
enjoy pleasure but face many dangers.
Thus, the bird of prey is confined for its fierce strikes,
the talking bird is cherished for its wit,
jade is cut for its auspicious patterns,
the three metals are smelted for their rare beauty,
orchids are cut for their fragrance,
the patterned catalpa is felled for its resonant wood.
Therefore, the emerald dragon observed Huà Yì and ascended to the dark clouds,
the divine phoenix met Mèng Xì and returned to the cinnabar cave,
Zǐyǒng lamented the greatness of natural bonds,
the Qīyuàn master grieved for the embroidered sacrificial ox.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When ten thousand deer lower their antlers,
the fierce tiger sheathes its fangs;
when a thousand birds gather scale-like,
the bird of prey clenches its claws.
Thus, when slander spread through four states,
Duke Zhōu could not stop it;
when critics filled the roads,
Zǐchǎn had no way to silence them.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The beauty of Wēishī
cannot be enhanced by powder and paint;
the qi of the two solstices
cannot be increased by blowing.
Thus, those possessing heroic and lofty capacity
do not strive for peculiar style to show uniqueness;
those embodying transcendent and uncommon ability
do not seek minor acclaim to curry favor.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The scales' halt and phoenix's bearing
are scarce, which is the concern;
the fox's cry and owl's call
are numerous, which the world detests.
Thus, though the court is full of talents,
the search for the worthy does not cease;
though slanderers wield power,
the loyal and steadfast gnash their teeth.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
One need not be Mèng Bēn or Wū Huò to possess great strength,
nor must one be Zhèng Dàn or Máo Qiáng to have surpassing beauty;
swift as the storm is not limited to Huáliú or Sùshuāng,
sharp and decisive is not unique to Chényú or Gànjiàng.
Thus, one who can establish the uncrowned king's legacy
need not be the Qiū of Eastern Lǔ;
one who can practice the kindness covering the dead
need not be the Chāng of Western neighbor.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The divine phoenix trills at the morning sun,
bringing no tangible benefit to creatures,
yet all below listen intently.
Owls gather at night on walls and eaves,
causing not a fraction of harm,
yet all cover their ears and aim arrows.
Thus, good words sent forth
are welcomed no matter how far;
evil words arriving
are rejected no matter how near.
Just as the sun and moon never fail in their constant brightness,
the crooked arrow is forgotten after its brief appearance.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A shadow never takes a form contrary to the object;
a name never bears writing detached from reality.
Thus, water that turns from its source
can never surge in long streams to spread eastward;
flowers blooming out of season
can never retain their brilliance and elegance through frost and ice.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A beast with saw-like teeth,
even when crouching low, is feared;
an insect wielding axe-like limbs,
even when silent and intact, inspires no awe.
Hence, a nobleman in coarse cloth,
though impoverished, must not be despised;
a petty man in carriage and crown,
though successful, deserves no respect.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The soaring unicorn roams beyond the vast wilderness,
thus avoiding traps and snares;
the divine swan flaps its wings atop Xuānpǔ's peaks,
evading the peril of nets and cages.
Why must one dwell in crooked caves, forever anxious?
Why clutch reeds in the mouth, filled with dread and sorrow?
Therefore, those who fulfill the role of slaughter
must cherish the livestock they raise;
those who provide sumptuous feasts
must find contentment in the courtyard's offerings.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The wise value discerning echoes from a thousand years past,
to trace the footsteps of rise and fall;
the discerning treasure spotting the exceptional among the destitute,
to draw forth talents that rectify the world.
But to hear a symphony's rich harmonies
and seek advice from mediocre craftsmen
is not the keen hearing of Yánzhōu.
To waste extraordinary genius
by consulting the ordinary
is not the unique insight of a visionary.
Thus, discussing superior tools with those who cannot appreciate them
is like asking the blind to point out colors;
plotting to promote virtuous foes with the envious
is like debating fur robes with a fox.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The noble steed endures hardship on perilous peaks,
disdaining the tedium of safe pastures;
the divine horse suffers hunger in icy deserts,
rejecting the fattening of sacrificial offerings.
Gūzhú would not trade his fasting for the wealth of Lùtái;
Zǐlián would not barter his poverty for the abundance of copper mountains.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those united in purpose find no distance in mountains and seas;
those at odds in Dao find no closeness in mere inches.
Thus, some journey afar to gather,
while others stay near yet remain unconnected.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The resplendent imperial robe's brilliance
is not the work of a single hue;
the loftiness of Sōng and Dài peaks
is not piled by one basket of earth.
Thus, with the Nine Ministers appointed, Kāngníng's achievements flourished;
with the Twenty-Eight Constellations entrusted, supporting merits became renowned.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The emerald dragon flies skyward without wings;
the winged serpent darts like lightning without feet;
the turtle, earless, hears keenly at the pass;
the earthworm, mouthless, projects its voice.
Thus, Gāoyáo, though mute, rivaled the eloquent in accomplishment;
Jīnyě, though blind, matched Lízhū in clarity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
High officials may have talents unfit for their posts;
the highly praised may have deeds unmatched to their fame.
Thus, saw teeth cannot chew;
a winnowing basket's tongue cannot distinguish flavors;
a pot's ears cannot tune music;
straw sandals' noses cannot detect scents;
a cauldron's eyes cannot grasp the moon's glow;
a bed's legs cannot traverse ordinary distances.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A passerby cannot draw a strong bow yet recognize Yǎng Yóu's archery;
Yánzǐ cannot handle reins yet foresee Dōngyě's downfall.
Thus, some who cannot play chess discern wins and losses at a glance;
some who cannot pluck strings understand Zhèng and Yǎ melodies upon hearing.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
What casts shade over ten thousand acres
must emerge from towering ridges;
what floods heavens and drowns hills
must spring from Kūntóng's source.
Transcendent achievements
must come from peerless talent;
strategies to avert collapse
must arise from extraordinary vision.
Thus, in the nests of tiny gnats,
there are no feathers to ride the wind;
in drainage ditches,
no gems shine like night stars.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Whirlwinds and fiery gales
feed the prairie fire's intensity,
yet candles meeting them are extinguished;
sweet rain and nourishing dew
make fine crops flourish,
yet dry wood rots faster from them;
vermilion carriages and ornate wheels
are great treasures for the talented,
yet usurpers who steal them invite disaster;
feasts of tripods and ten thousand measures
are grand rewards for contributors,
yet the incompetent given them bring ruin to the feast.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Slaughtering rhinos for armor
to clothe expedition commanders,
splitting kingfisher feathers for adornments
to crown empresses and consorts—
though they leave deep valleys
for lofty trees,
for these two creatures' sake,
it is不如 hiding in dense woods,
preserving life in thickets and marshes.
Thus, the divine turtle prefers dragging its tail in the mud
over being treasured in boxes and cloth;
the marsh pheasant delights in pecking within ten steps,
avoiding the calamity of chickens and ducks.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Partial talent is insufficient for comprehensive use;
a single strength cannot compensate for many weaknesses.
Thus, the rooster knows dawn's approach
but cannot fathom yīn-yang's calendric laws;
the crane recognizes midnight
but cannot master the path of sundials' shadows;
the mountain dove senses coming rain or shine
but cannot comprehend astronomy;
snakes and insects know where hidden springs lie
but cannot grasp geography.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
With unclear prohibitions,
using harsh punishments to quell chaos;
with imprecise court strategies,
waging endless war to invade neighbors—
is like cutting grain to exterminate locusts,
felling trees to kill borers,
eating poison to eliminate fleas and lice,
dismantling houses to drive off sparrows and rats.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Sharp blades are born from dull stones;
bright flames blaze from dark wood;
precious pearls come from lowly clams;
beautiful jade emerges from ugly rough stone.
Thus, one cannot judge Chónghuá by his parents,
nor measure Wèi and Huò by their ancestors.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
With ambitions fulfilled, the face beams;
with hopes lost, the expression saddens.
When the root decays, the branches wither;
when the source is shallow, the flow is brief.
What lies within must manifest without;
what starts nearby must resonate afar.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Elegant poses and charming looks
vary in form and color,
yet bring equal joy to the heart;
strings, bamboo, metal, and stone,
with five tones and diverse melodies,
yet please the ear alike;
arrows flying, hooks sinking,
nets raised, traps set,
all achieve the same catch;
establishing merits or setting forth words,
though paths of action differ,
the value placed on them is one.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Great benefits bring heavy harms;
fine quality summons disaster.
Thus, southern birds are killed for their brilliant plumage;
cave leopards die for their patterned fur;
carp and sturgeon accumulate till dark abysses dry;
deer and elk gather till dense forests burn;
gold and jade pile up till bandits arrive;
fame and high position bring worries and duties.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When autumn winds blow chill at night, thin fans are discarded;
when climbing perilous heights, light boats are abandoned;
when weapons cloud the land, scholars retreat;
when turmoil and loss are quelled, warriors are dismissed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
What is worth ten thousand in gold
needs no viewing for its quality to be discerned;
branches that span armfuls
need no measuring for their size to be assessed.
Thus, seeing billows reaching the sky,
one knows they do not rise from puddles;
observing the vastness of literary grace,
one knows it does not come from mere pedants of texts.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The crimson blossom and the green grass
are not confined to twisted and withered stalks;
the purple mushroom's fragrant beauty
is not limited to saline and barren soil.
Thus, the one who receives the dark jade tablet to announce success
is born from a family of four criminals;
the one who inherits the mandate from Wénzǔ
emerges from a household of the stubborn and unruly.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Good words spoken within a room
will find response even from afar;
if crooked or straight miss the mark,
then none nearby will remain.
Thus, in Sòng's wilderness, Yínghuò retreated from its station;
in the Yīn court, close relatives fled abroad.
Sìhuán arrived from beyond Shàoguǎng,
while deer and horses were confused within the palace walls.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Jīng Qīng and Zhū Hài
do not display bravery among the timid and weak;
Mèng Bēn and Féng Fù
do not brandish weapons among rustic bravos.
Eminent scholars and great minds
do not elaborate subtle arguments before the shallow;
profound individuals and lofty persons
do not alter their daily scrutiny amidst the vulgar.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Circling and bowing in courtesy
are not the demeanor for repelling invaders;
donning armor and fastening helmets
are not the adornments for the temple court.
Hanging sashes and shaking pendants
cannot wield blades in fierce combat;
walking in strict conformity
cannot rescue from fire or drowning.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Heaven and earth nurture all,
yet the multitude of things do not recognize their grace—
because their benefits are boundless;
the great man transforms spiritually,
and the petty do not perceive his actions—
because he governs before things arise.
Thus, what can be known is small,
what is easy to predict is few.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
É Huā, Nǚ Yīng, Rèn Sì
are not praised primarily for sericulture and weaving;
Tāng, Wǔ, Hàn Gāo
do not attract recent acclaim through minor conduct.
Therefore, one who gazes clearly at the three luminaries
has no leisure to peer down into wells and valleys;
one who listens purely to Sháo and Huò music
how could spare an ear for the songs of Sāngjiān?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The surface may not reflect the inside,
appearance may not verify ability.
Zhòngní resembled a homeless dog,
Gōng Dàn looked like unhewn timber,
Gāo Yáo's face was like a masked exorcist,
Yī Yǐn's form akin to a dried-up skeleton,
yet Lóng Yáng and Sòng Cháo,
are like earthen figures crowned with night-shining pearls;
Jí Rú, Dǒng Xián,
are like brocade wrapped around dust.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Yáo and Shùn cannot transform the most foolish,
hence their teachings fail with their own sons;
Zhòu and Jié cannot alter the wisest,
thus their evil does not taint the Three Benevolent Ones.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The greatest has what it cannot change,
the tiniest has what it cannot be deprived of.
Thus, icy frost's stern kill
cannot wither the luxuriance of beans and wheat;
scorching summer's stifling gloom
cannot melt the frozen snow of mountains;
typhoons churning the sea
cannot make hidden springs raise waves;
spring rains enriching all things
cannot make withered plants bloom.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The treasure that weeps blood
relies on Shíjiànshízhū to cast its light;
Shěn Lǘ and Mèng Láo
need Chǔ's whetstone to hone their edge;
a steed like Liú daily awaits the noble to achieve distance;
fine talent awaits correction to perfect virtue.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The perched phoenix and hidden yuè
though hungry and thirsty, will not consent to be caged in the cook's room;
the mythical Chénghuáng and Tiānlù
though starved in seclusion, will not delight in fodder at Zhuólóng's stable.
Thus, the old man catching cicadas
forgets all things in the fragrant woods;
the student angling with a line
disregards holding jade in Southern Chǔ.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Square and round differ in shape,
movement and stillness have different ends.
Thus, the celestial sphere is honored for its vigorous motion,
Earth is valued for its peaceful steadfastness.
The seven regulators and four seasons
accomplish through constant flow;
the five peaks and six pillars
serve as anchors through steadfast stillness.
Thus, Sòng Mò and Chǔ Shēn
saved their states through urgent missions;
Gān Mù and Hú Míng
repelled the enemy through non-action.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those content in hills and gardens
suffer in body but are serene in spirit;
those who toil themselves to aid others
are free in form but toil in heart.
Hence, one who carries a jar to water the garden
finds more joy than a prime minister;
one who dines on ferns and bitter herbs
finds more beauty than in cauldron-feasts;
one who leaves Bīn with a staff
appears as content as in the twelfth moon;
one who stays awake till dawn
wears out life with diligent worry.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Benevolence and cruelty are as far apart as sky and abyss,
good and bad are as distinct as having and lacking.
The zōuyu bends its foot to tread on emptiness,
while wolves wipe out herds to harm life.
Yú Qīng gave up his ministerial seal to relieve the poor,
Huà Gōng declined high office to yield to worthies.
Lǐ Sī, jealous of his superior, killed Hán Fēi;
Páng Juān, fearing being outshone, mutilated Sūn Bìn.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Use one's strengths rightly,
and no talent will be wasted;
focus solely on shortcomings,
and nothing will be acceptable.
Thus, light gauze and misty crepe
are beautiful for ceremonial dress,
but cannot ward off flying arrows;
Shěn Lǘ and Jùquē
are excellent for cutting and slashing,
but cannot pick or stab.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Small flaws do not impair a great vessel,
shortcoming does not burden a vast talent.
The sun and moon bear the blemish of birds and insects,
yet do not hinder their brilliance in the sky;
the Yellow River carries the mud's turbidity,
yet does not harm its flow past mountains.
Blocking trees should not lead to discarding Guǎn Zhòng,
seizing fields should not justify belittling Xiāo Hé,
wife-stealing should not cause the rejection of Xiàng Rú,
accepting gold should not warrant condemning Chén Píng.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Tigers and leopards cannot fight in the waves,
téng snakes cannot ascend on fogless days,
in catching pheasants and hares, the luán and fèng are no match for eagles and yào,
in pulling plows, the lóng and lín cannot compare to a pair of oxen.
Thus, warriors and brave men
are of no use in peaceful times;
great scholars and extraordinary talents
are not valued in eras of violent struggle.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If tethered by two reins around the neck,
then the qílí and a lame donkey are the same;
if out of the forest and in a cage,
then the yuán and yuàn and the huān and hé are equal;
if sheathed and not used to strike,
then the Lóngquán sword and a lead knife are identical;
if talent is vast but the task is small,
then the hero and the mediocre are comparable.
If one seeks a thousand-mile trace from a tethered steed,
demands epoch-making deeds from a worthy burdened with trifles,
and calls this not deluded,
I do not believe it.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who discard sweet herbs and eat bitter ones
surely lack a palate that recognizes sweetness;
those who abandon jade and pick up gravel
certainly lack the vision to discern treasures.
Those who scorn the Jiǔchéng melody and prefer the northern rustic tunes,
I know they cannot move the spirits and attract the soaring phoenix.
Those who forsake the elite and rely on commoners,
I know they cannot set in order the constant virtues and achieve peace and prosperity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who comprehend the ultimate principle of通畅 and blockage
do not fret over poverty and obstruction;
those who understand that fate is natural
do not become complacent in times of smooth passage.
Thus, when trapped in deep waters,
they leave behind a resentful heart;
when shining in the imperial court,
they show no smug expression.
Thrice appointed and thrice dismissed—
such is that kind of person.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Adversity and prosperity depend on fate,
poverty and success are insufficient to judge a scholar;
gain and loss lie in circumstance,
honor and disgrace cannot measure talent.
Time and destiny cannot be sought by force,
encounters cannot be avoided by wisdom.
Thus, Shàngfǔ [Lǚ Shàng]
was an old woman's discarded husband;
Hán Xìn,
a starving beggar;
Xiāo Hé,
a petty official;
Qíng Bù,
a punished and banished slave.
When they displayed dragon grace among lizards,
or coiled phoenix wings among quail flocks,
those reptiles and fowls
deemed them their peers.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The four auspicious beasts hide in obscurity,
yet become omens of great peace;
recluses excel in withdrawal,
yet become treasures of the state.
Why must one crow at dawn with a bit in mouth,
tethered by worries and duties?
There is the usefulness of being used by others,
and the usefulness of not being used by myself.
Those devoted to self do not disturb harmony for fame;
those cultivating life do not burden themselves with things.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
One who assigns posts by measure of talent
does not expect achievements beyond capacity;
one who accepts by assessment of ability
bears no blame when strength is exhausted.
Thus, to extinguish a candle flame, one need not trouble the vast sea;
to lift a few pounds, one need not employ Wūhuò.
Transporting firewood and hauling salt
should not waste the feet of a Qíjì;
trivial duties and petty tasks
are unworthy of bending a uniquely talented genius.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Streams in fields and ditches
cannot carry giant white-sailed ships;
vessels of pints and quarts
cannot hold thousand-zhōng quantities.
Glimmering lights cannot outshine the faintest glow;
common talents cannot distinguish extraordinary instruments.
For what creation bestows,
wisdom and intelligence have their roots.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The people of Yǐng admire the vulgar songs of Xiàlǐ,
and belittle the harmonious notes of Liùjīng;
mediocre men favor pleasing, flashy praises,
and dislike beneficial, well-guided actions.
Thus, Sòng Yù abandoned his ethereal, exquisite melodies,
while wise men seek uniquely insightful, far-reaching plans.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Though jade and gemstones pile like mountains,
there cannot be flawless vessels among them;
though the Dèng Forest spans a thousand miles,
it cannot lack withered trees.
In valuing treasures, one should not discard great beauty for minor flaws;
in speaking of greatness, one should not negate abundance for slight faults.
A betrayer of his lord was Liáng Píng [Zhāng Liáng],
yet he offered six wondrous strategies to secure the throne;
a bandit leader was Péng Yuè,
yet he achieved grand merits in aiding the mandate.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The five peaks stand majestic,
not harmed in their sky-touching height by hidden flaws;
the vast sea stretches boundless,
not burdened in its endless breadth by containing impurities.
Thus, the nine virtues esteem tolerance to win the multitude;
Xuānní [Confucius] embraced broad love to uplift others.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Establish virtue and fulfill words,
conduct whole and integrity pure—
this is true wealth;
why must it be exalted with jades and silks?
Hold your aspirations high,
neither yielding nor disgracing—
this is true nobility;
why must it be doubled with official insignia?
Common folk cannot fathom their measure,
mediocre men cannot gauge their standards—
this is true loftiness;
why must it soar through clouds and tread on rainbows?
Questioners may not sound their depths,
seekers may not find their shortcomings—
this is true profundity;
why must it pierce rivers and sink into seas?
If the four seas are within,
though the house has the poverty of hanging chimes,
one need not envy mining mountains and boiling seas.
Dwelling among birds and beasts,
one need not thirst for vermilion wheels and ornate carriages.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Hidden dragons await auspicious clouds to soar aloft;
perching swans need strong winds to ride the void.
The white fish required Jī Fā to leap forth;
the white pheasant waited for Gōngdàn to appear.
Jiāng Lǎo [Lǚ Shàng] met Xībó and cast his line at Pánxī;
Hán Yīng [Hán Xìn] encountered Hàn Gāo and unleashed his talent to quell chaos.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who clarify spirit in profound unity
can forget their physical forms;
those who distance themselves with lofty virtue from external things
can discard wealth and honor.
Thus, the cripple Zhīlí
marveled at creation with a joyful face;
the northern recluse Jīsǒu
dwelt on Sōng peaks in contentment.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Coarse principles cannot encompass all;
capable deeds cannot achieve everything.
Thus, the bright constellations can be obscured;
mountains and rivers may stagnate or shift;
gold and jade, though hard, can be softened;
solid ice, though dense, can be split.
Gōngdàn could not compete with Bóshì in climbing Féngyún's heights;
Zhòngní could not match Lǚliáng in skill at a hundred-rèn gorge.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Thunder cannot soften its roar
to match the harmony of metal and stone;
sun and moon cannot privatize their light
to alter the grace of impartial illumination;
great rivers cannot shorten their banks
to suit the desire for quick crossing;
the five peaks cannot reduce their steepness
to satisfy climbers' wishes.
Thus, a wide cart cannot narrow its tracks to force a narrow path;
a noble scholar cannot lower his integrity to blend with narrow customs.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Yīn and yáng broadly nurture and aid all things;
the three lights shine universally to illuminate;
Sōng and Huà mountains are vast for concealing flaws;
the northern sea is called great for containing filth;
great Confucians advance others to expand the Way;
far-sighted strategists embrace all with broad love.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The shell of the divine turtle
need not be deployed for battle;
the horn of the qilin and claws of the phoenix
need not be set for combat.
Thus, the talented do not sheathe their swords in times of peace;
watchmen do not cease preparations in thoughts of danger.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Southern gold does not devalue itself in obscurity;
fine jade does not cease purity in depth.
Those devoted to the Way do not change plans due to obstruction;
those upholding righteousness do not compromise for lack of appreciation.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who ascend the Xuánpǔ Garden
realize the lowliness of hills and mounds;
those who sail the vast sea
recognize the narrowness of ponds and marshes.
Studying the nine classics makes one aware of the blindness of facing a wall;
hearing the ultimate Way reveals the delusion of clinging to customs.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
From the origin of chaos,
no clear, pure streams emerge;
from roots of hair's breadth,
no arms-span branches grow;
from embers of inch and fraction,
no far-reaching heat flares;
within cracks and crevices,
no splendid multitudes gather;
from hooked and crooked shapes,
no straight-shadowed images cast;
above unevenness,
no uniformity lies below.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Without seeing the glitter of fine jade,
one does not feel the worthlessness of tiles and gravel;
without witnessing the splendor of tigers and leopards,
one does not know the mediocrity of dogs and sheep.
Hearing the nine movements of White Snow,
then one realizes the extreme vulgarity of the Bāman's song;
recognizing the profundity of Confucian elegance,
then one grieves over the stubborn ignorance of lacking learning.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A jade bowl without a base
is inferior to a whole earthen vessel;
brocade embroidery torn to shreds
is not as good as sturdy leather and cloth.
Thus, Xià Jī's lack of propriety
is less than the purity of the Gūzhú woman;
the many crimes of wealth and honor
are inferior to the path of poverty and humility.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Fierce beasts do not exert themselves beyond their scope;
eagles and hawks do not flap wings in reckless strikes.
If temple calculations do not assess virtue internally,
and advances do not measure strength externally,
it is like light feathers sinking into a great furnace,
flying snow falling into a boiling cauldron,
morning mushrooms testing Gànjiàng's blade,
lambs and calves confronting a martial tiger.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When the three luminaries are obscured in the heavens,
the clear light dims upon the earth;
when roots wither here,
branches wither there;
when the Way is lost nearby,
calamity reaches afar;
when governance errs above,
the people suffer below.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those focused on distant matters may err in close ones,
those governing external affairs may find troubles arising within.
Covering the head does not ensure the feet stay dry,
shielding the belly does not guarantee the back remains unharmed.
Thus, Qín Shǐhuáng built walls to block the Hú, yet disaster arose within his tent;
Hàn Wǔdì displayed banners over ten thousand miles, yet turmoil sprouted by his screen wall.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Talent has no fixed value,
utility follows no constant rule;
the straightforward become remarkable by fitting the age,
the employed prove skillful by aligning with the times.
Thus, when deep ice forms, the five illuminations are abandoned;
when summer heat blazes, fur robes and stoves retreat;
when high-flying birds gather, fine bows are drawn;
when cunning rabbits multiply, hounds and falcons dash;
when weapons rise, warriors strive;
when Sháo and Xià music plays, literati emerge.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
To stir long streams and lift tides to the sea,
one cannot turn from the five cities and leap over Jīshí;
to spread green leaves and bloom red flowers,
one cannot abandon great roots and discard lush branches.
Ruin the source, lose the foundation,
and few will not wither dry;
betray the sages, defy the classics,
and principle cannot broadly save.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The four great rivers trace distinct origins,
the five streams flow divided,
yet all rush low to fill the sea,
different paths converging alike.
Colors vary, yet all are vibrant;
sounds differ, yet all stir sorrow;
scents are not one, yet all are fragrant;
tastes unequal, yet all are delightful.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Things are valued for aiding affairs, yet adornment is secondary;
transforming customs with virtue, words are not the root.
Thus, silk cloth can ward off cold,
no need for sable or fox;
purity can shape things,
without ornate debate.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When fierce winds calm, tumbleweeds stand like mountains;
when the broad net is spread, all meshes fall in order.
Hence, never has a superior prized humility while inferiors were arrogant,
or a ruler scorned treasures while the people were poor.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Some matters start subtle and become prominent,
some things managed nearby affect the distant.
Thus, dig a pond of stepping-stone size,
and draw deep-scaled fish from rivers and seas;
enrich forests facing the morning sun,
and lure divine birds from Dānxuè;
set images on plates and urns,
and emerald dragons descend from dark skies;
scatter ashes on a foot of water,
and the moon goddess transforms at the cosmic pivot.
So, Jìn Wéngōng turned his chariot for a brave insect,
and warriors flocked like clouds;
Gōu Jiàn bowed to an angry frog,
and soldiers scorned death.
When the "nine times nine" was displayed, the talented with tapping horns arrived;
when dry bones were buried, the kindness of threefold rule spread.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Rich soil at the roots,
and withered leaves hold glory;
lead customs by example,
and transformation occurs without words.
Thus, the Táng era achieved peace with deerskin robes;
Qí Huánggōng discarded purple to curb extravagance.
Zhānghuá Tower built, and the fault of lavish halls was born;
the dew terrace halted, and silent virtue spread.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The perceptive,
foresee rise and fall in fading echoes;
the clear-sighted,
discern principles in unseen subtleties.
Thus, the Yuè person saw signs of Qí Huánggōng's decline in an unperceived ailment;
Jīzǐ recognized the disaster of Yīn's Lùtái at the first ivory chopsticks.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Heaven and earth cannot omit spring and autumn to make a year;
an enlightened ruler cannot discard punishment and virtue to achieve order.
Thus, punishment establishes authority when applied to the noble;
reward encourages goodness when given to the lowly.
When penalties reach high,
villainy is crushed, not something the weak can wield;
when kindness extends low,
distant people are won, not something the stingy can accomplish.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those sailing the vast sea
must keenly observe winds and weather,
thus securing fortune in safe passage.
Those skilled in governance
must tread cautiously on gains and losses,
thus enjoying lasting blessings.
What a blind ruler轻视,
an enlightened master may prize;
what a falling state discards,
a well-ruled age implements.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A hair's breadth error at the trigger,
becomes a yard's deviation at the target;
misjudgment here in giving and taking,
distorts good and bad there.
If evil and right mix equally,
moral order is disrupted;
if merit and fault go unmeasured,
all achievements collapse.
So, the wise ruler's rewards are like spring rain, without excessive deluge;
punishments mimic autumn frost, without untimely harshness.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those wielding fair scales
cannot be deceived in what they value;
those upholding laws
cannot show favoritism to their loved ones.
Thus, to win others,
one must first win oneself;
to lose others,
one must first lose oneself.
None have gained themselves yet lost others,
or lost themselves yet gained others.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The enlightened ruler personally wields authority and grace,
not lending sharp tools to others;
the blind ruler inverts spear and shield,
though titled尊, power departs.
Thus, controlling rewards to gain masses—
how Tián Cháng seized Qí;
monopolizing power and dominating court—
how Wáng Mǎng usurped Hàn.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Fixed rules cannot handle change,
a single path cannot answer infinite ways;
a carved boat cannot retrieve a dropped sword,
a glued tuning peg cannot harmonize clear notes.
So, no emerald canopy under clear skies,
no red wheels for crossing rivers;
if flavor is bland, add salt;
if boiling overflows, increase water and reduce fire.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Vermilion pledges on iron tablets,
blood oaths with sacrificed animals,
cannot save from the flaw of broken vows—
then it's hard to bind with knotted ropes.
The five punishments and nine chastisements,
the terror of clan extermination,
cannot stop the treachery of covetousness—
then one cannot transform with shield and axe dances.
Thus, the "Shū" has texts on generational emphasis,
the "Yì" speaks of adapting to the times.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those with eyes to discern truth
cannot be deceived by falsehoods;
those with wisdom to plumb depths
cannot be fooled by shallowness.
Otherwise,
they'd take a viper for a soaring dragon,
a fox or owl for a qílín or phoenix.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Worldly praise may be echoed, but not necessarily worthy;
common slander may be noisy, but not necessarily evil.
So, rather than welcoming and approving,
better examine deeds and test utility;
rather than rejecting and resisting,
better hear words and verify facts.
Then, flatterers won't advance with empty talk,
the capable won't retreat due to isolation;
nags will cease eyeing the grand carriage,
while dragon-steeds raise bits and gallop like lightning.
Then, what great feat cannot be achieved?
What distant Way cannot be reached?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Rotten wood, hidden away,
cannot withstand mountain-toppling winds;
cliffs riddled with cracks
hardly face sky-sweeping waves.
Thus, a reign of seven hundred years,
thirty generations' span,
did not hinge solely on the victory at Mùyě;
the defeat of turned spears,
the fall of Lùtái,
did not begin on the morning of Jiǎzǐ.
Its strength had long been firm,
its decline long foreshadowed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
To value the distant and disdain the near
is the common sentiment of ordinary people;
to trust the ears and doubt the eyes
is a perennial affliction throughout history.
Thus, the Qín emperor sighed over Hán Fēi's writings and longed for his presence,
while Emperor Wǔ of Hàn admired Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's essays yet felt disconnected across eras;
but when they finally obtained these men,
they failed to truly elevate them.
One accepted slander and executed the scholar,
the other relegated him to idle posts—
this resembles Lord Yè's fondness for painted dragons
turning to terror at the sight of a real one.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If the pearl fails to shine brightly,
it differs not from common gravel;
if the transformed kūn fish cannot soar above clouds,
it resembles the tiny wren.
Should Mián Jū silence his songs,
he'd blend with the mute;
if extraordinary talent is suppressed,
it stands alongside mediocrity.
Thus, when eels mock crimson dragons in muddy ponds,
or nags shame steeds in wilderness,
they fail to see how stillness unites,
but movement distinguishes.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Discard gold on the roadside,
and travelers will pause in awe;
cast brocade into mud,
and bystanders gasp in shock.
Yet when transcendent scholars are placed among the crude,
or statecraft talents left in obscurity,
critics don't decry their plight,
the influential don't rescue them,
some praise their writings but neglect their persons,
employ their strategies but forget their merits.
This malady
has persisted since antiquity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Dig a spring not fathoms deep,
and no flood will cover hills;
raise peaks not scraping skies,
and no clouds will veil heaven.
Without abundant wealth,
benevolence remains limited;
without profound talent,
eloquence falls short.
Seeing a foot-long tusk,
we know it grew not from an inch-wide mouth;
beholding a hundred-foot bough,
we know it springs not from a hair-thin trunk.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The phoenix rises at dawn from Dānxuè,
gathers by dusk at Xuānqiū,
before the sun shifts its shadow,
circling the nine heavens,
treading wind and cloud,
unhindered and unstoppable—
all through six pinions light yet mighty.
Great talent, too,
forms the six pinions of a state.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The Qíwèi bow "Forget-Return"
cannot shoot far without its string;
the dust-stirring melody
cannot evoke sorrow without instruments.
Transcendent virtue
achieves no deeds before its time.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Verdant blooms
adorn not withered branches;
mountain-toppling torrents
flow not from dried springs.
The firefly's nightly glow
cannot illuminate all things;
ambition fixated on gain
cannot leave fragrance through ages.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Unless abysses plumb earth's depths,
they cannot host hornless dragons
nor swallow ship-sized fish;
unless mountains pierce the sky,
they cannot conceal rare gems
nor summon clouds and rain;
unless virtue transcends common customs,
it cannot gather fair renown
nor establish solid achievements;
unless resolve surpasses the crowd,
it cannot attain success
nor engrave great deeds.
Yet mortals doing cicada-wing good at dawn
expect mountain-high gains by dusk,
like planting millet
then sitting to demand harvest.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Deeds lacking transcendent mark
yet seeking lofty praise;
self devoid of skill and principle
but busy with faction schemes—
to win pure honor now,
spread virtuous fame hereafter,
is like lifting robes to cross oceans,
tiptoeing to leap ninefold heavens.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Clay dragons, though brightly painted,
answer not auspicious clouds' call;
wooden birds, though finely gilded,
ride not the winds in flight;
straw dogs, though decked in gold and jade,
cannot chase shadows in gallop;
petty talents, though lavished with honors,
cannot bring celestial order to earth.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Where rich wine is served,
there gather gut-rotting rats;
where torches blaze at night,
there swarm fire-seeking insects.
Well-fattened livestock
ends on sacrificial altars;
small talent bearing great tasks
weeps tears of blood.
Sāng Hù's warning runs deep,
Fàn Shū's lesson shines clear.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Ocean waves rolling miles high
cannot sweep mountain dust away;
gales felling towering trees
cannot uproot tender grass.
The roaring tiger
cannot intimidate gnats;
world-surpassing genius
cannot conform to vulgar trends.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Steadfast will
masters achievement and fame;
unrelenting effort
teaches all virtues.
Climb mountains without halting at hardships,
and you'll reach lofty peaks;
accumulate goodness without complaining of plight,
and you'll earn lasting renown.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Though Yī Hé and Biǎn Què weren't immortal,
acupuncture cannot be deemed useless for saving lives;
though scholars often dwell in poverty,
classics cannot be deemed worthless for cultivating virtue.
Some plantings may fail,
yet farming must continue;
some virtue may meet misfortune,
yet moral practice must persist.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Overloading without cease
sinks our vessel;
charging blindly without retreat
endangers our selves.
Scorpions gnawing the base
—though temporarily stable—
signal impending collapse.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Dark clouds herald dragons' rise,
not summoned by lizards;
whirlwinds accompany tigers' roar,
not conjured by foxes.
Thus when great leaders receive mandate,
extraordinary talents gather;
when jade and silk seek recluses,
geniuses emerge from hills and gardens.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Metal breaks for its hardness,
water survives through softness;
mountains crumble for their height,
valleys endure through lowness.
Hence, those holding feminine grace avoid rivalry's harm,
while the domineering invite resentment's sting.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Huáiyīn hid his courage, crawling under legs,
yet remained dragon-leaping, tiger-gazing;
Yìnghóu concealed brilliance, trapped in mats,
yet still phoenix-soared, simurgh-ascending.
One became southern-facing sovereign,
the other rose to ministerial heights.
Thus dipping and rising
lets light swans soar through voids;
bending and stretching
lets fine talent await its hour.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The tiny gnat in humble dwelling
won't screech like owl catching mice;
the cicada fasting in purity
won't feast like dung beetle in filth.
Thus Yùkòu declined Zhèngyáng's bounty,
Zēng Shēn prized not Jìn-Chǔ's treasures.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A slight breeze cannot stir the waves of the great sea;
A fine hair cannot move a bell of ten thousand jun.
Thus, the master of the Qìyuán pondered on wisdom,
And sighed over discarding his axe;
Bó Shì lamented his time,
And felt indignation at cutting the strings.
A short chant is insufficient to achieve grand harmony,
Worldly power is inadequate to shift a heart of indifference.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Bears do not compete in agility with foxes;
Golden eagles do not vie in striking with small sparrowhawks.
Thus, Zhāng Ěr concealed his strength while holding the gate,
Zhū Hài hid his courage while wielding the knife.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The suspended fish is deluded by the fragrant bait;
The caged tiger dies because of the trapped fox.
What cannot be caught by fishing line,
Must be a qíu chī dragon;
What cannot be lured by traps,
Must be a lín yú mythical beast.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who soar in the clouds,
Do not know the filth of dwelling in mud;
Those in high positions,
Seldom sympathize with the toils of their subordinates.
Yet when roots decay,
Even a towering tree cannot maintain its lushness for a thousand days;
When the people resent,
Even Yáo and Shùn cannot rely on lasting blessings.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If an ordinary tree takes root on a sacred mountain,
Even craftsman Shí would lay down his axe and hatchet;
If a small fish dwells in the dragon's pool,
Even the fisherman would cease his nets.
When mosquitoes gather on an eagle's head,
Even sparrows dare not peck;
When a mouse stays by a tiger's side,
Even wildcats and dogs dare not glance askance.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The spiritual tortoise remains silent,
Yet fortune and misfortune are clearly revealed without form;
Spring frogs croak incessantly,
Yet their ugly sounds are despised for grating on the ears.
Thus, sparse sounds produce mighty echoes,
Few words make trust prominent.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
In cultures where sitting cross-legged is customary,
They despise the demeanor of graceful turns;
In lands where hair is worn loose,
They detest the adornment of formal caps.
Hence, the loyal and upright are rejected in an era where slander prevails;
The refined are not tolerated in customs that hate honesty.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A liter of water cannot extinguish the burning grass of a marsh;
A handful of soil cannot stop the roaring torrent at Dǐzhù;
An inch-long blade cannot clear the forest of Chángzhōu;
A solitary person cannot halt the faults of cliques.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A thousand sheep cannot fend off a single tiger;
Ten thousand sparrows cannot withstand one eagle.
Even if all courtyard torches are raised together,
They cannot match the last glow of Xīhé's sun;
Even if a hundred drums are beaten at once,
They cannot equal the residual sound of a thunderclap.
Thus, if mediocrities fill the court,
They cannot set the moral order right;
If a lone talent is entrusted,
He can make all affairs take root and grow.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Unexpected success beyond one's lot,
Is like flowers blooming in winter on trees and plants;
Adhering to the Way in poverty,
Is like bamboo and cypress enduring frost.
Therefore, those who discern fortune and misfortune with unique insight,
Even if threatened with sharp blades,
Will not lose their integrity or change their path;
How could they flatter and smile to conform to the vulgar?
Those who embody square virtue and dwell in uprightness,
Even if tempted with a fiefdom,
Will not betray their principles to follow the times;
How could they take shortcuts to gain favor?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The roar of thunder,
Cannot convey sound to deaf ears;
The brilliant light shining in the sky,
Cannot bend its rays into deep caves;
The bitter cold that freezes ice,
Cannot wither the flower of the kuǎndōng plant;
The scorching wind that melts stones,
Cannot consume the trees of Xiāoqiū.
Thus, even the highest virtue cannot change some things.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The crossbow at full draw is a critical danger,
With sharp arrows set on the string,
Extremely fearsome,
Yet the brave pheasant dashes against it without suspicion;
Dark governance that disrupts the state,
Hating the upright and envying the capable,
Is profoundly unpredictable,
Yet greedy people compete and do not avoid it.
Thus, flying blades suddenly gather unnoticed,
And calamity swiftly arrives without recovery.
Therefore, what fools delight in,
Is what the wise mourn;
What the mediocre strive for,
Is what the greatly wise abandon.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If the wind never ceases, fans are not used;
If the sun never sets, candles are not lit;
If flowers do not fall, fruits do not form;
If riverbanks do not erode, valleys do not fill.
When the nine regions are well-governed and peaceful,
Then the merits of Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ are not prominent;
When a wise ruler continues the path,
Then the achievements of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng are not accomplished.
Thus, illness highlights the value of a good doctor,
And chaos in the world elevates loyalty and integrity.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Loving glory makes one desire praise excessively;
Fearing disgrace makes one urgently resent slander.
But as for those who penetrate the essence of unity,
Whose fate aligns with creation,
Who blend fullness and emptiness into one strand,
And equate gain and loss in a single point—
Their loves and hates have never been attached,
And poverty or success cannot disrupt their harmony.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those whose spirit is not disturbed by gain or loss,
Are of the purest essence;
Those whose harmony is not stained by profit or harm,
Are of the most refined character.
Vast and boundless, they are not to be measured by gourds or cups;
Limitless and deep, they are not to be sought by short steps.
Sparse sounds constitute the great sound,
Scarcity of harmony enhances my own worth.
The profound and distant universe does not share their expanse;
Life and death are monumental,
Yet they do not alter their integrity.
Common trivialities,
Why should they care about them?
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When the forest is dense, craftsmen enter;
When pearls are beautiful, clams are split open.
Stones containing gold are smelted;
Grasses useful as medicine are cut and dug up;
A sharp blade is the first to chip;
A taut string snaps quickly.
Using things for self-cultivation,
Is the treasure of the true person;
Talents that meet worldly demands,
Are the disaster of the skilled.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When the target is set, flowing arrows fly towards it;
When a fine reputation arises, slanderous attacks follow.
Hoarding rare treasures brings no invitation for resentment, yet resentment comes;
Full of tools and proud in heart brings no summons for disaster, yet disaster arrives.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A treasure worth multiple cities,
Cannot be purchased by the poor and cold;
A vessel of extraordinary caliber,
Cannot be recognized by the shallow and vulgar.
Yet, a precious gem of full chi,
Does not conceal its quality for being unknown;
An outstanding scholar,
Does not diminish his integrity for being obstructed.
Rejoicing in heaven and accepting fate,
What complaint, what blame!
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The great roc has no use for dawn warnings;
The giant elephant has no talent for chasing.
Thus, Jiǎng Wǎn failed in a small district,
Yet became a model for the Three Terraces;
Chén Píng struggled in managing a household,
Yet harbored strategies of six wonders.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Brightness and dimness,
Are matters of talent,
Natural and not to be adorned;
Poverty and success,
Are matters of timing,
Encountered by chance and not to be forced.
Lǚ Shàng was not ignorant early and wise late,
But shook off plain clothes and barely met opportunity;
Hán Xìn was not timid at first and brave later,
But faced peril and hardship before achieving success.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
A galloping steed cannot catch up with past mistakes;
A thousand pieces of gold cannot undo the flaw of a spoken word.
Therefore, broadening one's generosity,
Is not as good as guarding against subtle faults;
Diligently seeking,
Is not as good as speaking sparingly.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When a person of fervent loyalty loves his country as his own family,
and serves his ruler as his own parent,
then acts of disloyalty
will not be counted among his faults.
When a benevolent person regards others as himself,
and treats the distant as intimately as the close,
then grievances arising from lack of forgiveness
will not be laid to his charge.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If dark ice had not formed,
and white snow had not accumulated,
then the luxuriance of the green pines would not be revealed;
if common customs were not corrupt,
and moral teachings had not declined,
then pure and unsullied conduct would not be distinguished.
Amidst a perilous state and sinking into poverty,
thus Zhuāng Lái upheld the lofty ideal of rejecting glory;
dwelling in a chaotic land and suffering hunger and cold,
thus Zēng Shēn and Liè Yùkòu spread the reputation of forgetting wealth.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Heaven resides on high and observes the lowly,
thus its net, though wide, lets nothing slip through;
the divine is intelligent and upright,
thus its way rewards the genuine and punishes the false.
Therefore, when kindness and harmony flow through the nine regions,
then the seven luminaries move correctly in the dark heavens;
when cruelty and harm are manifest among all things,
then the two forces err in the four seasons and eight nodes.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Heaven's ranks hold honor without limit,
but human titles confer no nobility that violates virtue.
Thus, though Confucius was but a commoner, he is sacrificed to for a hundred generations;
though King Zhòu and King Jié were emperors, even servants and slaves disdain to be compared to them.
Shāng Róng and Lǎo Zǐ, the lower their status, the more esteemed their names;
King Yōu and King Lì, the heavier their ranks, the more notorious their crimes.
Thus, the life of the King of Qí
is not equal to the tomb of Liǔ Xiàhuì;
the palace of the King of Qín
cannot match the lane of Zhèng Xuán.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Echoes and shadows cannot manifest without sound and form;
accumulated blessings cannot be summoned without virtue.
Thus, Emperor Yáo governed for over seventy years,
and only then did the auspicious star radiate its brilliance;
Yáng Gōng accumulated good deeds,
unwearyingly even in old age,
and only then did gold fall and rain gather.
For those on a long journey, arrival must be slow;
for those who give late, recompense is often delayed.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
One who has exhausted his principles cannot be blamed for not having more;
one who has achieved one thing cannot be asked to accomplish all.
Thus, at the end of a great wave,
it cannot float duckweed;
after a gust of wind,
it cannot lift light dust;
with the remaining strength of a strong crossbow,
it cannot pierce a gauzy veil;
with the setting glow of the western sun,
it cannot illuminate the east of the mountains.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Though the suspended heavenly bodies may suffer eclipses,
they cannot be compared to the steadfast glow of fireflies and candles;
though the Yellow River may be turbid,
it cannot be likened to the clear purity of a small pond.
Though a mountain may collapse,
it is still higher than a mound;
though a tiger may be emaciated,
it is still fiercer than jackals and wolves.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
If Shénnóng had not suffered the nine ailments,
then the ways of the four classics would not have been handed down;
if the Great Yǔ had not toiled until his hands and feet were calloused,
then the blessing of the dark jade tablet would not have been bestowed.
Thus, prolonged hardship is the foundation of great joy,
and temporary toil is the beginning of eternal ease.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Though a golden hook and cassia bait are precious,
they cannot control the sunken scales in the deep abyss;
though conspicuous favor and generous emoluments are noble,
they cannot attract reclusive people without desires.
Thus, at the Lǚliáng waterfall, there are men standing like cranes,
and by the riverbanks, dwell the people who cut the sandalwood.
Silks and jades are vainly gathered at the lane of Yán Zǐlíng,
and the chariot with rushes returns empty from the gate of Xú Shèng.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Observations and hearings differ in preference,
likes and dislikes are hard to align.
Birds see Xī Shī and flee in alarm;
fish and turtles hear the Jiǔsháo music and dive deep.
Thus, the dazzling brilliance of ornate patterns
cannot please the eyes of the naked village;
the clear sounds of the biànlíng flute
cannot delight the ears of Chǔ slaves.
The benevolence of Gǔgōng Dǎnfù
could not enlighten the Dí who desired his land;
the eloquence of Duānmù Cì
could not release the tethered horse from the commoner.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The ritual of dignified circling
is despised in the land of naked squatting;
the carpenter with his ink line
is resented in the market of crooked wood.
The greedy and gluttonous
detest the pure whiteness of plain silk;
those who form cliques and are numerous
envy the solitary stance of high integrity.
It is like merchants hating those who share their profits,
or ugly women harming the nation's beauties.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
When a noble man rises to prominence,
he recommends the worthy and distributes his emoluments;
when a mediocre person attains his ambition,
he boasts of his rank and neglects the scholars.
He bestows favors abundantly on flatterers,
and uses his wealth for petty kindnesses.
Not sharing safety with the wise,
yet hoping for rescue in times of danger;
not sharing joy with extraordinary men,
yet expecting sympathy in times of sorrow;
this is like when a calamitous fire blazes to the sky,
only then praying for rain on a famous mountain;
when a flood rises to the heavens,
only then building a boat at the eastern gate;
is it not too late?
Someone said:
"The square and round of heaven and earth,
are not achievements of compass and square;
the three luminaries casting their light,
are not due to the power of polishing;
the brilliant blossoms of spring,
are not distinguished by gradual dyeing;
the fragrance of chǎi and huì orchids,
is not borrowed from any scent.
Know that the utmost genuineness
is valued for its naturalness.
Meaning is considered extraordinary for its rarity,
and diction is esteemed as beautiful for its uncommonness.
Yet, reviewing through the ages the masters of literary composition,
few can produce outstanding elegance from their brush tips,
most deliberating over the words of predecessors.
Why is this?"
Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Clear tones are valued for their harmonious elegance,
and writings are treasured for their discernment of subtleties and analysis of principles.
Thus, the eight musical instruments differ in form, but their tones follow the same pitch pipes;
embroidered patterns vary in design, but the five colors are balanced.
Merely, in the interplay of complexity and simplicity, there is a host and guest;
in beauty and ugliness, there is a sequence.
This means the music hall has no constant tune,
and the great kitchen has no fixed flavor.
Though catalpa and evodia wood pile up like mountains,
without a master craftsman like Lǔ Bān, they cannot be made into ingenious works;
though numerous books are without limit,
without outstanding talent, one cannot extract their richness.
Why must one seek wood from a thousand miles away
to build a great mansion;
or wait for words from ghosts and spirits
to compose a chapter!"
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Talents have clarity and turbidity,
thoughts have length and shortness.
Though all engage in writing,
they vary into ten thousand grades.
Some are vast and overflowing but not deep and cohesive;
some are rich in substance but dull in expression;
some violate natural principles yet are skilled in style.
This is due to a consistency in partial strengths,
not the talent of comprehensive mastery.
Being obscure in self-assessment,
and forcefully attempting to encompass all,
contravening one's talent and changing one's pursuit,
thus they cannot avoid ridicule.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
The five flavors differ yet each is sweet;
various colors conflict yet all are beautiful.
In human nature,
people love similarity and hate difference,
valuing what agrees with themselves,
and despising divergent paths.
Now, the styles of literary writing,
are particularly difficult to appreciate in detail.
If one considers only what pleases the ear as excellent,
and what suits the heart as satisfying,
few understand the ninefold music that makes one forget the taste,
or the elegant grace of the Yǎ and Sòng.
This is what is meant by examining the saltiness and sourness of salted plums,
yet not knowing the unadorned nature of the grand broth;
appreciating the delicacy of fluttering lightness,
while being blind to the profound and vast depth.
Those who are outstanding and broad-minded
roam beyond the realm of dark and yellow;
those who are constrained and petty
are tethered within the confines of cages.
If the wings differ in sharpness and dullness,
then soaring and perching vary in height and lowness;
if the strides differ in speed and slowness,
then progress and retreat vary in distance and nearness.
The dull and sharp cannot be tuned by gluing the pegs.
Writing values richness and abundance;
why must it be praised with one unanimous voice?
If it cannot save the drifting customs,
or the decline of worldly paths,
clear the way for the doubtful,
or relieve the destitution of the poor,
how is it different from spring blossoms that do not serve as food,
or fragrant herbs that do not rescue from the urgency of cold and hunger?
Ancient poetry criticized faults,
thus it was beneficial and valued;
modern poetry is purely empty praise,
thus it is harmful and despised.
Bàopǔzǐ says:
Those who engage in writing
each have their own flaws.

Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Those who create tools value them for meeting urgent needs,
not for adorning appearances with elegance;
those who establish doctrines prize them for aiding instruction,
not for conforming to vulgar tastes to gather praise.
If one merely flatters and toadies,
praising falsely and concealing faults,
how can this rectify errors and admonish against transgressions,
awaken the deluded and remedy shortcomings?
To fear lack of harmony and abandon the melody of 'White Snow',
or disdain the value of a city's worth for being hard to sell—
I find nothing commendable in this.
It is not that I cannot compose flowery words to please,
nor that I am unaware of the risks in upholding blunt honesty,
but I cannot bear to distort truth with biased writing,
confusing authenticity and falsehood.
I wish for heart and speech to align,
facing my reflection without shame,
hoping for understanding from future kindred spirits.
Fortune and misfortune are fated,
success or blockage lies with heaven—
why must writings and words be put to use,
bringing glory in one's lifetime?
When a noble person speaks or writes,
they must guard against delusion and obscurity,
rectifying the slant of conformity,
polishing away the filth of waywardness.
Yet some authors merely embellish with ornate rhetoric,
expanding on impractical vagaries,
crafting unverifiable, useless phrases,
cultivating the beauty of empty, extravagant words.
They resemble the writings on 'Hard and White' or 'Sharpening Cultivation',
or Gōngsūn's discourses on names and punishments—
though they may roam beyond heaven and earth,
probing into the infinitesimal,
untying linked rings,
separating sameness and uniting differences,
claiming a bird's shadow does not move,
a chicken's egg has feet,
a dog can be a sheep,
or speaking of giant turtles and long snakes.
These only serve to display cleverness and strangeness to deceive the vulgar,
no different from painting the Áocāng granary to relieve hunger,
or gazing at the Milky Way to quench thirst.
Speaking of the abundance of jade in the Kūnlún Mountains
cannot relieve Yuán Xiàn's poverty;
perusing the records of a medicine cabinet
cannot cure a critical illness;
Mòzǐ carving a wooden kite to soar the sky
is inferior to a three-inch metal arrowhead;
Guǎn Qīng casting a golden statue of a qíjì steed
is less useful than a nag for daily tasks.
Words that soar to autumn skies yet cannot be applied—
even Confucius would not exchange for them."
Bàopǔzǐ says:
I have long considered Wáng Zhòngrèn's composition of over eighty chapters of 'Lùnhéng'
to be the work of a supremely talented individual.
A fellow student, Lǔ Shēng, challenged me:
"Jade is prized for its rarity,
while gravel is deemed cheap for its abundance.
Thus, Fúxī's hexagrams, fewer than ten, encompass the cosmos;
Lǎozǐ's words, under ten thousand, fully expound the Dàodé.
Wáng Chōng's writings,
filling cases and bundles,
waver in and out,
sometimes Confucian, sometimes Mohist.
His phrasing and ideas
are not entirely excellent—
like weeds on a slope,
they cannot match the millet and grains at one's feet."
Bàopǔzǐ replied:
"Moreover, creators are called sages,
transmitters are called worthies;
we observe the quality of their works,
not their quantity.
You, sir, are like one who dwells in the gloom of a nest,
unaware of the boundless eight directions;
clinging to the glow of a lamp,
ignorant of the brilliance of the three lights;
swimming in shallow puddles,
unacquainted with the vastness of the Southern Sea;
stuck on a low mound,
unenlightened to the heights of Sōng and Dài peaks.
The cosmos is called great
because it embraces all realms,
stretching endlessly beyond measure;
mountains and seas are deemed rich
for their vast containment,
holding myriad complexities.
If, as you elegantly argue,
we value few and disdain many,
then the heavens' grandeur has no merit for its expanse,
and the earth's breadth no worth for its support.
In puddle waters,
there are no fish that swallow boats;
on inch-long branches,
no wings that shade the sky;
atop ant hills,
no forests of Fúsāng;
in ditch sources,
no floods that淹没 hills.
The giant turtle crowns Yíngzhōu,
its waves surging over Fāngzhàng;
the great peach tree spreads on Dùlíng,
the Jiànmù tree towers in Dūguǎng;
the leviathan swims across the celestial lake,
the cloud-borne péng soars to the dark heavens.
Furthermore, the crash of thunder
cannot soften its roar;
the rush of the Yellow River
cannot confine its flow;
the qíjì steed chasing the wind
cannot shorten its stride;
the swan spreading its wings
cannot lower its flight.
Thick clouds bring heavy rain;
a strong bow shoots far arrows.
How could Wáng Shēng, with his vast learning and great talent,
be sparing in this!
"You say:
'Jade is precious for its scarcity,
stone cheap for its abundance.'
Yet beneath the Xuánpǔ garden,
atop Jīnghuà peaks,
in the marshes of Jiǔyuán,
the depths of Zhéfāng abyss,
línláng jade piles into mountains,
yèguāng pearls blaze to the skies—
are they not splendid?
