You cite Fúxī's few works,
but if Zhōu Gōng elaborated on the Yì,
adding rites and music,
and Confucius composed the 'Spring and Autumn Annals',
supplementing it with ten commentaries—
exceeding Fúxī,
outnumbering Lǎozǐ—
should they be贬斥 too?
Sparse words may lack complete truth,
scant phrases fail to express all affairs.
Thus, accumulated chapters and volumes
are necessary to present a comprehensive outline.
Xīhé's rise brings dawn,
Wàngshū's glow illuminates the night;
the five materials coexist with diverse uses,
hundreds of herbs flourish with varied cures;
four seasons unite to complete the year's work,
five colors blend to make brocades beautiful;
eight harmonies create the beauty of Sháoxiāo music,
myriad words combine to distinguish principles and arts.
Hoarding the wealth of Yī Dùn yet using little—
how is this different from Yuán Xiàn's poverty?
Possessing immeasurable capacity
yet writing meager, shallow works—
how does it differ from trivial mediocrity?
Music is treasured by those who understand,
books are transmitted by those who recognize;
the blind music master Kuàng tuning bells
need not seek approval in his time.
Should profound words and lofty writings
fear lack of appreciation and be reduced?
Moreover, the foul things in rivers and seas
are countless,
yet they don't diminish the depth;
the crooked trees on the Five Peaks
are beyond measure,
yet they don't impair the heights.
The jade of Xià Hòu,
though with tiny flaws,
shines with such brilliance and color
as to compensate fully.
Tens of millions of words,
though some lack elegance,
if their themes are lofty and profound,
suffice to overshadow flaws.
Thus it is said:
The turbidity of the four great rivers
does not compare to the clarity of jar water;
the leanness of a giant elephant
differs not from the fatness of a lamb."
"You also criticize, saying:
'Now entering, now exiting,
sometimes Confucian, sometimes Mohist.'
What is spoken from the mouth becomes speech,
what is written on paper becomes books.
Books serve to convey speech,
speech serves to record affairs.
If writing should not mix various records,
then discussions should always adhere to one single matter.
In the past, when feudal lords inquired about governance,
and disciples asked about benevolence,
Confucius answered them
with different words for each person.
This is because he adapted his guidance to the circumstances,
addressing what was urgent at the time.
It is like the thousands of medical treatments,
where acupuncture points are not fixed,
using warmth to dispel cold,
using coolness to remove heat,
aiming only to save lives and preserve health.
How can one insist that all travelers must take the same road to Qí or Chǔ,
without changing paths?
Táo Zhū and Bái Guī's wealth did not come from one source -
that is abundance;
the myriad things born in Yúnmèng and Mèngzhū -
that is vastness.
Therefore, the Huáinán Hóngliè
begins with 'Yuán Dào' and 'Chù Zhēn',
yet also contains 'Bīng Lüè' and 'Zhǔ Shù'.
Zhuāng Zhōu's writings,
while treating life and death as one,
also contain fears of sacrificial animals, admiration for turtles, requests for grain, and relief from hunger.
If we discard writings because their content is not pure,
it would be like removing a cataract by gouging out the eye,
treating damp paralysis by amputating the foot,
worrying about weeds and cutting down the grain,
hating dead branches and felling the tree."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
"The words of the hundred schools,
though not all possess elegant brushwork and sharp rhetoric,
nor grand magnificence and profound depth,
yet all represent what talented scholars have entrusted,
the clarified thoughts of focused minds.
The classical texts are the deep sea of moral principles,
while the philosophical texts are the rivers that increase its depth.
Looking up to compare them,
they are like the auspicious star assisting the three luminaries;
looking down to measure them,
they are like the woods and thickets complementing Mount Sōng.
Yet scholars who specialize in one field alone,
swimming in a well while ignoring the ocean,
consequently stumble in the mud,
and stagnate in immovable困境.
Philosophical texts unfold the profound and vast,
remote and deep,
gathering unfathomable sources,
spreading flows that leave nothing out,
changing without being bound by the square and round of rules,
extending widely without sinking into heretical paths that deviate from correctness,
their style lofty and strict,
their depth like multiple walls, difficult to exhaust.
Thus those with biased tastes for sour or sweet
cannot appreciate their flavor;
those with limited thinking capacity
cannot discern their spirit.
The ancients lamented the rarity of talent,
so for a hundred generations they followed in footsteps,
not discarding night-shining jewels
because the uncarved jade doesn't grow on Kǔntóng Ridge;
not rejecting words that aid teaching
because the books didn't emerge from the schools of Zhōu and Confucius.
They are like those carrying water -
though their vessels differ, they fight fire the same;
just as acupuncturists -
though their techniques vary, they attack illness equally.
Those with narrow views,
stubbornly clinging to one thing,
abandoning broad and refined discourse,
thinking without understanding,
adding up ounces and calling them as heavy as mountains,
gathering hundreds and thousands thinking they make millions and billions,
fascinated by the trivial writings of poetry,
while neglecting the deep and beautiful words of philosophical discourse,
confusing true and false,
mixing jade and stone,
equating magnificent music with rustic songs,
putting dragon patterns on plain cloth,
how lamentable and regrettable -
is this just one instance!"
Some say:
"Moral conduct
is the root;
literary composition
is the branch.
Therefore in the order of the four disciplines,
literature does not rank highest.
Thus what is written on paper
is the leftover matter of dregs;
what can be transmitted
is like the straw dogs after the sacrifice.
The pattern of high and low
is thus to be criticized."
Bào Pǔzǐ replied:
"The fish trap may be discarded but before the fish is caught,
one cannot be without the trap;
writing may be abolished but before the Way is practiced,
one cannot be without writing.
As for the breadth and narrowness of literary traces and rhythmic patterns,
the beauty and ugliness of composing phrases and comparing meanings,
the length and shortness of tracing sources and reaching destinations,
the depth and shallowness of containment and drawing forth,
the gap between them
is such that even the space between heaven's surface and a hair's tip
cannot比喻 its distance,
even the three luminaries shining brightly
cannot compare to their greatness and smallness.
Dragon's pool lead and iron ingots
cannot比喻 their sharpness and dullness;
wild goose feathers and accumulated gold
cannot compare their lightness and heaviness.
Yet common scholars, merely seeing the ability to dip brushes and paint paper,
generalize everything as one category,
this is why Bó Yá forever missed Zhōng Zǐ,
and why the Yǐng man's axe remained motionless.
Though woodcarvers stand shoulder to shoulder,
Bān and Dí alone hold the name of peerless hands;
though many play the zither,
Kuí and Xiāng exclusively possess the reputation of pure tones.
Though a stable may have thousands of horses,
Qíliú alone has the value of surpassing the herd;
though beauties may number in the tens of thousands,
Wēishī alone possesses transcendent beauty -
this is because they far exceed the multitude.
Moreover, literature and moral conduct
are like ten chǐ compared to one zhàng -
to call one secondary
has never been heard.
The eight trigrams were born from the flight of hawks,
the six jiǎ emerged from the celestial turtle's back,
where literature exists,
though we value the root, we need not necessarily neglect it,
nor must we necessarily despise the branches.
Like brocade relying on plain silk,
pearls and jade depending on clams and rocks,
clouds and rain born from tiny spaces,
rivers and seas beginning from minute distances -
if the principle is truly thus,
then your elegant argument is flawed."
He also said:
"The winged dragon rises slowly,
with a glance soars to the clouds;
the sweat-blood horse walks leisurely,
with one breath covers a thousand lǐ.
Therefore ants marvel at its reaching heights without steps,
and clumsy horses are shocked that it surpasses them without gradual progress.
As for galloping within the realm of poetry and discourse,
maneuvering within a single classic,
viewing great wonders with ordinary feelings,
measuring the boundless with narrow capacity,
starting from childhood,
continuing until white-haired age,
one cannot attain it.
Moreover, common customs generally value ancient times and disdain the present,
respecting what they hear while disrespecting what they see.
Though there may be steeds that chase the wind and outrun shadows in our time,
people still say they cannot match what Bó Lè drove.
Though there may be uncut jade worth multiple cities,
people still say it cannot match what Chǔ's Hé wept over.
Though there may be swords that cut horses and point to carving,
people still say they cannot match what Ōu Yě forged.
Though there may be medicines that revive the dead and resurrect the decayed,
people still say they cannot match what Hé and Què compounded.
Though there may be scholars who stand out among the crowd and walk alone,
people still say they cannot match the ancients."
Bào Pǔzǐ said:
Jī Kāng considered Tàiyuán's Guō Línzōng,
who ultimately did not accept appointment to the three highest offices,
whose learning encompassed everything,
whose reputation outweighed previous generations,
and who additionally possessed the knowledge of people -
to know people is wisdom,
making him a vessel approaching sagehood.
Living in a declining age,
restless and anxious,
without even warming his mat,
his aspiration focused on rectifying deviation and promoting the Way,
he resembled Confucius.
I replied:
"Wisdom or lack thereof
lies in a single word;
a flaw in the pivotal mechanism
mars the pure white jade.
I believe the title of 'Second Sage'
should not be lightly bestowed.
The so-called Second Sage
must embody the whole in miniature,
be peerless in his generation,
with no room for others between him and the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius.
How could such a person be worthy of this rank!
Línzōng stood out prominently,
with clear and penetrating judgment;
compared to ordinary people's discussions,
he was indeed often elevated above them,
but still insufficient.
This man had witty eloquence and graceful demeanor,
skillfully presenting himself and making good use of it,
and with enthusiasts acting as his wings,
extending his reputation in all directions,
thus enabling him to be admired in turbulent times,
and promoted by those who listened without verification.
Once he praised with a brief word,
it carried more weight than a thousand pieces of gold;
wherever he traveled,
both wise and foolish were stirred,
deeming it as the gathering of dragons and phoenixes,
the emergence of rare auspicious signs.
When he spoke, his lingering tones were emulated;
where he stepped, his footprints were copied.
He could be called one skilled at beating the great drum and unveiling the sun and moon,
but not a true recluse.
For wishing to serve at court, but the world was in great chaos;
wishing to live in seclusion, yet finding it unbearable;
leaping forward, he feared calamity;
standing firm, he felt uneasy.
Restless and unsettled,
now fat, now lean,
yet people chased his glamour without examining the substance,
admired his form without probing his spirit.
Thus even when his rain-soaked headgear was ruined,
it was still imitated,
without realizing its shortcomings—
all such cases are similar.
The common people's pursuit of fame
reaches such extremes.
Thus even though he had flaws,
none dared point them out.
Línzōng, learned and perceptive about people,
was not without his merits.
Yet he failed to avoid the reputation of being overrated,
and was unenlightened about self-assessment.
When urged to take office and advance,
Línzōng replied:
'By day I observe human affairs,
by night I watch celestial signs;
what Heaven has abandoned
cannot be supported.
Now fortune lies in the míngyí hexagram,
in a position of inaction,
a time for hesitation and seclusion,
not for meeting the favorable moment to appear.
Even on the plains,
I fear the wild seas may overflow.
I would become a fish,
how could I brave the storm and ride the turbulent waves!
Better to nourish the spirit in mountain caves,
delight the heart with Péng and Lǎo,
leisurely and carefree,
to pass the years.'
Judging by Línzōng's words,
he knew the Hàn could not be saved,
and clearly understood it was beyond his ability to do so.
He should have ascended to Shāngluò,
sailed on the Five Lakes,
followed Cháofù to the steep mountains,
sought the Fisherman by the Cānglàng River;
if unable to join the mountain hermits,
to leave the crowd and go alone,
then he should have hidden in deep abysses,
concealed his scales and tied his bag,
yet instead he traveled east from west,
without warming his mat,
aspiring to the busy pursuits of Confucius and Mòzǐ.
Sages worry about the world,
traveling everywhere,
yet even they were criticized
by retired scholars.
Línzōng's talent did not meet the times,
his capability was not peerless;
in public, he could not stabilize the rulers and govern the people,
nor transform customs;
in private, he could not wield the brush to write,
expounding the Six Arts;
his self-promotion
was already excessive,
gaining a resounding fame,
and receiving ample support.
Yet ultimately, in advancement he did nothing to improve order or chaos,
in retreat he left no traces in history.
Observing his wavering and drift,
melting like ice, bending like grass,
he was no different from ordinary people.
Without reason, he floated on waves,
stumbled in the dust,
gathered in the capital,
associated with noble wanderers,
with worn-out wheels and boxes,
no time to rest,
thus making his reputation glitter,
with foreigners following like shadows,
alleys lined with red-wheeled carriages,
halls filled with guests in red sashes,
streets packed with light chariots,
carriages arriving in succession,
truly a wandering knight,
not fitting the category of a recluse.
Even in an era of good governance, such behavior
would not qualify as noble and pure,
nor as an outstanding figure in hermitage,
yet he cultivated this in times of danger and chaos—
how commendable is that!
Who would not say he was blind to the rise and fall of Heaven and human affairs,
obscured in assessing his own strengths and weaknesses!
Vainly forsaking the path of tranquility,
ultimately gaining no benefit from action,
escaping disaster and downfall
was merely his luck.
To consider this as worrying for the world and nation,
hoping to emulate the Unadorned King,
is like a lame horse seeking the dragon-steed,
a quail chasing the swan,
a midge comparing itself to the roc,
a shrew matching the giant elephant.
"Thus, Línzōng can be said to have the talent to shine in society,
but not the quality to hold firm;
his understanding was not incomplete,
nearly fit for great use,
with discernment outwardly displayed,
but spirit inwardly empty,
unable to bear restlessness,
words and actions contradictory,
claiming quiet retreat with his mouth,
yet craving glory and gain in his heart,
failing to attain the roosting birds of Xuánpǔ,
the hidden spirits of the deep abyss.
Self-display and self-promotion
are disgraceful for scholars.
Knowing it's wrong yet imitating and emulating it—
how could the vessel of a Second Sage
reside in this?
Though said to know people,
the clarity to know people
was difficult even for Táng and Yú,
a trouble for Confucius.
With vision matching the sun and moon,
seeing the end from the beginning,
they still had errors,
unable to always be accurate,
let alone Línzōng with his firefly's light,
half-understood gains and losses,
which was already not little.
Yet his fame was weighty in his time,
praise flourished after his death;
thus what he gained
was widely circulated,
but what he lost
went unrecognized.
Though he somewhat selected unknown scholars from the grassroots,
pointed out unpolished jade in the countryside,
he failed to promote loyal and brave men to the court,
establish defenders on the frontiers,
relieve the signs of collapse in desperate times,
thwart the rush of rebellious plots.
Like Bào's recommendation of Guǎn,
or Píngzhòng's promotion of Rángjū,
Línzōng's name vibrated in the court,
respected for a time;
the high officials
all revered him,
his strength sufficient to elevate talent,
his words enough to rouse the stagnant,
yet he only nurtured his illness in the capital,
gathered guests,
without advancing anyone
to save the crisis,
merely able to know people,
unwilling to recommend them.
How different is this from knowing fertile soil is fit for fine crops,
discussing straight wood suitable for beams,
yet never plowing to sow good grain,
nor cutting to construct pillars?
How does it solve hunger,
or save from exposure?
His refusal to be nominated
was indeed a noble act,
but his incessant wandering
was also his flaw."
Jī Shēng further said:
"Línzōng in life served as a model for an entire generation,
and after death, his lasting fragrance spreads far and wide.
Eminent Confucian scholars and outstanding men,
none have pointed out his faults,
yet I alone criticize his shortcomings in my lifetime.
Wouldn't this make me an object of ridicule for future generations!"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"How could that be so?
If my words are indeed accurate,
they should be passed down to posterity.
Future generations who recognize the truth,
why worry about lack of agreement?
Moreover, many previous worthies have also criticized him,
only Huáng Shēng excessively praised him.
Thus, the late Grand Tutor Zhūgě Wúxùn also said:
'Línzōng in seclusion did not cultivate reclusion,
in public life did not benefit his time,
but actually sought only to spread his fame and nurture his reputation.
He considered street gossip and alley talk as eloquence,
mocking superiors and criticizing government as nobility,
yet the customs of the time valued him,
admiringly like Guō Jiě and Yuán Shè,
who were pursued in former times.
Those later admirers of reputation,
failed to examine the classics of sage kings,
or discuss the conduct of earlier worthies,
merely confused by flowery fame,
all competing to take him as their standard,
those learning from him acted as if fearing to fall behind,
those speaking of him filled one's ears,
even average people remained unaware,
how could the ignorant youth understand?
' Therefore, the former governor of Línglíng, Lord Yīn Bóxù of the prefectural office,
a man of high talent and profound discourse, also said:
'Línzōng formed friendships with generals and ministers,
traveled through various states,
promoted private discussions to move the masses,
manipulated praise and blame at the imperial court.
Those he favored would rise like wind and rain,
changing their value and appearance;
those he disliked would be crushed and submerged,
becoming despised by scholars.
Considering him a famous worthy,
who encountered chaos and lived in seclusion,
concealing his light and hiding his traces,
falls far short indeed.
The nobleman practices the Way,
to rectify his ruler,
to correct customs,
but when the ruler cannot be rectified,
and customs cannot be corrected,
Línzōng moved about,
engaging in pure conversation in the lanes,
bringing no rescue to the decaying world order,
offering no solution to the suffering of the people.
' Also, the former Central Secretariat official Zhōu Shēng Gōngyuǎn,
an outstanding famous Confucian, also said:
'To encounter good governance and praise it,
is called delighting in the Way;
to meet with chaos and rescue it,
is called worrying about the Way;
when chaos cannot be rescued and one avoids it,
is called preserving the Way.
Emperor Shun was one who delighted in the Way,
Confucius was one who worried about the Way,
Wēizǐ was one who preserved the Way.
As the Hàn dynasty was collapsing,
with worldly affairs focused on social connections,
Línzōng by principle should have been filled with righteous indignation and open-mindedness,
seeking like-minded noble men,
together to correct and set things right,
yet he busily made himself a leader among them,
which was not appropriate for saving the world.
At that time, even the various eunuchs,
were merely self-serving animals.
As for those like Chén Fán and Dòu Wǔ,
though holding high positions as ministers and governors,
all valued Línzōng highly,
believed his speeches and discussions,
determined right and wrong based on him,
couldn't they have hoped to rescue danger and change customs?
Yet Línzōng could neither recommend capable men,
nor establish the slightest benefit,
while those who fled and avoided office,
he compared to Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu;
those who neglected duties to entertain guests,
he likened to the Duke of Zhōu;
those who nurtured followers to avoid service,
he equated with Confucius;
those who abandoned family to依附 powerful families,
he matched to Zǐyóu and Zǐxià.
Thus the world was dazzled by name and reality,
and great chaos grew increasingly severe.
If we say Línzōng didn't know,
then we cannot call him intelligent;
if we say he knew but didn't change,
then we cannot say he worried about the Way.
Previously, the Four Lords resembled the Duke of Zhōu but couldn't become the Duke of Zhōu,
now Línzōng resembles Confucius but cannot become Confucius.
'" Then the questioner sighed with emotion and said:
"So then this man was merely one who avoided chaos,
not one of the lofty complete recluses."
Bàopúzǐ said:
"At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was Mí Héng,
twenty-three years old.
Kǒng Wénjǔ was over fifty,
served in the nine highest offices,
his literary talent surpassed all,
praised since youth,
his fame and position were exceptionally high,
yet he befriended Héng when Héng was a commoner,
and also recommended him to the Hàn court,
suggesting he should begin his career as a court gentleman.
He said:
'When the sacred mountain descends its spirit,
extraordinary men appear together.
Whatever his eyes see once,
he can recite from memory.
Whatever his ears hear briefly,
he doesn't forget in his heart.
His nature harmonizes with the Way,
his thinking seems divinely inspired.
' Such was his admiration for him.
When Héng traveled in Xǔxià,
from dukes, ministers, and state scholars downward,
Héng never addressed them by their official titles,
but called them all 'So-and-so',
or called them by surname as 'So-and-so boy',
calling Kǒng Róng 'the big boy',
calling Yáng Xiū 'the little boy'.
Only Xún Yù could勉强 be spoken with,
beyond him,
all were like wooden puppets and clay dolls,
resembling humans but lacking human spirit,
all just wine jars and drinking bags.
At a grand assembly of all officials,
Héng was present,
when suddenly he frowned with grief and sorrow,
sighing mournfully and passionately.
Someone criticized him, saying:
'Heroes are happily gathered,
this is nothing to sigh about.'
Héng glanced around at the dense crowd and replied:
'Amidst this accumulation of corpses and array of coffins,
how can a humane man not feel sorrow?'
Lord Cáo often gnashed his teeth, wanting to kill him,
but again there was no proper legal reason for capital punishment,
and he also regretted having the reputation of killing Confucian scholars,
so he demoted him to drum official.
Héng showed no regret or shame,
but tied horns to pillars,
putting his mouth to them to blow,
producing extraordinary sounds,
while simultaneously shaking the drum and striking it,
listeners didn't know it was one person.
And his discussions became even more intense,
without any restraint or fear,
soon he fled and went to Liú Biǎo, governor of Jīng Province.
Biǎo wanted to write a letter to Sūn Quán,
the Rebel-Subduing General at that time already fully controlled Jiāngdōng,
with a million armored troops,
wanting to form a mutual support alliance,
to jointly resist the Central Kingdom,
he had various literary scholars draft it,
but after exhausting their thoughts, they couldn't capture Biǎo's intent.
Then he showed it to Héng.
Héng examined it and said:
'You only want to make Sūn's sword-bearing attendants look at it,
then this can be used,
but if you let Zhāng Zǐbù see this,
it would be greatly humiliating.'
Immediately he destroyed it and threw it to the ground,
Biǎo looked disappointed and displeased,
saying to Héng:
'Is it really not even worthy for weeding?'
'It's a pity.'
Héng requested paper and brush,
then rewrote it,
there were over ten versions by the various scholars,
Héng merely glanced through them once,
memorized and wrote them,
finished and returned them to Biǎo.
Biǎo returned them to their authors,
some had kept copies of their original drafts,
compared them with Héng's version,
not a single character was wrong,
then all were greatly astonished.
Biǎo then asked Héng to compose another,
Héng immediately composed it,
his hand never stopping,
Biǎo considered it excellent and used it."
Héng grew increasingly arrogant,
to the point where everyone in the province
loathed and resented him.
Even Liú Biǎo could no longer bear it
and wanted to kill him.
Someone advised that even Lord Cáo, known for his severity,
could still tolerate him,
and since Héng had some empty reputation from youth,
if he were killed suddenly,
then wandering scholars across the land
would no longer set foot in Jīngchǔ.
So Biǎo sent him away.
Héng went to Xiàkǒu,
relying on General Huáng Zǔ,
who treated him as an honored guest.
Zǔ's eldest son, Huáng Shè,
traveled with Héng,
passing by someone's tomb,
where they both read the stele inscription once before leaving.
After some time,
Shè said:
"The stele text we saw earlier was excellent;
it's a pity we didn't copy it."
Héng replied:
"You only remember the title.
I still recall it after one glance."
He then wrote it from memory,
but at the end, one character
was damaged on the stone,
making it unclear.
Héng supplied half the character,
saying:
"I suspect this should be such-and-such character.
I fear it may not be accurate."
Shè examined and agreed
(text missing below).
Though his words and actions slighted others,
he still desired honor and prominence,
thus soaring high among phoenix trees,
unable to hide in the weeds.
Yet in cultivating himself, he was contradictory and critical,
deluded and unaware,
so opening his mouth brought hatred,
and every step trod into disaster.
With such skills as these,
how could he find a place in the world and die a natural death?
It's like an owl's hoot or a fox's cry—
all dislike it;
if the sound doesn't change,
what good does moving elsewhere do?
Xǔxià
was a sea of talents.
Wénjǔ served as its host;
relying on him could lead to arrival,
yet feeling unsettled there
already showed what was to come.
Like a terminal illness,
even Yúfù or Yuèrén
could do nothing.
Rotten wood or lead ingots—
even Bānshū or Ōuyě couldn't craft them.
And yet he fled to the Jīngchǔ region,
ultimately meeting extreme harm—
this was the result of Héng's blindness.
He desired but could not attain,
not that he could attain but wouldn't use it.
Alas, talented men,
must you not take warning!
Jī Shēng said:
"What perplexes me
is Héng's empty fame;
what you discuss
is Héng's real flaws.
How dare I not day and night follow this guide,
and lay down my staff at the balanced path!"
Bào Shēng Jìngyán,
fond of the books of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzǐ,
delved into sharp debates,
believing that ancient times without rulers
were better than the present age.
Thus, in his writings, he argued:
"The Ruists say:
'Heaven gave birth to the people and set rulers over them.'
How could it be that August Heaven earnestly intended this as a justification!
The strong bully the weak,
so the weak submit to them;
the clever deceive the foolish,
so the foolish serve them.
Submission
gives rise to the way of ruler and minister;
service
leads to the control of the less powerful.
Thus, enslavement and domination
stem from contending over strength and comparing wit.
But that blue heaven truly has no part in it.
In primal chaos, namelessness is valued;
all beings find joy in following their nature.
So stripping cinnamon bark or cutting lacquer trees
is not the tree's wish;
plucking pheasant feathers or tearing kingfisher plumes
is not the bird's desire;
tight reins and bits
go against the horse's nature;
bearing carts and hauling heavy loads
bring no joy to the ox.
The sprouting of deceit and cunning,
relying on force against truth,
severs the root of life
to adorn the useless,
capturing flying birds for ornamental play,
piercing the nose of the whole and natural,
hobbling the feet of heaven's freedom—
this is not the intent of all things living together.
To enslave those multitudes,
to support those in office,
where the noble have lavish stipends and the people are impoverished.
If dying and then returning to life
brings boundless joy,
how much better never to have died?
Declining titles and refusing salaries
to fish for empty fame—
better never to have had to decline.
Only when the world is in rebellion do loyalty and righteousness appear;
only when the six relations are discordant do filial piety and kindness become evident.
In ancient times,
there were no rulers or ministers;
people dug wells to drink,
plowed fields to eat,
rose at sunrise to work,
rested at sunset,
carefree and unbound,
expansive and content,
neither competing nor striving,
without honor or disgrace,
mountains without paths,
marshes without boats or bridges.
Rivers and valleys impassable,
so no annexation occurred;
masses of people not gathered,
so no attacks were launched.
Thus, high nests were not raided,
deep waters not drained;
phoenixes perched in courtyards,
dragons swam in groups in garden ponds;
hungry tigers could be trodden upon,
venomous snakes could be grasped;
wading through marshes, gulls wouldn't fly away;
entering woods, foxes and rabbits wouldn't startle.
No budding of power or profit,
no occurrence of calamity or chaos,
no use of weapons,
no fortification of walls,
all things mysteriously one,
forgetting each other in the Way,
plagues did not spread,
people lived to old age,
purity in their hearts,
no scheming minds born,
they nursed and played,
drumming their bellies as they roamed.
Their words unadorned,
their actions unembellished—
how could there be gathering of taxes to seize people's wealth,
how could there be harsh punishments as pitfalls and traps!
"As we descend to the degenerate age,
cunning and artifice arise,
morality and virtue decline,
distinctions between noble and humble become established,
elaborate rituals of social hierarchy develop,
ornate ceremonial garments are adorned,
towering palaces reach for the clouds,
vermilion and green decorate the rafters,
precipitous mountains are searched for treasures,
deep abysses are plumbed for pearls.
Jade gathered like forests
cannot satisfy their extravagance;
gold accumulated into mountains
cannot meet their expenditures.
They wallow in realms of wanton excess,
betraying their primordial origin,
departing daily from their ancestral roots,
growing ever more distant from simplicity.
Honoring worthiness makes people contend for fame,
valuing goods causes thieves and robbers to arise,
seeing desirable things disorders genuine hearts,
displaying power and profit opens paths to plunder.
They create sharp weapons,
prolonging the misery of invasion and division,
fearing crossbows aren't strong enough,
armor isn't sturdy enough,
spears aren't sharp enough,
shields aren't thick enough.
Were there no violent oppression,
all these could be discarded.
Therefore it is said:
If white jade isn't cut,
how can it become guīzhāng tablets?
If morality isn't abandoned,
how can benevolence and righteousness arise?
Thus tyrants like Jié and Zhòu
could burn people and punish remonstrators,
make dried meat of feudal lords,
mince regional chiefs,
cut out human hearts,
break people's shinbones,
indulge in extreme arrogance and depravity,
employ the cruelty of the heated bronze pillar.
Had these men been commoners,
though their natures were violent and extravagant,
how could they have practiced such things!
That they could indulge their cruelty and desires,
butchering and dividing the world,
was because they were rulers,
thus able to follow their whims.
Once ruler and subject are established,
various evils daily multiply,
yet we wish to roll up our sleeves amidst shackles,
labor exhaustively in mud and charcoal.
The sovereign worries and trembles in his court,
the common people seethe and struggle in hardship,
constrained by ritual measures,
regulated by punishments and penalties -
this is like opening a source flooding to heaven,
arousing an immeasurable torrent,
then trying to block it with a handful of soil,
or stem it with a palm."
Bàopǔzǐ refutes:
"I have heard that when primal chaos first opened,
the turbid descended and the clear ascended,
heaven arched overhead covering all,
earth extended broadly supporting below.
Heaven and earth took their positions,
above and below assumed form,
looking to distant things,
we see heaven honored and earth humble,
looking to what is near,
we see the head and limbs,
demonstrating the order between ruler and minister.
This hierarchy of high and low
has existed from the beginning.
As for the Great Ultimate in chaos,
the two primal forces without substance -
this cannot compare to the separation of dark and yellow,
the seven luminaries displaying their images,
the molding power of yīn and yáng,
the division of all things into categories.
From this perspective,
we also know that when birds flock and beasts scatter,
nesting in trees and hiding in caves,
eating raw flesh and blood,
wearing knotted grass,
within families there's no respect between the six relations,
in society there's no hierarchical dignity -
this cannot compare to sheltering in great houses,
enjoying fine millet and delicious food,
wearing embroidered silks,
withstanding winter and summer heat,
with enlightened rulers overseeing affairs,
able ministers ordering the world,
establishing offices and dividing duties,
making the universe harmonious.
When nobility and baseness have clear patterns,
people admire rewards and fear punishments;
when power is equal and strength matched,
they contend and plunder without fear.
Therefore when sages arose,
receiving mandate from heaven,
some made nets for hunting and fishing,
some observed stars to drill for fire,
some tasted plants to select grains,
some built dwellings for shelter.
They prepared things for use,
removing harm and promoting benefit,
the common people joyfully supported them,
serving and honoring them.
Thus the way of ruler and minister was born -
how could there be principle to deceive the foolish and bully the weak?
When the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors successively arose,
the way of governance flourished,
distinguishing encouragement and restraint,
virtue abundant and punishments clear,
songs of enlightened goodness were composed,
the transformation of vast virtue accomplished,
the great steps leveled,
the seven governors following their measures,
the wúqín bird singing at sunrise,
the qílín and yǔ beast manifesting their numina,
turtles and dragons displaying patterns at riverbanks,
the jǐnglǎo shining on celestial paths,
imperial influence vibrating through nine regions,
weapons of violence stored in armories.
Thus when ritual is established the ruler is secure,
when music is composed punishments are set aside.
As for extravagance, license, violence and tyranny,
these come from the individuals themselves -
must there necessarily be a ruler
for these to occur?
Yet Bào Shēng exclusively cites the crimes of degenerate ages,
not discussing the principles of perfect governance -
why is this?
Moreover, in remote antiquity's simplicity,
when transformation hadn't yet occurred,
people were still childlike and ignorant,
scheming minds not yet active,
comparable to infants
whose wisdom hasn't yet sprouted -
this isn't knowing yet not acting,
or desiring yet restraining.
If person vied with person for grassland profits,
family disputed with family over nesting grounds,
with no officials above to rectify wrongs,
and factions below repeating offenses,
then private fighting would exceed public warfare,
wood and stone would be sharper than shields and spears,
corpses would litter the fields,
blood would dye the roads crimson.
Long without a ruler,
living creatures would be utterly destroyed.
As for taming dragons and phoenixes,
the Hé Tú and Luò Shū diagrams,
some with unicorns holding tablets on their backs,
some with yellow fish surging in waves,
some with vermilion birds flying to present,
some with whirlwinds gathering thrice -
all occurred in ages with rulers,
never in times without kings.
These signs of auspicious responses
point to the profound ultimate,
some indicating portents of dynastic change,
some manifesting the flourishing of perfect governance.
If having rulers
didn't accord with heaven's intent,
then who caused
these fine responses to come?
Do you consider chaotic darkness beautiful?
Then heaven and earth shouldn't have separated;
do you esteem the nameless as lofty?
Then the eight trigrams shouldn't have been drawn.
Could the creator be mistaken,
and Tàihào blind?
Your elegant discourse exalts
only what values spontaneity.
May I ask: recognizing the mother but forgetting the father -
this is the nature of all living things;
the reverence of bowing and prostration -
this is the world's later ornament.
Yet nature cannot be followed completely -
the father must be honored;
ornament cannot be abolished -
there must be bowing.
If you follow nature and abolish ornament,
would you be content?"
"In ancient times, the living had no houses,
the dead had no burials,
rivers had no boats,
land had no use of carriages or horses.
People consumed poisonous substances,
leading to their demise.
There was no medical skill for illnesses,
resulting in countless unjust deaths.
Later sages
reformed and bestowed
benefits that people still rely on today,
enjoying their profound grace.
The advantages of ingenious tools
are not easily discarded.
Now, if you were made to live in crude nests and caves,
discard the dead in the wilderness,
swim across waters when blocked,
walk mountain paths carrying loads on foot,
abandon cauldrons for raw, rank food,
forsake acupuncture and rely on nature's course for illness,
use nudity as adornment,
without clothing;
mate with any woman encountered,
without matchmakers.
You would also say:
'It cannot be.'
How much more so without a ruler?
If people of antiquity were like trees and stones,
unaffected by frozen ice's chill,
unfamished despite lacking supplies,
then it might be acceptable.
But desires for food and clothing,
once rooted in the heart,
lead to conflicts not necessarily over gold and jade,
nor competitions solely for glory and status!
Acorns and grass can provoke disputes,
even wild greens, if sufficient,
can incite plunder.
The nature of desire
sprouts at the moment of conception;
the tendency to prioritize oneself
manifests upon forming a body.
Harm, killing, and annexation
arise naturally.
To expect no disorder—
what logic supports this?
When an enlightened king reigns above,
all lords offer admonitions,
sitting awake till dawn,
toiling from early morn till late, skipping meals.
They welcome criticism to correct faults,
urge close associates to supplement oversight,
heed public songs to reflect and introspect,
heed warnings and remain vigilant evening and night.
They raise clear winds to sweep away filth,
wield autumn's severity to discipline all things.
With strict and dense laws,
offenders are shown no mercy;
punishments and executions deter minor crimes,
nine punitive campaigns chastise great evils.
Yet, like wolves blocking the path,
they feel the disorder in human relations,
worry about tyrannical families,
fear traitors harming the state.
Thus, stern officials soar like hawks to punish transgressions,
tiger ministers wield axes at the frontiers.
Still, rebellious plots
never cease through the ages.
If allowed to run free,
made fearless,
then robbers like Zhì would rampage, killing and looting,
while the good stand idly awaiting disaster,
with no ruler to appeal to,
no strong support to rely on.
To hope every family is like Yí Qí's,
every person like Liǔ Xiàhuì's,
is no different from carrying a pig and expecting no stench,
crossing a river and hoping not to get wet,
riding a runaway horse without reins,
sailing a light boat without oars or rudder—
I see no feasibility in that."
Bào Shēng further objected:
"In the position of heaven and earth,
the two energies mold all things.
Those fond of yang soar like clouds;
those preferring yin dwell in rivers.
Following softness and hardness according to nature,
transforming with the four seasons and eight nodes,
each adheres to what suits them,
inherently without nobility or baseness.
Once rulers and subjects were established,
changes and complexities multiplied.
Too many otters disturb the fish;
too many eagles chaos the birds.
Offices set up oppress the common people;
lavish support for superiors impoverishes those below.
Hoarding precious goods,
adorning towers and pavilions,
dining with tables spread wide,
clothing embroidered with dragon patterns,
gathering unmarried women inside,
leaving many widowers outside,
disputing over rare treasures,
valuing strange objects,
creating useless vessels,
indulging insatiable desires—
if not by ghosts or spirits,
whence comes this wealth and power?
When grain and silk accumulate, the people suffer hunger and cold;
with numerous officials, sitting idly consumes resources for their upkeep.
Guards include many who eat without labor;
the commoners support idle hands.
People lack food and clothing,
struggling to sustain themselves,
yet taxes are increased,
burdensome labor imposed heavily.
Those below cannot bear it,
facing cold and hunger,
they recklessly break laws,
and thus it happens.
The king toils anxiously above,
ministers frown worried below,
treading on thin ice, facing depths,
fearing disaster's approach.
Fearing the unused of wisdom and courage,
they offer high ranks and rich emoluments to lure them;
fearing unforeseen treachery,
they build strong walls and deep moats for defense.
Yet they don't realize that rich emoluments empty the people and make ministers arrogant,
strong walls lead to heavy labor and clever attacks.
Thus, distributing the gold of Lùtái,
doling out the grain of Jùqiáo,
brought universal joy;
how much better not to amass gold
nor collect people's grain in the first place?
Returning oxen to Táolín,
releasing horses on Huàshān,
storing away shields and spears,
sheathing bows and arrows,
was still considered excessive;
how much better to have no armies
and neither war nor garrison duties?
Thatched roofs, earthen steps,
abandoning weaving, uprooting mallows,
using rough sacks as curtains,
washing fur coats, wearing cloth covers,
concubines not wearing silk,
horses not fed grain—
such frugality to lead by example
is praised as virtuous tales,
but it's like the robber Zhì dividing spoils,
taking less being called modesty,
or fish stranded on land,
moistening each other with spit.
"When individuals have no public duties,
families bear no tribute or levies,
content with their land and happy in their work,
following heaven and sharing the earth,
internally sufficient in food and clothing,
externally free from struggles for power and profit,
then taking up arms for robbery
goes against human nature.
Under the teaching of symbolic punishments,
none among the people transgressed;
when laws and decrees proliferate,
thieves and bandits abound.
Is it that they lacked self-interest then and are solely greedy now?
Rather, when we are tranquil, the people correct themselves;
when those below are exhausted and resentful, cunning arises.
Leaving things to nature,
we still fear violence;
laboring them incessantly,
seizing from them endlessly,
fields lying waste, granaries empty,
looms void of thread,
food not filling the mouth,
clothes not covering the body—
to expect no chaos,
how can it be possible?
Thus, trying to save from disaster only deepens it;
strict prohibitions fail to stop it.
Passes and bridges are meant to forbid wrongs,
but crafty officials use them for wrongdoing.
Measures and scales are to detect falsehood,
but wicked people use them for deception."
Ministers exist to support the state in crisis,
while treacherous ministers fear that their ruler might not face peril.
Arms are meant to quell turmoil,
yet rebels steal them to create chaos.
All these stem from the actions of the ruler.
When people have gains to pursue,
they develop contentious hearts;
wealthy and noble households
have the heaviest stakes.
Moreover, the disputes among common folk
are but minor affairs,
mere individuals contending in strength—
how far could they go?
They have no vast lands to covet,
no cities to profit from,
no treasures to desire,
no authority to compete for;
their influence cannot gather followers,
their might is insufficient to drive others—
how can this compare to a king's majestic wrath,
deploying armies and rallying troops,
pushing innocent people
to attack guiltless states,
leaving corpses numbering in the tens of thousands,
with blood flowing enough to dye shields and fields red?
Unprincipled rulers
exist in every era;
indulging in cruelty and chaos,
they leave the world without stable states,
where the loyal and good are harmed within,
and the common people lie exposed to bones abroad—
is this merely the worry of petty conflicts?
As for shifting filial duty from father to ruler,
abandoning piety for loyalty,
proclaiming orders that deny the father's role—
such things also occur.
In ancient times, houses
were enough to shelter from wind and rain,
but now they are draped in crimson and purple,
adorned with gold and jade;
in ancient times, clothing
sufficed to cover the body,
but now there are dark yellows and embroidered patterns,
silks and fine linens;
in ancient times, music
was enough to settle human emotions,
but now it is filled with excessive sounds,
startling the soul and harming harmony;
in ancient times, food and drink
merely satisfied hunger,
but now they involve burning forests and draining depths,
slaughtering living creatures.
(The following is Bàopúzǐ's refutation) "How can one abolish something entirely just because it has excesses?
If a ruler like Yáo were on the throne,
with Jì and Xiè assisting in governance,
humble palaces and light taxes,
employing the people in due seasons,
promoting the pure ethos of frugality,
enforcing clear prohibitions on luxury—
those who are simple and modest
would be honored and elevated;
those who disrupt order and harm the people
would be dismissed or executed;
then praises would arise, and the masses would be at peace.
Why must one fear fire and destroy houses,
or dread waves and block great rivers?"
Bàopúzǐ said:
"I have already refuted Bào Shēng's theory valuing the ancient era without rulers.
The responses he later gave me
are too numerous to fully record;
I have somewhat organized his arguments and documented my rebuttals as follows."
Bào Shēng said:
"Rulers distinguish rare treasures,
collect strange objects,
adorn useless things,
and satisfy endless desires."
Bàopúzǐ retorted:
"May I ask, have all emperors throughout history
indeed distinguished rare treasures
and collected strange objects?
There are those who did not.
I have heard that when Táng Yáo ruled,
he discarded gold in the mountains;
when Yú Shùn abdicated,
he cast away jades into valleys.
With coarse food and plain clothing,
comparable to a gatekeeper—
he did not drain abysses for pearls,
clear cliffs for jade,
mine rocks for gold and silver ores,
cross seas to pluck kingfisher feathers,
net tortoiseshell in remote lands,
or dig for pigments in Mín and Hàn—
this is evident.
If attire shows no distinction,
then authority is not emphasized;
if status differs,
then ceremonial items vary in measure.
Thus, the Duke of Zhōu distinguished the differences between noble and common, high and low:
in palace and dwelling structures,
there were limits of walls and measures;
in caps, canopies, and banners,
there were ornate decorations;
in chariots, robes, and utensils,
there were regulations on quantity;
in kitchen provisions and offerings,
there were grades of ritual feasts;
in years of disaster and calamity,
these were reduced or withdrawn.
Endless desires
do not exist under the Way;
what you mention
may condemn the crimes of Jié and Zhòu,
but it is insufficient to prove a refined argument."
Bào Shēng said:
"Rulers have three thousand consorts in the rear palace—
is this all heaven's will?
When grain and silk accumulate, the people starve and freeze."
Bàopúzǐ retorted:
"The number of royal consorts
was set by the sages.
Sages
are those whose virtue aligns with heaven and earth.
Their virtue matching heaven and earth—
how could it be merely different?
Was it only to fulfill desires and indulge emotions?
It was to assist the six palaces,
regulate yin and yang,
teach reverence in ancestral worship,
respectfully conduct grand sacrifices,
provide dark ceremonial robes,
and broaden the lineage paths.
Moreover, according to the Zhōu records of the nine regions
and Hàn dynasty geographical texts,
the number of women in the world
exceeds that of men.
Could the consorts honored by the king
truly pressure all marriageable men?
The Duke of Zhōu's considerations
seem already thorough.
Emperors lead officials in ceremonial plowing,
empresses direct noblewomen in sericulture and weaving;
extending to the common people,
farming duties have limits,
diligent farming is rewarded,
laziness is punished,
with a one-tenth tax
to serve public use.
Households have stores for calamities,
the state has reserves for nine years;
each follows heaven's timing and shares the land,
not seizing their seasons,
with light taxes and sparse labor,
so the people have no hunger or cold.
Once food and clothing are sufficient,
ritual and deference arise.
In the eras of Wén and Jǐng,
the people focused on farming,
households were well-supplied and prosperous,
granary rice rotted red beyond measure.
Yet nobles and commoners still wore marquis' robes and dined from tripods,
cattle and horses covered the marshes—
because taxation was moderate,
not harming the lower classes.
In degenerate times,
officials lost farming regulations,
private pursuits turned to frivolous trades,
grain production narrowed,
and idle eaters multiplied,
so upper and lower shared hardship,
and lawbreakers were many—
Bào Shēng blames this on having rulers.
If one criticizes excessive selection of consorts
or condemns unrealistic farming quotas,
rebukes three thousand revelries,
or denounces heavy land taxes—
simply ensure rear palaces follow Zhōu rites,
and taxes are not imposed arbitrarily;
that would suffice.
Must there be no rulers at all?
If one rises late for a day,
affairs fall into disarray;
pursuing deer without a guide,
they vanish into the forest—
how could it ever end?
Without a central authority,
the virtuous lose their support,
the wicked achieve their ambitions;
even a loose net catches some—
should we have no net at all?"
Bào Shēng said:
"In human life,
food and clothing are already burdensome,
let alone adding taxes and levies,
compounding them with forced labor,
so that hunger and cold arrive together,
the people below cannot endure their fate,
and thus risk breaking laws and committing wrongs,
from this they arise."
Bàopúzǐ retorted:
"Spiders spread their webs,
fleas and lice do not starve;
endowing humans with intelligence and skill,
to employ all things in service,
feeding mouths and clothing bodies,
how can this be considered burdensome?
The only worry is that the wealthy lack a mind to know contentment,
and the noble have unlimited desires.
How can one, because of a single stumble,
refrain from walking for life,
or due to the tyranny of Jié and Zhòu,
think of having no ruler?
If one says the ruler's affairs are overly expansive,
that taxes are heavier than in the past,
that the people's strength is exhausted by trivial tasks,
and that hunger and cold stem from this,
it is acceptable to criticize accordingly.
But to claim that having labor duties and taxes
causes the state to fall into chaos—
I ask, in the peaceful age of Táng and Yú,
or the era of the Three Dynasties under the Way,
were there no taxes or labor services to support the state,
so that the sovereign and his ministers
tilled the land themselves to be self-sufficient?
Bào Shēng only knows that when hunger and cold come together,
none can remain steadfast in poverty,
but does he not know that when food and clothing are both sufficient,
the people understand honor and shame!"
Bào Shēng said:
"The king treads on deep waters and a tiger's tail,
which is not enough to describe his peril;
he dozes in waiting for dawn,
neglecting meals until the sun is late,
yet what does he fear that disaster might reach him?"
Bàopúzǐ challenged:
"If he can truly be like this,
then he is a sage ruler.
What ails kings
lies in arrogance and extravagance,
in not employing the worthy,
or employing the unworthy.
Xià Jié pointed to the sun to justify himself,
Qín Shǐ Huáng worried about sharing the same posthumous title for myriad generations,
thus leading to their downfall,
and becoming laughingstocks for the future.
If one can fear danger and be vigilant at night,
widely accepting admonitions and advice,
consulting grass-cutters and wood-gatherers for their opinions,
nurturing the elderly to seek their words,
why worry about state affairs going awry,
or fear that all governance will not be well?
With caution and reverence, the constant relationships are in order;
with negligence and indulgence, treachery and crime arise.
How much more, without a ruler,
could there be no chaos?"
Bào Shēng said:
"Kings admire and long for rare auspicious signs,
luring those from remote wilderness,
wishing to exalt virtue and display might,
to overawe those not yet subdued,
but what good are white pheasants and jade rings
to the common people?"
Bàopúzǐ retorted:
"When a king's virtue reaches heaven, there are heavenly auspices;
when it reaches earth, there are earthly responses.
As for the radiant star spreading its light,
to aid the glow of the Moon;
or the corona encircling the sun,
marking the shadow of the sun's path;
the divine birds singing in harmony at the palace gates,
the golden elephant gleaming in the clear pond—
are these achieved by humble words,
or lured by rich gifts?
Wáng Mǎng, treacherous and cunning,
harboring ill intent,
embellished a false peace,
deceiving the court and the public,
bribed foreign regions,
to have them send auspicious objects;
how can one use this to say it was always so in antiquity?
Seeing a tail a full zhang long,
one knows it is not from a small body;
observing teeth spanning several ren,
one knows they are not from a tiny mouth.
Thus, the Queen Mother's sending of envoys
illustrates her mysterious influence connecting with the spiritual,
reaching even the remotest places;
the repeated translations from Yuèshang
suffice to show kindness touching distant lands,
with grace covering all without exception.
Remote regions cannot be subdued by force,
barbaric tribes cannot be intimidated by might;
if not for the most perfect governance,
how could it be so?
Why does Bào Shēng say they are of no use?
The Zhōu court did not lack jade and need the Queen Mother's ring for wealth,
nor were they frugal with meals and thirsty for Yuèshang's pheasant to fill their kitchens;
the reason they valued them
was truly that these things signified great peace.
Then, above, there were no harsh or oppressive policies,
below, no people who had lost their place;
even the flying and crawling insects
all found their joy.
Among the beauties of possessing a state,
what could be greater than this?
Yet you say they are of no use,
of no benefit to the common people.
The source is distant, the substance great,
and certainly not easy to perceive;
are Bào Shēng's words
not quite fitting then?"
Bào Shēng said:
"The ruler fears unforeseen treacheries and conflicts,
hence he strengthens the walls to prepare for them."
Bàopúzǐ retorted:
"For lords and kings to set up defenses,
is esteemed in the Great Yì (Classic of Changes);
I do not see why strengthening walls
should be criticized.
Since the two primal forces began to separate,
and the myriad things transformed and were born,
both evil and upright have existed.
The sages knew that malevolence is natural,
and that the dull-witted are hard to change,
just as the spring sun cannot revive the withered and rotten,
or blazing flames cannot melt metal and stone.
Adorning beauty and carelessly storing treasures
teaches licentiousness and summons thieves;
therefore, they take the model from repeated dangers,
preparing before anything sprouts.
Multiple gates require the vigilance of the night watchman's clapper,
managing the military to prevent the violence of intruders;
yet you wish to abolish these,
what principle supports this?
The horn of the rhinoceros,
the spur of the phoenix—
heaven indeed lends them,
but must they be used daily?
Bees and scorpions carry poison to defend themselves,
intelligent birds hold reeds to guard against nets;
badgers curve their burrows,
to prepare for direct attacks;
water buffalo form arrays,
to repel the savagery of tigers and leopards.
Yet Bào Shēng wishes to discard armor to stop sharp blades,
demolish city walls to halt charging attacks.
If armor is discarded yet sharp blades do not cease,
city walls are ruined yet charges still gather,
even Gōngshū and Mò Dí
could not preserve themselves;
I wonder, for our lives,
what plan would you propose?"
Someone said:
"If desirable things are absent,
even without the solidity of city walls,
the enemy will not come."
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"As for desirable things,
why must they be gold and jade?
Even the tip of an awl or knife
can make foolish people compete.
The great battle of the Yuè people
arose from a disagreement over a python;
the war between Wú and Chǔ
started over a mulberry leaf.
In times of famine,
people eat each other,
bare-handed and barefoot.
In ancient times, Fǔ Hóu and Zǐ Gāo,
more recently, Yú Gōng and Shì Zhī,
controlled passions and examined punishments,
splitting hairs and analyzing minutiae.
Those executed swallowed their voices and sang of virtue,
the punished bore no grudges for life;
these were not times without a ruler.
In the past, a widower was below, yet the Four Peaks did not conceal him;
promoting the obscure and lowly, Yuán and Kǎi were all recommended.
Some cast aside their butcher knives to enter the golden gates;
some left their mortar and pestle to tread the jade hall;
some abandoned their livestock to become ministers;
some rose from being fugitives to become great generals.
Bó Liǔ reconciled with his enemy,
Xiè Hú recommended his foe;
Fáng Huí kowtowed to attract scholars,
Qín Xī broke his head to promote the worthy.
I dare ask, at that time,
was there a ruler or not?"
It is also said:
"Fields lying waste and granaries empty,
all stem from having a ruler."
"For the ruler is not the weeds choking the fields,
nor are the ministers the sparrows and rats depleting the storehouses.
Whether they lie waste or empty,
ultimately results from the movement of the heavenly stems and earthly branches,
floods, droughts, and pestilences,
leading to famine and scarcity.
Could it be due to taxes and levies
that cause such conditions?
As for food being the first of the eight governmental affairs,
it is called the people's heaven.
Hòu Jì personally engaged in farming,
Yǒuyú himself plowed the fields,
in bountiful years there was much millet and much rice,
our granaries held hundreds of millions,
the people ate from the old stores.
When the Bái Canal was opened, saline land became fertile soil;
when Shào Fù raised the embankment at Yánglíng, accumulated grain stood like mountains;
when Shū Áo created Qīsī, every household had rotting grain;
when Zhào Guò invented the clever triple plow, the area west of Hángu Pass prospered;
when Rèn Yán taught farming in Jiǔzhēn, the black-haired masses were well-fed and prosperous.
Was this a time without rulers?!"
Bào Pǔzǐ says:
No prayer is greater than having no desires,
no blessing is richer than knowing when to stop.
Those who embrace fullness yet dwell in emptiness
are sure to preserve themselves completely;
those who indulge in comfort and abundance
face perils difficult to avert.
As for those like Shàn Juǎn, Cháo Fǔ, Xǔ Yóu, Guǎn Zhòng, and Hú Qiú,
they all tread on clouds to soar high,
relying on dragons and phoenixes to elevate their traces,
perceiving hidden dangers within tempting baits,
awakening to overturned carts on the road ahead,
avoiding perilous paths to cross afar,
thus they could escape Zhān Hé's fishing line,
they may be said to善于 foresee subtle shadows beyond form,
to see solid ice before frost forms,
to move firewood and bend chimneys when the fire is blazing,
to moor boats and rest oars before strong winds arise,
to gaze upon nine oxen and retreat deeply,
to look at dense foliage and soar away,
not building nests on reed tips,
not lying down to sleep on crumbling mountain cliffs.
These all had vast capacity and broad-mindedness,
discerning opportunities and recognizing outcomes,
surpassing peers and walking alone,
not bound by common desires,
their spirits partaking in creation,
their hearts leaving behind all things,
desirable things could not stain their purity,
worldly principles could not disturb their clarity.
Without such naturalness of these men,
truly it is hard to reach their extraordinary path.
They merely let it be known that those who achieve success should withdraw,
that those bearing great toil go unrewarded,
when the cunning hare dies, one knows the hunting dog is no longer needed,
when the high-flying birds are gone, one realizes the fine bow will be discarded.
Reflecting on Péng Yuè and Hán Xìn as clear mirrors,
one thinks of the method of withdrawing the hairpin;
witnessing the hidden mechanisms for Yuè Yì and Zhǒng Lí,
one recognizes the value of the golden statue.
Like Fàn Lǐ sailing away to vanish from sight,
or Xuē Yǎn withdrawing from chaos to preserve purity,
or the two Shūs returning their seals at the peak of fullness,
or Tián Yù laying aside his official ribbon before his time was up,
advancing, they escaped the blame of excess and regret,
retreating, they had no sting of being drenched at the tail,
their pure wind足以 lift the dust of a thousand years,
their virtuous words足以 dispel future confusion.
Compared to Chén Bǎo,
are they not far superior?!
Some with small wisdom fail in great schemes,
some with weak axles break under heavy loads,
some with singular correctness sink into collective wrongs,
some exhausting loyalty are slandered in concurrent meetings,
some proposing lofty plans suffer Cháo Cuò's calamity,
some exerting all heart and mind meet Wú Qǐ's harm.
Thus, even with restrained speech and thick-backed caution,
one may still not avoid it.
The exile of Duke Zhōu,
the travels of Zhòngní,
Jiǎ Yì being relegated among lower officials,
Sīmǎ Qiān suffering punishment though innocent,
Yuè Yì pacifying Qí,
Wǔ Yún crushing Chǔ,
Bái Qǐ expanding borders with a hundred victories,
Wén Zhòng霸越 with nine strategies,
Hán Xìn's merits overshadowing the empire,
Qíng Bù destroying his family to assist the mandate,
glory did not last a moment,
disgrace already reached them.
Not avoiding such calamities,
could they be called wise?!
Being a minister is not easy,
how could there be only one path?
To put it succinctly,
the key lies in choosing a lord.
That I am not reliable,
is evidenced thus.
To announce retirement and yield to the worthy,
is pure and moreover safe,
with fine reputation and solid gain,
no blessing is greater than this.
Those able to cultivate this art,
are not one in ten thousand.
Fortune and misfortune depend on man,
can one not ponder this?!
Words that grate on the ears,
few delight in them;
offering advice hoping for glory,
will hasten personal disaster,
saving oneself from slander leaves no leisure,
how can one expect faithful acceptance?!
When arrows and strings are numerous, the young phoenix hovers and turns its wings;
when pits and traps fill the paths, the qilin and unicorn收敛 their traces.
Passions should not be extreme,
desires should not be full,
the enlightened control passions with the Way,
and dispatch desires with strategy.
Those planning for others should still advocate loyalty,
how much more should one be meticulous in planning for oneself?!
For the contented are always satisfied,
the discontented never have enough.
The always satisfied
are where blessings gather;
the never satisfied
are where calamities accumulate.
Excessive nurturing of life,
kills what it seeks to grow.
The Sòng man pulling up seedlings,
the Yǐng man stretching leather,
truly wishing for speed,
but actually hastening withering and splitting.
Knowing advancement but forgetting retreat,
is this not what it means?
Those galloping without stopping
rarely avoid falling;
those riding waves without rest
seldom escape drowning;
those playing with blades incessantly
invite stabbing wounds;
those chopping and striking without cease
are the source of breakage and ruin.
Fullness leads to loss,
this is the natural principle.
The vessel in the Zhōu temple,
does it deceive me?
Thus, in Yǎng Yóu's shooting,
a passerby recognized when to loosen the string;
in Dōngyě's driving,
Yánzǐ knew it was about to fail.
Beneath success,
it is not easy to remain long.
Those who drink wine do not necessarily all become disorderly,
but many disorderly ones are among them;
those wealthy and noble are not all in danger,
but some in danger are among them.
The wise foresee events in the table of changes,
and cut wood at the beginning of the slightest sign.
They do not utter lofty words when tiles are piled high,
nor discuss making fur robes amidst a pack of foxes.
The ancients feigned madness and played the fool,
was it for pleasure?!
It was what the times deemed appropriate,
unavoidable.
There are also those who deeply escape yet on land encounter waves,
secludedly retreat yet in water suffer burning,
like Gōng Shèng starving to death to end his life,
or Lǐ Yè distressed and swallowing poison,
due to traces they left behind,
and shadows they could not extinguish.
If one's steps were like treading on ice,
one's body like dwelling in shadows,
moving without留下 tracks to follow,
resting in unity with non-action,
how could such troubles exist?!
How much more so for those who raise the sun and moon to hide their forms,
or beat the great drum to parade sharp weapons?!
Meeting an enlightened age, one excels in aiding the world;
encountering a perilous era, one is inferior in preserving oneself.
Lamenting this forever,
is not the plight of just one scholar.
I have heard that no flame fails to extinguish,
no fullness escapes diminishment.
Brilliance holds the omen of turning to ashes;
spring grass marks the beginning of autumn's withering.
The sun at its zenith must decline;
the moon at its fullness must wane.
In the sequence of the four seasons,
what has accomplished its task withdraws.
Looking afar to external things:
when constructing lofty, towering heights without limit,
one only worries about their collapse and ruin;
looking close at one's own self:
when indulging in fine food and sweet wine without restraint,
one accumulates illness and injures one's nature.
How much more so for those whose loftiness reaches the clouds yet accumulate without cease,
whose might shakes the sovereign yet grow ever more exalted,
without ever resting!
If a mosquito or gadfly falls down a mountain,
it is light enough to flutter about;
but if a rhinoceros or tiger falls,
it shatters into pieces.
This saying illustrates that great things
must not be out of place.
Moreover, to criticize wrongs with upright demeanor,
to act with straightforward principles,
to strike at those who violate the law,
without considering personal enmities,
will deepen resentments and accumulate hatred.
Yet if one abandons the law to tolerate faults,
responding to requests like an echo,
spitting out the hard and swallowing the soft,
bending the rules and measures,
then loyalty is lost and ruined.
Those who occupy such positions,
do they not find it wearisome?
Therefore, those who preserve both body and reputation are very rare,
while those who "break a leg and overturn the sacrificial offerings" are not lacking.
Yet indoors, they dwell in elegant orchid-scented chambers,
with crimson curtains and ornate hangings,
patterned mats spread out in splendid mansions,
dazzling beauties radiant on either side,
with light bodies and soft voices,
clear songs and exquisite dances,
the skill of Sòng and Cài,
the beauty of Yáng'ē,
mouths singing the "Biànlíng" and "Yánlù" melodies,
feet keeping time to the "Lǜshuǐ" and "Qīpán" rhythms,
pleasing tunes for the connoisseur's ear,
alluring forms to delight the heart,
intimate banquets following one after another,
fine wines never withdrawn,
ascending ornate pavilions to look up,
leaning over to gaze into clear pools below,
strolling through the reds and greens of fruit groves,
playing amid the fragrance of huì gardens,
with patterned fish darting about,
and red-feathered birds fluttering up and down,
shooting arrows to bring down cloud-high swans,
casting lines to hook bream and carp,
rare treasures gathering without seeking,
amusements and splendors arriving of their own accord.
Outdoors, vermilion wheels illuminate the road,
high canopies line up carriage after carriage,
crimson banners cloudlike and lush,
command flags resplendent and majestic,
metal instruments clamorous and vibrant,
spears and armor glittering and intricate,
satisfaction entrusted to the following chariots,
fine delicacies filling the attendant carriages,
exhausting the pleasures of travel and sightseeing,
reaching the height of joy in hunting and fishing.
Praises of sage brilliance
fill the ears as they enter;
flattering and pleasing words
come from different mouths in unison.
At such times, haughtily,
they look down upon the ancients,
saying that Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Guǎn Zhòng, and Yàn Yīng
are not worth considering.
How could they realize that rise and fall alternate as head and tail,
sorrow and joy follow each other like morning and evening,
and would they ever resign from high office,
beg for retirement,
turn their backs on vermilion gates and return to the hills and gardens?
As for when a sage reigns above,
with great worthies assisting in affairs,
and the hundred officials cannot be ordered without me,
the millions of people cannot be saved without me,
then being high without worrying about danger,
being full without fearing overflow—
such cases are not discussed here.
Someone asked:
"Men of the same caliber of talent,
some end in obscurity, others achieve prominence;
what is the reason for this?
Is it a regret that the outstanding are held back?"
Bàopúzǐ replied:
"When instruments and abilities do not differ,
yet some are suppressed and others advanced,
it is due to lacking those who understand them.
Thus, adversity and prosperity depend on the times;
success and obstruction are matters of fate.
Those who understand the times—why should they resent obscurity?
Those who know fate—why should they hate lowly hardship?
Thus, the Shěn Lú and Tíng Jūn swords,
fine and sharp as they are,
if not used for striking,
cannot even cut the morning mushroom;
Yáohuá and Lílù jades,
treasures worth multiple cities,
if cast into the mud,
will have tiles and rubble piled upon them.
Hence, one may be precious without necessarily being recognized as such,
useful without necessarily being employed.
Mediocre and vulgar men,
blind in distinguishing things,
cannot tell red from purple,
nor distinguish beans from wheat.
They only consider the successful as worthy,
unaware that those who succeed may have gained it by chance or seeking;
they only regard the obscure as inferior,
ignorant that those in obscurity may be upholding the Way.
Moreover, if the heavenly bodies were not suspended in the sky,
they could not shine with great light illuminating all beyond;
if Mount Sōng and Tài did not rest on the earth,
they could not tower steeply, reaching the clouds.
A rabbit relies on level ground to run swiftly;
a dragon boat rides turbulent streams to show its speed;
fire's brightness does not blaze without the Suìrén's drill;
Chǔ's metal does not sharpen without Ōuyě's forging;
lush flowers await spring's arrival to display their beauty;
roosting swans wait for strong winds to soar lightly;
if the Four Peaks had not clearly recommended,
the widower would not have been appointed;
if Shū Yá had not recommended the worthy, [137 then Yí Wú would not have been greatly honored;
Rángjū leaped high relying on Píngzhòng;
Huáiyīn soared like an eagle thanks to Lord Xiāo;
Jùnshéng rose through Shèngzhī's words;
Qū Nì advanced due to Wúzhī's recommendation;
Yuánzhí aroused the dragon-crouching Kǒngmíng;
Gōngjǐn presented the tiger-reclining Xìngbà;
thus they could leave fine names in imperial records,
and grand achievements noted in their time.
"In the late Hàn dynasty,
the final years of Wú,
it was not so.
In recommending scholars,
they placed those attached to themselves first;
in selecting men,
they decided based on those with many partisans;
yet those attached to themselves were not necessarily worthy of advancement;
being like me,
they could not be omitted;
and those with many partisans were not necessarily talents surpassing the crowd;
trusting the multitude's mouth,
they deemed them acceptable.
Some trusted these mediocre and vulgar types,
unable to dismiss their narrow affections;
some recognized the excellence of others,
yet could not be impartial in utmost fairness.
Thus, they set aside the balance of judgment,
using closeness or distance to determine weight;
discarded measures and standards,
using connections to decide quantity.
In those times, the so-called elegant men of high tone,
those holding the state's authority,
deciding promotions and demotions by themselves,
with praise and blame coming from their mouths—
few escaped this burden.
How much more so when in their hearts they often harbored hatred for the independent,
aversion for the non-partisan,
jealousy of those surpassing themselves,
and neglect for the poor and humble?
Alas!
Unconventional scholars,
ungrouped individuals,
thus encountered one after another without meeting opportunity,
too numerous to count,
some suppressed in marshes and wilds,
some dismissed even while serving at court."
When one cultivates virtue but the Way does not prevail,
harbors talents but encounters no opportune time,
some wait for the Yellow River to run clear yet their teeth are already gone,
others exhaust loyalty and diligence but remain unrecognized.
Their distant journeys find no gallop in this age,
their merits and grace do not reach the living people.
The treasures on the mat
lie stifled in mud,
the talent to aid all things
ends without application.
Carrying a builder's tool but not meeting Wǔdīng,
holding a fishing rod but not encountering Xībó,
from past till present,
how many such cases exist?
To grieve over this alone—
is that not narrow-minded?
Gazing at the distant path
yet feeling ashamed to tread it;
knowing the Great Way is blocked
yet refusing to change it.
To equalize smoothness and obstruction in one course,
entrust honor and disgrace to nature—
would such a one harbor depression over being rarely understood,
or sigh eternally over the river's flow?
To suspect they have regrets
is to fail to comprehend the heart of the ultimate person.
The short-lived not knowing the long-lived,
the well frog not understanding the vast sea—
this has existed since ancient times.
Bàopǔzǐ said:
My friend Xuánbó Xiānshēng,
at the age of determination for learning,
had already thoroughly studied the six categories of books,
and comprehensively mastered the Hé and Luò diagrams.
By day he raced with the last rays of Xīhé's sun,
by night he used the remaining glow of Wàngshū's moon.
No Dao was too distant for him to explore,
no saying too subtle for him to fathom.
Taking Confucianism and Mohism as his city walls,
using wit and spirit as his weapons,
thus debaters all acknowledged defeat upon seeing his dust,
and scholars blinked in awe, laying down their brushes.
Suddenly he awakened to the wise man's silence,
realized that preserving unity brings no blame.
When meaning is grasped, even the finest trap may be discarded;
when Dao diverges, one feels the song is too lofty and few join in.
Thereupon he observed Lǎozǐ's warning about many failures,
pondered the meaning of the golden man's triple seal.
He sheathed his sharpness as if dulled,
restrained his writing brush in its red tube.
Holding gold and embracing jade,
he suppressed his brilliant eloquence.
Throughout the day until late evening,
he might not utter a single word.
A disciple came forward and said:
"Master, you remain silent—
what shall we disciples relate?
Moreover, you appear no different from ordinary men.
I humbly suggest that a bell that does not ring
is no different from accumulated bronze;
a musical stone that produces no sound
remains undistinguished from gathered stones."
Xuánbó Xiānshēng replied:
"I specifically seek lasting fame for ten thousand generations,
and search for understanding friends in the future.
How could I compete to be recognized in the present day,
or set a model for just one era?
If a ritual vessel is used to hold wine,
though beautiful, it is not appreciated for its ceremony;
if one is lowly yet speaks of lofty matters,
though correct, one is not believed.
Merely rolling the tongue and exhausting the voice—
how can this save the drifting and escaping?
The ancients at sixty laughed at their fifty-nine-year-old selves,
not far gone in confusion and return,
thus realizing there was reason for it.
The hardness of jade,
the strength of metal,
the coldness of ice,
the heat of fire—
do these require self-proclamation
to then become evident?
Moreover, even with the eight tones and nine performances,
one cannot avoid the flaw of long and short;
even Yǎng Yóu with a hundred shots cannot prevent
eventually having one miss.
Those who enjoy crossing rivers
often drown in water;
those fond of intense debate
frequently leak through the mouth.
Bóyá was cautious in handling the strings,
thus ultimately avoiding the trouble of discordant notes;
the Confucian is respectful in his speech,
therefore finally escaping the shame of pivotal moments.
Superficial people
are not like this.
They debate the impracticality of emptiness,
contend over trivial matters with wasteful words,
discuss broad studies of useless theories like hardness and whiteness,
recite various masters' books that criticize sages and exceed propriety,
damaging teaching and increasing confusion,
calling this profundity,
abandoning the orthodox classics,
competing to cultivate heterodox learning.
Some compete with the ignorant in verbal victories,
present elegant conversations to those who don't understand,
with no worthy opponents,
and no appreciative audience nearby.
How different is this from performing refined music beside wooden puppets,
or displaying dark and yellow before clay figures?
Only to parch the mouth and exhaust the breath,
beating breasts and clapping hands,
the axe blade damaged yet the gnarl unbroken,
bursting with combativeness while estrangement grows farther,
causing angry expressions to show on faces,
ugly words to come from mouths,
sly and shallow changes
