arising between them,
the stain of error once made
cannot be ground away.
Better to embrace the faint sound that doesn't complete the great music,
and speak sparingly while waiting for those who understand."
Bàopǔzǐ,
whose surname is Gě,
given name Hóng,
courtesy name Zhìchuān,
was from Jùróng in Dānyáng.
His ancestor was Gětiānshì,
who ruled the world in ancient times.
Later they descended to feudal states,
and took this as their surname.
Gě Hóng's ancestor served as Governor of Jīng Province;
during Wáng Mǎng's usurpation,
the gentleman felt shame serving a traitor,
abandoned his office and returned home,
joining with Zhái Yì, Governor of Dōng Commandery, to raise troops.
They intended to execute Wáng Mǎng,
but were defeated by him,
and were spared disaster by amnesty.
He then claimed illness and cut himself off from the world.
Wáng Mǎng, considering his clan strong,
feared eventual rebellion,
relocated him to Lángyá.
The gentleman's son Pǔlú
raised troops to support Guāngwǔ,
achieving great merit.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Lú as Chariot and Horse General.
He was further promoted to Piàoqī Great General,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Tóng County in Xiàpī,
with a fief of five thousand households.
At the dynasty's founding,
the Marquis's brother Wén
accompanied the Marquis on campaigns,
repeatedly achieving great victories.
The Marquis repeatedly petitioned the throne regarding Wén's merits,
but officials claimed Wén had privately followed his elder brother
without military appointment,
thus no reward was granted.
The Marquis said:
"My brother and I together faced arrows and stones,
covered with wounds head to toe,
he lost his right eye,
yet receives not an inch of reward.
How can I feel at peace
while heavily adorned with gold and purple?"
He then petitioned to transfer his marquisate to his brother.
The document was submitted for approval,
the Hàn court wishing to honor his noble righteousness,
specially permitted it.
Wén declined,
but had no alternative.
He accepted the rank and residence,
building a mansion for the Piàoqī General in Bówàng Lane.
Its foundation and stone bases remain to this day.
He further divided his rental income to support officials and soldiers,
providing for them as if serving two lords.
The Piàoqī General earnestly劝阻 but he wouldn't listen.
The Piàoqī General said:
"This further troubles the state's people—
how can this be called yielding?"
He then traveled elsewhere on pretext,
crossed the river southward and settled in Jùróng.
His children and grandchildren farmed personally,
finding amusement in classical texts.
Wén repeatedly sent messengers to welcome the Piàoqī General back,
but the General never returned.
He also had people guard the Bówàng Lane mansion,
hoping for the Piàoqī General's return,
yet for generations none resided there.
My grandfather's learning encompassed all fields,
delving into the profound and subtle,
with literary artistry so elevated
that none in his time could match him.
Possessing talent for governing the state,
he served Wú,
successively administering the three counties of Hǎiyán,
Lín'ān,
and Shānyīn.
He entered the court as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
Imperial Censor,
Governor of Lúlíng,
Minister of Personnel,
Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
Secretariat official,
Chamberlain for Dependencies,
Palace Attendant,
Superintendent of the Imperial Household,
General Who Supports Wú,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wúshòu County.
My father was known for his filial piety and fraternal duty,
his conduct serving as a model for scholars,
and he exhaustively studied
all records in the classics and texts.
He served Wú as Gentleman of the Five Offices,
Impartial Judge,
Magistrate of both Jiànchéng and Nánchāng counties,
Secretariat郎,
Commandant of Justice,
Army Protector,
and Governor of Kuàijī.
Before he could resign, the Jìn army advanced along the river,
and the western borders were lost.
The court broadly selected talents versed in both civil and military arts,
and public opinion,
unanimously recommended him.
Thus, he was transferred to alert five commanderies.
As Grand Commander, he was given five thousand personal troops,
commanding the expeditionary forces
to guard the borders.
What Heaven destroys,
no man can uphold.
Thus, the former ruler submitted,
and all under heaven became guests.
He, retaining his former office,
was appointed as a Gentleman of the Interior.
Gradually promoted to Grand Master of the Palace,
he served as Grand Impartial Judge,
and Magistrate of Féixiāng.
The county had twenty thousand households,
and was the best governed in the province,
with particularly exceptional moral influence,
kindness pervasive and punishments clear,
praises heard in the countryside,
no traces of corruption on the roads,
he did not farm public fields,
yet people crossed borders as to a market.
Gifts as slight as an autumn hair
did not enter his gate;
the use of paper and brushes
all came from his private funds.
Punishments were set aside yet prohibitions held,
he spoke little yet transformation spread.
He left office due to illness,
but was summoned by decree to serve as Chief Steward to the Prince of Wú.
With stern countenance he corrected errors,
promoted the capable and replaced the unfit,
recommended the good and impeached the crooked,
bringing solemn harmony to the military and state.
He was promoted to Governor of Shàolíng,
and died in office.
I, Hóng,
am the third son of my father.
Born late,
I was indulged by both parents,
and not early supervised in studies and histories.
At the age of thirteen,
my kind father passed away.
Having lost parental instruction early,
suffering hunger, cold, and hardship,
I personally engaged in farming,
rising with stars and treading on grass,
diligently continuing the work.
Moreover, repeatedly affected by war and fires,
the ancestral texts were completely lost.
With nothing to read during farming breaks,
I carried book boxes and went on foot to borrow.
Often, from one household,
I could only obtain partial books,
so I increased my efforts, cutting firewood to afford paper and brushes,
and in the fields and gardens,
wrote books by柴火 light.
Due to these circumstances,
I could not early immerse in the arts and letters.
Often lacking paper,
whatever I wrote,
had characters layered over,
making it hard for others to read.
At sixteen,
I began reading the "Classic of Filial Piety," "Analects," "Book of Songs," and "Book of Changes."
Too poor to seek teachers and friends afar,
isolated and ill-informed,
with shallow understanding and short thoughts,
I often couldn't grasp the main principles,
but greedy for broad reading,
I memorized and mastered all books I encountered.
What I had covered,
from the classics, various histories, and hundred schools' words,
down to short miscellaneous writings,
amounted to nearly ten thousand volumes.
Being forgetful by nature,
and lacking literary grace,
with unfocused will,
what I retained was very thin,
and I couldn't avoid confusion,
yet when writing, I could still make references,
ultimately not becoming a pure Confucian scholar,
unfit to be a teaching master.
As for the Hé-Tú and Luò-Shū diagrams and weft texts,
I glanced and stopped,
not dwelling on them.
I disliked books on astrology, arithmetic, Jiǔgōng, Sānqí, Tàiyī, and Fēifú arts,
and never followed them,
for they are laborious and lack flavor.
Later, I studied wind angles, cloud gazing, Sānyuán, Dùnjiǎ,
Liùrén, and Tàiyī methods,
roughly understanding their essentials,
but not delving deeply.
Considering that these are mostly for serving others,
and aligned with personal motives,
I saw no urgency in toiling over them;
it's better to save time for beneficial books,
so I abandoned them too.
According to the "Bié Lù" and "Yìwén Zhì,"
there were thirteen thousand two hundred ninety-nine volumes,
and since the Wèi dynasty,
writings have multiplied,
doubling past counts,
making me realize how much I haven't seen.
Books in Jiāngbiǎo
are generally incomplete;
I once wanted to go to the capital to seek rare ones,
but encountered great turmoil,
and turned back halfway.
I often sigh in regret.
Now approaching forty,
my simple aspirations wane,
thinking only to reduce and reduce further,
acting through inaction,
farming occasionally in marshes,
merely preserving my life.
My broad learning endeavors
thus daily decline.
As for my character,
I am rustic and wild,
slow-witted and tongue-tied,
ugly in appearance,
yet never argue or boast to adorn myself.
My hat and shoes are dirty and worn,
clothes sometimes ragged,
but I feel no shame.
Fashionable attire
changes frequently and bewilderingly:
sometimes wide collars with large belts,
sometimes tight bodies with long sleeves,
sometimes long robes dragging on the ground,
sometimes short ones not covering the feet.
I aim to uphold constancy,
not following worldly changes.
My speech is straightforward,
eschewing teasing and jest;
unless with the right person,
I remain silent all day.
Thus, my countrymen all call me the "Embracing Simplicity" scholar.
Therefore, when I write books,
I use this as my pen name.
I am naturally frail and sickly,
compounded by frequent illnesses,
impoverished without carriage or horse,
unable to endure walking on foot,
and walking is also something I inherently dislike.
Moreover, troubled by corrupt customs,
where people abandon the root to chase the trivial,
and social interactions exceed proper bounds,
I thus set aside my brush and live in seclusion,
guarding tranquility behind a wicker gate with no place to rush to or follow others.
As for the powerful and arrogant types,
even if they are in close proximity,
I have no acquaintance with them whatsoever.
My clothes do not ward off the cold,
my room cannot avoid leaks,
my food does not fill my emptiness,
and my name does not leave my doorstep,
yet I do not worry about it.
Poor and without servants,
the fence is broken and collapsing,
thorns and brambles cluster in the courtyard,
weeds block the steps and eaves,
I push through bushes to go out,
and part grasses to enter my room.
Critics think I neglect the near for the distant and lack consideration
for my lack of assistance.
Not understanding the etiquette of visits, I have never sought to meet officials.
As for attending major funerals
or visiting the sick and distressed,
my heart wishes to exert myself,
and I force myself to go whenever possible,
but when I am ill and barely recovered,
I often cannot manage it fully,
and am frequently criticized and blamed by commentators.
I accept the blame without resentment.
If my intentions are sincere but illness thwarts my heart's desire,
I only care not to feel ashamed of myself;
why should I mind if others do not understand?
Only those with clear discernment
will forgive my sincere embrace of simplicity,
not as a means to cultivate aloofness.
Many people admire the intimacy of close friendships
and the secrecy of private chambers,
but I believe knowing others is very difficult,
something even the highest sages find challenging.
Superficial and mixed associations,
where mouths agree but spirits part,
are harmful rather than beneficial.
Though I cannot cut them off entirely like Zhū Gōngshū,
I must clarify and examine them thoroughly
before deciding how to engage.
For this, I am disliked by many, yet I do not change.
Those who rush about seeking advancement
or stand obsequiously at the gates of the powerful
also resent my difference from them
and find fault, slandering me,
calling me arrogant and dismissive of customs.
But as for my character,
I act with sincere belief,
ignoring both slander and praise.
My greater concern is that some people,
relying on their own strengths, look down on others' weaknesses.
Humbly positioned at the end of the scholars,
whenever I speak with others,
I often gauge their understanding and discuss accordingly,
not forcing them into topics they haven't heard of.
And when debating with learned scholars,
I always raise the main points.
If they cherish their shortcomings
and find the core meaning hard to grasp,
I roughly explain the direction of my thoughts,
just enough to enlighten them,
not pressing the reasoning hard
so they don't feel cornered.
Those with calm minds,
pondering carefully,
often realize and grasp it on their own.
For those I deem not worth speaking with,
even if they sometimes ask,
I often decline by saying I don't know,
to avoid the fault of wasting words.
By nature, I deeply dislike troubling officials.
From youth to adulthood,
I have helped several suppressed friends in need,
but only when不得已,
did I speak to those in power,
yet those individuals never knew of my concern.
I couldn't bear to see them fall into injustice,
so I secretly assisted them.
For others, even close relatives,
if they hold power and influence
and have no bond with me,
I never burden them with a single word or half a character.
As for times when food and supplies are desperately lacking
or medicine is needed, I call upon friends and peers;
if some provide aid,
I do not refuse.
When I receive others' help,
I always gradually repay it over time,
without letting them notice.
From those not of my kind, I do not recklessly accept their gifts.
If I have food stored for ten days,
I share it to relieve others' needs;
if I am seriously short myself,
I do not cut into my own share.
I do not engage in showy minor virtues
or cultivate conspicuous small integrities.
When ordinary villagers considered good and kind
occasionally bring wine and food to visit me,
even if they are not my peers,
I do not refuse them.
Later, I repay them in kind,
but not immediately.
I once said that Shǐ Yún not eating with his brothers
and Huà Shēng being overly clean with close guests
are hypocritical acts for seeking fame,
not the broad measure of court and temple.
I particularly detest unrighteous people
who neglect the fundamental work of farming and sericulture
and crave illicit profits from unrighteousness.
Those who control local discourse
sell elections for gratitude;
those with power and influence
issue documents to extort wealth.
Some take bribes from the guilty,
or wrong families in the right;
some become havens for fugitives,
harboring outlaws;
some conscript laborers,
hindering public duties;
some forcibly collect money and goods,
demanding high prices;
some monopolize marketplaces,
seizing the people's profits;
some annex others' fields,
robbing the weak and orphaned of their livelihoods.
They loiter around government offices,
seeking gains through extortion,
boasting to their wives and concubines inside,
fishing for fame and position outside.
For those like this,
I do not associate with them.
Thus, common people hate me for despising their ways,
and naturally keep their distance,
so my lane has no tracks of carriages or horses,
my hall no guests with differing intentions,
my courtyard could set a sparrow trap,
and my mats gather dust.
From when I gained awareness until approaching old age,
my mouth has not spoken of others' faults,
nor discussed people's private matters,
as it comes naturally.
Even if servants have their shortcomings
or shameful incidents,
I do not mock them for it.
I have never evaluated the merits and flaws of individuals,
nor do I enjoy criticizing the likes and dislikes in social interactions.
If pressured by elders to answer,
and unable to decline,
when discussing people,
I only mention their outstanding qualities.
When discussing writings,
I extract the excellent parts they've achieved
without pointing out flaws or faults,
thus avoiding resentment from praise or blame.
When nobles occasionally ask about officials or commoners,
"How is so-and-so?"
For the pure, lofty, and capable,
I point out their commendable deeds;
for the greedy, violent, and obtuse,
I reply that I happen not to know them well.
For this, I am often criticized,
accused of being too protective,
unable to clearly distinguish good from bad,
to separate black from white,
yet I dare not change.
Whenever I see people in the world fond of judging others,
comparing and ranking them,
often inaccurately,
and their praises, criticisms, approvals, and rejections
sometimes lack proper standards,
those praised take it as their due,
not necessarily trusting the virtue behind it;
those offended bear a deep-seated hatred,
sharper than a blood feud.
I take this as a warning,
and thus no longer speak of scholars.
Even for clansmen and disciples,
their evaluation I leave to the community,
not lightly assigning them a value.
Some people criticized Gě Hóng,
to which he replied:
"I am the one who knows myself best,
so it should be easy for me to understand.
Suppose someone asks me
to compare myself with the ancients,
or to find my peers among contemporaries,
I truly cannot know myself well enough
to determine who my equal would be.
Moreover, since I am not others,
how can I presume to select and judge them?
In the late Hàn dynasty, customs were corrupt,
with factions dividing into groups,
and figures like Xǔ Zǐjiāng
used their words to impose restrictions.
Disputes and debates
turned families into enemies.
Thus, in Rǔnán, there was no fixed evaluation of individuals, only the monthly assessments.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi deeply despised this,
wanting to take their heads,
forcing them to flee and scatter,
nearly leading to their extermination.
The past mirror is not far away,
offering a lesson to learn from.
Moreover, people are not easily understood;
even fathers and elder brothers may not fully know their sons and younger brothers.
Are those who agree with me necessarily right?
Are those who differ from me necessarily wrong?
Some start but do not finish;
Táng Yáo, the Duke of Zhōu, Zhòngní, and Jì Zhá
all had regrets of incompleteness.
How can we trust the flickering light of trivial insights from recent times
and lightly evaluate people?
Is this not selling short those great sages and worthies?"
In the past, during the Tài'ān era,
when Shí Bīng rebelled,
across six provinces,
like branches shaking and leaves falling,
many turned away from righteousness to join the rebels.
The Grand Commander of the righteous army invited Gě Hóng to serve as a military captain,
repeatedly urging and pressuring him.
Fearing for his homeland and the threat of invasion,
the danger was deep and worries great.
The ancients had a principle of responding to urgency,
and he also feared military law,
not daring to follow his own will,
so he recruited several hundred men,
and advanced with the various troops.
Once, attacking a subordinate general of the rebels,
on the day of victory,
money and silk piled up like mountains,
treasures and curios covered the ground.
The other troops all let their soldiers loose to gather wealth,
loading carts and carrying loads continuously.
Gě Hóng alone strictly ordered his command
not to recklessly leave their formations.
When a soldier picked up some loot,
Gě Hóng immediately beheaded him as a warning.
Thus, no one dared to abandon their posts,
and indeed, several hundred hidden rebels emerged,
injuring the other troops.
Those troops were all dispersed,
without organization,
each man and horse burdened with heavy loads,
losing all will to fight.
This led to panic and chaos,
with casualties scattered everywhere,
nearly causing a collapse.
Only Gě Hóng's army remained orderly and well-deployed,
suffering no losses.
In rescuing the other troops from a major collapse,
Gě Hóng played a key role.
Later, in another battle, he beheaded a minor rebel leader,
capturing many armored heads,
and reported the victory to the headquarters.
Thereupon, the Grand Commander promoted Gě Hóng to General Who Calms the Waves,
and by regulation, awarded him a hundred bolts of cloth.
Many generals stored theirs away,
or sent them home,
but Gě Hóng distributed his among the officers and soldiers,
and gave to impoverished acquaintances,
keeping only ten bolts for himself,
which he used directly to buy meat and wine,
to feast the officers and officials.
At that time, he privately enjoyed a day of fine reputation.
After the matter was settled,
Gě Hóng laid down his weapons and armor,
and went straight to Luòyáng,
wishing to broadly seek rare books,
utterly disregarding his military achievements.
He secretly admired Lǔ Lián for not accepting the gold from Liáochéng,
and Bāo Xū for not taking the reward for saving Chǔ,
upholding the principle of not dwelling on success.
Just then, the central state was in great turmoil,
and the northern route was blocked.
Moreover, Chén Mǐn rebelled in Jiāngdōng,
cutting off the return path.
It happened that an old friend, Qiáo Guó's Jī Jūndào,
was appointed as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He submitted a request for Gě Hóng to serve as an army advisor.
Although it was not what he desired,
it offered a chance to escape southward,
so he reluctantly accepted.
Sent ahead to hasten troops,
but Jī Jūndào was later killed,
so Gě Hóng remained in Guǎngzhōu.
Frequently invited by commanding officers for positions,
he declined them all.
He deeply reflected that wealth and honor can be gradually attained but not instantly achieved,
and the trivial pursuits in between
are enough to weary a person.
Moreover, glory, status, power, and profit
are like passing guests;
they are not permanent possessions,
and once they leave, they cannot be retained.
The lofty fall,
the illustrious perish,
like spring flowers,
withering in an instant.
Gaining them brings no joy,
losing them—why sorrow?
Regrets and troubles abound,
with worries, fears, and anxieties
beyond description.
It is not worth pursuing.
Furthermore, he considered his nature indolent and his talents meager;
with laziness governing limited ability,
even if he hunched his shoulders and bent his knees,
rushing through the dusty world,
he would still likely fail to achieve great fame and status and avoid troubles,
let alone if he could not even do that.
It would be better to cultivate the way of Sōng and Qiáo,
which lies within myself,
not dependent on others.
He planned to ascend famous mountains,
consume elixirs, and nurture his nature.
Not that he would abandon all duties,
but one cannot manage both worlds;
unless he cuts off worldly affairs entirely,
how could he pursue the path of profound tranquility?
Besides, true understanding is hard to attain,
and he could not spare the time to discuss it with others.
Therefore, the tracks of his carriage and horse
never passed through the domains of the noble and powerful;
not a single written character
was exchanged with families in office.
Also, among the scholarly community,
though he could not withdraw completely,
when visitors came to see him,
he felt unable to refuse them,
which interfered with his work,
preventing full concentration.
So he sighed and said:
"There is no path in the mountains and forests themselves.
But the ancients who cultivated the Way
always entered the mountains and forests
precisely to distance themselves from noise and clamor,
ensuring their minds remained unperturbed.
Now, I shall follow my original intent,
leave my homeland behind,
and go to Sōng Mountain,
to seek the path of Fāng Píng and Liáng Gōng."
The earlier work of my philosophical writings, the Inner and Outer Chapters,
fortunately had already been diligently worked on,
so I compiled them again,
to show to future generations.
When I, Hóng, was fifteen or sixteen years old,
the poems, rhapsodies, and miscellaneous essays I composed,
at the time I thought could circulate in the era,
but upon reaching the age of capping (around twenty),
and examining them more carefully,
I found many quite unsatisfactory.
It's not that my natural talent necessarily increased,
but simply that my reading had broadened somewhat,
and I became aware of the distinction between the beautiful and the ugly.
Therefore, I greatly restricted them,
discarding nine out of ten, not preserving even one.
Now, aside from my philosophical writings,
only over a hundred volumes of miscellaneous works remain,
yet I haven't fully grasped the principle of what to add or remove,
and being often distressed and resentful,
I have no leisure to further sort and preserve them.
Others, once their writing is finished,
immediately call it satisfying,
but my talent is dull and thoughts slow,
I truly cannot do that.
In writing, each time I revise a character,
it naturally becomes better,
but I worry about laziness,
and also that I often cannot review my works repeatedly.
When I was over twenty years old,
I then considered that writing trivial short pieces
wasted time and hindered work,
and it was not as good as establishing a school of thought,
so I began drafting philosophical works.
I encountered times of military chaos,
drifting in exile and displacement,
suffering some losses,
continuously on the road,
I did not pick up the brush again for over ten years,
until during the Jiànwǔ era,
when I finally settled on writing the Inner Chapters in twenty volumes,
the Outer Chapters in fifty volumes,
stele inscriptions, eulogies, poems, and rhapsodies in one hundred volumes,
military documents, proclamations, transfers, memorials, and letters in thirty volumes,
also compiling what common works do not include,
as the Biographies of Immortals in ten volumes,
and compiling about those of high virtue who did not serve in office,
as the Biographies of Recluses in ten volumes; also copying from the Five Classics, Seven Histories, and the sayings of the Hundred Schools,
military affairs, techniques, and short miscellaneous essential wonders in three hundred and ten volumes,
with a separate catalog.
The Inner Chapters discuss matters of immortals, elixirs, ghostly transformations, nurturing life to prolong years, warding off evils and averting disasters,
belonging to the Daoist school;
the Outer Chapters discuss the successes and failures in human affairs,
the rights and wrongs of worldly matters,
belonging to the Confucian school.
I saw the self-narration in Emperor Wén of Wèi's Diǎnlùn,
which did not cover matters like playing liubo or fencing,
and I intended to briefly speak of what I know,
but in truth, I do not have many skills,
and cannot falsely praise myself.
Now I will fully speak,
of what I am not versed in.
My nature is simple and dull,
with few hobbies or interests,
from the time of binding my hair as a child,
even throwing tiles or hand wrestling,
I did not join in children's groups,
never engaged in cockfighting or duck racing,
dog or horse racing,
seeing people gambling at games,
I did not even glance at them.
If forced to watch,
I could not get into it at all,
as if sleeping with eyes open.
Thus, to this day, I do not know how many lines are on a chessboard or the names of chūpú dice.
I also consider these trivial skills,
扰乱思绪 and waste time,
for officials, they harm governance,
for scholars, they disrupt lectures and recitations,
for common people, they make them forget farming,
for merchants, they cause loss of goods and wealth.
As for when胜负未分,
and they contend in the marketplaces,
hearts burning within,
faces worried without,
calling it pleasure,
but in reality, it is torment and exhaustion,
losing the virtue of integrity and shame,
giving rise to the seeds of contention,
exchanging heavy bribes,
secretly forming grudges and enmities.
In the past, Duke Mǐn of Sòng and the Crown Prince of Wú brought upon themselves the disaster of shattered heads,
giving rise to rebellions and turmoil,
overthrowing seven states,
nearly toppling the imperial court.
A warning for a hundred generations,
its lesson is clear.
Whenever I observe players,
shame and anger intermingled,
hands and feet coming to blows,
hurling ugly insults at each other,
severing ties and ruining friendships,
such cases often occur.
Resentment lies not necessarily in great matters,
nor only in small ones,
often summoning regret and misfortune,
it is not worth doing.
Although Confucius had the admonition against sleeping during the day,
comparing it with me,
I truly do not concede that it is better than daytime sleeping.
Why?
Sleeping during the day is only unbeneficial but does not have the worry of resentment,
the turmoil of fights and disputes;
the sage still wore out the leather thongs of his bamboo books three times,
diligently pursuing classical studies,
how can a person of ordinary talent,
manage to cultivate both?
All such games are not as good as showing a foot of writing,
so because I originally did not like them and did not engage in them,
probably this is what common people are fond of.
In youth, I once learned archery,
but my strength was slight and I could not draw a strong bow,
only like Yán Gāo's bow.
I thought that since archery is among the six arts,
and it can also be used to resist bandits and avoid robbery,
as well as catch birds and animals,
therefore I practiced it.
In the past, during military campaigns,
I once personally shot at pursuing cavalry,
and they fell with the twang of the string,
killing two bandits and one horse,
thus managing to escape death.
I also received training in sword and shield, single sword, and double halberds,
all with oral formulas and essential techniques,
waiting to capture others,
indeed having secret methods,
their skill reaching spiritual levels.
If using these arts against those unaware,
one can achieve complete victory alone,
unrivaled wherever directed.
Later, I also learned the seven-foot staff technique,
which can enter amidst naked blades,
and seize large halberds,
yet it is also an unimportant minor skill.
Knowing it is like having the horn of a qilin or the spur of a phoenix,
why must one use it?
Beyond this,
I know nothing else.
From youth, I had a firm resolve,
determined not to enter official service,
whenever I read the biographies of Cháo Fǔ, Xǔ Yóu, Zǐzhōu, the Stone Door man of Běirén, two Jiǎngs, two Yuáns, Fǎ Zhēn, and Zǐ Lóng,
I often put down the book and sat up on the mat,
admiring their character.
I aspired to master the Five Classics thoroughly,
write a work of philosophy,
so that later generations would know me as a literary scholar, that is all.
Later, when the provincial and commandery authorities and the Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry summoned me,
I did not accept any.
When recommended to the office of the Chancellor, Prince of Lángyá,
after previously raising righteous troops,
and after the bandits were pacified,
I never sought fame or visited the offices,
nor discussed merits with the authorities,
forever without expectation of reward or recognition.
The Prince of Jìn responded to Heaven and complied with the people,
bringing order out of chaos and correcting deviations,
tying the imperial network when it was nearly severed,
restoring the abandoned sacrifices of the ancestral temples,
mindful of the overdue rewards of the previous court,
and universally rewarded to encourage the future.
I followed the precedent and went there,
in the year Gēngyín,
an imperial edict granted me the title of Marquis within the Passes,
with a fief of two hundred households in Jūróng.
I privately thought that campaigning against bandits to save my homeland,
the toil was not worth recording,
the command of gold and purple,
was not my original wish.
I originally wished to emulate Lǔ Lián from afar,
and cite Tián Chóu from recent times,
submitting a letter to firmly decline,
to fulfill my humble ambition.
But there happened to be a general rule,
and alike, it was not permitted.
In the past, Zhòng Yóu declining due rewards discouraged doing good,
and with the ugly barbarians not yet pacified,
the world having many affairs,
the state just wanting to clarify rewards and enforce punishments,
to make the laws and codes clear,
how dare I, a petty person, merely cling to my insignificant stubborn will,
and oppose the great system of universal application?
Therefore, I abandoned my intention and respectfully accepted the imperial command.
Having already composed the piece "Autobiography,"
someone questioned me, saying:
"In the past, Wáng Chōng, at the age of sixty,
found his path blocked and his hopes extinguished,
fearing that both his person and his name would perish together,
thus wrote his own record as a final work.
You, sir, in the prime of your thirties,
encounter an era of virtuous governance,
about to receive the silk gifts like Shēn Gōng,
ascend the chariot of cushioned wheels like Mù Shēng,
shine your literary brilliance before the emperor,
and make your fame resound like Kūnwú's metal—
why worry that your fragrance will not spread,
and instead engage in the tasks of an old scholar?"
I replied:
"The two spheres of heaven and earth are vast and distant,
and human existence is like a sojourn;
with the morning mushroom's fleeting beauty,
it withers before a moment passes,
akin to spring blossoms' brief glory,
fading and falling before ten days change.
Even the gale that sweeps the sky,
or the sudden flash of lightning,
may not be as swift.
For the prime of life is like a shooting star trailing smoke,
and old age like an arrow shot through a crack.
How much more those who fall like unopened bamboo shoots,
or wither against autumn's dew?
Thus, Xiàng Zǐ sighed over containing grain yet dying young,
and Yáng Wū lamented an early demise.
Surveying ancient times,
men of extraordinary talent,
some through arts and letters soared like dragons,
others by military feats stood firm like tigers,
their high achievements recorded in the archives,
their virtuous sounds set to music.
Though their physical forms have sunk,
submerged in deep soil,
their fine tales flutter and are daily recounted,
so even after hundreds of generations,
they remain revered.
I, with my mediocrity and simplicity,
suppressed and struggling,
my abilities out of sync with the times,
my conduct at odds with the world,
my words echo contrary to customs,
my steps leave tracks that clash with the crowd.
Within, I lack the support of influential families,
without, I have no friends to dust off hats for mutual advancement.
Though the path may be level,
I have no steed like a qílín;
though the cosmos is vast,
my wings are not those of a great péng.
Above, I cannot soar like an eagle to save the state,
below, I have no means to honor my family or leave a name.
My virtues won't be entrusted to fine historians,
my voice won't adhere to bells and tripods.
Therefore, in the spare time from my writings,
I compose this autobiographical piece,
though it may not aid in poverty or success,
I rely on future generations to have something to recount!"

Outer Chapters
